title: Harnessing strain-release driven reactivity of a chiral SuFEx reagent: Stereocontrolled access to sulfinamides, sulfonimidamides, and sulfoximines
field_subfield: Chemistry — Organic Synthesis and Medicinal Chemistry
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can the N,N-diisopropyl urea protecting group of t-BuSF be repurposed as an enabling group that undergoes torsional strain-release–driven amine exchange to provide stereocontrolled access to sulfinyl (S(IV)) and sulfonimidoyl (S(VI)) ureas? (2) What are the scope, functional group tolerance, and stereochemical outcomes across diverse amines and complex substrates? (3) Can the method be integrated into late-stage diversification and streamlined syntheses of clinically relevant scaffolds, including DFV-890?

Hypotheses: (i) Sterically congested N,N-diisopropyl ureas in sulfinyl/sulfonimidoyl intermediates will exhibit large amide torsional strain that is efficiently relieved by primary/secondary amines, enabling rapid amine exchange at room temperature for S(IV) and at elevated temperatures for S(VI). (ii) Enantiopurity at the S(IV) center will be preserved under mild conditions but may erode at higher temperatures. (iii) The method will tolerate late-stage functional groups and deliver high yields and enantioenrichment, enabling practical medicinal chemistry and organocatalyst synthesis.

Support/refutation criteria: Successful amine exchange with high yields and >99% e.e., scope across primary/secondary amines and complex drugs, stereochemical fidelity at room temperature, and improved synthetic efficiency for DFV-890 would support the hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Reagents and intermediates: The chiral SuFEx reagent t-BuSF is SuFEx-activated to enantiopure tert-butyl sulfoximines (e.g., 12, 22, 26, 29). S-activation converts sulfoximines to sulfinyl ureas (e.g., 7), which undergo amine exchange to sulfinyl ureas (9). Sulfonimidamides (8a, 8b) undergo analogous amine exchange to sulfonimidoyl ureas (10). Oxidative amination (t-BuOCl, NH3) converts S(IV) to S(VI) sulfonimidamides.

General conditions: S-activation of tert-butyl sulfoximines typically uses t-BuOK in 2-MeTHF at 80 °C for 2 h, followed by neutralization to give sulfinyl ureas. Amine exchange for S(IV) is performed at room temperature (23 °C) for 3–4 h with 1 equiv of amine; TFA (1 equiv) accelerates reactions with less basic aromatic amines. For S(VI), amine exchange is conducted at 60–80 °C in THF or MeCN. Reaction scales are 0.1–0.25 mmol unless otherwise noted; gram-scale examples are reported for select transformations.

Stereochemical assessment: Enantiomeric excess (e.e.) is determined by chiral HPLC. Enantiopure sulfoximines (e.g., 12, 22, 26, 29) are prepared from t-BuSF via SuFEx. During S(IV) amine exchange, the S(IV) stereocenter is preserved at 23 °C and 60 °C; prolonged heating at 80 °C leads to stereochemical erosion for secondary/tertiary sulfinyl derivatives and eventual decomposition.

Scope and substrates: Primary/secondary aliphatic amines (including benzylic, cyclic, and heterocyclic amines) and aromatic amines (with TFA) are evaluated. Complex drug molecules (oseltamivir, amlodipine, sitagliptin, kinase pharmacophores) are used to test late-stage compatibility. Tertiary sulfonimidamides are unreactive under tested conditions (120 °C, dioxane) and with Brønsted/Lewis acids; a one-pot S(IV) amine exchange followed by S-activation is used to access them.

Combinatorial workflow: A 48-well plate is used to perform sequential transformations over 8 h. Starting from tert-butyl sulfoximines, S-activation is performed on gram scale (t-BuOK, 2-MeTHF, 80 °C, 2 h), partitioned into quadrants, and amine exchange is initiated with 22 amines. After 3 h, products are split and further transformed: Quadrant 1 undergoes oxidative amination (t-BuOCl, NH3) to primary sulfonimidamides; Quadrant 2 targets 12 products from the S(VI) amine exchange scope; Quadrant 3 forms 12 secondary/tertiary sulfonimidamides; Quadrant 4 uses sulfonimidoyl fluorides and turbo-Grignards to make sulfoximines. LC-MS monitors conversions; isolated yields are cross-checked by isolation.

Analytical methods: Enantiomeric excess determined by chiral HPLC; conversions estimated by LC-MS; yields reported as isolated unless noted. Stability analyses are referenced to Supplementary Information.

title: Novel dynamic residue network analysis approaches to study homodimeric allosteric modulation in SARS-CoV-2 M pro and in its evolutionary mutations
field_subfield: Computational Biology — Structural Biology and Drug Discovery
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a symmetry-aware DRN framework using multiple centrality metrics (BC, CC, DC, EC, KC) identify conserved and ligand-induced allosteric communication hubs in the homodimeric Mpro? (2) How do six SANCDB-derived allosteric modulators alter network topology and hub distributions across protomers? (3) How do early-pandemic mutations affect hub persistence, communication paths, and ligand stability? (4) Are there mutation cold spots that remain robust across ligands and mutations?

Hypotheses: (H1) Allosteric binding will induce protomer-specific hub gains/losses that are detectable via DRN metrics, revealing asymmetric allosteric effects in the homodimer. (H2) Persistent hubs will be metric-specific but collectively highlight key functional regions (e.g., dimer interface, antiparallel beta strands). (H3) Mutations will disrupt hub persistence and communication paths, with some regions (cold spots) remaining robust. (H4) Certain ligands will show superior stability across mutants, indicating scaffold-level robustness. Outcomes supporting H1–H4 include metric-specific persistent hubs, ligand-induced hub transitions, loss of hub persistence under mutations, and identification of CC super-persistent hubs. Outcomes refuting would include no hub changes upon ligand binding, uniform hub persistence across mutations, or no ligand stability differences.
reference_methodology:
Structures and preparation: The SARS-CoV-2 Mpro dimeric structure was retrieved from PDB (5RFV). A homology model of HCoV-OC43 Mpro was built with MODELLER (automodel, slow refinement, loop deviation 2.5 Å) after sequence alignment (PROMALS3D). The lowest z-DOPE model was selected from 50 models. Protonation states were assigned at pH 7.0 using PROPKA via PDB2PQR. Fifty early-pandemic mutations (GISAID) were introduced into the SARS-CoV-2 Mpro dimer using Discovery Studio Visualizer; all structures were protonated consistently.

Virtual screening: 623 SANCDB compounds were prepared with Gasteiger-Hückel charges (AutoDockTools). Docking used AutoDock Vina (PyMOL plugin) with a grid centered at (0.00, 0.65, 0.00), size 65×71×80 Å, 1 Å spacing, exhaustiveness 1000, and 20 poses. Blind docking (QuickVina-W) was run in parallel (12 cores/job) at CHPC. PDBQT poses were split, converted to PDB, and filtered by an in-house C++ script to retain poses within 10 Å of allosteric pockets (irrespective of binding energy). Manual curation in PyMOL removed off-pocket poses. For SARS-CoV-2, the top six compounds by residue interactions in lowest-energy poses were selected; HCoV-OC43 underwent the same steps.

Molecular dynamics: GROMACS 2019 was used. AMBER03 force field and ACPYPE generated topologies. Systems were solvated in TIP3P water with a 1.0 nm buffer and neutralized with 0.15 M NaCl. Minimization: 5000 steps steepest descent to 1000 kJ/mol/nm. Equilibration: NVT at 300 K (modified Berendsen thermostat) and NPT at 1 bar (Parrinello–Rahman barostat), with 0.1 ps coupling groups and constraints. Bonds were constrained with LINCS; PME handled long-range electrostatics. Simulations: 100 ns for reference and HCoV-OC43 apo and ligand-bound complexes; 20 ns for each of 50 mutants per ligand. Coordinates were saved every 10 ps; PBC were removed. Total CPU hours: ~2,921,472 (384 cores).

DRN analysis: DRN metrics were computed on the last 10 ns of trajectories using MDM-TASK-web (cal_network.py). Residues were nodes; edges were Cβ–Cβ (Gly Cα–Cα) within 6.7 Å. Metrics: averaged BC, CC, DC, EC, KC. Persistent hubs were defined as residues in the top 5% of centrality values across all samples (e.g., 212 elements from 304 residues × 2 chains × (1 apo + 6 bound) systems × 0.05). For each metric, a threshold was set from the concatenated sorted vector; binary matrices were built to select rows with non-zero row sums. Subnetworks were constructed by merging apo and ligand-bound hub nodes and edges, tracking protomer labels to assess hub gains/losses. Jaccard similarity quantified hub overlap between KC and DC/EC (ranges reported).

title: Slip Control during Slope Descent for a Rover with Plowing Capability
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a plow-based slip controller, using monocular optical flow slip estimation, autonomously regulate rover slip during direct descents on steep, unconsolidated slopes? (2) Do PI and fuzzy logic controllers achieve comparable performance across slopes and commanded speeds? (3) Can the system handle nonzero slip references (e.g., −5%) and deviations from visual odometry assumptions?

Hypotheses: (H1) A plow actuator can be used as the sole control input to drive slip to a reference (typically zero) without modifying commanded track speeds, thereby minimizing odometry error and energy waste. (H2) Both PI and fuzzy logic controllers will meet performance objectives: steady-state error within ±5% slip, time to enter the allowable band <10 s, and robustness to disturbances and noise. (H3) The PI controller will exhibit smoother response near nonzero references, reducing oscillations compared to a fuzzy controller with a steep control surface near zero. (H4) The system will remain effective under mild deviations from visual odometry assumptions (e.g., local nonplanarity, camera height changes), though performance will degrade.

Support/refutation: The experiments support H1–H4: slip was regulated to within ±5% across conditions; both controllers met time and disturbance/noise objectives; PI outperformed FLC for −5% references; performance degraded but remained acceptable under assumption violations.
reference_methodology:
System: Icebreaker tracked rover with a one-DOF plow (0–0.20 m depth) mounted at the centerline. Slip is defined as i_vehicle = (x_dot − V_T)/V_T, where x_dot is forward speed and V_T is theoretical speed from sprocket radius and angular speed. The slip control loop is SISO: input is slip error e = i_ref − i_vehicle; output is commanded plow depth u (discrete increments Δu via zero-order hold).

Slip estimation: Monocular optical flow visual odometry using a single camera (640×480, 60 FPS, IEEE 1394, FOV 96.25°×71.85°) mounted at the back of the left track. Pipeline: (1) Grab sequential images; (2) Create a feature selection mask to avoid robot shadow edges via K-means clustering (λ=1.5) and Canny edge parsing; (3) Select Harris corners within a ROI sized by expected maximum displacement; (4) Compute pyramidal Lucas–Kanade optical flow (one-level pyramid, 9-pixel window); (5) Undistort and map features to robot frame via homography (estimated from a chessboard target); (6) RANSAC (Challis method) enforces rigidity with inlier threshold 0.002 m; (7) Estimate linear and angular velocities using a non-inertial frame motion relation and pseudoinverse solution; (8) Outlier rejection via median replacement with fixed and MAD thresholds; (9) Low-pass filtering with a first-order transfer function H(s) = (ω/(s+ω)) (ω tuned by trial-and-error). Estimation frequency ~12 Hz.

Rover-terrain model: Adapted from Wong’s terramechanics for rigid tracks, with tractive effort derived from shear stress–shear displacement relations (eq. 2.8) and uniform normal pressure. Kinematics (eq. 2.9) compute slip parameters (i_L, i_R, σ=tanα). Dynamics sum forces/moments (eq. 2.10), including tractive effort F_i, longitudinal resistance R_i, lateral resistance R_l, and plow force F_plow. F_plow is zero for depth <0.05 m; otherwise a quadratic in depth: F_plow = a0 + a1·depth + a2·depth^2 (eq. 2.14). Longitudinal resistance uses a constant friction coefficient f_r; lateral resistance uses μ_t. The model neglects CG translation due to plow, load transfer due to centrifugal acceleration, and CG shift; landslides are treated as disturbances.

Parameter identification: Simulink Design Optimization with nonlinear least squares and trust-region-reflective algorithm. Planar terrain: optimize f_r and μ_t from two datasets (curved paths at 0° and straight-line driving). Inclined terrain (31° descents): optimize f_r (initial value from planar case) and plow force coefficients a0, a1, a2 from three datasets with constant plow depths (0.07, 0.14, 0.20 m). Data from NASA GRC SLOPE facility: GRC-1 lunar simulant (T3 preparation for some runs), precision instruments (position 5 mm, <0.0014°), fiber-optic gyroscope (random walk 4°/hr/√Hz). Speed computed from total station timestamps; yaw rate from gyroscope.

Controllers: PI (velocity form, incremental output Δu) tuned via Simulink Design Optimization with bounds on process output and Δu (max 0.012 m per cycle). Final gains: K=0.0246, T_i=0.0948, T_d≈0 (discarded). Sampling period T_s=0.5 s (plow movement completes before next cycle). FLC (SAM model): inputs normalized error e_n and normalized change in error ce_n (n_e=2.5; n_ce≈22.22), output normalized Δu_n (−1 to 1) denormalized by 0.012 m and integrated with saturation. Seven-term sets per input/output (LN, MN, SN, Z, SP, MP, LP). Rule-base (Table 5.1) encodes aggressive action at band edges, preventive action when ce_n indicates rapid change, and asymmetry near Z to avoid lingering at band borders. Sampling T_s=0.5 s.

Experimental protocol: Direct descents on tilt bed (20°, 25°, 31°) and Dunes (max 20°). Zero-slip reference for most tests; nonzero reference −5% for some. Commanded sprocket speeds: 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 rad/s. Data logging at 0.5 s (controllers) or 1 s (on-off proof-of-concept). Ground truth from total station for SLOPE; vision vs ground truth comparisons for estimator accuracy. Performance objectives: steady-state error within ±5% slip; time to enter allowable band <10 s; avoid slip >5%; robustness across speeds/slopes.

title: Anomalies of a Nonequilibrium Spinor Polariton Condensate in a Magnetic Field
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does Zeeman splitting, circular polarization degree, and diamagnetic shift of LP modes vary across linear, polariton condensate, and photon lasing regimes under an external magnetic field? (2) Can a unified non-equilibrium model explain the observed anomalies, including sign reversal of Zeeman splitting in the condensate regime? (3) Can magnetic response serve as a diagnostic to distinguish polariton lasing from photon lasing?

Hypotheses: (H1) In the polariton condensate regime, Zeeman splitting will be quenched at low magnetic fields and exhibit a sign reversal above a critical field due to competition between Zeeman energy and interaction-induced blueshifts in a quasi-equilibrium spinor condensate. (H2) Diamagnetic shift will increase in the condensate regime due to phase-space filling and exciton screening (increased Bohr radius), yielding a larger effective κ_eff. (H3) In the photon lasing regime, Zeeman splitting and diamagnetic shift will vanish, indicating loss of polaritonic origin. (H4) The quasi-equilibrium model (thermal equilibrium within each spin component, no equilibrium between components) will reproduce the measured polarization degree and explain the sign reversal and increased diamagnetic shift. Outcomes supporting H1–H4 include: sign-reversed Zeeman splitting above B_C ≈ 3 T in the condensate regime; κ_eff,Con > κ_eff,LP; absence of Zeeman/diamagnetic response in photon lasing; and model fits to polarization degree vs B.
reference_methodology:
Device and conditions: A high-Q (~10,000) Fabry–Pérot microcavity was grown by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). Experiments were conducted at T ≈ 5 K under non-resonant pumping with a top-hat laser spot of 40 μm diameter. The magnetic field was applied along the growth direction (Faraday geometry). Photon lasing required pulsed excitation with ~50 ps pulses due to limited continuous-wave (cw) powers.

Operating regimes and power series: Three regimes were identified by varying excitation power: (i) linear regime at P ≈ 0.2 P_th; (ii) polariton condensate regime at P ≈ 1.2 P_th; and (iii) weak-coupling photon lasing regime at P ≈ 20 P_th. Input/output characteristics, energy shift, and linewidth of the k = 0 ground state versus power were measured, consistent with literature. The threshold power P_th was 5 mW.

Magnetic field and detuning: Magnetic fields up to B = 5 T were applied. Detunings δ were set at B = 0 T but shifted with B due to exciton diamagnetic shift. For example, δ = +2.7 meV at B = 0 T decreased to δ = +1.6 meV at B = 5 T. The exciton g-factor g_X(B) is known to vary with B, especially in wide quantum wells (QWs).

Measurements: Fourier-space-resolved (momentum-space) spectra were recorded to map dispersion and mode shifts. Polarization-resolved spectra (σ+ and σ−) were integrated over k = ±0.25 μm^-1 around the ground state to extract Zeeman splitting and circular polarization degree. Diamagnetic shifts were quantified by fitting ΔE_Dia(B) = κ_eff B^2. Zeeman splitting in the linear regime was modeled as ΔEZ_X(δ, B) = X(δ, B) k^2 g_X μB B, where X(δ, B) is the exciton Hopfield coefficient and μB is the Bohr magneton. Effective g-factors were extracted by fitting ΔEZ vs B at fixed detuning.

Model parameters and assumptions: The theoretical model assumes thermal equilibrium within each spin component (σ+ and σ−) but no equilibrium between components, consistent with fast energy relaxation (tens of ps) and slow spin relaxation (~300 ps) at δ ≈ −6.5 meV. Interaction constants satisfy α1 − α2 > 0 for typical microcavity polaritons. The condensate fraction ρ_c and polariton density n were treated as parameters; n was inferred from the relative increase in κ_eff via phase-space filling and exciton screening (increased a_B).

title: CircPLXNA2 Affects the Proliferation and Apoptosis of Myoblast through circPLXNA2/gga-miR-12207-5P/MDM4 Axis
field_subfield: Molecular Biology — Non-coding RNAs and Skeletal Muscle Biology
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which circRNA-miRNA-mRNA axes are differentially expressed during chicken myoblast proliferation (GM) versus differentiation (DM), and which pathways are implicated? (2) Does circPLXNA2 function as a ceRNA to sponge gga-miR-12207-5p, thereby derepressing MDM4 and modulating p53 signaling to regulate proliferation and apoptosis in CPMs?

Hypotheses: (a) circPLXNA2 is differentially expressed between GM and DM and is predominantly cytoplasmic, enabling miRNA sponging. (b) circPLXNA2 directly binds gga-miR-12207-5p, reducing its availability to repress MDM4, thereby increasing MDM4 expression. (c) MDM4, as a p53 inhibitor, promotes proliferation and suppresses apoptosis in myoblasts. (d) Overexpression of gga-miR-12207-5p will decrease MDM4 and circPLXNA2, reduce proliferation markers, increase apoptosis markers, and lower EdU incorporation; conversely, circPLXNA2 overexpression will increase proliferation and reduce apoptosis. (e) Co-overexpression of circPLXNA2 will reverse the inhibitory effects of gga-miR-12207-5p on MDM4 and downstream markers.

Predicted outcomes supporting the hypotheses include: circPLXNA2–gga-miR-12207-5p binding confirmed by luciferase and pulldown assays; gga-miR-12207-5p overexpression decreasing MDM4 and proliferation markers while increasing apoptosis markers; MDM4 overexpression decreasing p53 and caspase expression while increasing cyclins and EdU incorporation; and circPLXNA2 co-transfection restoring MDM4 and reversing gga-miR-12207-5p-induced changes.
reference_methodology:
Cell source and culture: Thigh muscles from 11 embryo-aged chickens were minced and digested with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA at 37°C for 15 min. Cells were cultured in high-glucose DMEM with 10% FBS and 0.2% penicillin/streptomycin (GM). For differentiation, at 90% confluence, medium was switched to RPMI-1640 with 2% horse serum (DM). Adherent purification was performed twice (40 min each) to remove chick embryo fibroblasts. Cells were used at 60–80% confluence for transfections.

Omics profiling: Three biological replicates were prepared for GM and DM. Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol, treated with RNase R, and DNase I. circRNA-seq libraries were constructed using Illumina Ribo-Zero rRNA removal, RNase R treatment, and VAHTS Total RNA-seq kits; cDNA was synthesized with random primers, second-strand cDNA synthesized with dUTP, and libraries sequenced on Illumina Novaseq 6000. Ribo-seq libraries were generated by immunoprecipitation of monosomes with anti-HA magnetic beads after RNase I treatment, following an Illumina mammalian ribo-seq kit; libraries were sequenced on Novaseq 6000.

CircPLXNA2 validation: Divergent and convergent PCR primers were used with cDNA and gDNA templates. RNase R treatment assessed circularity. Sanger sequencing confirmed the back-splice junction. Subcellular localization was assessed by qRT-PCR using GAPDH (cytoplasmic) and U6 (nuclear) as controls.

Plasmids and oligos: circPLXNA2 overexpression used a pCD25-ciR vector constructed by homologous recombination of a synthesized linear circPLXNA2 sequence with EcoRI/BamHI sites and cyclization sequences. MDM4 overexpression used pcDNA3.1 with HindIII/XhoI cloning. gga-miR-12207-5p mimic and si-MDM4 were synthesized (RiboBio). Dual-luciferase reporter constructs (pmirGLO) contained circPLXNA2 or MDM4 3′UTR segments with predicted gga-miR-12207-5p sites (WT) or mutated sites (MUT).

Transfection and assays: Lipofectamine 3000 was used at 60–80% confluence; miRNA mimics, siRNAs, and plasmids were diluted in OPTI-MEM. Final miRNA/siRNA concentration was 100 nM. Dual-luciferase assays were performed 48 h post-transfection using a BioTek plate reader; firefly luciferase was normalized to Renilla. EdU assays used 50 µM EdU for 2 h after 36 h transfection; cells were fixed (4% PFA), glycine-neutralized, permeabilized (0.5% Triton X-100), stained with Apollo reagent, and imaged (Leica DMi8). At least three random fields per well were quantified with ImageJ to compute EdU-positive rates. Biotin-coupled miRNA pulldown used 3′-biotinylated gga-miR-12207-5p mimic or NC; RNA was eluted and analyzed by RT-qPCR. Western blotting used RIPA lysis, SDS-PAGE (12%), transfer to nitrocellulose, blocking with 5% milk, primary antibodies overnight at 4°C, and secondary antibodies for 60 min at room temperature; detection used LI-COR Odyssey Fc. Antibodies: cleaved caspase-3 (p17), cleaved caspase-8 (Asp391), caspase-9, and GAPDH.

Statistics: Data are mean ± SEM with 3–6 independent replicates. Independent-sample t-tests were used; significance thresholds: p<0.05 (*), p<0.01 (**), p<0.001 (***).

title: Short-term mortality after primary and revision total joint arthroplasty: a single-center analysis of 103,560 patients
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the in-hospital mortality rate after primary and revision TJA across hip, knee, shoulder, elbow, and ankle procedures in a high-volume specialty center? (2) What are the causes of death among in-hospital deaths, and do they differ by procedure type and revision status (primary, aseptic revision, septic revision)? (3) Which patient- and procedure-level factors (e.g., preoperative hemoglobin, comorbidity burden, blood loss, operative time, anesthesia type) are associated with mortality risk?

Hypotheses: (a) In-hospital mortality is low overall but higher after revision than primary TJA; (b) septic revisions carry higher mortality than aseptic revisions due to greater comorbidity burden and complications; (c) preoperative anemia is more prevalent in septic revisions and associated with higher mortality risk; (d) causes of death differ by group, with thromboembolic events more frequent in primary/aseptic revisions and septic shock in septic revisions; (e) longer operative times and greater blood loss in revisions contribute to higher mortality risk. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include higher mortality rates in revision groups, significant differences in preoperative Hb and CCI, and distinct COD distributions by group.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Retrospective cohort study at a single specialty arthroplasty center. Institutional Review Board approval was obtained (WF-080/18). The study period spanned January 1996 to December 2018.

Participants: All primary and revision arthroplasty procedures of the upper and lower extremities, including septic cases, were included. Total N=103,560: 73,130 primary (41,868 THA; 28,939 TKA; 1,572 TSA; 85 TEA; 666 TAA) and 30,430 revision (21,002 THA; 8,781 TKA; 467 TSA; 64 TEA; 116 TAA). In-hospital deaths were identified and analyzed.

Data collection: Variables included age, sex, weight, height, BMI, number of prior surgeries, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), CHA2DS2 score, pre- and postoperative hemoglobin (Hb), operative time, intraoperative blood loss, length of stay, days from surgery to death, diagnosis, medical history (e.g., liver disease, diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, COPD, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism), postoperative complications (e.g., infection, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, MI, epilepsy, cardiac arrest, delirium, sepsis, intestinal obstruction, multiorgan failure, shock, renal failure, cardiac decompensation), and cause of death (COD) for patients who died during hospitalization.

Outcomes: Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality by procedure type and revision status (primary, aseptic revision, septic revision). Secondary outcomes included preoperative Hb, CCI, CHA2DS2, blood loss, operative time, anesthesia type, complication frequencies (e.g., wound infection), and COD distributions.

Statistical analysis: Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages; continuous variables as means and ranges. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. For normally distributed data (p≥0.1), two-group comparisons used t-tests and multi-group comparisons used F-tests. For non-normal data, two-group comparisons used Mann–Whitney U tests and multi-group comparisons used Kruskal–Wallis tests. Categorical variable comparisons used Fisher’s exact test. All tests were two-sided. Analyses were conducted in SAS 9.4 for Windows.

Ethics and funding: Ethical approval was obtained (WF-080/18). No funding was reported. Authors declared no conflict of interest but listed royalties/payments from Waldemar Link and Zimmer.

title: Very Large Telescope Interferometer observations of the dust geometry around R Coronae Borealis stars
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the geometry of the inner circumstellar dust around RCB stars on sub-arcsecond scales? (2) Do asymmetries (e.g., off-center clumps) exist and are they persistent or variable? (3) How do inner-shell sizes and dust masses compare across RCB stars, and how do these relate to dust formation timing inferred from light curves? (4) What is the composition and spatial extent of dust responsible for MIR emission features in V854 Cen?

Hypotheses: (H1) RCB dust forms in clumps near the photosphere, with episodic ejection producing asymmetries detectable in interferometric visibilities. (H2) Over time, random clump ejections yield a spherically symmetric shell, with occasional asymmetries. (H3) Inner-shell sizes (R_DUSTY) are comparable across RCB stars and can be inferred from radiative transfer fits to SEDs and visibilities. (H4) Emission features in V854 Cen arise from extended, over-resolved dust (e.g., PAH-like/HAC/C60) that reduce visibilities at their wavelengths.

Support/refutation criteria: H1/H2 are supported if geometric models require asymmetries (clusters) and if DUSTY spherical shells fit the SEDs and visibilities. H3 is supported if R_DUSTY is consistent across sources within uncertainties. H4 is supported if visibilities drop at feature wavelengths in proportion to SED excesses.
reference_methodology:
Targets: RY Sgr, V854 Cen, and V CrA (RCB stars). Distances and stellar parameters (Table 4): RY Sgr: M_V = −5 mag, A_V = 0.06 mag, V = 6.4 mag, T_eff = 7250 K, D = 1800 pc; V CrA: M_V = −4 mag, A_V = 0.37 mag, V = 9.9 mag, T_eff = 6250 K, D = 5200 pc; V854 Cen: M_V = −4.5 mag, A_V = 0.00 mag, V = 7.1 mag, T_eff = 6750 K, D = 2100 pc. Reddening corrections used CCM law with E(B−V) = A_V/3.1.

Observations: VLTI/MIDI in 2007 June (11 runs) using two telescope pairs (U2–U3 and U3–U4) with N-band (7.5–13.5 µm) dispersed visibilities (R = 25 and 230). Typical sequence: single-dish acquisition (250 mas FWHM at 8.7 µm), fringe search (OPD scan 40–80 µm in ~2 µm steps), self-fringe tracking, and high-sens mode photometry recorded after fringes. Baselines and PAs (Table 1): RY Sgr (2005): B1–B7 (U1–U4; U3–U4) with projected lengths 57–128 m and PAs 34–135°; RY Sgr (2007): B1–B5 (U2–U3; U3–U4) with 34–59 m and PAs 32–129°; V CrA (2007): B1–B4 (U2–U3; U3–U4) with 32–61 m and PAs 45–128°; V854 Cen (2007): B1–B2 (U3–U4) with 56–60 m and PAs 101–153°. Absolute flux calibration accuracy <10%. Atmospheric fluctuations introduce correlated errors in absolute visibilities at 8–15% depending on conditions; differential visibility slopes are more reliable. Differential phases were not used due to limited sensitivity to slow spectral phase changes and similar clump spectral signatures.

Data reduction and calibration: MIA+EWS (V1.5.1). Calibration stars: HD 152334 (K4III; 3.99 ± 0.07 mas), HD 163376 (M0III; 3.79 ± 0.12 mas), HD 169916 (K1III; 3.75 ± 0.04 mas), HD 177716 (K1III; 3.72 ± 0.07 mas). ISO/SWS spectra (1996–1997) and Spitzer/IRS SL spectra (2005–2008) were re-reduced (SMART; modified SWS routines) for cross-checks.

Geometric modeling: Combinations of (i) central point source (PS), (ii) Gaussian shell (G; spherical clump distribution), (iii) uniform disc (UD), (iv) elliptical uniform disc (EUD), and (v) off-center cluster (C; 180° ambiguity). Monochromatic fits minimized reduced χ² across baselines using errors in mean visibility levels. Chromatic fits allowed wavelength-dependent FWHM and fluxes (cluster separation and PA fixed across wavelengths). Closure phase was not available (telescope pairs), so cluster position is ambiguous by 180°.

Radiative transfer modeling (DUSTY): 1D plane-parallel/spherical code with inputs: T_eff (blackbody), dust composition (amorphous carbon; Hanner 1988), grain size distribution (MRN: n(a) ∝ a^−3.5; a_min–a_max varied), density distribution r^−P (P constrained by visibility slopes), T_inner (from SED), τ_V (from V-band photometry), and shell thickness (R_out/R_in; poorly constrained beyond ~90–100). Outputs: SED, surface brightness, radial profiles, and visibilities at 15 N-band wavelengths. DUSTY results were scaled to stellar luminosity and distance (Table 4) and corrected for reddening. A Gaussian fit to the 1D collapsed intensity at 9 µm yielded R_DUSTY (HWHM) for comparison with geometric shell radii.

Ancillary data: AAVSO/ASAS light curves (2001–2010) to infer dust ejection timing relative to VLTI epochs.

title: Summary: Patients with ileostomy and OHT may be at risk of rejection given the lack of EHC of MPM. Therapeutic monitoring of MPA with AUC or conversion to other immunosuppressants should be considered in this population
research_question:
The first case implicitly tests whether donor HLA-specific B-cell compartments (plasma cells and circulating mBc) can detect active anti-donor humoral responses that are not fully captured by DSA assays, and whether such responses correlate with rejection risk and inform therapy. The hypothesis is that persistent donor HLA-specific B-cell activation, even with negative CDC crossmatch, indicates ongoing humoral risk and may necessitate combined immunosuppression.

The second case examines whether high cPRA detected by Luminex SAB after HBV vaccination reflects pathogenic HLA sensitization and whether multi-assay corroboration (LABScreen PRA, 4-digit typing, FC/CDC crossmatch) can identify non-pathogenic antibodies, thereby avoiding unnecessary donor pool restriction. The hypothesis is that negative LABScreen PRA and negative FC/CDC crossmatches, despite high SAB cPRA, indicate non-pathogenic antibodies and permit safe transplantation.
reference_methodology:
Case 1: A 44-year-old female with advanced Chagasic cardiomyopathy refractory to therapy was listed with PRA 67% in March 2019 and transplanted in November 2019. Pre-transplant CDC crossmatch was negative. Induction therapy included basiliximab, and maintenance was tacrolimus-based triple therapy with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and steroids. Post-transplant, five C3q-fixing DSAs were detected (A3, DR1, DR7, DPB1, DQ2, DQ5). The 14-day endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) showed acute cellular rejection G2R with pAMR1 i+ and persistent DSAs. Treatment comprised high-dose steroids, IVIG, and plasmapheresis. On day 25, SAB showed persistent DSAs with lower mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) levels. To characterize B-cell responses, a novel HLA-specific B-cell FluorSpot assay was used on bone marrow aspirate and peripheral blood, demonstrating high frequencies of donor HLA-specific IgG-producing plasma cells and circulating donor-specific mBc against multiple donor HLA specificities. No additional therapy was initiated beyond the initial regimen. At 12 months, the patient remained clinically stable with negative ACR/pAMR EMB.

Case 2: A 50-year-old Caucasian male with ARVD developed recurrent ventricular tachycardia and worsening right ventricular dysfunction, leading to HTx evaluation. He had no history of transfusion, surgery, or mechanical circulatory support. Luminex SAB at listing and serially was negative. After HBV vaccination, broad class II HLA sensitization (cPRA 98%) was detected by SAB, with multiple antibodies persisting at 1:8 dilution, including antibodies against his own HLA (autologous flow XM negative). At donor availability, four DSAs were identified on the most recent SAB. To assess pathogenicity, the team combined Luminex SAB with LABScreen PRA, 4-digit donor HLA typing, and prospective crossmatches by flow cytometry (FC) and CDC. LABScreen PRA was negative, and both FC and CDC crossmatches were negative. The patient underwent successful HTx with no rejection and normal graft function.

Across both cases, immunosuppression included basiliximab induction and tacrolimus-based triple therapy with MMF and steroids. Monitoring included serial DSA testing (SAB), CDC/FC crossmatches, EMB grading for ACR and pAMR, and, in Case 1, a novel HLA-specific B-cell FluorSpot assay. No IRB/consent details, randomization, or statistical analyses were reported.

title: SARS-CoV-2-related Guillain-Barré syndrome: a systematic review of published cases
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the demographic and clinical characteristics of GBS cases temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection? (2) What diagnostic patterns (CSF, electrophysiology) are observed in these cases? (3) What treatments are used, and what are the clinical courses and outcomes? (4) Do findings support a direct viral etiology or a post-infectious immune-mediated mechanism?

Hypotheses: (a) SARS-CoV-2 infection is temporally associated with GBS, with a post-infectious interval between COVID-19 symptoms and neurological onset; (b) CSF will not show SARS-CoV-2 RNA, supporting an immune-mediated mechanism; (c) GBS subtypes and clinical features will resemble non-COVID GBS, with AIDP predominating; (d) IVIg and PLEX will be effective, with a subset requiring ICU and mechanical ventilation. Support for (a) would be demonstrated by consistent intervals (e.g., 8–23 days) between infection and GBS onset. Support for (b) would be demonstrated by uniformly negative CSF PCR. Support for (c) would be shown by AIDP predominance and typical GBS signs/symptoms. Support for (d) would be shown by high response rates to IVIg/PLEX and documented ICU/ventilation needs.
reference_methodology:
Design: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance. Protocol was not published and not registered in PROSPERO.

Data sources and search: Electronic databases (Embase, MEDLINE, Google Scholar, Cochrane Central Trials Register) were searched with terms including “Guillain-Barré Syndrome” and “COVID-19.” The initial search was performed on 24 September 2020. Reference lists of included studies were screened for additional relevant reports.

Eligibility criteria: Included studies were original data reports (case reports and case series) of patients with GBS and suspected, probable, or confirmed recent SARS-CoV-2 infection, any age, gender, or setting. Exclusions: GBS within 3 months after vaccination or other proven triggering infections (e.g., C. jejuni), and studies lacking information on residence and at least one clinical variable of interest.

Screening and selection: Titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers (PS, LGG). Full texts were assessed by the same reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (MCP). The PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) summarizes selection.

Data extraction: Conducted independently by one of three reviewers (PS, LGG, MCP) using a predefined protocol, with cross-checking and consensus resolution. Extracted variables: demographics; COVID-19 symptoms; GBS symptoms/signs; CSF (protein, cell count, SARS-CoV-2 PCR); electrophysiology (subtype classification); treatments (IVIg, PLEX, steroids); clinical course (ICU, ventilation, death); outcomes. Continuous variables (age, intervals, durations) were extracted as medians/means as reported.

Diagnostic classification: GBS diagnosis was classified using the Brighton Collaboration Criteria (2011). SARS-CoV-2 infection certainty was classified per WHO criteria. For unreported symptoms, the authors assumed absence to mitigate reporting bias.

Synthesis: Descriptive synthesis of proportions (n/N) and counts; electrophysiology and CSF results summarized; treatment regimens and outcomes tabulated. No meta-analysis or pooled effect estimates were performed due to heterogeneity and small sample sizes.

Ethics: Not applicable (systematic review of published cases).

title: EgoNet identifies differential ego-modules and pathways related to prednisolone resistance in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can EgoNet identify differential ego-network modules that discriminate prednisolone-resistant from sensitive childhood ALL samples? (2) Do these modules enrich for biologically coherent pathways implicated in glucocorticoid resistance? (3) Do the identified modules and their enriched pathways exhibit strong predictive performance in cross-validated classification? (4) How do EgoNet-derived modules compare to modules identified by an established attractor method on the same data?

Hypotheses: (H1) EgoNet will recover ego-network modules with high classification accuracy that are significantly enriched for pathways relevant to prednisolone resistance. (H2) The enriched pathways will implicate mechanisms consistent with glucocorticoid action and resistance (e.g., cell cycle regulation). (H3) SVM-based AUC for the enriched pathways will exceed 0.7, indicating clinically useful predictive performance. (H4) Compared to attractor modules, EgoNet modules will have comparable or superior predictive performance and/or larger size, reflecting more informative sub-networks.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if modules pass FDR thresholds and achieve high classification accuracy. H2 is supported if pathway enrichment (FDR<0.01) aligns with known resistance mechanisms. H3 is supported if AUC>0.7. H4 is supported if EgoNet modules outperform attractor modules in AUC or node count.
reference_methodology:
Data source and cohort: Microarray data (Affymetrix Human Genome U133A, GPL96) from GSE19143 comprising 52 pediatric ALL patients stratified by in vitro prednisolone sensitivity: 27 sensitive (LC50 <0.1 lg/ml) and 25 resistant (LC50 >150 lg/ml). Prednisolone LC50 thresholds were used to define group labels.

Preprocessing: Probe–gene annotation mapping was performed using TXT annotation. Expression preprocessing included: (1) background adjustment via RMA; (2) quantile normalization; (3) PM/MM correction using Microarray Suite (MAS); (4) summarization via median polish; (5) probe set mapping to gene symbols. The final expression profile included 12,442 genes.

Network construction: A STRING-derived PPI network (787,896 interactions; 16,730 genes) was intersected with the microarray gene set to obtain a filtered PPI network with 41,244 interactions and 6,722 genes. A differential co-expression network (DCN) was constructed by computing absolute Pearson correlation coefficients (PCC) between gene pairs and retaining edges with |PCC| > δ (δ=0.8). This yielded 605 genes and 845 edges (Figure 1; Supplementary Table 1 lists gene/interaction content).

Ego gene selection: An importance function g(s) was defined using a degree-normalized weighted adjacency matrix A′ and a diagonal matrix D to compute node importance in the DCN. For each gene, g(s) was converted to a z-score; genes with degree >1 were ranked by z-score, and the top 5% were designated ego genes (30 ego genes identified).

Ego-network module growth: Starting from each ego gene, ego-network modules were grown via snowball sampling. For a current module C and neighbor y, the change in classification accuracy ΔS(C′, C) = S(C′) − S(C) was computed. If ΔS > 0, y was added to C; otherwise, growth stopped. Random selection was used when multiple neighbors improved accuracy. Growth continued until classification accuracy decreased. Modules with classification accuracy <0.9 or fewer than 15 nodes were removed.

Statistical significance: Significance was assessed via 1,000 random permutations of the same ego-network modules. The null distribution of classification accuracy was used to compute p-values as the probability of observing smaller accuracy under the null. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied; FDR=0.01 was the significance criterion.

Pathway enrichment: Reactome reference pathways (human) were intersected with the filtered PPI network to retain informative pathways with 5–100 genes. Module genes were mapped to pathways; enrichment was tested using Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Pathways with FDR<0.01 were considered enriched. For each module, the pathway with the smallest FDR was selected as the significant pathway.

Validation and benchmarking: SVM was used to compute AUC for each significant pathway using 3-fold cross-validation. AUC=1.0 indicates perfect classification; AUC>0.7 was considered good. The attract method (per Wang et al.) was applied to the same microarray profile to identify differential attractor modules with FDR<0.05; pathway enrichment for attractor modules followed the same criteria.

title: Forgiveness, Blame, and Punishment
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What does it mean to forgive a criminal, and under what conditions is forgiveness warranted? (2) How is the justification for punishment connected to the conditions under which forgiveness becomes possible? (3) What distinguishes contingent from necessary unforgivable cases? (4) What practical implications follow for punishment, legal restrictions, and reconciliation after restoration?

Hypotheses/theses: (a) Fully forgiving a criminal is warranted only if the offender has undertaken all the punishment they deserve; once fully forgivable, no further punishment is justified. (b) Forgiveness is the suspension of warranted moral blame for the right object-based reason: the offender has restored trustworthiness by credible signaling of reform. (c) There are two senses of unforgivable: contingent (capable of reform but has not signaled it) and necessary (lacks capacity to restore trustworthiness to a minimally acceptable degree). (d) Forgiveness is not mercy (state-based reasons) or condoning (approval of the crime), and it is not obligatory but not elective in the sense of being morally permissible to withhold after restoration. (e) After credible signaling, certain legal restrictions (e.g., denial of voting rights, employment bans, public shaming) are morally impermissible.
reference_methodology:
The essay employs conceptual analysis and normative argumentation. It begins by distinguishing forgiveness from related concepts (mercy, condoning) and clarifying that forgiveness involves suspending warranted moral blame for object-based reasons. It then develops a theory of punitive desert grounded in an unfair advantage framework: unexcused crimes undermine the offender’s minimally acceptable degree of trustworthiness, thereby posing unacceptable risks to others (future harms, costs of insecurity, and fear). To avoid this unfair advantage, offenders incur an obligation to restore trustworthiness expeditiously.

The author specifies that credible signaling of reform must be costly, observable, and sustained over time, evidencing a sufficiently benevolent character. Costly signaling is contrasted with “cheap talk” (e.g., apologies, compensation) that is not credible absent sacrifice of sufficiently important personal interests. The burdens necessary to fulfill the obligation of restoration determine the severity of deserved punishment; punishment is proportional to these burdens. The essay argues that no acceptable system of deterrence or incapacitation can fully mitigate risks posed by untrustworthy offenders, and that there is no reliable way to induce reform, necessitating offender-provided signals.

Forgiveness is analyzed as a suspension of blame for the right reason: the offender has restored trustworthiness by signaling reform. Degrees of forgiveness (full vs partial) track the degree of restoration (to a minimally acceptable degree vs less). Perspectives include personal (victim), impersonal (any third party), and self-reactive (self-forgiveness). The essay also articulates five values potentially promoted by forgiveness: marginal trust-warranting effects, reduced costs of insecurity, relief from the burden of blame, reconciliation, and improved self-esteem. Practical implications are drawn: once full forgiveness is warranted, additional punishment is unjustified; and after credible signaling, certain legal restrictions are morally impermissible.

The essay engages counterarguments: (1) epistemic abstinence (forgiveness as abstaining from negative inferences about character) is rejected as psychologically implausible and lacking the honorific nature of forgiveness; (2) releasing obligations due to hardship is rejected as conflating mercy with forgiveness. The analysis presumes practical constraints (no extraordinary means to assess or change dispositions) and relies on established theories of trust, signaling, and moral responsibility.

title: Bienestar animal en hatos lecheros especializados de Costa Rica asociados a una cooperativa de productores de leche
field_subfield: Veterinary Medicine — Animal Welfare and Dairy Production
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the distribution of animal welfare scores among specialized Costa Rican dairy farms associated with a national cooperative, and how do they map to Welfare Quality® categories? (2) Which freedoms (nutrition, housing, health, behavior) are strongest and weakest, and what specific measures drive these outcomes? (3) How do management systems (stalled, semi-stalled, sesteo, continuous grazing) and geographic zones (Central, North, Pacific) relate to welfare scores? (4) Are there correlations between welfare criteria that suggest leverage points for improvement?

Hypotheses: (a) Grazing systems will outperform stalled systems in housing and behavior due to natural environments and movement, but will lag in nutrition/water control; (b) Water supply (quantity/quality) will be a primary constraint on nutrition scores; (c) Lack of analgesia/anesthesia for painful procedures will depress health scores; (d) There will be positive associations between adequate nutrition and positive emotional state. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include higher Housing/Behavior scores in grazing systems, lower Nutrition scores linked to water deficits, lower Health scores due to unmanaged pain, and significant positive correlations between Nutrition and positive emotional state.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional, observational assessment of animal welfare using the Welfare Quality® Project protocol for adult dairy cattle, with calf-specific measures applied to replacement calves.

Population and sampling: Sixty farms affiliated with a national dairy cooperative were selected by proportional allocation across three geographic zones (Central 38%, North 45%, Pacific 17%). Exclusion criterion: refusal to participate. Farms were specialized dairy with mechanical milking, concentrate supplementation, mineral salts, veterinary services, and cooperative advisory. Average herd size was 60±7.7 cows in milk; average milk yield 20.9±4.6 kg/cow/day (large breeds) and 15.9±3.8 kg/cow/day (small breeds), with hybrids intermediate. Open days ranged IQR 85–115. Major breeds: Holstein (large), Jersey (small), each >90% in their category.

Sample size: Calculated to detect a mean compliance score of 55% from 1500 farms, expected SD 20, error 5, 95% confidence.

Measures and instruments: The Welfare Quality® protocol for adult dairy cattle was applied to adults; for 47 farms, the calf protocol was used for animals aged 3–6 months. Animal-based measures included: (1) Nutrition: absence of prolonged hunger (body condition), absence of prolonged thirst (water provision, drinker cleanliness, flow, functionality); (2) Housing: rest comfort (bedding, collisions, cleanliness of udders/flanks/paws), thermal comfort (no measure developed), facility movement (tie-stalls, access to air/pasture, slippery floors); (3) Health: absence of lesions (skin, hoof, joint, bursa, ear/tail biting, lameness), absence of disease (cough, nasal/ocular discharge, dyspnea, diarrhea, vulvar discharge, somatic cell count, mortality, dystocia, fallen cows), absence of pain from management procedures (dehorning, tail docking, castration); (4) Behavior: expression of social behaviors (agonistic), expression of other behaviors (pasture access, play, abnormal behaviors), human-animal relations (flight distance), positive emotional state (qualitative behavior assessment). Scoring followed protocol-specific formulas; liberty scores were summed to obtain farm-level scores.

Procedure: Each farm was visited once. Visual observations of adult behavior and health were conducted post-morning milking, followed by calf assessments, then interviews with farm managers to obtain management and health data. The evaluation adhered to Welfare Quality® methods.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics (absolute/relative frequencies by category; mean, median, SD, percentiles P25/P75) were computed for farm-level scores and liberty/criterion scores. Pearson correlations assessed relationships among criteria. Software: InfoStat/S 2013. No inferential tests beyond correlations and group comparisons (as reported) were described. Ethics/IRB approvals were not reported.

title: Celtiberia en las fuentes grecolatinas: replanteamiento conceptual de un paradigma obsoleto
field_subfield: Classics — Ancient History (Hispanic antiquity; historiography and geography)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What geographic and conceptual boundaries does the term “Celtiberia” denote in Greco-Latin sources? (2) Is Celtiberia an ethnic-political entity or a geographic interior region? (3) How do classical sources (Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy) and the Punic/Roman war narratives (Polybius, Livy, Appian, Diodorus) describe Celtiberia’s extent and character? (4) What are the implications of a geographic redefinition for cultural syntheses (language, religion, material culture) and origin theories of Iberian Celts?

Hypotheses: (H1) Celtiberia in classical sources is a geographic interior region of the Iberian Peninsula (Meseta), not an ethnic bloc. (H2) Strabo’s III,4,13 does not define intrinsic ethnic divisions; the mention of Lusones is a generic boundary marker. (H3) Pliny’s references to “Celtiberi” are geographically broad and do not support the traditional Meseta image; the identification of Clunia as the “finis” is erroneous. (H4) Ptolemy’s list reflects a patchwork solution to fill an ethno-geographic vacuum rather than an ethnic partition. (H5) The Citerior/Ulterior dichotomy and Numantia-centric narrative are misreadings of the sources. Support for these hypotheses would be demonstrated by textual analysis showing geographic boundaries, administrative references, and the generic use of “Celtiberi” in war narratives.
reference_methodology:
Design: Historiographical and philological analysis of Greco-Latin sources, focusing on Book III of Strabo, Pliny’s Naturalis Historia (Books III, IV, VI), and Ptolemy’s Geography (Book II), with cross-referencing to Polybius, Livy, Appian, and Diodorus. The study also engages with modern historiography (e.g., Schulten; Burillo; Salinas; Tovar; Ciprés) to assess how classical texts have been interpreted.

Sources and passages analyzed: Strabo III,2–5 (Bética, Lusitania, Citerior, interior Celtiberia; III,4,12–14 for explicit boundaries; III,4,13 for the contested four-part division; III,4,19–20 for administrative references). Pliny Nat. III.3.13 (Celtici from Lusitania); III.4.19–20 (Citerior order: Bastuli, Mentesani, Oretani, Carpetani; Vaccaei, Vettones, Celtiberi Arevaci); III.4.25–27 (Conventus Cluniensis; Arevaci civitates; Clunia as “Celtiberiae finis”); IV.36.119 (Cassiterides); VI.39.211–218 (climatic circles and paralels). Ptolemy II,6,57–59 (Celtiberi civitates and boundaries). Polybius III,17,1–2 (Celtiberia delimitation via Sagunto); Livy XXVIII,1,4; XL,39; XL,47 (Celtiberia Ulterior in Bética); Appian Ib.1,42–47,50–54 (Celtiberi as generic rebels; Vaccei among Celtiberi); Diodorus V,33–35 (Celtiberi in Punic/Roman wars).

Procedure: The author reconstructs the geographic scope of Celtiberia by synthesizing Strabo’s Book III, which systematically describes the Peninsula and defines Celtiberia as the interior region bounded by the Idubeda (Ebro) and Orospeda (Duero) and by the Provincia Citerior/Ulterior. The analysis distinguishes Strabo’s geographic framing from later administrative overlays. For Pliny, the study examines the context of “Celtiberi” in Citerior and the Conventus Cluniensis, arguing that the term denotes geographic inclusion rather than ethnic identity. Ptolemy’s list is read as a patchwork solution to fill an ethno-geographic vacuum. The Punic/Roman war narratives are used to show the generic use of “Celtiberi” for interior rebels.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable (textual analysis of classical sources).

title: Extracting Linked Data from statistic spreadsheets
field_subfield: Computer Science — Semantic Web and Information Retrieval
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can statistical tables from government portals (e.g., INSEE) be systematically converted into a structured RDF model that preserves hierarchical headers and aggregated relations, enabling precise, machine-readable access? (2) Can a keyword-based search algorithm, leveraging semantic similarity and location-aware scoring, efficiently retrieve the most relevant datasets and return the most precise cell-level answers for fact-checking queries? (3) Does the proposed approach achieve effectiveness comparable to or better than existing baselines (INSEE search, Google) while maintaining practical efficiency?

Hypotheses: (H1) A rule-based extraction pipeline can achieve high accuracy in identifying data cells, headers, and hierarchical relations in INSEE Excel sheets, enabling reliable LOD generation. (H2) A content- and location-aware scoring function, augmented by semantic similarity (word2vec) and Geonames for places, will improve dataset relevance ranking over simple keyword matching, yielding higher MAP scores. (H3) The system can return precise cell-level answers with minimal latency, supporting real-time fact-checking workflows. (H4) The approach will match or exceed the effectiveness of INSEE’s own search and be comparable to Google search on the same corpus.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if extraction accuracy on held-out sheets is high (e.g., ≥90%). H2 is supported if MAP scores improve with semantic similarity and location weighting. H3 is supported if average query time is low (seconds) and cell-level answers are returned. H4 is supported if MAPp and MAPh are at least comparable to baselines.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: The authors crawled INSEE under categories Data/Key figures, Data/Detailed figures, Data/Databases, and Publications/Wide-audience, obtaining ~11,000 pages, 20,743 Excel files (36 GB), and 20,116 HTML tables. The extraction focused on Excel files; HTML tables were also processed for corpus building.

Extraction pipeline: Using Python’s xlrd, each sheet is parsed. Data cell identification proceeds in three steps: (DCI1) Identify leftmost data locations (ldl) per row by detecting the first non-header cell with numeric or interval content; (DCI2) Compute row signatures (counts of non-empty string/numeric cells) and find the largest set of rows with identical signatures (the data table seed); (DCI3) Grow the seed by adding adjacent rows (within 1–2 rows above/below) that contain at least one data cell, iteratively until no more qualify. Header detection: (HCE1) If a horizontal border separates the first header row from the data, the header area spans from that border down to the first data row; otherwise, inspect rows above the first data row, starting at ldl[i], to identify header rows (no empty header cells are allowed). (HCE2) Group fused header cells (spanning multiple adjacent cells) by tracking visible borders to form conceptual header cells. (HCE3) Identify column headers by collecting cells to the left of ldl[i] across data rows. Relationships: connect each data/header cell to its (row, column) location; each data cell to its closest row and column header; and hierarchical headers via aggregated by.

RDF model: Entities include dataset, table, cell (data/header), outline, and variable/measure mappings. Each entity has a URI; relationships are represented as RDF resources with roles. The model captures hierarchical headers and aggregated-by relations.

Search setup: A scraper converts Excel/HTML tables to RDF and stores them in Apache Jena TDB. At query time, keyword queries are transformed into word sets W via KEA tokenization, Geonames for multi-word French locations, lowercasing, stopword removal, and accent normalization. Words are mapped to word2vec vectors (trained on French news), with bigrams/trigrams considered. For datasets, word-dataset scores are computed: score(w) = 1 if w appears; otherwise, if any of the top-50 word2vec similar words appears, score(w) is the similarity; for Geonames places, score(w) is (p+1−i)/(p+1) where p is the number of places returned by the hierarchy API and i is the rank of the place appearing in the dataset. Location-aware scoring aggregates occurrences in title (T), row headers (HR), column headers (HC), and comments (C) with coefficients αT, αC, αHR, αHC, and αH. A variant discards datasets without title matches. Fagin’s threshold algorithm efficiently retrieves top-k datasets.

Data cell search: For each dataset, precomputed located occurrences (w, score(w), location, dataset) are used. For each data cell D_r,c, count the unique w≺W in its characterizing headers (including ancestors). Return either cell(s) with highest counts, or rows/columns if no cell answers exist. SPARQL 1.1 property paths identify characterizing headers.

Evaluation: Extraction validation used 100 randomly selected Excel files (2,432 tables), with manual annotation of headers/data and hierarchy. Search evaluation used 55 queries derived from Les Décodeurs fact-checks (2014) that reference INSEE. A development set of 29 queries tuned parameters; a test set of 26 queries measured MAPp and MAPh. Baselines: INSEE’s own search and Google search restricted to INSEE. Hardware: 126 GB RAM, 40 CPUs (Intel Xeon E5-2640 v4 @ 2.40 GHz).

title: A Novel, Low-Volume Method for Organ Culture of Embryonic Kidneys That Allows Development of Cortico-Medullary Anatomical Organization
research_question:
Primary questions: (1) Can embryonic kidney rudiments be cultured in very low volumes (≈85 µL) directly on glass to achieve superior organotypic development and cortico-medullary zonation compared to conventional filter-based culture? (2) Does the low-volume glass system respond normally to known positive (GDNF) and negative (TGF-β) morphogens? (3) Is the improved development associated with reduced cellular stress, as reflected in cytokine profiles? (4) Is the gas–liquid interface and/or surface tension at the air–medium boundary a key factor for improved development?

Hypotheses: (H1) Low-volume glass culture will increase organ area, UB branching, and nephron number relative to conventional filters. (H2) The low-volume system will exhibit normal morphogen responses (GDNF upregulates; TGF-β inhibits). (H3) Low-volume culture will reduce stress-associated cytokines (TIMP1, MCP1, CXCL1, IFNγ). (H4) Lowering surface tension (via DOPC) will impair development in low-volume cultures, supporting a role for surface tension; high-volume cultures will be less sensitive to surface tension changes. Outcomes supporting H1–H3 include quantitative improvements in morphometrics, normal morphogen dose–response, and reduced cytokine signals. H4 is supported if DOPC significantly reduces UB branching and nephron number in low-volume but not high-volume cultures.
reference_methodology:
Organ sources: E11.5 NMRI or CD1 mouse embryos. Right and left kidneys from the same embryo were dissected and randomly assigned to conventional or low-volume culture groups.

Conventional culture: Rudiments were placed on 5 mm pore-size polycarbonate filters at the bottom of a well insert in a six-well plate (Corning, Costar) or on top of a stainless steel Trowell grid in a 3.5 cm culture dish. Culture medium (KCM) was Eagle’s minimal essential medium with Earle’s salts and non-essential amino acids (GIBCO), 10% fetal bovine serum (Biochrom/Biosera), and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma). For some experiments, 1 nM TGF-β (Sigma T7039) or 100 ng/mL GDNF (Sigma G1777) were added.

Low-volume culture: Sterilized silicone rings (FlexiPERM Cone shape A, Greiner BioOne) were placed on 22622 mm coverslips (Menzel Gläser, Germany). Coverslips were cleaned in 5:1:1 H2O:H2O2:NH4OH (10 min, 70°C). Rudiments were positioned near the center of the ring. After pipetting, residual medium was removed and replaced with final KCM (70–200 µL), wetting the entire enclosed area. The surrounding dish was filled with PBS containing 1% penicillin/streptomycin. All cultures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2, with medium changes every 2 days.

Imaging: Time-lapse movies were acquired in an incubation chamber of a Zeiss Axiovert 200 microscope, imaging every 10–15 min. Phase-contrast images of living cultures were taken every 12 h using an Olympus IX50 microscope. NIH ImageJ 1.37v was used for time-lapse assembly and morphometric analysis.

Immunostaining and lectin: Rudiments were fixed in methanol at −20°C, washed in PBS (10 min), and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C in PBS: anti-laminin (1:100, Sigma L9393), anti-calbindin-D28k (1:100, Sigma C9848), anti-megalin (1:150), anti-WT1 (1:50, Dako M3561), anti-Pax2 (1:100, Covance PRB-276P), anti-E-cadherin (1:100, BD 610181). After ≥30 min PBS washes, secondary antibodies were applied overnight at 4°C: anti-rabbit IgG-TRITC (1:100, Sigma T6778), anti-mouse IgG-TRITC (1:100, Sigma T5393), anti-mouse IgG-FITC (1:100, Sigma F6257). For co-staining, solutions contained 1% milk powder in PBS and 10 ng/mL Dolichos biflorus-FITC lectin (Sigma L9142) with secondary antibodies. Samples were washed, mounted, and imaged by confocal microscopy (Leica TCS SP5). Serial 5 µm optical sections were acquired; FITC, TRITC, and DAPI emissions were collected sequentially.

Proliferation and apoptosis: BrdU (5-bromo-2-deoxyuridine) was added 4 h before fixation to a final concentration of 100 µM. Detection followed [26], with In Situ Cell Death Detection Kit, TMR red (Roche 12156792910) added with primary antibodies. After 30 min PBS washes, secondary antibodies were applied overnight at 4°C. After washes, 1 µg/mL DAPI (Sigma) was added for 20 min. Samples were washed and mounted.

Morphometrics: Ureteric bud tips and nephrons were counted manually. Area was defined and measured using ImageJ. For cytokine arrays, conditioned media from 0–2 d and 2–4 d were collected, diluted to 3 mL total, and analyzed using R&D Systems’ mouse cytokine array panel (40 cytokines), per manufacturer’s instructions. Experiments were performed in triplicate.

Surface tension: DOPC (1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine; Sigma P6354) was dispersed at 1 mg/mL in KCM by 30 min sonication on ice. Surface tension was measured by pendant drop (Young–Laplace) using a Contact Angle System OCA 30 (DataPhysics Instruments), calibrated with degassed water.

Ethics: Animals were bred and kept under UK Home Office guidance (Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act, 1986). Euthanasia was performed by trained staff under Schedule 1 methods. Ethical approval was granted by the University of Edinburgh.

title: A COMPARISON IN VITRO STUDY OF PERMEATION OF SELECTED DRUGS FROM LIPOPHILIC SOLUTIONS TROUGH HUMAN SKIN
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does a lipophilic vehicle (highly liquid paraffin) affect the permeation of model drugs with varying lipophilicity through HSE? (2) How do C_sat, K_sc/don, K_soebuffer/SC, Kp, and Jmax relate across drugs and vehicles? (3) Is permeation vehicle-insensitive for highly lipophilic steroids like testosterone?

Hypotheses: (H1) Hydrophilic drugs will show higher permeability from lipophilic vehicles than from aqueous vehicles due to favorable partitioning from the vehicle to SC. (H2) Lipophilic drugs will show lower permeability from lipophilic vehicles due to high affinity to the vehicle, reducing effective release and SC partitioning. (H3) Jmax will primarily depend on C_sat and correlate with drug lipophilicity (log K_oct/water). (H4) For highly lipophilic steroids (e.g., testosterone), permeation may be vehicle-insensitive because SC partitioning and viable epidermis diffusion dominate. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include higher Kp for hydrophilic drugs from paraffin, lower Kp for lipophilic drugs from paraffin, Jmax scaling with C_sat, and minimal Kp differences for TST between paraffin and buffer.
reference_methodology:
Skin and donors: Human skin from three donors was used. Immediately after excision, subcutaneous fat was removed. Skin was cut into 10×10 cm pieces, wrapped in aluminum foil, and stored at -26°C (max 6 months). At use, HSE was prepared by heat separation: 25 mm skin disks incubated in 60°C water bath for 90 s, then epidermis pelted off with forceps; HSE sheets were floated in water for 30 min before use. SC was isolated by trypsin digestion (0.15% trypsin in PBS, 24 h at 32°C; repeated as needed), washed three times with distilled water, freeze-dried, and stored in an exsiccator.

Vehicle and solubility: Highly liquid paraffin was used as the donor vehicle. Saturation solubility (C_sat) was determined by suspending excess drug in 10 ml paraffin (or 5 ml in some sections), stirring at 500 rpm, 32°C for 24 h; undissolved solids were removed by 0.2 µm PTFE filtration. Supernatants were diluted 1:10 with dichloromethane and analyzed by UV/VIS (Perkin Elmer Lambda 35) at drug-specific wavelengths: BA 228 nm, CAF 277 nm, FA 287 nm, TST 238 nm. Calibration curves were constructed to quantify C_sat.

Partition coefficients: K_sc/don was determined by incubating dried SC (donors 2 and 3) with 5 ml paraffin containing three drug concentrations (24 h, 32°C). After incubation, 2.5 ml supernatant was diluted to 25 ml with dichloromethane and analyzed by UV/VIS. The remaining drug in paraffin was used to compute K_sc/don. For K_soebuffer/SC, SC (donors 2 and 3) was incubated with 5 ml Soerensen phosphate buffer pH 7.4 containing three BA concentrations (24 h, 32°C); K_soebuffer/SC for TST, CAF, and FA were taken from literature. Blank SC-paraffin incubations were used to correct for endogenous testosterone in SC.

Permeation experiments: Franz diffusion cells (FDC) with diffusion area 1.767 cm² were used. HSE was mounted on a cellulose support membrane (pre-hydrated with buffer). Donor compartment: 500 µl paraffin with drug at 0.4 mg/ml (TST, FA, BA) or 0.1 mg/ml (CAF). Acceptor compartment: Soerensen phosphate buffer pH 7.4, stirred at 500 rpm. Temperature was maintained at 32°C. Samples of 0.4 ml were collected at intervals (10–29 h depending on drug), replaced with fresh buffer. Air bubbles were checked to avoid area reduction. No preservative was added to acceptor fluid. Quantification used validated HPLC methods with external standards: Testosterone (λ 250 nm; methanol/water 70/30; 1.2 ml/min; 5 min; RT 4.8±0.2 min), Caffeine (λ 262 nm; buffer pH 2.6/acetonitrile 90/10; 1.2 ml/min; 6 min; RT 5.08±0.2 min), Flufenamic acid (λ 284 nm; methanol/McIlvaine pH 2.2 80/20; 1.2 ml/min; 5 min; RT 3.1±0.2 min), Benzoic acid (λ 228 nm; buffer pH 6.5/methanol 95/5; 1.2 ml/min; 5 min; RT 3.5±0.03 min). Limits of detection/determination were reported (e.g., BA LOD 6.25 µg/ml; LOQ 12.5–100 µg/ml).

Analysis: Cumulative amount permeated per area vs time plots were constructed; lag time was defined as the x-intercept of the linear steady-state portion. Steady-state flux (J) was the slope of the linear region. Apparent permeability coefficient (Kp) was computed as J divided by donor concentration. Maximum flux (Jmax) was calculated as Kp × C_sat. Calculations were performed in Microsoft Excel 2003 and SigmaPlot 10.0. For inter-donor variability, analyses focused on skin 2 (used for both permeation and partitioning).

title: Histones H1° and H5 Share Common Epitopes with RNA Polymerase 11
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do H1° and H5 share epitopes with RNA polymerase II, and if so, where are these epitopes located within H1°? (2) Do the observed cross-reactions reflect structural homology consistent with known sequence similarities among VLR histones? (3) Could shared epitopes imply a common binding site on nucleosomes, potentially explaining H1°-mediated modulation of transcriptional accessibility?

Hypotheses: (a) Antiserum to Pol II will cross-react with H1° and H5, with strength paralleling their sequence homology; (b) Antisera to GH1° and GH5 will cross-react with Pol II subunit IIc; (c) Mapping with H1° fragments will localize the Pol II–recognized epitope to the junction between the globular and C-terminal domains; (d) Sequence analysis will reveal homologous regions between H1°/H5 and Pol IIc, supporting structural homology.

Support/refutation criteria: Strong cross-reaction of Pol II antiserum with H1° and weaker with H5 supports (a). Cross-reaction of GH1°/GH5 antisera with IIc supports (b). Fragment mapping showing epitope enrichment in the globular–C-terminal junction supports (c). Identification of homologous segments between H1°/H5 and IIc supports (d).
reference_methodology:
Protein sources and purification: RNA polymerase II was purified from calf thymus as previously described. Total histones were extracted from isolated nuclei of lamb thymus, beef liver, and chicken erythrocytes using 0.2 M H2SO4. H1° was extracted from whole beef liver with 5% perchloric acid and purified by ion exchange chromatography.

H1° fragmentation: H1° was cleaved at Met30 by cyanogen bromide: purified H1° (0.25 mg/ml) in 70% formic acid was incubated at room temperature under nitrogen with a 100-fold excess of cyanogen bromide for 1 day; reaction was stopped by water addition and lyophilization. N-bromosuccinimide cleavage targeted tyrosines 27, 52, and 57: equal volumes of purified H1° (0.7 mg/ml) in 0.9 N acetic acid and 200 mg/ml N-bromosuccinimide in 0.9 N acetic acid were incubated at room temperature for 5 min; reaction was stopped by electrophoresis sample buffer. Chymotrypsin cleavage targeted Phe92 and Phe106 and tyrosines: H1° (0.2 mg/ml) in 100 mM Tris-Cl, pH 6.8, 1 mM CaCl2, 5 mM mercaptoethanol, 10% glycerol was incubated at 37°C with 0.02 mg/ml chymotrypsin for 5 min; reaction was stopped by sample buffer and boiling. GH1° was prepared by limited trypsin digestion: H1° (1.2 mg/ml) in 1 M NaCl, 50 mM Tris-Cl, pH 8, was digested 1 h with trypsin (1/300 w/w); reaction was stopped by phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride and sample buffer.

Gel electrophoresis and transfer: Proteins were separated on 17.5% SDS-PAGE (optimized for histones and H1° fragments) or 5–17.5% gradient SDS-PAGE (optimized for Pol II subunits). Proteins were transferred to nitrocellulose; transfers were stained with Amido Black or Coomassie Blue or used without staining.

Antibodies and immunoblotting: Antiserum to calf thymus Pol II was elicited in New Zealand White rabbits. GH1° and GH5 antisera were prepared as previously described. Immunoblotting followed Howe and Hershey: transfers were blocked with 5% milk, incubated with Pol II, GH1°, or GH5 antiserum at 1:1000, followed by 125I-protein A and exposure on Kodak XAR film. Monospecific antisera were prepared by affinity purification: proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to diazophenylthioether (DPT) paper, localized with antiserum and 125I-protein A; antibody-containing bands were excised and used to purify antibodies from polyclonal serum.

Sequence analysis: Homologies among human H1°, chicken H5, rabbit H1.3, and yeast/Drosophila Pol IIc were determined using Beckman’s MicroGenie Sequence Analysis Program (1986) for complete sequences.

Controls and conditions: Pre-immune serum served as negative control. Core histones and other basic proteins (e.g., high mobility group proteins) from 0.2 M H2SO4 extracts did not bind antibody. Exposure times varied (e.g., 2–40 h) to visualize signals; autoradiograms were typically 3 days for peptide panels.

title: WP/19/226 Instruments of Debtstruction: A New Database of Interwar Debt
research_question: The paper asks: (1) How did interwar governments manage rollover risks when public debt was largely unsustainable? (2) How did the external public debt network’s structure and evolution contribute to the collapse of the international financial system in the early 1930s? The authors hypothesize that debt management mattered under imperfect commitment and segmented investor bases, and that network topology (interconnectedness, centrality, clustering) amplified shocks and propagated defaults. They further posit that instrument design (e.g., redemption options, sinking funds, tax incentives) and central bank exposure (fiscal dominance) influenced credibility and rollover outcomes. Evidence supporting these hypotheses would include non-stationary debt and weak fiscal responses (Bohn’s criterion), network metrics indicating increased interconnectedness and circular dependencies, and documented rollover strategies (e.g., conversions) that reprofiled maturities and reduced short-term service burdens. Evidence refuting them would include stationary debt with cointegration to primary balances, a centralized network with low clustering, and rollover strategies that failed to mitigate short-term service pressures.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: The primary source is the League of Nations’ Public Finance and Public Debt publications (1913–1946), supplemented by Money and Banking and Statistical Yearbooks for central bank balance sheets and exchange rates, Moody’s Analyses of Investment for instrument-level qualitative attributes, and national sources (budgets, yearbooks, manuals, bulletins). The authors document sources exhaustively in Appendix A and provide country-specific notes (e.g., France’s changing public debt perimeter; Germany’s reparations; Japan’s marks; Russia/USSR’s Lend-Lease exclusion).

Data construction: The IDD records amounts outstanding (local currency, USD, or gold equivalent) and instrument characteristics. Where the League’s sporadic reporting left gaps, the authors used inference and interpolation, and converted fiscal years to calendar years (end-December) to harmonize timing. Currency harmonization used Federal Reserve (1943) exchange rates; amounts were converted to USD and gold equivalents, with gold used as a universal reference given the period’s gold standard context. The database includes non-marketable instruments (e.g., advances, annuities) and excludes municipal and sub-central debts and guaranteed securities unless assumed by the central government.

Instrument taxonomy: Instruments are classified by promised cash flows: bonds (principal and coupons), perpetuals (consols/rentes), bills (discounted, short-term), credits (annual principal+interest, bilateral), advances (low/no interest, open-ended), accounts (demand/term deposits), annuities (annual budget payments), and other (e.g., arrears). Attributes include coupon rate (nominal, excluding premia), interest payable months, issuance and maturity dates, redemption (who can call, lottery/SF), grace period, sinking fund (Y/N/NA), taxability (Y/N/NA), and purpose (e.g., war, reconstruction, defense, economic development).

Sustainability tests: Following Bohn (1998), the authors test stationarity of debt and debt-to-revenue ratios (DF, ADF, PP, KPSS) and run Engle–Granger cointegration tests with fiscal series (Mauro et al., 2013; Mitchell, 1998). They estimate Bohn equations relating primary balance to lagged debt and controls. Robustness includes panel unit root tests and alternative currency conversions (USD vs gold). The analysis also examines debt-to-revenue ratios and their stationarity.

Network analysis: The external debt network is modeled as a dynamic, directed graph with nodes as countries and directed edges as outstanding debts (in gold equivalents). Metrics include in/out-degree (weighted by debt amounts), degree centrality, in/out-closeness (exposure/systemicity), betweenness (contagion), clustering (circular dependencies), and central point of dominance (centralization). The authors compute these over time and compare weighted vs unweighted measures. Appendix G provides formal definitions and formulas (e.g., weighted average maturity, remaining maturity, betweenness, clustering, central point of dominance).

title: Triazenolysis of Alkenes: Aza-version of Ozonolysis
field_subfield: Chemistry — Organic Synthesis and Mechanistic Chemistry
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can an aza-version of ozonolysis be realized to cleave alkenes into two C–N bonds via a [2+3] cycloaddition/rearrangement sequence? (2) What reaction conditions and additives enable efficient and selective rearrangement of the triazane intermediate? (3) What is the mechanistic role of Lewis acid catalysis (BH3) in lowering barriers and accelerating the process? (4) What is the substrate scope, including strained cyclic alkenes and potential acyclic systems?
