Hypotheses: (i) A triazadienium cation generated from a triazene will undergo [2+3] cycloaddition with an alkene to form a triazolium salt that reduces to an N–H triazane (Q). (ii) The triazane will rearrange via reverse cycloaddition to a diaza-Criegee zwitterion and an imine, yielding an aminohydrazine product that can be hydrogenated to a diamine. (iii) BH3, generated in situ from NaBH4 with I2 or BF3·Et2O, will act as a Lewis acid mediator, stabilizing charged intermediates and lowering the rearrangement barrier relative to a non-mediated pathway. (iv) Substrate scope will favor strained cyclic alkenes; acyclic alkenes may require further optimization.

Support/refutation criteria: High isolated yields of diamines under optimized conditions, solvent dependence consistent with BH3 stabilization, DFT showing lower barriers for BH3-mediated pathways, and successful transformations across diverse cyclic alkenes would support the hypotheses. Failure with non-strained acyclic alkenes and lack of BH3 dependence would nuance or refute the Lewis acid mediation claim.
reference_methodology:
General three-step sequence: Step 1 (generation of triazolium salt): Alkene 1 (2 eq) and triazene 2 (1 eq) are combined with KPF6 (2 eq) in acetone (0.033 M) at −78 °C under N2. tert-Butyl hypochlorite (tBuOCl, 1.1 eq) is added dropwise, and the mixture warms to room temperature overnight in the dark. The mixture is filtered (to remove KCl), washed with acetone, evaporated, and the residue is triturated with diethyl ether and ultrasound, then filtered and dried. Step 2 (reduction and rearrangement): NaBH4 (6 eq) in THF (0.1 M) is cooled to 0 °C. I2 (1 eq) is added and the solution is stirred 5 min (colorless). The triazolium salt 3 (1 eq) is added; the mixture is stirred 15–90 min at RT (TLC-monitored). The reaction is quenched with MeOH (1 ml), solvent is evaporated, and the residue is dissolved in MeOH (4 ml) for Step 3. Alternatively, BF3·Et2O (1 eq) can be used instead of I2. Step 3 (hydrogenation to diamine): The MeOH solution is degassed, Ni–Raney (40 mg per 0.1 mmol of 4) is added, and the flask is charged with H2 (1 atm). The mixture is stirred overnight at RT, filtered through Celite, and the product is purified by silica gel chromatography.

Optimization (Table 1): For norbornene 1a and triazene 2a, Step 2 was varied. NaBH4 in MeOH (0% yield) or THF (81% at RT then 90 °C) gave high yields; LiBH4 in THF (82%) was comparable; LiAlH4 in THF (32%) was less effective; PhSiH3/CsF in THF (0%) failed. Solvent screening showed only ethers effective: Et2O (61%) and dioxane (12%) were modest; toluene (0%) and DMF (0%) failed. Temperature: RT (77%) and 40 °C (1.5 h) were inferior to 90 °C (81%). Reducing NaBH4 to 3 eq (64%) lowered yield. Generating BH3 in situ via I2 (1 eq) at RT (85%) or BF3·Et2O (1 eq) (72%) increased yield and eliminated heating; even 0.2 eq I2 (81%) was effective.

Scope and scale-up: The sequence can be run one-pot without isolating intermediates. Diamines 5 are generally more stable than hydrazines 4 and are the focus of the scope. Examples include para-substituted N-aryl triazenes (Me, OMe, Cl, F, CF3) giving 5c–5f in ~50–80% yields; meta-substitution (5h) maintained yields; ortho substitution (5i) reduced yield to 32%. N-alkyl triazenes did not rearrange (SI). Cyclopropene 1g gave 5o in good yield; cyclopentene 1h gave 4p (Step 2) with hydrogenation challenges; indene 1i and acenaphthylene 1j gave 5q/r. Acyclic 1,1-diphenylethylene 1k gave 5s in 45%. Cyclobutenes 1l/m underwent ring expansion to 6 via 1,6-cyclization. Indole 1n underwent N–C2 cleavage to 7. 6–8-membered cyclic alkenes (cyclohexene 1o, dihydrodioxepine 1p, cyclooctene 1q) and styrene 1r failed under standard conditions.

DFT: Free energy profiles (Figure 3) were computed at bp86/def2SVP-D3(BJ) for geometries and M06-2X/def2tzvp-D3(THF) for energies. The non-mediated rearrangement of triazane 9 to diaza-Criegee/imine 10 has ΔG‡ = 36.6 kcal/mol and is endergonic; BH3-mediated conversion of 9 to 11 and rearrangement to 12 has ΔG‡ = 25.7 kcal/mol and is exergonic. BH3 stabilizes the charged transition state and product, consistent with experimental acceleration in THF and with I2/BF3·Et2O additives.

Characterization and data: Experimental and characterization data are in the SI. X-ray crystallographic data for 5e·2HCl (CCDC 2290229) and 5g·2HCl (CCDC 2290228) are deposited.

title: A Guided Web-Based Intervention for Convicted Individuals Who Sexually Abused Children and Individuals Who Consumed Child Sexual Exploitation Material Under Community Supervision: A Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial Protocol
research_question:
Primary research questions: (1) Does a guided web-based intervention for ISAC/ICCSEM under CS reduce dynamic risk factors (as measured by the Index of Desistance, IoD) and official recidivism over 5 years compared with a placebo web-based condition? (2) Do individual modules produce targeted reductions in their respective risk domains? (3) Is the intervention cost-beneficial relative to the placebo condition?

Hypotheses: (a) Participants in the web-based intervention will show significantly greater reductions in self-reported dynamic risk factors (IoD) and fewer officially recorded re-offenses over 5 years than the placebo group, controlling for baseline risk levels and randomization strata. (b) Each module will yield pre–post improvements in its targeted risk factors: motivation module (increased motivation to change), supervision module (reduced negative social influences and resistance to rules; increased interest in emotionally intimate adult relationships), emotion management module (reduced impulsivity and dysfunctional coping), problem-solving module (increased rational problem-solving), offense-supportive attitudes module (reduced agreement with cognitive distortions), and sexuality module (reduced emotional congruence with children, sexual preoccupation, and sexual fantasies with children). (c) The intervention will yield a positive net economic benefit, with tangible (e.g., reduced victim- and offender-related costs) and intangible benefits outweighing intervention costs. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include statistically significant between-group differences in IoD and recidivism, module-specific pre–post improvements with adjusted p-values, and NB > 0 with benefit-cost ratio > 1.00.
reference_methodology:
Design: Parallel-group, placebo-controlled, randomized, add-on trial with two arms: (1) guided web-based intervention (experimental) and (2) guided web-based placebo (control). Both arms are add-on to CS as usual (CSaU), which includes court-ordered f2f contacts with supervision officers (SOs), external psychotherapeutic/medical treatment (if ordered), and medical care.

Participants: Male and female offenders under CS (§§56, 57, 68 ff. StGB) for child abuse (§§176, 176a, 176b StGB) or child sexual exploitation material use (§184b StGB), aged ≥18 years. Inclusion requires current CS for at least one qualifying offense. Exclusion: probation period <6 months at enrollment; no access to a PC/tablet/smartphone; severe acute psychiatric disorder (e.g., acute psychosis); severe cerebro-organic disorder; severe cognitive impairment; withdrawal of consent; no written consent.

Assessments: Baseline and follow-up measures include: SSQ-P (participant demographics, lifestyle, treatment/offending history); SSQ-SO (SO’s reports on living conditions, offending/clinical history, index offense); SSQ-rSO (repeated SO reports during probation); SSQ-CF (court file coding to confirm inclusion and populate Static-99 for ISAC or modified Static-99 for ICCSEM); PHQ-D (screening for mental disorders); SSPI-2 (pedophilic interests); ICD-11-Sexuality-Screener (screening for sexual dysfunction/gender dysphoria/paraphilic disorder; not diagnostic).

Intervention and placebo: Both arms consist of six modules (four sessions/module; ~60 minutes/session), completed over 24 weeks (one session/week). Sessions unlock after 1 week and completion of guided tasks. Experimental modules target empirically supported dynamic risk factors using RNR-aligned CBT techniques (motivational interviewing, DBT/ACT skills, PST, cognitive restructuring). Placebo modules cover unrelated topics (e.g., healthy nutrition, physical activity, sleep) with non-sustained exercises. Coach support is identical in both arms; feedback is manualized.

Randomization and blinding: 1:1 allocation via centrally generated lists (SecuTrial), stratified by offense type (ISAC vs ICCSEM), CS type (§§56,57 vs §§68 ff), external treatment (yes/no), and baseline risk (Static-99 or modified Static-99). Blinding of SOs and coaches is not feasible; participants, DSMB, and analysts are blinded until end of analysis.

Adherence and monitoring: Participants receive usernames/passwords; initial passwords are changed post-login. Sessions include psycho-education, exercises (self-guided with automated feedback; coach-guided with manualized feedback), in-app messaging with SO/coach, gamified rewards (virtual awards/coins; up to €120 payout), and a personalized first-aid kit. Duration per lesson is recorded to assess attention; coach-guided tasks ensure engagement. SOs and coaches monitor progress; reminders are sent if sessions are delayed.

Outcomes: Primary—(1) officially recorded re-offenses at 5-year follow-up; (2) IoD (pre–post change) as composite of Acute-2007-SR, CTE (module-specific changes), and CMC (offense-related behaviors). Secondary—validated questionnaires at pre/post each module: CVTRQ (treatment readiness), RCQ-D (readiness to change), OQMPR (psychological reactance), F-SozU K-7 (social support), UCLA (loneliness), BMS (cognitive distortions), SPSI-R (problem-solving styles), DERS-impulsivity (emotion regulation), NARQ (negative affect repair), BIS-15 (impulsivity), CUSI (sex as coping), HBI-19 (hypersexuality), EKK-R (emotional congruence with children), SSIC-Scale (self-efficacy to modify sexual interest in children), ESIQ (explicit sexual interest), SOI-R Item 2a (desire for sexual activity with children). Additional measures: WAI-SR (therapeutic alliance), SBV-R (pressure of pain), WHO-5 (well-being), ATQ (technology acceptance), MRQ (session-level mood/risk), QNP (reasons for non-participation).

Sample size and power: Assuming 50% consent among 1,165 eligible (N=582), 26.4% dropout, N=428 completers (214 per arm). With α=0.05 and 80% power, the trial is powered to detect small effects (d=0.27).

Statistical analysis: Primary IoD analyzed via Gaussian linear mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with treatment, time (six post-module timepoints), treatment-by-time interaction, and randomization strata as factors; baseline IoD as covariate; unstructured covariance; least squares mean changes with 95% CIs; between-group differences with 95% CIs and p-values; Intention-to-Treat (ITT) population (≥1 module completed). Recidivism analyzed via Cox proportional hazards with treatment, number of completed modules, and randomization strata; baseline risk included. Module-level pre–post changes via Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni-Holm correction. Economic evaluation: NB = tangible + intangible benefits − intervention costs; benefit-cost ratio; 5-year horizon; sensitivity analyses. Stopping rules: trial stops at 12 months if experimental arm shows significantly higher risk (main outcome or events), higher proportion of significant events, or increased proportion of high-risk subjects vs baseline.

title: Design and Manufacture of a Head-Neck Movement Robot using 3-D Printing Technology of PLA Material and Implementing BCI Sensors
field_subfield: Mechanical Engineering — Robotics; Biomedical Engineering — Assistive Devices
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a 3-RRS parallel manipulator 3D-printed from PLA be designed and fabricated to realize six primary head–neck movements (rotation, flexion/extension, lateral flexion) with acceptable deformation and stress under realistic loads? (2) Does an EEG-based BCI pipeline (OpenBCI 16 channels, SVM classifier) enable discrimination of the six movement classes and identification of responsive electrode locations? (3) Among candidate materials (316L steel, ABS, PLA), which balances structural integrity, deformation, and wearability for a wearable neck brace?

Hypotheses: (H1) PLA will provide sufficient structural integrity under a 5 N load, with deformation and Von Mises stress below yield limits, enabling a lightweight, low-cost brace. (H2) EEG signals will contain discriminative features across six movement classes, with a subset of electrodes contributing most to classification. (H3) The 3-RRS mechanism will achieve clinically relevant ranges (rotation ±40°, flexion/extension ±20°, lateral flexion ±15°) using three actuators.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if FEM shows deformation and stress below yield; H2 is supported if SVM classification separates classes and identifies responsive electrodes; H3 is supported if kinematic simulations and tests achieve the stated ranges.
reference_methodology:
Design and kinematics: The device is a 3-RRS parallel manipulator with three revolute–spherical limbs connecting a fixed base to a moving platform. Revolute joints allow rotation about a single axis; spherical joints allow rotation about three axes. CAD was created in SolidWorks 2019, and motion analysis was performed to verify kinematic feasibility and workspace. A MATLAB package was used to verify forward/inverse kinematics, velocity analysis, and workspace/range of motion.

3D printing and materials: FDM printing used a Creality Ender-3 Pro (dimensions 220×220×250 mm; 0.4 mm nozzle; 1.75 mm filament; ±0.01 mm precision; max extruder 250°C; build plate 100°C; SD card/LCD). CR-PLA 1.75 mm filament (density 1.24 g/cm³; print temperature 190–220°C) was used. The total device weight is reported as 1.8 kg. Material selection compared 316L stainless steel, ABS, and PLA via FEM.

FEM simulations: ANSYS R23.1 performed static structural analyses under a 5 N load applied at the head triangle. Outputs included total deformation and equivalent Von Mises stress. Reported material properties (Table 2): 316L steel (tensile yield 290 MPa; ultimate 560 MPa; shear 370 MPa; density 8 g/cm³; Poisson’s 0.28; modulus 193 GPa); ABS (tensile yield 2–77 MPa; ultimate 40 MPa; shear 24.63 MPa; density 1.04 g/cm³; Poisson’s 0.37; modulus 0.778–21.2 GPa); PLA (tensile yield 8–103 MPa; ultimate 65 MPa; shear 26.74 MPa; density 1.24 g/cm³; Poisson’s 0.39; modulus 2.96–3.6 GPa). Deformation and stress distributions were visualized (Figures 9–12; 13–14 for PLA stress).

Actuation and control: Three high-torque digital servos (DCS16942CHV; 50 kg·cm torque; 6.0 V; 0.18 s/60°; 180° limit; 60×30.2×60.5 mm; 186±1 g) were driven by an Arduino Uno R3 (ATmega328P; 14 I/O, 6 PWM; 6 analog inputs; 16 MHz crystal; USB; power; ICSP; reset). The servos implement the six neck movements.

EEG acquisition and processing: OpenBCI Cyton+Daisy (16 channels) recorded EEG with wet electrodes. Sampling was 125 samples/s. The acquisition protocol involved six trials, each comprising six movement classes (left/right rotation, up/down flexion/extension, left/right lateral flexion). Signals were filtered using a Savitzky–Golay filter. Features were extracted and normalized; SVM classification used an 80/20 train/test split. Confusion matrices were computed. The study reports that 10/16 electrodes were most responsive to movement classes. No details on feature types, hyperparameters, or cross-validation are provided.

Ethics and human subjects: Not reported. No human trials are described.

title: Design on Face Recognition System with Privacy Preservation Based on Homomorphic Encryption
field_subfield: Computer Science — Computer Vision and Cryptography
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a face recognition system that operates entirely in ciphertext using CKKS (SEAL) achieve competitive accuracy relative to plaintext FaceNet systems while preserving privacy? (2) What is the practical latency of feature processing, encryption, and ciphertext comparison on commodity hardware? (3) How robust is the system to pose variations and occlusions in real-world image conditions?

Hypotheses: (H1) CKKS-based ciphertext operations on FaceNet embeddings will yield recognition accuracy comparable to plaintext FaceNet on standard benchmarks (e.g., LFW), with a threshold-based decision rule in the embedding space. (H2) The total end-to-end latency for ciphertext recognition will be acceptable for practical deployment, with feature processing dominating total time. (H3) The system will remain effective within moderate pose biases (≤30 degrees) and small occlusions, though performance will degrade with larger pose deviations.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if accuracy on LFW is within a small margin (≤2.3%) of recent plaintext systems. H2 is supported if total time per comparison is on the order of seconds and processing time constitutes the majority. H3 is supported if multi-person tests show clear separation of same- vs different-person distances and if tests indicate effectiveness up to 30 degrees of pose bias.
reference_methodology:
Implementation environment: Python 3.6 with PyCharm on Windows 10 Home, running on a Lenovo 310S-14IKB laptop (Intel i5 7200U 2.4 GHz, 4 GB RAM). The system uses the SEAL library (CKKS scheme) for homomorphic encryption and FaceNet for feature extraction and training.

Data: FaceNet training uses the 20180402-114759 dataset derived from VGGFace2. The authors tested both 20180402-114759 and 20180408-102900 (CASIA-WebFace-derived) and selected 20180402-114759 based on higher recognition accuracy. Recognition evaluation uses the LFW dataset. For multi-person reliability testing, 20 images from 10 persons were used, with two images per person.

Pipeline: (1) Client extracts face features using FaceNet, normalizes embeddings to unit norm (||f(x)||2 = 1), and encrypts them with CKKS (SEAL). (2) Server performs ciphertext computations (e.g., distance comparisons) and returns encrypted results. (3) Client interprets results without decrypting features. The system relies on order-preserving properties of CKKS to compare distances in ciphertext.

Evaluation metrics and thresholds: Recognition uses Euclidean distance in the 128D embedding space. A threshold of 0.7 is used to classify pairs: distances ≤0.7 indicate same-person; >0.7 indicate different-person. For multi-person tests, average judgment values are reported for same- vs different-person pairs. Efficiency is measured as: t1 (processing time per image), t2 (encryption time per feature), t3 (ciphertext comparison time), and total time tall = t1 + t2 + t3.

Experimental design: LFW accuracy is measured across 820 tests with 40 persons, varying the threshold to select 0.7 as optimal. Multi-person reliability tests use 20 images from 10 persons, comparing all pairs under the 0.7 threshold. Efficiency tests include: (a) processing time distribution for 120 images (20 sets × 2 images per set), (b) encryption time for 20 feature vectors, and (c) ciphertext comparison time for 20 groups of ciphertexts. Pose robustness is assessed qualitatively, with the authors reporting effectiveness within 30 degrees of face bias and noting effectiveness up to 90 degrees in a separate test scenario.

Analysis: Accuracy is reported as a percentage on LFW. Time distributions are summarized via averages and ranges. No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or random seed settings are reported. Details on FaceNet training hyperparameters, CKKS parameters (moduli, scaling factors, rescaling steps), batching, and security levels are not provided.

title: Analysis of single nucleotide variants of HFE gene and association to survival in The Cancer Genome Atlas GBM data
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are HFE SNVs (including H63D and C282Y) enriched in TCGA GBM blood normals compared to population controls? (2) Do H63D and/or C282Y genotypes associate with overall survival in GBM, and are these associations gender-specific? (3) Is 1-year survival status associated with H63D/C282Y? (4) Does HFE genotype correlate with HFE gene expression, and is high HFE expression associated with poorer survival?

Hypotheses: (H1) H63D and C282Y are enriched in GBM NB samples relative to 1000Genomes. (H2) H63D/C282Y carriers have poorer overall survival than WT, potentially with gender-specific effects (e.g., worse outcomes for male H63D and female C282Y carriers). (H3) 1-year survival is reduced among H63D/C282Y carriers. (H4) HFE expression is higher in carriers and predicts poorer survival; genotype influences expression levels.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported by higher genotype frequencies in NB with significant exact binomial tests. H2/H3 are supported if Kaplan–Meier curves and Fisher tests show significant survival differences; otherwise refuted. H4 is supported if t-tests show genotype–expression differences and high expression predicts poorer survival; otherwise refuted.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: TCGA GBM primary tumor (TP) and blood normal (NB) samples, accessed via the TCGA data portal and NCI Cancer Genomics Hub (CGHub). Due to lack of VCF/MAF files in the portal, whole genome BAMs were downloaded using GeneTorrent and processed with GTFuse to extract HFE regions. Variant calling followed GATK best practices. Population allele/genotype frequencies were obtained from UCSC Table Browser (dbSNP Build 142) and 1000Genomes VCF via tabix. Clinical data (gender, age, race, ethnicity, histology, survival, outcomes) were downloaded from the TCGA portal. Samples were linked by TCGA IDs.

Cohort selection: Caucasian-only analyses were performed because HFE variants are most prevalent in Caucasians. For SNV and genotype analyses, 340 TP samples were available; 11 duplicates were removed, yielding 329 TP samples with SNVs. Clinical data were available for 511 patients; the merged TP+clinical dataset included 296 TP samples: 264 Caucasian, 6 Asian, 18 Black, and 8 unknown. NB genotype data were available for 332 samples; 291 had both genotype and clinical data: 261 Caucasian, 5 Asian, 18 Black, and 7 unknown. Age in TP ranged 21–89 years; median age was 61 (male) and 63 (female). Two NB–TP pairs showed discordant genotypes (e.g., NB C282Y heterozygote vs TP WT or homozygote).

Statistical analysis: Genotype frequencies in NB were compared to 1000Genomes using exact binomial tests with 95% CIs. Associations between survival and HFE genotype, gender, and 1-year survival status were tested using Fisher’s exact test. Kaplan–Meier curves assessed overall survival by genotype and gender; log-rank tests provided p-values. Two-sample t-tests compared HFE expression levels across genotypes. Analyses were conducted in R 3.2.1 with alpha = 0.05. Site-specific analyses used Henry Ford Hospital samples (n = 100) to mitigate regional confounding.

Outcome measures: Primary outcomes were overall survival and 1-year survival status. Secondary outcomes included genotype–expression associations and enrichment of HFE SNVs in NB vs population controls. HFE expression was categorized as high (>50%) vs low (<50%) using PROGgeneV2 thresholds.

Ethics: Retrospective analysis of publicly available data; no IRB details reported.

title: Detection of Cryptosporidium in stool samples of immunocompromised patients
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the intestinal parasitic profile among immunocompromised patients in this clinical setting? (2) How accurate is the ImmunoCard STAT ICT for detecting Cryptosporidium spp. compared with PCR as the gold standard?

Hypotheses: (a) PCR will outperform ICT and microscopy in sensitivity for detecting Cryptosporidium, given its molecular sensitivity and ability to detect low burdens; (b) Cryptosporidium will be a common enteric pathogen in immunocompromised patients, with species predominantly C. parvum and C. hominis; (c) ICT will show lower sensitivity than PCR, potentially limiting its utility in low-burden settings. Supportive outcomes would include higher PCR-positive counts than ICT/microscopy, identification of C. parvum/C. hominis by sequencing, and ICT sensitivity below PCR. Refutation would involve ICT matching or exceeding PCR sensitivity and/or absence of Cryptosporidium in the cohort.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Analytical diagnostic accuracy study conducted in the Department of Microbiology at a tertiary care hospital (October 2013–June 2015), in collaboration with Pediatrics and Medicine. Institutional Research and Ethics Committee approval was obtained. Written informed consent was collected from all participants.

Participants: Two groups were enrolled. Group I (study): immunocompromised patients (n=73), including HIV seropositive (n=21), transplant recipients (n=16), long-term steroid users (n=14), malignancy patients on chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy (n=18), and primary immunodeficiency (n=4). Group II (control): non-immunocompromised individuals (n=73) attending outpatient services for reasons other than gastrointestinal illness and not admitted. Groups were age- and gender-matched. Exclusion: individuals on antimicrobials within one week prior to sampling.

Sampling: A total of 146 nonduplicate stool samples were collected. For OPD attendees, one sample per person was collected; for admitted patients, multiple samples were collected. The number of patients included on OPD basis was 100 (68.4%), and 46 (31.5%) were admitted.

Demographics: Among the 146 participants, the majority were aged 21–30 years (30%). The youngest was 11 months. Mean age was 36.6 years (range 11 months to 83 years). Six children were included; two were HIV-seropositive, two had primary immunodeficiency, one had celiac disease, and one had atopic dermatitis with Grade I protein-energy malnutrition.

Diagnostic procedures: Microscopy was performed using saline and iodine wet mounts after concentration by Sheather’s sucrose floatation technique, with modified acid-fast staining using 1% concentrated sulfuric acid. ICT used the ImmunoCard STAT Crypto/Giardia rapid assay (Meridian Bioscience, Europe) for qualitative detection of Cryptosporidium and Giardia intestinalis antigens in aqueous fecal extracts, following manufacturer instructions. DNA extraction employed the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit per manufacturer’s protocol.

PCR: Conventional PCR was performed on an Eppendorf Mastercycler gradient thermocycler. The Cryptosporidium genus was targeted using 18S rRNA gene primers: Forward 5'AGTGACAAGAAATAACAATACAGG3' and Reverse 5'CCTGCTTTAAGCACTCTAATTTTC3'. Reaction volume was 25 µl, with primers at 12.6 pmol each and 4 µl of DNA. Cycling conditions: 96°C for 2 min; 35 cycles of 94°C for 30 s, 58°C for 30 s, 72°C for 30 s; final extension 72°C for 8 min. Amplicon size was 298 bp. Post-amplification analysis used 1.5% agarose gel electrophoresis in 25× TBE buffer, stained with ethidium bromide. Positive amplicons were sequenced using the ABI BigDye terminator method (BioServe Biotechnologies, India), and species identification was performed via BLASTN (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast).

Analysis: Data were summarized as frequencies and distributions. PCR was designated as the gold standard for diagnostic accuracy assessment. No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or randomization/blinding procedures were reported.

title: MULTIPLE IMPUTATION: STEP BY STEP 0 Multiple Imputation of Missing Data in Longitudinal Organizational Research: A Stepby-Step Guide
field_subfield: Psychology — Organizational/Occupational Psychology; Methodology — Missing Data
research_question: The article’s central aim is to guide researchers in applying MI to longitudinal organizational data, not to test a single hypothesis. It addresses the following practical questions: (1) How to specify imputation models that reflect longitudinal dependencies and intended analyses (e.g., mediation, LCM) while preserving flexibility? (2) How to choose between wide-format (model-agnostic) and long-format (model-based) MI strategies for balanced designs? (3) How to extend MI to item-level data and second-order LCMs? (4) What auxiliary variables to include to strengthen MAR plausibility? (5) How to select the number of imputations and assess convergence? (6) How to analyze and pool results (including fit indices) under MI? The authors provide worked examples and recommendations rather than formal hypotheses. Outcomes that support the guidance include successful convergence of the imputation algorithm, plausible auxiliary variable inclusion (e.g., gender associated with negative affect), and coherent substantive results (e.g., significant indirect effects in mediation; acceptable LCM fits). Outcomes that would refute the guidance would include poor convergence, implausible auxiliary variable associations, or analyses that contradict substantive theory despite appropriate MI; such cases would motivate sensitivity analyses or alternative MI specifications.
reference_methodology:
Design and data: The example dataset derives from a German diary study (2019–2020) of schoolteachers (Hesse). After excluding seven participants (six incomplete pre-diary questionnaire; one different federal state), N=179 remained (female 80.4%; age M=40.24, SD=9.51). Diary prompts occurred three times daily (morning 05:00–10:30, afternoon 15:00–18:15, evening 20:30–23:30) over five days (Wednesday morning through Sunday evening). Constructs: sleep quality (morning, single item; 1–5 Likert), vitality (noon, three items; 1–5 Likert), negative affect (evening, three items; 1–5 Likert). For examples, the authors used: Example 1 (day 1 only); Example 2 (five days, one indicator per construct); Example 3 (five days, three items per construct). Pre-diary questionnaire included gender and age (no missingness).

Missingness: Across 2,685 diary entries, 306 were missing (11.3%). Per-day missingness: sleep quality 5.6%–19.6% (10–35 missing), vitality 7.3%–18.4% (13–29 missing), negative affect 6.7%–24.0% (12–43 missing). Patterns (Example 1): 123 participants had all variables observed; 22 had missing sleep quality only; 14 had missing negative affect only; missing vitality or multiple variables were rare.

Auxiliary variables: Gender and age were examined for associations with observed values and missingness. Gender showed weak positive association with negative affect; age showed no meaningful associations. Gender differed between missing and observed groups for some variables (Figure 2), supporting its inclusion as an auxiliary variable.

Imputation: FCS via R package mice was used. Example 1: three submodels (one per target variable) with all other variables (including gender, age) as predictors; 100 imputations (100 iterations × 20 cycles); convergence assessed via mice diagnostics (excellent). Example 2: wide-format MI (17 variables: gender, age, 15 repeated measures) with 15 submodels (each repeated measure predicted by all others and time-stable variables); 100 imputations; convergence checked. Long-format MI (five variables: gender, age, sleep quality, vitality, negative affect, plus person/time indicators) with multilevel submodels for time-varying variables (fixed and random effects of time); 100 imputations. Example 3: wide-format MI at the item level (37 variables: gender, age, five repeated measures for sleep quality [1 item], vitality [3 items], negative affect [3 items]); 35 submodels (one per item with missingness), including correlated residuals over time; 100 imputations.

Analysis and pooling: Analyses were conducted separately on each imputed dataset and pooled using Rubin’s rules. Example 1: mediation via semTools; indirect effect computed per dataset and pooled. Example 2: LCM for negative affect via semTools; pooled fit indices (χ², RMSEA, SRMR) computed using D3 pooling. Example 3: second-order LCM for vitality/negative affect with metric constraints on first-order factors and time-invariant loadings; pooled estimates and fit indices reported. Software: mice (imputation), semTools (analysis/pooling), mitml (as noted in software section).

title: Comparison of Real-Time DSP-Based Edge Detection Techniques for License Plate Detection
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Among Canny-Deriche-FGL, Haar (Daubechies-1), Daubechies-4, and Sobel, which edge detection algorithm achieves the best real-time performance (per-image edge and LP detection times) and LP detection success on a TI C64plus DSP? (2) How does the addition of a sharpening filter affect speed and detection success, and what are the trade-offs in false positives? (3) Can DSP-specific optimizations (cache, assembly, and C code) enable all tested edge detectors to meet <40 ms/frame requirements while maintaining high detection success?

Hypotheses: (H1) Wavelet-based edge detectors (Haar/Daubechies-1 and Daubechies-4) will outperform Sobel in speed and/or detection success on a DSP due to their computational efficiency and suitability for embedded architectures. (H2) Canny-Deriche-FGL, while accurate, will be slower than wavelet/Sobel on this DSP without further optimization. (H3) Sharpening will modestly improve detection success but increase false positives, necessitating thresholding and rectangle filtering to maintain accuracy. Support for H1 would be demonstrated by lower per-image edge/LP detection times and higher detection success for wavelets relative to Sobel. Support for H2 would be shown by significantly higher per-image times for Canny-Deriche-FGL. Support for H3 would be indicated by small accuracy gains with sharpening and an explicit increase in false positives.
reference_methodology:
Hardware and tools: A Texas Instruments C64plus DSP (fixed-point, enhanced VLIW architecture) with a minimum clock speed of 600 MHz and 1 MB RAM was used. Code Composer Studio (CCS) version 3.3 was employed for development and debugging. A JTAG interface debugger connected the DSP to a Windows host PC and monitor. The exact DSP host board details were not provided.

Dataset: 45,032 UK images at 768×288 resolution were provided by CitySync Ltd. The dataset includes images with both flat (weak) and sharp edges due to varying lighting conditions. The abstract reports 45,032 images; Table II lists 45,035 images for some metrics, indicating a discrepancy.

Pipeline: (1) Normalization: a threshold based on the difference between maximum and minimum intensity levels was applied to address varying lighting. (2) Optional sharpening: a standard 3×3 sharpening kernel was applied to enhance flat edges. (3) Edge detection: four detectors were tested—Sobel (3×3 standard mask), Canny-Deriche-FGL (optimized Canny variant), Haar wavelet (Daubechies-1), and Daubechies-4 wavelet. For wavelets, a 1D kernel was applied to rows and columns to decompose into horizontal (Eh) and vertical (Ev) edges; the absolute sum |E(r,c)| = |Eh| + |Ev| formed the edge image. (4) Post-processing: contrast stretching and a variable threshold were used to suppress noise and strengthen edges. (5) Adding edges back: the thresholded edges were added to the original grayscale image. (6) Connected Component Analysis (CCA): CCA labeled connected regions to identify potential rectangles. (7) Rectangle filtering: rectangles were filtered against LP characteristics (e.g., resolution, pixel counts, edge counts) to select the best candidate.

Optimizations: DSP memory optimization (L1/L2 cache architecture; application/procedure-level cache analysis; elimination of conflict misses), linear assembly optimization (compiler-generated assembly), and C code optimization (loop unrolling, vectorization, and other standard techniques) were applied. The authors note that Canny-Deriche-FGL was not fully optimized as per [5], contributing to its slower performance.

Evaluation metrics: Per-image edge detection time (ms), per-image LP detection time (ms), and LP detection success rate (%). Sharpening was evaluated both with and without. The study emphasizes real-time performance (<40 ms per frame).

title: A robust multi-task Representation Learning methodology for sustainable management of Radio Access Networks
field_subfield: Computer Science — Networking/Telecommunications (Wireless Networks, Representation Learning, Reinforcement Learning)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a hybrid SOM-TCAN framework provide accurate, scalable traffic forecasting across BS clusters in a HAPS-integrated RAN? (2) Does TCAN outperform TCN and LSTM for forecasting BS traffic? (3) Does SOM-TCAN reduce model count and variance in errors relative to per-series LSTM baselines? (4) Can DRL be effectively applied to optimize WFQ weights within HAPS using forecasted traffic priorities?

Hypotheses: (H1) SOM clustering will identify compact, meaningful traffic regimes, enabling fewer forecasting models with comparable or improved accuracy. (H2) TCAN will achieve lower MSE/RMSE/MAE than TCN and LSTM due to its dilated convolutions and attention. (H3) SOM-TCAN will reduce variance in errors and model count versus per-series LSTM. (H4) A DRL-WFQ agent trained on forecasted priorities can learn WFQ weights that improve queue stability, delay adherence, and throughput. Outcomes supporting H1–H3 include lower aggregate errors and fewer models; H4 is supported conceptually by the defined state/action/reward design but remains untested empirically in this work.
reference_methodology:
Data: 5G network traffic demand (bits) from a major Italian MNO in Milan, covering 112 BSs (16 clusters × 7 BSs) with 1,420 hourly observations per BS over approximately two months (April 1–May 30, 2020). Traffic zones include Business, Rho, San Siro, FS (Milan Central Train Station), and Residential. Spatial distribution was visualized (Figure 3.1). Statistical analyses included cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) (Figure 3.2), hourly/daily averages (Figure 3.3), and weekday/weekend patterns (Figure 3.4).

Preprocessing: Min–max normalization to [0,1]. SOM clustering used a 4×4 grid with learning rate α=0.05, neighborhood σ=0.3, and training length T=50,000 steps. SOM converged to 8 winning neurons (Table 4.1; Figure 4.3). Neuron (2,1) captured a single high-traffic BS (mean 68.90 Gbits, SD 43.03); neuron (0,1) captured two low-traffic BSs (mean 1.27 Gbits, SD 0.76). Trustworthiness and neighborhood preservation were computed for k=2–5 (Table 4.2): e.g., k=5 yielded trustworthiness 0.882 and neighborhood preservation 0.90.

Forecasting: TCAN architecture used causal dilated convolutions with kernel size 2 and residual blocks; attention (Bahdanau) was applied after TCN outputs to weight relevant time steps. Dilation sequences were tied to look-back length (Table 5.2): e.g., look-back 24 used [1,2,4,8,16] with 5 residual blocks. Look-back was selected by minimizing MSE (Figure 5.1), with 24 chosen as optimal. TCAN was trained on SOM neuron weights (85% training/15% validation) and evaluated on the corresponding BS time series. Metrics: MSE, RMSE, MAE, MARE (Equations 5.1–5.4). Baseline: per-series LSTM trained on 60% of each time series and tested on 40% (Figure 4.5). TCN and LSTM baselines were also evaluated for comparison.

Evaluation: Aggregate metrics across 8 SOM neurons were reported for TCAN, TCN, and LSTM (Table 5.3). Scatter plots assessed alignment of predictions with actuals (Figure 5.4). Boxplots compared distributions of MSE per neuron and across clusters (Figures 5.2–5.6). No random seeds, optimizer settings, or detailed hyperparameters for TCN/LSTM are reported. No statistical significance tests are provided. Ethics/IRB: not discussed.

title: A Clinical Study of Autologous Bone Marrow Mononuclear Cells for Cerebral Palsy Patients: A New Frontier
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Is intrathecal autologous bone marrow mononuclear cell transplantation combined with neurorehabilitation feasible and safe in CP patients over 6 months? (2) Does the intervention produce clinically meaningful improvements in motor, speech, cognitive, and tone outcomes across CP subtypes? (3) Do metabolic changes on PET-CT correlate with clinical improvements?

Hypotheses: (H1) The combined intervention is safe with acceptable adverse events. (H2) A majority of CP patients will show improvement in predefined functional domains at 6 months. (H3) Improvements will be significant in diplegic and quadriplegic subgroups by McNemar’s test. (H4) PET-CT will demonstrate increased glucose metabolism in brain regions corresponding to clinical gains. Support for H1 would be low rates of serious adverse events and resolution of minor events. Support for H2 would be high proportions of patients achieving mild-to-major improvements. Support for H3 would be statistically significant McNemar’s test results for key symptoms in diplegic and quadriplegic groups. Support for H4 would be increased 18-FDG uptake in frontal, temporal, parietal, basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum correlating with clinical domains (speech, cognition, motor control, balance).
reference_methodology:
Design: Open-label, nonrandomized, single-center clinical study conducted at one hospital from August 2010 to August 2013. Primary aim: evaluate efficacy over 6 months; secondary aim: assess effects by CP subtype. No placebo or rehabilitation-alone control group.

Participants: N=40 CP patients (26 males, 14 females), age 17 months–22 years. Subtypes: diplegic (n=11), quadriplegic (n=23), miscellaneous (n=6; 3 dystonic, 2 athetoid, 1 ataxic). Inclusion: diagnosed CP of any type; age >12 months. Exclusion: acute infections (HIV/HBV/HCV), malignancies, bleeding tendencies, pneumonia, renal failure, severe liver dysfunction, severe anemia (Hb <8 g/dL), bone marrow disorders, intracranial space-occupying lesions, and other acute medical conditions (respiratory infection, pyrexia).

Ethics and registration: Conducted per the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki; approved by the Institutional Committee for Stem Cell Research and Therapy (IC-SCRT) under ICMR guidelines; registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01978821). Written informed consent obtained from adults and parents; consent explained in detail with possible adverse events; consent video recorded.

Preintervention assessment: Detailed neuroevaluation; serology, biochemistry, hematology; brain MRI and EEG for all patients. GMFCS used to classify severity. PET-CT introduced later in the study.

Cell procurement and isolation: G-CSF administered 48 h and 24 h prior to aspiration. Bone marrow aspirated under general anesthesia from the anterior superior iliac crest (80–100 mL depending on age/weight) into heparinized tubes. Mononuclear cells isolated by density gradient. Viability assessed by propidium iodide on a TALI machine (Invitrogen); average viability 98%. CD34+ counts measured by FACS using CD34-PE antibody (BD Biosciences).

Transplantation: Autologous BMMNCs injected intrathecally via an 18G Tuohy needle and epidural catheter between L4–L5 by experienced medical personnel. Mean dose 10.23 × 10^6 cells. Concomitant methylprednisolone 20 mg/kg in 500 mL Ringer lactate IV to enhance cell survival. Patients monitored for procedure-related adverse events.

Neurorehabilitation: 4 days of intensive rehabilitation post-transplantation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, psychological intervention), followed by a personalized home program for at least 6 months. Patients generally continued prior rehabilitation before intervention.

Outcome measures and timing: Neurological evaluations at 1 week, 3 months, and 6 months. A grading system categorized improvement as: no improvement (<10% symptom improvement), mild (10–35%), moderate (35–70%), major (>70%). Video recordings were made pre- and post-intervention to document functional changes. PET-CT (18-FDG) performed before and 6 months after intervention in a subset (n=6) using a Siemens Biograph mct 64-slice PET/CT (3D PET True V; intrinsic resolution 0.6 mm FWHM; 45–50 transverse planes; 21.6 cm axial FOV). Data processed with Scenium Software.

Statistical analysis: McNemar’s test (df=1) applied to symptoms with ≥10 affected patients to assess association between intervention and improvement in diplegic and quadriplegic subgroups; no analysis for the small miscellaneous group. Percentage analyses were conducted for symptoms. No effect sizes, confidence intervals, or multivariable adjustments were reported.

title: Dynamic evolution of bitter taste receptor genes in vertebrates
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How have T2R gene numbers evolved across vertebrates via birth-and-death processes? (2) Are there lineage-specific expansions or contractions in teleosts, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals? (3) How do T2R repertoire dynamics relate to dietary habits and ecological niches? (4) Do reconciled-tree analyses provide a more detailed and reliable picture of gains/losses than linearized-tree approaches?

Hypotheses: (H1) T2R repertoires exhibit extensive birth-and-death evolution with lineage-specific expansions/contractions, reflecting adaptation to diet and environment. (H2) Teleost T2R families are more divergent from tetrapods than previously appreciated, indicating independent evolutionary trajectories. (H3) Herbivorous and omnivorous taxa will have larger T2R repertoires than carnivores, and aquatic/semi-aquatic taxa will have reduced repertoires. (H4) Reconciled-tree reconciliation will reveal more detailed and plausible gains/losses than linearized-tree methods, including mammalian expansions and Laurasiatheria contractions.

Predictions: Support for H1/H2 would be observed as multiple independent expansions (e.g., teleosts, frogs, lizards, mammals) and phylogenetic divergence. H3 would be supported by larger intact gene counts in herbivores and smaller counts in carnivores. H4 would be supported if reconciled trees recover expansions/contractions consistent with prior reports and provide additional resolution (e.g., opossum expansion; dog contraction).
reference_methodology:
Species and genomes: The study analyzed 16 vertebrates, including mammals (human, rhesus macaque, mouse, rat, dog, cow, horse, opossum, platypus), birds (chicken), reptiles (lizard), amphibians (frog), and teleost fishes (fugu, puffer fish, zebrafish, stickleback). Genome assemblies were high-coverage where available (e.g., rheMac2, 5.1×; danRer5, 7.6×; xenTro2, 7.6×; tetNig1, 7.9×; gasAcu1, 7.6×). Some genomes were unassembled into chromosomes, necessitating scaffold-level analyses for frogs and lizards.

Gene identification: T2R genes were identified using TBLASTN (E-value 1e-10) against each genome with previously published T2R sequences from human, mouse, dog, opossum, chicken, frog, and zebrafish as queries. Hits overlapping the same genomic region were collapsed to non-overlapping sequences with the lowest E-value. Candidate sequences >100 amino acids were extended in both 3′ and 5′ directions along the genome, then validated by BLASTP against NCBI databases. Coding sequences with proper ATG and stop codons were classified as intact T2Rs (~300 aa). Sequences with interrupting stop codons or frameshifts were pseudogenes; sequences with only an initiation or stop codon were partial T2Rs. Partial genes were also identified from draft genomes to avoid underestimation.

Phylogenetic analysis: Amino-acid sequences of intact T2Rs were aligned with MAFFT v5 (FFT-NS-I). The phylogeny was constructed in MEGA3 using Neighbor-Joining with the JTT substitution model and evaluated by 500 bootstrap replicates. Only intact genes were included; partial and pseudogenes were excluded due to length differences. The tetrapod clade was supported at 82% bootstrap. Ten phylogenetic families (A–J) were defined manually, requiring >70% bootstrap support and >5 genes per family; smaller nested families were subsumed into larger ones. Family A–J bootstrap supports were mostly >90%.

Reconciled-tree analysis: To estimate gains and losses, the authors used the reconciled-tree method (Niimura et al.) to map gene trees onto species trees. For mammals, the species tree followed Murphy et al. and Glazko et al., with mouse VR genes as outgroups. A condensed tree (50% bootstrap) was used to mitigate uncertainty in low-support branches. Ancestral gene counts were inferred via parsimony. The same approach was applied to all 16 vertebrates using a conventional vertebrate phylogeny. Results were compared to prior linearized-tree estimates to assess consistency.

Chromosomal clustering: For families with ≥2 genes, chromosomal/scaffold locations were compared. Genes within families clustered on the same chromosomes/scaffolds, consistent with tandem duplication. Due to incomplete assemblies, scaffold-level locations were reported for frogs and lizards.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; analyses used publicly available genomes and computational methods.

title: More complex societies have more complex kinship lexicons
research_question: Research question: Does societal complexity (exotericity) correlate with the complexity of kinship lexicons across languages? Hypothesis: Languages spoken by exoteric societies (Type X) exhibit more complex kinship lexicons than those spoken by esoteric societies (Type S). Predictions: A negative association between the Sociopolitical Complexity Index (SCI; more negative = more complex society) and kinship complexity (higher gzip-compressed extension list length = more complex system) will be observed globally and remain after controlling for language relatedness and geographic proximity. Alternative outcomes: No association after controls, or associations reversed, would refute the hypothesis; heterogeneous effects across language families would nuance it. Outcomes supporting the hypothesis include significant negative coefficients in linear and Bayesian mixed-effects models, with credible intervals excluding zero in the expected direction, and stronger effects in families with more exoteric sociopolitical structures.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: Kinship features from KinBank (1235 languages; 440 analyzed), which lists core kinship concepts and, where attested, lexical forms per language. Societal features from Ethnologue (EGIDS 1–13; EGIDSnat 1/2), Glottolog (language family size), and D-Place (EA033 jurisdictional levels; EA031 local community size; EA202 population size; SCCS156 population density; SCCS150 residence fixity; B014 distance moved annually). Geographical coordinates from KinBank/AUTOTYP; phylogeny from the EDGE tree.

Preprocessing: Duplicates in KinBank were removed (e.g., English/German entries in Latin vs IPA; Russian entries in Latin vs Cyrillic). For SCI computation, nine features were normalized and missing values imputed using missForest (R). Principal component analysis (prcomp) was run; the first principal component (PC1) explained 56.8% of variance and was used as SCI. More negative SCI indicates more complex (exoteric) societies.

Kinship complexity metric: KinBank’s primitive concepts and modifiers were re-coded to a more compositional set (Ego E; Parent P; Sibling S; Child C; Spouse O; modifiers: male m, female f, younger y, elder e, exchange X, agnatic a, cognatic c, co-, or, not). For each kinship term, the extension (set of concepts it refers to) was compiled. For each language, extension lists for all terms were concatenated with slashes and compressed using gzip; the compressed length served as the complexity score. Longer compressed length indicates higher complexity due to less redundancy and more essential information.

Statistical analysis: A global linear regression related SCI to kinship complexity. To control for Galton’s problem, a Bayesian mixed-effects linear regression (brms) included random effects for language relatedness (covariance matrix from pairwise distances on the EDGE tree) and geographic proximity (Matérn covariance from great-circle distances; normalized to maximal covariance). The fixed effect was SCI. Four Markov chains, 10,000 iterations, 5,000 warm-up, uninformative priors were used. Significance was defined as both 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles having the same sign (excluding zero). Posterior means, 2.5%, and 97.5% quantiles were reported. Family-level analyses (Figure S1) examined heterogeneity across language families.

title: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Chemical Shift as Probe for Single-Molecule Charge Transport
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does single-molecule conductance correlate quantitatively with NMR chemical shifts (1H/13C) of diagnostic nuclei across molecular series and substituents? (2) Can NMR-derived parameters inform a simple analytical model that reproduces experimental conductance trends and transmission features? (3) Does the correlation generalize across different termini and experimental conditions?

Hypotheses: (H1) A semilogarithmic relationship exists between single-molecule conductance and the chemical shift δ of diagnostic nuclei (β-protons or β-carbons) across molecular series. (H2) Incorporating β-site on-site energy perturbations in a TB+NEGF model will capture the observed decrease in conductance with heavier chalcogens and reveal chalcogen-induced quantum interference (from constructive to destructive). (H3) The δ–conductance correlation persists across literature datasets with matched or comparable NMR/STMBJ conditions, even when termini and solvents differ.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if conductance vs δ plots show a clear semilog trend across series and substituents. H2 is supported if TB transmission and Landauer-derived conductance histograms match experimental trends and interference patterns when εβ is included. H3 is supported if literature datasets exhibit consistent δ–conductance correlations under varied conditions.
reference_methodology:
Synthesis and characterization: The authors synthesized 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)chalcogenophenes 1–4 (1: furan; 2: thiophene; 3: selenophene; 4: tellurophene). 1–3 were prepared by Suzuki coupling of 2,5-dibromo chalcogenophenes with 4-pyridinylboronic acid. 4 was synthesized by treating 1,4-di(pyridine-4-yl)buta-1,3-diyne with sodium telluride generated in situ from Te and NaBH4. All compounds were purified by chromatography and recrystallization (1 reprecipitated). NMR spectra (1H, 13C) were recorded on a Bruker Avance III 500 MHz spectrometer in CDCl3, referenced to TMS and residual solvent; 1H δ for β-protons is highlighted. Mass spectra were recorded on an Agilent Q-TOF 7200. Crystal structure of 4 deposited at CCDC (2219092). Data (NMR, STMBJ) from Liverpool are available at DOI: https://doi.org/10.17638/datacat.liverpool.ac.uk/2141.

STMBJ measurements: A modified Keysight 5500 SPM with a custom 4-channel preamplifier (per Meszaros et al.) and NI9215 DAQ (16-bit, 10 kSa/s) was used. Au substrates (~200 nm Au on freshly cleaved muscovite mica) were briefly annealed with a butane torch. Tips were cut from 99.998% Au wire (0.25 mm Ø). Measurements were performed in mesitylene:THF 4:1 v:v at 1 mM target concentration, room temperature, at 100 mV bias. The Au tip was driven into the Au substrate to form a microcontact (G ≫ G0), then retracted at 12 nm/s while monitoring current; conductance G = I/V. The microcontact thinned to G = G0, then ruptured to form atomically sharp electrodes. Molecules in solution or preadsorbed on electrodes self-assembled in the nanogap. The tip was further retracted to stretch the junction to rupture. The process was repeated thousands of times to collect statistically robust datasets. Data were aligned to G0 rupture and compiled into log-binned conductance histograms and 2D density maps without selection. Acquisition was stopped if the system failed to engage at G ≫ G0 or if conductance did not decay to the noise level (10^−5.3 G0 at 100 mV) within 6 nm of withdrawal.

DFT and CST analysis: Chemical shift tensors (CST) for β-protons were computed to assess electronic structure changes across 1–4 (details in SI). The YY component (along the chalcogen) and anisotropy were analyzed.

Transport modeling: A TB Hamiltonian with single p-orbitals per atom and nearest-neighbor coupling γ = −1 eV was constructed. Initial on-site energies for all carbon atoms were set to zero; transmission T(E) was computed between α sites. On-site energies for the chalcogen site (εC) were varied (O, S, Se, Te: −0.6, −0.8, −1.0, −1.2 eV). To capture β-site perturbations, εβ was also varied (O, S, Se, Te: −0.48, −0.64, −0.83, −1.0 eV). Transmission coefficients were calculated using GOLLUM (nonequilibrium Green’s function) and converted to conductance via the Landauer formula at room temperature. Robustness was assessed by randomizing εC and εβ within ±0.2 eV and recalculating T(E) and histograms.

title: Reachable Set and Robust Mixed Performance of Uncertain Discrete Systems with Interval Time-Varying Delay and Linear Fractional Perturbations
field_subfield: Control Theory — Discrete-time systems with time-varying delays and switched control
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can we derive LMI conditions that guarantee asymptotic stability, bounded reachable set, and mixed H2/H∞ performance for uncertain discrete systems with interval time-varying delays and linear fractional perturbations? (2) Can a switched controller with gains scheduled by the delay mode achieve these properties while improving reachable set bounds and disturbance attenuation? (3) Does incorporating a slow variation constraint on the delay reduce conservatism relative to unconstrained switching?

Hypotheses: (H1) A switched Lyapunov function with mode-dependent LMI constraints can simultaneously ensure stability, mixed H2/H∞ performance, and a hyper-spherical reachable set bound under LFPs. (H2) A switched controller u(k) = −Kσ(k)x(k) designed via LMI can stabilize the system and improve performance relative to non-switched designs. (H3) Imposing |τ(k+1) − τ(k)| ≤ λ (small λ) reduces conservatism by limiting mode transitions, yielding tighter bounds and feasible solutions where unconstrained switching fails.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if LMI feasibility yields stability, γ and α bounds, and a reachable set radius. H2 is supported if the switched controller yields feasible gains and improved γ and α. H3 is supported if feasible solutions exist under slow variation with smaller radii and γ than under unconstrained switching or prior methods.
reference_methodology:
System model: Consider a discrete-time system with interval time-varying delay τ(k) ∈ [τm, τM], bounded peak disturbance w(k) with wT(k)w(k) ≤ w2, and regulated output z(k). The state and output equations are x(k+1) = −A0(k)x(k) − A1(k)x(k − τ(k)) − Bxw(k)w(k) and z(k) = −Az0(k)x(k) − Az1(k)x(k − τ(k)) − Bzw(k)w(k). Perturbations satisfy linear fractional forms: [ΔA0(k) ΔA1(k) ΔBxw(k)] = Mx • Δ1(k) • [N0 N1 N2w] and [ΔAz0(k) ΔAz1(k) ΔBzw(k)] = Mz • Δ2(k) • [N3 N4 N5w], with Δj(k) = I − Γj(k)Ξj−1Γj(k), ΞjΞjT < I, and Γj(k)TΓj(k) ≤ I. The delay satisfies |τ(k+1) − τ(k)| ≤ λ.

Switched representation: Define σ(k) = τ(k) − (τm − 1) ∈ {1, …, N}, N = τM − τm + 1, and τσ(k)(k) = τ(k). Stack the state vector X(k) = [xT(k) xT(k−1) … xT(k−τM)]T. The system becomes X(k+1) = [AX0(k) + AX1(k)Eσ(k)]X(k) + BXw(k)w(k), z(k) = [AZ0(k) + AZ1(k)Eσ(k)]X(k) + BZw(k)w(k), where AX0, AX1, AZ0, AZ1, BXw, BZw are block matrices with identity shifts and Eσ(k) selects the appropriate delay block.

Lyapunov framework: Use mode-dependent Lyapunov functions Vi(X(k)) = X(k)T Pi X(k), i ∈ {1, …, N}. For stability and reachable set bounds, require Vj(X(k+1)) − αji Vi(X(k)) − (1 − αji)w2 wT(k)w(k) < 0 for all i, j, with 0 < αji < 1. This implies asymptotic stability and Vi(X(k)) ≤ 1 for all k if Vi(X(0)) ≤ 1, and the reachable set is bounded by a hyper-sphere S(r) with r = min δi, where δi are bounds from a diagonal dominance condition.

Mixed performance: Define V(X(k)) = X(k)T P X(k) and analyze zT(k)z(k) − γ2 wT(k)w(k) + ΔV(X(k)) < 0 along trajectories. Using an augmented Lyapunov function and LFP slack variables (Lemma 2), derive LMI Ωi < 0 that enforces H∞ performance γ and H2 measure α via additional constraints. The optimization procedure minimizes γ (then α, then δi) subject to LMI feasibility.

Controller design: For systems with control input u(k), use u(k) = −Kσ(k)x(k). Substitute into the switched dynamics and derive LMI conditions (Theorem 2) involving Pi = diag(Pi1, Pi2) and slack variables to handle uncertainties. The gains are Ki = Kĩ P−1i1, with Kĩ obtained from the LMI. The optimization steps (Remark 3) first fix δi, then minimize γ, then α.

Implementation: All LMIs are solved using MATLAB’s LMI toolbox. The slow variation constraint |τ(k+1) − τ(k)| ≤ λ reduces the number of i–j couplings by restricting σ(k+1) to a small neighborhood of σ(k).

title: La previdenza obbligatoria in Italia tra crisi globale, strategie europee e vincoli di bilancio
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How have EU strategies and fiscal constraints shaped Italy’s mandatory pension reforms (2011–2012), and do these reforms achieve long-term sustainability? (2) To what extent do the reforms address pension adequacy, particularly for low earners and precarious workers? (3) How do labor market policies and gender disparities intersect with pension adequacy? (4) What are the implications of the Fiscal Compact for social rights and pension adequacy?

Hypotheses: (H1) The 2011 reforms improve long-term sustainability via higher retirement ages and contributory design. (H2) Adequacy remains insufficient due to low replacement rates, low complementary pension participation, and labor market precarity. (H3) Indiscriminate age indexing without labor market supports risks shifting burdens to other welfare pillars. (H4) Fiscal constraints may limit future adequacy unless complementary pensions and labor policies are strengthened. Outcomes supporting H1 include RGS sustainability projections; outcomes supporting H2/H3 include replacement rate projections and OECD/CESE critiques; H4 is supported by the Fiscal Compact’s debt targets and the thesis’s constitutional adequacy analysis.
reference_methodology:
Design: Doctrinal legal analysis and policy evaluation. The thesis synthesizes primary legal sources (Italian laws and decrees: Law 421/1992; Law 335/1995; Law 247/2007; Law 102/2009; Law 122/2010; Law 214/2011; EU directives and regulations; CESE opinions; OECD reports), official statistics (RGS, INPS, ISTAT, COVIP), and secondary literature. It maps legal provisions to policy outcomes and evaluates them against EU guidance and constitutional principles (Art. 38 Cost. on adequacy; Art. 39 Cost. on freedom of private provision; Art. 81 Cost. on budgetary balance).

Data and measures: The analysis reports quantitative parameters from legislation and official sources: minimum pension at 1.5× social allowance (2013: ≈€663.45/month; social allowance ≈€442.30/month), retirement age for old-age pensions set at 66 (with biennial updates from 2019; not below 67 from 2021), transformation coefficients extended to age 70 (biennial updates from 2019), gender parity in public sector retirement age (achieved), and private sector parity schedule (2018). It cites RGS projections of ≈€80B savings by 2021 and exodati safeguards totaling ≈139,130 people. It references OECD replacement rate projections (net ≈71.3% by 2040; total with integration ≈88.1%) and complementary pension participation (≈27% as of mid-2013). The thesis also references ISTAT youth unemployment (≈39.5% in 2013) and labor market precarity.

Procedures: The thesis conducts a chronological review of reforms, contrasts Italian measures with EU strategies, and evaluates adequacy and sustainability trade-offs. It analyzes the exodati issue’s fiscal impact and discusses constitutional adequacy (Art. 38 Cost.) and the Bundesverfassungsgericht’s MES/Fiscal Compact jurisprudence as constraints on future fiscal commitments. No experimental or statistical modeling is performed; the study is narrative and evaluative, relying on official statistics and doctrinal reasoning.

title: Вестник психологии и педагогики АлтГУ 2017-4 24
research_question:
Research question: How are components of self-concept (e.g., global self-concept, self-sympathy, self-confidence, self-respect, self-control, self-understanding, self-interest, expected attitude from others) associated with sexual attitudes (e.g., sexual satisfaction, sexual neuroticism, depersonalized sex, aggressive sex, pornography, permissiveness, aversion to sex) among young adults with non-traditional sexual orientations?

The article does not state explicit a priori hypotheses. The analysis is exploratory, using Spearman correlations to identify associations between self-concept scales and sexual attitude scales. Outcomes that would support the research aims include statistically significant correlations (with reported p-values) between specific self-concept components and sexual attitude dimensions. The authors interpret the direction and magnitude of correlations to infer potential psychological mechanisms (e.g., higher self-acceptance linked to lower sexual satisfaction; higher self-confidence linked to more objectifying/aggressive sexual attitudes).
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional correlational study using self-report questionnaires.

Participants: 30 young adults aged 17–25 years who identify with non-traditional sexual orientations. The sampling method, recruitment procedures, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and demographic breakdowns (e.g., gender identity, sexual orientation subtypes, region, education) are not reported.

Measures: (1) Eysenck’s Sexual Attitudes Inventory (SAI), oriented to predicting marital satisfaction, identifying deviations in sexual behavior, and diagnosing femininity–masculinity. The specific scales analyzed include sexual satisfaction, sexual neuroticism, depersonalized sex, aggressive sex, pornography, and permissiveness. (2) Self-Concept Questionnaire by Stolin and Pantileev, assessing components such as global self-concept, self-sympathy, self-confidence, self-respect, self-control, self-understanding, self-interest, and expected attitude from others. The operational definitions and scoring procedures for each scale are not provided.

Procedure: Participants completed the two questionnaires. The language of administration, administration setting, and duration are not reported. No details are provided on instructions, response format (e.g., Likert scales), or handling of missing data.

Analysis: Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients were computed to examine associations between self-concept scales and sexual attitude scales. The significance thresholds reported include p ≤ 0.02, p ≤ 0.04, p ≤ 0.05, p ≤ 0.06, and p ≤ 0.08. No adjustments for multiple comparisons, confidence intervals, or effect size estimates beyond r are reported. No regression analyses, subgroup analyses, or control variables are described.

Ethics: No information is provided on ethical approvals, informed consent, or data privacy protections.

Reproducibility notes: The study lacks details on sampling frame, recruitment, instrument reliability/validity, scoring, and data handling, which are critical for replication.

title: A Light-Activated Hypervalent Iodine Agent Enables Diverse Aliphatic C-H Functionalization
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a hypervalent iodine(III) reagent be designed to release a potent hydrogen atom abstractor (HMDS•) under mild visible-light conditions, thereby decoupling HAT from radical trapping? (2) Does such a reagent enable selective, modular diversification of aliphatic C–H bonds across a broad substrate scope, including complex molecules? (3) Can the platform be generalized to diverse functionalizations by simply varying the radical trapping agent (RTA)?

Hypotheses: (i) PIMS will undergo photoinduced homolysis of weak I–N bonds to generate two HMDS• radicals and iodobenzene, with HMDS• acting as the HAA for C–H activation. (ii) The decoupling of HAT and trapping will allow RTAs that do not need to turnover a photocatalyst or sustain a radical chain, expanding accessible functional groups and improving functional group tolerance (including base-sensitive groups). (iii) For allylic C–H bonds, SPT• generated in situ from SPT–SPT under light will initiate a radical chain, enabling efficient allylic thiolation without PIMS. Supportive outcomes would include: successful PIMS synthesis and characterization; visible-light-driven HAT with high yields and selectivity; broad substrate scope; generality across multiple RTAs; and minimal reactivity without PIMS. Refutation would involve failure of PIMS to release HMDS•, lack of selective C–H functionalization, or inability to generalize across RTAs.
reference_methodology:
Reagent synthesis and characterization: PIMS was synthesized in one step on multigram scale from commercially available lithium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (LiHMDS) and [bis(trifluoroacetoxy)iodo]benzene (see Supplementary Information for full synthesis and characterization). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction revealed a T-shaped geometry at iodine with N–I–N = 179.08(5)° and N–I–C angles 90.08(6)–90.81(6)°. I–N bond distances were 2.2069(13) and 2.1953(13) Å (both > sum of covalent radii, 2.10 Å). DFT predicted a mean I–N bond energy of ~20 kcal/mol, consistent with facile homolysis. Differential scanning calorimetry showed melting at 82.6 °C and subsequent degradation to iodobenzene. UV–Vis spectra exhibited UV absorption with a visible tail.

Optimization and conditions: Reactions were typically performed on 0.2 mmol scale unless noted. For model thiolation, PIMS was the limiting reagent with excess alkane. Irradiation used 440 nm blue light for 18 h. Control experiments established that both PIMS and light are required: no product without PIMS; dark reactions gave substantially lower yields (20%) presumably via slow thermal decomposition of PIMS to HMDS•. For allylic thiolation, PIMS was unnecessary; SPT• generated in situ from SPT–SPT under light initiated a radical chain. Reaction times varied with light source/intensity; full conversion could be reached within 4 h under more intense illumination, but 18 h was used for optimized reproducibility.

Substrate scope and analysis: The optimized conditions were applied to cycloalkanes (e.g., cyclododecane 2, trans-decalin 5, trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane 6), linear alkanes (e.g., 13–16), bicyclic alkanes (e.g., 7–9), organosilanes (11, 12), and heterocycles (e.g., pyrrolidine 24–27, morpholine 26, furane 30, quinuclidine 28, 1,4-diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane 29). Regioselectivity and yields were determined by quantitative 1H NMR (for many entries) or 13C NMR (for selected entries). Gram-scale synthesis of norbornane-derived product 8 was achieved (59% yield vs 63% on smaller scale). For allylic substrates (e.g., (+)-valencene 41, (+)-α-pinene 42, cholesteryl chloride 43, abiraterone acetate 44), excellent diastereoselectivity was observed.

Generality with varied RTAs: Using cyclododecane as substrate, the platform was extended to thiolations with diphenyl disulfide, di-tert-butyl tetrasulfide, or S-(trifluoromethyl)benzenesulfonothioate; halogenations with benzenesulfonyl chloride, N-bromosuccinimide, and iodine; azidation (62), cyanation (63), vinylation (64), and alkynylation (65) with arylsulfonyl-based RTAs; and aminoxylations using persistent TEMPO•. In all cases, little to no product formed without PIMS.

Derivatizations: SPT-bearing products underwent Lewis-acid-promoted nucleophilic substitution (e.g., 43-SPT to 45), SNAr removal of the tetrazole (2-SPT to 47), oxidation to sulfones (e.g., Julia–Kocienski olefination to 48), and SNAr to sulfinate followed by one-pot conversion to sulfone (51), sulfonyl fluoride (52), or primary sulfonamide (53).

title: Performer: A Novel PPG-to-ECG Reconstruction Transformer for a Digital Biomarker of Cardiovascular Disease Detection
field_subfield: Computer Science — Machine Learning (Biomedical Signal Processing)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a Transformer-based architecture with a tailored tokenization scheme (SPA) reconstruct ECG from PPG with state-of-the-art accuracy, enabling continuous cardiac monitoring? (2) Does combining PPG with reconstructed ECG as a multimodal digital biomarker improve CVD detection compared to single-modality baselines? (3) Is the approach generalizable across datasets and tasks (CVD subtypes and diabetes)?

Hypotheses: (H1) SPA’s hierarchical, shifted-patch tokenization will improve PPG-to-ECG reconstruction accuracy over prior methods (GAN, CNN encoder-decoder, vanilla Transformer) by capturing local features and cross-patch context while denoising. (H2) The multimodal digital biomarker (PPG + reconstructed ECG) will outperform raw PPG or reconstructed ECG alone and perform comparably to raw PPG+ECG pairs. (H3) The model will generalize to different datasets (MIMIC-III, PPG-BP) and tasks (CVD subtypes, diabetes), achieving competitive accuracy.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if RMSE on BIDMC is lower than prior methods. H2 is supported if ablation shows superior or comparable performance for the multimodal input. H3 is supported if accuracy on MIMIC-III and PPG-BP is competitive with reported baselines.
reference_methodology:
Datasets: Reconstruction training uses paired PPG and Lead-II ECG from UQVSD (≈3000+ minutes), DaLiA (≈1800+ minutes), and BIDMC (≈400+ minutes), totaling ≈5200+ minutes. Lead-II is emphasized for its clinical relevance (P and R wave visibility). For detection, MIMIC-III (40,000 patients) provides PPG paired with four CVD labels: coronary artery disease (CAD), congestive heart failure (CHF), myocardial infarction (MI), and hypotension (HOTN), with class distribution 7:7:7:12. PPG-BP (219 patients) provides PPG paired with diabetes labels (37:182 distribution).

Preprocessing: All signals are resampled to 128 Hz. A BioSPPY standard denoising filter is applied, followed by a 1D convolutional layer to amplify waveform patterns. Signals are normalized to [-1, 1]. Data are segmented into 4-second windows with 2-second overlap. For SPA, waveforms are split into multiple patch sizes (32, 64, 128, 256, 512 points) across hierarchical stages.

Training: Implemented in PyTorch. Training environment: AWS Deep Learning AMI, Tesla T4 GPU. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 0.0001. Training duration: 50 epochs. Loss for reconstruction: RMSE between ground-truth ECG y_i and reconstructed ECG ŷ_i over N sampling points per segment. The reconstruction Transformer is trained end-to-end on paired PPG/ECG. The multimodal Transformer is trained on PPG paired with CVD labels, using the reconstructed ECG generated by the reconstruction Transformer as an additional modality.

Evaluation: Reconstruction accuracy is measured by RMSE on BIDMC and compared to prior methods (DCT/XDJDL, GAN, CNN encoder-decoder, vanilla Transformer). CVD detection performance is reported as accuracy on MIMIC-III and PPG-BP, with confusion matrices referenced (Table 2). An ablation compares inputs: raw PPG, reconstructed ECG only, raw PPG+ECG pairs, and the multimodal digital biomarker (PPG + reconstructed ECG) (Table 4). Attention maps from the last layer visualize focus on clinically salient regions (Figure 6). No details are provided on train/validation/test splits, random seeds, batch sizes, or statistical tests (e.g., CIs, p-values).

title: Who is Tom Bombadil?: Interpreting the Light in Frodo Baggins and Tom Bombadil's Role in the Healing of Traumatic Memory in
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does Frodo Baggins become “transparent” and filled with a “clear light,” and what is the nature of that light? (2) Who is Tom Bombadil, and what is his role in Frodo’s healing from traumatic memory? (3) How do Tolkien’s letters and medieval interpretive frameworks inform these readings?

Hypotheses: (a) Frodo’s “clear light” is a symbolic manifestation of Christ-light, emerging through trauma and sustained in healing interludes; (b) Tom Bombadil’s identity is intentionally enigmatic but can be read simultaneously as prelapsarian Adam (Eldest, fearlessness, naming) and Second Adam (Jesus), with his song effecting Frodo’s salvation from death and initiating trauma healing; (c) Tolkien’s letters and medieval exegesis support these interpretations and clarify Tom’s function as an exemplar rather than an allegory. Supportive outcomes would include textual evidence of light symbolism tied to the Phial and Eärendil’s Silmaril, narrative scenes where Tom’s song rescues Frodo from the barrow-wight (framed as drowning and resurrection), and Tolkien’s explicit statements about Tom’s role and identity. Refuting outcomes would include narrative or letter evidence contradicting the Christ-light linkage or Tom’s Christ-like role.
reference_methodology: The study employs close textual analysis of The Lord of the Rings (The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers, The Return of the King), The Silmarillion (Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Voyage of Eärendil), and The Adventures of Tom Bombadil, alongside Tolkien’s letters (Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien; The Return of the Shadow). It uses medieval hermeneutics (literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical) to interpret symbols and character roles. Primary textual anchors include Gandalf’s Rivendell observation of Frodo’s “clear light” (FR 222–23), Sam’s perception of Frodo’s inner light in Ithilien (TT 651–52), the Phial of Galadriel’s origin and function (TT 376), the barrow-wight rescue scene (FR 142–43), and the lembas motif (e.g., TT 213). Tolkien’s letters to Naomi Mitchison (April 1954) and Peter Hastings (September 1954) clarify Tom’s intended function and identity, while The Return of the Shadow provides early drafts and notes on Tom Bombadil (e.g., “aborigine” references). Biblical and Old English sources (e.g., Christ III, Bickling Homily 10) are used to contextualize light imagery and resurrection symbolism. The analysis also draws on secondary scholarship (e.g., Flieger, Shippey, Basso, Gay, Rogers) to situate interpretations within existing debates. No empirical data, statistical analyses, or experimental procedures are used; the methodology is interpretive and hermeneutic. Ethical approvals are not applicable.

title: Assembly and Testing of a Radioisotope Power System for the New Horizons Spacecraft AIAA 4th International Energy Conversion Engineering Conference and Exhibit (IECEC)
research_question: The central objective was to assemble and qualify a GPHS RTG for the New Horizons spacecraft at INL’s SSPSF and to demonstrate that the facility and procedures meet mission requirements. The implicit hypotheses were: (1) The INL SSPSF can safely and effectively perform all required RPS assembly and testing operations (fuel handling, module assembly, reduction monitoring, inert atmosphere assembly, vibration, mass properties, and thermal vacuum testing) under DOE hazard category II standards; (2) The assembled RTG will meet New Horizons power specifications, specifically BOM power ≥237 W and 9.5-year power ≥191 W; (3) The RTG will survive simulated launch/transport environments and function in vacuum. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include successful completion of all assembly/test steps, measured BOM power exceeding the minimum requirement (243 W vs 237 W), and successful launch and in-space operation.
