Outcomes refuting them would include facility safety/operational failures, power shortfalls, or test failures. The paper reports successful outcomes consistent with the hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Facility and safety: The SSPSF comprises two physically connected buildings (original facility 792 and annex 792A) constructed to DOE hazard category II standards with performance category 3. The facility supports Pu-238 handling, module assembly, reduction monitoring, inert atmosphere assembly, vibration, mass properties, and thermal vacuum testing. Remote operation and contamination controls are emphasized.

Fuel handling: Pu-238 fuel was shipped from LANL in multiple nested welded containers. Opening operations used a metal cutting device within a polycarbonate/stainless steel fume hood to remove primary and secondary containment vessels and transfer fuel product cans to a module assembly glovebox. Operations were conducted under an inert argon atmosphere with slight positive pressure relative to the SSPSF.

Module assembly: Eighteen (18) GPHS modules were assembled in a dual-glovebox system (two gloveboxes interconnected by a pass-through airlock). Modules were then placed into Module Reduction Monitoring (MRM) cans, which were welded within the glovebox. The MRM system provided ultra-high purity argon, argon/carbon monoxide/helium, and vacuum via a manifold; each MRM can station could be evacuated. Operators controlled the manifold from a console outside the MRM room.

Fuel reduction: The MRM process reduced PuO2 to substoichiometric PuO1.98, mitigating thermoelectric performance degradation and enhancing safety (reducing vent plugging, plutonium migration within aeroshells, and iridium grain growth). After reduction, MRM cans were backfilled with argon and transferred to the Inert Atmosphere Assembly Chamber (IAAC).

Inert Atmosphere Assembly Chamber (IAAC): The IAAC comprised two gloveboxes (an opening glovebox and an assembly/loading glovebox) connected by a pass-through airlock. The assembly/loading glovebox was equipped with master/slave manipulators. Assembly steps included disassembling MRM cans, exposing modules, assembling two nine-pack assemblies, inserting them into the RTG generator, leak checking, and initial power checks. The IAAC maintained an argon atmosphere at positive pressure relative to the building. All equipment met 5 mil particle cleanliness requirements. Vacuum handling tools and specialized fixtures/gauges were used.

Testing sequence: After initial power checks, the RTG underwent vibration testing to simulate transport and launch environments, mass properties testing (center of gravity, mass, and derived moments of inertia), and thermal vacuum testing in a 1.83 m diameter, 2.74 m long chamber. Power output was monitored via a Read Out Console (ROC) during tests. Vibration testing used an electrodynamic vibrator, slip table assembly, hydraulic power unit, field coil power supply, power amplifier/transformer, control system, and sensors/signal conditioners. Mass properties testing used a newly purchased mass machine with remote operation. Thermal vacuum testing used a chamber with power, signal, thermocouple, and gas feed-throughs.

Transportation and integration: The RTG was packaged in a DOT-certified container and transported to Kennedy Space Center (KSC). INL involvement continued until shortly after launch. The New Horizons spacecraft with the RTG launched January 19, 2006, and is en route to Pluto-Charon and the Kuiper Belt.

title: Nutritional profile of preschool children of fishermen
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the anthropometric nutritional status (height-for-age, weight-for-age, MUAC, head/chest ratio) of preschool children (4–5 years) from fishermen families in coastal Thrissur district? (2) What are their actual food and nutrient intakes relative to Indian RDA? (3) Which nutrients are most limiting (energy, protein, micronutrients)? (4) How do socio-demographic and health factors relate to nutritional status?

Hypotheses: (H1) Preschool children in this community exhibit significant deficits in anthropometric indices relative to Indian standards, with higher prevalence of moderate malnutrition by weight-based indices. (H2) Energy intake is inadequate, with protein intake relatively adequate due to energy sparing, leading to deficits in micronutrients (e.g., vitamin A, C, calcium, iron). (H3) Energy and protein will be significant predictors of weight in regression analyses. (H4) Clinical signs of vitamin A deficiency will be detectable. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significant t-tests for anthropometric deficits, intake percentages below RDA for energy and key micronutrients, significant regression coefficients for energy and protein, and clinical signs consistent with vitamin A deficiency.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional survey with socio-demographic, anthropometric, clinical, and dietary assessments.

Setting and sampling: Coastal Thrissur district, Kerala. A list of anganwadis was compiled; 10 anganwadis (Thalikkulam, Nattika, Valappad) were randomly selected. From each anganwadi, families not engaged in fishing or related activities were excluded. Ten families per anganwadi were randomly selected, yielding 100 preschool children (4–5 years) as the main sample. Subsamples: 50 children for clinical examination; 20 children for a one-day food weighment survey.

Measures: Socio-demographic data (family type, size, religion, education, occupation, income, housing, sanitation, transportation, information sources, ICDS participation) were collected via pre-tested structured interviews with mothers. Anthropometry: height (fiberglass tape; standing without shoes), weight (bathroom balance calibrated with standard weights; minimal clothing), head circumference (tape around frontal bones and occipital prominence), chest circumference (tape at xiphisternal level), and MUAC (tape at mid-point between acromion and olecranon; arm relaxed). Clinical examination (qualified physician) assessed signs of malnutrition and micronutrient deficiency (e.g., dental caries, phrynoderma, fluorosis, eye pigmentation, dry conjunctiva). Food weighment: raw ingredients and cooked foods consumed by the child in one day were weighed using standard measuring cups/spoons and a food weighing balance; cooked food was converted to raw equivalents. Nutrient intakes were computed using Indian food composition tables (Gopalan, 1989).

Standards and indices: Anthropometric means compared to ICMR (1990) and NIN (1991) standards. Malnutrition classification: height-for-age (Waterlow, 1972), weight-for-age (Gomez, 1956), weight/height² (Rao & Singh, 1970), MUAC (Gopaldas & Seshadri, 1987), and head/chest circumference ratio (Gopaldas, 1987).

Statistical analysis: Student’s t-tests compared observed means to standards. Multiple regression modeled weight as a function of energy, protein, calcium, iron, vitamin A, thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and vitamin C; R² and p-values were reported. Additional analyses included ANOVA, correlation, and descriptive statistics for socio-demographics and dietary patterns.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. Informed consent procedures are not described. Clinical examination was conducted by a qualified physician; no adverse events are reported.

Data availability: Not reported. No preregistration or code links are provided.

title: DEVELOPING ASSESSMENT INSTRUMENTS OF HUMAN COORDINATION SYSTEM FOR GRADE XI HIGH SCHOOL
research_question:
Research question: How to develop and formulate assessment instruments for the human coordination system in Grade XI high school biology that comprehensively cover cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains and are practical for classroom use?

Implicit hypotheses: (1) A development process combining expert validation, one-to-one tryouts, and small-group tryouts will yield instruments with acceptable content and evaluation validity (mean scores ≥ 3 on a 1–3 scale) and high reliability (α ≥ 0.7) for cognitive and affective instruments; (2) The psychomotor instrument will be valid but may exhibit lower reliability due to fewer items and limited inter-item correlations; (3) Teachers and students will judge the instruments as practical and attractive for classroom application. Support for these hypotheses would be indicated by post-revision expert validation scores meeting or exceeding 3.00, high reliability coefficients for cognitive and affective instruments, and positive practicality feedback. Refutation would involve low validation scores, low reliability, or negative practicality judgments.
reference_methodology:
Design: Developmental research following a three-stage model (preliminary, development, formative evaluation). The preliminary stage included literature review and field study (classroom observations and teacher interviews). The development stage formulated learning objectives from Standard Competence 3 and Basic Competence 3.6 (human coordination system) and designed initial instruments (Prototype 1). The evaluation stage included expert validation, one-to-one tryouts with teachers and students, revisions, and a small-group tryout.

Participants: Two biology teachers and five students participated in one-to-one tryouts; forty-one students participated in the small-group tryout. No demographic details were reported. Ethics/IRB approvals were not mentioned.

Instruments: (1) Cognitive instrument: multiple-choice test (30 items) aligned with content standards (facts, concepts, principles, procedures) for the human coordination system. (2) Affective instrument: attitude questionnaire targeting attitudes on content (15 items). (3) Psychomotor instrument: observation sheet (4 items) capturing practical skills related to the topic. Prototype 1 was revised based on validator feedback to produce Prototype 2.

Validation and reliability procedures: Item validity was assessed using point-biserial correlation for test items and product-moment correlation for non-test items; items with r ≥ 0.3 were deemed valid. Reliability was assessed using KR-20 for test data and Cronbach’s alpha for non-test data; instruments with α ≥ 0.7 were considered reliable. Expert validation involved one content expert and one evaluation expert, rating instruments on a 1–3 scale. Practicality was assessed via teacher and student feedback during one-to-one tryouts and descriptive analysis of small-group tryout outcomes.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics summarized expert validation scores and item validity/reliability. No inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or effect sizes were reported. The study did not report randomization, blinding, or detailed scoring rubrics beyond the psychometric thresholds.

Setting and materials: Instruments were developed for Grade XI high school biology, with content aligned to the KTSP curriculum and Permendiknas standards. The study references classroom observations and interviews to inform instrument design and revisions.

title: Psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy: Where is the psychotherapy research?
research_question: The review poses three central questions: (1) What are the necessary and sufficient components of psychotherapy within PAP, and how should they be standardized? (2) Which psychotherapeutic mechanisms (e.g., alliance, insight, corrective experiences, reality testing) mediate clinical change in PAP, and how should they be measured? (3) How can trial designs (beyond standard RCTs) better detect differences among psychotherapeutic approaches and identify active ingredients? The authors do not test explicit hypotheses but advance propositions: psychotherapy is likely necessary for safety and efficacy; specific psychotherapeutic components may be more influential than pharmacology alone; and RCTs may be insufficiently sensitive to psychotherapy differences due to common factors. Outcomes that would support these propositions include: demonstration that removing or varying psychotherapeutic elements reduces efficacy; evidence that alliance and insight predict outcomes; and trial designs (dismantling, CLPMs) isolating psychotherapy effects. Outcomes that would refute them include: no differences in outcomes when psychotherapy is removed or varied; lack of association between alliance/insight and outcomes; and RCTs robustly detecting psychotherapy differences.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review synthesizing published clinical trials, theoretical models, and methodological literature on PAP and psychotherapy. The authors outline the standard PAP sequence: preparation (psychoeducation, expectations, goal setting, therapeutic alliance), dosing (≥6 hours in a relaxed environment with music and psychotherapeutic support), and integration (meaning-making and generalization of insights). They describe the dominant non-directive supportive approach (derived from psychedelic peak therapy) and note adjunctive modalities (CBT, CBT+MI, eclectic existential/psychodynamic/CBT, ACT, mindfulness, EMDR, IFS, psychoanalysis, group therapy, VR, common factors). The review also references a 2018 RCT (N=75 healthy participants) that manipulated dose and spiritual support to probe psychotherapeutic context.

Methodological recommendations from traditional psychotherapy research are emphasized: (1) manualization—explicitly list all psychotherapy ingredients and their order; publish manuals/supplements detailing hours, principles, and therapist eligibility; (2) mechanism measurement—assess transtheoretical principles (hope/expectations/motivation, alliance, insight, corrective experiences, reality testing) and PAP-specific mechanisms (e.g., mystical-type experiences, awe, acceptance, cognitive flexibility); (3) trial designs—dismantling studies to remove hypothesized active ingredients while holding other factors constant; comparative efficacy/non-inferiority trials to compare active psychotherapeutic approaches; and CLPMs to track within-patient temporal associations and improve causal inference. The review also highlights ethical and regulatory considerations: licensure and training for psychedelic therapists to mitigate boundary violations and coercion risks, and alignment with FDA guidance on psychotherapy in PAP trials. No new data collection, statistical analyses, or preregistration are reported.

title: Identification of Stable Reference MicroRNAs for Normalization of Plasma Exosomal MicroRNA Quantification in Pediatric Hematological Malignancies
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which miRNAs are stably expressed across healthy donor plasma exosomes and pediatric hematological malignancy exosomes, suitable as endogenous reference miRNAs for qRT-PCR normalization? (2) Do candidate miRNAs recommended for plasma/serum (e.g., miR-191-5p) maintain stability in plasma exosomes? (3) Are candidate reference miRNAs stable across disease subtypes (ALCL, BL, HL, mALL) and across therapy (pre- vs post-chemotherapy in ALCL)?

Hypotheses: (a) Certain miRNAs identified as abundant and low-variability in HD plasma exosomes will remain stably expressed across pediatric hematological malignancies and HDs, making them suitable normalizers. (b) miRNAs previously considered stable in plasma/serum may not be stable in exosomes, leading to biased normalization if used. (c) A robust reference miRNA will not differ significantly across disease subtypes or treatment status. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include non-significant differences in Ct values across groups for candidate normalizers, and significant differences for miRNAs known to vary. The study tests these predictions using RNA-seq-based ranking and qRT-PCR validation with appropriate statistical tests.
reference_methodology:
Data sources and preprocessing: The authors retrieved small RNA-seq datasets of HD plasma exosomes from GEO (GSE128359 and GSE100467). Samples with fewer than 2 million reads were excluded. An equal number of samples was randomly selected from each dataset to yield 69 HD samples. miRNAs were identified and quantified using miR&moRe2 v0.2.3. Small RNAs with read sums ≥10 across samples and detected in ≥80% of samples were retained as consistently expressed. Raw counts were normalized with DESeq2, and batch effects were corrected using limma v3.42.2. Corrected normalized expression estimates were used to compute modified Z-scores (Peltier et al.) to rank miRNAs by abundance and variability.

Clinical sample collection: Peripheral blood from pediatric patients enrolled in AIEOP protocols was collected with written informed consent. Healthy donor plasma was also collected. Ethics approval was obtained from each participating institution. At diagnosis, 72 plasma samples were collected: ALCL (n=14), BL (n=15), HL (n=15), mALL (n=15), and HD (n=13). Follow-up plasma from 23 ALCL patients before the last chemotherapy cycle was also collected.

Exosome isolation and characterization: For each plasma sample, two 500 µL fractions were filtered (0.22 µm) and processed independently. Exosomes were isolated using exoRNeasy Midi kit (Qiagen) per MISEV 2018, yielding exosome-enriched fractions. One fraction was used for characterization; the other for RNA extraction. Exosomes were eluted in XE buffer and quantified with FluoroCet Exosome Quantitation Kit. NTA was performed on a Nanosight NS300 (488 nm laser, high-sensitivity sCMOS camera, syringe pump) with samples diluted 1:1000 in particle-free PBS to 1–10 × 10^8 particles/mL. Standard SOP measurements captured 3 videos of 60 s each; 1500 frames per sample were analyzed using NTA 3.1 build 54. TEM (Tecnai G2 Spirit) used formvar/carbon-coated grids with 2% ammonium molybdate negative staining; exosome diameters of 30–150 nm were imaged up to 300 kX.

RNA extraction and qRT-PCR: Exosomes were eluted in 700 µL Qiazol; RNA was extracted with exoRNeasy Midi kit. RNA quality was assessed on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. cDNA synthesis used TaqMan Advanced miRNA cDNA Synthesis Kit. Due to low RNA input, 2 µL RNA per reaction was used for equal loading. Exogenous cel-miR-39 (10 pM) was added as a technical control. qRT-PCR used TaqMan Advanced assays for hsa-miR-26a-5p (ID_477995_mir), hsa-miR-486-5p (ID_478128_mir), hsa-miR-423-5p (ID_478090_mir), hsa-miR-191-5p (ID_477952_mir), and cel-miR-39 (ID_478293_mir). RT products were used in 5 µL PCR reactions at 1:10 dilution. Cycling: 95 °C 20 s; 40 cycles of 95 °C 1 s and 60 °C 20 s. Three technical replicates were run on a ViiA 7 system.

Statistics: GraphPad Prism 7 was used. Shapiro–Wilk tested normality. Two-group comparisons used unpaired t-test (normal) or Mann–Whitney (non-normal). For >2 groups, ordinary one-way ANOVA (normal) or Kruskal–Wallis (non-normal) compared Ct values; Dunn’s test (non-parametric) or Tukey’s test (parametric) performed pairwise comparisons. Significance threshold was p ≤ 0.05.

title: Gene Expression Analyses Support Fallopian Tube Epithelium as the Cell of Origin of Epithelial Ovarian Cancer
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do EOC gene expression profiles cluster more closely with fallopian tube (FN/FA) than with normal ovary (ON), supporting a fallopian tube origin? (2) Are EOC markers (FOLR1, MSLN, MUC16, HE4, etc.) overexpressed in EOC relative to the true cell of origin (FN), or are they retained from the origin (passengers)? (3) How do folate transporters/receptors and one-carbon metabolism/folate homeostasis genes differ between EOC and normal tissues, and what do these differences imply about folate handling and methylation in EOC?

Hypotheses: (H1) EOC originates from fallopian tube epithelium, so EOC will show gene expression profiles more similar to FN/FA than to ON. (H2) EOC markers previously considered overexpressed in EOC are not overexpressed relative to FN, indicating they are retained from the cell of origin rather than drivers of tumorogenesis. (H3) FOLR1 is highly expressed in EOC due to retention from FN, not de novo upregulation in ON. (H4) One-carbon pathway genes will show tumor-associated changes (e.g., TYMS upregulation, altered folate turnover via GGH), reflecting increased metabolic demands and methylation requirements in tumors.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if EOC clusters with FA/FN and separates from ON. H2 is supported if EOC vs FN comparisons show no significant upregulation of EOC markers. H3 is supported if FOLR1 is not differentially expressed in EOC vs FN. H4 is supported if TYMS and GGH are upregulated in tumors and methylation pathway genes are downregulated.
reference_methodology:
Design: Focused gene expression profiling using a custom TaqMan Low Density Array (TLDA) targeting folate transporters/receptors, one-carbon metabolism/folate homeostasis, known EOC markers, signal transduction, steroid receptors, and miscellaneous genes. Statistical thresholds for differential expression were p ≤ 0.05 and ≥2-fold change.

Samples: Fresh-frozen tissues were obtained from ProteoGenex Inc. Total RNA was sourced from Asterand and Origene. ON (n=22) and FN (n=9) were from unrelated donors. EOC (n=68) and NAT (n=30) were from Asterand; 21 EOC, 30 NAT, and 8 FA were from ProteoGenex. All institutions had IRB approval for human subject research. Samples were from individual donors. Donor demographics and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 2 (mean age ON 62.5±12.3; FN 57.7±10.3; EOC 52.4±12.6; FA 60.1±4.9; race predominantly White/Caucasian). Tumor grading (EOC) included Grade 1 (17/68, 25.0%), Grade 2 (18/68, 26.4%), Grade 3 (23/68, 33.8%), unspecified (10/68, 14.7%); FA grade distribution was not reported. Stage distribution (EOC): I (19/68, 27.9%), II (6/68, 11.7%), III (27/68, 39.7%), IV (8/68, 11.8%). FA stage distribution was not reported. No macrodissection or tumor enrichment was performed; tissues may contain mixed cell populations.

RNA isolation and quality control: Total RNA was isolated using TRI Reagent (Sigma). Concentration and quality were assessed by Nanodrop and Agilent Bioanalyzer.

Gene selection: An Affymetrix Exon Array ST 1.0 (100 ng RNA) was used to identify genes correlating with FOLR1 expression in EOC samples. Using GeneData Analyst, 27 genes with |correlation| > 0.8 were selected as additional targets.

TLDA design and qPCR: The TLDA (384-well microfluidic card) included 96 genes (90 genes of interest; 6 endogenous controls) grouped into: folate transporters/receptors (6), one-carbon metabolism/folate homeostasis (19), known EOC markers (13), signal transduction (19), steroid receptors (3), miscellaneous (30), and endogenous controls (6) (Table 1; Supplemental Table S1). cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg total RNA using High Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Life Technologies) for ovarian samples and SuperScript VILO MasterMix (Life Technologies) for fallopian samples. For each sample, 100 ng equivalent cDNA was combined with TaqMan Gene Expression Master Mix and run on the ABI 7900HT with standard cycling. Ct thresholds were automatically calculated; TYMS was manually set due to software limitations. ΔCt was computed using the six endogenous controls in ExpressionSuite v1.0. 2^-ΔCt values were exported to Excel and analyzed in GeneData Analyst.

Clustering and PCA: Two-dimensional hierarchical clustering used Manhattan distance and complete linkage with row-scaled gene expression (values represented as ratios above/below row mean). PCA used a covariance matrix. Analyses were performed in GeneData Analyst. Comparisons included EOC vs ON and EOC vs NAT, and EOC vs FN and EOC vs FA, with emphasis on using the tissue of origin (FN) as comparator.

title: Epidote-bearing hydrothermal ductile shear zones: Evidence of tectonically driven fluid flow in the Larderello geothermal field (Northern Apennines, Italy)
field_subfield: Geology — Structural Geology and Geothermal Systems
research_question:
Research question: Did ductile shear zones act as channelized conduits for hot metasomatic fluids during the early evolution of the Larderello geothermal field, enabling heat advection from deep magmatic/metamorphic sources to shallow crustal levels?

Hypotheses: (1) Epidote-bearing layers and skarn pods formed synkinematically with ductile shear deformation, indicating channelized fluid flow localized within a narrow zone. (2) Mineralogical and microstructural evidence (synkinematic growth of epidote, illite, amphibole; C/S fabrics; dynamic recrystallization) will constrain temperatures >300°C and support a ductile regime. (3) The presence of REE- and Th/U-enriched allanite/monazite in epidote layers indicates involvement of residual volatile-rich fluids from shallow intrusions. (4) The inferred ductile shear zone connects deep (4–5 km) hot sources to shallow (1.5–2 km) levels, explaining thick thermal aureoles and widespread metasomatic assemblages.

Support/refutation criteria: Support would include synkinematic growth textures, ductile microstructures, consistent geothermometry (~300°C), absence of fracture-controlled vein networks, and spatial association of skarn with epidote-bearing shear layers. Refutation would involve purely brittle vein-controlled mineralization without synkinematic growth or ductile fabrics, or temperatures inconsistent with ductile deformation.
reference_methodology:
Study area and sampling: The Sasso 22 geothermal well (SA-22) was drilled in the central Larderello field. The Phyllite Complex sequence, affected by Pliocene thermal metamorphism, hosts decimetre-thick skarn levels cored at 1600 m depth. The core was drilled vertically but not oriented with respect to geographic coordinates, limiting structural orientation determination to dip only.

Petrography and thin-section preparation: Hand-specimen observations and thin sections were prepared normal to foliation and parallel to the mineral lineation (XZ plane of the strain ellipsoid). Thin sections were examined under plane-polarized and crossed-polarized light to document fabrics, grain size, shape-preferred orientations, and synkinematic growth of epidote, illite, and amphibole.

SEM-EDS mineral chemistry: Analyses were performed using a Philips XL30 micro-analytical system coupled with EDAX DX4 at 20 kV accelerating voltage, 0.1 nA beam current, and 100 s live time. Analyses were normalized to 100% by EDAX software. Representative analyses were reported for epidote and amphibole (calculated on 12.5 and 23 oxygen atoms, respectively; total Fe in epidote as Fe2O3, amphibole as FeO) and for illite and muscovite (formula proportions calculated assuming Fe3+ = 86.5% of total Fe; 11 oxygen atoms). Illite compositions were evaluated using Al–Fe–Mg diagrams and geothermometry relationships (Bishop & Bird, 1987) to estimate formation temperatures.

Structural analysis: The presence of C/S fabrics (Lister & Snoke, 1984) and shear planes cutting S-planes at low angles (15°–30°) was documented. Dynamic recrystallization of quartz and white mica, synkinematic growth of epidote and illite on C and S planes, and quartz porphyroclast deformation were used to infer ductile deformation conditions and synkinematic mineral growth. The absence of fracture systems and vein-controlled mineralization was noted.

Geothermometry and fluid inferences: Illite geothermometry (Bishop & Bird, 1987) was applied to hydrothermal illite in epidote layers and to metamorphic muscovite in phyllites to estimate temperatures (~300°C). The presence of allanite and monazite in epidote layers, enriched in REE, Th, and U, was used to infer involvement of residual volatile-rich fluids from shallow intrusions.

Comparative context: The study situates findings within the known polyphase hydrothermal evolution of Larderello (450–670°C early magmatic/metamorphic fluids; later meteoric-dominated propylitic assemblages) and the regional tectonic framework of Upper Miocene–Pliocene extension and low-angle normal faulting.

title: ДОСЛІДЖЕННЯ ВИЛУЧЕННЯ ФОСФАТІВ НА АНІОНІТАХ ТА СТВОРЕННЯ БЕЗВІДХОДНОЇ ПЕРЕРОБКИ РЕГЕНЕРАЦІЙНИХ РОЗЧИНІВ
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which anion exchanger (AB-17-8 vs Dowex Marathon WBA) achieves higher phosphate removal capacity under dynamic conditions in distilled and tap water? (2) How do competing anions (chloride, sulfate) and pH affect phosphate uptake capacity and breakthrough? (3) Can regeneration with NaCl or NH4Cl (10–15%) achieve high desorption of phosphate and sulfate, enabling reuse of regeneration solutions? (4) Can phosphorus be recovered as struvite from ammonium chloride regeneration streams, and what conditions (pH, MgCl2 stoichiometry) maximize recovery?

Hypotheses: (H1) AB-17-8 (highly basic) will exhibit higher phosphate capacity than Dowex Marathon WBA (low basic) due to stronger affinity for phosphate anions and pH effects. (H2) Sulfate, being a strong-acid anion, will compete more strongly with phosphate than chloride, reducing phosphate capacity; OH-form will increase phosphate dissociation and capacity relative to Cl-form. (H3) NH4Cl regeneration will enable efficient phosphate desorption and, with MgCl2 addition at pH ≥9, will precipitate struvite, allowing reuse of regeneration solutions. (H4) Sulfate can be removed from regeneration streams by gypsum precipitation to facilitate reuse.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if AB-17-8 shows higher capacities than Dowex. H2 is supported if sulfate presence reduces phosphate capacity and OH-form outperforms Cl-form. H3 is supported if desorption reaches ≥95% and struvite precipitation reduces phosphate and Mg2+ concentrations. H4 is supported if gypsum precipitation removes sulfate sufficiently for reuse.
reference_methodology:
Design: Dynamic ion-exchange experiments in columns with two anion exchangers: AB-17-8 (highly basic) and Dowex Marathon WBA (low basic). Two forms were tested for AB-17-8: chloride (Cl−) and hydroxide (OH−). Regeneration and recovery experiments used NaCl and NH4Cl (10–15%).

Materials and media: Ion-exchange beds of 20 cm3 volume (19 mm diameter) were used. Distilled water and tap water (characteristics close to Bortnichy aeration station wastewater) served as feed. Tap water sulfate concentrations were varied (e.g., 36.7–57 mg/m3 in experiments; up to 570 mg/m3 in performance tests). Phosphate solutions included Na2HPO4 at 170 mg/m3 and 90 mg-ekv/m3 (as reported in figures). AB-17-8 was converted to OH-form using 4% NaOH.

Operating conditions: Feed flow rates were 10–15 cm3/min. The volume of feed processed per run ranged from 0.1 to 1.0 m3. Regeneration flow rate was 1–3 cm3/min. Specific regeneration consumption (qn) was reported in cm3/cm3.

Measurements: Phosphate concentration was determined by spectrophotometry using the molybdenum blue method. Sulfate concentration was measured by titration with barium chloride. Chloride was analyzed by titration (method not fully specified). pH was measured by potentiometry. Alkalinity and hardness were determined by titrimetry. Breakthrough curves tracked outlet concentrations of phosphate, chloride, sulfate, and pH versus volume processed.

Capacity and efficiency calculations: Total dynamic capacity (ПОДЄ) and breakthrough capacity (ОДЄпр) were computed from mass balance: m = V(Cп − Cр), where V is volume processed, Cп initial concentration, and Cр equilibrium concentration. Regeneration efficiency Z was calculated as Z = 100% × mд.с.і / mс.і, where mд.с.і is the mass of desorbed ions and mс.і is the mass of the corresponding ion initially sorbed.

Regeneration and recovery procedures: AB-17-8 in phosphate form was regenerated with 10% or 15% NaCl or NH4Cl. For struvite recovery, ammonium chloride regeneration solutions were treated with MgCl2 at pH 9 (adjusted with ammonia) in stoichiometric amounts; struvite precipitate was collected on a “blue ribbon” filter, and filtrate was analyzed for phosphate and Mg2+. For sulfate removal from regeneration streams, calcium chloride was added to precipitate gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O), followed by settling, filtration, and reuse of the clarified solution.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human or animal subjects.

title: Risk Adjusted Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions for the Management of COVID-19 in South Africa
field_subfield: Public Health — Epidemiology and Infectious Disease Modeling
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can the OxCGRT stringency index be mapped to South Africa’s 5-tier alert system in a way that supports quantitative prediction of COVID-19 transmission? (2) What is the magnitude and uncertainty of the linearized transmission coefficient αs for South Africa relative to global estimates? (3) How do different alert levels (L1–L5) affect epidemic trajectories (peak timing, amplitude, cumulative cases) under a latent SIRD model with dynamic β(t,p)? (4) What is the required rate of change of αs relative to p to maintain sub-criticality and avoid overwhelming healthcare capacity? (5) How does adherence to NPIs (αs) evolve in a province like Gauteng, and how should parameters be re-calibrated to improve predictive accuracy?

Hypotheses: (H1) Transmission can be linearized with respect to OxCGRT stringency, yielding a stable αs with small statistical uncertainty. (H2) South Africa’s αs is compatible with the global average. (H3) Relaxing stringency (Δp<0) delays the apex but increases its amplitude; staged, slow relaxation is necessary to remain sub-critical. (H4) A sub-critical condition exists where the rate of increase of αs must exceed the rate of decrease of p. (H5) Increased adherence to NPIs (higher αs) in Gauteng can be empirically detected and re-calibrated to improve forecasts. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include consistent αs estimates with narrow CIs, predicted delays/amplitude changes under Δp, and improved fit after re-calibration.
reference_methodology:
Model: A latent SIRD model with dynamic infection characteristics is used, incorporating both asymptomatic and symptomatic infections. The transmission rate β(t,p) depends on the OxCGRT stringency index p(t) and is parameterized as β(t,p) = βf − (1 + e^{−br t}) β0 αs Δp (Eq. (4)), where t=0 corresponds to the end of the initial lockdown period (pmax=100), Δp = p − pmax, and br is an adjustment time. The model assumes constant daily recovery rate γ0 and daily mortality rate d0 during the post-lockdown phase.

Data and parameter estimation: South African COVID-19 time-series case data from the NICD and Department of Health are used to fit parameters before and during lockdown. Global analysis indicates αs ≈ 0.01 ± 0.0017 (95% CI) on average; South Africa’s αs is estimated as 0.0078 ± 0.00036 (95% CI). For South Africa, fitted parameters are γ0=0.022 (68% CI: 0.022 ± 0.001), β0=0.28 (68% CI: 0.28 ± 0.003), βf=0.06, pm=100, and αs=0.0078. The adjustment time br is reported as ~1 day from South African specifics but ~10 days from global analysis; the study adopts br≈10 days for temporal evolution. A mortality rate of 2.5% is targeted (25% 68% CI), based on a Wuhan mortality matrix and multi-dimensional Gauteng data; the text notes current national mortality stabilized at ~2%.

OxCGRT mapping and stringency index: The OxCGRT stringency index p is computed as a normalized average of indicators S1–S7 (Eq. (3)), omitting the general/targeted distinction in South Africa. Indicator cardinalities are set as N1=4, N2=4, N3=1, N4=4, N5=1, N6=4, N7=2. For each alert level L1–L5, S1–S7 values are assigned (e.g., S2: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1; S3 and S5: 1 for all levels; S4: 0, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1; S6: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1; S7: 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 1). S1 is time-dependent due to staged school reopening (June 1, 2020 onward), making p(t) time-varying (Figure 1). Stringency boundaries for L1–L5 are reported as minima and maxima (e.g., L3: 60.7–75.0; L5: 85.71–100).

Uncertainty and validation: Two main uncertainty sources are considered: (1) αs with 2–3% statistical error and ~10% inter-country variation; (2) β0 and γ0 with 68% CIs (β0=0.28 ± 0.003; γ0=0.022 ± 0.001). Predictions are presented with uncertainty bands (Figures 3 and C.7). Gauteng Province predictions (Levels 4–5) using national parameters underpredict May 2020 cases, attributed to increased adherence; re-calibration of αs using May data (up to May 26, 2020) yields a 20% increase in αs relative to pre-lockdown. The model excludes local hot-spot dynamics, which are acknowledged as a limitation.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported.

title: Building Evalution Tools to Assess the Usability of Primary Care Clinics
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How can a usability assessment framework for primary care clinics integrate ISO-aligned parameters (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction) with psychosocially supportive design theory to produce actionable evaluation tools? (2) What design features in a primary care clinic most strongly influence effectiveness (functionality, privacy, safety), efficiency (workflow, adjacency, circulation), and satisfaction (physical, social, psychological comfort) for staff, patients, and visitors? (3) Can a case study clinic analysis using behavioral observation, staff survey, and a Usability Matrix yield practical design recommendations and a validated toolkit for future evaluations?

Hypotheses: (H1) A literature-derived Building Usability Framework can be operationalized into a Usability Matrix that systematically maps observed design features to effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction subdimensions. (H2) Empirical observations and staff feedback will reveal specific, clinic-specific usability issues (e.g., exam room size/location, lab counter space, check-out wayfinding) that align with the framework’s dimensions. (H3) Integrating the framework with the Usability Matrix will produce a revised survey and toolkit that can be used by architects and researchers to evaluate and improve clinic usability. Outcomes supporting H1–H3 include successful mapping of observed features to the matrix, identification of actionable design problems, and compilation of a practical tool kit.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-site case study of a primary care clinic in a Maryland suburb. The clinic is a one-story facility (~9,000 sq ft), with five full-time providers, 16 exam rooms, and approximately 18 full-time staff (5 providers, 5 certified medical assistants [CMAs], 5 medical office assistants [MOAs], 2 registered nurses [RNs], 1 office manager; plus part-time administrative assistant and specialists). The clinic sees ~100 patients/day. Programmatic elements include waiting area, check-in/reception, exam rooms, procedure room, lab area, staff lounge, provider offices, workstations, and storage (clean utility, soiled utility, biohazardous waste, medical supply closets, sharps room).

Data collection: (1) Initial interview with the head nurse to gather preliminary clinic operations and spatial information. (2) Behavioral observation totaling 40 hours: 24 hours across three areas (check-in, waiting, lab) on full workdays (9 a.m.–5 p.m.), and 16 hours in periodic 2–3 hour sessions across exam rooms, procedure room, provider offices, and workstations until core workflows were understood. (3) Staff survey administered to clinic staff (professions recorded: provider, CMA, MOA, RN). The survey comprised eight sections (check-in/waiting; exam room; procedure room; lab; communication systems; workstations/offices; check-out; storage) with 1–5 Likert items and open-ended questions. The survey also collected staff role and work location on the facility plan.

Instruments: (a) Usability Observation Tool (Table 4) documented furniture, equipment, tasks, interactions, and spatial attributes at observation points. (b) Coding Analysis Table (Table 5) categorized observations into effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction dimensions and color-coded spatial attributes (green: working; red: missing/not working; black: other ideas). (c) Staff survey sections (Tables 6–13) mapped to observed issues (e.g., exam room size, lab counter space, check-out wayfinding).

Analysis: Observations and coding were analyzed using JMP Pro 9 to organize and compare ratings across staff roles and sections. The Usability Matrix (Table 15) was used to integrate findings into the Building Usability Framework (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction) and to identify gaps for survey refinement. The final survey and matrix were compiled into a Building Usability Evaluation Tool-Kit (Appendix E).

Ethics: No IRB approval, consent procedures, or data privacy protocols are reported. The study is a single-site observational case study with staff surveys.

title: MAGNETO cardiography parameters to predict future Sudden Cardiac Death (MAGNETO-SCD) or ventricular events from implantable cardioverter defibrillators: study protocol, design and rationale
research_question:
Primary research question: Can MCG parameters measured with the Vitalscan device accurately and precisely predict future ICD therapies for ventricular arrhythmias in patients meeting current ICD/CRT-D criteria? Secondary questions: (a) Do MCG parameters predict future VA events? (b) Does the Vitalscan device replicate findings from prior SQUID-based MCG studies (e.g., late QRS fields, fragmentation, QT spatial dispersion)? (c) How does MCG compare to ECG parameters and LVEF in predicting VA? (d) How do MCG parameters correlate with LVEF and CMRI LGE? (e) What is the effect of ICD therapy on QoL? (f) Can MCG identify patients at risk of inappropriate ICD therapies despite low SCD risk?

Hypotheses (implicit from protocol rationale): (1) MCG depolarization features (e.g., QRS fragmentation) and repolarization features (e.g., QT spatial dispersion SIn) will predict appropriate ICD therapies and VA events with clinically useful sensitivity and specificity. (2) The Vitalscan device will reproduce prior SQUID-based MCG findings. (3) MCG may outperform ECG metrics in certain subgroups (e.g., non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with normal QRS duration). (4) MCG parameters will correlate with LVEF and CMRI LGE. (5) MCG may identify patients at risk of inappropriate therapies, informing implant decisions. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include high sensitivity/specificity for MCG features, replication of prior SQUID results, superior predictive performance vs ECG/LVEF in specified subgroups, and significant correlations with LVEF/LGE.
reference_methodology:
Design: Prospective multicentre observational study at University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust and University Hospital North Midlands NHS Trust, UK. No randomization; all eligible participants receive MCG.

Participants: Adults ≥18 years listed for first-time ICD or CRT-D implantation per national/international guidelines (primary or secondary prevention, any etiology), without an existing device. Exclusions: inability to lie still on a bed (max 30° upright) for 15 minutes; ongoing MI or active ischemia (ECG changes, chest pain, elevated biomarkers); clinically unstable; thoracic metallic implants (pacing/defibrillator devices, metallic valves) due to magnetic interference.

Baseline assessment: Demographics, medical history, medications, LVEF (echocardiography, CMRI, or nuclear imaging), resting 12-lead ECG, and MCG. MCG acquisition: Vitalscan device, 2100 Hz sampling, 37-array hexagonal sensor head; recording duration 15 minutes to enable signal averaging. Bed: MRI-safe aluminum to reduce vibration. Patient positioning: horizontal with up to 30° head-up tilt if tolerated. Sensor alignment: center of hexagonal array at the 5th intercostal space, 3–7 cm left of the left sternal border (~V3). Periodic archiving from the device ensures data integrity and storage capacity.

ICD programming and follow-up: ICDs programmed with extended detection algorithms to avoid labeling non-sustained arrhythmias as therapy candidates. Standard ICD clinic follow-up (6 weeks post-implant, then 6–12 monthly; remote monitoring per patient preference). Data collected include arrhythmia events, ventricular ectopy burden, and QoL. Baseline biomarkers: high-sensitivity troponin, NT-proBNP, CRP, high-sensitivity CRP, interleukin-6.

Endpoints: Primary—delivery of appropriate ICD therapy for VA (reviewed by principal investigators and Trial Steering Committee). Secondary—future VA; replication of prior SQUID findings; comparison of MCG vs ECG and LVEF predictive power; correlations with LVEF; QoL impact of ICD therapy; identification of patients at risk of inappropriate ICD therapies.

Sample size and power: Target N=270 based on an event rate of 23% at 20 months (from primary and secondary prevention ICD trials). Sensitivity is prioritized (prevalence <50%), aiming for ≥80% sensitivity with a 5% margin of error; NPV >90% is targeted. Minimum follow-up 4.5 years; maximum 6 years.

Ethics and oversight: Approved by Yorkshire and Humber Sheffield Research Ethics Committee (19/YH/0143) and Health Research Authority (IRAS 254466). Conducted under Good Clinical Practice and the Declaration of Helsinki. Trial Steering Committee (TSC) includes arrhythmia specialists and a Patient and Public Engagement representative; annual meetings to review recruitment, endpoints, and adverse events. Data protection under GDPR and the Data Protection Act.

title: Implementation of Learning Models To Improve Elementary School Students' Critical Thinking Abilities
research_question: Research question: Which learning models are associated with improvements in elementary school students’ critical thinking abilities, and how do these models align with the components of critical thinking? The review does not state explicit hypotheses. Implicit expectations are that student-centered, collaborative, and problem-solving learning models will be linked to enhanced critical thinking outcomes compared to traditional, teacher-centered, memorization-focused instruction. Outcomes supporting this expectation include reports of increased critical questioning, analysis, and reflection, as well as improved performance on tasks requiring evaluation and synthesis. Outcomes that would refute or nuance the expectation would include evidence of no effect, adverse effects, or inconsistent findings across contexts. The review aggregates qualitative and quantitative findings from prior studies to assess the strength and consistency of these associations.
reference_methodology:
Design: Analytical descriptive literature review. The authors followed Kuhlthau’s library research process, which includes topic selection, information exploration, determination of research focus, collection of data sources, preparation for data presentation, and report preparation. The analysis technique is descriptive content analysis, used to obtain valid, context-relevant inferences by selecting, comparing, combining, and sorting meanings until relevant data are identified. The approach is not designed to test causal relationships between variables but to describe aspects and characteristics of the reviewed literature.

Data sources: The review synthesizes multiple prior studies on learning models and critical thinking in elementary education. Specific cited works include: Dewi (2018) on experiential learning; Intan (2018) and Putra (2019) on Contextual Teaching and Learning (CTL); Fajar (2020) on flipped classroom; Utami (2020) on technology-based learning; Mira (2018) on jigsaw; Gita (2019) on STEM integration; Endah (2022) on collaborative learning; Cahya (2021) and Taufik (2022) on Problem-Based Learning (PBL); Sari (2018) on inquiry-based science reading; Kurnia (2019) on problem-solving-based science learning; Joko (2020) on inquiry-based learning; Oktaviani (2020) on project-based learning; Lestari (2021) on mind mapping; Rina (2021) on reciprocal teaching; Nia (2022) on blended learning; and foundational work by Ennis (2000) on critical thinking components. The review also references contextual observations and prior reports on the state of critical thinking in Indonesian elementary education (Wulandari, 2019; Purwanto & Santosa, 2020; Andayani, 2018; Setiawan, 2017).

Procedures: The authors systematically identified and examined studies that apply specific learning models to elementary school settings and report outcomes related to critical thinking. They organized findings into three categories: student-centered learning, collaborative learning, and problem-solving models. The synthesis emphasizes reported mechanisms (e.g., active exploration, contextualization, collaboration, structured inquiry) and outcomes (e.g., improved analysis, questioning, reflection). No meta-analytic procedures, effect size calculations, or formal quality appraisal criteria are reported. No details are provided on databases searched, search strings, inclusion/exclusion criteria, screening processes, or risk-of-bias assessments.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable for a literature review; no new human subjects data were collected.

title: Education and Science
field_subfield: Education — Educational Leadership and School Effectiveness
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do student-level SES and academic self-efficacy directly predict academic achievement? (2) Do school-level instructional leadership and school culture predict achievement directly or indirectly via collective teacher efficacy? (3) How do instructional leadership and school culture relate to each other and to collective teacher efficacy?

Hypotheses: H1: As students’ SES increases, their academic achievement scores increase. H2: Higher academic self-efficacy perceptions are associated with higher academic achievement. H3: Teachers’ perceptions of instructional leadership behaviors of principals significantly predict perceptions of school culture. H4: Teachers’ perceptions of school culture significantly predict collective teacher efficacy. H5: Higher collective teacher efficacy is associated with higher student achievement. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would show significant positive standardized paths from SES and self-efficacy to achievement, from instructional leadership to culture, from culture to collective efficacy, and from collective efficacy to achievement, with acceptable multilevel SEM fit.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional, two-level structural equation modeling (SEM) with hierarchical data (students nested within schools).

Setting and sampling: 30 secondary schools in Çankırı province, Turkey, selected via stratified sampling proportional to the number of teachers and students. The population included 40 secondary schools across 8 districts; the sample included 194 teachers and 948 eighth-grade students. Teachers were those assigned to the sampled classes; students were eighth graders. Data collection occurred in the 2017–2018 academic year.

Participants: 194 teachers (response rate 97% of 200 distributed) and 948 students (response rate 94.8% of 1000 distributed). Table 1 reports district-level counts and descriptive statistics for students (mean score 76.40, SD 15.40; range 21.6–100). Gender distribution: 492 female and 456 male students.

Measures: Academic achievement was the average of six course scores (Turkish, Mathematics, Science and Technology, English, Religious Culture and Moral Knowledge, History of Revolution and Kemalism). SES was constructed from three indicators (monthly income, mother’s education, father’s education) via EFA, which explained 62% of variance. The composite SES was computed as SES = 0.807*(mother’s education) + 0.827*(father’s education) + 0.728*(income)/1.864. Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (ASES; Jinks & Morgan, 1999; Turkish adaptation by Öncü, 2012) measured student self-efficacy across three dimensions (skills, learning environment, quality of teaching) with 19 items on a 5-point Likert scale. Instructional Leadership Scale (ILS; Alig-Mielcarek, 2003; Turkish adaptation by Şahin, 2011b) measured teacher perceptions of instructional leadership across three dimensions (professional development, shared goals, feedback) with 23 items on a 5-point Likert scale. Organizational Culture Scale (OCS; Şahin, 2011a) measured five dimensions (school leadership, collegiality/personal support, teacher cooperation, development culture, teaching culture) with 37 items on a 5-point Likert scale. Collective Teacher Efficacy Scale (CTS; Goddard et al., 2000; Turkish adaptation by Kurt, 2012) measured collective efficacy with 21 items on a 5-point Likert scale.

Reliability and validity: ASES—Cronbach’s alpha .71; CFA fit indices reported as close to cut points (χ²=376.64, df=149, p>.05; RMSEA=.07; NNFI=.92; CFI=.93). ILS—Cronbach’s alpha .95; CFA fit indices close to cut points (χ²=581.06, df=227, p>.05; SRMR=.04; NFI=.96; NNFI=.98; CFI=.98). OCS—Cronbach’s alpha .97; CFA fit indices close to cut points (χ²=1502.67, df=619, χ²/df=2.42, p>.05; NFI=.95; NNFI=.97; CFI=.97). CTS—Cronbach’s alpha .80; CFA fit indices close to cut points (χ²=578.62, df=312, p>.05; RMSEA=.08; CFI=.99; NFI=.97; NNFI=.97). Prior adaptation reports for ASES indicated KMO=.83, Bartlett χ²=927.03 (df=186, p<.000), reliability .80, and dimension reliabilities ranging .81–.51.

Procedures: Scales were administered to teachers and students by the Çankırı Provincial Directorate of National Education Research and Development Unit. Completion time was ~10 minutes for students and ~20 minutes for teachers. Data were checked for normality via scatterplots and descriptive statistics; skewness and kurtosis were <±3, and means/medians were similar.

Analysis: Correlations were computed within and between schools. Two-level SEM (Mplus 8; LISREL 9.30; SPSS 23) estimated standardized paths and model fit. Model fit indices reported: χ²=136.72, df=58, RMSEA=.05, CFI=.98, TLI=.93. Standard errors and p-values were reported for key paths. No details on missing data handling, random effects, or robustness checks were provided.

title: Diffusion-Equation-Based Electrical Modeling for High-Power Lithium Titanium Oxide Batteries
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a diffusion-equation-based ECM that explicitly models diffusion polarization (via a SOL shift term) accurately predict terminal voltage of LTO batteries across SOC and current rates, including near cutoffs? (2) Does embedding diffusion polarization reduce the need for SOC-dependent tuning of circuit elements (R0, R1, C1) compared to conventional ECMs? (3) How does the proposed model compare to a second-order RC (Thevenin) model under galvanostatic and dynamic profiles?

Hypotheses: (H1) Diffusion polarization dominates voltage loss in LTO cells and varies with SOC; modeling it explicitly will improve voltage prediction accuracy relative to models that rely on interfacial polarization alone. (H2) The proposed model will maintain low terminal voltage error (<3%) across 1C–8C galvanostatic tests and dynamic DST/FUDS profiles, outperforming a second-order RC model whose errors increase with C-rate and dynamic stress. (H3) The diffusion term can be parameterized with a linear current dependence (λ, μ) and a diffusion time constant (τ), enabling accurate identification from three-electrode and JEVS tests.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if diffusion polarization is quantitatively larger than interfacial polarization and exhibits SOC dependence. H2 is supported if maximum voltage errors remain <3% across conditions, with clear superiority over the Thevenin model. H3 is supported if identified parameters yield accurate voltage reconstructions across tests.
reference_methodology:
Tested cell: LTO battery with Li4Ti5O12 anode and LiCoO2 cathode (nominal capacity 25 Ah; voltage range 1.8–2.8 V; max charge current 8C/200 A; max discharge current 12C/300 A). Temperature was held at 25°C in a GIANT FORCE CO. chamber (−60°C to 100°C, 0.1°C resolution).

Test platform: Arbin multi-channel 5V–100A tester (voltage accuracy ±0.02%; current accuracy ±0.05%).

Galvanostatic tests: Constant-current charge/discharge at 1C, 2C, 4C, 6C, and 8C. Protocol: charge/discharge at 1C to cutoff; then charge/discharge in the opposite direction at the five rates. Additional JEVS-based internal resistance characterization was conducted between 10% and 90% SOC at 10% SOC intervals (details of JEVS steps not fully enumerated in the text).

Three-electrode configuration: Positive electrode LiCoO2, negative electrode Li4Ti5O12, and lithium metal as reference electrode. Three channels measured: full-cell voltage and the voltages of the positive and negative electrodes relative to the reference. Two representative current conditions were used: 0.1C (2.5 A; quasi-equilibrium) and 8C (200 A; high-rate). The full-cell voltage is U = UPE − UNE. Steady-state vertical voltage differences between electrodes reflect ohmic and interfacial polarization; R1 was obtained by dividing the difference by current and subtracting R0.

OCV and OCP characterization: Full-cell OCV vs. SOC was reconstructed by averaging low-rate charge/discharge curves. Electrode OCP vs. SOL was obtained from half-cells (positive material from disassembled full cell; negative material Li4Ti5O12; reference Li metal). OCP curves were scaled (αPE, αNE) and offset (βPE, βNE) to match the full-cell OCV, ensuring electrode capacities are consistent (QFull = QPE/αPE = QNE/αNE). SOL(t) is computed by integrating current over time (Equation (7)).

Model structure and identification: The proposed model includes two controlled OCP sources (positive and negative), series R0, and an interfacial RC branch (R1, C1). Diffusion polarization is represented by a SOL shift ΔSOL(I) = λ·I + μ with time constant τ. The terminal voltage is U = OCPPE[SOLPE(t)] − OCPNE[SOLNE(t)] − R0·I − R1·I·(1 − e^(−t/(R1·C1))). SOL(t) = SOL(t0) − (1/Q)∫I(t)dt (Equation (7)). Identification steps: (1) Reconstruct full-cell OCV from electrode OCPs and identify α, β, and R0; (2) Fit three-electrode data at 0.1C and 8C to obtain λ, μ, and R1; (3) Fit JEVS 60 s pulses to identify τ (with C1 set to infinity) and JEVS 10 s segments to identify C1. Final parameters were averaged across SOCs. Particle swarm optimization was used for τ identification.

Validation protocols: Galvanostatic charging and discharging at 1C and 8C; dynamic DST and FUDS profiles (typical current profiles shown in Figure 4). Errors were computed as absolute voltage differences between model predictions and measurements. No random seeds or statistical tests were reported; no degradation or temperature-variation robustness tests were reported.

title: The N3RO trial: a randomised controlled trial of docosahexaenoic acid to reduce bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants < 29 weeks' gestation
research_question:
Primary research question: Does enteral DHA supplementation (60 mg/kg/day) reduce the incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) at 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age (PMA) in preterm infants born before 29 weeks’ gestation compared with an iso-caloric control emulsion without DHA?

Secondary questions: Does DHA reduce the composite endpoint of death before 36 weeks’ PMA or BPD? Does it shorten duration and reduce intensity of respiratory support (including endotracheal ventilation, non-invasive positive pressure support, and supplemental oxygen), and reduce use of caffeine, postnatal steroids, and diuretics for lung disease? Does it improve BPD severity, feeding tolerance, growth (weight, length, head circumference z-scores), and reduce length of hospital stay? Does it reduce major morbidities (retinopathy of prematurity, intraventricular haemorrhage, cystic periventricular leukomalacia/porencephaly, sepsis, necrotising enterocolitis)?

Hypotheses: The primary hypothesis is that DHA supplementation will reduce BPD incidence at 36 weeks’ PMA by 10% absolute (from 51.4% to 41.4%; 19% relative reduction). Secondary hypotheses include reductions in the death-or-BPD composite, shorter respiratory support duration, lower need for assisted ventilation and supplemental oxygen, reduced steroid/diuretic use, improved BPD severity, better feeding tolerance, and improved growth. Exploratory subgroup hypotheses posit potential effect modification by sex and gestational age (<27 vs 27–28 completed weeks). Outcomes supporting the hypotheses would include statistically significant relative risk reductions for BPD and related endpoints; null or adverse findings would refute or nuance the hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Design: Multicentre, parallel-group, randomised, blinded, controlled trial with two arms (DHA emulsion vs control emulsion). Blinding is maintained for participants, families, clinicians, data collectors, outcome assessors, and data analysts. The intervention and control emulsions are identical in viscosity, colour, packaging, and labelling, differing only in DHA content.

Setting and centres: Sponsoring institution and Trial Coordinating Centre: Women’s and Children’s Health Research Institute, Adelaide, South Australia. Participating centres: 13 perinatal centres across Australia, New Zealand, and Singapore (e.g., Flinders Medical Centre, Women’s and Children’s Hospital, Royal Women’s Hospital, John Hunter Hospital, Monash Medical Centre, King Edward Memorial Hospital, Mercy Hospital for Women, Liverpool Hospital, Royal Hospital for Women, Mater Mothers’ Hospital; Wellington Hospital; Waikato Hospital; KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital).

Participants: Preterm infants born before 29 weeks’ gestation, within 3 days of first enteral feed, with a legally acceptable representative able to provide informed consent. Exclusion criteria include major congenital or chromosomal abnormalities; breastfeeding mothers taking >250 mg DHA/day who do not wish to stop; participation in another fatty acid study; and receipt of intravenous lipid emulsions containing fish oil as early parenteral nutrition support (e.g., Omegaven, SMOFlipid, Lipoplus).

Interventions: DHA emulsion provides 60 mg/kg/day DHA via a microencapsulated aqueous emulsion of DHA-rich triglyceride, delivering 60 mg DHA in 0.5 mL. Dosing: three divided doses of 0.17 mL/kg/dose, total 0.5 mL/kg/day. Control emulsion contains soy oil and is administered at the same volume and dosing schedule. Both emulsions are iso-caloric and identical in appearance. Administration: enterally via naso/orogastric tube immediately preceding a scheduled feed; dosing is adjusted weekly based on current weight (birthweight used until regained). If feeds are stopped, emulsions are withheld and resumed upon restart of feeds. The emulsions are manufactured under GMP, labeled for clinical trial use, supplied in boxes of four 30 mL bottles (20 mL per bottle), refrigerated, and have a 9-month shelf life with a 28-day opened-bottle discard. Pharmacists or nominees dispense; registered/enrolled nurses administer per local practices. Compliance is monitored by research nurses via medication charts.

Concomitant care: All clinical management follows neonatologist-directed local protocols. Use of fish oil-containing IV lipid emulsions for Parenteral Nutrition-Associated Liver Disease rescue is at neonatologist discretion.

Outcomes: Primary outcome is BPD at 36 weeks’ PMA (or discharge), defined physiologically: infants on endotracheal mechanical ventilation, continuous positive airway pressure, or high-flow oxygen ≥2 L/min are classified as BPD without additional testing. For nasal cannula <2 L/min, effective oxygen concentration is calculated using the Benaron–Benitz formula. Infants on supplemental oxygen ≥30% with saturations 90–96% are classified as BPD without testing. Infants on <30% oxygen with saturations ≥90% or ≥30% with >96% undergo a 20-minute stepwise reduction to room air; failure (saturation 80–89% for 5 consecutive minutes, <80% for 15 seconds, or apnoea/bradycardia with saturation <90%) or failure in the room-air phase (saturation <90% over 30 minutes) classifies as BPD. Infants in room air undergo a 15-minute oximetry assessment; saturation <90% classifies as BPD. Secondary outcomes include death before 36 weeks’ PMA or BPD; respiratory support duration (birth to 36 weeks’ PMA and to 40 weeks’ PMA or discharge); discontinuation of endotracheal ventilation, non-invasive positive pressure support, and low-flow/supplemental oxygen to 40 weeks’ PMA or discharge; caffeine use and total days; postnatal steroids and diuretics for lung disease and total diuretic days; BPD severity (mild/moderate/severe); BPD classification at 36 weeks’ PMA or discharge; feeding tolerance (days to enteral intake ≥120 mL/kg/day; days with feed interruptions); growth (weight, length, head circumference z-scores at 36 weeks’ PMA and at 40 weeks’ PMA or discharge); and major morbidities (retinopathy of prematurity stage ≥3 and treated; intraventricular haemorrhage any grade and grade III/IV; cystic periventricular leukomalacia/porencephaly; sepsis; necrotising enterocolitis). Data collection follows Australia and New Zealand Neonatal Network definitions.

Timeline and assessments: Baseline (30 μL infant blood for fatty acids; weight, length, head circumference; demographics). Weekly compliance and monthly anthropometrics. At 36 weeks’ PMA: primary outcome assessment; anthropometrics; 30 μL infant blood for fatty acids; if available, 30 μL breast milk for fatty acids. Secondary outcomes collected up to 40 weeks’ PMA or discharge. First discharge date recorded.

Sample size and power: Target 1244 infants (622 per group) to detect a 10% absolute reduction in BPD incidence (from 51.4% to 41.4%; 19% relative reduction) with 90% power, two-tailed α=0.05, accounting for clustering (variance inflation factor 11%) and deaths (4%). Clustering parameters: 26% of infants <29 weeks’ GA from multiple births; intracluster correlation coefficient for BPD 0.52; average cluster size 2.07 (from DINO).

title: Bayesian Adaptive Exploration
field_subfield: Statistics — Experimental Design; Astronomy and Engineering (Applications)
research_question:
Research question: Can a Bayesian adaptive framework that iteratively updates beliefs and selects next observations to maximize expected information gain significantly improve observational efficiency in nonlinear scientific problems compared to non-adaptive or random sampling?

Hypotheses: (1) When noise statistics are independent of signal properties (e.g., additive Gaussian noise), the optimal adaptive design reduces to maximum entropy sampling of the predictive distribution, which is computationally efficient and intuitive. (2) In nonlinear models with well-defined structure, BAE will substantially reduce posterior uncertainty faster than random sampling, as measured by reductions in posterior volume and correlation structure. (3) The entropy-guided design will outperform naive or nonoptimal observation placements by avoiding regions of low predictive uncertainty.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if the expected information gain simplifies to maximizing predictive entropy under the stated noise conditions. Hypothesis (2) is supported if posterior volume decreases by factors exceeding √N scaling across cycles. Hypothesis (3) is supported if nonoptimal observations yield larger posterior volumes and persistent correlations compared to entropy-guided choices.
reference_methodology:
Framework: BAE iterates Observation–Inference–Design. Inference computes posterior distributions p(θ|D, M) via Bayes’ theorem, marginalizing over nuisance parameters φ to obtain p(ψ|D, M) for parameters of interest ψ. Design uses predictive distributions p(d|D, Me) (Me includes experimental setup) and Bayesian decision theory to select the next observation e that maximizes expected utility. For inference-focused goals, utility is the information in the posterior p(θ|D, Me), measured by negative Shannon entropy.

Analytical simplification: Using Shannon’s theorem, the expected information gain simplifies to I[prior] + I[sampling] − I[predictive]. When I[prior] and I[sampling] are independent of e (e.g., additive noise with noise properties independent of signal), the optimal e maximizes the entropy of the predictive distribution, yielding maximum entropy sampling.

Computation: Posterior sampling (e.g., MCMC) is used to approximate predictive distributions and expected information. For a set of N posterior samples {θi}, the predictive density at a candidate observation time/location is approximated by averaging the sampling distribution over samples. Expected information EI(e) is estimated via Monte Carlo integration over e and d, with entropy curves computed over candidate e values to identify the maximum.

Example 1 (Exoplanet radial velocity): Model V(t; τ, e, K) with Gaussian noise n ~ N(0, σ2), σ = 8 m s−1. Initial setup: 10 equispaced observations. True parameters: τ = 800 d, e = 0.5, K = 50 m s−1. Inference produces marginal posteriors for τ and e (100 samples shown), and derived posteriors for semimajor axis a and m sin i by evaluating nonlinear functions on posterior samples. Design computes entropy curves over candidate times; the next observation is placed at t = 1925 d (Figure 2d). Subsequent cycles incorporate single optimally timed observations.

Example 2 (1D Gaussian object localization): Hidden object with peak x0 = 5.2, amplitude A = 7, FWHM = 0.6. Initial scan: 11 noisy observations (σ = 1) spaced over the object width. Inference yields samples for A and x0 (Figure 4b). Design selects next observation near the peak (σ = 1/3). Subsequent cycles alternate inference and design, with entropy curves guiding placement (Figures 5b, 5d). A nonoptimal final observation is contrasted (Figure 5f).

Metrics: Posterior volume (product of parameter standard deviations), posterior correlation structure, and entropy curves. No IRB/ethics required; all analyses are simulations.

title: Five years of Hospital at Home adoption in Catalonia: impact and challenges
field_subfield: Health Services Research — Integrated Care and Hospital-at-Home
research_question: The study addressed three objectives: (i) assess regional adoption of HaH (AA and ESD) across 27 providers from 2015–2019; (ii) compare AA and ESD with matched conventional hospitalizations on in-episode and 30-/90-day outcomes (mortality, readmissions, ER visits, expenditure) and case-mix complexity; and (iii) characterize value generation and heterogeneity across providers to inform quality assurance and monitoring recommendations. The implicit hypotheses were: (1) HaH (AA/ESD) would be safe and deliver outcomes comparable to conventional hospitalization; (2) AA would demonstrate value-based benefits (e.g., bed capacity release, patient satisfaction, cost efficiency) under regional reimbursement; (3) provider-level heterogeneity in patient profiles and episode complexity would be substantial, necessitating provider-profiled KPIs and continuous quality assurance. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include non-inferiority of HaH to conventional care on mortality and utilization, small effect sizes indicating comparable complexity, and expert consensus on AA’s value and the need for tailored monitoring. Refutation would involve inferior outcomes, large effect sizes favoring conventional care, or lack of consensus on value and monitoring needs.
reference_methodology:
Design: Mixed-methods observational study combining a population-based retrospective analysis of registry data with qualitative expert panel discussions. The quantitative component followed STROBE guidelines; the qualitative component followed SRQR.

Setting and data: The Catalan Health Surveillance System (CHSS) provided comprehensive administrative data for Catalonia’s population (7.7 million), including resource utilization across tiers, drugs, and billable costs (e.g., nonurgent transport, outpatient rehabilitation, respiratory therapies, dialysis). The analysis period was January 1, 2015–December 31, 2019, spanning sustainable regional adoption and avoiding SARS-CoV-2 pandemic effects.

Participants and episodes: All AA and ESD episodes recorded in CHSS during 2015–2019 were screened. Providers were categorized by bed capacity and role: community hospitals (50–250 beds; internal medicine/general surgery), general/district hospitals (200–800 beds; multiple specialties), and high-technology hospitals (300–1,500 beds; regional reference centers). A total of 58,547 HaH episodes were identified: 31,901 AA and 26,646 ESD.

Controls and matching: For each HaH modality, a 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) with Genetic Matching (GENOUD) was used to create matched conventional hospitalization controls. Matching variables included demographics (age, sex), prior-year healthcare utilization (hospital admissions, ER visits, number of prescriptions, total expenditure), clinical/social risk (Adjusted Morbidity Groups [AMG] score; presence of health-related social needs [HRSN] Z-codes), and Medicare DRG category. Matching was restricted to contemporary admissions within the same hospital and identical DRG category. Balance was assessed using Mahalanobis distance, Rubin’s B (acceptable if <0.25), and Rubin’s R (acceptable if 0.5–2).

Variables and outcomes: Baseline characteristics included age, sex, AMG, prior-year hospitalizations, ER visits, and expenditure. Episode characteristics included LoS and complexity via Case Mix Index-APR-DRG v35 (CMI) and Queralt index. Outcomes included in-episode mortality, 30- and 90-day mortality, readmissions, ER visits, and expenditure at 30 and 90 days. Expenditure was derived from reimbursements by the Catalan Health Service; operational costs were unavailable for the full cohort.

Statistical analysis: Incomplete records, duplicates, and outliers (Z > |3|) were removed. Effect sizes were estimated using Cohen’s D (continuous) and Cohen’s W (categorical), with magnitude thresholds: weak (<0.20), small (0.20–0.50), moderate (0.50–0.80), large (0.80–1.30), very large (>1.30). For categorical variables, weak (<0.10), small (0.10–0.30), moderate (0.30–0.50), and large (>0.50) were used. One thousand bootstrap replicates generated 95% CIs. Heterogeneity across providers was assessed descriptively (age, AMG, severity, LoS, repeat episodes) and via K-means clustering (MacQueen algorithm) with silhouette method to determine optimal clusters, incorporating hospital category (beds/role).

Ethics and governance: The Ethical Committee for Human Research at Hospital Clinic de Barcelona approved the study (HCB/2021/0768) within the EU JADECARE project. Data were handled under GDPR (2016/679) and the Biomedical Research Act (14/2007). No interventions beyond routine care were applied. Analyses used only registry data.

title: Chemical Availability of Bromide Dictates CsPbBr3 Nanocrystal Growth
research_question:
Research question: How does bromide chemical availability influence the nucleation, phase evolution, and final product of CsPbBr3 nanocrystal growth under hot-injection conditions? Specifically, do intermediates exist, and if so, what sequence of phases is formed, and which reaction parameter (bromide vs lead availability) dictates the product phase?

Hypotheses: (1) Slow release of Br− from 1-bromohexane will extend reaction times sufficiently to observe sequential phases in Cs–Pb–Br systems. (2) The initial product will be CsBr (Br− complexation with Cs+), followed by Cs4PbBr6, and finally CsPbBr3 as Br− availability increases. (3) The product phase will be determined by bromide concentration and ligand equilibria, not by lead concentration. (4) The growth mechanism will deviate from a single-species LaMer nucleation model and instead involve nucleation of CsBr, followed by phase conversion to Cs4PbBr6 and then CsPbBr3.

Predictions: If (1)–(3) hold, time-resolved XRD/HRTEM will show CsBr → Cs4PbBr6 → CsPbBr3 transitions, PL will emerge only after CsPbBr3 forms and red-shift with growth, and increasing Br− (e.g., via 1-bromohexane) will drive conversion to perovskite while increasing Pb-OA will not. If (4) holds, conventional controls (precursor concentration, temperature) will have limited effect on product phase compared to Br− availability.
reference_methodology:
Synthesis of cesium oleate (Cs-OA): 0.1 g Cs2CO3 was reacted with 0.3 mL oleic acid (OA) in 5 mL 1-octadecene (ODE) at 120 °C under vacuum for 1 hour until fully dissolved.

Typical slow-kinetics CsPbBr3 synthesis: 0.046 g PbO was loaded into a 25 mL flask with 5 mL ODE and 0.16 mL OA, dried at 120 °C under vacuum for 1.5 hours. After dissolution, 0.7 mL Cs-OA was injected under Ar, and the mixture was heated to 150 °C. Then 0.8 mL oleylamine (OAm) and 0.6 mL OA were added, followed by injection of 0.13 mL 1-bromohexane 2 minutes later. Aliquots were removed at various times and quenched in cold toluene. Products were purified by centrifugation at 3300 rcf for 20–50 minutes, redispersed in toluene, centrifuged again, and finally collected and dispersed in hexane for characterization.

CsBr synthesis (bromide-deficient, lead-abundant): 0.019 g PbBr2 was loaded into a 25 mL flask with 2.5 mL ODE, dried at 120 °C under vacuum for 1 hour. Under Ar, the solution was adjusted to a desired temperature, then 0.4 mL OAm and 0.1 mL OA were added. After PbBr2 dissolution, 0.7 mL Cs-OA was injected and reacted for 2–10 minutes. The solution turned cloudy within 15 seconds to 2 minutes depending on temperature. Products were cooled in an ice bath, purified as above, and stored in hexane. To study Pb concentration effects, 0.5 mL Pb-OA (0.1822 g PbO, 0.64 mL OA, 4.8 mL ODE) was added either before or after Cs-OA injection.

CsBr-seeded growth of CsPbBr3: CsBr seed solution was prepared at 120 °C without cooling/purification. To the crude CsBr solution, 0.5 mL Pb-OA (0.1822 g PbO, 0.64 mL OA, 4.8 mL ODE) was added, followed by injection of 0.29 mL 1-bromohexane. Aliquots were collected at different times and quenched in cold hexane. Products were centrifuged at 8000 rcf for 10 minutes at 20 °C, redispersed in hexane, and centrifuged again at 2500 rcf for 10 minutes. Supernatants from early stages (no products) and later stages were also analyzed.

Characterization: XRD was measured on a Bruker D8-Focus Bragg–Brentano diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation. PL spectra were collected on an Ocean Optics Flame-S-UV-Vis spectrometer with a DH-200-Bal deuterium lamp. HRTEM images were acquired on a FEI Tecnai G2 F20 ST FE-TEM operated at 200 kV with a Gatan CCD camera.

Control experiment for slow Br− release: A mixture of Pb-OA, OA, OAm, and 1-bromohexane was aged for 30 minutes at 150 °C. Cs-OA was then injected, and CsPbBr3 nanocubes formed instantly (Figure S4), confirming that slow Br− release, not precursor incompatibility, governs the kinetics.

title: Waning COVID-19 Vaccine Effectiveness for BNT162b2 and CoronaVac in Malaysia: An Observational Study
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19 infection wane over three to five months post-full vaccination for BNT162b2 and CoronaVac in Malaysia? (2) Does VE against COVID-19-related ICU admission and death wane over the same period? (3) Are there age-specific differences in waning patterns?

Hypotheses: (a) VE against infection declines over time for both vaccines, consistent with prior mRNA vaccine findings; (b) VE against severe outcomes may decline less than against infection, but could wane for CoronaVac; (c) older adults may exhibit greater waning than younger adults due to lower immunogenicity and higher baseline risk. Support for these hypotheses would be indicated by lower VE estimates in the early (3–5 months post-vaccination) versus late (1–2 months post-vaccination) groups, with larger declines in older age strata. Refutation would be indicated by stable VE across periods or no age-stratified differences.
reference_methodology:
