Design and data sources: Retrospective observational study using nationally representative data from Malaysia’s national electronic COVID-19 cases register (confirmed cases), COVID-19 vaccine recipients line listing, ICU admissions register, and COVID-19 deaths line listing. Case and personal identification numbers enabled deterministic linkage. The study period was 1 September–30 September 2021, when Delta predominated. Individuals with infections outside this period or recipients of non-homologous vaccines (excluding AZD1222 due to insufficient follow-up) were excluded. Full vaccination was defined as ≥14 days after the second dose of BNT162b2 or CoronaVac.

Cohorts: (1) Population cohort for infection incidence: ages 15+ (reflecting census availability), with vaccination timing categorized as early (fully vaccinated April–June 2021; 3–5 months post-vaccination during the observation period) versus late (fully vaccinated July–August 2021; 1–2 months post-vaccination). Unvaccinated individuals were derived from census-based population estimates. (2) Confirmed-case cohort for severe outcomes: ages ≥18, with confirmatory test dates 1–30 September 2021; outcomes included ICU admission and death recorded through November 2021 to account for delays.

Statistical analysis: For infection, negative binomial regression estimated VE by comparing infection rates between early and late vaccinated groups relative to unvaccinated, adjusting for age groups, sex, and state, with cumulative person-days as the offset. For severe outcomes among confirmed cases, logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for ICU admission and death, adjusting for age (continuous), comorbidities, sex, nationality, and state. VE was computed as 1 − adjusted OR. Sensitivity analyses included: (a) combining ICU admission and death into a single outcome; (b) age-stratified analyses (18–39, 40–59, ≥60 years); and (c) robustness checks cycling through all combinations of covariates. Software: Python 3.9 and R 4.1.2.

Ethics: Commissioned by the Ministry of Health, Malaysia; registered in the National Medical Research Register (NMRR-21-1660-60697). Conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki; ethical approval by the Medical Research and Ethics Committee (MREC), Ministry of Health, Malaysia.

title: Costs of Saving Water in South Texas with Irrigation District Infrastructure Rehabilitation - Using Capital Budgeting with RGIDECON?
field_subfield: Agricultural Economics — Water Resources and Irrigation Management
research_question:
Research question: What are the life-cycle costs of saving water via rehabilitation of irrigation district infrastructure in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, and how do these costs vary by project type and district? A secondary question is whether the RGIDECON capital budgeting approach provides a consistent, comparable metric for prioritizing projects.

Hypotheses/predictions: (1) Rehabilitation measures (e.g., canal lining, pipeline replacement, metering/telemetry, pumping plant upgrades) will yield measurable annual water savings at life-cycle costs that are economically competitive relative to alternative supply enhancement strategies. (2) On-farm metering/telemetry and canal lining will be among the most cost-effective measures, while certain pipeline and pumping plant projects may be more expensive due to higher capital and longer lifetimes. (3) Aggregating across components will produce an overall average life-cycle cost that reflects the distribution of project types and savings.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if the reported life-cycle costs are within a plausible range relative to other supply options and if total savings are substantial. Hypothesis (2) is supported if grouped averages show on-farm meters/telemetry and lining at lower $/af than pipelines and pumping plants. Hypothesis (3) is supported if the overall average aligns with the distribution of component costs and savings.
reference_methodology:
Design: A capital budgeting analysis using Net Present Value (NPV) and annuity equivalent (AE) values to compute a single annual life-cycle cost per acre-foot of water saved for each project component. The approach integrates initial construction costs, annual operation and maintenance (O&M) costs, expected annual water savings, and expected useful life.

Data: Twenty-five project components across multiple irrigation districts (Harlingen, Edinburg, San Juan, Brownsville, San Benito I/II, Eagle Pass, United, San Juan III) completed between 2002 and 2009. For each component, the report provides: estimated initial construction cost ($), NPV of net total cost ($), NPV of lifetime water savings (af), useful life (years), annual water savings (af), and cost of saving water ($/af). Component-level data are summarized in Table 1; aggregated district-level and type-level summaries are in Table 2.

Modeling assumptions and parameters: The analysis uses 2.04% inflation and a 6.125% discount rate for dollar cash flows. Water savings are discounted at 4.0%. AE values are computed assuming perpetuity, zero salvage value, and replacement of capital items with similar assets at the end of their useful lives. The report states that the NPV of lifetime water savings and NPV of net total cost are used to derive the AE life-cycle cost per af.

Procedures: For each component, the RGIDECON spreadsheet model calculates the NPV of net total cost (initial construction plus discounted O&M) and the NPV of lifetime water savings (annual savings discounted at 4.0%). The AE of these NPVs is then converted to an annual $/af life-cycle cost. Components are aggregated within districts (weighted by af of water savings) to produce district-level costs. Components are further grouped by project type (on-farm meters/telemetry; in-system meters/telemetry; lining; pipeline; pumping plant) to compute type-level averages.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human subjects or sensitive data are involved.

Reproducibility notes: The report provides component-level inputs and outputs (Table 1) and type-level averages (Table 2), but does not detail O&M cost structures, water savings estimation methods, or uncertainty quantification. The discount rates, inflation, and AE assumptions are specified.

title: Secondary flow in contour currents controls the formation of moat-drift contourite systems
field_subfield: Earth and Environmental Sciences — Marine Geology and Sedimentology
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Under what hydrodynamic conditions do moat–drift contourite systems self-emerge? (2) How do current speed and slope steepness control moat–drift morphology (width, relief, aspect ratio, drift angle)? (3) Does a secondary across-slope flow near the seafloor exist, and how does it depend on along-slope velocity and slope steepness? (4) Can moat–drift morphology be used to reconstruct paleo-ocean current strength and direction?

Hypotheses: (H1) Moats and drifts migrate upslope with higher sediment availability; (H2) moat–drift morphology depends on current speed; (H3) a secondary across-slope flow near the seafloor, dependent on along-slope velocity and slope steepness, is necessary for moat–drift formation. Predictions: If H1 holds, adding sediment should reverse moat migration direction relative to no-input conditions. If H2 holds, increasing along-slope velocity and slope steepness should increase drift angle and moat relief. If H3 holds, secondary flow should be detectable near the bed, with direction and magnitude varying with velocity and slope; its presence should correlate with moat–drift emergence. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses include observed upslope migration under sediment input, monotonic increases in drift angle with velocity and slope, and measured secondary flow confined within the moat with a helicoidal structure.
reference_methodology:
Experimental setup: A 6 m wide, 11 m long, 1 m deep flume tank (EUROTANK) at Utrecht University was used. The floor morphology comprised a gentle lower slope (not part of the study area), a flat terrace, and an upper slope of 18° or 26°. The base morphology was built from sediment and stabilized with artificial grass (plastic). A thin 1.5 cm layer of walnut shells covered the grass before the first experiments; for experiments 2–6, a 0.5 cm layer was used. All added walnut shells were removed after each experiment.

Flow generation: Three pumps created a clockwise, circular current parallel to the slope at the study area, analogous to a contour current along a continental margin. The circular flow provides a barotropic pressure gradient via run-up against the slope, inducing radial acceleration; this is considered a simplified analog to the Coriolis effect in natural systems (Supplementary Note 1). The Earth’s Coriolis force was not modeled due to the tank’s small size.

Sediment analog and transport: Sediment was supplied as crushed walnut shells (200–450 μm; density 1350 kg/m3) with settling velocity 1.9 cm/s (Stokes’ law). During the initial 2 h of the sediment input phase, a side pump injected water mixed with 80 dm3 of walnut shells (volume concentration <2%). The contour current transported the particles to the study area, where they settled and were reworked. The non-dimensional bed shear stress (Shields parameter) exceeded the critical threshold (0.05) for all tested velocities: 0.11 (11 cm/s), 0.22 (16 cm/s), 0.28 (18 cm/s). Calculated flow shear velocities were 1.1 cm/s (11 cm/s), 1.6 cm/s (16 cm/s), and 1.8 cm/s (18 cm/s) (Supplementary Note 2). Walnut shells were used as an analog for silt because similar current speeds transport them as bedload; their larger size allowed experiments in a smaller setup.

Experimental phases and durations: All experiments began with the same base morphology. Two phases were distinguished: (1) sediment input phase (3 h; 80 dm3 added) and (2) reworking phase (4 h; no input). In Experiment 1, an additional input phase (7 h) and extended reworking (8 h) were used to test migration under input/no-input conditions. For Experiments 2–6, one input phase (3 h) and one reworking phase (4 h) were used.

Measurements: Bathymetry was measured with a laser scanner before and after each experiment, scanning predefined across-slope profiles every 2 mm with a 50 cm swath, yielding a 5 mm grid. For morphological analysis, the average along-slope elevation of a 70 cm wide swath in the tank’s middle was computed and plotted as a cross-section to average out small ripple perturbations. Velocity was measured with a UDOP 4000 velocimeter (~15 cm above bed). One 1 MHz probe was the emitter; three probes were receivers. Data within the first 5 cm near the emitter were of poor quality and excluded. For Fig. 4, measurements were taken within the first 20 min (before moat–drift formation). For across-slope profiles at the fastest current (18 cm/s) and 18° slope, velocities were measured every 5–10 cm for 2 min. When not measuring, the instrument was positioned in the tank center to avoid disturbing flow.

Derived metrics: After moat–drift formation, the study quantified moat width (cm), moat relief (cm; depth between moat trough and drift crest), moat aspect ratio (relief/width), and drift angle (°; slope angle of the drift adjacent to the moat).

title: A base promoted one pot solvent free version of the Ramachary reductive coupling/alkylation reaction for the synthesis of 2,2-disubstituted ethyl cyanoacetates
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a solvent-free, base-promoted one-pot RRC/A reaction be developed to synthesize 2,2-disubstituted ethyl cyanoacetates from aldehydes, ethyl cyanacetates, alkyl halides, and Hantzsch ester with high yields? (2) Which base and reaction conditions (temperature, equivalents) optimize the process? (3) What is the substrate scope for aryl and heteroaryl aldehydes, and how do electron-withdrawing groups affect outcomes? (4) Can a complementary solvent-free two-step RRC/A process be established for malononitriles and 4-nitrophenyl acetonitriles?

Hypotheses: (i) A weak base (e.g., DIEA) under solvent-free conditions will efficiently promote both the Knoevenagel/hydrogenation (RRC) and subsequent alkylation (RRC/A) steps, outperforming strong bases and organic bases. (ii) Elevated temperature (≈90°C) and sufficient base equivalents (2 equiv DIEA) will maximize yields, while lower temperatures or insufficient base will reduce conversion. (iii) Electron-rich aryl aldehydes will be more reactive than strongly electron-withdrawing aryl aldehydes; ketones and aliphatic aldehydes will be poor substrates. (iv) A two-step solvent-free protocol will enable RRC/A for malononitriles and 4-nitrophenyl acetonitriles, with DIEA required in both steps for the latter.
reference_methodology:
Optimization: The model reaction used ethyl cyanacetate, 4-bromobenzaldehyde, benzyl bromide, and Hantzsch ester. Without base, no RRC/A product formed at 80°C. With 2 equivalents of sodium bicarbonate, the RRC/A product was obtained in 40% yield. Using 2 equivalents of sodium carbonate or potassium carbonate improved yields to 60% and 76%, respectively. Sodium hydroxide (2 equiv) gave only 5% yield. Organic bases (triethanolamine, 2-diethylaminoethanol, triethylenediamine) gave ≤50% yield. N,N-diisopropylethylamine (DIEA) at 2 equivalents afforded 90% yield; 1 equivalent reduced yield to 50%, while 3–4 equivalents gave low yields. Temperature studies showed trace product at 60°C and 70°C; at 90°C, yields increased to 92% at 2 hours. Shorter reaction times (0.5 h and 1 h) gave 67% and 75% yields, respectively. The optimal conditions were identified as heating the four-component mixture at 90°C for 2 hours with 2 equivalents of DIEA.

Substrate scope: Aryl aldehydes were screened. 4-Chlorobenzaldehyde and 4-fluorobenzaldehyde delivered 95% and 96% yields, respectively. 4-Methylbenzaldehyde gave 94%. 4-Methoxybenzaldehyde afforded 73%. 4-Cyanobenzaldehyde gave 24%. 4-Nitrobenzaldehyde provided 76%. 1-Naphthaldehyde gave 92%. Heteroaryl aldehydes furan-2-carbaldehyde and thiophene-2-carbaldehyde yielded 94% and 88%, respectively. Acetophenone and propionaldehyde were poor substrates; the latter’s low boiling point and lower reactivity of ketones were noted as likely causes.

Two-step solvent-free RRC/A: For malononitrile, a self-catalyzed RRC step with aldehyde and Hantzsch ester produced 2-(4-bromobenzyl)malononitrile in 95% yield. After completion, benzyl bromide and DIEA were added without workup to give the RRC/A product in 93% isolated yield. For 4-nitrophenyl acetonitrile, both the RRC and alkylation steps required one equivalent of DIEA. No additional procedural details (e.g., exact stoichiometries beyond equivalents, reaction times, or purification methods) are provided in the text. No IRB/ethics approvals are applicable.

title: Family physicians supporting patients with palliative care needs within the Patient Medical Home in the community: An Appreciative Inquiry qualitative study
field_subfield: Medicine — Family Medicine and Palliative Care; Health Services Research
research_question:
Research question: What essential components are required to best support patients and families with palliative care needs in their communities, and how can these inform system changes to empower family physicians to provide community-based palliative care within the Patient Medical Home?

The AI approach did not test explicit hypotheses but sought to discover, dream, and design a future “destiny” state for community palliative care. Implicit expectations were that (a) FPs’ longitudinal relationships with patients would be central to effective CPPC; (b) interprofessional communication and team relationships would be foundational; (c) system flexibility and resources would be necessary; and (d) public education about palliative care beyond end-of-life would facilitate earlier engagement. Outcomes supporting these expectations would include convergent themes across stakeholder groups emphasizing these elements and the development of a coherent framework that integrates them. Outcomes refuting them would include stakeholder emphasis on acute care-centric models, lack of consensus on team roles, or absence of system-level enablers. The study’s qualitative design prioritized depth and triangulation over hypothesis testing.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative study using Appreciative Inquiry (AI) to identify strengths and possibilities for community-based palliative care. The design adhered to SRQR standards.

Setting and recruitment: Urban and surrounding rural health authority zones of Calgary, Alberta, Canada. FPs were recruited via Primary Care Networks (PCNs) through newsletters and email lists, with snowball sampling and theoretical sampling to diversify perspectives across urban and rural practices. PHC clinicians were recruited from two PHC teams in different city quadrants. Patients and bereaved caregivers were recruited through Alberta Health Services’ Patient and Family Advisory Group, an arms-length organization to protect privacy and ensure ethical recruitment.

Participants: 18 FPs (9 female, 9 male; years of practice 2–42); 8 bereaved caregivers; 1 patient; 26 PHC team members. Among FPs, 12 self-identified as actively providing palliative care, while 6 did not include palliative care as a substantial portion of practice but philosophically endorsed its scope.

Data collection: FPs participated in individual semi-structured interviews (in person, telephone, or Skype for Business) using an AI-informed guide. Demographic data included gender, years of practice, palliative care training, and country of medical school. PHC teams, patients, and bereaved caregivers participated in distinct focus groups using a semi-structured guide that incorporated AI principles and the “possibility statements” derived from FP interviews. Demographics for PHC and patient/caregiver groups were collected (Table 1). All sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim by a confidential service, and checked for accuracy. Field notes informed iterative sampling.

Analysis: Line-by-line thematic analysis was conducted by all three authors and a research assistant (SD). Emerging themes from FP interviews were used to generate “possibility statements” (affirmative, present-tense future states) to frame focus groups. Focus group transcripts were analyzed inductively by the principal author and a research assistant (CP) and deductively against the possibility statements to test the future destination from other perspectives. Consensus on themes was reached through iterative meetings. Memos and an audit trail supported constant comparison and theme saturation. Triangulation across stakeholder groups was performed to develop a conceptual framework. The team also sought feedback from non-participant stakeholders to validate the framework.

Ethics: Ethical approval was granted by the Conjoint Health Research Ethics Board (CHREB), University of Calgary. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. Patient/caregiver recruitment via an arms-length organization addressed privacy and ethical concerns.

Rigor: Pilot testing of interview guides; purposeful and theoretical sampling; intercoder reliability checks; iterative coding and consensus; constant comparison; saturation; triangulation with non-participant stakeholders. No quantitative outcomes or statistical tests were applicable.

title: microRNA-130a-5p suppresses myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury by downregulating the HMGB2/NF-κB axis
research_question:
Research question: Does miR-130a-5p overexpression attenuate MIRI in vivo, and does it do so by targeting HMGB2 to suppress NF-κB signaling, thereby reducing oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, and inflammation?

Hypotheses: (1) miR-130a-5p overexpression will improve cardiac function and hemodynamics, reduce serum injury biomarkers (CK, cTnT), and mitigate histological injury and apoptosis in MIRI mice. (2) miR-130a-5p will reduce oxidative stress (higher SOD, lower MDA/ROS) and mitochondrial dysfunction (higher MMP/ATP, lower Ca2+), and decrease pro-apoptotic proteins (Bax, Cyt-c, AIF) while increasing anti-apoptotic Bcl-2. (3) miR-130a-5p will downregulate HMGB2 and inhibit NF-κB pathway activation (lower p-p65, p-IκBα) and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β). (4) HMGB2 overexpression will reverse the protective effects of miR-130a-5p, restoring MIRI phenotypes. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significant improvements in functional and molecular readouts with miR-130a-5p and their reversal upon HMGB2 upregulation; failure to observe these changes would refute the hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Animals and groups: Sixty healthy male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks, 20–25 g; Guangzhou General Pharmaceutical Research Institute, SYXK (Guangdong) 2018-0003) were randomized by body weight into six groups (n=10/group): sham, MIRI, agomir negative control (NC), miR-130a-5p agomir, miR-130a-5p agomir + pLVX-Puro, and miR-130a-5p agomir + pLVX-Puro-HMGB2.

MIRI model: Mice were anesthetized with 4% pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg, i.p.). For MIRI, the left anterior descending coronary artery was ligated for 30 min and reperfused for 120 min. Sham mice underwent thoracotomy without ligation. For the four intervention groups, intramyocardial injections were administered 24 h before MIRI: agomir NC (RiboBio), miR-130a-5p agomir (50 µL, 300 nmol/kg; RiboBio), miR-130a-5p agomir + pLVX-Puro (1×10^7 pfu; Gaining Biotechnology), and miR-130a-5p agomir + pLVX-Puro-HMGB2 (1×10^7 pfu; Gaining).

Cardiac function and hemodynamics: Echocardiography (Philips Sonos 5500) measured left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) and fraction shortening (FS). After echocardiography, catheters were inserted via the right common carotid artery into the left ventricle (LV) for measurement of LV systolic pressure (LVSP), LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), and maximal rates of pressure rise/fall (±dp/dtmax) using a multiconductive physiological recorder (Chengdu Medical Instruments).

Sample collection: At endpoint, mice were euthanized with pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg, i.p.). Blood (1 mL) was collected by cardiac puncture, allowed to clot for 10 min, centrifuged at 3000 g for 10 min, and serum stored at −80 °C. Myocardial tissues were harvested; 4 samples per group were used for homogenate assays; 6 samples per group were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h and paraffin-embedded for histology.

Biochemical assays: Serum CK, cTnT, LDH, SOD, and MDA were measured (Nanjing JianCheng Bioengineering). Serum TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β were quantified by ELISA (Shanghai Enzyme-linked Biotechnology).

Mitochondrial function: Mitochondria were isolated from tissue homogenates using reagents (Beyotime), with sequential centrifugations (600 g, 4 °C, 5 min; 1100 g, 4 °C, 10 min). Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) was assessed with JC-1 (Beyotime). ATP, ROS, and Ca2+ were measured using commercial kits (Shanghai Enzyme-linked Biotechnology; Sigma-Aldrich).

Histology and apoptosis: HE staining was performed on paraffin sections (hematoxylin 3 min; 1% hydrochloric alcohol differentiation 15 s; eosin 2 min; Olympus microscope). TUNEL staining (Shanghai Yeason) and DAPI nuclear counterstain (Beyotime) were used to quantify apoptosis under fluorescence microscopy.

Molecular assays: Total RNA was extracted (TRIzol, Beyotime) and reverse-transcribed (ReverTra Ace qPCR RT Master Mix, Toyobo). qPCR used SYBR Premix Ex Taq II (Takara) with 2^-ΔΔCt normalization to GAPDH. Primers: miR-130a-5p (F: 5′-CCAGGGCTTTTAAAATGA-3′; R: 5′-CCGATCCAA TCTGTTCTGGT-3′), U6 (F: 5′-GTGCTCGCTTCGGCAGCA-3′; R: 5′-AAAAATATGGAACGCTTTC-3′), HMGB2 (F: 5′-GGGAAGAGCACAA GAAAGAAC-3′; R: 5′-AAACAGGAAGAAGGCAGATGG-3′), GAPDH (F: 5′-GTCACCGATTGGTCTGTATT-3′; R: 5′-AGTCTTCTGGTGGCAGTGAT-3′). Western blotting used SDS-PAGE and PVDF transfer; membranes were blocked with 5% milk and probed with primary antibodies (Abcam): Bcl-2 (ab59348, 1:1000), Bax (ab182733, 1:2000), Cyt-c (ab216971, 1:1000), AIF (ab32516, 1:1000), HMGB2 (ab124670, 1:10,000), p65 (ab16502, 0.5 µg/mL), IκBα (ab109300, 1:1000), p-p65 (ab86299, 1:2000), p-IκBα (ab133478, 1:10,000). HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (ab32152, 1:2000; ab205719, 1:2000) were used. GAPDH (ab8245, 1:1000) served as loading control.

Target validation: TargetScan predicted miR-130a-5p binding sites in HMGB2 3′UTR. PCR-amplified WT and MUT 3′UTR fragments were cloned into pmiR-GLO (Promega). 293T cells were co-transfected with WT/MUT constructs and miR-130a-5p mimic or mimic NC using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen). Luciferase activity was measured at 48 h; experiments were repeated three times independently.

Statistics: SPSS 21.0 was used. Normality was assessed by Kolmogorov–Smirnov. Data are mean ± SD. One-way or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc tests were used; two-tailed p<0.05 indicated significance. Sample sizes: n=4 for molecular assays; n=6 for histology; n=10 for echocardiography and ELISA.

title: Hydroerosion in foothills of the coastal plain of cozoaltepec, oaxaca, Mexico
field_subfield: Environmental Science — Soil Erosion and Hydrology
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the magnitude of soil loss during rainfall in an agricultural plot in Barra del Potrero, Cozoaltepec, Oaxaca? (2) How do runoff plot measurements compare with USLE-based estimates of potential and actual erosion? (3) What is the scale of sediment deposition in the adjacent coastal plain, and how much sediment is exported to the ocean? (4) How do soil physicochemical properties and ionic profiles reflect erosion processes and sediment transport?

Hypotheses: (a) USLE will predict higher erosion than the runoff plot due to broader consideration of rainfall energy, topography, and management factors. (b) A significant fraction of gross erosion will be transported downstream, contributing to coastal sedimentation and potential salinization. (c) Ionic migration will be evident, with more mobile ions (e.g., Na+, Cl−) accumulating in coastal soils. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include AE > plot-measured erosion, substantial downstream sediment accumulation, and geochemical evidence of ionic migration. Refutation would involve plot-measured erosion exceeding USLE AE, negligible downstream sedimentation, or no geochemical signal of transport.
reference_methodology:
Study area: Barra del Potrero, Cozoaltepec, Oaxaca, Mexico, located ~6 km northeast of La Salina lagoon and Escobilla, within the Santa María Tonameca jurisdiction. Climate: warm subhumid (Aw0(w)); mean annual temperature 27.4°C (25.5°C in January; 29.4°C in May); annual rainfall 1057.8 mm; driest month March (1.4 mm), wettest September (255.2 mm). Soils: foothill eutric regosols (sandy loam, low clay <10%, kaolinite dominant, massive structure) on metamorphic Paleozoic rocks (Xolapa complex); coastal plain eutric cambisols (sandy loam, apparent density 1.47 g cm−3, porosity ~40%). Slope: ~25% in foothills; ~2% in coastal plain.

Soil sampling and analysis: Dry season (Dec–May 2014) field reconnaissance identified uniform geomorphology/geochemistry. Infiltration measured with two absorption wells (0.30 m diameter, 0.40 m depth): 4.5 cm h−1 (foothills) and 2.4 cm h−1 (plains). Two soil profiles: upstream (foothills) and downstream (coastal plain, 300 m away). Samples (2 kg each) collected in 0.20 m increments to 0.80 m depth. Samples dried in air, weighed (wet/dry), dried at 104°C, sieved at 2 mm. Texture and apparent density via Bouyoucos hydrometer and texture triangle; porosity calculated from density; color via Munsell cards. Chemical analyses: saturation paste pH and EC (Hanna HI98129); TDS from dry calcined residues (600°C); Ca2+, Mg2+, CO3 2−, HCO3 −, Cl− by titration; SO4 2− by turbidimetry (Perkin Elmer spectrophotometer); Na+ and K+ by flame photometry (IL-653).

Runoff plot: Site selected for steep slope and trough toward the coast, on a peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) field. Plot dimensions: 2.5 m × 5 m (12.5 m²), oriented N–S (upstream–downstream). Fencing: wooden boards (5 m × 0.25 m), buried 0.1 m. Outflow: PVC tube (1 m × 4 in) connected to a 100 L buried container (0.20 m depth) at the southern end. Sediments collected monthly, dried, weighed (100 kg scale), and projected to Mg ha−1 yr−1; lab analyses of sediments followed the same protocols.

USLE and rainfall KE: KE computed via Hudson’s equation using I30 = 51.88 mm h−1 (June–Nov 2014). R factor from Lombardi & Moldenhauer using 30-year monthly (P = 82.06 mm) and annual (P = 984.8 mm) rainfall for the coast of Oaxaca. K factor from Wischmeier & Smith modified for Mexican soils (Irurtia & Cruzate). LS factor from slope length and steepness (LS = 3.6). C factor = 0.8 (eroded, sparse vegetation); P factor = 0.7 (contour lines). AE = PE × C × P.

Runoff estimation: Maximum daily rainfall (Id) from 30-year records: 300 mm; average maximum intensity I1 = 100 mm h−1. Time of concentration (Tc) via Pilgrim et al. Runoff coefficient (C) via USDA Soil Conservation Service formula using Id = 300 mm and rainfall threshold = 19 mm. Runoff volume via Pilgrim et al. equation.

Downstream sediment accumulation: Eight PVC collectors (4 in diameter, 50 cm length) installed randomly in the coastal plain adjacent to the property, covering ~45×10³ m² (180 m width × 250 m shoreline). Sites marked with Garmin 76S GPS. Sediments averaged and projected to Mg ha−1 yr−1. Gross erosion and downstream migration estimated using field area (2 ha), land-use fractions (Cn = 10%, Ac = 60%, Pa = 30%), sediment transport coefficient (C = 0.79), apparent density (1.46 g cm−3), and arable layer depth (0.10 m).

title: Host Erythrocyte Environment Influences the Localization of Exported Protein 2, an Essential Component of the Plasmodium Translocon
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does Exp2 localize to cytoplasmic vesicles in Plasmodium-infected reticulocytes, and is this localization host-dependent? (2) Are Exp2-positive vesicles conserved across Plasmodium species that infect reticulocytes (P. yoelii, P. berghei, P. falciparum)? (3) Does the host erythrocyte environment influence the distribution of Exp2 between PVM-associated PTEX and cytoplasmic vesicles? (4) Is Exp2 essential for blood-stage parasite viability in P. yoelii?

Hypotheses: (a) Exp2, a PVM-localized PTEX component, will also localize to distinct cytoplasmic vesicles in reticulocyte-infected parasites, reflecting a reticulocyte-specific export pathway. (b) The formation of Exp2-positive vesicles will be preferentially observed in reticulocytes and absent in mature RBCs, indicating host environment dependence. (c) Exp2-positive vesicles will be conserved across Plasmodium species that infect reticulocytes. (d) Exp2 will be essential for parasite growth, consistent with prior reports in P. berghei and P. falciparum.

Predictions: Support for (a) and (b) would include immunofluorescence and 3D-SIM evidence of Exp2-positive vesicles in reticulocytes but not mature RBCs, with quantification of positive cells. Support for (c) would include analogous vesicle localization in P. berghei and P. falciparum reticulocytes. Support for (d) would include failure to delete pyexp2 and successful tagging without altering localization.
reference_methodology:
Animals and parasites: Male BALB/cByJ mice (5–6 weeks) were infected with P. yoelii 17X (nonlethal, reticulocyte-prone), P. yoelii 17XL (lethal, normocyte-prone), or P. berghei ANKA. Parasites were maintained as cryopreserved stabilates. All procedures were IACUC-approved.

Sample preparation: Infected blood was collected at defined parasitemias (e.g., P. yoelii 17X day 9: 9.2% ± 4.3%; P. yoelii 17XL day 4: 11.2% ± 3.0%). Reticulocytes were enriched by 70% Percoll gradients. For P. yoelii 17XL reticulocytes, phenylhydrazine (0.55 mg/mouse/day, i.p., days −5, −3, −2, −1) induced mild anemia and reticulocytosis; reticulocytes were isolated on day 4 (7.2% ± 5.3% parasitemia).

Proteomics: Reticulocyte membrane-enriched fractions from P. yoelii 17X-infected cells were prepared by saponin permeabilization (0.05% saponin, 10 min), low-speed centrifugation (800 × g, 15 min), and solubilization (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate). A 29–32 kDa band was excised, trypsin-digested, and analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an LTQ ion trap coupled to nano-UHPLC (Dionex). Peptides were separated on a 75 μm × 15 cm C18 column with a 4–50% acetonitrile gradient (60 min) and 50–80% (120 min) at 250 nL/min. MS/MS dynamic exclusion was 180 s; collision energy 30. Proteome Discoverer v1.3 (Sequest) searched Swiss-Prot (375–1,500 Da), with manual verification.

Antibodies and recombinant proteins: Polyclonal rabbit anti-rPyExp2 and anti-rPY04481 sera were generated (Lampire) with adjuvanted immunizations; mouse anti-rPyExp2 sera were generated in BALB/c mice (Quil A adjuvant). NYLS3 (IgG1) recognizes PyExp1 (PyHep17). Mouse anti-clathrin heavy chain (BF-06) cross-reacts with host clathrin. Recombinant PY04481 (pyst-a family) was expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) pLysS, purified by nickel affinity after refolding, and validated by SDS-PAGE.

Immunofluorescence and microscopy: Indirect immunofluorescence used mouse anti-rPyExp2 (1:400) and rat anti-mouse CD71 (1:200) for reticulocyte identification; secondary antibodies were Alexa Fluor 488 and rhodamine-conjugated goat anti-rat/rabbit. Wide-field imaging used Olympus BX60 with Sensicam QE; z-stacks (200 nm steps) were deconvolved. 3D-SIM used DeltaVision OMX V4 (Olympus Plan Apo N 60×/1.42 NA; 405/445/488/568/642 nm lasers; 125 nm z-steps; SoftWorx 5.0). Bodipy TR ceramide (20 μM, 30 min, 37°C) stained membranes; cells were fixed (1% paraformaldehyde) and permeabilized (0.1% saponin).

Quantification: For each mouse (n=5/group), 500 infected cells per stage were scored for Exp2 vesicle positivity; data are mean ± SD. Two-tailed, unpaired Student’s t test assessed differences (p<0.05).

Subcellular fractionation: Saponin-treated iRBCs were separated into parasite-associated and host cytoplasmic fractions (800 × g). Cytoplasmic fractions were further partitioned into soluble (supernatant) and particulate (pellet, 20,000 × g, 45 min) fractions. Integrity controls used anti-PyMSP8 (GPI-anchored parasite plasma membrane protein) and anti-aldolase (cytosolic).

Transgenesis: A double-crossover pyexp2 knockout targeting construct (Tg-dhfr-ts pyrimethamine resistance) was generated with 5′ (292 bp) and 3′ (331 bp) homology arms; 10 μg linear DNA was transfected (Amaxa Basic Parasite Nucleofector, U33 program). Drug selection began 24 h post-infection with pyrimethamine (0.8 mg/kg/day). At least two independent transfections per construct were performed. A single-crossover 3HA tagging construct (pSE02-3HA) fused a 495 bp 3′ pyexp2 fragment to triple-HA; EcoRI-linearized DNA was transfected. Drug-resistant parasites were passaged to increase numbers.

P. falciparum reticulocyte invasion assay: P. falciparum FVO was cultured in RPMI 1640 with supplements at 2% hematocrit of O+ human RBCs under 90% N2/5% CO2/5% O2. Mature schizonts were enriched by Percoll. Human cord blood reticulocytes were enriched by Percoll. Schizonts and reticulocytes were co-cultured 1:1 for 48 h; samples were fixed at 16, 24, and 36 h for IFA. Invasion of reticulocytes vs normocytes was assessed by Giemsa staining.

title: Практика ведения пациентов с позиционным головокружением: ошибки в диагностике и лечении
research_question:
Research question: What are the common diagnostic errors and management practices in the outpatient management of positional vertigo, and what is the distribution of etiologies after standardized otoneurological evaluation?

Hypotheses: (1) Many initial referral diagnoses (e.g., chronic cerebral ischemia, vertebral artery syndrome, vegetative-vascular dystonia) are incorrect when evaluated with standardized positional tests and nystagmus assessment. (2) BPPV and vestibular migraine are the predominant etiologies after specialized evaluation. (3) Diagnostic errors frequently arise from reliance on complaints without otoneurological testing and from improper execution of positional tests. (4) Appropriate management involves targeted repositioning maneuvers for BPPV and vestibular rehabilitation for vestibular migraine, rather than neuroprotective/vasoactive medications.

Support/refutation: The results support all hypotheses: initial vascular/cervical diagnoses were not confirmed; BPPV and vestibular migraine predominated; diagnostic errors were common (62.5% based on complaints only; improper test performance); and repositioning maneuvers were underutilized, with many patients receiving non-targeted medications.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-center observational study of patients presenting with positional vertigo to a specialized outpatient clinic. The study period, recruitment timeframe, and setting beyond the clinic are not specified.

Participants: N=64 patients with complaints of positional vertigo. Exclusion criteria: persistent postural-perceptual vertigo; conditions impeding communication or clinical testing (including dementia); refusal to participate. Demographics: 57/64 (89.1%) female; 37/64 (57.8%) elderly (age threshold not specified).

Assessments: Clinical and neurological examination; otoneurological examination including positional diagnostic tests (Dix-Hallpike, McClure-Pagnini); assessment of spontaneous nystagmus using Frenzel glasses; tests of smooth pursuit, saccades, head-shaking, and Fukuda test. The study emphasizes correct head positioning relative to horizontal, observing the latent period of nystagmus onset, and differentiating peripheral from central nystagmus features. Specifics of test sequence, number of repetitions, and thresholds for abnormality are not reported.

Outcomes and definitions: Etiological diagnoses included BPPV (posterior, horizontal, multichannel), vestibular migraine, vestibular neuronitis, demyelinating disease, brain tumor, and MS exacerbation. Nystagmus characteristics were categorized by direction (rotatory-vertical, horizontal geotropic, vertical downbeat), latency (1–5 s typical for BPPV), duration (up to 1 min), and gaze dependence. Atypical features included strictly torsional nystagmus, prolonged or non-fatiguing positional nystagmus without latency, and positional vomiting without nystagmus.

Interventions: For BPPV, repositioning maneuvers included Epley and Semont for posterior canal, and Lempert and Gufoni for horizontal canal. Vestibular rehabilitation was recommended for vestibular migraine. In practice, many patients received neuroprotective and vasoactive drugs without sufficient indication.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics (counts and percentages) were used. No inferential statistics, effect sizes, or confidence intervals were reported. MRI was not performed in this cohort; indications for MRI are discussed based on literature. Ethical approvals, consent procedures, and data management are not reported.

title: Effects of manual lymphatic drainage on breast cancer-related lymphedema: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does adding MLD to standard postoperative care reduce the incidence of lymphedema after breast cancer surgery with axillary lymph-node dissection? (2) Does MLD reduce arm volume in patients with established lymphedema compared with standard therapy?

Hypotheses: The authors implicitly tested whether MLD confers a clinically meaningful reduction in lymphedema incidence (prevention) and/or arm volume (treatment) relative to standard care. Outcomes supporting efficacy would include a pooled RR <1 (for incidence) or a pooled WMD favoring MLD with a 95% CI excluding zero (for volume reduction). Outcomes refuting efficacy would be pooled estimates not significantly different from the comparator. Given heterogeneity in techniques and comparators, the analysis also considered whether subgroup or sensitivity analyses would clarify effects; however, such analyses were not reported. The review further examined whether MLD outperforms simple lymphatic drainage (SLD) and whether adding sequential pneumatic compression (SPC) to MLD improves outcomes.
reference_methodology:
Search strategy: Comprehensive searches of PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, PEDro, SCOPUS, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ClinicalTrials.gov (http://clinicaltrials.gov/) were conducted using MeSH and free-text terms: 'manual lymph drainage', 'breast cancer OR neoplasm', 'lymphoedema OR lymphedema'. The PubMed 'related articles' feature was used to broaden retrieval. No language restrictions were applied. The final search was performed in December 2012. Reference lists of relevant papers and expert contacts were also screened.

Eligibility criteria: Included RCTs or quasi-RCTs evaluated MLD for prevention or treatment of breast cancer–related lymphedema. Trials had to report: (1) inclusion/exclusion criteria, (2) MLD technique, (3) compression strategy, (4) lymphedema definition, and (5) evaluation of lymphedema severity. Exclusions: no axillary lymph-node dissection (e.g., sentinel node only), unclear outcomes, or duplicate cohorts.

Study selection and data extraction: Two authors independently extracted participant characteristics, inclusion/exclusion criteria, MLD technique, compression strategy, lymphedema parameters, and complications. Disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. Methodological quality was independently appraised by two authors, focusing on randomization adequacy, allocation concealment, blinding, follow-up duration, dropout rates, and intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis.

Outcomes and measures: Prevention outcome was incidence of postoperative lymphedema at 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Treatment outcome was reduction in arm volume measured by water displacement volumetry at baseline and at 1, 3, and 12 months. Absolute edema volume was defined as the difference between affected and contralateral arm volumes. Lymphedema definitions varied: >10% volume difference vs contralateral arm; ≥200 ml increase vs pre-surgery; ≥20 mm circumference increase vs pre-surgery.

Statistical analysis: Analyses were conducted in Review Manager 5.1 (Cochrane Collaboration). Dichotomous outcomes were summarized as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs; continuous outcomes as weighted mean differences (WMD) with 95% CIs. When necessary, standard deviations were estimated from reported CIs, standard errors, or ranges. Pooled estimates used a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model to accommodate heterogeneity, yielding conservative CIs. Heterogeneity was quantified with I². Data were pooled only when clinical and methodological similarity was adequate. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed.

title: Projected epidemiological consequences of the Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variant in England, December 2021 to April 2022
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the projected epidemiological consequences of Omicron in England (December 2021–April 2022) under plausible immune escape and booster effectiveness scenarios? (2) How do Omicron’s relative transmissibility and immune escape compare to Delta, and what growth dynamics does this imply? (3) What is the potential impact of existing and additional control measures (mask-wearing, Plan B, roadmap steps) on hospitalizations and deaths? (4) How sensitive are outcomes to booster uptake, rollout speed, and early seeding rates?

Hypotheses: (a) Omicron will outcompete Delta in England due to immune escape, leading to rapid growth and increased healthcare burden; (b) Booster effectiveness and immune escape jointly determine the magnitude of hospitalizations and deaths, with high escape and low booster effectiveness producing the largest burden; (c) Additional NPIs (Step 1/2) will reduce peak admissions and deaths relative to Plan B, but may increase exit waves; (d) Increasing booster uptake will substantially mitigate burden, while slower rollout will have limited impact if prioritization targets older adults. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include modeled increases in SGTF, rapid growth (r ≈ 0.29/day), and scenario totals/peaks consistent with the stated ranges.
reference_methodology:
Design: Deterministic compartmental transmission model fitted to England’s epidemic data (March 2020–November 2021) and extended to project December 2021–April 2022 under Omicron. The model tracks multiple variants (wild-type, Alpha, Delta, Omicron) and includes compartments for susceptible, infected (with variant-specific parameters), recovered, and vaccinated (primary and boosted) individuals. Variant-specific parameters include transmission rates, vaccine effectiveness against infection and severe outcomes, and waning.

Data: Model fit uses hospital admissions, hospital bed occupancy, ICU bed occupancy, PCR prevalence, seroprevalence, SGTF (proxy for Omicron), genomic sequencing (Alpha and Delta introductions), and vaccine coverage. SGTF growth is used to calibrate Omicron’s spread. Mobility is assumed unchanged from November 30, 2021 levels, with a 7.5% transmission reduction from mask-wearing (30 Nov 2021–30 Apr 2022). Plan B measures (12 Dec 2021) include certification (modeled as a 17% increase in vaccination uptake for ages 18–29), work-from-home guidance (workplace mobility set to March 15, 2021 levels), and face coverings (no additional effect beyond existing mandates). Roadmap steps (Step 0/1/2) are modeled by returning mobility indices to levels observed during equivalent steps in early 2021.

Vaccine and immune escape assumptions: Neutralization studies inform immune escape relative to Delta: 5.1-fold (EL) and 12.8-fold (EH) reductions in neutralization titre. Using Khoury et al.’s relationship between neutralization titre and protection, vaccine effectiveness against infection and severe outcomes is derived. Booster effectiveness is informed by neutralization increases after Moderna (2.5-fold) and Sinovac (4.9-fold) boosters; for AstraZeneca primary recipients boosted with Pfizer or half-dose Moderna, protection against infection is assumed to reach Pfizer/Moderna levels, then scaled to severe outcomes via the Khoury relationship. Individuals previously infected are assumed to have protection against Omicron equivalent to two doses of Pfizer/Moderna. Baseline severity for Omicron and Delta is assumed identical; average severity per infection is lower for Omicron due to immune escape.

Calibration and projections: The model is fitted to historical data (Fig. 2a; Fig. S2) and then used to project variant proportions (Fig. 1d) and outcomes under four immune escape–booster effectiveness combinations. Omicron’s transmissibility relative to Delta is calibrated to match SGTF growth (Fig. 1b). Growth rate r is estimated from SGTF; Rt is computed assuming a 5.5-day generation interval (SD 1.8 days). Sensitivity analyses vary initial seeding rates (5, 10, 20 infections per NHS region/day), booster uptake (0%, 50%, 99%), and booster rollout speed (200,000, 350,000, 500,000/day). Ethics approval: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine Ethics Committee (project ID: 22828).

title: Feasibility, SAR Distribution, and Clinical Outcome upon Reirradiation and Deep Hyperthermia Using the Hypercollar3D in Head and Neck Cancer Patients
field_subfield: Medicine — Oncology (Head and Neck Cancer; Hyperthermia)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Is deep hyperthermia using the Hypercollar3D feasible in patients with recurrent or SP HNC undergoing reirradiation, in terms of patient tolerance, treatment duration, and achievable tumor-targeted cfSAR? (2) What are the oncologic outcomes (CR, LC, OS) and toxicity profiles of thermoradiotherapy with Hypercollar3D in this population? (3) Does the interval from prior radiotherapy predict LC in this cohort? (4) How does the Hypercollar3D compare to the earlier Hypercollar in tumor-targeted cfSAR delivery?

Hypotheses: (a) Hypercollar3D will enable feasible deep hyperthermia with improved tumor-targeted cfSAR compared to the earlier Hypercollar; (b) Thermoradiotherapy will achieve CR rates comparable to literature for reirradiation ± chemotherapy; (c) Longer intervals from prior RT will be associated with better LC; (d) Protocol adjustments to mitigate normal tissue toxicity (e.g., masseter SAR threshold) will reduce trismus without compromising oncologic outcomes. Support for these hypotheses would be demonstrated by high treatment completion rates, higher cfSAR than prior applicator, CR/LC/OS within reported ranges, significant LC differences by interval, and reduced trismus incidence after protocol changes.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Retrospective cohort study at a single institution (Erasmus MC Cancer Institute, Rotterdam) with ethics approval (MEC-2018-1453) and consent waived due to retrospective design and use of non-identifying data. Inclusion: patients with recurrent or SP HNC treated with reirradiation plus deep hyperthermia using Hypercollar3D between 2014 and 2018 with curative intent. Exclusion criteria for hyperthermia: systemic temperature >39°C, claustrophobia, tumor caudal to a tracheostomy, anatomical constraints preventing applicator positioning, and presence of a pacemaker.

Participants: N=22 patients. Definitive thermoradiotherapy: n=13; postoperative thermoradiotherapy: n=9. Median follow-up for LC: 17.5 months (IQR 6.0–31.0). Median follow-up for OS: 24.5 months (IQR 11.0–48.0). Median interval from prior radiotherapy: 51.5 months (IQR 17.5–122.0). Thirteen patients had local recurrence; fourteen had any recurrence; fourteen died during follow-up.

Radiotherapy: Techniques at treating physician discretion: CyberKnife stereotactic radiotherapy (n=7) and external beam IMRT/VMAT (n=15). Fields included primary tumor site with or without elective neck irradiation. Fractionation schemes are listed in Table 1 (not provided in text). Dose and fractionation details are not reported in the provided text.

Hyperthermia: Weekly, after each RT fraction, for 75 minutes, targeting GTV with margins; in postsurgical cases, the radiation CTV often served as the hyperthermia target; if too large, a high-risk zone was prioritized. Planning: automatic segmentation of planning CT; SEMCAD-X for electromagnetic field calculations per antenna; VEDO for SAR optimization to maximize THQ (THQ_1% defined as total hotspot volume of 1% of total volume). Real-time monitoring used applied cubic filtered SAR (cfSAR) estimated from measured power/phase and precomputed antenna fields. Re-optimization occurred if patient discomfort indicated hotspots (diagnosed by briefly turning off total power). Protocol adjustments after early trismus: power increments reduced from 20 W to 10 W per 5 minutes; absolute SAR threshold of 175 W/kg in the masseter region. Invasive thermometry was mandatory if predicted treatment quality (TC25) <75%; optional otherwise. Optional normal tissue temperature measurements were performed if distinct hotspots were predicted. Hyperthermia sessions were marked as prematurely aborted if duration <70 minutes. Effective treatment time per session was defined as input power >1 W during the session.

Data collection: Patient/tumor/treatment details extracted from records; radiotherapy and hyperthermia characteristics from planning/recording systems. Outcomes: local recurrence (LC), distant recurrence, survival status, date and cause of death, and acute/late toxicity. Toxicity scored per CTCAE v4 at baseline, end of RT, and at 3–4 and 12 months; grade 1 toxicities excluded due to retrospective unreliability. After evaluating the first five patients, range of motion (ROM) of the jaw was measured before and after each treatment to better capture trismus.

Statistical analysis: LC and OS calculated from RT start to event. LC failure defined as physician-diagnosed local recurrence (clinical/imaging). Censoring: LC after last physician visit for recurrent disease or death; OS after civil registry consultation. Kaplan–Meier methods with log-rank tests compared groups (e.g., interval from prior RT).

title: Performance of three rapid antigen tests against the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant Authors
research_question:
Research question: Does the Omicron variant’s nucleocapsid protein mutations affect the analytic sensitivity of three widely used at-home rapid antigen tests (BinaxNOW, FlowFlex, iHealth) relative to the Delta variant across a range of viral loads?

Hypotheses: The primary hypothesis was that Omicron’s N protein mutations would reduce RADT analytic sensitivity compared to Delta, potentially lowering positivity rates at comparable Ct values. The alternative hypothesis was that sensitivity would remain unchanged, reflecting robustness of the antigen targets and assay performance to Omicron’s mutations. Secondary questions included whether inter-assay differences exist among the three RADTs and whether there is a practical detection threshold (e.g., Ct ≥27.5 on the Roche cobas E gene target) beyond which no RADT detects infection. Outcomes supporting the primary hypothesis would include significantly lower Omicron positivity rates versus Delta within matched Ct strata. Outcomes supporting the alternative hypothesis would include similar positivity rates across variants and Ct strata. Inter-assay differences would be indicated by significant contrasts in positivity or Ct overlap ranges between devices.
reference_methodology:
Design: Analytic sensitivity comparison of three rapid antigen tests (BinaxNOW, FlowFlex, iHealth) using clinical nasal samples from patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, stratified by RT-PCR Ct and variant (Omicron vs Delta).

Samples: 30 Omicron-positive and 30 Delta-positive samples collected from anterior nares in universal transport medium (UTM) at Massachusetts General Hospital. Omicron samples were collected Nov 30, 2021–Dec 27, 2021; nine Delta samples were collected Aug–Nov 2021. Samples were not heat-inactivated. Variant assignment used a combination of TaqPath COVID-19 Combo Kit (for spike gene target failure, SGTF, a proxy for Δ69–70) and the TaqMan SARS-CoV-2 Mutation Panel (amplifying six spike mutations characterizing major variants). One Omicron sample was positive for only the K417N target due to low nucleic acid; it was assumed Omicron because of SGTF. All other samples were verified by multiple targets from the mutation panel.

RT-PCR and Ct stratification: All samples were run on the Roche cobas SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR assay targeting the envelope (E) and ORF1ab genes. For each variant, 10 samples were selected per Ct category: <20, 20–30, and >30 (E gene Ct). The study reports a detection threshold of Ct ≥27.5 for the E gene target on the cobas assay.

RADT procedures: For each RADT, the kit-supplied swab was mixed with 50 μL of sample for 15 seconds, followed by the manufacturer’s instructions for use. Samples underwent one freeze-thaw cycle prior to examination on the iHealth assay and two freeze-thaw cycles for all other assays. Each sample was tested in duplicate. Results were read after 15 minutes by two independent readers blinded to variant status and Ct values. All three RADTs were tested over a 2-day period.

Statistical analysis: Chi-squared tests compared the distribution of RADT results by variant within each Ct stratum and overall. Logistic regression estimated the impact of variant and RADT on the likelihood of test positivity, controlling for Ct values. No additional details on model specification (e.g., covariate handling, interaction terms, or random effects) were provided.

Ethics: The study was deemed non-human subjects research and approved by the Brigham Institutional Review Board (protocol 2021P003604).

title: Pulmonary Artery Sling Presenting as Pneumonia and Inhalation of a Foreign Body
research_question:
The implicit clinical questions were: (1) In an infant with recurrent respiratory infections and pneumonia following a choking episode, could PAS be the underlying cause of persistent respiratory symptoms despite removal of a suspected foreign body? (2) Would surgical correction of PAS (LPA reimplantation) combined with management of tracheal stenosis (slide tracheoplasty) resolve respiratory distress and reduce RRTI incidence? (3) Could OM-85 immunomodulatory prophylaxis reduce infection burden pre- and postoperatively in PAS-associated RRTI?

No explicit hypotheses were stated. Outcomes that would support these questions include confirmation of PAS by echocardiography and CT angiography, demonstration of airway stenosis, resolution of respiratory distress after surgical correction, and a documented reduction in RRTI frequency following surgery and prophylaxis. Outcomes that would refute them would include persistent symptoms without vascular anomaly, lack of improvement after surgery, or continued high RRTI incidence despite prophylaxis.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-patient clinical case report with longitudinal follow-up.

Patient: 13-month-old male with a 3-day history of worsening cough following a choking episode while eating rice. History included 8–9 RRTIs since 3 months of age (primarily bronchitis/bronchopneumonia). No asthma or family history of asthma.

Initial evaluation (January 13, 2014): Local hospital auscultation revealed diminished left-sided breath sounds. Chest X-ray showed bronchopneumonia, mediastinal right shift, and left-sided emphysema (Figure 1). Computed tomography virtual bronchoscopy (CTVB) suggested pneumonia and a bronchial foreign body (Figure 2). Auscultation confirmed reduced left breath sounds with rales and wheezing.

Intervention 1 (foreign body removal): Under general anesthesia, rigid electronic bronchoscopy was performed. No foreign body was seen in the left bronchus; a rice-like foreign body was visualized in the right bronchus and removed. No residual foreign body was identified in either bronchus. Postsurgery diagnosis: bronchial foreign body with bronchopneumonia. Postoperative course: cough and wheezing persisted for 3 days. Sputum culture and viral rapid antigen tests were ordered; bronchodilator therapy (budesonide, ipratropium bromide, salbutamol) was administered. Two days later, symptoms improved, but predischarge chest X-ray showed no improvement in pneumonia, mediastinal shift, or emphysema. Parents declined further examination and requested discharge.

Follow-up (one month later): Readmitted with 5-day history of cough. Physical exam: reduced left breath sounds, rales, wheezing. Chest X-ray: persistent bronchopneumonia, mediastinal right shift, left-sided emphysema (Figure 3). Immunological analysis by turbidimetric inhibition immunoassay showed reduced C3 and C4. Diagnosis: bronchopneumonia and RRTI. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed airway dysplasia, an O-shaped tracheal cartilage ring, and stenosis of the left bronchus (Figure 4). Echocardiogram identified PAS (Figure 5). Cardiac CT angiography confirmed PAS (Figure 6). The left bronchus stenosis measured approximately 0.8 cm.

Management: OM-85 immunomodulatory prophylaxis was prescribed for 3 months prior to surgery. Two months later, the patient underwent LPA reimplantation and slide tracheoplasty via median sternotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass. Postoperative course: resolution of respiratory distress. Subsequent years included mild acute infections (likely rhinovirus in 2014; mild hand-foot-mouth disease in 2015) with additional 3-month OM-85 courses in 2015 and 2017; no recurrence of RRTI was reported.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. Consent: Not reported.

title: Adherence to Antiretroviral Therapy and Associated Factors Among Children Living With HIV in East Wallaga Zone Public Health Institutions, Ethiopia
field_subfield: Public Health — HIV/AIDS and Pediatric Care
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the level of ART adherence among children living with HIV attending public health institutions in East Wollega Zone? (2) Which sociodemographic, clinical, and care-related factors are associated with adherence?

The study did not state explicit a priori hypotheses. Implicit expectations, based on prior literature, included that disclosure of HIV status, caregiver–provider relationship quality, and proximity to health facilities would be positively associated with adherence. The analysis tested these associations via logistic regression, with adherence defined as caregiver-reported missed doses over 3, 7, and 30 days. Outcomes supporting the implicit hypotheses would include statistically significant adjusted odds ratios (AORs) >1 for disclosure, good caregiver–provider relations, and shorter travel distances. Conversely, non-significant associations or AORs near 1 would refute or nuance these expectations.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Institution-based cross-sectional study conducted from July to September 2018 in seven public health facilities in East Wollega Zone, Oromia, Ethiopia: Nekemte Specialized Hospital, Gida Ayana District Hospital, Jima Arjo, Gutin, Gudtu Arjo, Sire, and Nekemte Health Center.

Participants: Under-15 children living with HIV on ART for >6 months and their primary caregivers were eligible. Inclusion required caregiver consent and presence with the child in the prior month. Exclusions: caregivers not with the child in the past month; caregivers of children with terminal illness or major disability (e.g., deafness). Children were selected by simple random sampling.

Sample: The analysis comprised 237 children and their caregivers among 259 research participants (92% response rate). The median child age was 12 years. Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics (Table 2) included caregiver sex (74.3% female), age (31–40 years: 46.8%), marital status (married: 59.9%), education (no formal: 27.0%; primary: 39.2%; secondary: 23.2%; college/university: 10.5%), occupation (farmer: 23.6%; day laborer: 29.1%; government employee: 13.1%; unemployed: 15.2%), income (<500: 40.9%; 501–1000: 34.6%; 1000–2000: 14.3%; >2000: 10.1%), residence (urban: 70.5%; rural: 29.5%), proximity to ART facility (<10 km: 81.4%; >10 km: 18.6%), caregiver HIV status (positive: 82.3%), caregiver on ART (82.3%), disclosure of child’s HIV status (yes: 38.4%), WHO stage at ART initiation (stage I: 21.5%; II: 36.3%; III: 40.5%; IV: 1.7%), current treatment stage (T1: 86.5%; T2: 7.2%; T3: 6.3%), baseline CD4 count (<500: 50.2%; >500: 49.8%), current CD4 count (<500: 26.2%; >500: 73.8%), current viral load (<1000: 79.3%; ≥1000: 20.7%), and ART duration (<5 years: 32.5%; >5 years: 67.5%).

Measures: Adherence was caregiver-reported via structured questionnaire items on missed doses in the previous 3, 7, and 30 days. Adherence percentage was computed as (pills taken/prescribed)*100. Operational definition: adherence if ≤1 dose missed in the past month or none missed in the past 3 or 7 days (>95% of prescribed doses). Variables included sociodemographics, healthcare delivery factors (caregiver–provider relationship quality), therapy-related factors (regimen line, WHO stage at initiation), environmental factors (residence, proximity), and disclosure status.

Data collection and quality: The questionnaire was adapted from ART guidelines, follow-up forms, and prior literature. It was pretested (5% of items), and data collectors/supervisors received 2 days of training. The instrument was administered in English, translated to Afaan Oromo, and back-translated to ensure consistency.

Statistical analysis: Data were entered into SPSS v20. Bivariate logistic regression identified candidate predictors (p≤0.20). Multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit was computed. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

Ethics: Institutional Review Board approval was obtained from Wallaga University (DPH/114/12). A formal letter was provided to facilities. Written informed consent was obtained from participants; verbal consent was repeated prior to interviews. Confidentiality and participant rights were protected.

title: Fakability of Interest Tests
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are women able to alter their SVIB scores as easily as they alter KPR scores when instructed to fake highest and lowest categories in the opposite direction? (2) Does intelligence (Otis IQ) influence the ability to fake interest test scores within a superior-IQ range? (3) Can the Michigan Vocabulary Profile Test identify individuals attempting to fake interest test scores?

Hypotheses (implicit from aims): (a) The KPR would be more susceptible to faking than the SVIB; (b) Faking would be possible in both upward and downward directions without directional preference; (c) IQ would not systematically predict faking success within the sampled range; (d) Vocabulary knowledge would align with genuine interest (higher vocabulary for higher interest) and oppose faked scores (low vocabulary for upward fakers; high vocabulary for downward fakers). Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include significant negative original–faked correlations and significant differences for KPR categories, balanced success rates for upward/downward faking, no IQ-related differences in faking success, and consistent vocabulary–interest relationships.
reference_methodology:
Design: Two-session experimental study with a within-subjects manipulation of response honesty versus deliberate faking. Session 1 (baseline): SVIB Form W, KPR Form eH, and Otis Self-Administering Test of Mental Ability Form D were administered in that order under instructions to respond honestly, following test manuals. Session 2 (faking): Two weeks later, SVIB Form W, Michigan Vocabulary Profile Test Form BM, and KPR Form eH were administered in that order. Subjects were explicitly instructed to fake the highest and lowest interest categories from Session 1 in the opposite direction (i.e., if a category was high in Session 1, fake it low in Session 2, and vice versa). The study focused on the highest and lowest categories per test to isolate faking attempts.

Participants: Thirty female college seniors (mature, unsophisticated) from Rosary College (Loyola University Chicago). The sample was limited to women to align with the thesis’s focus on female fakability. No further demographic details were reported.

Measures: (1) KPR Form eH: nine broad interest areas (mechanical, computational, scientific, persuasive, artistic, literary, musical, social service, clerical). Scoring: percentile ranks. (2) SVIB Form W: seventeen occupational categories (artist, author, buyer, elementary school teacher, business education teacher, English teacher, mathematics teacher, physical education teacher, social science teacher, home economics teacher, housewife, laboratory technician, life insurance saleswoman, office worker, social worker, stenographer, nurse). Scoring: standard scores. (3) Otis Self-Administering Test of Mental Ability Form D: IQ scores used to assess the effect of intelligence on fakability. (4) Michigan Vocabulary Profile Test Form BM: seven domain scores (human relations, government and commerce, physical sciences, biological sciences, mathematics, fine arts) used to identify fakers by comparing vocabulary with original and faked interest scores.

KPR verification score (V-score): A previously developed scale based on common response patterns on the KPR; a V-score between 38–44 indicates sincere responding; scores <38 or >44 indicate faked responding.

Procedure: In Session 1, subjects completed SVIB, KPR, and Otis under honest-response instructions. In Session 2, they completed SVIB, Michigan Vocabulary Profile, and KPR with explicit faking instructions targeting the highest and lowest categories from Session 1. The two-week interval aimed to reduce memory effects and practice.

Analysis: For KPR, original and faked percentile ranks were compared using t-tests for differences and correlations between original and faked scores per category. For SVIB, original and faked standard scores were compared similarly. Correlations were computed between IQ and faking success, and between Vocabulary Profile domain scores and both original and faked interest scores. The V-score was examined to distinguish sincere from faked KPR responses. Significance thresholds were reported at 1% and 5% levels. No details were provided on randomization, blinding, or statistical software.

title: Los estudios superiores en Santo Domingo durante el período colonial. Bibliografía crítica, metodología y estado de la cuestión
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the historical and legal status of the Universidad de Santo Domingo founded by the 1538 bull In apostolatus culmine, and does it constitute the first university in the Americas? (2) What is the authenticity and legal force of the bull, given the absence of surviving originals and the lack of royal pase regio? (3) How did the Universidad de Santiago de la Paz (Gorjón) originate, evolve, and interact with Santo Domingo’s university, particularly under Jesuit management? (4) What governance structures and statutes regulated these institutions, and how did they change over the 18th century?

Hypotheses/predictions: (a) The 1538 bull is authentic and functionally effective as a papal instrument of university erection, despite lacking royal pase regio; (b) Santo Domingo’s university predates and is legally distinct from Santiago de la Paz; (c) Jesuit management revitalized Gorjón/Santiago de la Paz but did not alter its foundational legal status; (d) The 18th-century statutes (1754) formalized governance and curtailed conventual dominance, reflecting secularizing trends. Outcomes supporting these include archival corroboration of the bull’s issuance (Vatican perpetual inventory; Dominican petition with papal autograph), documentary evidence of the 1558 real cédula and 1747 brief, and the 1754 statutes’ approval. Outcomes refuting would include conclusive proof of forgery or non-issuance of the bull, or evidence that royal pase regio was indispensable and absent.
reference_methodology:
Design: Critical historiographical synthesis with primary-source-based verification. The author organizes the work into: (1) historical evolution of the two universities; (2) sources and bibliography; (3) state of the question; and (4) an extensive bibliographic appendix.

Data/sources: Primary sources include the Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Santo Domingo Audiencia records (e.g., patronato, contratación, escribanía de cámara, justicia, contaduría, gobierno, indiferente general), Vatican archives (Bullarium Ordinis FF. Praedicatorum; perpetual inventory of Paul III; briefs and cédulas), Jesuit and Dominican order archives, Archivo Nacional de Bogotá (including the 1583 Estatutos de Gorjón), Archivo Nacional de La Habana, Archivo General de la Nación (Caracas), and local repositories. The article also references printed collections (e.g., Recopilación de Leyes de Indias; Cedulario Americano de los XVIII; Hemández’s collection of American and Philippine documents) and university publications (e.g., Anales de la Universidad de Santo Domingo; Historia y Sociedad series).

Key documents: (a) 1538 bull In apostolatus culmine (Paul III) erecting the Universidad de Santo Domingo; (b) 1558 real cédula elevating Gorjón to university status; (c) 1703–1745 Jesuit management of Gorjón; (d) 1745 royal cédula granting Jesuits perpetual ownership of Gorjón’s assets; (e) 1747 brief In supereminenti (Benedicto XIV) erecting Santiago de la Paz as a pontifical university; (f) 1747 royal cédula equalizing degree-conferring rights of Santo Domingo and Santiago de la Paz; (g) 1754 royal cédula approving Santo Domingo’s statutes; (h) 1747 royal provision requiring four years of apprenticeship before admission to the bar; (i) Dominican petition with papal autograph (1538) and Vatican perpetual inventory entry.

Procedures: The author applies a three-stage method: (1) heuristic documentation (systematic identification and cataloging of sources); (2) hermeneutic critique (external criticism: provenance, dating, authenticity; internal criticism: content validity, legal interpretation); (3) synthesis (interpretation of facts into broader narratives). The analysis triangulates multiple repositories to corroborate claims (e.g., Vatican inventory and Dominican petition for the bull’s authenticity). It also reconstructs institutional chronologies (e.g., 16th–18th century) and legal disputes (e.g., 1704–1747 litigation over degree conferral and primacy).

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; historical archival research. No human subjects or sensitive data are involved.

title: How Well Do We Know the Surface Impact of Sudden Stratospheric Warmings?
field_subfield: Atmospheric Science — Stratosphere–Troposphere Coupling and Climate Variability
research_question: The study addresses two questions: (1) How robust are the observed composite surface responses to SSWs to sampling variability? (2) Is the spread in composite surface anomalies explained by differences in the stratospheric conditions sampled (e.g., NAM strength, descent characteristics) or by unrelated tropospheric variability? The authors hypothesize that while the sign of key responses (negative NAO, Eurasian cooling, Canadian/US cooling) is robust, their magnitudes and spatial patterns vary due to internal atmospheric noise. They further hypothesize that the spread in surface anomalies is not primarily determined by the spread in stratospheric vortex strength or NAM descent, but rather by unrelated tropospheric variability. Evidence supporting the hypotheses would include: (i) consistent sign across bootstrap composites with large magnitude/pattern variability; (ii) weak correlations between surface anomalies and stratospheric strength (e.g., z10-5 day), and modest correlations with lower stratospheric anomalies that still explain limited variance; and (iii) limited ENSO modulation of North Pacific SLP shifts. Evidence refuting the hypotheses would include strong, monotonic relationships between surface anomalies and stratospheric strength across composites.
reference_methodology:
Data: JRA-55 (Japan Meteorological Agency; Kobayashi et al., 2015) covering 1958–2019, with 60 vertical levels and daily fields. The dataset is chosen for its top above the stratopause (0.1 hPa), fine vertical resolution, and suitability for SSW studies. Fields analyzed include winds, SLP, temperatures, precipitation, and geopotential heights.

SSW detection: Following Charlton & Polvani (2007; corrigendum Charlton-Perez & Polvani, 2011), an SSW is defined as a reversal of zonal mean zonal winds at 10 hPa and 60°N from westerly to easterly during extended boreal winter (NDJFM). The central date is the first day with easterly winds. No day within 20 days following the central date is considered a separate SSW. If winds do not return to westerly for at least 10 consecutive days before April 30, the event is classified as a final stratospheric warming and excluded. This definition is among those described in Butler & Gerber (2018) as optimal. The procedure identifies 39 SSWs in JRA-55 (1958–2019).

Composite construction: Synthetic SSW composites are formed by resampling with replacement (bootstrap) from the 39 observed SSWs to create 2,000 composites of 39 events each. This isolates variability across composites rather than event-to-event variability. To verify sampling consistency, the authors examine the distribution of the number of unique events per composite and the maximum repetition of any single event; these match multinomial expectations (Figure S1).

Climatological baseline: 2,000 climatological composites are formed by randomly selecting 39 winter 60-day periods (matching the seasonal distribution of SSWs) and assigning each to a random year from 1958–2019, preserving seasonality while forming a climatology independent of vortex state.

Anomalies and indices: Daily anomalies are computed by subtracting the climatological daily mean (mean of each calendar day over 1958–2019). The NAM is computed as a deseasonalized, detrended daily mean geopotential height anomaly averaged over 65–90°N, normalized to unit variance with a sign convention such that negative NAM indicates a weak polar vortex. Regional indices are defined as area-weighted averages over specified boxes: (1) NAO: SLP difference between 62.5–90°N, 45°W–10°E and 35–50°N, 45°W–10°E; (2) North Atlantic precipitation: 30–50°N, 40°W–10°E; (3) North Pacific SLP: 30–60°N, 175°E–135°W; (4) Northern Eurasian Ts: 60–75°N, 30–120°E; (5) Eastern Canadian Ts: 45–70°N, 45–90°W; (6) Eastern United States Ts: 25–42.5°N, 65–90°W. Significance is assessed via two-tailed Student’s t-tests at the 95% level in figures.

ENSO modulation analysis: For North Pacific SLP, observed SSWs are separated by ENSO phase (El Niño, La Niña, neutral) using NOAA ONI. Composites of 10 SSW events per phase are formed (reduced sample size due to phase availability).

title: Simulations multi-échelles de matériaux polymères
field_subfield: Materials Science — Polymer Physics and Computational Modeling
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Can bottom-up, chemical-specific mesoscopic potentials derived from atomistic configurations reproduce polymer melt structure, thermodynamics, and dynamics quantitatively? (2) Are such potentials transferable across polymer chemistries (cis-PB, PIB, PDMS), chain lengths, and temperatures? (3) Can DPD with these potentials capture viscoelastic relaxation, entanglement statistics, and network elasticity? (4) How do polymer–silica interfacial interactions and grafting density affect chain conformation, interphase structure, and dynamics?

Hypotheses: (i) IBI-derived mesoscopic potentials, when corrected for pressure, will match experimental densities, R2ee/M, and αp at 300 K; (ii) transferability will hold for different polymers and chain lengths, enabling entanglement analysis; (iii) DPD will reproduce entanglement modulus G0N and network elasticity consistent with phantom network theory; (iv) grafting density will increase brush thickness (R2ee/M) and slow grafted-chain dynamics, while free-chain dynamics will be slowed only at high φg where interphase overlap is eliminated. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include quantitative agreement with experiments and theory, and systematic trends with φg and confinement.
reference_methodology:
Atomistic MD: Systems of monodisperse cis-PB (200 monomers per chain; 800 carbons; M ≈ 10.8 kg mol−1) were equilibrated at 600 K (2 ns, NpT, 0.1 MPa, Berendsen) then quenched to 300 K (2 ns). Five independent configurations were generated to reduce statistical uncertainty. Validation included Gaussian end-to-end distributions, R2ee/R2g ≈ 6, and αp from dilatometry (Tg slightly below experimental 165 K). Segmental relaxation was quantified via P2(t) fits (KWW) and MSD(t) to assess reptation onset.

Coarse-graining: Bead size λ = 5 monomers per bead (cis-PB bead mass ≈ 270 g mol−1). To increase statistics, beads were slid along chains (sliding coarse-graining). RDFs were computed for nonbonded pairs, bonded pairs, and bond angles; potentials were initialized as ω(r) = −kBT ln g(r). IBI iteratively adjusted potentials to match target RDFs: ωi+1(r) = ωi(r) + kBT ln[gi(r)/gcible(r)], with 5 ns equilibration between iterations and 5 iterations to convergence.
