Tabulated potentials with cubic spline interpolation were used; bond-angle potentials were included to enforce realistic bond-angle distributions.

Pressure correction: IBI overestimated pressure (e.g., 72 MPa at 300 K). A short-range attractive correction Δωpress(r) = A(1 − r/rc) was added to the nonbonded potential to restore NpT pressure to 0.1 MPa; A was tuned iteratively. Post-correction, RDFs remained accurate while pressure fluctuations centered on 0.1 MPa.

DPD simulations: Real units were used (time in ns, length in nm, energy in J mol−1). Conservative forces included realistic nonbonded and bonded terms; friction γ = 300 kg mol−1 ns−1; noise amplitude set by fluctuation–dissipation (σ2 = 2γkBT). Integration used DPD-VV with δt = 50 fs. Periodic boundary conditions; minimum-image convention; cutoff rc = 4 nm. Systems: 40 chains × 40 beads (cis-PB, PIB, PDMS) for bulk; 40 chains × 40 beads for network simulations; 40 chains × 40 beads between two silica planes (9 × 9 nm2 each) separated by D = 10 nm for confinement studies. For networks, PIB was crosslinked by converting entanglement nodes to covalent junctions (functionality f = 4) with subchain length Mcl ≈ 6.4 kg mol−1.

Observables: Thermodynamics (ρ, v = 1/ρ), structural (R2ee, R2g, R2ee/R2g, R2ij/Mij vs segment length), dynamics (Ree autocorrelation, MSD, diffusion coefficients D), viscoelasticity (G(t) via Green–Kubo from pressure tensor autocorrelations; multiple-correlator algorithm with m = 2, p = 16), entanglement analysis (PPA at 0 K with intramolecular interactions disabled and bond potentials shifted to enforce non-crossing), and interfacial structure (RDFs g(z), density profiles, R2g∥ and R2g⊥ components). For networks, uniaxial traction was simulated by anisotropic barostat imposing σzz = 0.10–0.30 MPa while Pxx = Pyy = 0.1 MPa; strain ε = (Lz − Lz(0))/Lz(0) and Poisson’s ratio ν were computed.

title: Modeling the use of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination to safely relax non-pharmaceutical interventions
research_question:
Research questions: (1) When can NPIs be safely relaxed as vaccination proceeds, and how does the timing depend on rollout speed and dosing strategy? (2) How do vaccine mechanisms (susceptibility-only vs susceptibility+severity) and baseline immunity affect the safety and timing of relaxation? (3) What is the population risk if vaccinated individuals relax NPIs earlier than unvaccinated individuals? (4) What policy thresholds (e.g., delays, speeds) minimize deaths and health system burden?

Hypotheses: (a) Rapid two-dose vaccination enables safe relaxation within 2–9 months, substantially reducing deaths and shortening the epidemic compared to relaxing without vaccination. (b) The extent of delay needed to safely reopen depends primarily on rollout speed, with vaccine mechanism playing a secondary role. (c) Allowing vaccinated individuals to relax earlier poses limited population risk. (d) One-dose strategies can accelerate coverage but may be suboptimal or risky if relative efficacy is low (RE<80%).

Support/refutation criteria: Hypotheses are supported if modeled deaths and hospitalizations under delayed, rapid two-dose rollout are markedly lower than immediate relaxation without vaccination, and if allowing vaccinated individuals to relax earlier yields minimal additional risk. Hypotheses are nuanced if lower baseline immunity or susceptibility+severity mechanisms require longer delays or slower relaxation to avoid surges.
reference_methodology:
Model structure: A seven-compartment SEAIRH model (S: susceptible; E: exposed; A: asymptomatic infectious; I: symptomatic infectious; H: hospitalized; R: recovered; D: deceased) is stratified by age (<20, 20–64, ≥65) and risk (high vs low). High-risk individuals include those with underlying health conditions (size estimates from Clark et al.) and those with occupational exposure (NAS framework). Relative infection risk for high-risk groups is parameterized from Clark et al. (see SI for values).

Baseline immunity: Baseline immunity is set to 32% (approximately 4× reported cases as of Feb 23, 2021), with a sensitivity analysis at 16%. Immunity is assumed to confer protection against infection for the simulation horizon. Age distribution of prior infection is derived from CDC seroprevalence in Georgia, California, Wisconsin, and New York, averaged and adjusted for age sampling weights (ACS 2019).

Vaccination: Vaccination is implemented by adding vaccinated compartments (S_V, E_V, A_V, I_V, R_V, H_V, D_V) with reduced susceptibility and/or severity. Vaccination prioritization follows NAS/CDC guidance: high-risk elderly first, then low-risk elderly, high-risk adults, and low-risk adults. Doses are allocated to each group until 80% coverage is reached, then redistributed to remaining eligible groups. Children are not modeled due to trial exclusion and low initial uptake. The overall daily vaccination rate λ is converted to monthly two-dose series and then to age/risk-specific rates. Two-dose series are assumed for mRNA vaccines; one-dose scenarios approximate J&J’s single-dose strategy with high efficacy.

Vaccine mechanisms: Two mechanisms are modeled. Susceptibility-only: VE_susceptibility=0.9, VE_infectiousness=0, VE_progression=0. Susceptibility+severity: VE_susceptibility=0.67, VE_infectiousness=0, VE_progression=0.70 (chosen so (1−0.67)×(1−0.70)=0.03≈1−0.97). Vaccination does not reduce infectiousness once infected. One-dose relative efficacy (RE) is varied at 100%, 80%, and 60% (main text focuses on 80%).

Contact patterns and NPI relaxation: Age-stratified contact matrices are from Prem et al. At simulation start, contacts are 45% of baseline (calibrated to match early February hospitalizations with a 75% reporting rate and 55% baseline reduction). Relaxation is modeled as a linear increase in contacts to pre-pandemic levels. Scenarios vary: (i) start time of relaxation (0–240 days after vaccination begins) and (ii) time to reach pre-pandemic contacts (1 month–1 year). Elderly and unvaccinated individuals have a delay; vaccinated individuals can either relax immediately after completing their series or wait with the general population. For vaccinated individuals, social contacts are not fully restored until the general population relaxes due to ongoing restrictions.

Calibration and outputs: The model is calibrated to US hospitalization data in early February 2021. Outcomes include deaths, hospitalizations, and epidemic duration. Sensitivity analyses include lower baseline immunity (16%), lower one-dose efficacy (60% RE), and susceptibility+severity vaccine.

title: Covariant nucleon electromagnetic form factors from the Goldstone-boson-exchange quark model
research_question:
Research question: Can the Goldstone-boson-exchange constituent quark model, formulated in a covariant point-form relativistic quantum mechanics framework, reproduce the proton and neutron electromagnetic form factors, charge radii, and magnetic moments without introducing constituent quark form factors or other phenomenological parameters beyond the model wavefunctions?

Hypotheses: (1) A covariant treatment with proper relativistic boosts (point-form) and one-body currents (PFSA) will yield e.m. form factors that agree with experimental data across the studied Q² range. (2) The GBE hyperfine interaction contributes essential mixed-symmetry components necessary to reproduce the neutron charge radius. (3) Nonrelativistic impulse approximations will fail to capture the observed momentum dependences and low-Q² behavior. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses include close agreement with experimental charge radii, magnetic moments, and form factors; a small residual discrepancy in magnetic moments; and systematic failure of NRIA. Outcomes refuting the hypotheses would include large discrepancies without additional parameters, or success of NRIA without relativistic boosts.
reference_methodology:
Model and Hamiltonian: The three-quark Hamiltonian includes a relativistic kinetic-energy operator for constituent quarks (masses mi, three-momenta ki), a linear confinement potential, and a pseudoscalar Goldstone-boson-exchange hyperfine interaction. The hyperfine interaction is taken as the spin-spin component, consistent with the model’s success in baryon spectroscopy. The total Hamiltonian yields a mass operator constructed via the Bakamjian–Thomas (BT) construction in the point-form, ensuring Poincaré covariance.

Wavefunction generation: The three-quark eigenstates are obtained in the center-of-momentum frame (P = 0) using the stochastic variational method (SVM). SVM provides accurate eigenenergies and eigenstates, with ground-state and resonance energies independently confirmed by modified Faddeev equations. The resulting wavefunctions are interpreted as eigenstates of the interacting mass operator in the point-form.

Relativistic kinematics and boosts: The point-form approach places all dynamics in the four-momentum operators, which commute and can be simultaneously diagonalized. Lorentz boosts are kinematic (interaction-free), enabling exact transformations of three-quark states. Velocity states are introduced by applying a canonical boost to center-of-momentum states, simplifying Wigner rotations so that quark spins can be coupled to a total spin state analogous to nonrelativistic theory. General Lorentz transformations are implemented using Wigner rotations, with the velocity-state formalism ensuring correct spin rotations and momentum dependences.

Current operator and matrix elements: The invariant nucleon form factors are computed as matrix elements of the one-body current operator jν in the standard Breit frame, where the momentum transfer Q is along the z-axis (qst = (0, 0, 0, Q)). Due to wavefunction symmetry, only the case where quark 1 is struck (quarks 2 and 3 are spectators) is evaluated and multiplied by 3. The initial and final nucleon velocities are vin = (sqrt(mN² + (Q/2)²), 0, 0, −Q/2)/mN and vout = (sqrt(mN² + (Q/2)²), 0, 0, Q/2)/mN, respectively. The single-particle current matrix element uses Dirac spinors u(pi, λi) and momentum transfer qρ = p′ρ − pρ with Q² = −q². Constituent quark form factors are taken as pointlike: f1(Q²) = 1 and f2(Q²) = 0. The Sachs form factors are obtained from the ν = 0 (electric) and ν = 2 (magnetic) components of the current tensor; the ν = 1 component yields GM, and the ν = 3 component vanishes due to current conservation.

Comparative setups: Results are compared to (i) a nonrelativistic impulse approximation (NRIA) using a nonrelativistic current operator and no Lorentz boosts, and (ii) a confinement-only case with a larger nucleon mass mN = 1353 MeV. The physical nucleon mass is mN = 939 MeV. Scaling arguments are used to relate charge radii and magnetic moments to the mass shift when adjusting mN.

title: A Truncated Form of IKKa Is Responsible for Specific Nuclear IKK Activity in Colorectal Cancer
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Is a truncated, active nuclear IKKα isoform present in CRC and associated with malignancy? (2) What proteolytic mechanism generates this isoform in CRC cells? (3) Does the truncated isoform form specific nuclear complexes and phosphorylate nuclear substrates (SMRT, histone H3) to drive oncogenic transcription? (4) Is cleavage of IKKα required for CRC cell survival and tumor growth?

Hypotheses: (a) CRC cells contain a proteolytically generated nuclear IKKα isoform (p45-IKKα) that is active and enriched in the nucleus; (b) cathepsins B/L mediate IKKα cleavage; (c) p45-IKKα forms a complex with nonactive FL-IKKα and NEMO, enabling phosphorylation of SMRT and histone H3, thereby activating Notch-target genes; (d) cleavage of IKKα is necessary for CRC cell survival and tumor growth in vitro and in vivo. Supportive outcomes would include detection of p45-IKKα in CRC nuclei, correlation with P-IKK, cathepsin-dependent cleavage, HMW complex formation with NEMO/FL-IKKα, substrate phosphorylation, and rescue of growth/apoptosis only when cleavage-competent IKKα is present. Refutation would involve absence of p45-IKKα, lack of cathepsin dependence, failure to phosphorylate nuclear substrates, or inability of cleavage to influence growth.
reference_methodology:
Human samples: 288 colorectal samples (147 adenomas, 141 carcinomas) with paired distal normal mucosa from 98 patients were analyzed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) for phosphorylated IKK (P-IKK; Ser180/181) using two antibodies (Cell Signaling #2681; Santa Cruz sc-23470). Nuclear localization was assessed by confocal microscopy. Additional cohorts included 183 colon tumors and 55 normal mucosas for p45-IKKα IHC. Ethics: written consent obtained; institutional ethics committee approval.

Antibodies and reagents: Monoclonal antibody 881H3 against IKKα aa 241–424 (Abyntek) specifically recognized p45-IKKα in nondenatured lysates. Blocking peptide controls were used. Phospho-IKK antibodies recognized Ser180/181. NEMO and IKKα/β antibodies were used for western blots. Protease inhibitors (complete protease inhibitor cocktail, Roche) and z-FA-FMK (cathepsin B/L inhibitor) and z-VAD (caspase inhibitor) were used in vitro. Calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase (CIAP) tested phosphorylation status.

Cell lines and models: CRC cell lines (HCT116, SW480, Ls174T, HT-29) and nontransformed HS27 fibroblasts. IKKα knockout (KO) MEFs and WT MEFs. Retroviral vectors expressed FL-IKKα (myc- or HA-tagged), truncated p45-IKKα, or noncleavable IKKα mutants (e.g., 3M with mutations disrupting caspase/cathepsin sites). shRNA targeting IKKα 3′ UTR (shRNA #4) depleted endogenous IKKα; scrambled shRNA controls. Rescue constructs were shRNA-resistant.

Proteolytic processing assays: IKKα aa 300–450 fragment (containing predicted caspase 3/6/7 and cathepsin B/L/K sites) was expressed in HEK293T cells. Processing was assessed at pH 5.5 (acid) versus pH 8.0 with or without z-FA-FMK or z-VAD. Mutants disrupting individual or all three sites (3M) were tested for cleavage efficiency. Mass spectrometry of tryptic peptides identified cleavage products.

Biochemistry: Subcellular fractionation (cytoplasmic and nuclear) and gel filtration (Superdex S200) of nuclear extracts. Fractions 19–25 (HMW) and 38–45 (LMW) were immunoprecipitated with anti-IKKα or anti-P-IKK and assayed for kinase activity on GST-NCoR (aa 2256–2452) and GST-SMRT. NEMO co-precipitation from HMW fractions confirmed complex formation. Pull-down assays tested binding to histone H3. Leptomycin B assessed nuclear export.

Functional assays: In IKKα-deficient MEFs, FL-IKKα, p45-IKKα, or combinations were expressed; SMRT phosphorylation (Ser2410), histone H3 phosphorylation, and transcription of SMRT-repressed genes (hes1, herp2, hes5) were measured by western blot and qRT-PCR. In CRC cells, IKKα knockdown effects on growth, apoptosis (annexin V), and proliferation were quantified; rescue by WT IKKα or 3M + p45-IKKα tested. Xenografts: HCT116 and HT-29 cells transduced with IKKα constructs, sorted by YFP, selected with puromycin, and injected (2×10^4 cells in Matrigel) subcutaneously into nude mice; tumor growth measured after 3 weeks.

Statistics: Fisher’s exact test for categorical comparisons; Spearman’s rho for correlation; t-tests for qRT-PCR; nonparametric ANOVA with rank transformation for ordinal P-IKK data; significance threshold p<0.05 (two-sided).

title: УДОСКОНАЛЕННЯ ІННОВАЦІЙНОЇ ДІЯЛЬНОСТІ ВНЗ ШЛЯХОМ ВПРОВАДЖЕННЯ СИСТЕМИ МЕНЕДЖМЕНТУ ЯКОСТІ
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How can TQM principles and ISO 9000/9001 requirements be systematically aligned with the core principles of modern higher education to support innovation? (2) What structural model and implementation mechanisms can HEIs adopt to operationalize a QMS that enhances educational quality, graduate competitiveness, and institutional effectiveness? (3) What requirements must a HEI QMS meet to be practical, understandable, minimally documented, informationally supported, and certification-ready?

Hypotheses/expectations: (a) Mapping HEI principles to TQM/ISO constructs will reveal strong correspondences that enable coherent QMS design; (b) A three-level process model (key, management, support) with an iterative implementation algorithm will provide a reproducible pathway for QMS adoption; (c) Such a QMS will improve the learning process, graduate quality, employer satisfaction, research productivity, and infrastructure efficiency. The paper does not state explicit statistical hypotheses; instead, it advances conceptual propositions supported by literature and comparative analysis.
reference_methodology:
Design: Analytical and theoretical synthesis of international experience and standards. The authors review the Bologna Process context, the Bergen Declaration (2005), and the evolution of ISO 9001 (2008 revision) and IWA 9001:2009. They analyze TQM principles and their applicability to HEI operations.

Data/materials: The study draws on prior literature and institutional experience, including the authors’ own work within a state-funded research project at the Kyiv National University of Technologies and Design (metrology, standardization, and certification department). No primary empirical datasets, participant samples, or statistical analyses are reported.

Procedure: (1) Identify core principles of modern higher education (e.g., quality-oriented preparation, accessibility, lifelong learning, innovation, adaptability, systemic approach, humanistic orientation, partnerships, global standards, motivational orientation, continuous improvement, information-communication infrastructure). (2) Map these principles to TQM elements and ISO 9001 requirements, producing a comparative table. (3) Derive a structural model of HEI activity organized into three process levels: key processes, management processes, and support processes. (4) Develop an implementation algorithm (block diagram) detailing steps: leadership training, documentation development (process maps, procedures, methods), audit and certification, process monitoring, performance evaluation, and continuous improvement via corrective/preventive actions. (5) Specify requirements for an effective HEI QMS (practical utility, clarity, minimal documentation, computer-networked information support, certification suitability).

Analysis: Qualitative alignment and conceptual modeling. No quantitative metrics, statistical tests, or effect sizes are reported. The paper references the increased adaptability of ISO 9001:2008/IWA 9001:2009 to service contexts and reduced mandatory documentation as contextual factors enabling QMS adoption in HEIs.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human subjects or sensitive data are involved. No preregistration or data/code availability statements are provided.

title: Hepatocarcinogenic Susceptibility of Fenofibrate and Its Possible Mechanism of Carcinogenicity in a Two-Stage Hepatocarcinogenesis Model of rasH2 Mice
research_question: Research questions: (1) Do rasH2 mice exhibit hepatocarcinogenic susceptibility to fenofibrate in a two-stage model initiated by DEN after partial hepatectomy? (2) What molecular changes accompany FF-induced hepatocarcinogenesis in rasH2 mice? Hypotheses: (H1) FF increases the incidence of preneoplastic foci in rasH2 mice relative to DEN-alone controls; (H2) FF elevates proliferation markers (PCNA) and cytokeratin 8/18-positive foci; (H3) FF upregulates the human H-ras transgene and downstream ras/MAPK pathway and cell cycle genes (c-myc, c-jun, ATF3, cyclin D1). Support for H1 would be a significant increase in preneoplastic foci in FF groups. Support for H2 would be significantly higher PCNA-positive indices and larger CK8/18-positive foci in FF groups. Support for H3 would be significant increases in transgene and downstream gene expression at FF doses (1200–2400 ppm). Refutation would be no differences or decreases in these measures versus controls.
reference_methodology:
Animals: Male rasH2 mice (6 weeks old) were obtained from CLEA Japan. Housing: plastic cages (five per cage), absorbent bedding, 22 ± 2°C, 55% ± 5% humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle. Diet: powdered Oriental MF; water ad libitum. Acclimation: 1 week prior to experiments. Ethics: Conducted per institutional guidelines.

Chemicals: Fenofibrate (CAS 49562-28-9; purity >99%; Sigma-Aldrich) and N-diethylnitrosamine (DEN; Nacarai-tesque). All other reagents were analytical grade.

Experimental design: Two-thirds partial hepatectomy (PH) to enhance hepatocellular proliferation. Twenty-four hours post-PH, mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of DEN (30 mg/kg) in saline. One week later, mice were randomized to receive powdered diet containing 0, 1200, or 2400 ppm FF for seven weeks. The FF dosing was selected based on FDA data (200 mg/kg/day induced liver carcinomas in mice). At study end, mice were euthanized by exsanguination under ether anesthesia; livers were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for histology. Some livers were snap-frozen in RNAlater at −80°C for RNA analysis.

Histopathology: Five liver pieces per mouse were paraffin-embedded, sectioned at 3 μm, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE). For each mouse, the number of hepatocellular-altered foci across all HE sections was counted under light microscopy; foci area was not measured. The amount of tissue examined was standardized across groups; evaluation was blinded.

Immunohistochemistry: Serial sections were used for CK8/18 and PCNA. CK8/18: deparaffinization in xylene, rehydration in ethanol; antigen retrieval in 0.1 M citrate (pH 6.0) with 0.1% NP-40 (autoclave 120°C, 10 min; microwave low power 5 min; cool 40 min). Endogenous peroxidase blocked with 3% H2O2 (10 min). Blocking with PBS + 1% BSA, 0.05% saponin, 0.2% gelatin. Primary antibody (PROGEN) overnight at 4°C in PBS + 0.5% casein; secondary guinea pig peroxidase-conjugated antibody; DAB chromogen; hematoxylin counterstain. Quantification: five sections per liver from five animals per group; foci (≥3 cells) were counted and categorized by size; number and area of CK8/18-positive foci/cells per mm² were quantified using WinRoof (Mitani). PCNA: deparaffinization and rehydration; antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) with microwave (30 min, low power); peroxidase block with 0.3% H2O2 (20 min); blocking with Histofine solution A; primary antibody (Dako) 1:300 in 0.5% casein-PBS overnight at 4°C; Envision detection; DAB; hematoxylin counterstain. Quantification: sections from five mice per group; multiple liver regions examined; PCNA-positive hepatocytes counted (≥3000 per section) in a blinded fashion; PCNA-positive index calculated as % positive cells.

Real-time RT-PCR: Total RNA (2 μg) isolated with Trizol; cDNA synthesized with SuperScript III and random primers. SYBR Green qPCR on ABI Prism 7000. Primers designed with Primer Express; β-actin as endogenous reference; relative quantification by 2ΔΔCt. ATF3 primers: forward 5'-CAGCATTTGATATACATGCTCAACCT-3'; reverse 5'-TCCGGTGTCCGTCCATTCT-3'. Other primers (human Ha-ras, mouse Ha-ras, raf, c-fos, c-myc, cyclin D1) from prior studies.

Statistics: StatLight v2.0. Data as mean ± SD. Bartlett’s test for homogeneity; Dunnett’s multiple comparison test (or Dunnett’s rank sum test if heterogeneous). Significance at p < 0.05.

title: Estimation of true number of COVID-19 infected people in Japan using LINE questionnaire
research_question:
Research question: Can the true number of COVID-19 infections in Japan be estimated as of April 1, 2020, by relating prefecture-level PCR positivity to the proportion of respondents reporting high fever in a large-scale LINE questionnaire, while accounting for symptom-to-confirmation lag and recovery?

Hypotheses: (1) There is a statistically significant positive correlation between the ratio of accumulated PCR positivity per population and the ratio of high fever per LINE respondents across prefectures. (2) A linear relationship N_C = a N_T holds, where N_C is the number of high fever cases attributable to COVID-19 and N_T is the confirmed positives, enabling nationwide estimation. (3) Modeling the decay of confirmed positives with an exponential half-life improves alignment between survey and PCR data, modestly increasing correlation and precision. (4) Excluding outlier prefectures yields a stronger correlation than including all 47 prefectures.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if Pearson’s r is significantly positive (e.g., r > 0 with p < 0.05). Hypothesis (2) is supported if the regression slope a is positive and statistically significant, and if applying N_C = a N_T yields a plausible nationwide estimate. Hypothesis (3) is supported if r increases and confidence intervals tighten when using a half-life model. Hypothesis (4) is supported if r decreases when all prefectures are included.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: (1) LINE questionnaire (March 31–April 1, 2020) with prefecture-level counts of respondents and high fever cases; (2) J.A.G. Japan COVID-19 dataset (initial symptom dates and confirmation dates) to estimate symptom-to-confirmation lag; (3) National Population Census 2015 for prefecture populations.

Preprocessing and alignment: The LINE survey is treated as quasi-randomized and sufficiently large to approximate population proportions. The authors compute the ratio of high fever cases to respondents per prefecture. For PCR data, they calculate the ratio of accumulated PCR positives to population per prefecture as of April 5, 2020. To temporally align the LINE survey (March 31–April 1) with PCR data, they use J.A.G. data to estimate the lag between initial symptom and confirmation. A Gaussian distribution is fitted to the distribution of days from symptom onset to confirmation, indicating a 4–5 day lag. Thus, PCR data as of April 5 are used to represent the period corresponding to the LINE survey.

Outlier handling: Four prefectures (Tottori, Okinawa, Hokkaido, Fukui) are excluded as outliers due to extreme deviations from the main cluster; Tokyo is retained despite its high values. The rationale is that excluding outliers improves the linear relationship and robustness.

Statistical analysis: Pearson’s correlation coefficient r is computed between the ratio of accumulated PCR positivity per population and the ratio of high fever per respondents across 43 prefectures. Linear regression (Ordinary Least Squares) is performed using statsmodels in Python 3.7 (Anaconda). The regression slope (a) and intercept (b) are estimated, and 95% confidence intervals are reported. The authors derive the relationship N_C = a N_T, where N_C is the number of high fever cases attributable to COVID-19 and N_T is the confirmed positives, by summing across prefectures and assuming N_fLp/N_Lp = N_fnp/Pp + N_Cp/Pp and N_Cp/Pp = a N_Tp/Pp.

Recovery adjustment: To account for recovery/death, the authors model the decay of confirmed positives with an exponential half-life τ_HL: dN_Tp/dt = -ln(2)/τ_HL · N_Tp. The number of confirmed positives as of a given day is computed as the sum over days i of new positives N_Ii multiplied by exp(-ln(2)(n-i)/τ_HL). They test τ_HL = 9, 3, and 14 days and recompute the correlation and estimate.

Software and libraries: Anaconda Python 3.7 for data acquisition, analysis, and plotting; statsmodels for OLS regression.

title: A Comprehensive Review Of Inventory Models In Rainwater Harvesting For Resource Management
research_question: The review articulates four objectives: (i) evaluate the role of inventory modeling in improving RWH efficiency and sustainability; (ii) examine EOQ and other inventory techniques for optimizing water resource utilization; (iii) identify emerging trends and challenges in integrating inventory modeling with RWH; and (iv) highlight research and development opportunities. No explicit hypotheses are stated, as the work is a narrative synthesis rather than a hypothesis-testing study. Implicit expectations include: (a) inventory-based approaches (e.g., EOQ) can reduce operational costs and enhance resilience in RWH by aligning storage and distribution with variable rainfall and demand; (b) successful integration requires addressing data scarcity, model complexity, and stakeholder engagement; and (c) interdisciplinary collaboration and participatory frameworks are necessary for real-world adoption. Outcomes supporting these expectations would include reported cost reductions, improved reliability, and documented barriers and solutions in the cited literature.
reference_methodology: The review followed systematic review protocols. Electronic databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by academic repositories and scholarly publications. Search terms combined keywords such as “rainwater harvesting,” “inventory modeling,” “water resource management,” “Economic Order Quantity,” and related terms using Boolean operators. Inclusion criteria required studies that integrated inventory modeling techniques with RWH practices and discussed implications for water resource management. The review restricted inclusion to English-language publications up to the present date (search end date not specified). Screening proceeded in stages: initial title/abstract screening for relevance, followed by full-text retrieval and evaluation against inclusion/exclusion criteria. Data extraction focused on study methodologies, key findings, and limitations, with synthesis organized thematically by methodology, geographic scope, and outcomes. The review reports no quantitative meta-analysis, no PRISMA flow diagram, and no risk-of-bias assessment. No details are provided on search dates, number of records identified, screening counts, or inter-rater reliability. Ethical approvals are not applicable as no human subjects data were collected. The review does not report specific case study datasets, parameter values, or model calibration details, as it synthesizes prior studies rather than conducting new experiments.

title: An analysis of integrative outcomes in the Dayton peace negotiations
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the integrative versus distributive characteristics of negotiated outcomes across the eight issues of the Dayton Peace Agreement? (2) Which of Pruitt’s five integrative mechanisms (expanding the pie, cost cutting, non-specific compensation, logrolling, bridging) are used, and how? (3) Can integrative agreements emerge in redistribution contexts, and how do mechanisms interact within and across issues? (4) What role did mediator pressure (U.S./NATO) play in shaping outcomes?

Hypotheses (implied by the framework and aims): (a) Real-world international negotiations can achieve integrative outcomes even when redistribution of existing resources is central; (b) Multiple mechanisms may be used simultaneously within a single issue; (c) Some mechanisms (e.g., non-specific compensation, bridging, cost cutting) can satisfy underlying interests without fully redistributing the pie; (d) Mediator pressure can facilitate integrative solutions by aligning parties and enabling post-agreement implementation. Support would be demonstrated by identifying integrative mechanisms across issues, documenting how underlying interests are satisfied, and noting cases where mechanisms co-occur within issues. Refutation would involve finding only distributive outcomes or mechanisms that fail to satisfy underlying interests.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative case study analysis of the Dayton Peace Agreement (1995) using a structured framework to classify outcomes as integrative or distributive and to identify Pruitt’s mechanisms.

Units of analysis: Eight issues/sub-issues: (1) Percentage of territory each party would get; (2) Control of Gorazde and the land link between Sarajevo and Gorazde; (3) Control of Eastern Slavonia; (4) Posavina Corridor and Brcko; (5) Integrity of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina; (6) Political authorities of the state; (7) Name of the state; (8) Sarajevo.

Parties: Official participants (e.g., Muslim-Croats, Bosnian Serbs, Croatia, rebel Croatian Serbs). The authors avoid naming individual representatives to avoid legitimacy debates.

Timeline: Initial positions set at the start of U.S. involvement (February 1994). Key milestones include the Contact Group’s 49–51% proposal (May 13, 1994), the Geneva Accord (September 8, 1995) on state integrity, the New York Accord (October 5, 1995) on constitutional arrangements, and the Dayton Agreement signed on December 14, 1995.

Data sources: (a) Primary news resources (Keesing’s Record of World Events, Facts on File, Summary of World Broadcasts, OMRI Daily Digest, 1991–1995); (b) the Dayton Agreement text; (c) daily newspapers; (d) memoirs of diplomats. The authors also reference the International Herald Tribune for corridor width estimates.

Operationalization: Distributive outcomes are defined as (a) fixed-resource allocation among parties; (b) cooptation (one party gets all it wants; the other gets nothing); or (c) concessions converging toward resistance points. Integrative outcomes satisfy both parties’ underlying interests via mechanisms: expanding the pie (increasing total resources), cost cutting (reducing the other’s costs), non-specific compensation (compensation unrelated to the original issue), logrolling (trading concessions across issues), or bridging (creative solutions that satisfy underlying interests). The authors pose six standardized questions per issue/sub-issue: (1) What is the issue/sub-issue? (2) Who are the parties? (3) What are each party’s positions? (4) What are the underlying interests? (5) What are the priorities? (6) What did each party get at the end?

Analysis: For each issue, the authors identify initial positions, underlying interests, priorities (where available), and final outcomes, then classify outcomes as integrative/distributive and map mechanisms. They note that logrolling requires explicit priority data, which was not available from public sources, limiting its identification. They also note that some negotiation records are classified, constraining access to underlying interests. No statistical tests or quantitative benefit measures are reported; the analysis is descriptive and mechanism-based.

title: Recommendations for COVID-19 Vaccination in People with Rheumatic Disease: Developed by the Singapore Chapter of Rheumatologists
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are PRD at increased risk of adverse COVID-19 outcomes? (2) Are COVID-19 vaccines safe, immunogenic, and efficacious in PRD? (3) How do immunomodulatory therapies (including rituximab) affect vaccine immunogenicity and timing? (4) What are the implications for household contacts? (5) Should post-vaccination antibody titres be measured in PRD?

Implicit hypotheses: (a) PRD have higher COVID-19 severity risk than the general population; (b) COVID-19 vaccines are safe and beneficial in PRD, with timing around rituximab improving immunogenicity; (c) household vaccination reduces transmission risk to PRD; (d) post-vaccination antibody titres are not routinely necessary in PRD due to uncertain correlation with clinical protection. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include higher severe outcome rates in PRD, absence of safety signals in PRD subgroups within vaccine trials, preserved cellular immunity with rituximab and improved humoral responses when timing is optimized, and evidence of reduced household transmission with vaccination. Outcomes refuting them would include high rates of autoimmune flares or severe adverse events in PRD, poor immunogenicity despite timing, or lack of benefit from household vaccination.
reference_methodology:
Design: Systematic literature reviews and a modified Delphi consensus process with GRADE-based recommendation grading.

Core Working Group (CWG): Comprised AS, CX, WF, ML. They reviewed primary clinical trials and performed systematic literature reviews to answer four research questions. Where appropriate, they also reviewed international best practice guidelines and rheumatology society recommendations on non-live, non-COVID-19 vaccinations in PRD, as well as other academic bodies’ recommendations for COVID-19 vaccination and immunocompromised conditions.

Task Force Panel (TFP): Eight adult rheumatologists from public and private institutions in Singapore, one pediatric rheumatologist, and one infectious diseases specialist. All members declared no conflicts of interest.

Literature searches: PubMed searches used MeSH terms including “Consensus” and “Guidelines as Topic,” with filters for English and Humans. The CWG screened titles/abstracts, excluded non-guideline, non-PRD, live-vaccine-only, pediatric-only, non-systematic reviews, duplicates, and outdated recommendations. Four additional citations were added via manual search. Eleven full-text articles were included after screening (Figure 1; Table 2). Definitions of PRD and immunomodulatory drugs were clarified (Table 3).

Delphi process: The CWG drafted statements based on reviewed evidence. The TFP independently rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree) via an online platform. Agreement was defined as scores of 4 or 5. Consensus was defined as ≥70% agreement. After the voting round, the CWG and TFP convened via teleconference to discuss and refine statements. No further voting rounds were needed as consensus was achieved on all statements.

GRADE: The TFP applied GRADE to determine recommendation strength, considering the level of evidence and the balance of benefits and risks of vaccination versus omission in PRD. Recommendations were categorized as strong (benefits/risk clearly outweigh) or conditional (benefits/risk closely balanced or uncertain).

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; this is a guideline development study without patient data collection. Conflict-of-interest declarations were required and all members reported none.

Data sources: Primary COVID-19 vaccine trials (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2; Moderna mRNA-1273; Johnson & Johnson JNJ-78436735; Gamaleya Sputnik V; Oxford-AstraZeneca AZD1222; Novavax NVX-CoV2373; Bharat Biotech BB-152/Covaxin) and their interim efficacy data were summarized (Table 1). PRD outcomes with COVID-19 were synthesized from a meta-analysis and registry data.

title: Global exponential stability for a delay differential neoclassical growth model
field_subfield: Mathematics — Dynamical Systems (Delay Differential Equations; Economic Growth Models)
research_question:
Research question: Under what explicit parameter conditions does the unique positive equilibrium of the delay differential neoclassical growth model x'(t) = β x(t−τ)^γ e^{−δ x(t−τ)} − α x(t) (γ ∈ (1,2)) exhibit global exponential stability? Secondary questions include: (i) Do solutions remain positive and uniformly bounded away from zero and infinity (uniform permanence)? (ii) Does a unique positive global solution exist for admissible initial conditions?

Hypotheses: (1) If α exceeds a threshold proportional to h(γ + √γ) (the maximum of a function tied to the production term), then the unique positive equilibrium is globally exponentially stable. (2) Under inequalities involving κ (the maximizer of h(x)) and a threshold K, solutions are uniformly permanent with explicit lower and upper bounds. (3) For admissible initial conditions, there exists a unique positive global solution on [0, ∞). Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include: (i) a Lyapunov functional V(t) = y(t) e^{λ t} with negative definite derivative under α > (β/δ^γ) h(γ + √γ), yielding exponential decay of deviations; (ii) bounds m = κ/δ and M = K/δ for lim inf and lim sup of x(t); and (iii) proof of existence and uniqueness of the global positive solution. Outcomes refuting would include failure of the Lyapunov derivative to be negative definite or counterexamples to permanence.
reference_methodology:
Model: The delay differential equation x'(t) = β x(t−τ)^γ e^{−δ x(t−τ)} − α x(t) with parameters α, γ, δ, β > 0 and delay τ ≥ 0. The function h(x) = e^{−x} x^{γ−1} (γ x) is decreasing on [1, γ + √γ) and increasing on (γ + √γ, ∞), attaining a unique maximum at κ ∈ (1, γ). The authors define K ∈ (κ, κ) (as per the text) and use inequalities involving β, γ, δ, K, e^{γ}, and e^{κ} to derive bounds.

Function spaces and initial conditions: Let C = C([−τ, 0], ℝ) with supremum norm and C_+ = C([−τ, 0], ℝ_+). Admissible initial conditions are ϕ ∈ C_+ with ϕ(0) > 0. The map f: C_+ → ℝ defined by f(ϕ) = β ϕ(−τ)^γ e^{−δ ϕ(−τ)} − α ϕ(0) is locally Lipschitz, ensuring existence and uniqueness of solutions for admissible ϕ.

Preliminary results: (1) Uniform permanence: If there exists K ∈ (κ, κ) such that β γ^γ δ^{−γ} K^γ e^{γ} < α < β δ^{2−γ} e^{κ}, then all solutions satisfy m = κ/δ < lim inf_{t→∞} x(t) ≤ lim sup_{t→∞} x(t) < M = K/δ. The proof uses differential inequalities and comparison with auxiliary linear equations. (2) Existence of a unique positive global solution: Using the variation of constants formula and contradiction arguments, the authors show that solutions remain positive for all t ≥ 0 and that the maximal interval of existence is [0, ∞). They also exclude blow-up by bounding x(t) via comparison with an auxiliary linear differential inequality.

Main stability result: Theorem 3.1 states that if α > (β/δ^γ) h(γ + √γ), then the unique positive equilibrium x* is globally exponentially stable. The proof constructs a Lyapunov functional V(t) = y(t) e^{λ t} with y(t) = x(t) − x*. They choose λ ∈ (0, γ] such that λ − α + (β/δ^γ) h(γ + √γ) e^{λ τ} < 0. Using the differential mean value theorem, they bound the nonlinear term by h(γ + √γ) |x(t−τ) − x*|, leading to D−V(t) ≤ (λ − α) V(t) + (β/δ^γ) h(γ + √γ) e^{λ τ} V(t−τ). A contradiction argument rules out the possibility of V(t) attaining a positive maximum, yielding V(t) ≤ K e^{−λ t} for t sufficiently large.

Numerical example: The authors provide a concrete parameter set (values partially obscured in the provided text) and compute κ ≈ 0.9... and K = 0.9..., verify the inequality α > (β/δ^γ) h(γ + √γ), and report x* ≈ 0.4009 with convergence rate λ ≈ 0.3. Simulations (Figure 1) with initial values ϕ(s) ≡ 0.1, 1, 3 for s ∈ [−1,0] show convergence to x*.

title: Serum levels of specialised pro-resolving molecule pathways are greatly increased in SARS-CoV-2 patients and correlate with markers of the adaptive immune response
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do serum levels of pro- and anti-inflammatory bioactive lipids differ between hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients and age- and sex-matched controls? (2) Are levels of these lipids associated with adaptive immune responses (anti-nucleocapsid and anti-spike binding titers)? (3) Do lipid mediator levels differ by clinical outcome (survival vs death) and by age strata?

Hypotheses: (a) SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with increased activation of both pro-inflammatory and pro-resolving pathways, reflected in elevated levels of omega-6–derived pro-inflammatory mediators and omega-6/omega-3–derived SPMs compared with controls. (b) Higher adaptive antibody responses (anti-spike binding) correlate with higher levels of SPMs and related mediators, consistent with a link between adaptive immunity and resolution signaling. (c) Patients who die exhibit impaired resolution-associated lipid signaling (e.g., lower LA and 5,6-DHET; altered EET/DHET ratios). Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significant between-group differences in lipid concentrations, positive correlations between anti-spike titers and SPM/EET levels, and mortality-associated differences in specific lipid mediators. Outcomes refuting them would include no differences in lipid profiles, null correlations with antibody titers, or no mortality-associated lipid differences.
reference_methodology:
Design and participants: Cross-sectional observational study of 50 hospital-admitted inpatients (22 female, 28 male) with symptomatic RT-PCR–confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and 94 age- and sex-matched pre-pandemic controls from the iBEAT-OA cohort (n=94). Controls were collected prior to the pandemic; lack of SARS-CoV-2 infection was not confirmed. Clinical characteristics included 30 recoveries, 20 deaths, and 25 ICU stays among SARS-CoV-2 patients.

Specimen handling and assays: Serum samples were collected for clinical chemistry testing; excess sera were anonymized for research. Samples were stored at 4°C for 24 h, then inactivated using the WHO-approved protocol (4 h at room temperature with 1% Triton X-100 in PBS). Viral genomic sequencing (subset) was performed as part of COG-UK; circulating variants were Hu-1 or 20B lineage (D614G), with no nucleocapsid amino acid variability. Anti-nucleocapsid and anti-spike quantitative binding assays were performed by ELISA following Tighe et al. (2020). CRP was measured clinically; the median interval between CRP sampling and lipid/antibody sampling was 5 days.

Lipidomics: Serum bioactive lipids were extracted and quantified using a published LC-MS/MS method (updated to include SPMs and precursors), quantifying 44 mediators across pro- and anti-inflammatory classes (e.g., HETEs, ODEs/HODEs, PGE2, PGD2, TBXB2, LTB4, SPMs including 17-HDHA, RvD4, Maresin 2, LXA4/LXA5, EETs/DHETs, endocannabinoids). Detailed methods are in Supplementary Information. For undetected lipids, an arbitrary value of 0.001 was used for statistical analysis.

Statistical analysis: GraphPad Prism v8.2.1 was used. Normality was assessed with D’Agostino–Pearson; group comparisons used Kruskal–Wallis with Dunn’s multiple-comparison correction. MetaboAnalyst 4.0 was used for PCA and PLS-DA; cross-validation was applied. Variables with VIP>1 were considered key discriminants. Spearman’s rho correlations assessed associations between lipid concentrations and antibody titers. Patients were stratified by age (<60, 61–74, >75 years) for PLS-DA and univariate analyses.

Ethics: University of Nottingham School of Life Sciences Ethical Review Committee deemed the study not requiring full ethical review. Approval for use of anonymized clinical data was provided by NHS Health Research Authority (HRA) and Health and Care Research Wales (HCRW; ref. 20/HRA/4843). Samples were not deemed relevant materials by the Human Tissue Authority. Risk assessments were approved by the UK Health and Safety Executive (ref. CBA1.470.20.1).

title: Scenario Evolution of Waste NIMBY Crisis: A Grounded Theory and Dynamic Bayesian Network Approach
field_subfield: Environmental Science — Public Health and Risk Management
research_question: The central research questions are: (1) Why does the waste NIMBY crisis occur? (2) How does the waste NIMBY crisis evolve across stages? The authors hypothesize that a structured set of factors—external environment, risk cognition, public trust, interest games, facility location, enterprise operations, and government behavior—interact over time to drive NIMBY crises through latent, explosive, continuous, and solved stages. They further hypothesize that modeling these interactions with a DBN can capture the dynamic, uncertain evolution of scenarios and support identification of effective emergency measures that steer crises toward disappearance. Evidence that would support these hypotheses includes: (a) GT-derived categories that coherently explain observed cases; (b) a DBN that reproduces the observed evolution of a representative case (Xiantao) with increasing probabilities of favorable scenario states and disappearance; and (c) explicit conditional and prior probabilities that align with expert judgment and historical patterns. Evidence that would refute the hypotheses would include a failure of the GT framework to organize case data coherently, or a DBN that mispredicts key transitions or fails to align with the case timeline.
reference_methodology:
Design: Mixed-methods approach combining qualitative Grounded Theory (GT) and probabilistic modeling with a case study. GT was used to inductively derive factors and evolution laws of NIMBY crisis scenarios; DBN was used to formalize and compute dynamic scenario evolution.

Data sources and selection: The study focuses on Chinese waste NIMBY crises (2006–2019). Typical cases were identified via web searches (Baidu, Google, official websites, government microblogs, professional forums) using keywords such as “waste NIMBY,” “NIMBY crisis,” “NIMBY risk,” and “waste incineration.” Selection criteria emphasized representativeness, diversity in location/time, and comprehensive supporting materials (media reports, academic papers, forum posts, blogs, microblogs, publicity letters, press conferences). Twenty-six cases were selected. Peer-reviewed literature was retrieved from CNKI using “NIMBY” combined with “conflict,” “crisis,” “syndrome,” and “incident,” yielding 128 items; after screening, 69 studies were retained for GT analysis.

GT procedures: Nvivo11 was used for coding. Open coding labeled all data, extracting keywords related to NIMBY influencing factors; axial coding grouped initial categories into 10 main categories (e.g., external environment, risk cognition, public trust, interest game, public demand, facility location, enterprise operations, government response strategy, government behavior/attitude); selective coding identified the core category “scenario evolution factors of waste NIMBY crisis” and organized it along a storyline of latent, explosive, continuous, and solved stages. Two coders conducted precoding under supervision; inter-coder consistency was assessed before independent coding. From open coding, 514 initial concepts and 43 initial categories were derived; axial coding summarized to 10 main categories (Table 2).

DBN construction and analysis: The DBN models three elements: external situation (E), scenario state (S), and emergency management (M). Nodes: eight scenario states (S0–S8), seven external environment nodes (E0–E7), seven emergency management nodes (M0–M7). Variable types: E is a binary sequential variable (Positive/Negative); S and M are Boolean (True/False). Prior probabilities for E and M were set using historical experience and expert judgment (e.g., E0 P=0.40, N=0.60; M0 T=0.90, F=0.10). Conditional probabilities for S given E and M were specified for each node (e.g., S0 T|E0=P,M0=T=0.65; S0 T|E0=N,M0=F=0.75). The model was implemented in Netica (Norsys Software Corp., Canada) to compute posterior probabilities and visualize evolution paths. The case study (Xiantao, Hubei) provided the timeline and context for node definitions and parameterization.

Ethics: Ethical review and approval were waived; the study did not involve biological human experiments or patient data.

title: Improving Reading Achievement through the Implementation of a Balanced Literacy Approach
research_question:
Research question: Does implementing a multilevel, strategy-focused literacy program (Four Block Balanced Literacy) augmented with motivational supports (AR, incentives, parent engagement) improve reading fluency, comprehension, and motivation among elementary students in grades 1, 3, and 6 over a five-month period?

Hypotheses: (1) Students will show improved reading levels on Running Records and BRI from August to December 2001. (2) Students will demonstrate increased motivation and positive attitudes toward reading on the student attitude survey. (3) Teacher observations will indicate greater independent reading behaviors (e.g., use of classroom library, school library checkouts, reading for recreation). (4) S.T.A.R. Reading scores will show growth relative to August baselines.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypotheses are supported if post-intervention measures show statistically or practically meaningful improvements relative to pre-intervention baselines. Given the descriptive design, support is inferred from direction and magnitude of changes rather than inferential tests. Refutation would involve no change or declines across measures.
reference_methodology:
Design: Action research with pre–post assessment across two elementary schools in a central Illinois community. No control group; no randomization. Duration: August–December 2001.

Participants and setting: Two elementary schools in a growing, lower-to-middle-class community. Targeted grades: 1, 3, and 6. Total n=55 students. School B demographics: 9% Caucasian, 91% African American; 94% attendance; 30% mobility; 1% chronic truancy; 98% low-income families. School A was recognized for high academic achievement. District context: 7,000 students; 430 teachers; 19:1 pupil–teacher ratio; 91.3% Caucasian, 7.5% African American, 1.2% Hispanic teachers; student ethnicity 62.7% Caucasian, 30.8% African American, 5.6% Hispanic, 7% Asian.

Measures: (1) Running Records and Beginning Reading Inventory (BRI) to assess vocabulary and comprehension levels; administered in August and December. (2) S.T.A.R. Reading assessments to measure reading growth; administered in August and December (posttest in December). (3) Student attitude survey (“My Ideas about Reading”) with Agree/Disagree responses; administered in August and December. (4) Teacher observation checklists capturing independent reading behaviors (e.g., use of classroom library, school library checkouts, reading for recreation, reading for personal interests, talking about reading, favorite authors, topic requests); administered in August and December.

Intervention procedures: The Four Block Balanced Literacy Approach was implemented across all targeted grades. Components included: (a) Word study: phonics and decoding (e.g., RIVETS, Making Words, “Guess the Covered Word,” “Word Splash,” “Mystery Word Match,” “What looks right,” “Word cycle,” vocabulary sorting); (b) Guided reading: teacher-selected texts, group instruction, strategy use (main idea, facts/details), discussions, and teaching points; (c) Self-selected reading: student choice across genres and levels, reflection, and sharing; (d) Writing: mini-lessons, conferencing, and sharing of published pieces. Motivational supports included AR challenges, incentive charts, parent newsletters, a literacy center with diverse materials, buddy reading (intermediate–primary), daily read-alouds, and student-led book displays. Teachers conducted weekly conferences, updated the literacy center, and held parent teacher conferences (October). A planned parent informational night was rescheduled due to staff constraints. Some activities (guest speaker, Reading Riot) were canceled due to scheduling.

Timeline: August—introduction of Four Blocks, parent informational night, baseline assessments, initial activities (e.g., RIVETS, Making Words, literacy center setup). September—introduction of “Guess the Covered Word,” “Word Splash,” daily read-alouds, incentive charts, AR challenges, buddy reading, and monthly reading challenges. October—midterm reports, conferences, parent teacher conferences, and updates to the literacy center. November—introduction of “Mystery Word Match,” literacy center activities (two-column response charts), tongue twisters compilation, and rescheduling of book exchange. December—Running Records/BRI and S.T.A.R. posttests, book exchange (grades 1 and 6), student attitude survey, and final observations.

Analysis: Descriptive comparisons of pre–post measures (percentages, counts) across grades. No inferential statistics, effect sizes, or confidence intervals reported.

title: Topological properties of function spaces C_k(X,2) over zero-dimensional metric spaces X
research_question:
The central questions are: For a zero-dimensional metric space X, under what conditions on X does C_k(X,2) satisfy the following properties: (i) Ascoli, (ii) k-space, (iii) sequential, (iv) Fréchet–Urysohn, (v) normality, and (vi) countable tightness? Additionally, what is the topological and algebraic structure of C_k(X,2) when these properties hold?

Hypotheses/predictions: (1) Ascoli and k_R properties for C_k(X,2) are equivalent and characterized by X being locally compact or X not locally compact but X′ compact. (2) The k-space property holds iff X is a topological sum of a separable metrizable locally compact space and a discrete space, or X not locally compact with X′ compact. (3) Sequentiality holds iff X is Polish and either X is locally compact or X not locally compact with X′ compact. (4) Fréchet–Urysohn property holds iff C_k(X,2) is Polish iff X is Polish locally compact. (5) Normality holds iff X′ is separable. (6) Countable tightness holds iff X is separable. The structural hypotheses include: when X is locally compact, C_k(X,2) is a product of Polish abelian groups; when X not locally compact but X′ compact, C_k(X,2) contains an open subgroup isomorphic to ⊕_{n∈N} 2^{κ_n} with the box topology; and for sequentiality, C_k(X,2) is homeomorphic to (2^ω)^∞.
reference_methodology:
The paper employs standard tools from general topology and function space theory. Definitions used include: Fréchet–Urysohn (every cluster point has a convergent sequence), sequential (every non-closed set has a sequence converging to a point outside it), k-space (every non-closed set intersects some compact set non-closed), k_R-space (a real-valued function is continuous iff its restriction to every compact set is continuous), and Ascoli space (every compact set in C_k(X) is evenly continuous; equivalently, the canonical evaluation map X → C_k(C_k(X)) is an embedding). The evaluation map ψ: X × C_k(X,Y) → Y is used to analyze even continuity.

Key constructions and lemmas: (i) The countably infinite metric fan M and its generalization M_{κκκ} with a complete metric ρ are used to model spaces where compact subsets have finite intersections with clopen layers. (ii) Proposition 2.1 establishes that for a sequence of compact topological groups G_n, the box topology on the direct sum ⊕_{n∈N} G_n is k_ω and separable locally compact iff G_n is finite for all but finitely many n. (iii) A sufficient condition for non-Ascoli spaces is given via a family of functions {f_{p,q}} with disjoint supports and a cluster point 0, showing failure of even continuity on compact sets. (iv) A retraction argument is used: if X contains a closed subspace Y homeomorphic to a known non-Ascoli space (e.g., a space L constructed from M and N × s), then C_k(Y,2) is a retract of C_k(X,2), implying non-Ascoli.

Proof strategies: For Theorem 1.4(i), necessity follows from Proposition 3.1 (if X is not locally compact and X′ is not compact, then C_k(X,2) is not Ascoli). Sufficiency uses clopen outer bases for X′ and a continuous map T: X → M_{κκκ} collapsing X′ to ∞ and mapping clopen layers injectively, yielding a topological isomorphism C_k(X,2) ≅ H × 2^D, where H is an open subgroup isomorphic to ⊕_{n∈N} 2^{κ_n} with the box topology. For Theorem 1.4(ii), if X is locally compact, X decomposes into a disjoint union of separable metrizable locally compact spaces; if X is not locally compact but X′ is compact, the open subgroup is as above. For Theorem 1.4(iii), sequentiality implies κ_n ≤ ω for all n (since compact abelian groups are sequential iff metrizable), forcing X to be Polish and X′ compact; in the locally compact case, C_k(X,2) is Polish. For Theorem 1.6, Lemma 3.6 constructs a closed copy of N^{ω_1} in C_p(X,2) when X′ is not Lindelöf, implying non-normality; conversely, normality implies separability of X′. For Theorem 1.7, if X is not separable, C_k(X,2) contains an isomorphic copy of 2^{ω_1}, which has uncountable tightness, contradicting countable tightness.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable.

title: Structured Liquid Batteries
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can charge-complementary polyelectrolytes form a stable, ion-conductive coacervate membrane at high salt concentrations at the interface of ATPS-based liquid electrodes? (2) Does ion-pairing between polyelectrolytes and oppositely charged actives sufficiently slow active-material crossover to enable long-term cycling? (3) Can patterned, under-oil structured liquid batteries access theoretical capacity and operate for hundreds of hours while powering an external circuit?

Hypotheses: (H1) PSS–PDADMA coacervate membranes will form over time at high salt and provide structural support and ionic conduction. (H2) Ion-pairing will reduce diffusion coefficients of actives by increasing effective size, thereby limiting crossover. (H3) With optimized formulation and geometry, devices will access full theoretical capacity and cycle stably for extended durations. Outcomes supporting H1 include visible membrane formation after 24–48 h and mechanical strength sufficient to hold 10 mL after 4 days. Outcomes supporting H2 include reduced diffusion coefficients upon adding polyelectrolytes and low measured crossover after cycling. Outcomes supporting H3 include full-capacity access within a few cycles and long-term cycling under defined protocols.
reference_methodology:
Materials: Dextran (Mr 450,000–650,000), PEG (Mn 20,000), Na4Fe(CN)6·10H2O (99%), MV dichloride hydrate (98%), PSS-Na (Mw 70,000), PDADMA-Cl (Mw 200,000–350,000), NH4Cl (99.5%), PFOTS (97%), 3-mercaptopropionic acid (99%), hexanes (99.9%), silicone oil (10 cSt). Milli-Q water (18.2 MΩ). Ammonium ferrocyanide heptahydrate prepared per literature.

Electrochemistry: BioLogic VMP3 potentiostat in a N2 glovebox. Working electrode: 3 mm glassy carbon; counter: Pt wire; reference: AgCl/Ag in 3.0 M NaCl. CV scan rates: 10–200 mV s^-1. Diffusion coefficients determined from peak current vs scan rate (Randles–Sevcik) with OLS regression. Ep/2 and ΔEp measured at 20 mV s^-1; error bars: SD of five scans after the first.

Formulations: Six aqueous solutions were prepared: (a) 10 mg mL^-1 Na4Fe(CN)6·10H2O + 0.5 M NH4Cl; (b) 100 mg mL^-1 PEG + 10 mg mL^-1 Na4Fe(CN)6·10H2O + 0.5 M NH4Cl; (c) 100 mg mL^-1 PEG + 10 mg mL^-1 PDADMA + 10 mg mL^-1 Na4Fe(CN)6·10H2O + 0.5 M NH4Cl; (d) 10 mg mL^-1 MV + 0.5 M NH4Cl; (e) 150 mg mL^-1 dextran + 10 mg mL^-1 MV + 0.5 M NH4Cl; (f) 150 mg mL^-1 dextran + 10 mg mL^-1 PSS + 10 mg mL^-1 MV + 0.5 M NH4Cl. Active materials were added to final concentrations of 0.2 M in each phase after diffusion.

Device fabrication: Microslides cleaned by UV-ozone, patterned with polyimide tape, and metallized with 5 nm Cr and 100 nm Ag by thermal evaporation (0.05–0.1 nm s^-1 Cr; 0.2–0.5 nm s^-1 Ag). After aging ≥24 h, slides were immersed in 0.1% PFOTS in hexanes (1 min), rinsed, then treated with 1% 3-mercaptopropionic acid (1 min), washed, and neutralized with 1% NH3. The surface chemistry was hydrophilic on Ag and superhydrophobic on glass. Two electrode geometries were tested: parallel plates and interdigitated arrays. The interdigitated array was redesigned with thick fingers to mitigate Laplace pressure-driven flow.

Assembly: In the glovebox, 0.45 mL of PEG-rich solution (100 mg mL^-1 PEG, 10 mg mL^-1 PDADMA, 0.5 M NH4Cl) and 0.45 mL of dextran-rich solution (150 mg mL^-1 dextran, 10 mg mL^-1 PSS, 0.5 M NH4Cl) were dispensed onto opposite current collectors until they merged at the gap. Silicone oil (10 cSt) was added to cover the aqueous phases. Ag rods connected the collectors to WE/CE/RE. Solutions aged overnight. MV and ferrocyanide were added to their respective phases to 0.2 M and equilibrated 24 h before cycling.

Cycling protocol: Galvanostatic charge to 1.0 V or theoretical capacity; rest 2 h; galvanostatic discharge to 0.2 V; CCCV discharge at 0.2 V up to 5 h or current <3 μA; rest 2 h. For interdigitated arrays, current rates of 13.5, 27, 54, 135, and 270 μA were tested (5 cycles each). Parallel plates were cycled at 54 μA for 884 h.

Crossover quantification: After cycling, oil was removed; films were peeled and cut at the interface. Each phase was diluted to 5.0 mL in 0.5 M NH4Cl. CV was used to measure MV in PEG and ferrocyanide in dextran against calibration curves. Calibration phases were prepared with known crossover percentages (5.2–45.2% increments). Effective diffusion coefficient Deff was calculated using Eq. S2: Deff = Cperm(t) l V / (C0 A t), where C0 = 0.2 M, V = 0.5 cm³, A = 0.16 cm², t = 3.27×10^6 s, and l was assumed up to 500 nm from literature.

title: Effect of Particle Size and Solution Leaching on Water Retention Behavior of Ion-Absorbed Rare Earth
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does particle size (and associated fine/coarse particle content) affect the SWCCs (drying and wetting) of ion-absorbed rare earth soils? (2) How does ammonium sulfate solution leaching alter water retention capacity and SWCC parameters? (3) What microstructural mechanisms explain observed changes in water retention?

Hypotheses: (H1) Smaller particle size and higher fine particle content increase water retention capacity at a given matric suction, due to greater surface porosity and capillary retention. (H2) Ammonium sulfate leaching reduces water retention capacity by increasing double electric layer thickness and pore water pressure, thereby lowering matric suction. (H3) Larger particle size reduces the amplitude of water content change during drying/wetting due to increased pore size and earlier formation of macroscopic air channels that stabilize water loss. (H4) SWCCs can be accurately captured by Fredlund & Xing and Van Genuchten models, with parameter trends consistent with pore-scale physics.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if θ decreases with particle size at fixed suction and if amplitudes decrease with particle size. H2 is supported if θ after leaching is lower than before at fixed suction and if θr and a/n/m parameters shift in directions consistent with reduced retention. H3 is supported if larger particle size shows smaller amplitude changes and earlier stabilization. H4 is supported if model fits achieve high R² and parameter trends align with theory.
reference_methodology:
Materials: Ion-absorbed rare earth samples were collected from the Nanzudong Rare Earth Ore (Jiangxi Province) at 0.5–1 m depth. Basic physical properties (Table 1): density 1.66 g/cm³; natural water content 16.26%; specific gravity 2.68; void ratio 0.88; liquid limit 40.56%; plastic limit 30.27%; plastic index 10.29%. Particle size distribution (Figure 3) indicated silty clay; particles <0.5 mm comprised 48.22% of the undisturbed sample.

Sample preparation: Samples were sieved into three particle size classes: <0.075 mm, 0.075–0.25 mm, and 0.25–0.5 mm, and an undisturbed reference. Particles >0.5 mm were excluded due to poor adhesion and differing engineering properties. Samples were remolded into 70 mm × 19 mm cylinders, compacted to a water content of 15% and dry density 1.3–1.5 g/cm³. All samples were vacuum-saturated for 24 h (Figure 5) prior to testing.

Leaching protocol: Following the Chinese industry standard XB/T619-2015, control groups were leached with ammonium sulfate solution (20 g/L), then statically deposited and dried. The leaching design is summarized in Table 2 (S1–S4: not leached; L1–L4: leached).

Apparatus and procedure: A Geo-Experts stress-related soil–water characteristic curve pressure plate apparatus (Figure 4) was used, comprising a pressure plate, vertical loading system, pressure control, and water volume measurement. Drying tests applied matric suctions of 0, 10, 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, and 480 kPa. Wetting tests reduced suction stepwise to 0 after drying. Equilibrium was defined as <0.1 mL water change in 24 h (per Pham, 2005). The ceramic plate (high inlet air) forms a shrink film that prevents air entry while allowing water flow; matric suction was taken as the applied air pressure when water volume stabilized (u_w ≈ 0).

Measurements and calculations: Saturated mass water content ws was computed from masses (mt, ms, m0) (Equation 1). Mass water content w at each suction was derived from the equilibrium water volume change Δvi and water density ρw (Equation 2). Volumetric water content θ was computed from w and dry density ρd (Equation 3). Drying and wetting SWCCs were constructed.

Modeling: SWCCs were fitted with (i) Fredlund & Xing 3-parameter model (θ/θs = 1 / [1 + (ψ/a)^n]^m, assuming θr = 0), (ii) Fredlund & Xing 4-parameter model (θ−θr)/(θs−θr) = 1 / [1 + (ψ/a)^n]^m, with θr estimated by fitting), and (iii) Van Genuchten model (θ−θr)/(θs−θr) = 1 / [1 + (aψ)^n]^m, with m = 1 − 1/n. Fitting parameters and R² are reported in Tables 3–4.

Microstructural analysis: SEM images at 5000× were processed with the PCAS system to quantify surface porosity, probability entropy (0–1; higher indicates more chaotic structure), and mean shape coefficient (narrower shapes lower). Results are in Table 5.

title: Feed Control, May, 1907. Information Regarding the New Feed Law
field_subfield: Agricultural Science — Feed Chemistry and Regulation
research_question: The bulletin does not state formal hypotheses. Its objectives are: (1) to summarize the amended Texas Feeding Stuff Law (House Bill No. 399) and its enforcement procedures; (2) to provide compositional benchmarks for concentrated feeding stuffs sold in Texas to guide realistic guarantees and detect adulteration; and (3) to explain how producers can comply with registration, sampling, and tagging requirements. Implicit expectations are that compositional data will reveal typical ranges for protein, fat, crude fiber, nitrogen-free extract, ash, and water across feed types, and that crude fiber content will be a sensitive indicator of adulteration (e.g., hulls, cobs, chaff). Outcomes supporting these objectives include tabulated averages and ranges for key constituents and digestibility coefficients that contextualize nutritional value. Outcomes that would refute them would include inconsistent or non-informative compositional data or evidence that crude fiber is not a reliable adulteration indicator; such outcomes are not reported.
reference_methodology:
Sampling and analysis: The law requires that before offering a concentrated feeding stuff for sale, the manufacturer, importer, or party causing the sale must deposit with the Director of the Experiment Station a sealed glass jar or bottle containing not less than one pound of each kind or brand of the product, accompanied by an affidavit that it is a fair average sample and corresponds within reasonable limits to the product’s protein, fat, crude fiber, and nitrogen-free extract. The Director is empowered to take samples from not less than five percent of the whole lot inspected, with samples drawn in the presence of the parties or their representatives, or in the presence of two disinterested witnesses if absent. Each sample is thoroughly mixed and divided into two, sealed in glass or metal vessels, and labeled with the name/brand, party sampled, date, and place. One duplicate is retained by the Director for comparison with certified statements; the other is left with the sampled party.

Analytical methods: The bulletin states that constituent determinations follow methods adopted at the time by the Association of Official Agricultural Chemists of the United States. Specific laboratory protocols (e.g., Kjeldahl for protein, ether extraction for fat, acid/alkali fiber methods, ashing, moisture determination) are not detailed in the text. Digestibility coefficients are reported for selected feeds (e.g., protein digestibility 59.7% in green corn), but the animal models, diets, and procedures used to derive these coefficients are not described.

Registration and tagging: Manufacturers/importers must file a certified copy of the required statement (net weight, brand, manufacturer/importer details, and chemical guarantees) and pay a 10¢/ton inspection tax. The Director issues tax tags certifying payment. The Director may refuse registration for misleading names or nonconformity with standards and may cancel registration ten days after notice if violations are discovered. Re-registration is required for changes in guarantees or ingredient percentages; new sealed samples are needed if guarantees or ingredient percentages change.

Scope and exclusions: The law applies to concentrated feeding stuffs (e.g., wheat bran, wheat shorts, cottonseed meal, rice bran/polish, corn chops/bran/corn and cob meal, etc.) but excludes hay and straw and whole or unground grains/seeds. Mill products have standardized net weights (e.g., flour 196 lb/barrel or 48 lb/sack; corn meal 35 lb/sack; rice bran 143 lb/sack; rice polish 200 lb/sack; other cereal feeds 100 lb/sack).

title: KARAKTERISTIK GEOMORFOLOGI DAN HUBUNGANNYA DENGAN SEBARAN LITOLOGI DAERAH WAY LAGA DAN SEKITARNYA, KOTA BANDAR LAMPUNG, PROVINSI LAMPUNG
research_question:
Research question: What are the geomorphological characteristics of the Way Laga area and its surroundings, and how do these characteristics relate to the distribution of constituent lithologies?

Hypotheses (implicit): (1) Distinct lithologies (tuff, clays, schist) produce characteristic landform morphologies and drainage patterns that can be delineated into geomorphological units; (2) Structural controls (e.g., faults) and lithological properties jointly determine the observed hillslope morphology and valley forms; (3) Exogenous erosion processes, influenced by lithology, dominate valley development, with vertical erosion exceeding horizontal erosion in clay-rich settings.

Support/refutation criteria: Support would be demonstrated by consistent associations between mapped lithologies and specific geomorphological units (e.g., tuff on higher elevations, schist in V-shaped valleys, clays in lower terrains), and by drainage patterns (e.g., rectangular patterns linked to structural controls) that align with slope ranges and lithology. Refutation would involve inconsistent or non-corresponding distributions or drainage patterns that do not align with lithology and structural interpretations.
reference_methodology:
Study area: Desa Way Laga, Bandar Lampung City, Lampung Province, Indonesia, covering 2.5 × 2.5 km². The area is part of the Bukit Barisan mountain range and coastal terrains of Lampung.

Data: SRTM DEM (resolution not reported) and compiled geological maps from prior studies at 1:12,500 scale. The regional geological map (Tanjung Karang sheet, WGS84 UTM 48S) is referenced for structural context. No additional geospatial datasets (e.g., LiDAR, field surveys) are reported.

Software: Global Mapper and ArcGIS for DEM compilation, zoning, and geomorphological mapping.

Analytical approach: The study applies three geomorphological aspects: (1) Morphography: identification and classification of landforms and drainage patterns based on visual characteristics (size, shape, slope, pattern) and absolute elevation, referencing Van Zuidam (1983) and Van Zuidam (1985) (modified from Howard, 1919). Drainage pattern analysis is used to infer lithological resistance and tectonic influence. (2) Morphometry: quantitative analysis of slope and other landform attributes to infer erosion, slope stability, and landform evolution, using Van Zuidam (1985) for slope classification (percent or degrees). (3) Morphogenetics: assessment of the origin and processes shaping landforms, integrating endogenous (e.g., tectonic faulting) and exogenous (e.g., erosion, sedimentation) processes. Morphogenetic interpretation compares drainage patterns with geological structure, landform morphology, and lithology.

Procedure: The study area was divided into zones based on topographic appearance in 2D and 3D DEM to facilitate analysis. SRTM DEM was compiled with geological maps to produce a thematic geomorphology map. Morphographic units were delineated by landform type and drainage pattern; morphometric units were delineated by slope ranges; morphogenetic interpretation linked these to lithology and structural controls. The final geomorphology map integrates these analyses to show the spatial distribution of lithologies within geomorphological units.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human or animal subjects reported.

title: Investigation of an Electrooptic Tunable Filter in Lithium Niobate
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a polarization-independent EOTF in LiNbO3 be realized with a narrow -3 dB bandwidth (~1.56 nm) at 1.55 μm using zero-gap PBSs and strain-induced TE↔TM converters? (2) What fabrication parameters (Ti thickness, diffusion temperature/time, PBS Lc) optimize PBS ER and overall filter performance? (3) What thermal and electrooptic tuning rates are achievable, and how do they compare across TE and TM polarizations? (4) Is the device polarization independent under both tuning mechanisms?

Hypotheses: (H1) A converter with 765 gratings (Λ = 21 μm) will yield ~1.56 nm FWHM and high conversion efficiency near the phase-matched wavelength. (H2) PBS ER can be increased to ≥20 dB for TM and ≥16 dB for TE by optimizing Ti thickness (≥1300 Å), diffusion temperature (~1055°C), and Lc (~280 μm). (H3) Electrooptic tuning will produce linear wavelength shifts with rates on the order of 0.06–0.09 nm/V, limited by electrode gap and breakdown. (H4) Thermal tuning will shift the center wavelength with a negative rate (~-0.8–-1.0 nm/°C). (H5) The assembled filter will be polarization independent, with comparable drop and add spectra and similar tuning behavior for TE and TM. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include measured FWHM, ER, tuning rates, and polarization-insensitive spectra.
reference_methodology:
Substrate and waveguides: x-cut LiNbO3 wafers (1 mm thick, 3 inch diameter) were diced into 9 mm (z) × 14 mm (y) or 9 mm × 25 mm chips. Ti films (~1050 Å for waveguides; ~1330 Å for splitters) were deposited by DC sputtering. Photolithography (AZ-5214) defined channel waveguides (5–10 μm widths) and PBSs (v-junctions with opening angle α = 0.55° and central interaction length Lc = 200–280 μm). RIE (CHF3:75 sccm, Ar:2 sccm, He:7.5 sccm; ~350 W) removed non-patterned Ti; residual Ti was wet-etched (HF:H2O = 1:25, 10–12 s). Photoresist was stripped (90°C, 15 min). Diffusion used wet air (bubbler) at 1025–1055°C for 9–11 h (e.g., 1055°C, 9 h for 1350 Å Ti). Ends were polished (UV epoxy mounting, 3 μm and 0.3 μm diamond) for fiber coupling.

Strain-induced gratings: A 1.45–1.60 μm SiO2 film was deposited at 360°C (e-beam evaporation with O2) on top of electrodes. Positive photolithography (AZ-5214) patterned 765 uniform strips with Λ = 21 μm. RIE (300 W, 20 min) defined the grating; BOE (25–30 s) removed residue. The grating thickness and deposition temperature were varied to optimize Δn5 and conversion efficiency.

Electrodes: Cr/Au/Ti (650/800/650 Å) were deposited by e-beam evaporation and patterned by lift-off. Electrode gaps g were 13–17 μm; electrode lengths d were 13–15 μm.

Testing: Insertion loss was measured with a 1.55 μm DFB laser (32 mA), polarization controller, butt coupling to polished waveguide ends, and detection via a 20× lens and Ge photodiode (Newport 818-IR). Mode profiles used a vibrating mirror and slit (100 μm) with a 20× lens and oscilloscope/LabVIEW. ER was measured using ASE from an EDFA (980 nm pump LD; 5 m EDF; WDM coupler; isolator) coupled through a polarizing fiber (PZ) to select TE/TM. Output spectra were recorded with an OSA (Anritsu MS9710C). Thermal tuning used a TEC on a Cu plate with a thermistor (Omega 44030) to control substrate temperature. Electrooptic tuning applied DC voltages from -100 to +60 V (converter) or -80 to +80 V (filter) and measured wavelength shifts. Polarization dependence was evaluated by repeating measurements for TE and TM inputs.

Analysis: Waveguide propagation loss was estimated by subtracting Fresnel and mode-mismatch losses from measured insertion loss. PBS ER was computed from output port powers (Eq. 71).
