Converter conversion efficiency was computed from Eq. (81)/(82). Thermal tuning rate was computed from Δλ/ΔT. Electrooptic tuning rate was computed from Eq. (85) assuming ΓTE ≈ ΓTM for overlap factors.

title: The clinical effectiveness of Neuromidin and its influence on the processes of neuroplasticity in cranial-cerebral injury
research_question:
Research question: Does adding Neuromidin to standard therapy improve clinical outcomes and neuroplasticity-related measures in patients with mild-to-moderate TBI during the acute and early recovery periods compared with standard therapy alone?

Hypotheses: (1) Neuromidin will produce greater improvement in neurological symptoms and cognitive function than standard therapy, reflected in reduced P300 latency and improved EEG reactivity/spectral characteristics. (2) Neuromidin will increase serum beta-NGF levels post-treatment, indicating enhanced neuroplasticity, to a greater extent than standard therapy. (3) Neuromidin will improve subjective measures of fatigue, headache, emotional symptoms, and socialization more than standard therapy. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include statistically significant between-group differences favoring Neuromidin in P300 normalization, beta-NGF increases, and clinical symptom scales; outcomes refuting them would be no differences or worse outcomes with Neuromidin.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Observational clinical study at the Kharkiv Regional Clinical Hospital — Center for Emergency Medicine and Disaster Medicine (Kharkiv, Ukraine). Patients were assessed at 1–2 days post-admission and after a 60-day treatment course.

Participants: 80 patients with mild-to-moderate TBI (79% concussion; 21% mild contusion). Inclusion criteria: age 25–60 years; first-time TBI; acute or early recovery period; informed consent. Exclusion criteria: severe somatic or neurological diseases; two or more prior TBIs; hepatic or renal dysfunction; substance dependence; pregnancy; injury during alcohol intoxication; age >60 years; refusal to participate. Neuromidin contraindications: epilepsy, extrapyramidal disorders, angina, marked bradycardia, bronchial asthma, hyperthyroidism, peptic ulcer, urolithiasis, hypersensitivity.

Interventions: Two equal groups (n=40 each). Group I (intervention): standard therapy plus Neuromidin (Oleinfarm, Latvia). Group II (control): standard therapy only. Neuromidin dosing: intramuscular 15 mg twice daily for 10 days, followed by oral 20 mg tablets three times daily for 1.5 months (acute TBI) or 2 months (early recovery TBI). Total course: 60 days. Standard therapy details (e.g., specific medications, dosages, rehabilitation protocols) are not reported.

Measures: (1) Clinical neurological status (polymorphic, polysyndromic symptomatology; vegetative dysregulation; emotional-personality disturbances; coordination; pyramidal signs; sleep disorders). (2) EEG: spontaneous activity patterns (normal, hypersynchronous, flat, disorganized, paroxysmal), reactivity, and spectral characteristics; assessment of midbrain and subcortical dysfunction via paroxysmal activity/irritability. (3) Cognitive P300: auditory oddball paradigm with significant and non-significant stimuli; P300 latency interpreted against age norms (Sadovsky, 1993). (4) Serum beta-NGF: ELISA. (5) Subjective symptom scales (fatigue, headache, emotional symptoms, socialization) and qualitative patient-reported outcomes.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics and group comparisons are reported; specific statistical tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and p-values are not provided. No randomization or blinding is described. Ethics: informed consent obtained; IRB approval not reported.

title: Augmented Reality Enabling Disassembly Sequence Planning
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which disassembly sequence for a two-way valve minimizes disassembly time when evaluated using multiple DSP methods? (2) Can AR-based simulation effectively visualize and validate the optimal sequence in a real-world context before physical disassembly? (3) Do geometric constraints, precedence, and time-based modeling jointly yield a sequence that is faster than common-practice heuristics?

Hypotheses: (H1) A time-based DSP method (Favi et al., 2019; Mandolini et al., 2018) will identify a sequence with lower disassembly time than a CAD-based wave method (Jianjun et al., 2008) and common-practice heuristics. (H2) AR visualization will successfully render the optimal sequence in a real scenario, demonstrating feasibility for pre-production evaluation. (H3) Incorporating geometric feasibility (SDR/CD) and collision detection (Mitrouchev et al., 2015) will reduce non-optimal paths and improve sequence quality.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if the time-based sequence yields the minimum reported time. H2 is supported if the AR simulation reproduces the sequence in a real environment. H3 is supported if the DGCG method reduces search space and aligns with the optimal sequence.
reference_methodology:
Design: A case study of a two-way valve with 13 components. The authors model the assembly in PTC CREO from construction drawings (Straneo et al., 1972). Components are numbered for sequence tracking. The study compares four disassembly sequences: (1) common-practice heuristic, (2) CAD-based disassembly wave method (Jianjun et al., 2008), (3) time-based DSP method (Favi et al., 2019; Mandolini et al., 2018), and (4) DGCG-based selective disassembly (Mitrouchev et al., 2015). Sequences are evaluated by converting operations to disassembly time using Mandolini et al. (2018) and selecting the minimum-time sequence.

DSP methods: (1) CAD-based wave method: Generate disassembly waves starting from the most internal component (component 11) to propagate removal directions; four waves are produced. (2) Time-based method: Construct a level matrix and precedence relationships; identify levels of disassembly (e.g., level 1: components 1 and 7; level 2: 12, 4, 8A, 6; level 3: 2, 7; level 4: 8B, 3; level 5: 5, 11; level 6: 11). Optimize by minimizing disassembly time to reach the target (BDSTx = min(Seq_iTx)). (3) DGCG method: Build a Disassembly Geometry Contacting Graph with SDR, CD, and collision detection (projection-based, Jimenez et al., 2001). Use a Gaussian sphere to represent feasible removal directions; collisions reduce feasible directions. The method reduces search complexity by focusing on lowest-level disassembly.

Evaluation: Operations are converted to time using Mandolini et al. (2018). The best sequence is selected by minimum time. The authors report that sequence 3 (time-based) is optimal but do not provide numerical time values, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. No human user studies or physical timing trials are reported.

AR simulation: The authors use PTC CREO’s Target/ThingMark to anchor the CAD model in a real environment and Unity with Vuforia for marker-based AR. The AR pipeline recognizes a marker, stabilizes tracking (SLAM), and overlays the disassembly steps. Videos (MPG) are created to visualize sequences. The final AR scene shows all parts disassembled (Figure 7).

title: Effect of inclusion education on the perceptions of sighted school children about the abilities of students living with severe visual impairment and blindness
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does inclusion education influence sighted students’ perceptions of the abilities of SWVI compared to sighted students in sighted-only schools? (2) Do SWVI in inclusion schools perceive their own abilities similarly to SWVI in special schools? (3) How do perceptions differ across domains (educational prospects, leadership, social participation, routine tasks)?

Hypotheses (implicit from the abstract): (a) Inclusion education positively affects sighted students’ perceptions of SWVI abilities relative to sighted-only peers; (b) SWVI in inclusion schools do not differ in self-perceptions from SWVI in special schools. Support for (a) would be evidenced by SSIS endorsing higher academic attainment and leadership potential for SWVI, citing supports and resources available in inclusion settings. Support for (b) would be evidenced by similar SWVIIS and SWVIBS narratives about their own capabilities and experiences. Alternative outcomes would include no change in SSIS perceptions or divergence in SWVI self-perceptions across school types.
reference_methodology:
Design: Phenomenological qualitative study using focus group discussions (FGDs) and thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke). The approach aimed to elicit how participants experience, describe, and judge the abilities of SWVI.

Setting and participants: Three junior high schools in Ghana’s Central Region were purposively sampled: (1) Cape Coast School for the Deaf and Blind (special school), (2) Ghana National Inclusion Basic School (inclusion school), and (3) Kwegyir Aggrey Basic School (mainstream, sighted-only). Total N=58: 10 blind students from the special school; 34 students from the inclusion school (21 sighted, 13 blind); 14 sighted students from the mainstream school. The inclusion school sample included both sighted and blind students to capture peer perceptions within inclusive settings.

Data collection: Structured FGDs explored perceptions across four domains: educational prospects (e.g., academic attainment, class ranking, appropriate educational setting), leadership (religion, politics, academic leadership, counseling), participation in social activities (social media, hobbies, entertainment), and routine tasks (school chores, home errands). Each FGD lasted approximately 60 minutes and was informal. Participants were informed of the study’s purpose and encouraged to provide candid responses. Sessions were recorded and transcribed verbatim.

Analysis: Thematic analysis followed Braun & Clarke’s six-phase framework: familiarization, coding, theme development, review, definition, and reporting. The authors identified themes within each domain and synthesized cross-domain insights. Excerpts were used to illustrate themes; the text notes that presented excerpts are representative of similar opinions.

Ethics: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Cape Coast. Written informed consent was obtained from parents/guardians; written assent from participants; and consent from schools. Confidentiality and anonymity were maintained (no names/personal details reported). Participation was voluntary with the right to withdraw. No emotional trauma was reported.

Limitations of reporting: The text does not report inter-coder reliability, sampling procedures beyond purposive selection of three schools, or demographic details (e.g., age, gender, impairment severity distribution). No quantitative measures or statistical analyses were conducted.

title: Rebound in asthma exacerbations following relaxation of COVID-19 restrictions: a longitudinal population-based study (COVIDENCE UK)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Did relaxation of COVID-19 restrictions in the UK coincide with changes in behaviors (face coverings, social mixing, travel) and with temporal increases in COVID-19, non-COVID-19 ARI, and moderate/severe asthma exacerbations? (2) Is incident ARI independently associated with increased risk of moderate/severe asthma exacerbations, and are the associations similar for COVID-19 versus non-COVID-19 ARI? (3) Does the strength of association between COVID-19 and asthma exacerbations differ before versus after the emergence of the omicron variant?

Hypotheses: (a) Relaxation of restrictions would be associated with reduced face covering use and increased social mixing, leading to higher incidence of respiratory infections and asthma exacerbations. (b) Incident ARI would be independently associated with increased risk of moderate/severe asthma exacerbations, with effect sizes comparable across COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 ARI. (c) The association between COVID-19 and exacerbations would not be stronger after omicron dominance. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significant temporal increases in ARI and exacerbations during relaxation periods, adjusted aORs >1 for incident ARI, and similar aORs for COVID-19 pre- and post-omicron.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Prospective, population-based longitudinal cohort (COVIDENCE UK). Recruitment via national media campaign from May 1, 2020 to October 6, 2021. Baseline online questionnaire captured demographics, occupation, lifestyle, quality of life, anthropometrics, comorbidities, medication use, vaccination status, diet, and micronutrient intake. Monthly follow-up questionnaires (from November 12, 2020 to April 21, 2022) captured behaviors potentially influencing ARI transmission, incident ARI symptoms, RT-PCR/antigen test results for respiratory viruses, incident asthma and COPD exacerbations, and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination doses.

Participants: Inclusion criteria: participation in COVIDENCE UK; self-reported doctor-diagnosed asthma at baseline; ongoing use of at least one prescribed asthma treatment and/or at least one moderate/severe asthma exacerbation in the 12 months prior to enrolment; and completion of at least one monthly follow-up questionnaire between November 12, 2020 and April 21, 2022. Exclusion criteria: self-reported positive RT-PCR/antigen SARS-CoV-2 test; ongoing or prior chronic symptoms attributed to prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID); or hospitalization for COVID-19 prior to enrolment or at baseline. Of 19,981 baseline participants, 2,666 reported asthma; 2,312 (86.7%) had no prior COVID-19 and contributed follow-up data.

Variables: Behavioral variables included face covering use (proportion reporting “Always” use indoors in the prior week), visits to shops, other indoor public places, indoor visits to/from other households, public transport use, and foreign travel (proportion reporting any such event in the prior week or month). Respiratory outcomes: COVID-19 defined by self-report confirmed by positive RT-PCR/antigen; non-COVID-19 ARI defined by GP/hospital diagnosis of pneumonia, influenza, bronchitis, tonsillitis, pharyngitis, ear infection, common cold, or other upper/lower respiratory infection, or symptom-defined ARI with at least one negative RT-PCR/antigen test and no positive tests. Symptom-defined ARI used modified Jackson criteria (upper respiratory), modified Macfarlane criteria (lower respiratory), and a triad of cough, fever, and myalgia (influenza-like illness). Moderate/severe asthma exacerbations required systemic corticosteroids and/or precipitated ED attendance or hospital admission.

Potential confounders: Age, sex (assigned at birth), ethnicity (White vs minority), current tobacco smoking, educational attainment, BMI (<25, 25–30, >30 kg/m²), asthma treatment level (reliever only; ICS±reliever; LAB±ICS/reliever; monoclonal antibody±other), prior moderate/severe exacerbation (yes/no), index of multiple deprivation (IMD) 2019 quartiles, self-rated general health, and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination status (primary course completed vs not). Variant attribution: episodes occurring from December 16, 2021 onward were imputed as omicron.

Statistical analysis: Univariable Poisson GAMs modeled temporal trends (month-year) for behaviors, ARI, and exacerbations; penalized regression splines visualized trends with means and 95% CIs. Multilevel logistic GLMs estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for associations between incident ARI and moderate/severe asthma exacerbations, adjusting for all listed confounders. Random intercepts for unique participant identifiers accounted for within-participant correlation. Missing data were assumed MCAR and handled by listwise deletion in mixed models. Analyses used R 4.1.1 with lme4. Ethics: Leicester South Research Ethics Committee approval (20/EM/0117); ClinicalTrials.gov registration (NCT04330599); informed consent obtained.

title: Imipramine, in part through TNF-α inhibition, prevents cognitive decline and Aß accumulation in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does imipramine prevent Aβ25–35-induced short-term (Y-maze) and long-term (water-maze) memory impairments? (2) Does imipramine reduce TNF-α expression in frontal cortex and hippocampus? (3) Does imipramine modulate APP processing and Aβ accumulation in these regions?

Hypotheses: (H1) Imipramine will prevent Aβ25–35-induced cognitive deficits in both Y-maze and water-maze tasks. (H2) Imipramine will attenuate TNF-α increases in brain regions affected by Aβ25–35, consistent with anti-inflammatory action. (H3) Imipramine will reduce Aβ accumulation and normalize APP/CTF profiles, reflecting amyloidogenic-to-non-amyloidogenic processing shifts. Supportive outcomes would include significant improvements in alternation and probe performance, reduced TNF-α levels by ELISA/IHC, and decreased Aβ immunoreactivity with normalization of CTFs and APP. Refutation would involve no differences in behavior or biomarkers, or increased TNF-α/Aβ despite treatment.
reference_methodology:
Animals: Male Swiss mice (Janvier, France), 4 weeks old, 27–32 g at start. Individually housed with ad libitum food/water (except during behavioral tests). Housing: temperature- and humidity-controlled, lights on 8:00–20:00. Experiments conducted 09:00–13:00. Ethical compliance: EU Directive 86/609/EEC.

Peptides and injection: Aβ25–35 and scrambled Aβ25–35 (NeoMPS, France) dissolved in sterile UHQ water (3 mg/mL), stored at −20°C. Aggregated at 37°C for 4 days. i.c.v. injection: 3 µL per mouse. Anesthesia: isoflurane (FORENE, Abbott). Stereotaxic coordinates: A −0.2 mm, L −1 mm from bregma, V 2.5 mm from skull; unilateral injection over 60 s.

Drug treatment: Imipramine (Cooper, France) dissolved in saline; i.p. 10 mg/kg once daily for 14 days starting the day after Aβ25–35 injection; volume 100 µL per 10 g body weight. Dose rationale: prior protective effects at 10 mg/kg; higher doses (20–40 mg/kg) caused reduced food intake and weight loss in prior studies.

Behavioral tests: Y-maze (day 9): three arms (34 cm length, 7 cm width, 10 cm walls), 120° apart. Mice placed at end of one arm; free exploration for 8 min. Arms entry defined as all four paws into an arm. Alternation score (%) = number of alternations / total possible alternations × 100. Water-maze (days 10–14): circular pool (140 cm diameter, 40 cm height), water 20 ± 1°C, 20 cm depth, opaque with Meudon white powder. Habituation: visible platform in varied positions across four trials. Training: submerged platform (1 cm below surface) centered in NE quadrant; one session of four trials/day for four days (days 10–13). Each trial: 60 s swim to platform; 10 s platform dwell; start positions randomized (all four used once/day). Probe test (day 14): platform removed; 60 s exploration. Visible-platform control: no differences in time/distance to platform among groups (not shown). Swimming speed computed and analyzed.

Biochemistry and histology: On day 14, mice were sacrificed by cervical dislocation; frontal cortex and hippocampus dissected. Lysis buffer: 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 50 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 50 mM NaF, 1 mM PMSF, 5% protease inhibitors, 1% phosphatase inhibitors. Supernatants quantified (Bradford). TNF-α quantified by ELISA (BioLegend) per manufacturer; standard curve in duplicate; OD 450 nm.

Western blotting: 15% Tris-glycine gels; transfer to PVDF. Blocking: TBST + 5% milk + 0.21% NaF, 2 h. Primary: rabbit anti-CTFs/APP (1:1000, Ozyme). Secondary: HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG (1:1000, 1 h RT). Detection: ECL (Amersham), imaging with Gbox (GeneSnap). Tubulin (1:10,000) used as loading control. Band intensities normalized to tubulin.

Immunohistochemistry: Anesthesia with sodium pentobarbital (40 mg/kg i.p.). Transcardial perfusion: 50 mL PBS, then 100 mL PBS + 4% paraformaldehyde. Brains fixed overnight in 4% PFA at 4°C; paraffin-embedded; 4–11 µm sagittal sections. Dewaxing and rehydration; antigen retrieval in 10 mM sodium citrate (pH 6), microwaved 2×10 min (650 W). Blocking: PBS/0.3% Triton X-100 + 5% BSA, 60 min RT. Primary antibodies: rabbit anti-TNF-α (1:100) and mouse anti-Aβ (4G8, 1:100) overnight at 4°C. Secondary: biotinylated anti-rabbit or anti-mouse (1:30) 1 h RT; streptavidin-FITC or streptavidin-RRX (1:30) 1 h RT. Mounting in aqueous medium. Imaging: Olympus DP70; Olympus DP-soft. Neurons counted in six fields by two experimenters blinded to treatment.

Statistics: Results as mean ± SEM. Two-way ANOVA for repeated measures (groups × days) for escape latencies; Tukey post hoc. One-way ANOVA for probe time, biochemical, and IHC measures with Tukey post hoc; normality and homogeneity checks (SAS 9.1). Significance threshold p<0.05.

title: Psychological Distress and Well-Being among Students of Health Disciplines: The Importance of Academic Satisfaction
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the levels of psychological distress (depression, anxiety, stress) and psychological well-being among undergraduate students in multiple health-related disciplines in Geneva? (2) Which factors—gender, age, academic year, discipline, and academic satisfaction—are associated with these outcomes? (3) Does academic satisfaction predict distress and well-being beyond demographic and programmatic factors?

Hypotheses: (a) Lower academic satisfaction would be associated with higher depression, anxiety, stress, and lower psychological well-being; (b) Female gender would be associated with higher anxiety and stress; (c) Older age would be associated with higher psychological well-being; (d) Academic year (first/second years) would be associated with higher distress; (e) Discipline would show differential associations with distress and well-being; (f) Academic satisfaction would account for a substantial proportion of variance in outcomes beyond demographic and programmatic predictors.

Support/refutation criteria: Significant regression coefficients (p ≤ 0.05) for the hypothesized predictors and meaningful increases in R² when entering academic satisfaction would support the hypotheses. Null or non-significant coefficients for academic year or discipline would refute or nuance those hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Cross-sectional survey conducted in October 2019 among bachelor-level students at the Geneva School of Health Sciences and the Faculty of Medicine, School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, and Psychology Department of the University of Geneva.

Sampling and participants: Random sampling stratified by health disciplines; all students were invited. No exclusion criteria. Of 2835 invited, 915 completed the survey (32% response rate); 3 were excluded for invalid birth years, yielding n=912 for analysis. The sample was 82.3% female (n=753). Age ranged 16–61 years (mean 22.15, SD 4.25). The sampling pool’s female proportion ranged from 64% (Faculty of Medicine) to 81% (Psychology Department). Mean age ranged from 21 (Faculty of Medicine and School of Pharmaceutical Sciences) to 24 (School of Health Sciences Geneva).

Measures: Socio-demographic variables included gender, age, academic year, and health discipline. Mental health outcomes were measured with: (1) Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), with depression and anxiety subscales (7 items each; 0–3 scale); (2) Cohen Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-14), 0–4 scale; (3) Psychological Well-Being Scale (BEP-18), 1–6 scale; (4) Scale of Satisfaction with Studies (SSS-5), 1–7 scale. Descriptive statistics were reported as means ± SD.

Data collection: Recruitment via email from student secretariats. Participation via a secure online platform (EvaSys Education Survey Automation Suite v7.1). After informed consent, participants completed socio-demographics and the four scales. Data were collected shortly after the academic year began. Data were handled confidentially and archived on a locked office hard drive accessible only to investigators.

Statistical analysis: Hierarchical linear regressions were run separately for each outcome (depression, anxiety, stress, well-being). Four blocks of predictors were entered sequentially: Block 1 (gender, age); Block 2 (academic year); Block 3 (health discipline); Block 4 (academic satisfaction). Predictors were considered significant at p ≤ 0.05. The increase in R² between consecutive blocks was evaluated for significance. No missing data were present due to mandatory fields. Analyses were conducted in SPSS v25 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA).

Ethics: The Ethics Research Committee of the Geneva University Hospitals reviewed the protocol and waived the need for an internal review board review due to anonymity (reference 2019-00696). Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

title: Analysis of Antioxidant Activity and Flavonoids Metabolites in Peel and Flesh of Red-Fleshed Apple Varieties
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do phenotypic traits, total anthocyanins, total phenols, and antioxidant activities vary across four red-fleshed apple cultivars at three developmental stages? (2) Which flavonoid metabolites differ between XJ4 and DH at maturity, and how are these differences distributed across early and late biosynthetic genes? (3) Do specific anthocyanin profiles explain coloration differences and antioxidant activity differences?

Hypotheses: (a) Higher anthocyanin content correlates with stronger antioxidant activity, particularly DPPH scavenging; (b) XJ4 exhibits unique anthocyanin accumulation (e.g., pelargonidin- and cyanidin-based compounds) that underlies its intense coloration and higher antioxidant activity; (c) Differences in upstream (early) versus downstream (late) biosynthetic gene-regulated metabolites explain stage-specific changes in anthocyanin content (e.g., larger decreases in XJ4 peel at maturity). Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include positive correlations between anthocyanins and DPPH scavenging, detection of unique XJ4 anthocyanins, and pathway-level enrichment consistent with early/late domain regulation.
reference_methodology:
Plant materials and sampling: Four red-fleshed apple cultivars (XJ4, QN-5, DH, HX1) grafted on Malus Robusta were grown for 8 years at Qingdao Agricultural University (Qingdao, China). Fruits were harvested at 30 days after anthesis (young), 90 days (developmental), and 140 days (mature). Peel and flesh were sampled separately, freeze-dried in liquid nitrogen, lyophilized, and stored at −80 °C.

Anthocyanins extraction and quantification: Total anthocyanins were extracted with methanol-HCl (99:1, v/v) at 1:10 (w/v) for 15 h in the dark. Supernatants were filtered (0.45 μm) and stored at −4 °C. Total anthocyanins were measured by the pH differential method. For each sample, 1 mL extract was mixed with 9 mL sodium acetate buffer (0.4 mol/L, pH 4.5) and 9 mL potassium chloride buffer (0.025 mol/L, pH 1.0), incubated 1 h at room temperature, and absorbance read at 510 nm and 700 nm. Absorbance A was calculated as A = (A510 − A700) pH 1.0 − (A510 − A700) pH 4.5. Total anthocyanins (cyanidin 3-O-glucoside equivalents, mg•kg^-1 FW) = A × MW × DF / (ε × W), where MW = 449.2, DF = dilution factor, ε = 26,900 (cyanidin 3-O-glucoside), W = fresh weight.

Total phenols: Determined by Folin-Ciocalteu method (modified Cai). Gallic acid standards were prepared with 10% sodium carbonate; absorbance at 765 nm after 1 h at 50 °C. Total phenols (gallic acid equivalents, mg•kg^-1 FW) = C × V × N / m, where C = concentration from standard curve, V = final volume, N = dilution times, m = sample weight.

Antioxidant assays: DPPH radical scavenging (modified He): 2 mL extract + 2 mL DPPH (0.2 mmol/L); blank: 2 mL extract + 2 mL ethanol; control: 2 mL DPPH + 2 mL ethanol. After 30 min in the dark at room temperature, absorbance at 517 nm. Scavenging rate (%) = [1 − (As − Ab)/Aw] × 100%, where As = sample absorbance, Ab = blank absorbance, Aw = control absorbance.

Hydroxyl radical (•OH) scavenging (modified Ma): 1.5 mL phenanthrene (5 mmol/L) + 9 mL PBS (0.01 M, pH 7.4) + 1 mL FeSO4 (7.5 mmol/L). Sample: add 2.5 mL extract; injured: add 2.5 mL H2O2 (1%); uninjured: add 2.5 mL H2O. After 1 h at 37 °C, absorbance at 536 nm. Scavenging rate (%) = (As − Ai)/(Au − Ai) × 100%, where Ai = injured absorbance, Au = uninjured absorbance.

Superoxide anion (O2•-) scavenging (modified pyrogallol autoxidation): 4.5 mL Tris-HCl (0.05 mol/L, pH 8.0) + 0.1 mL extract (sample) or 0.1 mL H2O (blank) + 0.4 mL pyrogallol (2.5 mmol/L). After 5 min at 25 °C, stop reaction with 2 drops HCl (8.0 mol/L). Absorbance at 325 nm. Scavenging rate (%) = (Ab − As)/Ab × 100%.

Metabolomics: Mature-stage peel and flesh of XJ4 and DH were ground (MM400, 30 Hz, 1.5 min), extracted overnight at 4 °C with 1.0 mL 70% aqueous methanol per 100 mg powder, centrifuged (10,000×g, 10 min), filtered (0.22 μm), and SPE (CNWbond Carbon-GCB, 250 mg, 3 mL). LC-MS/MS used UPLC (Shimadzu CBM30A; ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3, 1.8 μm, 2.1 × 100 mm) with mobile phases A (water + 0.04% acetic acid) and B (acetonitrile + 0.04% acetic acid). Gradient: 100:0 at 0 min; 5:95 at 11.0 min; 5:95 at 12.0 min; 95:5 at 12.1–15.0 min. Flow 0.40 mL/min; column 40 °C. ESI-QTRAP-MS/MS (AB Sciex 6500 QTRAP): TurboSpray, 500 °C; IS 5500 V; GSI 55 psi; GSII 60 psi; CUR 25 psi; CAD high; nitrogen collision gas 5 psi; MRM transitions. Identification used MWDB, MassBank, KNApSAcK, HMDB, METLIN, MoToDB. QC and MRM ensured accuracy and repeatability; PCA/OPLS-DA and permutation tests validated models.

Statistics: Three biological replicates; data as means ± SE. One-way ANOVA tested differences. Metabolite significance: VIP ≥ 1 and fold change ≥ 2 (up) or ≤ 0.5 (down).

title: Recruitment of lymphoblasts derived from peripheral and intestinal lymph to synovium and other tissues in normal rats and rats with adjuvant arthritis.
field_subfield: Immunology — Lymphocyte Trafficking and Autoimmune Arthritis
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are lymphoblasts from peripheral and intestinal lymph recruited to synovium and other tissues in normal and arthritic rats? (2) How do donor (normal vs arthritic) and recipient (normal vs arthritic) disease states modulate recruitment? (3) Does the anatomic origin of lymphoblasts (TD vs MD) determine tissue preferences, including synovium? (4) Does synovial recruitment reflect viable cell entry rather than free nucleoside uptake or cell death?

Hypotheses: (a) Inflamed synovium recruits more lymphoblasts than normal synovium; (b) Arthritic donors produce lymphoblasts with enhanced joint-seeking properties; (c) Peripheral-origin lymphoblasts preferentially enter inflamed synovium and lungs, whereas intestinal-origin lymphoblasts preferentially enter intestine and lymph nodes; (d) Joint-associated radioactivity primarily reflects viable cell recruitment rather than free nucleoside or nonviable cell iodide release. Supportive outcomes would include higher foot counts in arthritic recipients, higher foot counts with arthritic donors, origin-dependent tissue distributions (TD > lungs; MD > intestine), and minimal contribution of free nucleoside and nonviable cells to joint counts.
reference_methodology:
Animals: Female inbred specific pathogen-free Dark Agouti rats (Animal Resource Centre, Perth; Gilles Plains Animal Resource Centre, Adelaide). All rats in each experiment were from the same source and weaning.

Adjuvant arthritis (AA) induction: At 7 weeks, rats received 0.1 ml CFA subcutaneously at the tail base. Adjuvant: IFA containing 10 mg/ml heat-killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37RA. All Dark Agouti rats developed polyarthritis under this protocol. Donor rats cannulated on day 9 post-CFA were termed “arthritic donors,” though not all manifested disease at cannulation.

Lymph collection: Thoracic duct (TD) and mesenteric duct (MD) cannulation per prior methods. Lymph collected overnight (typically 15 h) at room temperature into flasks with 5 ml PBS containing 25 U/ml preservative-free heparin. Cells were isolated by centrifugation (350 × g, 7 min), washed twice in RPMI + 10% FCS, resuspended at ~1 × 10^7 cells/ml, and labeled with [251I]IUdR (1 μCi/ml) for 60 min at 37°C, then washed three times. Autoradiographic smears estimated labeled cell proportions.

Adoptive transfer: Recipients received labeled cells intravenously in 2 ml medium over 1 min. Each recipient received the equivalent of one donor’s overnight lymph output. Donor cells were pooled and divided equally among recipients, which were either normal age-matched controls or rats with established arthritis (day 12 post-CFA).

Tissue sampling and gamma counting: Rats were euthanized 24 h post-transfer. Harvested tissues included stomach, kidneys, uterus, lungs, liver, spleen, thyroid, small intestine, cecum, large intestine, thymus, mesenteric, cervical, inguinal, iliac, and popliteal lymph nodes, plus quadriceps muscle, proximal tail segment (including adjuvant site), front and hind paws, and knees. Tissues were fixed in 10% neutral formalin, rinsed in PBS, and counted with an Auto-Gamma counter (10 min/sample). Net activity was expressed as % of total recovered counts or % of injected counts.

Autoradiography: Perfusion fixation (halothane-nitrous oxide anesthesia; heparinized perfusion; 4% paraformaldehyde/2% glutaraldehyde/2.5% PVP in 0.1 M phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; 2.5 ml/min flow) followed by decalcification and paraffin embedding. Dewaxed 7-μm sections and ethanol-fixed smears were coated with LM-1 emulsion, exposed 3–5 weeks at 4°C, and developed in D19.

Arthritis severity: Paw score per paw (0–4) summed to a joint score (max 16). Day 12 mean joint score was 10.9 ± 2.5.

Statistics: Two-way ANOVA for Figures 1 and 2; weighted ANOVA for heteroscedastic tissues. Planned contrasts tested recipient and donor effects. Some tissues were log-transformed to stabilize variance. Significance thresholds included p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001.

Controls: (1) Nonviable cells (heat-killed at 56°C, 30 min) showed only 3–4% recovery (75% in thyroid), versus ~20% for viable cells; (2) Free [251I]IUdR administered i.v. contributed at most ~0.1% of viable cell counts to feet; (3) Urine excretion accounted for ~50% of injected radioactivity within 24 h; (4) Thyroid uptake (~10–15%) was similar across donor/recipient states.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported.

title: PRoPoZyCJA noWeJ MetoDyKI BADAń …
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How can urban functional-spatial structures be reconstructed and quantified across long historical periods with standardized, comparable methods? (2) What are the persistent and changing contiguities (neighborhood relations) among functional components, and how do these relations shape urban development? (3) Which functions act as initiating or structuring forces, and how do natural, economic, and political factors condition functional succession, expansion, regression, and spatial localization?

Hypotheses/predictions: (a) A standardized functional classification and retrogressive cartographic reconstruction will enable reliable, period-specific mapping and quantification of functional areas. (b) Contiguity analysis will reveal persistent, frequent, and sporadic neighborhood relations that correspond to phases of urban development. (c) The transport function will exhibit initiating and structuring roles, with strong and persistent contiguities to residential and other core functions. (d) Incorporating natural, economic, and political conditioning factors will improve explanatory power for functional succession and spatial patterns.

Support/refutation criteria: Support would be demonstrated by reproducible period maps, consistent area shares and street/railway metrics, contiguity persistence thresholds, and coherent contiguity models aligned with known development phases. Refutation would involve inconsistent reconstructions, unstable contiguities, or inability to link conditioning factors to observed functional changes.
reference_methodology:
Design: A six-stage, standardized methodology for dynamic analysis of urban functional-spatial structures:

Stage I: Functional periodization and identification of causal functions. Using detailed analysis of historical and contemporary written and cartographic sources, the study delineates major development phases marked by significant spatial-functional changes. For Lublin, phases are: pre-colonial (VI–1317), dynamic (1317–1648), depressive–dynamic (1648–1815), moderately dynamic (1815–1944), and dynamic (1944–present). The base catalog of functions is defined to ensure comparability across periods.

Stage II: Reconstruction of functional-spatial structure for each phase. A. City boundary reconstruction: For periods lacking full administrative plans (commonly pre-18th/19th century), boundaries are reconstructed using partial maps, literature, and archival materials (e.g., monographs, municipal records, notarial acts, illustrations). Hydrographic networks (rivers, lakes, coasts) serve as a baseline for boundary and network reconstruction. B. Map redaction: Functional-spatial maps are created for a base year (preferably on a 1:10,000 topographic base) and for phases with major changes. Retrogressive cartographic reconstruction aligns historical sources to a uniform scale (e.g., 1:10,000) via rectification using fixed landmarks (e.g., town halls, churches, preserved walls). The principle of spatial form conservatism is applied to maintain continuity of structures.

Stage III: Quantitative GIS analysis. Using GIS (e.g., ArcView/ArcGIS), the study computes areas of functional components and their shares of total city area, and lengths of streets and railways for each period. Tables record the number of polygons, maximum, mean, and total areas (ha), and shares (%). Bar charts visualize area shares over time.

Stage IV: Contiguity (neighborhood) analysis. For each period, adjacency relations between functional components are tabulated (e.g., Table 2 for Lublin, 1482–2004). Persistence thresholds classify contiguities as persistent (>70% consistency), frequent (30–70%), or sporadic (<30%). A contiguity model is constructed (Figure 2) to summarize stable and changing relations.

Stage V: Conditioning factors analysis. Functional succession, spatial patterns, and change directions are interpreted in the context of natural (climate, topography, hydrology, soils), economic (trade routes, transport modes, technological change, infrastructure lines), and political (administrative decisions, privileges, territorial changes, wars) factors. This step identifies determinants and constraints of development.

Stage VI: Synthesis. Across periods, the study synthesizes the roles of key functions in driving development, evaluates the relative importance of conditioning factors, and highlights functions and relations that favored balanced growth versus those that hindered it. The synthesis informs planning by identifying functions to prioritize and problematic contiguities to mitigate.

Data sources: Archival cartography (partial plans, maps), written sources (historical, archaeological, municipal), and modern GIS layers. The base plan for Lublin’s reconstruction was S.J.n. Łąckiego (1783; ~1:4,500).

title: Benefits and Pitfalls in Utilization of the Internet by Elderly People
field_subfield: Computer Science — Human-Computer Interaction; Gerontology — Aging and Technology
research_question:
The study investigates: (1) What is the extent and nature of ICT use among elderly people in the Czech Republic, and how does it compare internationally? (2) What benefits and pitfalls arise from elderly Internet and ICT use, and how do these manifest in local programs? (3) How do stakeholder groups (senior citizens, pupils as lecturers, teachers as tutors, school directors) perceive the benefits of structured computer literacy courses? (4) How do institutional contexts (senior homes vs home care) influence device ownership and ICT use?

Implicit hypotheses include: (a) Elderly ICT adoption in the Czech Republic is lower than in the United States and some EU countries; (b) Structured training (intergenerational courses) improves computer literacy and social connectivity; (c) Stakeholder expectations of benefits vary by role, with educators/directors more optimistic than seniors; (d) Institutional ICT provision and accessibility are key determinants of elderly ICT engagement. Support for these hypotheses would be evidenced by descriptive statistics showing low adoption rates, positive stakeholder perceptions of training benefits, and observed differences in ICT use across institutional contexts.
reference_methodology:
Design: Mixed-methods study combining a literature review with a local empirical investigation. The literature review synthesized official statistics (CZSO, Eurostat) and international studies on elderly ICT use, benefits, and training. The empirical component focused on the municipal project “Internet for Senior Citizens” in Hradec Kralove (November–December 2016) and field observations in senior homes and home care.

Participants and sampling: Four stakeholder groups were surveyed: (1) Senior citizens (“Students”) who completed one of three courses (Internet for beginners, Internet for advanced, Digital photography); (2) Primary school pupils (“Lecturers”) who taught the courses; (3) Teachers (“Tutors”) coordinating courses; and (4) School directors overseeing the project. Responses were obtained from all 12 directors, 15 tutors, 99 lecturers, and 82 seniors. Field observations included interviews/contact with residents in three senior homes (approximately 200 residents) and caregivers in home care contexts.

Procedures: The local program involved 12 primary schools offering free, 10-week computer literacy courses (1 hour/week) taught by lower secondary school pupils. Data collection included questionnaires, interviews, discussions, and a closing ceremony presentation. The survey instrument comprised four modified questionnaires tailored to each group, with some shared items. A key item asked stakeholders to identify perceived benefits of attending the course. An interview with a young lecturer provided qualitative context on intergenerational dynamics and expectations.

Measures and variables: The primary outcome was perceived benefits of the course, captured via multiple-choice options (e.g., improved computer literacy, social communication, advanced skills, gaining information across disciplines, meeting others with similar interests, medical information). Secondary variables included device ownership and ICT use patterns in senior homes and home care. International comparative data were drawn from national surveys and Eurostat.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics (counts and percentages) were reported for stakeholder perceptions and international comparisons. No inferential statistical tests, effect sizes, or confidence intervals were reported. The study did not specify demographic characteristics, randomization, or control groups. Ethical approvals, consent procedures, and data handling protocols were not described.

title: Metabolic Improvement via Enhancing Thermogenic Fat-Mediated Non-shivering Thermogenesis: From Rodents to Humans
research_question:
The review addresses the following questions: (1) How do human BAT anatomy, distribution, and physiology differ from rodent BAT, and what are the implications for translational research? (2) Which non-invasive methods most reliably quantify human BAT mass and activity, and what are their strengths and limitations? (3) Which pharmacological and natural interventions can safely and effectively enhance thermogenic fat-mediated NST in humans, and what are their metabolic effects? (4) What biomarkers correlate with human BAT activity and could serve as diagnostics? (5) How do cold exposure and pharmacological stimulation compare in activating human BAT and increasing whole-body energy expenditure?

Implicit hypotheses include: (a) Human BAT is anatomically and physiologically distinct from rodent BAT, necessitating species-specific therapeutic strategies; (b) Non-invasive imaging (18F-FDG PET/CT) and complementary modalities (MRI, IRT, calorimetry) can quantify BAT activity and guide interventions; (c) Pharmacological activation of β3-AR and A2A pathways can increase human BAT activity and energy expenditure, improving metabolic biomarkers and insulin sensitivity; (d) Biomarkers (e.g., miRNAs, lysophosphatidylcholine-acyl C16:0, FGF21) correlate with BAT activity and may enable non-invasive diagnostics. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include increased BAT activity and resting energy expenditure with mirabegron and adenosine, biomarker correlations, and cold-induced BAT activation. Outcomes refuting or nuancing them include the absence of weight loss despite metabolic improvements and cardiovascular side effects with β3-AR agonists.
reference_methodology:
As a narrative review, the article synthesizes findings from human imaging studies, clinical trials, and rodent mechanistic research. Key human methods include:

- 18F-FDG PET/CT: BAT is identified as 18F-FDG–avid adipose tissue with SUVmean ≥1.5. PET/CT provides anatomical localization and dynamic metabolic imaging of BAT activity. Limitations include radiation exposure and potential variability in analysis methods.

- MRI: Measures intracellular triglyceride depletion in BAT before and after activation, offering non-radiation assessment of BAT function. Sensitivity is lower than PET/CT, and modeling is complex.

- Infrared thermography (IRT): Measures anterior supraclavicular temperature, which correlates positively with energy expenditure and PET SUV. IRT is limited to superficial adipose tissue and lacks precise anatomical localization.

- Whole-body calorimetry: Quantifies total energy expenditure and, when paired with serum metabolites (HDL, triglycerides, fasting glucose, non-esterified fatty acids), provides insights into whole-body energy metabolism.

- Serum biomarkers: BAT-derived exosomal miR-92a and miR-122-5p are negatively correlated with BAT activity; lysophosphatidylcholine-acyl C16:0 and FGF21 are positively correlated. These markers may enable non-invasive diagnostics in larger cohorts.

Pharmacological interventions summarized include:

- β3-AR agonists (mirabegron, vibegron, ritobegron, solabegron): Repurposed from overactive bladder indications. Clinical trials report acute (2 days) and chronic (28 days) administration increases BAT activity (PET/CT) and resting energy expenditure in healthy humans, with improvements in HDL, ApoA1, non-esterified fatty acids, total bile acids, adiponectin, and insulin sensitivity. In obese/insulin-resistant individuals, chronic mirabegron improves glucose tolerance and induces WAT beiging, with improved β-cell function. Side effects include increased heart rate and systolic blood pressure.

- Adenosine and A2A receptor agonists (e.g., CGS21680): Exogenous adenosine increases human BAT activity more than cold exposure. Cold exposure reduces radioligand-detectable A2A receptor density via endogenous adenosine release.

- Other agents: PPARγ agonists (potential beige fat induction), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (positive correlation with BAT thermogenesis), thyroid hormone receptor agonists (beige fat induction and heat generation in rodents), and natural molecules (secretin, natriuretic peptides, bile acids, myokines, capsaicin). Human mechanisms remain unclear.

Ethical/IRB details are not reported for the review. No systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessments are described.

title: Breaking rotational symmetry in a trapped-ion quantum tunneling rotor
field_subfield: Physics — Quantum Information and Quantum Optics
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does flipping the spin state of a single ion in an N-ion QTR alter the quantum tunneling dynamics between Wigner crystal orientations? (2) How does an applied magnetic flux threading the QTR modulate tunneling probabilities via AB interference? (3) Can the QTR dynamics be mapped to continuous-time cyclic quantum walks on a 2N-site cycle graph?

Hypotheses: (H1) Flipping a single ion’s spin breaks the rotational symmetry of the QTR, making tunneling-induced rotations distinguishable and creating coupling between spin states and rotational motion. (H2) AB phases θAB introduce a relative phase between clockwise and counter-clockwise tunneling paths, enabling destructive interference at specific θAB (e.g., θAB = π/2) that suppresses tunneling. (H3) The QTR’s tunneling dynamics can be described as continuous-time cyclic quantum walks on a 2N-site cycle graph, with the |↑ ion acting as a quantum walker.

Predictions: If H1 holds, simulations with a flipped spin should show distinguishable rotational dynamics compared to the symmetric case and localized probability patterns at specific sites under certain θAB. If H2 holds, tunneling probabilities should exhibit minima at θAB = π/2 and other destructive-interference points. If H3 holds, probability distributions of the |↑ ion should evolve in a manner consistent with cyclic quantum walks on a 2N-site graph.
reference_methodology:
System and Hamiltonian: N ions of mass m and charge e are confined in a 2D harmonic trap with frequencies ωx and ωz (ωy frozen out). The total Hamiltonian is HTotal = Σ_i p_i^2/(2m) + V, with V = Σ_i m(ωx^2 x_i^2 + ωz^2 z_i^2)/2 + Σ_{i>j} e^2/(4πε0 r_ij). The trap is tuned so that ωz ≈ ωx to form a near-regular polygon crystal. The rotational mode frequency ωRot decreases as ωx is ramped down adiabatically (dωRot/dt ≪ ωRot), enabling ground-state cooling of the rotational mode.

QTR formation and cooling: The protocol first cools the rotational mode to its motional ground state at a higher ωx (where ωRot is large), then adiabatically ramps ωx downward to make ωx ≈ ωz. For a 3-ion QTR, ωz = 2π×1.500 MHz and ωx/ωz = 1.001 are used; for a 5-ion QTR, ωx/ωz = 1.010. The effective potential shows two stable orientations (|ψup, |ψdown) with overlapping wavefunctions, enabling tunneling. The QTR is modeled as a superposition |ψ = α|ψup + β|ψdown with |α|^2 + |β|^2 = 1. Including spin, the state is expanded over site- and spin-dependent basis states: |ψ = α Σ_n c_{2n−1} |ψup,2n−1 + β Σ_n c_{2n} |ψdown,2n, with normalization constraints on α, c_{2n−1}, c_{2n}, and γn.

Spin-flip scenario: Flipping the internal state of the ion at a specific site (e.g., site 2n−1 or 2n) introduces spin-dependent basis states |ψup,2n−1 and |ψdown,2n with one ion in |↑ and others in |↓. The Hamiltonian is expressed in terms of creation/annihilation operators ân for |↑ at site n: H = j Σ_n (â_n â_{n+1}^† + â_{n+1} â_n^†), with periodic boundary conditions â1 = â_{2N+1}. This maps the QTR to a 2N-site cycle graph with tunneling rate j.

Magnetic flux and AB interference: A magnetic flux Φ = S·B through the QTR introduces a vector potential coupling to the ions. The AB phase difference between clockwise and counter-clockwise paths is θAB = πΦ/Φ0 (Φ0 = h/e). The Hamiltonian becomes H = j (ĴCL e^{iθAB} + ĴCCL e^{−iθAB}), where ĴCL and ĴCCL are clockwise and counter-clockwise tunneling operators. For identical ions, rotational direction is indistinguishable; AB interference modulates tunneling probabilities.

Simulations and parameters: Numerical simulations compute time evolution of probability distributions for the |↑ ion on a 2N-site cycle graph. For the 3-ion QTR, the numerically calculated tunneling rate is 4.95 Hz. Time is normalized to the tunneling rate. Scenarios include θAB = 0, π/24, π/12, π/6. For the 5-ion QTR, the same framework applies with ωx/ωz = 1.010 and overlapping |ψup and |ψdown wavefunctions. The analysis assumes perfect ground-state cooling of the rotational mode; decoherence sources (rotational mode heating, RF fluctuations) are discussed qualitatively.

title: Cortical morphogenesis during embryonic development is regulated by miR-34c and miR-204
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which miRNAs are differentially expressed in the porcine cortex during the period of cortical folding (E60 to E80)? (2) Do these miRNAs target key migration-related genes, notably DCX and LIS1? (3) Do miR-34c and miR-204, which show extreme upregulation at E80, functionally regulate neuronal migration in vivo?

Hypotheses: (a) A subset of conserved miRNAs is sharply upregulated at the time of cortical folding and targets migration-related genes. (b) miR-34c and miR-204 directly target DCX 3′UTR sites and thereby modulate neuronal migration. (c) In vivo modulation of miR-34c and miR-204 will alter the distribution of migrating neurons across cortical layers, consistent with altered migration.

Predicted outcomes: If miR-34c and miR-204 regulate DCX, then miRNA mimics should reduce DCX 3′UTR reporter activity and miRNA inhibitors should increase it; mutating target sites should abolish effects. If these miRNAs control migration, IUE with mimics should reduce CP and increase IZ/SVZ populations, whereas inhibitors should have the opposite effect. Support for these predictions would substantiate the role of miR-34c and miR-204 in timing cortical morphogenesis.
reference_methodology:
Porcine cortex sampling and small RNA-seq: Embryonic pig brain samples (E60, E80) were snap-frozen and stored in RNAlater-ICE. Low molecular weight RNA (<200 nt) was purified (MirVana kit), DNase-treated (TURBO DNA-free). Libraries were prepared with TruSeq Small RNA kit (Illumina) using 100 ng RNA. Fifty bp single-end sequencing was performed. One replicate per timepoint. Raw reads were quality-filtered (fastX toolkit), adapter-trimmed (cutadapt), and mapped to mature porcine miRNAs (miRBase v21) using Bowtie. Expression was normalized to RPM.

Target prediction and global targeting analysis: Conserved predicted targets were obtained from TargetScan v7. Unique miRNA family target sites per gene were noted. The change in targeting from E60 to E80 was defined as the number of matching upregulated miRNA families minus downregulated families. Significance was assessed by randomization: 100,000 iterations of randomly selecting the same number of conserved miRNA families to compute p-values for each expressed TargetScan-indexed gene. Expression threshold for genes was ≥1 FPKM in embryonic cortex (Venø et al., 2015; GEO GSE71832).

In situ hybridization (ISH): Brain slices (10 or 5 µm) from porcine E60 and E80 were ISH-hybridized as previously described. Alkaline phosphatase-labeled probes: miR-204 (22 nt), miR-34c (23 nt), GAPDH mRNA (26 nt), DCX mRNA (28 nt). Specificity controls included 100× unlabeled probe excess, RNase A pre-treatment, and buffer-only controls; all were negative. Co-localization of miRNA with DCX mRNA was performed on adjacent sections hybridized with each probe, developed for equal times.

Luciferase reporter assays: DCX and LIS1 3′UTR fragments were PCR-amplified from HEK293-H cDNA and cloned into psiCHECK2. Constructs: DcxUp-3′UTR_WT (chrX:110543495–110543999, 505 bp; miR-34c site), DcxDown-3′UTR_WT (chrX:110537676–110538698, 1023 bp; miR-204 sites), Lis1-3′UTR_WT (chr17:2586883–2588130, 1248 bp; miR-15a sites). HEK293-H cells were co-transfected with miRNA mimics/inhibitors and psiCHECK2 reporters via calcium phosphate. Mutant reporters carried site-directed, ligase-independent mutations in target sites. After 24 h, Dual-Luciferase assays (Promega) were performed. Experiments were in biological triplicate; data normalized to controls and analyzed by independent sample t-tests.

In utero electroporation (IUE): Pregnant mice were anesthetized (isoflurane), uterine horns exposed, and 1.7 µl saline/Fast Green (0.3 mg/ml) containing 30 pmol RNA construct and 1.5 µg EGFP was microinjected into one lateral ventricle per embryo at E14.5. Electroporation used 5 pulses (30 V, 50 ms, 950 ms interval) with a tripolar electrode. Embryos were fixed at E17.5 (4% PFA/PBS), cryoprotected (30% sucrose), sectioned at 20 µm (coronal), immunostained with anti-GFP (1:1000), counterstained with DAPI, and imaged (Zeiss Axioskop A1). Migration was quantified using ImageJ’s automated cell counting across five regions (marginal zone, cortical plate, layer 5–6, intermediate zone, SVZ). Statistical analysis used independent sample t-tests (SPSS). Ethics approvals: Danish Experimental Animal Inspectorate (pigs) and Dutch/EU regulations (mice).

title: Effect of Carbon Nanotube-based Catalyst Layer Surface Roughness on Polymer Electrolyte Membrane Fuel Cell Performance
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does the surface roughness of a CNT-based CL at the interface with the PEM affect PEMFC performance? (2) Does a smoother CL–PEM interface reduce interfacial resistance and thereby improve power density? (3) Are electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) and other electrochemical parameters comparable between MEAs with different CL surface roughness?

Hypotheses: (H1) A smoother CL surface in contact with the PEM will reduce interfacial resistance (RΩ), leading to higher power density. (H2) ECSA will remain comparable between MEAs with different CL surface roughness, indicating that roughness differences do not limit proton accessibility at the Pt interface. (H3) EIS will show lower RΩ for the smoother interface and trends in Rct and Rmt consistent with ORR and water production effects.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if the smoother-interface MEA exhibits lower RΩ and higher power density than the rougher-interface MEA. H2 is supported if ECSA values are statistically similar. H3 is supported if EIS trends align with literature and the smoother interface shows lower RΩ.
reference_methodology:
Materials: H2PtCl6·6H2O, 2-propanol, N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc), ethylene glycol (EG), Nafion solution (5 wt% in lower aliphatic alcohol), Nafion 212 membranes, Milli-Q water (15 MΩ cm), Sigracet GDL-29BC, and commercial Pt/C gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs; EC-10-05-7). Multi-walled CNTs (CVD-grown, metal-catalyst-free) were provided by Nikkiso Co.

Catalyst preparation: CNTs were coated with polybenzimidazole (PBI; 23.4 wt% DMAc) to introduce anchoring sites for Pt. Pt was deposited from H2PtCl6·6H2O. TEM (JEM-2010, 120 kV) showed Pt nanoparticles with diameter 3.7 ± 1.3 nm homogeneously dispersed on CNTs. XPS (AXIS-ULTRA DLD) confirmed PBI (N 1s ~400 eV) and Pt (Pt 4f7/2 at 71.7 eV; Pt 4f5/2 at 74.9 eV). TGA (EXSTAR TG/DTA7300) quantified Pt loading as 37 wt% (residual at 900 °C). Free-standing CNT/PBI/Pt sheets were obtained by vacuum filtration of the dispersion through a PTFE filter membrane; Pt loading was 0.35 ± 0.025 mg cm^-2.

Ionomer incorporation: 1 cm × 1 cm CNT/PBI/Pt sheets were dipped in 1 wt% Nafion solution (5 mL) for 24 h at 25 °C, then vacuum-dried at room temperature for 2 h. Ionomer content was determined by TGA: heating 30–550 °C under N2 (water evaporation and Nafion decomposition), isothermal at 550 °C for 10 min, then 200–900 °C under air (CNT decomposition). The weight loss between 30–250 °C reflected water evaporation; 250–550 °C reflected Nafion decomposition.

MEA fabrication: Gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) were formed by hot-pressing the CNT/PBI/Pt sheets with Sigracet GDL-29BC at 132 °C, 0.6 MPa, 20 s. Two configurations were prepared: top-GDE (top surface of the sheet exposed to air during filtration) and bottom-GDE (bottom surface contacting the PTFE membrane). MEAs were assembled by sandwiching a Nafion 212 membrane between the cathode GDE (CNT-CL) and an anode commercial Pt/C GDE, hot-pressed at 132 °C, 0.6 MPa, 20 s. The resulting MEAs are denoted top-MEA (top surface contacting PEM) and bottom-MEA (bottom surface contacting PEM).

Electrochemical testing: Single-cell performance was measured per NEDO protocol using an in-house system (Auto PEM-ER01, TOYO). Activation: 20 h at 0.5 V, 75 °C, 100% RH H2 (0.139 L min^-1) and air (0.332 L min^-1). Polarization curves: galvanostatic scan at 20 mA s^-1 under 100% RH H2 (0.1 L min^-1) and air (0.2 L min^-1) at 80 °C. In situ CV: activation by 100 cycles from 0.05 to 0.9 V vs RHE at 50 mV s^-1, 40 °C, H2 anode and N2 cathode (0.1 L min^-1 each). Then, with cathode N2 stopped, three CV cycles (0.05–0.9 V vs RHE, 50 mV s^-1) were recorded; the hydrogen desorption peak of the third cycle was used to determine ECSA. EIS: frequency 0.1–10 kHz, sinusoidal amplitude 10% of applied current, at 0.1 and 1.0 A cm^-2, 100% RH, 80 °C. Equivalent circuit analysis separated ohmic (RΩ), charge transfer (Rct), and mass transport (Rmt) resistances (Figure S1).

title: Ultrathin Boron Growth onto Nanodiamond Surface via Electrophilic Boron Precursors
field_subfield: Materials Science — Nanomaterials and Surface Chemistry
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can alcohol-terminated HPHT nanodiamonds template covalent boron overlayers via nucleophilic attack by surface alcohols on electrophilic trigonal boron precursors at room temperature? (2) What bonding environments (trigonal vs tetrahedral boron, B–B, B–C, B–O) are formed on the ND surface? (3) Does the growth self-terminate, analogous to ALD, and what is the thickness of the boron layer? (4) How do different boron precursors (BCl3, BBr3, BH3) influence surface chemistry and morphology? (5) Are the resulting boron-diamond nanostructures dispersible in solvents relevant to biomedical applications?

Hypotheses: (H1) Alcohol-rich ND surfaces will react with BCl3, BBr3, and BH3 to form covalent boron overlayers at room temperature without catalysts. (H2) The growth will be self-terminating, limited by the number of alcohol sites, yielding ultrathin layers (≤1 nm). (H3) The resulting surface will exhibit trigonal and tetrahedral boron centers, with evidence of B–B and B–C bonding. (H4) BH3 will induce hydrogenation and boric acid-like termination, whereas BBr3/BCl3 will retain more trigonal boron character. (H5) ND-B samples will aggregate in DCM and disperse in various solvents, enabling potential BNCT or imaging applications.

Support/refutation: The data support H1–H5: microscopy shows electron-transparent layers; DRIFTS/XPS/XAS confirm B–O, B–B, B–C; thickness remains ≤1 nm over 1–24 h; BH3 shows hydrogenation and boric acid-like features; DLS indicates aggregation and dispersibility.
reference_methodology:
Materials: HPHT nanodiamond powders (30–50 nm; Microdiamant, USA). Reagents: anhydrous DCM (≥99.8%), BBr3 (≥99%), BCl3 (1.0 M in DCM), BH3 in THF, boron carbide (95%, 42 µm), 400 mesh Cu TEM grids with ultrathin Lacey carbon film, boron powder (95%), 4-inch Si wafers with 10 nm Ti/Cr adhesion and 100 nm Au, KBr (Spectra Tech). All water-sensitive syntheses were conducted in an inert nitrogen glovebox; glassware and consumables were dried (140°C, 24 h) or vacuum-dried (40°C, 24 h).

ND oxidation: ~500–600 mg ND placed in a ceramic boat in a three-zone tube furnace (Thermo Scientific STF55346COMC-1). Typical protocol: 10°C/min ramp to 525°C, hold 5 h in air to tan color, then dried at ~140°C to remove water, yielding alcohol-rich ND-OH.

Synthesis: In glovebox, 40 mg ND-OH in a 100 mL round-bottom flask was combined with 39.38 mL anhydrous DCM and 0.62 mL BBr3 (161 mM) or BCl3 (1.0 M in DCM). A cup-horn sonicator (Fisher Scientific FB505, 75% of 500 W) was used for 2 min, followed by bath sonication at 40°C for 10 min. The reaction was stirred at 300 rpm under inert conditions at room temperature for 1–24 h. BH3 reactions used BH3 in THF. Post-reaction workup: centrifugation (5,000 rpm, 25 min) to pellet ND-B; supernatant analyzed by UV–vis; pellet resolubilized in 10–15 mL DCM with vortexing and bath sonication; purification cycles repeated 3× in DCM; samples stored as powders or in solution under inert conditions.

Solubility/DLS: Purified ND-BCl3 powders (1 mg) were dispersed in octane, toluene, octadecene, chlorobenzene, and water (2–3 min bath sonication), then analyzed by DLS (Malvern Nano-S). Settings: material = diamond (n=2.418), dispersant octane→water, equilibration 10 s at 25°C, quartz cuvette, run duration 10 s, 10 runs, 3 measurements. Histograms were processed in Excel (custom macro) and analyzed in Igor Pro 8.0 with Gaussian fits (Multi-Peak Fit 2.0).

DRIFTS: Harrick Praying Mantis DRIFTS attachment (DRK-3) with high-temperature reaction chamber (Harrick #HVC-DRM-5) and Thermo Fisher FTIR 6700 (MCT/A detector). Backgrounds: 80 mg KBr ground and packed; 128 scans, 2 cm−1 resolution. Samples: 3–4 mg ND-OH/ND-Br/ND-NH2 mixed with 80–90 mg KBr; percent reflectance mode; Kubelka–Munk transformation with linear background corrections in Igor Pro.

XPS: Thermo Scientific K-Alpha Surface Analysis (Al Kα micro-focused monochromator; 180° double hemispherical analyzer; 128-channel detector). Low-resolution pass energy 200 eV; high-resolution 50 eV; step sizes 1.0 eV and 0.1 eV; acceptance angle 55°; survey 0–1350 eV (3 scans, 10 ms dwell). B1s high-resolution: linear background subtraction; Voigt fits (FWHM 1.5–2.0 eV). Quantification: CASA-XPS with VAMAS files; Tougaard backgrounds; RSF: B 1.0, C 1.8, O 2.93, Au 2.8. Samples were transferred under inert atmosphere to the Molecular Foundry.

XAS: SSRL beamlines 8-2 and 10-1 (SLAC). TEY mode; spot size <1 mm²; slits 42×42 µm (8-2), 40×40 µm (10-1), 30×30 µm; incident E-field 54.7°; UHV ~5×10−9 torr. Pre-edge background subtraction (B: 180–190 eV; C: 260–280 eV; O: 510–530 eV); post-edge normalization at 340 eV (C) and 580 eV (O). Energy calibration via diamond core-hole exciton at 289.0 eV and Ni L3 reference.

TEM/EDS: HRTEM and EDS on Au-coated Si wafers (10 nm Ti/Cr adhesion, 100 nm Au). Wafers cleaned (piranha, 90 mL H2SO4 + 10 mL H2O2, ~10 min at 80°C), rinsed with 18 MΩ water, dried with N2. ND solutions (1 mg/mL in DCM or water) drop-cast and dried (140°C, 60 min). EELS used to confirm diamond cores (supporting information).

title: ЕКСПЕРИМЕНТАЛЬНЕ ДОСЛІДЖЕННЯ ПРУЖНИХ ВЛАСТИВОСТЕЙ ОБЛИЧКУВАННЯ ТАМПОННОГО ЦИЛІНДРУ РОТАЦІЙНОГО ТАМПОДРУКАРСЬКОГО АПАРАТУ
research_question:
Research question: Can the nonlinear viscoelastic behavior of silicone rubber shells used in rotary pad printing be adequately captured by a power-law stress–strain model σ = Ey ε^n, and what are the corresponding material constants Ey (conditional modulus) and n (exponent) for representative samples of different hardness and dimensions?

Hypotheses: (1) The stress–strain relationship for silicone rubber shells under indentation will be nonlinear and increasing, consistent with σ = Ey ε^n. (2) The constants Ey and n will vary with material hardness and geometry, reflecting the viscoelastic nature of silicone rubber. (3) The method described in reference [3] for computing Ey and n from limited deformation measurements will yield values that closely match experimental stress–strain data, with small discrepancies attributable to measurement and modeling approximations. Support for these hypotheses would be demonstrated by: (a) monotonic, nonlinear force–deformation curves; (b) distinct Ey and n values across samples; and (c) close agreement between calculated and measured stresses at given relative deformations.
reference_methodology:
Design: Experimental indentation testing to characterize viscoelastic behavior of silicone rubber shells used in rotary pad printing. The study focuses on determining the power-law constants Ey and n for σ = Ey ε^n.

Materials and samples: Three silicone rubber samples were prepared with dimensions and hardness reflecting typical tampon shell geometries (Tampoprint catalog): (1) 50×50×50 mm, 10 Shore units; (2) 18×50×20 mm, 40 Shore units; (3) 50×50×23 mm, 52 Shore units. The hardness range (10–52 Shore) was selected to cover common applications for fragile substrates.

Apparatus and procedure: A circular pin indenter with 30 mm diameter was used to simulate contact with a plastic cap. Absolute deformation of the sample was measured using a dial indicator with 0.01 mm resolution. Applied force was measured using a compression dynamometer (DOSM-3-1, class 3), with the dynamometer and pin weights accounted for. For each sample, four measurements at different loads were performed at various points on the sample. The two extreme deformation values (maximum and minimum) were used to compute Ey and n following the method in reference [3]. Force–relative deformation curves were constructed using the relative deformation values corresponding to the maximum and minimum loads for each sample.

Analysis: The stress–strain relationship was modeled as σ = Ey ε^n, where σ is stress, ε is relative deformation, Ey is the conditional modulus, and n is the exponent. For each sample, Ey and n were determined from the measured force–deformation data using the procedure described in [3]. The authors evaluated the fit by comparing calculated stresses at a given relative deformation to the experimental values, noting small differences. No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or error propagation analyses were reported. No details on sample preparation (curing, temperature control), environmental conditions, or repeatability across multiple trials were provided.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable for materials testing.

title: ‫الزراعية‬ ‫للعلوم‬ ‫ات‬ ‫الفر‬ ‫مجلة‬ -8 ( 3 :) 111 -111 , ( 6112 )
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do foliar gibberellin (0, 150, 250, 350 mg L^-1) and ethephon (0, 100, 200, 300 mg L^-1) affect growth traits (plant height, branches per plant) and yield components (capsules per plant, seeds per capsule, 1000-seed weight) of rapeseed under field conditions? (2) What are the effects of these treatments on seed yield and oil percentage? (3) Are there significant interactions between GA and ethephon concentrations that further enhance growth or yield?

Hypotheses: (H1) GA and ethephon will increase vegetative growth (plant height, branches) and yield components relative to the control, with optimal concentrations differing by trait. (H2) GA and ethephon will increase seed yield and oil percentage. (H3) Certain GA–ethephon combinations will produce synergistic effects on growth traits. Outcomes supporting H1–H3 include statistically significant increases in measured traits at specific concentrations and significant interactions. Outcomes refuting them would include no significant differences versus control or negative effects on yield components.
reference_methodology:
Design and site: Field experiment conducted at the Experimental Field of the Department of Field Crops, College of Agriculture, University of Baghdad, during the 2009–2010 season. A factorial design with three replications in a randomized complete block design (RCBD) was used.

Treatments: Gibberellin (GA) at 0, 150, 250, 350 mg L^-1; ethephon at 0, 100, 200, 300 mg L^-1. Sprays were prepared in water at 5% concentration. The text indicates that the factorial combinations were evaluated, including specific interactions (e.g., GA 150 mg L^-1 × ethephon 100 mg L^-1).

Crop and management: Cultivar Pioneer Green. Sowing date: 28 November 2009. Row spacing: 40 cm. Seed rate: 0.6 g m^-2. Fertilization: 195 kg P2O5 ha^-1 (as DAP) and 48 kg N ha^-1, split into two applications (first at early growth, second at flowering start). No additional irrigation or pest/disease management details were reported.

Measurements: Traits included plant height (cm), number of branches per plant, number of capsules per plant, number of seeds per capsule, 1000-seed weight (g), seed yield (kg ha^-1), and oil percentage (%). Oil percentage was determined by Soxhlet extraction following AOAC procedures 30 days after the last spray. The text does not specify the exact timing of other measurements (e.g., post-spray intervals for height/branch counts), but it notes that height and branch counts were measured at the first appearance of the second leaf.

Statistical analysis: Data were analyzed using Genstat and Steel’s method (ANOVA). Significance was assessed at p < 0.05. The text references significant main effects and interactions (e.g., GA 150 mg L^-1 × ethephon 100 mg L^-1) but does not provide full ANOVA tables, effect sizes, or confidence intervals.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human or animal subjects were involved.

title: Editorial peer review: its development and rationale
field_subfield: Health Sciences — Biomedical Publication and Peer Review
research_question:
The article addresses three interrelated questions: (1) Why has editorial peer review become so widespread despite acknowledged inefficiencies, costs, and biases? (2) What empirical evidence exists regarding peer review’s reliability, fairness, and impact on manuscript quality and innovation? (3) How can electronic publication and open review practices improve transparency, accountability, and the ethical standards of peer review?

Implicit hypotheses include: (a) Peer review persists because it is perceived as a necessary quality assurance mechanism and a democratic process that distributes editorial responsibility; (b) Peer review’s effects on manuscript quality and readability are positive but uncertain, and its reliability is limited by heterogeneity of expertise and criteria; (c) Transparency (e.g., open identities, public comments) does not degrade review quality and may enhance accountability; and (d) Electronic platforms can accelerate and broaden post-publication review, improving the system’s utility. The article evaluates these propositions by synthesizing historical accounts, empirical studies (including randomized trials), and contemporary practice changes.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review/commentary synthesizing historical accounts, prior empirical studies, and contemporary practice changes in biomedical peer review. The author cites: (1) historical analyses (e.g., Kronick on 18th-century practices; Burnham on 19th–20th century evolution); (2) congress proceedings and research agendas (JAMA congresses in 1989, 1993, 1997, 2001); (3) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies on peer review processes; and (4) journal-level reforms and their evaluations.

Key empirical references include: (a) RCTs at JAMA and BMJ assessing blinding and open peer review. The BMJ validated a Review Quality Instrument (RQI) to measure review quality and conducted RCTs showing that blinding reviewers to author identity and revealing reviewer identities to authors did not affect review quality. The BMJ then introduced signed referee opinions, with no observed quality degradation. (b) JAMA RCTs found masking success varies widely by journal and is often low, with negligible effect on review quality; and reported no bias in favor of positive results. (c) Studies at Annals of Internal Medicine showed peer review and editing improved manuscript quality and readability. (d) A systematic review (Jefferson et al., 2002) concluded effects of peer review are uncertain. (e) Additional studies documented reviewer biases (e.g., overreliance on statistical significance, sample size, complexity) and publication biases (e.g., faster publication for statistically significant findings).

The article also references electronic publication initiatives: rapid online posting of letters (BMJ within 24 hours) and open review experiments (e.g., Behavioral & Brain Sciences, which publishes articles with up to 100 invited commentaries and author responses). It notes legal considerations in the United States regarding confidentiality of peer review and the cultural shift toward transparency.

No single protocol, preregistration, or comprehensive search strategy is reported. The review does not specify inclusion/exclusion criteria, data extraction methods, or risk-of-bias assessments. Ethical approvals are not applicable to this narrative synthesis.

title: Integrated Reporting Disclosure Level in Malaysian Public Universities: Signalling and Institutional Theories Perspective
field_subfield: Accounting — Public Sector and Integrated Reporting
research_question:
Research question: Do Malaysian Research Universities (RUs) disclose higher levels of Integrated Reporting (IR) content than non-RUs in their annual reports?

Hypothesis (H1): RUs provide higher IR disclosure levels than non-RUs. Rationale: Signalling theory predicts that organizations with superior performance and reputational aspirations will disclose more to signal quality and differentiate themselves. Institutional theory predicts that RUs, established with government expectations and resource dependence, face coercive, normative, and mimetic pressures to report in ways that legitimize performance and align with societal expectations. Outcomes supporting H1 include significantly higher mean IR scores for RUs across total disclosure and key content areas. Outcomes refuting H1 would show no significant differences or higher disclosure by non-RUs. The study also explores whether differences vary by content area (e.g., governance, value creation, performance), consistent with institutional isomorphism patterns.
reference_methodology:
Design: Quantitative content analysis of annual reports from Malaysian public universities (2016–2018). The study is exploratory and focuses on disclosure levels rather than causal effects.

Sample: 16 public universities were analyzed over three years (48 annual reports total). The sample excludes the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM), which is a corporation under the Companies Act 1965. The final analysis sample comprises 15 RUs and 33 non-RUs across 2016–2018 (5 RUs per year; 11 non-RUs per year). Annual reports were sourced from online repositories and personal requests to institutions.

Framework and coding: The IIRC (2013) framework’s eight content areas were used: (1) Organisational Overview and External Environment (OEE), (2) Governance (GVN), (3) Value Creation Model (VCM), (4) Risk and Opportunity (RO), (5) Strategy and Resource Allocation (SRA), (6) Performance (PM), (7) Outlook (OLK), and (8) Basis of Preparation and Presentation (BPP). Each content area includes seven items scored 0–3: 0=no disclosure; 1=descriptive disclosure without linkage to strategy/governance/performance/prospects; 2=descriptive disclosure linked to strategy/governance/performance/prospects with comparison to past; 3=descriptive disclosure linked to strategy/governance/performance/prospects with comparison to past, present, and future. Each content area thus has a maximum of 21 (7×3), and the total maximum score is 168 (8×21).

Coder reliability: Two coders independently assigned scores. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus. This procedure follows Potter and Lehvine-Donnerstein (1999) as cited in Moggi et al. (2019). The authors note that absolute scores may not be comparable across studies due to coder judgment, so comparisons are limited to trends and relative differences.

Statistical analysis: Normality was assessed via skewness and kurtosis; most variables were normal, except SRA. Group differences between RUs and non-RUs were tested using independent-samples t-tests (parametric) and Mann–Whitney U tests (nonparametric) for robustness. Reported statistics include means, standard deviations, t-statistics, p-values, and Z-statistics with p-values for the nonparametric tests. The analysis covers total IR scores and each content area.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. No human subjects beyond document analysis were involved.

title: Internal Tremors and Vibration Symptoms Among People with Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2: A narrative review of patient reports
research_question:
