Research question: What are the common domains and themes of patient-reported internal vibrations and tremors among people with PASC, and how do these symptoms manifest in terms of onset, timing, triggers/alleviators, comorbidities, medical encounters, and impact on daily life?

The study is exploratory and does not test formal hypotheses. It aims to (1) identify recurrent themes in patient narratives; (2) characterize symptom phenomenology (anatomic distribution, severity, timing, triggers); (3) document changes from baseline health status; (4) summarize experiences with the medical establishment (diagnostic workups, skepticism, treatments); and (5) quantify the prevalence of related terms in social media communications. Outcomes that would support the aims include consistent domains/themes across emails, convergent term frequencies in word clouds, and poll data indicating high prevalence of vibrations/buzzing and neuropathic pain. No causal hypotheses or mechanistic predictions are specified.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative narrative review of patient-reported experiences, supplemented by social media text analysis. The approach was modified to analyze data generated by patients in response to a call for information.

Setting and sample: Survivor Corps, a grassroots COVID-19 patient advocacy group with a Facebook group of approximately 180,000 members, solicited reports of vibrations/tremors among PASC members. The study sample comprises 140 de-identified emails and 450 Facebook comments from members who self-reported these symptoms. The group is a convenience sample; no demographic or infection status data were systematically collected. The study received exemption from the Yale IRB.

Data collection: Emails were collected between July 15 and July 27, 2021, via Facebook and a newsletter. Facebook comments were analyzed on July 16, 2021. Exact dates and names were removed and replaced with month/year and five-year age brackets to protect anonymity. No structured prompts beyond the initial call were used; no secondary follow-up was conducted.

Email analysis: Emails were analyzed using common qualitative coding techniques and the constant comparative method. An initial code list was developed by two team members (HMK, DM) after initial data review and refined by the full team for logic and breadth. Two team members independently coded all transcripts, then met in joint sessions to achieve consensus and assign codes via negotiated group process. Coded data were managed in nVIVO v12 to support theme identification, cross-linking, and retrieval of supporting quotations.

Facebook comments analysis: Given brevity and less narrative content, comments were analyzed via word clouds to visualize term prevalence. Two sets of comments were analyzed: (1) 288 comments responding to a post soliciting information on tremors/internal vibrations (July 14, 2021 post; comments analyzed July 16, 2021); (2) 162 comments responding to a poll titled “Vibration/Buzzing/Pain Poll” (posted June 27, 2021; analysis as of July 16, 2021). Comments were coded by a clinician analyst (CC) as reporting symptoms, unrelated, or possibly related; only symptom-related or possibly related comments were included. Word clouds were generated in R v4.0.3 using quanteda, wordcloud, and tm packages with minimum term frequency 3, maximum 200 words, and removal of extraneous filler words.

Ethics: The study received IRB exemption from Yale. Data were de-identified by removing exact dates and names and replacing with month/year and five-year age brackets.

title: Sick individuals, sick populations revisited: a test of the Rose hypothesis for type 2 diabetes disparities
research_question:
The study addresses three questions: (1) How much of the variance in T2D genetic risk (PRS) and socioenvironmental deprivation (TI/IMD) occurs within versus between UK ethnic groups (Asian, Black, White)? (2) Are PRS and TI associated with individual-level T2D risk after adjusting for age and sex? (3) Do PRS and TI mediate ethnic disparities in T2D prevalence?

Hypotheses derived from Rose’s framework predict: (a) Genetic risk factors will show greater within- than between-group variance and will be associated with individual T2D risk but not with ethnic disparities; (b) Socioenvironmental risk factors will show greater between- than within-group variance and will be associated with ethnic disparities but not with individual-level risk. The study evaluates these predictions using UKB data and mediation analysis. Outcomes supporting Rose’s framework would include: PRS showing strong individual-level associations but negligible mediation of ethnic disparities, and TI showing strong mediation of disparities but weak individual-level associations. Outcomes refuting the framework would include both PRS and TI showing significant individual-level associations and meaningful mediation of ethnic disparities despite within-group variance dominance.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Observational cohort analysis using the UK Biobank (UKB), a prospective cohort of >500,000 UK adults recruited 2006–2010 via 9.2 million invitations (~5.5% response). Inclusion: adults aged 40–69, capacity to consent, within 20–25 miles of one of 22 assessment centers (England, Scotland, Wales). Baseline data included questionnaires (sociodemographics) and blood samples for DNA. EHR linkage to NHS enables clinical outcomes. Data accessed via UKB Access Management System (application 65206).

Participants: The analytic cohort comprised 26,912 participants self-identified as Asian (n=9,372; 34.8%), Black (n=7,540; 28.0%), or White (n=10,000; 37.2%). White participants were randomly downsampled from >94% of UKB to 10,000; downsampling repeated 100 times to assess representativeness. Exclusions: participants lacking ICD-10 code data or excluded by phecode criteria. For analyses including PRS, TI, or IMD, participants with missing data were excluded (complete case analysis).

Outcome: T2D case status defined by NHS EHR ICD-10 codes mapped to phecode 250.2; controls excluded by phecodes 249–250.99. Unadjusted T2D prevalence computed as [cases/(cases+controls)]×100.

Exposures: Genetic risk quantified by PRS using 359 T2D-associated variants (p<5e-8) from the Type 2 Diabetes Knowledge Portal (meta-analysis of 382 GWAS). PRS computed as the weighted sum of effect alleles using PRSice-2 with clumping and thresholding; MAF threshold 0.1. Socioeconomic deprivation measured by TI (data-field 189) and IMD (data-field 26410), both assigned by postcode output area; lower scores indicate less deprivation.

Covariates: Age (data-field 21003) and sex (data-field 31) included in all models.

Statistical analysis: Conducted in R 4.2.1 with ggplot2 for visualization. ANOVA (method of moments) and t-tests (aov, t.test) partitioned within- versus between-group variance for PRS and TI. Multivariable logistic regression modeled T2D by ethnicity (White reference), PRS, and TI with age/sex covariates (glm, binomial family). Multiple mediation analysis used the mma package with T2D as outcome, ethnicity as predictor, PRS and TI as mediators, and age/sex as covariates; parameters: alpha=0.4, alpha2=0.4, n2=10. Complete case analysis (listwise deletion) applied to all analyses.

Ethics: UKB approvals from CHIAG (Scotland), PIAG (England/Wales), and North West MREC (project ID 299116). Written informed consent obtained. Data de-identified; no subject identifiers accessible to the study team. Not considered human subjects research under NIH Revised Common Rule.

title: SVARM-IQ: Efficient Approximation of Any-order Shapley Interactions through Stratification
field_subfield: Computer Science — Explainable AI (XAI) and cooperative game theory
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a stratified, sampling-based algorithm approximate any-order Shapley-based interaction indices (and more generally CIIs) with provable unbiasedness and tight non-asymptotic error bounds under a fixed budget? (2) Does such an approach deliver superior approximation quality (lower MSE, higher Prec@10) compared to state-of-the-art baselines (SHAP-IQ, permutation sampling) across diverse XAI tasks and indices? (3) Can the method be extended to approximate multiple indices and orders simultaneously without additional budget cost?

Hypotheses: (H1) A stratified representation of CIIs by coalition size yields unbiased stratum estimates and enables efficient, simultaneous updates for all interactions with one ν(A) call, leading to improved variance and MSE scaling with budget. (H2) SVARM-IQ will outperform permutation sampling and SHAP-IQ for SII/STI on LM, ViT, and CNN tasks, and will match or exceed kernel-based regression for FSI where applicable. (H3) The method will generalize to multiple indices and orders, including k=1 (SV), without extra budget. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include unbiasedness proofs, explicit variance/MSE bounds, and empirical MSE/Prec@10 improvements over baselines; refutation would involve biased estimates, weaker bounds, or inferior empirical performance.
reference_methodology:
Cooperative game setup: A cooperative game (N, ν) with player set N={1,…,n} and value function ν: 2^N→R. The Shapley value (SV) is defined via weighted marginal contributions. Discrete derivatives generalize marginal contributions to higher-order interactions: for K⊆N, Δ_K(S) = Σ_{W⊆K} (−1)^{|K|−|W|} ν(S∪W). The Shapley Interaction Index (SII) is a weighted average of discrete derivatives: I^SII_K = Σ_{S⊆N\K} [1/(n−|K|+1) C(n−|K|,|S|)] Δ_K(S). CIIs generalize SII as I_K = Σ_{S⊆N\K} λ_{k,|S|} Δ_K(S), where λ_{k,ℓ} are index-specific weights (e.g., SII, STI, FSI, Banzhaf).

Approximation problem: Given (N,ν), order k≥2, budget B∈N, and weights λ_{k,ℓ}, approximate all CIIs I_K for K∈N_k={S⊆N:|S|=k} using at most B evaluations of ν. Quality measures: MSE = E[(Î_K − I_K)^2] and (ε,δ)-approximation P(|Î_K − I_K| ≥ ε) ≤ δ.

Stratified representation: The authors decompose CIIs by coalition size, splitting discrete derivatives into strata: I_K = Σ_{ℓ=0}^{n−k} [C(n−k,ℓ) λ_{k,ℓ}] Σ_{W⊆K} (−1)^{k−|W|} I^{W}_{K,ℓ}, where I^{W}_{K,ℓ} = (1/C(n−k,ℓ)) Σ_{S⊆N\K, |S|=ℓ} ν(S∪W). Estimates are Î^{W}_{K,ℓ} = sample mean over coalitions S of size ℓ in N\K, and the final estimate aggregates strata: Î_K = Σ_{ℓ=0}^{n−k} [C(n−k,ℓ) λ_{k,ℓ}] Σ_{W⊆K} (−1)^{k−|W|} Î^{W}_{K,ℓ}.

SVARM-IQ algorithm: (1) Compute border sizes S_exp={0,…,s_exp, n−s_exp,…,n} and S_imp={s_exp+1,…,n−s_exp−1} using ComputeBorders (Algorithm 2), evaluating all coalitions of sizes in S_exp exactly. (2) WarmUp (Algorithm 3) initializes each implicit stratum Î^{W}_{K,ℓ} with one sample ν(A∪W) for A⊆N\K of size ℓ, ensuring at least one sample per stratum. (3) Sampling loop (Algorithm 1): draw size a_b∈S_imp from P_k (uniform over {2,…,n−2} for k≥3; tailored P_2 for k=2), draw A_b uniformly among coalitions of size a_b, store ν(A_b), and update all relevant strata via W=A_b∩K and ℓ=a_b−|W| using UpdateMean (Algorithm 4). (4) Aggregate to CIIs: Î_k = Σ_{ℓ=0}^{n−k} [C(n−k,ℓ) λ_{k,ℓ}] Σ_{W⊆K} (−1)^{k−|W|} Î^{W}_{K,ℓ}.

Theoretical analysis: Under n≥4 and sufficient budget, Lemma E.1 proves unbiasedness of all stratum estimates, implying unbiasedness of CIIs (Theorem 4.1). Lemma E.2 bounds the expected number of samples per stratum m^{W}_{K,ℓ} ≥ B/γ_k, where γ_k=2(n−1)^2 for k=2 and γ_k=n^{k−1}(n−k+1)^2 for k≥3. Lemma E.3 bounds E[1/m^{W}_{K,ℓ}] ≤ γ_k/B. Theorem 4.2 bounds variance V[Î_K] ≤ (γ_k/B) Σ_{W⊆K, ℓ∈L_k} [C(n−k,ℓ)^2 λ_{k,ℓ}^2 σ^2_{K,ℓ,W}], and Corollary 4.3 gives MSE ≤ (γ_k/B) Σ_{W⊆K, ℓ∈L_k} [C(n−k,ℓ)^2 λ_{k,ℓ}^2 σ^2_{K,ℓ,W}]. For k=2, the MSE simplifies to (2/B) Σ_{W⊆{i,j}, ℓ∈L_2} σ^2_{i,j,ℓ,W}. Corollary 4.4 and Theorem 4.5 provide (ε,δ) bounds using Chebyshev and Hoeffding inequalities, respectively.

Experiments: Tasks include (i) LM (DistilBERT fine-tuned on IMDB; token removal; n=14; output Y∈[−1,1]), (ii) ViT (ViT-32-384; patch clustering into 3×3 or 4×4 grids; token removal; n=9 or 16; Y∈[0,1]), (iii) CNN (ResNet18 on ImageNet; SLIC superpixels; n=14; Y∈[0,1]), and (iv) synthetic SOUM (ν(S)=Σ_{d=1}^D c_d 1_{S_d⊆S}; D=50; closed-form CIIs). Baselines: SHAP-IQ and permutation sampling for SII/STI; kernel-based regression for FSI. Ground truth is computed exhaustively (2^n) per run. Performance metrics: MSE and Prec@10 (ratio of top-10 highest absolute interactions correctly identified). Runs: LM (50 runs), ViT (30 runs for n=16; 20 runs for n=9), CNN (50 runs).

title: Medical Imaging in Nuclear Medicine: Evaluation of Total Variation Noise-Reduction Algorithm for PET/MR Images Using MR-AC Dixon-CAIPI and MR-AC Dixon-GRAPPA Pulse Sequences
research_question:
Research question: Does a total variation (TV) noise-reduction algorithm improve PET image quality (CNR and COV) in integrated PET/MR compared to conventional Wiener and median filters, and how does performance vary with MR-AC sequences (Dixon-CAIPI vs Dixon-GRAPPA)?

Hypotheses: (1) TV will increase CNR and decrease COV relative to noisy images and to Wiener/median filters, due to edge-preserving denoising. (2) MR-AC Dixon-CAIPI, with shorter acquisition times, will yield higher CNR than MR-AC Dixon-GRAPPA, potentially reducing motion-related artifacts. (3) TV will outperform Wiener and median filters in preserving contrast and reducing noise, with minimal edge blurring.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if CNR increases and COV decreases for TV vs noise and vs Wiener/median across both AC sequences. Hypothesis (2) is supported if MR-Dixon-CAIPI shows higher CNR than MR-Dixon-GRAPPA. Hypothesis (3) is supported if TV shows the largest CNR gains and COV reductions and visual inspection indicates superior edge preservation.
reference_methodology:
Design: Phantom-based evaluation of denoising algorithms on PET/MR images reconstructed with two MR-AC sequences (Dixon-CAIPI and Dixon-GRAPPA). The study simulates noise and compares TV against Wiener and median filters using CNR and COV metrics.

System and phantom: Integrated PET/MR system (mMR, Siemens, München, Germany) with lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) scintillator crystals and avalanche photodiode (APD) detector arrays. Phantom: Jaszczak phantom with rods of various diameters. Phantom fluid: NiSO4+NaCl to reduce MR artifacts compared to water, which can cause high relative permittivity artifacts above 1.5 T.

MR-AC sequences: MR-Dixon-CAIPI (accelerated with controlled aliasing in parallel imaging) and MR-Dixon-GRAPPA (accelerated with generalized autocalibrating partially parallel acquisition). The study notes that MR-AC Dixon-CAIPI has a shorter acquisition time (9 s/bed) than MR-AC Dixon-GRAPPA, potentially reducing motion artifacts in breath-hold scans.

Noise simulation: Gaussian noise with variance 0.001 was added to PET images using MATLAB to emulate degraded conditions. The exact PET acquisition parameters, reconstruction settings, and ROI definitions are not reported in the provided text.

Denoising algorithms: (1) TV denoising implemented as a Rudin–Osher–Fatemi (ROF) model with L1-norm gradient regularization and L2 fidelity term; regularization parameter λ = 0.1. (2) Wiener filter (spatial-domain). (3) Median filter (spatial-domain). The iterative solution procedure for TV is described conceptually; implementation details (e.g., number of iterations, stopping criteria) are not provided.

Quantification: CNR and COV were computed from ROIs. CNR = |Hs − HB| / sqrt(σs^2 + σB^2), where Hs and σs are mean and SD in the sphere ROI, and HB and σB are mean and SD in the background ROI. COV = σs / Hs. ROI placement and sphere sizes are not specified in the provided text. Reproducibility: experiments were repeated 10 times under identical conditions.

Ethics: Not applicable (phantom study).

title: Natural Polymorphisms in Mycobacterium tuberculosis Conferring Resistance to Delamanid in Drug-naïve Patients
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the prevalence of polymorphisms in F420 pathway genes (ddn, fgd1, fbiA, fbiB, fbiC, fbiD) among drug-naïve Mtb isolates from diverse settings? (2) Do specific natural polymorphisms, particularly Tyr29del in ddn, confer elevated delamanid MICs in drug-naïve patients? (3) How do lineage-associated polymorphisms (e.g., fgd1 Lys270Met) relate to delamanid MICs? (4) What is the clinical outcome associated with isolates harboring such polymorphisms?

Hypotheses: (a) A substantial fraction of drug-naïve Mtb isolates carry F420 pathway polymorphisms; (b) loss-of-function or catalytically disruptive mutations in ddn or its coenzymes increase delamanid MICs, with Tyr29del in ddn associated with critical MICs; (c) lineage-specific markers may modulate MICs variably, with some increasing MICs and others not; (d) elevated MICs may correlate with poorer clinical outcomes. Support would be evidenced by high prevalence of F420 pathway mutations, MICs exceeding the ECOFF (0.04 mg/L) in isolates with specific mutations, and clinical associations (e.g., mortality). Refutation would involve low prevalence of such mutations, lack of MIC elevation in carriers, or absence of clinical associations.
reference_methodology:
Design and participants: Multicentre observational study of Mtb isolates from patients living with HIV (PLWH) and HIV-negative TB patients, recruited between 2013–2016 in Peru (n=52), Thailand (n=14), Côte d'Ivoire (n=51), DRC (n=14), Kenya (n=1), and South Africa (n=1). All patients were delamanid-naïve. Demographic and clinical characteristics were collected as part of the IeDEA network.

Ethics: Approvals were obtained from the Cantonal Ethics Committee in Bern, Switzerland, and local institutional review boards. Written informed consent was obtained at all sites except South Africa, where consent was not required for archived samples.

Sequencing and variant calling: Mtb DNA was extracted and sequenced on Illumina HiSeq 2500. Reads were aligned to the H37Rv reference (NC_000962.3) using bowtie2 v2.3.5, BWA v0.7.17, or minimap2 v2.16. Variants were called with SAMtools v1.9. TBProfiler was used for gene-level analysis. Polymorphisms with variant frequencies ≥75% were considered putative resistance-conferring mutations in F420 pathway genes (ddn, fgd1, fbiA, fbiB, fbiC, fbiD).

Selection for MIC testing: Isolates with at least one F420 pathway mutation were re-cultured in liquid medium. Selection criteria included: (i) mutations in regions predicted to be catalytic or structurally important by ARIBA and PhyResSE; (ii) availability of culture; (iii) suitability for microdilution. Ten isolates met these criteria and underwent delamanid MIC determination.

MIC determination and interpretation: MICs were measured by microdilution. The study assumed 0.04 mg/L as the critical MIC threshold, consistent with prior reports and WHO guidance. Additional drugs tested for susceptibility included isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, moxifloxacin, and amikacin.

Data availability: WGS data for the strains in Table 1 are deposited in NCBI under PRJNA300846. Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figure 1 are referenced for mutation cataloging and MIC workflow.

title: Identification of Novel Smyd1 Inhibitors for Cardiovascular Disease Treatment through Molecular Modelling
research_question: Research questions: (1) Can a reliable human Smyd1 homology model be generated from the mouse Smyd1 structure (PDB 3N71) to support structure-based virtual screening? (2) Can pharmacophore models derived from known cofactor-pocket ligands (SFG) and substrate-pocket inhibitors (lly507) identify compounds that bind Smyd1 with stable poses? (3) Do selected compounds modulate Smyd1 methyltransferase activity in vitro? Hypotheses: (H1) A high-identity mouse template will yield a reliable human Smyd1 homology model suitable for docking and MD. (H2) A cofactor-pocket pharmacophore based on SFG will retrieve molecules engaging conserved interactions (e.g., HBD/His206, HBA/His135 and Asn205, AR/Phe272), while substrate-pocket pharmacophores based on lly507 will capture a core binding region (HBA/Thr183, PI/Tyr252, HYD/Phe139 and HYD/Ile177/Val195) and a hydrophobic subpocket. (H3) Compounds passing multi-criteria scoring and MD stability will show significant inhibition or modulation of Smyd1 activity in a methyltransferase assay. Support/refutation: H1 is supported by model quality metrics (GMEAN -1.11; 98.4% Ramachandran favored). H2 is supported by pharmacophore construction and docking/MD outcomes. H3 is supported by the identification of three compounds with significant assay effects (n=3, ANOVA; **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
reference_methodology:
Target and modeling: Human Smyd1 sequence (UniProt Q8NB12; 490 aa) was modeled using SWISS-MODEL with ProMod3 alignment. Template: mouse Smyd1 (PDB 3N71; 2.3 Å; 94.49% identity). Model quality: GMQE 0.97; GMEAN -1.11; Ramachandran plot: 98.361% residues in favored/allowed regions. NME/ACE caps were added in PyMOL 2.5.0 for MD stability.

Library and preprocessing: MolPort (~7.4M molecules, April 2021) was preprocessed with RDKit (salts/ions removed; additional steps not detailed).

Pharmacophore modeling: LigandScout 4.3.3 was used. Cofactor pocket: c-01 derived from SFG in PDB 3N71, capturing HBD (His206 backbone carbonyl), HBA (His135 imidazole and Asn205 backbone amide), and AR (Phe272). Substrate pocket: lly507 (Smyd2 inhibitor; PDB 4WUY) was docked into the Smyd1 homology model using OpenEye HYBRID, followed by LigandScout energy minimization to deepen a hydrophobic subpocket (Phe139, Glu143, Leu147 inward; Glu142–Lys268 H-bond) and stabilize the pose. Two pharmacophores were defined: s-01 (3 features: HBA/Thr183, PI/Tyr252, HYD/Phe139 and HYD/Ile177/Val195) and s-02 (4 features: s-01 plus HYD/Phe139).

Docking and scoring: OpenEye HYBRID docking used SFG (cofactor) and lly507 (substrate) as templates. Docked poses were scored with Chemgauss4. For substrate-pocket poses, LigandScout energy minimization and binding affinity scoring were performed, followed by unaligned pharmacophore score calculation (without re-alignment) to ensure pose–pharmacophore consistency.

MD simulations: OpenMM 7.7.0 with Amber14SB (protein), OpenFF 1.2.0 (ligand), TIP3P water, PME electrostatics (1 nm cutoff), 300 K, 1 bar, 2 fs timestep. Total 105 ns (first 5 ns equilibration excluded). RMSD was computed to assess pose stability.

In vitro methyltransferase assay: Promega MTase-Glo kit. Recombinant Smyd1 (0.5 µg/100 µl) in reaction buffer (20 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 3 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mg/mL BSA, 1 mM DTT). Substrate: biotinylated Histone H3 (21–44) peptide (10 µM) and SAM (10 µM) in reaction buffer (40 mM Tris pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 6 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mg/mL BSA, 2 mM DTT). Test compounds at 100 µM; SFG at 100 µM; DMSO control. After 30 min incubation, MTase-Glo reagent and detection solution were added; luminescence (RLU) measured after 30 min. Negative control: enzyme without substrate; positive control: enzyme + substrate or DMSO. n=3; one-way ANOVA; GraphPad Prism; data shown as mean ± SD; significance thresholds indicated (**p<0.01, ***p<0.001).

title: The cerebellum is an active participant of sleep: oscillatory interactions with neocortex and thalamus during natural sleep in non-human primates
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do M1 and cerebellar oscillations exhibit coordinated sleep-stage-specific dynamics during natural sleep in non-human primates? (2) What is the directionality of cerebro-cerebellar interactions at slow-wave and spindle frequencies? (3) Does the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway mediate spindle-frequency communication? (4) Can a simple coupled-oscillator model explain observed phase–amplitude relationships between M1 and cerebellar spindle-band oscillations?

Hypotheses: (H1) M1 and cerebellar LFPs and spiking will show reciprocal slow-wave and spindle-band modulations aligned with the sleep cycle. (H2) Directionality will reverse with frequency: neocortex→cerebellum during SWS and cerebellum→neocortex during non-SWS spindles. (H3) Spindle-band communication will traverse the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway, with cerebellum leading thalamus and thalamus leading M1. (H4) A two-oscillator coupled model will better explain phase–amplitude relationships than reduced models (single-source or uncoupled). Outcomes supporting H1–H4 include significant coherence in both bands, frequency-dependent directed coherence, consistent cross-correlation lags across regions, and superior cross-validated fit and phase–amplitude reproduction by the full coupled model.
reference_methodology:
Subjects: Four female rhesus macaques (O: 11 y/o, 8.2 kg; U: 7 y/o, 7.7 kg; T: 10 y/o, 7.8 kg; Y: 6 y/o, 6.9 kg), housed in pairs. Procedures approved by the Animal Welfare Ethical Review Board and licensed by the UK Home Office under the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 (2013 revision).

Electrode implantation: Under sevoflurane anesthesia with postoperative analgesics/antibiotics, animals received head casings and combinations of fixed linear microelectrode arrays (LMAs; 16-channel, 12.5 μm platinum-iridium, 500 kΩ) and individually moveable flexible microwires (50 μm Teflon-insulated tungsten, 200 kΩ). Targets: M1 (hand area; anterior bank of central sulcus, 16 mm lateral to midline), cerebellar lobule IV/V (7 mm lateral from MRI), and contralateral VPL thalamus (in T and Y). For chronic M1, two LMAs (16 electrodes/shank, 0.5 mm spacing) and 12 microwires were implanted. For cerebellar spike recording (U, T), an LMA was attached to a 16-gauge guide-needle with 8 preloaded microwires; intraoperative LMA recordings verified tentorium penetration. For VPL verification (T, Y), antidromic responses were used.

Home-cage recording: A custom battery-powered data logger (two INTAN RHD2132 bioamplifiers; STM32 F407 microcontroller; 32GB microSD) enabled untethered recording. Spike channels: typically 5 M1 and 2 cerebellar microwires (0.1 Hz–7.5 kHz, 20 kHz sampling). LFP channels: LMAs (M1: 16 channels; cerebellum: 16 channels; thalamus: every other 8/16 channels; 0.1 Hz–300 Hz, 1 kHz sampling). Sessions began daily with fresh battery and SD card, capturing ~20 h of behavior and sleep.

Dataset: 145 LFP sessions (O: 48; U: 63; T: 29; Y: 5). M1 LFPs referenced to a local tungsten wire over dura; cerebellar LFPs referenced to the most superficial contact below the tentorium. Thalamic LFPs (T, Y) from deepest LMA contact (VPL) referenced to the overlying white matter; differential recordings used adjacent VPL contacts (1.2 mm separation). Spike discrimination: high-pass 300 Hz, PCA clustering. Spike counts: 265 M1 neurons (U: 235; T: 30) and 113 cerebellar neurons (U: 96; T: 17). Simultaneous spike pairs: 493 (U: 426; T: 67).

Preprocessing: MATLAB. Butterworth 4-pole filters (forward/reverse). LFP down-sampled to 250 Hz after anti-aliasing. Sleep start/end visually demarcated from M1 LFP spectrograms (512-sample Hanning, 50% overlap), validated with video (monkey O). Sleep phase: low-frequency (<1 Hz) power envelope low-pass filtered (2.7 cycles/hour) and Hilbert-transformed to yield continuous circular phase. Sleep phase binned into 10 equal bins for cycle-aligned analyses. SWS identified via circular mean phase in 30 s windows (−π/2→0→π/2: high <1 Hz power; outside: non-SWS). Non-SWS subdivided into nSWSs (with spindles) and nSWSns (without spindles) based on spindle presence in 30 s windows.

REM/arousal classification: Derived from prior dataset (monkey U; 33 sessions) using M1 spike firing and EMG: REM windows had spike rates > mean waking and EMG < 2 μV; arousal windows had spike and EMG ≥ mean waking. High-gamma (50–125 Hz) LFP power was elevated in both states. A high-gamma threshold (1.13× mean) was selected by averaging thresholds from ROC-derived points (closest to top-left corner; intersection with negative diagonal; Youden’s index). This threshold yielded REM/arousal proportions comparable to prior primate reports.

Spindle detection: Visual identification followed AASM criteria. Automated detection (method of [0010]) applied to 9–16 Hz band-pass filtered M1 LFP (analytic signal magnitude), with start-end threshold at +1 SD and detection threshold at +3 SD; events required >0.5 s and <2 s duration and peak magnitude exceeding detection threshold; adjacent events within 1 s merged. Windows with >5 SD 20–30 Hz power were removed to ensure spectral specificity. For dynamical modeling, a 7–15 Hz band was used to capture observed peaks.

Coherence and directed coherence: Spike events binned to 250 Hz. LFP–LFP, spike–LFP, and spike–spike coherence computed as |Pij(f)|^2/(Pii(f)Pjj(f)) using non-overlapping 512-point windows. 95th percentile significance threshold S = 1 − 0.05^(1/(N−1)). Directed coherence via bivariate autoregressive spectral Granger causality: LFP down-sampled to 83.3 Hz; model order 171; transfer matrix H(f) inverted; normalized directed coherence DirCoh_i←j(f) = |H_ij(f)H_ij*(f)C_jj| / |H_ij(f)H_ij*(f)C_jj + H_ii(f)H_ii*(f)C_ii|. Directionality assessed by paired t-tests across sessions. Time-reversed LFPs served as a control.

Spike metrics: Peak-to-peak spike width, mean firing frequency, irregularity index (Irregularity = (1/(N−1)) Σ|ln(I_i/I_{i−1})|).

Dynamical systems analysis: Hilbert-transformed 7–15 Hz LFPs yielded instantaneous phase difference binned from −π to +π. Amplitude and amplitude derivative were averaged per bin. A two-oscillator linear model with complex dynamics matrix (A_M1, A_Cb, A_M1→Cb, A_Cb→M1) and white-noise inputs (two real variances, one complex covariance) was fit by regressing real/imaginary components against one-sample shifts. Reduced models included: common-input single oscillator; uncoupled oscillators; one-direction coupling. Cross-validation (10-fold) assessed mean-squared residuals; Pearson R quantified phase–amplitude reproduction.

title: A New Analytical Method for Determination of Cathepsin L Based on the Surface Plasmon Resonance Imaging Biosensor
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can an SPRI biosensor using RKLLW-NH2 immobilized via ODM provide a selective, sensitive, and precise method for CTSL quantification in plasma? (2) What are the optimal inhibitor surface density and assay pH for maximizing CTSL binding and signal? (3) Does the method achieve a linear response range suitable for clinical quantification and meet LOD/LOQ targets? (4) Is the method selective against common plasma proteins and proteases? (5) Do SPRI results correlate with ELISA in human plasma samples?

Hypotheses: (a) Hydrophobic immobilization of RKLLW-NH2 on ODM will enable specific CTSL binding detectable by SPRI with a linear response over a clinically relevant range. (b) Assay conditions can be optimized to maximize signal (e.g., pH near CTSL’s activity optimum). (c) The method will achieve sub-ng/mL sensitivity (LOD/LOQ) and acceptable precision. (d) The assay will be selective against albumin and other proteases at high excess. (e) SPRI measurements will correlate strongly with ELISA in plasma. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include a defined linear range with saturation beyond it, LOD/LOQ values in the pg/mL range, precision within acceptable limits, negligible interference up to 10,000-fold excess, and Pearson r near 1 when compared to ELISA.
reference_methodology:
Biosensor fabrication and immobilization: Gold chips were prepared with a photopolymer and hydrophobic paint as described previously. A 20 mM ODM ethanolic solution was used to form a linker monolayer by immersing chips for ≥24 h at room temperature, followed by rinsing with ethanol and water and drying under argon. RKLLW-NH2 (Arg-Lys-Leu-Leu-Trp-NH2) was immobilized via hydrophobic interactions with ODM. For inhibitor concentration optimization, 2 µL of nine RKLLW-NH2 solutions (1.0–100.0 ng/mL) were applied to each of nine active spots on ODM-modified chips, incubated 24 h at 37°C, washed twice with HBS-ES buffer and ≥10 times with distilled water, and then exposed to 10.00 ng/mL CTSL in acetate buffer (pH 4.5) for 10 min at room temperature. SPRI measurements were taken immediately after preparation.

Assay pH optimization: Eight CTSL solutions (10 ng/mL) in buffers spanning pH 2.20–7.40 were applied to chips with ODM and RKLLW-NH2 (30.00 ng/mL) for 10 min. SPRI responses were measured in 12 repetitions per pH. The pH with maximal signal was selected for subsequent measurements.

Standard curve: CTSL standards (0.5–50.0 ng/mL) at pH 4.5 were applied to ODM/RKLLW-NH2 chips for 10 min, with 12 repetitions per concentration. The linear range was defined by the non-saturating portion of the curve; saturation was observed above 15.00 ng/mL.

Selectivity testing: Mixtures containing constant CTSL (8.00 ng/mL) with interferents (human albumin, MMP-1, MMP-2, cathepsins B, D, E, G) at 1:1 to 1:10,000 concentration ratios were applied to the biosensor. SPRI responses were measured to assess interference.

Precision: Precision was evaluated at 0.50, 5.00, and 15.00 ng/mL CTSL with 36 repetitions per concentration (pH 4.5; RKLLW-NH2 30 ng/mL).

Sample collection and processing: Plasma was collected from healthy donors (EDTA anticoagulant) and patients (ovarian tumor/cyst or gallbladder resection) at the L. Zamenhof Children’s Clinical Hospital (Bialystok, Poland). Two mL of whole blood was centrifuged (1000×g) for >15 min, filtered three times to separate plasma, frozen, and stored at −70°C. All subjects provided informed consent; the study adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical University of Bialystok (R-I-002/63/2013).

SPRI measurement and image processing: SPRI images were acquired at an angle maximizing contrast between background and active sites. Two images were captured: (1) with immobilized RKLLW-NH2 and (2) after CTSL interaction. The SPRI signal was computed by subtracting intensities and integrating contrast across pixels within each spot, then integrating over the spot area. ImageJ v1.32 was used for 2D image evaluation and digitization (A.U.). Non-specific binding was monitored by blank spots (no receptor), buffer-only spots (pH 4.5), and buffer application to some spots.

SEM characterization: A Phenom ProX SEM (CeB6 source, backscattered electron detector, 10 kV, 5000× magnification) was used to confirm layer formation (gold, ODM, RKLLW-NH2, immobilized CTSL).

title: Zamansal Evrişimli Ağlarla Siber Saldırı Tespiti: Karşılaştırmalı Bir Analiz
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does TCN perform on network intrusion detection compared to LSTM and FCN across binary classification, multi-class detection, and anomaly detection tasks on KDD99? (2) Does TCN achieve competitive or superior performance relative to classical machine learning baselines? (3) How do models perform on rare attack classes (R2L, U2R) that are underrepresented in KDD99?

Hypotheses: (H1) TCN will match or exceed LSTM in temporal sequence modeling tasks due to causal convolutions and dilation, potentially improving efficiency and performance. (H2) TCN will perform competitively with FCN on binary classification, leveraging temporal context where FCN’s independence assumption is suboptimal. (H3) TCN will be competitive with classical ML baselines on KDD99, except for decision tables. (H4) Performance on rare classes (R2L, U2R) will be constrained by class imbalance, requiring more training examples.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if TCN’s F1 is at least comparable to LSTM; H2 is supported if TCN’s F1 is close to FCN’s; H3 is supported if TCN’s metrics are within the range of classical ML baselines; H4 is supported if R2L/U2R detection rates are lower than for more frequent classes.
reference_methodology:
Dataset: KDD Cup 99 (KDD99), a labeled intrusion detection dataset derived from a simulated U.S. Air Force network. It contains 41 features, including connection duration, protocol type, service, flags, and counts of failed attempts, among others. The dataset includes four attack categories: DoS (Denial of Service), Probe (information gathering), R2L (Remote-to-Local), and U2R (User-to-Root). KDD99 comprises 38 continuous/binary and 3 categorical features; categorical features are one-hot encoded. Numerical features are normalized to [0,1]. The training set includes 494,019 examples with class distribution: 19.69% normal, 79.24% DoS, 0.83% Probe, 0.23% R2L, and 0.01% U2R.

Preprocessing and sampling: To mitigate class imbalance, temporal stratified sampling is applied: 2,000 examples per class are selected while preserving temporal connections; R2L and U2R are included fully due to their small counts. The test set is the standard KDD99 test split.

Tasks: (1) Binary classification (normal vs attack), (2) Multi-class detection (DoS, Probe, R2L, U2R), and (3) Anomaly detection using autoencoders trained on normal data only. For anomaly detection, sliding windows of length 64 are used; reconstruction error thresholds are determined using statistics from normal validation data (mean, standard deviation, etc.), and sequences with errors exceeding the threshold are flagged as anomalies.

Models and training: FCN, LSTM, and TCN are implemented. FCN uses Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.001, three hidden layers with 32–64–32 neurons, and ReLU activations. LSTM uses Adam, learning rate 0.001, two hidden layers with 32–20 neurons, and truncated BPTT (tBPTT) of 64 steps. TCN uses Adam, learning rate 0.0001–0.001, 64 filters, 4 kernels, dilation 1, ReLU, and sequence length 64. Autoencoders (AE) employ a 3-layer encoder (300–200–75) and a 3-layer decoder (75–200–300), with a 10-neuron latent representation; Adam optimizer is used. Hyperparameters are tuned via grid search; the best configurations are reported in tables.

Evaluation metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 are reported. For binary classification, metrics are computed over normal vs attack labels. For multi-class detection, per-class detection rates are reported. For anomaly detection, reconstruction error thresholds are set on normal validation data and evaluated on test data.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported.

title: Research Progress in the Prevention and Treatment of Perinatal Venous Thromboembolism and Nursing Care
research_question: The review addresses two primary questions: (1) What are the current best practices for preventing and treating VTE in the perinatal period, including nursing care strategies and pharmacologic management? (2) What gaps exist in evidence, particularly regarding early activity protocols and evaluation scales, and what future research is needed? The article does not test explicit hypotheses; rather, it synthesizes existing data to inform clinical practice and identify research priorities. It posits that improved early activity data and standardized evaluation scales are necessary to optimize prevention, and that prospective studies are required to determine optimal anticoagulation dosing and duration. Outcomes that would support these priorities include validated activity effectiveness scales demonstrating improved thromboprophylaxis outcomes and prospective trials comparing anticoagulation regimens with clear endpoints (e.g., VTE incidence, bleeding, maternal/fetal safety).
reference_methodology: This is a narrative review focused on perinatal VTE prevention and treatment, integrating clinical observations, nursing protocols, and pharmacologic management. The text cites multiple Chinese clinical studies and guidelines, including risk stratification, early mobilization, and anticoagulation protocols, as well as international references on point-of-care ultrasound and cancer-associated VTE. No systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessment is reported. The review does not describe statistical synthesis, meta-analysis, or predefined endpoints. Ethical approvals are not applicable as no new human or animal subjects were studied. The article provides practical, context-specific guidance for nursing care (e.g., positioning, activity schedules, dietary recommendations) and pharmacologic management (LMWH/UFH dosing, timing around delivery, warfarin transition, IVCF use). It also references management of thrombophilia in the peripartum period and the role of neuraxial anesthesia timing relative to anticoagulation. The absence of detailed methodological reporting (e.g., databases searched, time frame, selection criteria) limits reproducibility of the review process. The quantitative data presented derive from cited studies and case series, with small sample sizes (e.g., n=20 in a thrombolysis case series) and limited prospective evidence in China.

title: Seroepidemiological Study of Epstein-Barr Virus in Different Population Groups in Croatia
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the seroprevalence of EBV VCA IgG in the Croatian general population by age and sex? (2) How does EBV seroprevalence differ among clinical groups (MS, hemodialysis, heart transplant recipients, hematological malignancies, Crohn’s disease) compared with the general adult population? (3) What is the prevalence of EBV VCA IgM and the proportion of recent primary infections versus reactivation across age groups, as inferred by IgG avidity? (4) Are age and sex associated with EBV seropositivity?

Hypotheses: (a) EBV seroprevalence increases with age, reflecting cumulative exposure and primary infections in childhood/adolescence. (b) Female sex is associated with higher EBV seroprevalence. (c) High-risk clinical groups (MS, hemodialysis, transplant recipients) exhibit higher EBV seroprevalence than the general adult population. (d) IgM positivity in older adults predominantly reflects reactivation rather than primary infection, as indicated by high IgG avidity.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypotheses are supported if age shows a monotonic increase in IgG seropositivity (P < 0.05), female sex shows higher IgG seroprevalence (P < 0.05), high-risk groups show higher IgG seroprevalence than general adults (P < 0.05), and IgM-positive older adults have high avidity. Logistic regression AORs and 95% CIs quantify associations.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Cross-sectional seroepidemiological study conducted over 2015–2016 at two large Croatian institutions: University Hospital Centre Zagreb and the Croatian National Institute of Public Health. Samples were collected from Croatian residents residing in all counties.

Participants: 2,022 consecutive serum samples were tested. Demographics: 1,104 males (54.6%) and 918 females (45.4%), ages 1–84 years. Inclusion criteria were routine clinical testing for hemodialysis, hematologic check-ups, preoperative evaluations for cardiac and renal transplant programs, elevated liver transaminases, lymphatic disorders, neurological disorders (including multiple sclerosis), and Crohn’s disease. No exclusion criteria beyond routine testing are reported. Sampling frame and recruitment procedures are not described.

Laboratory assays: EBV VCA IgM and IgG were measured using commercial assays. The VIDAS ELFA (bioMérieux, Marcy l’Étoile, France) thresholds were: EBV IgM ≤0.11 negative; 0.12–0.18 equivocal; ≥0.19 positive. EBV VCA IgG ≤0.09 negative; 0.10–0.20 equivocal; ≥0.21 positive. The Virotech ELISA (Sekisui Virotech, Rüsselsheim, Germany) thresholds were: EBV VCA IgM and IgG <9 VE negative; 9–11 VE equivocal; >11 VE positive. IgM/IgG-positive samples underwent IgG avidity testing using Euroimmun ELISA (Lübeck, Germany). The avidity index (AI) was calculated from extinction values with and without urea treatment and expressed as a percentage. Interpretation: AI <40% = low avidity (acute primary infection); 40–60% = borderline (recent post-acute infection); >60% = high avidity (past infection). Assay calibration, inter-laboratory validation, and blinding are not reported.

Statistical analysis: Frequencies are reported with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests. Associations between dependent and independent variables were evaluated via logistic regression, reporting crude odds ratios (OR) and age/gender-adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% CIs. Software: STATA/IC v11.2 (StataCorp, USA). Significance threshold: α = 0.05. No details on handling of missing data, multiple testing correction, or model diagnostics are provided.

Ethics: The text does not report ethics approval, consent procedures, or data privacy measures.

title: Understanding THCV: A Review of Therapeutic Potential for Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
field_subfield: Pharmacology — Endocannabinoid System and Metabolic Disorders
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Does THCV, as a non-psychoactive CB1 antagonist/reverse agonist, improve metabolic parameters (body weight, adiposity, glycemia, insulin sensitivity, lipid profile) in obesity and T2D models? (2) Are THCV’s effects mediated via CB1 antagonism and/or interactions with TRPV1 and other receptors? (3) Does THCV mitigate THC’s psychoactive effects in humans? (4) Are THCV’s benefits associated with fewer psychiatric or anxiogenic adverse effects compared with rimonabant?

Implied hypotheses: (a) THCV will reduce food intake and body fat and improve glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in rodent models of obesity; (b) THCV will lower fasting glucose and improve β-cell function in T2D patients without psychoactive effects; (c) THCV will attenuate THC-induced psychotic and memory impairments in humans; (d) THCV’s metabolic benefits will be CB1-dependent, with additional contributions from TRPV1 modulation. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significant reductions in body fat and liver triglycerides, improved OGTT and fasting glucose, increased insulin sensitivity, and improved HOMA2 β-cell function in animals and humans, alongside blunting of THC’s psychoactive effects. Mixed or null glycemic outcomes would nuance or challenge the hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review. The authors conducted an electronic literature search of peer-reviewed articles published from January 1, 1970, to September 30, 2019. Inclusion criteria were based on relevance to THCV, THC, Cannabis sativa, obesity, body weight, metabolism, and diabetes. Specific databases, search strings, screening procedures, inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond topic keywords, and risk-of-bias assessments were not reported. No PRISMA flow diagram or quantitative synthesis was provided.

Preclinical studies summarized include: (1) DIO and GO mouse models (n=4 per group) treated with THCV orally at 0.3–12.5 mg/kg twice daily for 30 days (DIO) or 0.1–12.5 mg/kg once daily for 45 days (GO), with pilot dosing at 0.3–3 mg/kg once daily and a full range at 0.1–12.5 mg/kg once daily for 30 days in obese mice. THCV was diluted in sesame oil. A positive control CB1 inverse agonist AM251 was administered orally at 10 mg/kg once daily or 5 mg/kg twice daily. Outcomes included body weight, food and water intake, body fat content, fasting glucose, OGTT, insulin sensitivity, and liver triglycerides. (2) Zucker rats treated with rimonabant (CB1 antagonist) to assess lipid profiles (triglycerides, free fatty acids, total cholesterol, HDL/LDL ratio). (3) CB1 knockout mice to test CB1 dependence of anti-obesity effects. (4) Rodent studies of THCV’s interaction with CB1 and CB2, including dose-dependent antagonism/agonism of synthetic analogs (O-4394, O-4395) and THC-induced antinociception/hypothermia reversal.

Human studies summarized include: (1) A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group pilot in 62 non-insulin-treated T2D patients (HbA1c <10%) randomized to THCV 5 mg twice daily, CBD 100 mg twice daily, THCV:CBD 5:5 mg twice daily, THCV:CBD 100:5 mg twice daily, or placebo for 13 weeks. Outcomes included fasting glucose, HOMA2 β-cell function, adiponectin, ApoA, and HDL. (2) A placebo-controlled, double-blind, crossover pilot in 10 cannabis users (<25 uses/occasion) receiving 10 mg THCV for 5 days followed by 1 mg IV THC on day 5, assessing THC’s psychoactive and memory effects.

No details on randomization procedures, blinding implementation, statistical analysis plans, or ethics approvals for the summarized studies were provided in the review text.

title: Factors Associated with Re-Displacement after Nonsurgical Treatment of Distal Radius Fractures in Adults: A Retrospective Study
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which factors influence re-displacement after closed reduction and external fixation of adult distal radius fractures? (2) How do pre-reduction and immediate post-reduction radiographic parameters correlate with re-displacement? (3) What is the relationship between age and re-displacement? (4) How does AO/OTA type relate to re-displacement risk? (5) Can predictive thresholds be established for age and UV to inform prognosis and management?

Hypotheses: (a) Older age is associated with higher re-displacement risk due to osteoporosis and reduced healing capacity. (b) Higher AO/OTA complexity (B3, C1–C3) confers greater instability and higher re-displacement rates than A2. (c) Greater UV at pre- and immediate post-reduction predicts re-displacement. (d) Palmar tilt, RI, and RL changes are associated with re-displacement. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include significant associations in univariate and multivariable analyses, graded risk by AO/OTA type, and ROC-derived cutoffs with acceptable sensitivity/specificity. Null findings would include non-significant associations or lack of predictive value for UV.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Retrospective cohort study at the Reduction Room of the Orthopedics and Traumatology Department, Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine, Tianjin Hospital. Ethics approval: Medical Ethics Committee of Tianjin Hospital (2023YLS077).

Participants: Adults (≥18 years) with closed distal radius fractures (within 3 cm of distal articular surface) treated nonoperatively between July 2019 and December 2022. Inclusion: AO/OTA types A2, A3, B3, C1–C3; closed manipulative reduction with external fixation using plaster and/or splint; complete radiographic data at pre-reduction, immediate post-reduction, and 6–8 weeks; final radiograph showing blurred fracture line with continuous callus across the fracture line (clinical healing criteria). Exclusion: pathologic fractures; prior fracture or congenital deformity on the injured side; concurrent fractures elsewhere. B1/B2 AO/OTA types were excluded due to small numbers.

Sample characteristics: 884 patients (167 male, 717 female), age 18–92 years (mean 62.68 ± 11.73). Laterality: 498 left, 386 right. AO/OTA distribution: A2 (n=99), A3 (n=219), B3 (n=50), C1 (n=199), C2 (n=289), C3 (n=27). Fixation: plaster alone (n=418) or plaster combined with splint (n=466).

Interventions and follow-up: Closed reduction followed by external fixation. Plaster fixation immobilized the wrist in palmar flexion (or dorsal extension) with ulnar deviation for 4–6 weeks, extending no further than the elbow or metacarpophalangeal joint. Plaster combined with splint fixation used paper compresses along the fracture line and a splint with outer plaster; at 4 weeks, plaster was removed, leaving the splint. Follow-up radiographs at 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, 4 weeks, and 6 weeks to adjust position/tightness and monitor adjacent joint function.

Radiographic measurements: Digimizer v5.7.5 (MedCalc) measured UV, RL, PT, RI. UV: AP view, two lines perpendicular to the radius long axis through the ulnar distal articular surface and the ulnar margin of the distal radial articular surface; distance between lines. RL: AP view, two lines perpendicular to the radius long axis through the ulnar distal articular surface and the distal radial styloid; distance between lines. PT: lateral view, angle between lines connecting palmar/dorsal edges of the radius and a line perpendicular to the radius long axis. RI: AP view, angle between a line from the distal radial styloid to the ulnar point on the distal articular surface and a line perpendicular to the radius long axis.

Outcomes: Re-displacement at final examination defined by UV >3 mm, PT >20°, dorsal tilt >10°, or RI <15°. Patients with severe swelling/skin compromise could not meet guideline “acceptable standards” but were included if they met patient-acceptable reduction criteria after discussion.

Statistical analysis: SPSS v27. Dependent variable: re-displacement. Univariate analyses: one-way ANOVA for continuous variables; χ² for categorical variables; independent-samples t-test for normally distributed continuous variables; non-parametric tests for non-normal data. Variables with p < 0.05 entered binary logistic regression. ROC curves assessed predictive performance of age, pre-reduction UV, and immediate UV; optimal cutoffs determined by Youden index.

title: A smartphone ocular alignment measurement app in school screening for strabismus
research_question:
Primary research question: Is a smartphone app implementing a photographic Hirschberg test feasible for use by school nurses during routine vision screenings to detect strabismus, and what is the user experience? Secondary question: What threshold for the app’s measured deviation optimizes sensitivity and specificity for detecting strabismus when PACT is the ground truth?

Hypotheses: (1) The app will achieve high measurement success rates with minimal training, enabling routine use by school nurses. (2) The app’s measured deviations will correlate with PACT, supporting its validity. (3) An optimal threshold exists that balances sensitivity and specificity for screening; the app will outperform conventional acuity/stereopsis screening in identifying intermittent strabismus. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include ≥90% success rates, strong correlation with PACT (high R²), and ROC-derived thresholds with acceptable sensitivity/specificity. Outcomes refuting them would include low success rates, poor correlation, or thresholds with poor sensitivity/specificity.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional evaluation conducted at an elementary school (Norwell, MA) from November 2017 to January 2018. IRB approval was obtained from the William G. Vinal School; procedures adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from one parent per child.

Participants: 520 students in grades 1–5 were offered participation; 133 consented and were included. Age, gender, and race were not recorded in app data; iris color was documented from cropped images (55 dark [41.4%], 78 light [58.6%]).

Stage 1 (school screening and app capture): The school nurse performed standard screening: visual acuity with tumbling E at 10 ft., near acuity with OPTEC 2000, and stereopsis testing. For consenting children, the nurse captured three consecutive images per child using EyeTurn v1.0 on an iPhone 7. Children sat ~40 cm from the phone, fixated the camera lens, and the app displayed two purple boxes to guide positioning and minimize head tilt. The nurse used snapshot mode; video mode (cover/uncover) was not used. Overhead fluorescent lights were on. Glasses were removed (17 children required glasses for refractive correction). A successful measurement required correct detection of iris borders and corneal reflections. The app automatically cropped images to the eye region.

Stage 2 (image review and flagging): An ophthalmologist (WC), masked to gender, age, and ocular history, reviewed de-identified images offsite. Measurements with incorrect feature detection (iris border or corneal reflection) were rejected for analysis but documented. A flagging threshold of 2.4Δ was applied based on the app’s RMSE from prior evaluation, below AAPOS’s 8Δ referral criterion. This threshold aimed to minimize false negatives due to random noise (≈1% probability for AAPOS-positive cases) while acknowledging potential misses if errors were systematic.

Stage 3 (in-person evaluation): Identified students underwent unilateral cover test (to detect tropia) and PACT at near by a pediatric ophthalmologist (WC) and optometrist (KH), masked to app values. PACT used prism bars (Bernell) with base opposite the deviation; deviation was recorded when refixation movements were extinguished. Ground truth required intermittent or constant tropia with PACT >8Δ. Extraocular motility and near point of convergence (NPC) were also assessed. The examiners were aware that app measurements exceeded 2.4Δ but were masked to app values during testing.

Statistical analysis: Analyses used SPSS v23 and STATA v14.2. ROC analysis determined the optimal threshold for sensitivity/specificity with PACT as ground truth; PPV and NPV were also calculated. Pearson’s correlation coefficients assessed linear relationships. Random-effects multiple logistic regression evaluated failure types (eye closing, eye detection failure, iris misfitting, corneal reflection misfitting) as outcomes with iris color (light/dark) and class order (testing sequence) as covariates. Significance threshold was p<0.05.

title: Solar and stellar activity cycles
field_subfield: Astrophysics — Solar and Stellar Physics (Dynamo Theory, Activity Cycles)
research_question:
Central questions: (1) How do stellar cycle periods and amplitudes depend on rotation rate and convection-zone depth, and can these relations discriminate between interface and flux-transport dynamos? (2) Does the activity–rotation relation R_HK ∼ Ro^{-1} imply an increase in dynamo energy with rotation, or can it be explained by surface manifestations and storage constraints? (3) What roles do meridional flow and tachocline properties play in setting cycle periods and amplitudes? (4) How do energetics (differential rotation power, Reynolds stress saturation, potential energy conversion) constrain plausible dynamo scalings?

Hypotheses: (H1) Cycle periods scale with Rossby number P_cyc ∼ Ro^n (n ≈ 1.25–2), with dispersion reflecting convection-depth effects and meridional flow structure. (H2) Activity–rotation scaling R_HK ∼ Ro^{-1} arises from surface manifestations (e.g., longer active-region lifetimes, mixed polarities) rather than a direct increase in dynamo energy with rotation. (H3) Flux-transport/Babcock-Leighton models with meridional flow u_m ∼ Ω can reproduce observed period scaling, while interface models with steep α/ΔΩ scalings are less consistent with differential rotation observations. (H4) Energetics constraints (Q_RS ≈ 0.01 L; Lorentz feedback) limit toroidal field growth and necessitate storage or alternative energy sources (e.g., flux-tube explosions) for faster rotators. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include consistent scaling laws, model fits to observed relations, and energetics analyses showing saturation limits; refutation would involve inconsistent scalings or model fits requiring implausible parameter scalings.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review synthesizing observational datasets and theoretical models. Key datasets include: (1) Mt. Wilson H&K survey (≈110 stars, K–F), which established the prevalence of cyclic behavior (≈40% cyclic; ≈20% with well-determined cycles), period ranges (2.5–25 years), and the activity–rotation relation R_HK ∼ Ro^{-1} with saturation near Ro ≈ 0.3; (2) SSS (Lowell Observatory; since 1994) continuing Mt. Wilson monitoring; (3) CASLEO (Argentina; since 2000) covering M5–F6 to better separate convection-depth effects; (4) SMARTS (southern survey targeting asteroseismic targets). The review also references differential rotation measurements (e.g., Reiners 2006) and theoretical models (interface dynamos, flux-transport/Babcock-Leighton, mean-field energetics with Lorentz feedback).

Analytical approaches summarized: (a) Period–rotation analyses using Rossby number Ro = P_rot/τ_c, with scaling fits P_cyc ∼ Ro^n and two-branch separation; (b) Cycle amplitude scaling A_cyc = ΔR_HK/R_HK ∼ (ω_cyc/Ω)^γ with γ ≈ 0.66 (low activity) and 0.85 (high activity); (c) Differential rotation scaling ΔΩ ∼ Ω^0.7 and max shear near P_rot ≈ 3 days; (d) Energetics estimates: Q_RS ≈ 0.01 L for the Sun; magnetic energy E ≈ (1/4) R Φ B for Φ = 10^24–10^25 Mx and B ≈ 10 kG, implying energy demands over ≈10-year cycles; (e) Storage constraints: geometric storage at the convection-zone base requires B ≳ 10^6 G to avoid geometric limits if Φ ∼ Ω^2.

No new experiments, simulations, or statistical tests are reported in this review. Ethical approvals are not applicable. The review emphasizes the need for asteroseismology to determine convection-zone base location, rotation inclination, and differential rotation, and for broader spectral surveys to disentangle rotation and convection-depth effects.

title: Fingerprints of intrinsic phase separation: magnetically doped two-dimensional electron gas
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can intrinsic phase separation driven by Mn-induced ferromagnetism in a clean 2DEG produce distinct transport fingerprints that differentiate it from disorder-driven inhomogeneity? (2) What are the temperature, magnetic field, and density dependencies of resistivity in the IPS regime, and how do they compare to experimental observations in Mn-doped CdTe quantum wells? (3) How do AFM superexchange and finite temperature modify the IPS phase diagram and activation energy?

Hypotheses: (i) In the IPS regime, the activation energy E_g is density-independent because the chemical potential μ and local carrier density in FM domains are pinned at critical values; thus, resistivity will show strong temperature and magnetic-field dependence but very weak density dependence. (ii) Finite temperature induces re-entrant IPS (Pomeranchuk-like), producing a resistivity maximum on the metallic side of the MIT. (iii) An external magnetic field reduces the IPS region and lowers E_g, yielding negative magnetoresistance. (iv) The Mn-doped CdTe 2DEG system, with minimized disorder and Mn neither donor nor acceptor, will exhibit these IPS fingerprints, providing experimental support for the mechanism.

Support/refutation criteria: Agreement with experimental data on density-independent activation energy, temperature-dependent resistivity maxima, and negative magnetoresistance within the IPS region would support the hypotheses; deviations or disorder-dominated signatures would refute them.
reference_methodology:
System and model: The study considers a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) doped with magnetic ions (Mn), modeled as a lattice of classical spins S_i (Mn local moments) interacting with conduction electrons via s–d exchange J_sd and with each other via AFM superexchange J_ex. The conduction electrons are spin-polarized in the FM phase (J_sd → ∞ limit), with θ_ij = arccos(S_i·S_j) the angle between neighboring Mn spins. Long-range Coulomb interactions H_Coul prevent global phase separation while allowing local inhomogeneity. Weak disorder scattering H_imp is included, similar to conventional 2DEGs.

Ground-state IPS condition: At T=0 and J_ex = 0, the ground state is fully FM, maximizing conduction-electron kinetic energy. For J_ex > 0, at infinitesimal doping the FM energy gain is insufficient to overcome AFM superexchange, leading to IPS between FM carrier-rich domains and PM carrier-poor regions. The IPS condition is obtained by equating the grand thermodynamic potentials of FM and PM phases, Ω_FM = Ω_PM. In the FM phase, Ω_FM depends on the density of states ρ(ω) and half-bandwidth D; in the PM phase, Ω_PM = 0. IPS emerges when n < n_c, with n_c determined by this equality. Within IPS, n_FM = n_c and μ_FM = μ_c are pinned, making E_g = E_c − μ density-independent.

Finite-temperature analysis: The finite-T phase diagram is computed using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), which maps the lattice model to a single-site impurity problem with self-consistency. The local effective action involves Grassmann fields c_i(τ) and includes the s–d exchange and superexchange terms. The self-consistency defines the cavity field Δ_i(τ, τ′, S) and uses a semi-circular bare density of states ρ_0(ω) = (1/πD)√(D^2 − ω^2). The DMFT equations relate local Green’s functions G_av(iω_n) = ⟨c†(iω_n)c(iω_n)⟩ and G_m(iω_n) = ⟨S c†(iω_n)c(iω_m)⟩ to the magnetization m = ⟨S⟩. Ising spins (S = ±1) are used; Heisenberg spins yield only minor quantitative differences. Sommerfeld expansions provide analytic leading-order T-dependence: Ω_FM(T) ≈ Ω_FM(0) + O(T^2) and Ω_PM(T) ≈ −k_B T ln 2 + O(T^2), implying a T^2 correction to n_c(T) and a critical superexchange J_c_ex ≈ 0.025D (with C ≈ 0.88) above which IPS is suppressed.

Transport modeling: Phase-resistivities ρ_FM(n, T) and ρ_PM(n, T) are obtained from DMFT solutions, accounting for scattering off Mn spins in each phase. Weak impurity scattering is modeled as ρ_imp(n, T) ≈ ρ_o exp{−An} + C, fitted to high-temperature experimental data with ρ_o = 3600ρ_Mott, A = 850, and C = 0.2ρ_Mott. The net resistivity in the IPS regime is computed via an effective-medium approximation for percolation: ρ(n, T) = ρ_med(ρ_FM, ρ_PM) + ρ_imp. The percolation threshold is determined by the volume fraction x of FM domains, with x increasing as n increases until metallic transport sets in.

Magnetic field effects: An external magnetic field h reduces the IPS region by favoring FM alignment and lowers the activation energy E_g, producing negative magnetoresistance. The phase diagram and transport under h are analyzed to quantify the reduction of the IPS dome and the decrease of E_g with h.

Experimental comparison: The model’s predictions are compared to recent experiments on Mn-doped CdTe quantum wells, which exhibit low-density metallic behavior, strong temperature and magnetic-field dependence of resistivity, and CMR-like negative magnetoresistance. The analysis focuses on qualitative agreement and the presence of density-independent activation energy in the IPS regime.

title: Characterization of the focused beam from a 10-Hz desktop capillary-discharge 46.9-nm laser
field_subfield: Physics — XUV/X-ray lasers and laser-matter interaction
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the key focused-beam parameters (divergence, focus position, Rayleigh parameter, and focal spot size) of a desktop capillary-discharge 46.9-nm laser when focused by a spherical Sc/Si multilayer mirror? (2) How does the annular (TEM01*) beam profile manifest in ablation-induced craters in PMMA, and can crater area measurements be used to infer beam characteristics? (3) What are the dominant mechanisms of radiation-induced erosion under multi-shot irradiation below the single-shot damage threshold? (4) Does the beam exhibit sufficient coherence to produce LIPSS on the crater surface?

Hypotheses/predictions: (i) The CDL beam will exhibit an annular transverse intensity profile with measurable divergence and a well-defined focus; (ii) Eroded area versus longitudinal position will follow a Gaussian-like dependence with a minimum at the focus, enabling extraction of z_c and z0; (iii) Eroded area versus accumulated shots will scale linearly at low intensities, consistent with desorption-dominated removal, allowing determination of single-shot crater area S0 and pedestal area S1; (iv) The presence of LIPSS will indicate partial coherence in both transverse and longitudinal directions. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include: confirmation of annular profile and divergence; a Gaussian fit to eroded area vs z yielding z_c and z0; a linear fit to eroded area vs shots yielding S0 and S1; and observation of periodic surface structures consistent with LIPSS.
reference_methodology:
Laser source and operation: The capillary-discharge Ne-like Ar laser (CDL) lases on the 1P1 (2p1/2 3s1/2) J=1 to 1S0 (2p1/2 3p1/2) J=0 transition in Ar8+ ions. The capillary is filled with Ar at 50 Pa. Pre-ionization is achieved with a lower-current pulse, followed by a fast current pulse (~21 kA peak) generated by discharging low-inductance ceramic capacitors through a pressurized synthetic air spark gap. The Rogowski coil monitors discharge current. The pinch effect compresses the plasma column, creating high density and temperature on axis and a convex electron density profile that refracts amplified radiation into an annular intensity distribution. The beam exits through a pinhole in the cathode into a high-vacuum sector (~1 mPa) connected to the interaction chamber. Typical operation: pulse energy >10 μJ, pulse width ~1.5 ns (FWHM), repetition rate 5 Hz (up to 12 Hz), shot-to-shot stability reported as very good.

Beam imaging and temporal diagnostics: A phosphor-coated hybrid CCD camera placed 134 cm from the output aperture images the far-field beam. A 400 nm Al foil blocks incoherent radiation. The annular profile is measured, with a peak-to-peak diameter ~6 mm. Divergence is computed from this diameter. A vacuum photodiode with an Al photocathode measures pulse duration; the Rogowski coil measures discharge current. The temporal profiles (Fig. 5) yield a 1.5 ns FWHM pulse duration.

Focusing optics and sample: A spherical Sc/Si multilayer mirror with focal length 0.25 m and incidence angle ~6° focuses the beam onto a 500 nm PMMA layer spin-coated on a Si substrate (Silson, UK). The focusing geometry is illustrated in Fig. 6. The sample is translated along the beam axis to map eroded area versus position.

Ablation and microscopy: PMMA samples are irradiated with accumulated shots (15 shots per position in longitudinal scans; shot number varied in separate scans). Nomarski (DIC) microscopy provides crater pedestal areas; AFM in tapping mode provides crater depth and surface morphology. The authors assume linear accumulation of crater depth with shot number at low intensities and linear proportionality between single-shot crater area and transverse intensity, consistent with desorption-dominated removal.

Data analysis: The annular intensity profile is modeled as a TEM01* distribution I(r) = I0 exp[−2(r/r_foc)²] with r_foc the halfwidth of the focused beam. For crater area analysis, the annular tails are approximated by a Gaussian I(r) ~ exp[−2(r/r0)²] to avoid solving a transcendental equation involving the Lambert W function. Eroded area SI(z) versus longitudinal position z is fit to a Gaussian-like function with parameters z_c (focus position), z0 (Rayleigh parameter), and SI(0) (minimum eroded area at focus). Eroded area SI(N) versus accumulated shots N is fit to SI(N) = S0 + S1 ln(2N), where S0 is the single-shot crater area and S1 is a pedestal parameter reflecting microscope sensitivity. Fits yield z_c, z0, SI(0), S0, S1, and the ratio 2S1/S0. The ratio is checked for constancy across z to validate the model assumptions.

title: Robust antibody levels in both diabetic and non-diabetic individuals after BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccination
research_question:
Primary research question: Do adults with T2DM mount lower humoral responses (IgG and neutralizing antibodies) to BNT162b2 compared with non-diabetics? Secondary questions: Are obesity (BMI categories) and hypertension associated with differences in humoral responses? Do prior COVID-19 infection, age, gender, and time since second dose influence titers? What is the trajectory of antibody levels over time?

Hypotheses: (1) T2DM is associated with lower vaccine-induced IgG and neutralizing titers relative to non-diabetics due to immune dysregulation in metabolic conditions. (2) Obesity and hypertension are not significantly associated with humoral responses after adjustment. (3) Prior infection increases titers due to memory B-cell responses. (4) Antibody levels decline over time since vaccination; age is inversely associated with titers. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include statistically significant adjusted differences in IgG and neutralizing titers by T2DM status, non-significant effects of BMI and hypertension, positive associations for prior infection, and negative associations for age with titers.
reference_methodology:
Design and ethics: Observational cohort study approved by the Ethical Review Committee of Dasman Diabetes Institute (Protocol # RA HM-2021-008) and the Kuwait Ministry of Health (reference 3799; protocol 1729/2021), in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and US Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects.

Participants: Adults who completed two doses of BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) and were ≥3 weeks post-second dose. Exclusions: autoimmune diseases, immunosuppressants, arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and pregnancy. T2DM status was self-reported. Data collection via REDCap included age, gender, comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension), height/weight (BMI), and prior COVID-19 infection. BMI categories: <25 kg/m² (normal), 25–30 kg/m² (overweight), >30 kg/m² (obese). Cohort size: N=262 (non-diabetics N=181; T2DM N=81). Hypertension: normotensive N=193; hypertensive N=69. BMI: <25 N=65; 25–30 N=117; >30 N=74 (6 missing). Gender: female N=126; male N=136. Age: overall mean 49.7±15.1 years; non-diabetics 45.4±14.3; T2DM 59.4±12.0. Duration since second dose: overall mean 83.4±37.2 days; non-diabetics 84.3±37.1; T2DM 81.5±37.4.

Specimen collection and processing: Venous blood collected in EDTA tubes; plasma isolated by centrifugation at 400×g for 10 min at room temperature; aliquots stored at −80°C until assay.

Assays: IgG ELISA (SERION ELISA agile SARS-CoV-2 IgG; SERION Diagnostics, Würzburg, Germany) per manufacturer instructions. Samples thawed, clarified (10,000×g, 5 min, 4°C), diluted 100× in kit diluent, incubated 60 min at 37°C, washed 4×, incubated with antibody-specific enzyme conjugate 30 min at 37°C, washed 4×, incubated with TMB substrate 30 min at 37°C, stopped with stop solution, read OD at 405 nm (Synergy H5). Interpretation: <21 BAU/mL negative; 21.0–31.5 BAU/mL borderline; >31.5 BAU/mL positive.

Neutralizing antibodies: Surrogate virus neutralization test (sVNT; SARS-Cov-2 sVNT kit, GenScript, USA). Clarified plasma and controls diluted 1:1 with HRP-conjugated RBD; incubated 30 min at 37°C; 100 μL transferred to wells, incubated 15 min at 37°C; washed 4×; TMB added, incubated 15 min at 37°C; stop solution added; OD at 450 nm (Synergy H5). Inhibition (%) = (1 − ODsample/ODnegative control) × 100. Positive if >20% inhibition.

Statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics (mean, SD, median, IQR). Primary models: generalized additive linear models with IgG and neutralizing antibodies as outcomes; predictors: T2DM (yes/no), hypertension (yes/no), BMI (categorical: <25, 25–30, >30 kg/m²), age, gender, prior COVID-19 infection (yes/no), comorbidity score (sum of heart disease, stroke, COPD, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease, bleeding disorders, other chronic diseases), and duration since second dose. Penalized splines modeled non-linear effects of age and duration (REML estimation). Effect estimates reported as adjusted mean differences with 95% CIs. Post-hoc interaction analyses tested diabetes × age, gender, BMI, hypertension on IgG. Analyses in R 3.3.1 using mgcv for GAMs; p<0.05 considered significant.

title: Adaptive control for a class of nonlinear systems with time-varying delays in state and input
field_subfield: Control Engineering — Adaptive Control and Time-Delay Systems
research_question:
Research question: Can one design an adaptive state-feedback controller that guarantees Lyapunov stability and asymptotic convergence of the original state to zero for uncertain nonlinear systems with time-varying delays in both state and input, when the nonlinear uncertainties are bounded by unknown weighted norms of state and delayed-state vectors?

Hypothesis: If there exist positive definite matrices P, Q1, Q2, a matrix Y, and scalars ε > 0, d > 0 satisfying a specific LMI (Σ11 Σ12; Σ22 < 0), then the adaptive controller u(t) = K x(t) + μ In x(t) with adaptive laws for μ and θ will render the closed-loop system globally Lyapunov stable at (x, μ, θ) = 0 and ensure x(t) → 0 as t → ∞ for all initial conditions. The LMI condition is independent of delay magnitudes but requires the delay derivative bound 0 < d < 1. The adaptive factor μ and parameter θ are designed to counteract unknown bounds on nonlinear uncertainties, enabling asymptotic stabilization even when these bounds are arbitrarily large.

Support/refutation criteria: The hypothesis is supported if the LMI is feasible and the Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional derivative is negative definite under the controller and adaptive laws, and if simulations demonstrate state convergence and boundedness of adaptive parameters for test systems.
reference_methodology:
System class: Consider x(t) ∈ R^n, u(t) ∈ R^m with nominal dynamics ẋ(t) = A1 x(t) + A2 x(t−h1(t)) + B1 u(t) + B2 u(t−h2(t)) and nonlinear perturbation Δf(x(t), x(t−h1(t)), u(t), u(t−h2(t))). The initial condition is x0(τ) = ψ(τ), τ ∈ [−max{h1, h2}, 0]. The delays satisfy 0 ≤ hi(t) ≤ hi, ḣi(t) ≤ d < 1 (i = 1, 2), with hi > 0. The nonlinear uncertainty satisfies Δf(·) ≤ β1 x(t) + β2 x(t−h1(t)) + β3 x(t−h2(t)) with unknown βi. The matching condition is not imposed.

Controller and adaptive laws: The controller is u(t) = α(x(t), θ(t)) with θ(t) = β(x(t)). The proposed design is u(t) = K x(t) + μ In x(t), where K = Y P−1 is the state-feedback gain, In ∈ R^{m×n} is a matrix of ones, and μ(t) ∈ R is an adaptive factor. The adaptive laws are: μ̇(t) = −x^T P B1 In x − (1/2) ε μ x^T x − (1/2) μ θ x^T P P x, with a projection law to keep |μ(t)| ≤ 1; θ(t) = θ̄ − θ̄, where θ̄ estimates the norm bound of the nonlinear uncertainty (θ̄ = β2^2 + β2^2 + β3^2).

Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional and analysis: Define V(t) = x^T(t) P x(t) + Σ_{j=1}^2 ∫_{t−hj(t)}^t x^T(s) Qj x(s) ds + ε ∫_{t−h2(t)}^t μ^2(s) x^T(s) x(s) ds + μ^2(t) + (1/2) θ^2(t), with P > 0, Qj > 0. Compute V̇ along the closed-loop trajectories using the system dynamics and controller. Use the inequality 2 x^T P B2 μ t2 In x t2 ≤ ε(1−d) μ^2 t2 x^T t2 x t2 + ε^{−1}(1−d)^{−1} x^T P B2 In I_n^T B2^T P x. Bound Δf via the weighted norm inequality. Combine terms and apply the Schur complement to obtain a block LMI condition on Σ11, Σ12, Σ22 that must be negative definite. The LMI is independent of delay magnitudes but depends on d.

Feasibility and parameters: Solve the LMI (7) with variables P, Q1, Q2, Y, ε, d to obtain feasible gains and parameters. The adaptive factor μ is bounded by projection to ensure stability. The adaptive parameter θ estimates the unknown bound of the nonlinear uncertainty. The proof shows V̇ < 0 under the LMI and delay derivative bound, implying global Lyapunov stability and x(t) → 0.

Numerical experiments: Example 1 (linear system with input delay and parametric uncertainty) is compared against prior robust controllers. Example 2 (nonlinear system with time-varying state and input delays) is simulated with specified delays and initial conditions. MATLAB is used to solve LMIs and simulate responses. No random seeds or statistical analyses are reported.

title: Gastric Helicobacter species associated with dogs, cats and pigs: significance for public and animal health
research_question:
The review addresses the following questions: (1) What is the pathogenic significance of dog-, cat-, and pig-associated gastric NHPH in their natural hosts? (2) What are the prevalence rates and transmission routes to humans, and what is the zoonotic potential? (3) Which virulence mechanisms underlie NHPH pathogenesis, and how do they differ from H. pylori? (4) Are standard H. pylori eradication regimens effective for NHPH, and what resistance patterns emerge?
