(5) What are the implications for animal health (e.g., porcine growth and ulceration) and human disease (e.g., gastritis, ulcers, MALT lymphoma, and potential CNS associations)?

Implicit hypotheses include: (a) NHPH are clinically relevant in humans, particularly H. suis, with zoonotic transmission from dogs, cats, and pigs; (b) NHPH virulence mechanisms rely on urease, GGT, and OMPs rather than cagPAI/VacA; (c) standard triple therapy can eradicate NHPH and improve gastric pathology, though resistance may occur; and (d) porcine H. suis strains exhibit intrinsic antimicrobial susceptibility differences compared to non-human primate strains and other NHPH. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include epidemiological detection of NHPH in human biopsies, successful eradication with standard regimens, and molecular evidence of virulence factors. Contradictory findings (e.g., inconsistent associations in dogs/cats, variable prevalence) nuance these hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review that synthesizes published studies on gastric NHPH in dogs, cats, and pigs, and their zoonotic relevance to humans. The text does not report a systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessment. It integrates evidence from: (1) epidemiological studies estimating prevalence in animal and human populations; (2) clinical case series and cohort studies assessing associations with gastritis, ulcers, and MALT lymphoma; (3) experimental infections in rodents (mice, gerbils) to model pathogenesis and immune responses; (4) molecular diagnostics (PCR, histology, immunohistochemistry) for species identification; (5) antimicrobial susceptibility testing (MICs) for aminopenicillins and metronidazole; and (6) comparative genomics and proteomics to characterize virulence factors and OMP families.

Taxonomic identification methods include 16S rRNA and 23S rRNA sequencing to distinguish H. suis from dog/cat-associated NHPH, ureAB sequencing for differentiation among dog/cat NHPH, MLST for H. suis strain typing, and genome-based approaches (e.g., IceA, LpsA, whole-genome sequencing) to separate H. heilmannii s.s. from H. ailurogastricus. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry can differentiate cultured NHPH. Culture of NHPH is fastidious; only a few human isolates have been obtained to date.

Transmission studies report detection of NHPH DNA in saliva and feces of animals, with some studies detecting Helicobacter DNA in saliva/feces without H. suis-specific PCR positivity, suggesting other enterohepatic Helicobacter species may contaminate these matrices. In pigs, H. suis DNA was detected in saliva but not feces in some studies, supporting oral-oral or gastric-oral routes. Potential human exposure routes include direct/indirect contact with dogs, cats, or pigs, contaminated water, and consumption of contaminated pork for H. suis.

Treatment studies evaluate standard H. pylori eradication regimens (proton pump inhibitor plus two or three antibiotics) for NHPH, with follow-up via PCR and endoscopy. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing includes MICs for amoxicillin and metronidazole, comparing porcine vs non-human primate H. suis strains and other NHPH. No IRB/ethics approvals are reported, as the review does not involve new human or animal subjects.

title: Deconvolution of Intermixed Redox Processes in Ni-based Cation-Disordered Li-Excess Cathodes
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can intermixed TM and oxygen redox processes in Ni-based DRX cathodes be deconvoluted into quantitatively distinct contributions using isotopic labeling and gas-phase diagnostics? (2) What are the onset potentials and relative magnitudes of oxygen redox and TM redox in NTMF, and how do they evolve with state of charge? (3) How do surface carbonate and electrolyte degradation contribute to CO2 evolution and reactive oxygen species that influence electrolyte stability? (4) Does the sum of quantified capacities match the potentiostat-measured net electron transfer, validating the approach?

Hypotheses: (i) 18O-enrichment of the lattice and surface carbonate will enable unambiguous separation of O2 sources during DEMS and TiMS, allowing backcalculation of oxygen redox and TM redox capacities. (ii) Oxygen redox will occur in parallel with TM redox at high potentials, with lattice oxygen disproportionation and irreversible O2 loss dominating at higher states of charge. (iii) Surface carbonate oxidation will generate reactive oxygen species that drive electrolyte degradation below ~4.5 V, while lattice-derived oxidized oxygen will dominate above ~4.6 V. (iv) The sum of deconvoluted capacities will agree with potentiostat measurements within experimental error, supporting the method’s validity. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include isotopic consistency of O2 evolution onset, quantified Ni oxidation efficiency below 100%, and close agreement between summed capacities and potentiostat data.
reference_methodology:
Material synthesis: Li1.15Ni0.45Ti0.3Mo0.1O1.85F0.15 (NTMF) was synthesized via solid-state annealing. Precursors Li2CO3, NiCO3, TiO2, MoO2, and LiF were mixed stoichiometrically by high-energy milling (3 h) and annealed at 700 °C for 10 h in air. Powder XRD was performed on a Bruker D2-Phaser with Cu Kα radiation.

Isotopic enrichment: NTMF powders were enriched with 18O by heating at 600 °C under 97 at% 18O2 in N2 for 6 h. Surface native carbonate (NACN) was quantified by strong acid titration, yielding 39.9 mol% 18O enrichment with a near-uniform binomial distribution. The bulk mean 18O enrichment (excluding surface carbonate) was estimated at 11.7 mol% from headspace oxygen balance. XRD and first-cycle voltage profiles confirmed structural and electrochemical invariance after enrichment.

Electrochemical cell assembly: Modified Swagelok-type cells were used. Cathodes were prepared under Ar by casting slurry (70 wt% active material, 20 wt% Super P, 10 wt% PVDF, NMP solvent) onto 12 mm stainless-steel meshes, dried at 120 °C under vacuum overnight. Active material loading was 7–10 mg cm−2. Li foil disks (11 mm) served as anodes. Separators: Celgard 2500 (cathode side) and QM-A quartz microfiber filter (anode side), each 12 mm. Electrolyte: 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DEC (1:1 v/v), 80 µL. Cells were assembled in a glovebox.

In-situ DEMS: A custom-built DEMS system (calibrated for O2 and CO2 in N2 carrier gas) monitored gas evolution during charge. Cells were charged at 0.1 Li+ h−1 (29.5 mA g−1) to specified cut-off voltages, then held until current fell to 0.01 Li+ h−1 (2.95 mA g−1). Headspaces were purged with N2 every 10 min; swept gas was analyzed by mass spectrometry. Isotopic O2 evolution (16,16O2; 16,18O2; 18,18O2) and CO2 evolution were quantified.

Ex-situ TiMS: Custom glass vessels with separate solid and liquid compartments were used. Charged cathodes were extracted, rinsed with DEC (3×), dried under vacuum, and sealed with 10 M H2SO4 (N2-sparged) in the glovebox. The headspace was purged with N2; after mixing, gas was swept with 2 mL N2 pulses every 2 min and analyzed by mass spectrometry. O2 sources were decoupled: 18O-tagged O2 from lattice oxidized oxygen disproportionation and untagged O2 from water oxidation by oxidized Ni. A control experiment swapped labeling (untagged NTMF with H218O-containing H2SO4) to confirm water oxidation.

Quantification and analysis: DEMS isotopic distributions and cumulative O2 loss were recorded at cut-off voltages (e.g., 4.6–4.8 V). TiMS isotopic O2 fractions were used with known bulk 18O enrichment to backcalculate lattice oxidized oxygen and water-splitting contributions. Ni redox capacity was computed from the water-splitting stoichiometry (n = 3 or 4) and the measured O2 from water oxidation. Capacities were normalized to the net moles of active material. Differential capacity (∆Q/∆V−1) plots were reconstructed from deconvoluted components.

title: Why is patient safety a challenge? Insights from the Professionalism Opinions of Medical Students' (PoMS) Research
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do Australian medical students, doctors, and members of the public differ in their acceptability judgments of patient safety-related behaviors by medical students across multiple scenarios? (2) Do contextual variables (e.g., student seniority, health professional role, attendance vs non-attendance, PPE compliance) and participant demographics (gender, age/seniority) influence these judgments? (3) Is there evidence of a “transition effect” in which acceptability increases from public to students to doctors? (4) Are there indications of cognitive biases (e.g., in-group bias, moral self-licensing, cognitive dissonance, positional obedience) that may affect patient safety?

Hypotheses: (a) Doctors will show greater leniency toward certain unsafe behaviors than the public, particularly when peers are implicated (in-group bias). (b) Students’ opinions will bridge public and doctor attitudes, reflecting professional identity formation. (c) Contextual complexity (e.g., failure-to-report scenarios) will widen acceptable ranges and reveal subgroup differences (e.g., male doctors/students). (d) Fabricating results will be uniformly unacceptable, but public may be less stringent than clinicians. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significant cohort differences favoring doctors in leniency, monotonic transition effects, and subgroup effects aligning with bias constructs.
reference_methodology:
Design: National, multicentre, prospective, online cross-sectional survey using hypothetical vignettes. Ethical approvals: UWA HREC RA/4/1/8014 (students), RA/4/1/9195 (doctors), RA/4/1/9278 (public).

Participants and sampling: Convenience sampling via social media (Facebook), professional networks (Australian Medical Association; Australian Confederation of Postgraduate Medical Education Councils), and consumer forums (Australian Consumers’ Health Forum). Surveys closed in April 2018 when recruitment plateaued (<10 responses/month for 3 months). Cohorts: 2602 Australian enrolled medical students, 809 Australian doctors, and 503 Australian members of the public. Females predominated across cohorts (p<0.001). Public respondents were older than doctors (p<0.001). No denominator data for doctors/public; student participation rate was 15.2% of all Australian enrolled medical students (PoMS-I).

Instruments: Five patient safety scenarios (Table 1) with two randomized versions each, differing in a pre-specified contextual variable (e.g., student seniority, health professional role, attendance vs non-attendance, PPE compliance). Scenarios ranged from serious professionalism breaches to positive examples. Each vignette ended with “This student’s behaviour is…” and respondents rated acceptability on a four-point Likert scale (no equipoise option). The survey is included in Appendix A.

Procedures: Each participant received a random version of each scenario to test unconscious bias effects of contextual variables (e.g., seniority, role). Scenarios included: (1) Fabricating blood pressure results; (2) Infection control/presenteeism (attending vs not attending a clinical placement after a probable viral illness); (3) PPE compliance (agreeing vs refusing to proceed without appropriate PPE); (4) Failure to report a drug error by a junior doctor; (5) Failure to report potentially racist comments by a health professional. Student seniority was defined as junior (undergraduate years 1–3 or postgraduate years 1–2) vs senior (undergraduate years 4–6 or postgraduate years 3–4).

Analysis: Likert responses were dichotomized into acceptable vs unacceptable and summarized as frequencies. Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests compared acceptability across contextual variables and participant demographics (cohort, gender, age/seniority). Null/blank responses and “prefer not to say” for gender were excluded. SPSS Statistics 24 (IBM) was used; p<0.05 denoted statistical significance. Prevalence ratios (Thompson et al., 1998) were reported for significant subgroup comparisons. Tables note rounding and missing data may cause totals to vary.

title: Chapter 20: Vulnerability of island flora and fauna in the Great Barrier Reef to climate change
research_question:
Central questions: (1) How will climate change drivers (air/sea temperature, CO2, ocean acidification, sea level rise, storms, ENSO, and rainfall variability) affect the structure, function, and distribution of island flora and fauna in the GBR? (2) Which habitats (e.g., rainforest, montane heath, pisonia forests, freshwater wetlands, foreshore vegetation) and taxa (e.g., seabirds, shorebirds, turtles, endemic plants and animals) are most vulnerable? (3) What are the short-term (≤1 m SLR, 2–3°C air warming) versus long-term (>1 m SLR, >3°C air warming) trajectories? (4) How do stressor interactions (e.g., elevated CO2 with temperature and water stress; SLR with rainfall changes) shape outcomes?

The chapter does not state formal hypotheses but evaluates predictions: warmer, drier conditions and higher fire risk will favor sclerophyllous and salt-tolerant vegetation; SLR will erode/inundate cays and lowlands, salinize freshwater lenses, and reduce freshwater wetlands; elevated CO2 will enhance C3 growth and reduce foliar nitrogen; storms will increase habitat disturbance; and migratory species will face phenological mismatches and habitat loss. Outcomes supporting these predictions include observed seabird declines, documented storm impacts, and literature-based projections for vegetation shifts and wetland shrinkage.
reference_methodology:
Design: Narrative synthesis and vulnerability assessment integrating baseline ecological data, literature, and case studies. The chapter compiles island inventories, species lists, vegetation types, and historical trends, then projects impacts under IPCC-consistent climate scenarios.

Data sources: (1) Island inventories and geomorphology (e.g., ~900 islands; ~600 continental/high islands; ~300 coral cays; 44 low wooded islands in the northern GBR). (2) Flora: ~2000 native vascular plant species on continental islands and low sandy mainland islands; 70 rare/endangered species (<5%); eight plant endemics (Table 20.1). (3) Fauna: ~40 terrestrial reptiles; 38 islands with marine turtle nesting; 55 key seabird breeding islands; ~736,000 seabird pairs (1995) across ~24 species; significant terrestrial fauna (Table 20.2); seabirds and shorebirds (Table 20.3). (4) Case studies: seabird population trends on Raine Island (1979–1993 vs 1994–2003); Michaelmas Cay storm impacts (1999 cyclone); Tryon/Wilson Islands pisonia forests affected by soft scale; freshwater lens salinization on Pacific atolls; storm damage on Dunk/Frankland/Barnard Islands (Cyclone Larry, 2006). (5) Climate projections: air temperature increases (2–3°C short-term; >3°C long-term), sea surface temperature increases (1–2°C short-term; >2°C long-term), sea level rise (0.1–0.9 m by 2100; catastrophic multi-metre rise possible), and rainfall variability (more intense events, longer dry spells).

Procedures: The authors qualitatively link climate drivers to ecological processes (e.g., photosynthesis, water-use efficiency, fire regimes, dispersal, salinization, geomorphological dynamics) and to species-specific sensitivities (e.g., folivores under elevated CO2, montane heath species under warming, seabirds under habitat loss and food availability changes). They synthesize interactions among stressors (e.g., SLR with rainfall, CO2 with temperature and water stress) and evaluate short-term versus long-term thresholds (≤1 m vs >1 m SLR). No formal statistical models, experimental manipulations, or standardized monitoring protocols are reported; instead, the chapter relies on cited studies and observed patterns.

Analysis: The assessment is structured by habitat (continental islands, coral cays, freshwater wetlands, foreshore vegetation) and by stressor (temperature, CO2, ocean acidification, SLR, storms, rainfall). It summarizes quantitative examples (e.g., species counts, percentage declines, SLR ranges) and provides a summary table (Table 20.4) contrasting short-term and long-term impacts. Ethical approvals, sampling frames, and data access are not applicable to this synthesis.

title: MicroCT of Coronary Stents: Staining Techniques for 3-D Pathological Analysis
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can post-fixation radiopaque staining (I-KI, PTA, PMA, and combinations) increase soft tissue contrast and reduce beam hardening artifacts in microCT of stented vessels sufficiently to enable 3D pathological analysis? (2) Which staining protocol maximizes contrast between neointima and media while minimizing metal streaking artifacts? (3) Do microCT-derived morphometric measurements correlate with histology? (4) Can staining detect para-strut amorphous material (PAM) and differentiate it from other tissues?

Hypotheses: (H1) Radiopaque staining will increase soft tissue attenuation and improve contrast between vessel wall layers, enabling non-destructive 3D analysis. (H2) I-KI will provide superior contrast and artifact reduction due to high electron density and lipid binding, but may reduce specificity in lipid-rich regions. (H3) PTA and PMA will increase contrast and reduce artifacts, with PTA+PMA outperforming single agents. (H4) MicroCT morphometrics will correlate strongly with histology. (H5) Staining will highlight PAM regions, identifiable by TEM as pools of red blood cells with macrophages.

Support/refutation: The results support H1–H4: all stains increased contrast and reduced artifacts; I-KI achieved the highest media contrast (85%) and largest artifact reduction (38% SD decrease); PTA+PMA improved contrast and artifact reduction relative to single agents; microCT measurements correlated strongly with histology (R²=0.9884). H5 is supported: PAM regions were detected by PTA and I-KI and confirmed by TEM.
reference_methodology:
Design: Empirical evaluation of post-fixation radiopaque staining protocols for microCT of stented porcine iliac vessels. Samples were from necropsy-fixed vessels (10% neutral buffered formalin) implanted with metal stents (AUP#2005-102). The study period was October 2010–March 2011.

Materials and equipment: X-Tek HAWK 160XI microCT scanner (Nikon Metrology); reconstruction software CT-Pro; visualization VGStudioMAX (Volume Graphics). Stains: I-KI (aqueous), PTA (aqueous), PMA (solid in solution). Plastic histology: dehydration in graded ethyl alcohol (EtOH) to 99%, infiltration with Technovit 7200 (light-activated methyl methacrylate), embedding, sectioning with EXAKT diamond band saw, grinding (25–75 µm), H&E staining (formic acid, EtOH, Scott’s water, Gibb’s hematoxylin, eosin, phyloxine B). Imaging: Nikon Super Cool Scan 9000 for histology; TEM at Texas Heart Institute (JEOL 1230, AMT 600 camera) with toluidine blue, basic fuchsin, uranyl acetate, lead citrate.

Stain selection and optimization: Radiographic trials on non-stented porcine tissue determined optimal concentrations and penetration times. PTA: 0.5%, 1%, 5% in 70% EtOH; PMA: 0.5%, 1%, 5% in 70% EtOH; I-KI: 5%, 10%, 10% with 5 g KI buffer. Contrast percent was computed as ((AUO − AUB)/(AUO − AUB))/2, where AUO and AUB are object and background gray values. Based on trials, optimal concentrations were selected: PTA 3%, PMA 3%, I-KI 10% (with 5 g KI). PTA/PMA required ≥48 h for penetration; I-KI penetrated in ~3 h.

MicroCT acquisition: Unstained scans at 150 kV, 134 µAs, with an 8 mm aluminum pre-hardening plate; ~1000 projections per vessel; average resolution ~18 µm. After scanning, vessels were stained per protocol, then placed in 70% EtOH or distilled water to prevent dehydration during scanning. For I-KI, a subset was scanned after 3 h staining and then placed back in formalin overnight to remove I-KI before histology.

Combined staining: PTA+PMA (2:1) and PTA+PMA+I-KI (3% PTA, 1.5% PMA, 10% I-KI) were tested. All vessels were subsequently processed for plastic microground histology.

Analysis: ROI-based CT number measurements were taken for air (background), neointima, media, stent struts, and high-stain uptake regions. Strut region SD of CT numbers was used as a proxy for beam hardening artifact. Calibration: microCT slice calibration used FWHM of stent struts (150 µm) for Image-Pro measurements; histology used a standardized micrometer slide. Morphometric comparisons included lumen, stent, and media circumferences (Table 2). Correlation between microCT and histology measurements was assessed via linear regression (Figure 10). PAM detection: high-stain uptake regions were identified in microCT and validated by TEM.

title: Estimating social contacts in mass gatherings for disease outbreak prevention and management: case of Hajj pilgrimage
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do risky social contacts (within 2 m for ≥15 min) during Hajj rituals scale with total pilgrim numbers and density? (2) How do Tawaf and Sa'ay differ in contact generation given their geometries and movement patterns? (3) What congestion thresholds emerge in Mata'af and Masa'a, and how do they affect time spent and contact counts? (4) How do physical distancing policies (0.5–4 m) alter contact rates and unique contacts? (5) Can the model inform practical entrance-rate caps to maintain safe densities?

Hypotheses: (H1) Contact counts increase non-linearly with population, with congestion causing sharp increases beyond thresholds. (H2) Tawaf generates more contacts than Sa'ay due to rotational geometry and path overlap. (H3) Physical distancing reduces contacts up to a threshold; beyond it, increased path density can raise contacts. (H4) Entrance-rate caps aligned with safe densities can prevent congestion. Support for H1–H4 would be indicated by monotonic increases in contact metrics with population, higher Tawaf contact rates, a distancing effect that reverses at ≥4 m, and entrance-rate caps consistent with design criteria. Refutation would involve flat contact scaling, Sa'ay exceeding Tawaf contacts, no distancing effect, or entrance-rate caps failing to prevent congestion.
reference_methodology:
Design: Integrated agent-based modeling (ABM) and discrete-event simulation (DES) in AnyLogic to simulate pedestrian dynamics and contact generation during Hajj rituals in Masjid-Al-Haram. The model captures movement from entry to exit after completing Tawaf and Sa'ay, with two complementary contact calculation approaches.

Setting and geometry: A 3D representation of Masjid-Al-Haram (first floor only) includes the Kaaba, Place of Abraham, entrance gates, divider walls in Masa'a, and other architectural details. Tawaf occurs in Mata'af (open-air), with a maximum radius ~75 m and an open area ~15,000 m²; Sa'ay occurs in Masa'a (two 16 m corridors; Safa–Marwah distance ~450 m; seven trips ≈3.6 km). The free surface area for Tawaf is approximated as 11,000 m² (Kaaba radius 10 m; Mata'af radius 60 m). Historical throughput limits: ~30,000 Tawafs/hour for efficient, safe circulation; entrance/exit rates up to 55,000–65,000 p/hour in peak seasons.

Pedestrian dynamics: AnyLogic’s social force model governs movement, incorporating pedestrian mass/dimensions, desired speed, attraction to goals, and repulsive forces with pedestrians and obstacles. Pilgrims enter via five gates at predefined rates, are randomly distributed 0.5–50 m from the Kaaba, and circulate counterclockwise around the Kaaba for seven rounds (Tawaf). After prayer (≈5 min), they proceed to Masa'a for Sa'ay (seven trips), then exit via gates. Speed is set to 1.1±0.1 m/s in low-density areas; high-density speeds are density-dependent. Path control for Tawaf uses 36 radial lines each divided into 100 half-meter segments, enabling precise control of perpendicular motion and average path radii.

Contact definitions and methods: Close contact is defined per CDC guidance (within 2 m for ≥15 min). Two methods are used: (1) Monte Carlo snapshot sampling: random placement of individuals with 0.15 m² area; pairwise distances computed; distances <2 m counted as contacts; repeated runs until contact counts stabilize. (2) Simulation-based contacts matrix calculator: at each time step, each pilgrim identifies others within 2 m; if not previously counted, a new contact is recorded; accumulation begins at entrance and ends at exit. Contacts are normalized by total pilgrims and reported as total contacts, fraction with ≥1 contact, average and maximum contacts per person, and unique contacts.

Scenarios: Population sizes from 1,000 to 10,000 entering Masjid-Al-Haram. Steady-state conditions are identified by tracking pilgrim counts in Mata'af and Masa'a over time. Physical distancing scenarios enforce circular paths with 0.5–4 m spacing, using a triangular distribution favoring outer circles to spread density. Entrance rates are varied to reflect peak season variability (15–18 p/s). Validation checks include code walkthroughs and timing comparisons to literature-reported ritual durations and throughput.

Analysis: Contact metrics are computed per ritual and per area; polynomial trendlines (second-order) are fitted to contact vs population data. Congestion effects are inferred from increases in time spent and reductions in speed. Entrance-rate caps are derived from steady-state densities and design criteria.

title: An Integrative Approach to Decipher the Chemical Antagonism between the Competing Endophytes Paraconiothyrium variabile and Bacillus subtilis
field_subfield: Microbiology — Microbial Natural Products and Chemical Ecology
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which metabolites are produced during the interspecific competition between P. variabile and B. subtilis, and how are they spatially distributed? (2) Do B. subtilis surfactins mediate the observed balding effect on P. variabile? (3) Does P. variabile resist surfactin-mediated antagonism via enzymatic hydrolysis of surfactins? (4) What antimicrobial metabolites does P. variabile produce that can suppress B. subtilis?

Hypotheses: (H1) B. subtilis produces cyclic lipopeptide surfactins that inhibit P. variabile aerial hyphae development (balding effect). (H2) P. variabile counters by hydrolyzing surfactins, producing hydrolyzed analogs detectable in the competition zone. (H3) P. variabile produces tetronic acids (e.g., nivefuranone A) that inhibit B. subtilis growth. Support for H1 would be the spatial localization of native surfactins to bacterial zones and their association with hyphal inhibition; support for H2 would be detection of hydrolyzed surfactins in the competition area and enzymatic hydrolysis in biotransformation assays; support for H3 would be isolation of a tetronic acid with measurable antibacterial activity against B. subtilis.
reference_methodology:
Strains and isolation: P. variabile LCP5644 (MNHN collection) and B. subtilis 9E1a were isolated from inner needle tissue of Cephalotaxus harringtonia var. drupacea (reference N°2686, Arboretum de Chèvreloup, MNHN). Endophytes were cultivated on MEA (malt extract 20 g/L, glucose 20 g/L, bacteriological peptone 1 g/L, agar 20 g/L).

Competition assays: Co-cultures were set up on MEA in 12 cm Petri dishes (60 mL) by spotting 10 µL of each microbial suspension at 1.5 or 2.5 cm apart. Cultures were incubated at 24 °C under ambient light. Monocultures (fungus and bacterium) were controls (triplicate). To exclude volatiles, a divided Petri dish (9 cm, 25 mL MEA) with a plastic barrier was used; no competition was observed, indicating diffusible mediators.

LC-ESI-MS/MS for molecular networking: Extracts were analyzed on a Dionex U3000 nanoflow system coupled to a Thermo LTQ Orbitrap (nano-ESI). Separation: C18 PepMap 100 column (75 µm ID, 15 cm, 5 µm, 10 nm). Injection: pre-concentration column, 20 µL/min water/TFA (0.1%), 3 min wash, then 200 nL/min gradient 2–60% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid over 30 min. Orbitrap full scans m/z 200–1500 at 30,000 resolution (m/z 400), accumulating 500,000 charges in the LTQ. Up to four top ions were isolated for CID MS/MS (target 100,000 charges) and recorded in the Orbitrap at 7,500 resolution.

Molecular networking: RAW files were converted to mzXML (Trans-Proteomic Pipeline). GNPS workflow used MS-Cluster (parent mass tolerance 0.2 Da; MS/MS fragment ion tolerance 0.1 Da) to generate consensus spectra; nodes with <2 spectra were discarded. Edges required cosine >0.7 and >6 matched peaks; reciprocal top-10 filtering was applied. Spectra were searched against GNPS libraries and visualized in Cytoscape v3.2.1.

MALDI-TOF MSI: Competitions were prepared on MALDI plates (MTP 384 polished steel BC) with 5 mL MEA. After cooling, 2 µL bacterial suspension (10^4 cells/mL) and 5 µL mycelial suspension (50 mm^3 mycelium pieces vortexed/sonicated in 1 mL sterile water) were deposited at 1.5 or 2.5 cm. MALDI-TOF/TOF UltrafleXtreme (Bruker) in reflector mode; Smartbeam-II 355 nm laser at 2 kHz; shot number per pixel 500; pixel size 150 µm; extraction delay 210 ns; acceleration 25 kV; resolution 36,000 (bradykinin m/z 1060.57). Calibration used PepMix 5 (bradykinin [1–5] m/z 573.31; [1–7] m/z 757.40; bradykinin m/z 1060.57; angiotensin m/z 1296.68) with a quadratic/cubic enhanced algorithm; average mass accuracy 3.8 ppm. Acquisitions and image processing used flexControl 3.4 and flexImaging 4.0; spectra normalized by median.

TOF-SIMS MSI: After 26 days at 24 °C, filter paper with co-cultured microbes was removed, dried under vacuum (≥3 h), and a rectangular piece containing both microbes was mounted on a stainless steel plate with conductive tape (fungi removed to avoid topography). TOF-SIMS IV (ION-TOF) used Bi3+ cluster ions (25 keV) in high-current bunched mode (~0.4 pA at 10 kHz). Secondary ions were extracted (2 keV) and post-accelerated (10 keV) to a hybrid detector (micro-channel plate, scintillator, photomultiplier). Large-area analyses used 500 µm × 500 µm patches, 100 × 100 pixels, 10 pulses/pixel (ion dose ~1.0 × 10^10 ions/cm^2). A 21 eV pulsed electron flood gun compensated charge. Mass calibration used internal low-mass fragments (C−, CH−, C2−, C3−, C4H−) in negative mode. Data acquired and processed in SurfaceLab 6.5.

Biotransformation assays: P. variabile was grown in YMS medium (glucose 16 g/L, yeast extract 4 g/L, malt extract 10 g/L, peptone 5 g/L) from spore suspension (10^6 spores/mL). After 72 h at 27 °C (160 rpm), 1.5 g mycelium was harvested and stored in phosphate buffer (4 mL, pH 6). Commercial surfactin (DMSO, 20 mg/mL) was added (4 µL) to biomass; controls: surfactin in buffer (40 µL) or DMSO to biomass (40 µL). After 24 h, 300 µL methanol was added to 1.5 mL mycelium/supernatant, sonicated 20 min, centrifuged, and 10 µL supernatant was analyzed by UPLC-MS.

Fungal fermentation and isolation: P. variabile was grown on MEA (25 °C, 26 days) in 15 Petri dishes. Mycelium and broth were extracted with EtOAc (3×), dried over Na2SO4, filtered, and concentrated to 900 mg crude extract. Preparative HPLC (gradient 45–52% MeCN in H2O, 32 min; flow 20 mL/min; tR 28.5 min) yielded nivefuranone A (1).

Antibacterial assays: Agar diffusion used B. subtilis 9E1a (~10^6 CFU/mL) on MEA (40 mL). Ten µL of nivefuranone A (50 or 10 mg/mL in DMSO) or fungal crude extract (50, 10, 1 mg/mL) were spotted; inhibition zones measured after 48 h at 25 °C. Controls: econazole (10 µL, 5 mg/mL) and DMSO. MICs were determined by resazurin microdilution: 2 µL nivefuranone A (10 mg/mL in DMSO) added to 200 µL LB; serial dilutions 100–0.1 µg/mL in 96-well plates. Growth controls included DMSO and chloramphenicol (1 µg/mL to 1 ng/mL). Plates incubated at 26 °C for 2 days, then 30 µL resazurin (0.01% w/v) added and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h; MIC defined as lowest concentration preventing blue-to-pink reduction.

title: Biochemical characterization and cryo-EM studies of MlaFEDB
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the precise assembly and stoichiometry of the MlaFEDB complex? (2) Where are phospholipid-binding pockets located, and what residue-level interactions stabilize bound lipids? (3) How does ATP binding couple to conformational changes that drive phospholipid translocation? (4) Which subunit interfaces and residues are essential for function in vivo and in vitro?

Hypotheses: (a) MlaFEDB forms a defined stoichiometric complex with specific subunit interfaces that enable coordinated conformational changes. (b) The complex contains discrete lipid-binding cavities that accommodate phospholipid head groups and acyl chains through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. (c) ATP binding induces NBD dimerization and TMD rearrangements that collapse the central cavity, extruding lipids and enabling translocation. (d) Disrupting key MlaD–MlaE, MlaE–MlaF, or MlaB–MlaF interfaces will impair ATPase activity and OM integrity, increasing sensitivity to SDS/EDTA.

Predictions: Nucleotide-free structures will reveal bound lipids in specific cavities; ATP-bound structures will show NBD closure, TMD bending, and cavity collapse; mutations at identified contact residues will reduce ATPase activity and cause growth defects under OM stress. Outcomes supporting these predictions would validate an extrusion mechanism and clarify the mechanistic basis of Mla-mediated phospholipid transport.
reference_methodology:
Expression and purification: The mlaFEDCB operon (E. coli K-12) was cloned into pET20b (C-terminal His-tag on MlaB). E. coli C43(DE3) was grown at 37 °C in LB + 100 μg/mL ampicillin to OD600 1.0, induced with 0.5 mM IPTG, and incubated 12 h at 16 °C. Cells were lysed (microfluidizer), membranes pelleted (100,000 × g, 1 h, 4 °C), solubilized with 1% DDM (1 h, 4 °C), and purified by TALON affinity followed by Superdex 200 size-exclusion chromatography in 25 mM Tris pH 7.8, 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% DDM, 5% glycerol. Fractions were concentrated to 6 mg/mL and stored at −80 °C. SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry confirmed MlaFEDB; MlaC was not detected by SDS-PAGE but was identified by MS.

Nanodisc reconstitution: POPG (10 mM) was hydrated and re-suspended in 25 mM Tris pH 7.8, 150 mM NaCl, 100 mM sodium cholate. Mla complex proteins, MSP1D1, and POPG were mixed at 0.5:1:60 molar ratio with 15 mM sodium cholate, incubated 1 h at 4 °C, and detergent removed with Bio-Beads SM-2 (0.6 mg/mL, overnight, 4 °C). Nanodisc-embedded MlaFEDB was purified by Superdex 200 in 25 mM Tris pH 7.8, 150 mM NaCl.

ATPase assays: Using a Sigma ATPase/GTPase kit, 0.5 μg of nanodisc-embedded Mla complex was incubated in 40 μL reactions with 0–4 mM ATP for 30 min at 37 °C. Absorbance at 620 nm was measured. ATPase activities were determined from linear regression of standards. Each point represents mean ± SD; n = 3 biologically independent samples.

Lipid binding and MS: Lipids were extracted by Bligh–Dyer (buffer/chloroform/methanol phases). Accurate mass measurements were acquired on an Agilent 6545 QTOF (ESI-negative mode: capillary 2.5 kV, nozzle 1000 V, gas temp 320 °C, drying gas 8 L/min, nebulizer 35 psi, sheath gas 350 °C, 11 L/min; MS/MS collision energy 20–30 eV; m/z 100–1000). PG and PE were detected and confirmed by MS/MS.

Mutagenesis and complementation: Site-directed mutagenesis targeted MlaF E170Q, MlaE I14N, R97E, R237E/H241E, L99N; MlaD L106N/L107N; MlaB T52A, Q22A; and MlaF M127A. Mutants were transformed into an E. coli mlaFEDCB-null strain. Growth was assessed by spotting serial dilutions (10^−1 to 10^−6) on LB + ampicillin + IPTG ± 0.8% SDS and 2.5 mM EDTA at 37 °C overnight.

Cryo-EM sample prep and data collection: Nanodisc-embedded MlaFEDB (4 mg/mL) was applied to glow-discharged Quantifoil Au R1.2/1.3 grids. For ATP-bound samples, MlaF~EQ~EDB was incubated with 2 mM ATP and 2 mM MgCl2 for 30 min at room temperature. Grids were plunge-frozen in liquid ethane (Vitrobot Mark IV). Data were collected on a Titan Krios at 300 kV with a Gatan K3 detector and GIF Quantum energy filter (slit 20 eV, super-resolution mode, 81,000× nominal magnification; defocus −2.2 to −1.2 μm; 32 frames/frame exposure 0.08 s; total dose ~50 e−/Å2). Motion correction (MotionCor2), 2× binning (pixel size 1.087 Å/pixel), and dose weighting were applied; defocus estimated by Gctf.

Data processing and model building: RELION-3 was used for particle picking, 2D/3D classification, local defocus correction, auto-refinement, and post-processing. Adaptive masks were applied to MlaD (C6 symmetry) and MlaFEB/TM (C2 symmetry). For ATP-bound states, 3D classification used C1 symmetry; focused refinements targeted intracellular and TM regions. Resolutions were estimated by gold-standard FSC0.143 with high-resolution noise substitution. Models were built ab initio in PHENIX/COOT using aromatic residues as markers; MDFF was used to fit nucleotide-free models into ATP-bound maps, followed by manual refinement and PHENIX refinement with secondary structure and geometry restraints. Overfitting was monitored via half-map refinement and testing.

title: Effect of the Nanoparticles h-BN on Improving the Tribological Properties of Biodegradable Vegetable Oils
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does adding h-BN nanoparticles (70 nm) to biodegradable vegetable oils improve anti-wear (reduced wear scar diameter), anti-seize (increased welding load), and friction coefficient relative to base oils? (2) How does the surfactant (succinimide) affect dispersion and tribological outcomes? (3) Are improvements consistent across different vegetable oils, and do they differ from a commercial ester oil (Priolube 3967 LQ)?

Hypotheses: (H1) h-BN will reduce wear scar diameter and friction coefficient and increase welding load in vegetable oils due to lamellar lubrication and film formation. (H2) A surfactant will improve h-BN dispersion and suspension stability, indirectly enhancing tribological performance. (H3) Benefits will be base-oil dependent, with potential deterioration in ester oils due to different base-oil chemistry. Outcomes supporting H1 include statistically significant reductions in wear scar diameter and friction coefficient and increases in welding load versus base oils. Outcomes supporting H2 include improved dispersion and minor direct effects on wear metrics. Outcomes supporting H3 include consistent gains in vegetable oils and adverse effects in ester oil.
reference_methodology:
Materials: Base oils included rapeseed, sunflower, corn, and soybean oils (domestically produced; Silesia Oil, Łaziska Górne, Poland) and a commercial ester oil (Priolube 3967 LQ; CRODA Lubricants). h-BN nanoparticles were MK-hBN-N70 (Lower Friction M.K. IMPEX CORP, Mississauga, Ontario, Canada). The dispersant was succinic acid imide (succinimide; Merck, Darmstadt, Germany). The surfactant was used at 0.5% w/w; h-BN was added at 0.5%, 1.5%, and 2.5% w/w.

Sample preparation: For each test, the appropriate masses of base oil, h-BN, and surfactant were measured (PS 600.R2 balance, 1.5 mg accuracy) and mixed using an ultrasonic homogenizer (UP200St, 200 W, 26 kHz; S26d14 sonotrode; amplitude 20–100%; pulse 0–100%) for 15 min at 20°C and 55% RH. Mixtures were prepared immediately before testing to mitigate sedimentation.

Physicochemical tests: pH (WTW pH meter with SenTix 41 electrode), surface tension (Nima tensiometer), density (pycnometers in thermostat), kinematic viscosity at 40°C and 100°C (Höppler viscosimeter with thermostat), and refractive index (Abbe refractometer). Base-oil specifications (Table 1) included flash point temperatures (e.g., rapeseed 342°C; sunflower 338°C; corn 340°C; soybean 334°C; Priolube 316°C), kinematic viscosities at 40°C (35.43, 31.46, 33.18, 30.83, 90.62 mm²/s), at 100°C (8.05, 7.69, 7.86, 7.62, 13.09 mm²/s), viscosity indices (211, 229, 221, 231, 144), pH (6.42, 6.31, 7.16, 6.04, 6.69), surface tension (48.97, 50.77, 50.97, 65.20, 70.83 mN/m), and density (0.9195, 0.9222, 0.9125, 0.9223, 0.9104 g/cm³).

Anti-wear and anti-seize testing: Four-ball apparatus T-02U (ITEE, Radom, Poland) per PN-C-04362:2017-03. Tests used 100CR6 steel balls (12.7 mm ± 0.0005 mm; hardness 59–61 HRC; Ra 0.02). Conditions: ambient 20°C, 1500 rpm, constant load 39.23 daN, 3600 s. Ten milliliters of oil were drip-fed to cover the balls. Wear scar diameters were measured with an OMO 06192/06193 optical microscope (Keyence). Welding load (Ft) was determined by increasing load until seizure onset. Each measurement was repeated three times.

Friction coefficient testing: HFN5/E/16/029 (P.A. Hilton, Andover, UK) with a phosphor bronze sleeve (CC481K; Ra 2.5) and a steel pin (C45; Ra 1.25). Tests used light bearing lubrication at 400 rpm with variable loads (55–135 N). Friction torque was recorded; friction coefficient µ was computed via µ = F/N and µ = tan(ρ), where ρ is the slope of the torque–load line.

Suspension stability: Visual inspection of bottles over 14 days documented sedimentation; images were taken at day 0, ~1 week, and ~2 weeks. The authors note gradual h-BN deposition at the bottom, mitigated by immediate pre-test mixing.

Comparative context: Results were compared to prior work on PAO4 and CB30 oils (Urbaniak et al., 2018, 2022) to contextualize the magnitude of improvements and dispersant effects.

title: 聴覚障害児へのソーシャルスキルトレーニングの実践 ― コミュニケーションレベルにより分類したグループによる支援 ―
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does a 10-session, emotion-focused SST program, tailored to communication level, improve social skills and self-esteem among hearing-impaired middle/high school students? (2) Are gains consistent across communication-level groups (oral, sign, severe/overlap)? (3) What implementation factors facilitate or hinder SST effectiveness and generalization?

Hypotheses: (H1) Students will show pre-post improvements in social skills (reduced withdrawal and aggression) and self-esteem (reduced failure anxiety and social anxiety) on standardized scales. (H2) Improvements will be more pronounced in groups with more functional communication (oral and sign) than in the severe/overlap group. (H3) Teacher observations will corroborate student-reported gains, particularly in withdrawal and aggression. (H4) Qualitative feedback will identify practical constraints (e.g., time, duration) and supports (e.g., team-teaching, repeated sessions) that influence outcomes and generalization.

Support/refutation: H1 and H3 were supported for the oral/sign groups (significant improvements in withdrawal, aggression, and failure anxiety; significant withdrawal reduction by teachers). H2 was partially supported: the severe/overlap group showed no significant changes on teacher ratings, though descriptive means suggested some improvements. H4 was supported: qualitative data highlighted both facilitators (team-teaching, repeated sessions) and barriers (short duration, late timing, limited generalization).
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-group pre-post intervention with three communication-level groups (oral, sign, severe/overlap). The intervention was implemented during moral education classes over approximately 4 months (200X-11 to 200X+1-02), comprising 10 sessions. Each session followed a standardized sequence: instruction, modeling, role-play, feedback, and homework. Team-teaching (two teachers per session) was used to support students with lower communication proficiency.

Participants: Middle/high school students with hearing impairments at a Japanese school. Grouping by communication level: (1) Oral group (口話グループ): 5 students (3rd-year female leader; 2nd-year male; 1st-year female n=2, male n=1). Three of five had good hearing and used oral communication; two males were shy and hesitant to initiate conversations; one 1st-year female had limited vocabulary and difficulty with daily conversation. (2) Sign group (手話グループ): 5 students (1st-year male/female, 2nd-year male/female, 3rd-year male). The 3rd-year male was selected as leader to build leadership experience; overall cohesion appeared, but individual interest in others was low and self-centered tendencies were noted. (3) Severe/overlap group (重度・重複グループ): 4 students (1st-year male n=3, 2nd-year male n=1). Three had mild intellectual disability (愛の手帳 level 4) and one had high-functioning autism (愛の手帳 not acquired). All had prior experience in regular classes or regular elementary schools; language level was approximately that of lower elementary; they experienced conflicts and impulsive actions that upset peers. The severe/overlap group’s content was modified (repeated target skills) due to difficulty in regular classes.

Measures: (1) Social Skills Scale for Middle Schoolers (嶋田, 1999): 25 items; 4-point Likert (4=very applicable to 1=not applicable). Factors: pro-social (10 items), withdrawal (8 items), aggression (7 items). Example items: helping friends, listening attentively, apologizing, initiating conversations, interrupting, blaming others. (2) Self-Esteem Scale (modified for middle schoolers; 小塩, 1998; adapted by 渡辺・山本, 2003): 20 items; 2-point Likert (yes/no). Factors: others’ evaluation (6 items), self-worth (7 items), social anxiety (5 items), failure anxiety (2 items). Example items: concern about others’ opinions, fear of speaking in front of peers, worry about mistakes. (3) Teacher ratings: same scales administered by three teachers before and after SST. (4) Qualitative teacher feedback: free-text questionnaires after SST, analyzed via grounded theory coding into categories of effects and challenges.

Procedure: SST was based on DeRosier’s SS-GRIN-A with an emphasis on emotion monitoring and languageization to enhance metacognitive awareness and self-esteem. Sessions covered guidance, introductions, communication basics (language and nonverbal skills), active listening, self-esteem, respect, emotion control (two sessions), goal-setting, and a closing gratitude exercise. Team-teaching provided modeling and support. The severe/overlap group received repeated target skills due to difficulty in regular classes.

Analysis: Paired t-tests compared pre-post means within groups for each subscale. Significance thresholds were p<.05. No effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported. Qualitative data were coded into categories (effects: meaning, student motivation/skill use/knowledge gain; teacher: SST adaptations, daily instruction use, student understanding; challenges: session pacing, duration, generalization).

title: Reeling them in: taxonomy of marine annelids used as bait by anglers in the Western Cape Province, South Africa
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which marine annelid species are used as bait by anglers in the Western Cape Province, and how are they named by fishers? (2) Do morphologically similar bait species form cryptic complexes locally and globally that are not captured by morphology-only taxonomy? (3) How do common names map to taxonomic identities, and what are the implications for management?

Hypotheses: (H1) Common names are inconsistently applied across taxa and among user groups (recreational vs subsistence; regions), complicating enforcement and management. (H2) Morphologically similar species (e.g., Gunnarea gaimardi, Scoletoma tetraura, Lysidice natalensis) form cryptic complexes with distinct genetic lineages and/or morphological differences, detectable via mtCOI phylogenetics. (H3) Some species previously reported from the Western Cape under broad names (e.g., “coralworm,” “musselworm”) correspond to multiple families or species, reflecting both taxonomic complexity and naming inconsistencies.

Predictions: If H1 holds, multiple species will share common names, and names will vary by site or user. If H2 holds, COI trees will reveal well-supported clades separating morphologically similar groups with measurable genetic distances and corroborating morphological differences. If H3 holds, sequences will not match those from distant regions (e.g., China, India), and morphological traits will diverge from nominal species descriptions.
reference_methodology:
Sampling was conducted at 12 popular beach and estuarine fishing sites across the Western Cape Province (June 2016–May 2017), spanning sandy (e.g., Saldanha Bay, Muizenberg, Strand, Betty’s Bay, Pearly Beach, Struisbaai, Witsand, Knysna) and rocky (Velddrif, Melkbosstrand, Kommetjie, Betty’s Bay, Hermanus, Witsand) habitats. Fifteen recreational and six subsistence fishers donated 194 worms, which they identified by common name. Participants provided verbal consent; ethical clearance was granted by Stellenbosch University (SU-HSD-001609). Collection followed DAFF (2017) permit RES2017-27. Additional arenicolid samples were collected by the authors using the same techniques (per Simon et al. 2020). Sampling occurred during low tide; collection methods varied by taxa (e.g., hand collection, trowel digging, breaking Gunnarea tubes, pouring household bleach over mussel beds for nereidids). In some cases, only small pieces sufficient for genetic analysis were donated.

Specimen processing: Worms were relaxed in 7% MgCl2 in tap water, measured, and photographed. A mid-body or posterior section was preserved in 96% ethanol for molecular analysis. The remainder was fixed in 4% formalin in seawater for ≥2 days, washed in distilled water, and stored in 70% ethanol. Morphological examination used Leica DM1000/MZ75 and DM750/M80 microscopes with Leica EC3 or Olympus Targus TG5 camera attachments; images were stacked in Helicon Focus v7.6.4 and processed in Photoshop C6. Identification followed Day (1967, 1974) and recent literature as appropriate. All specimens were deposited at IZIKO South African Museum (Table 1).

Molecular methods: DNA was extracted from ~25 mg tissue (mid-section or posterior) using the Zymo Quick DNA MiniPrep Plus kit per manufacturer’s protocol. COI was amplified with universal primers LCO1490/HCO2198 (Folmer et al. 1994). PCR conditions: 94°C 3 min; 34 cycles of 94°C 45 s, 42°C 1 min, 72°C 1 min; final extension 72°C 7 min (Bleidorn et al. 2005). PCR products were visualized on 1% agarose gels with Quick-Load Purple 100 bp ladder. Sanger sequencing was performed at the Central Analytical Facility, Stellenbosch University. Newly generated sequences were deposited in GenBank (Table 1).

Phylogenetic analysis: Sequences were edited in BioEdit v7.2.6 and aligned with ClustalW (default parameters) in MEGA X. Neighbor-joining (NJ) trees were constructed per family. Nodal support was assessed via 10,000 bootstrap replicates using maximum composite likelihood, uniform rates, and pairwise deletion. Comparative analyses included sequences from prior studies (e.g., Simon et al. 2020; Kara et al. 2015; Sigamani et al. 2020; Zhou et al. 2010).

title: Self-Reported Sexual Engagement of Ethiopian Undergraduate Students in the Context of HIV/AIDS Pandemic
research_question: The study sought to answer two research questions: (1) How do female and male Ethiopian undergraduate students perceive HIV/AIDS? (2) What behaviors and practices expose students to HIV/AIDS? The work did not state formal hypotheses. Implicit expectations, grounded in prior literature, were that: (a) sexual engagement among undergraduates is common and influenced by peer and normative pressures; (b) environmental factors (e.g., alcohol, chat, access to pornography) facilitate risk-taking; (c) knowledge alone is insufficient to change behavior; and (d) certain partner patterns (e.g., student–sex worker, female–sugar daddy) are perceived as particularly risky. Outcomes that would support these expectations include high self-reported sexual activity, qualitative accounts of peer-driven initiation, descriptions of substance-related risk contexts, and negative perceptions of specific high-risk relationships. Outcomes that would refute them would include low sexual activity, minimal peer influence, absence of environmental risk factors, or positive perceptions of high-risk practices.
reference_methodology:
Setting and population: The study focused on Addis Ababa University (AAU), the oldest and largest university in Ethiopia, with over 40,000 students, many assigned from across the country. AAU’s urban setting and proximity to a vibrant sex industry motivated the site choice.

Participants and sampling: Approximately 600 students participated overall. The qualitative component included 20 undergraduates (10 female, 10 male) with diverse profiles (academic class, ethnicity, religion, place of origin). FGDs were conducted in two rounds, with each group’s discussion taped for about one hour, totaling 13 hours of audio and 150 pages of transcripts. The quantitative component surveyed 575 randomly chosen undergraduates. Random selection procedures, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and response rates were not detailed.

Instruments and measures: The survey was a 43-item questionnaire designed in accordance with Ajzen’s Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Items reportedly assessed factors constraining/facilitating condom use (means and standard deviations reported), but the full item content, scales, and reliability/validity metrics were not provided. The qualitative instrument comprised semi-structured FGD guides exploring sexual experiences, partner patterns, perceptions of HIV/AIDS, and mechanisms of relationship formation. Moderator gender matched participants’ sex to reduce bias.

Procedures: FGDs were moderated by a female colleague (Dr. Muluemebet Zenebe) for women and by the author for men. Discussions were recorded and transcribed. The quantitative survey was administered to randomly selected undergraduates; administration mode (paper vs. online), timing, and data collection procedures were not specified.

Analysis: Qualitative data were analyzed inductively, with categories, themes, and patterns derived from the data, guided by grounded theory methodology. The study reports descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations) for survey items related to condom use facilitators/constraints; no inferential statistics, effect sizes, or confidence intervals were reported. No details on coding reliability, inter-coder agreement, or software were provided.

Ethics: The text does not report IRB/ethics approval, informed consent procedures, or data privacy safeguards. No demographic breakdowns (e.g., age, year of study) were provided.

Limitations of methods: Single-institution sampling limits generalizability. Self-report measures are susceptible to social desirability and recall bias. The qualitative sample size (n=20) is modest. The survey’s psychometric properties and sampling frame details are not reported.

title: An inverse problem of reconstructing the electrical and geometrical parameters characterising airframe structures and connector interfaces
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a multilayered transmission line model with a Riccati difference equation formulation accurately predict reflection coefficients for air- and dielectric-filled plates, enabling inversion of spatially varying electrical and geometrical parameters? (2) Under what conditions are the parameters uniquely identifiable, and what parameter subsets can be recovered? (3) How should the connector interface be modeled to ensure consistent inversion of line parameters from VNA measurements? (4) How well can the method reconstruct plate separation profiles and dielectric properties in simulated and experimental resin-filled structures?

Hypotheses: (H1) The homogeneous case admits an exact analytic solution for the reflection coefficient, revealing parameter aggregation across layers. (H2) In the air-filled case, only two of the three geometric parameters (L, W, d) are uniquely identifiable, due to coupling in the governing equations. (H3) A connector model comprising excess capacitance, inductance, and an effective electrical length is necessary to reconcile measured and modeled reflection coefficients, enabling stable inversion of connector and line parameters. (H4) The multilayered inversion can recover plate separation profiles with reasonable fidelity, but resistivity recovery will be sensitive and may require staged inversion.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported by the derived analytic solution (Equation (5)). H2 is supported by the identifiability analysis showing only two of L, W, d can be uniquely recovered. H3 is supported by improved qualitative agreement when the connector model is included and by successful identification of Cc and Lc. H4 is supported by simulated reconstructions of plate separation and by experimental reconstructions showing underestimation and sensitivity to layer count, with resistivity requiring staged inversion.
reference_methodology:
Forward model: The structure is modeled as a multilayered transmission line with two aluminum plates bounding a dielectric slab. Transmission line theory yields a matrix telegrapher’s equation for voltage V(z) and current I(z) between plates (Equation (1)), incorporating frequency-dependent losses (skin effect, polarization). The reflection coefficient r(z) satisfies a Riccati differential equation (Equation (2)) with coefficients a_i and b_i depending on permittivity ε_i, permeability μ_i, angular frequency ω, plate width W, plate separation d_i, and characteristic impedance Z0. For layered media, a Riccati difference equation (Equation (3)) relates r_i and r_{i+1} via layer-specific parameters A_i and B_i, which depend on P_i = −a_i/b_i + sqrt((a_i/b_i)^2 − 1) and E_i = exp(−jθ_i), where θ_i = 2ω√(ε_i μ_i)′_i. Reindexing gives a Riccati difference equation (Equation (4)). In the homogeneous case, an exact solution is obtained (Equation (5)), showing r_m = (E^m − P^2) r0 + P(1 − E^m) / [P(E^m − 1) r0 + 1 − P^2 E^m], indicating parameter aggregation across layers.

Inverse problem: The objective is to estimate parameters from measured reflection coefficients r_d(ω_k) at 801 frequencies (7.5 MHz–6 GHz) using an Agilent 8753Es VNA. The objective function is the sum of squared magnitudes of errors between measured and modeled reflection coefficients (Equation (22)). The unknown vector s includes connector parameters (Cc, Lc) and line parameters (W, d, L, ρ, ε_i, μ_i). Constraints are set by experimental tolerances: W ∈ [20, 25] mm; d ∈ [1.7, 3.7] mm; L ∈ [180, 220] mm; ρ ∈ [10−8, 10−4] Ω·m; Lc ∈ [10−11, 10−9] H; Cc ∈ [10−13, 10−11] F (Table 1). For the air-filled case, an additional constraint set (Table 2) is used for certain inversions. Initial conditions are generated as 20 uniformly distributed samples within bounds, augmented by physically motivated guesses. The solver is a non-linear least squares method; convergence behavior is examined across initializations.

Connector modeling: The connector is modeled as a lossless 50 Ω coaxial line of effective electrical length Δz ≈ 15 mm (air-equivalent), plus excess capacitance Cc and inductance Lc at the coaxial–structure interface. The reflection coefficient at the calibration plane r_cal is related to the reflection coefficient at the connector–structure interface r0 by r0 = r_cal e^{−j2kΔz}. The interface impedance Z_L is computed from r0 via Z_L = Z0 (1 + r0)/(1 − r0). The total impedance at the interface Z_T includes series inductance Lc and shunt capacitance Cc (Equations (20)–(21)). Initial estimates: Cc ≈ 1 pF; Lc ≈ 0.1 nH; contact resistance < 0.01 Ω (neglected); conductance between inner/outer conductors ≈ 10−12 S (neglected).

Experimental setup (air-filled): Plates are tool plate aluminum (6 mm thick), flatness 50 μm over 1 m, roughness 0.6 μm. Plate separation d = 2.7 ± 0.05 mm; width W = 23.04 ± 0.02 mm; inner length 196 mm; outer length 200 mm; Z0 = 50 Ω. The VNA is connected via a coaxial cable terminating in a type N male connector; plates are held by type N female connectors controlling separation. No impedance matching is used to accommodate wide permittivity variation. Measurements are taken at 801 points between 7.5 MHz and 6 GHz.

Experimental setup (resin-filled): Eight structures (X1–X8) are manufactured with step-like (X1–X4) and tapered (X5–X8) geometries (Figure 3). Electrical property estimates (Table 3) include Δz = 14 mm; connector resistance R = 0.1 Ω; Lc = 1 nH; C1 = C2 = 1 pF; ρ = 1 Ω·m; static permittivity ε_s = 3.5; infinite permittivity ε_∞ = 2.5; termination capacitance C_t = 1 pF. Simulated reflection coefficients are generated by perturbing these properties by ±5%.

title: Оцінка технологічної складової конкурентоспроможності національної економіки
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the deep causes of changes in the high-tech market over 1993–2007 across leading economies? (2) Which indicators best explain observed trends in technological competitiveness? (3) How do input indicators (NO, SE, TI, PC) relate to the output indicator TS, and which components (e.g., A2, X) drive TS changes?

Hypotheses: (H1) Input indicators (NO, SE, TI, PC) and the output TS will track national competitiveness trajectories; (H2) PC and TS will be dominant factors explaining sectoral changes, with TS reflecting realized technological and technical status; (H3) China’s rise in HTM competitiveness is driven by growth in electronic devices production (A2) and high-tech exports (X), leading to increases in PC and TS; (H4) The US and Japan will show stable or declining TS despite high input indicators, indicating structural shifts or maturation. Support for H1–H4 would be evidenced by consistent TS trends aligned with changes in PC and A2/X, and by cross-country comparisons showing divergent trajectories.
reference_methodology:
Design: Comparative, longitudinal analysis of national HTM competitiveness using NSF-defined indicators. The study aggregates data for major producers (US, Japan, China, EU, and Asian countries) and examines trends from 1993 to 2007, with some global aggregates extending to 1986–2005.

Indicators and computation: Five indicators are computed, each normalized to a maximum of 100 units. Input indicators: NO = [Q1 + (Q2 + Q3)/2 + Q4 + F1V]/4; SE = (Q5 + Q10 + HMHS)/3; TI = [(Q7 + Q8)/2 + Q9 + Q11 + EDP + S&E]/5; PC = (2/3)[(Q6 + Q12 + Q13) + A2]. Output indicator: TS = (X + A2 + Q14)/3. Definitions: F1V is PRS Group investment risk index (1–12); HMHS is UNESCO human capital index based on secondary education coverage; EDP is purchases of electronic data processing equipment (thousands USD); S&E is total scientists and engineers engaged in research (UNESCO); A2 is total production of electronic devices (World Electronics Yearbooks); X is high-tech exports (COMTRADE); Q1–Q14 are expert responses to 14 questions (NSF methodology). The Input indicator is the average of NO, SE, TI, and PC.

Data sources: NSF Science and Engineering Indicators (2008, Chapter 6; http://www.nsf.gov/statistics/seind08/c6/c6h.htm); PRS Group Political Risk Letter (2007; http://www.prsgroup.com); World Electronics Yearbooks (1985–2007; http://www.rer.co.uk); UN COMTRADE (2007; http://comtrade.un.org). The EU aggregate excludes Cyprus, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, and Slovenia. Asian aggregates include China (with Hong Kong), India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand.

Procedure: (1) Compute NO, SE, TI, PC, and TS for each country-year using the NSF formulas and data sources. (2) Aggregate country shares of global HTM output and consumption (Figure 2). (3) Plot Input (average of NO, SE, TI, PC) and TS over time for leading countries (Figure 3). (4) Examine TS vs. Input and TS vs. PC relationships for the US, Japan, and China (Figures 4–5). (5) Analyze component trends (NO, SE, TI, PC) to infer drivers (e.g., A2, X, S&E).

Analysis: Descriptive statistics and trend visualization; no inferential statistical tests, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are reported. Figures present time series and comparative plots; some numerical values are explicitly stated in the text (e.g., TS levels in 1996–2007; global HTM output and share).

title: Heat-based N95 mask decontamination and reuse in a large hospital setting
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does a 70°C, 60-minute dry heat protocol preserve PFE and structural integrity of N95 masks across multiple brands? (2) Can this protocol be scaled to a large hospital setting using standard equipment while maintaining safety and operational efficiency? (3) What logistical constraints and SOPs are necessary for safe, high-throughput decontamination?

Hypotheses: (H1) After 70°C for 60 minutes, PFE at 0.3 μm remains unchanged relative to pristine masks across tested brands. (H2) SEM of filter layers will show no microstructural degradation after multiple cycles. (H3) A hot drying cabinet configured with a 75°C setpoint and open-top paper bags can achieve mask surface temperatures ≥70°C uniformly enough to ensure decontamination, with manageable temperature/humidity dynamics. (H4) Hospital-wide SOPs and scheduling can enable safe, high-throughput decontamination without compromising user safety. Support for H1–H2 would be demonstrated by stable PFE and unchanged SEM morphology; support for H3–H4 would be demonstrated by calibration data, operational metrics (e.g., ~10°C door-opening drop, ~15-minute re-stabilization, 96 masks/cycle), and successful deployment of 8193 masks. Refutation would include measurable PFE loss, structural changes, or operational failures.
reference_methodology:
Study design: Mixed-methods combining laboratory validation (filtration efficiency and structural integrity) and operational implementation (scaling and logistics) at a large hospital.

Laboratory validation: A 45 cm × 45 cm × 40 cm laboratory oven (Trishul Instruments, Mumbai) was used. Temperature and humidity sensors (Sensirion SHT-31 or EL-USB-2 logger) were taped to mask surfaces to monitor actual conditions. Target: 70°C for 60 minutes per cycle. Masks were placed directly on the oven rack or in open paper bags. Surface temperatures reached 70–75°C within 7–12 minutes depending on placement. Humidity was not controlled; ambient humidity in Mumbai was ~75–80%, yielding ~12–15% minimum humidity at 70°C; tissue paper saturated with tap water increased humidity to 25–40% during the 60-minute period. PFE at 0.3 μm was measured using a home-built setup: a vacuum pump (~10 LPM, approximating human breathing) drew air through a particle counter, with and without the mask, and PFE was computed as the ratio of particle counts. A stable 0.3 μm aerosol was generated using a saline nebulizer (0.9% NaCl). To prevent leakage, mask sides were taped to a holder. Tested brands included 3M 8822 (common at TMH), Venus 4400 and 4200, Chinese KN95, and Magnum 95001. Each brand underwent up to five 70°C, 60-minute cycles. SEM (Zeiss EVO) examined filter layers from pristine and post-treated masks to assess microstructural changes.

Operational scaling: A hot drying cabinet (Axyos Technologies) in the Central Sterilization Services Department (CSSD) was selected. The cabinet has two vertical halves (~180 cm × 60 cm × 90 cm) with grilled racks. Internal temperature displays monitored each half; external temperature and humidity sensors were added for spatial monitoring. Temperature uniformity around 70°C was evaluated: within ±1°C across a single rack, but ~5°C variation top-to-bottom due to convection. To ensure mask temperatures ≥70°C, a 75°C setpoint was used. Paper bags (open-top, with internal waterproof coating) were used to hold one mask per bag, labeled by user, to simplify logistics and minimize direct handling. To maintain airflow, a maximum of 12 bags per rack (of 16 slots) was loaded, enabling up to 96 masks per cycle. Opening the cabinet door caused a ~10°C temperature drop; ~15 minutes were required to re-stabilize to setpoint. A wet towel at the bottom yielded initial humidity ~35%, decreasing to ~10–14% by cycle end. Paper bags were pre-validated by heating to ~90°C for 2 hours to confirm material stability.

Hospital logistics: The hospital was divided into 65 subunits (departments, disease management groups, surgical/medical/radiation/radiology/nursing). Each subunit had a coordinator. SOPs were established for users (labeling, single-mask-per-bag, no direct mask handling), coordinators (scheduling, collection/distribution), and the decontamination team (prime oven at 8 AM, document deposits, load with adequate airflow, seal doors until >70°C, run 60 minutes, return between 3–4 PM). Operational windows were scheduled to avoid overcrowding and ensure distancing. The decontamination facility became functional on May 28, 2020. From May 28 to September 22, 2020, 8193 N95 masks from ~1400 users were decontaminated and reused. Rejection criteria included visible stains/mold and structural damage; masks with fungal patches were discarded. The authors note that filtration and structural integrity were tested in-house for 3M, Venus, and Filtra masks; other brands were not tested but literature suggests dry heat compatibility.

title: Discovery of Neurocognitive Phenotypes of Autism By Analyzing Functional Connectivity in the Default Mode Network and Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are there group differences in functional connectivity between ASD and non-ASD participants within the DMN and between DMN and DLPFC? (2) Do specific connectivity measures correlate with cognitive (FIQ, VIQ, PIQ) and autism severity (ADI-R subscores) phenotypes? (3) Can partial correlation-based connectivity estimates, after multiple-comparison correction, reveal reproducible neurocognitive phenotypes of ASD?

Hypotheses: (a) ASD participants will show altered DMN connectivity relative to controls; (b) DLPFC connectivity will differ between groups, reflecting executive dysfunction; (c) connectivity differences will correlate with cognitive and ADI-R subscores, with lower connectivity associated with higher RRB scores. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses would include significant ASD vs control differences in partial correlations (BH-corrected) and significant Pearson correlations between connectivity coefficients and phenotypic measures. Outcomes refuting would include no significant group differences or non-significant phenotype correlations.
reference_methodology:
Data source: ABIDE (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange), an open-access repository of resting-state fMRI scans from 1112 individuals across 17 research groups (as of March 2022). ABIDE provides preprocessed data via pipelines (e.g., Connectome Computation System, Neuroimaging Analysis Kit) and phenotypic data (age, gender, handedness, medications, ADI-R and ADOS subscores). The analysis used Talairach atlas .1D files (42 regions), with ROIs including mPFC (2001/2002), PCC (2101/2102), angular gyrus (4101/4102), DLPFC (4501/4502), and additional regions (4701/4702). The text states that males and females under 21 were analyzed, yielding 672 unique fMRI datasets.

Preprocessing and ROI extraction: Time series for each ROI were extracted from .1D files using AFNI’s 1dtool.py. The study references DensParcorr (Wang et al., 2016) for partial correlation estimation, chosen to account for effects of other brain networks. Specific preprocessing pipelines, scanner parameters, motion correction, nuisance regression, and harmonization across sites are not reported.

Connectivity estimation and group comparison: Partial correlations were computed between ROI time series to estimate functional connectivity. Correlation matrices were split by ASD vs non-ASD groups. For each ROI pair, mean correlation coefficients were compared using Student’s t-tests, and p-values were calculated. Age and sex differences in resting-state connectivity were acknowledged (seniors show more connectivity than adults under 60 and children; males show more general connectivity than females), but the analysis restricted to males and females under 21. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure with α=0.05.

Phenotypic correlations: For each participant, Pearson correlations were computed between connectivity coefficients and phenotypic scores: FIQ, VIQ, PIQ, and ADI-R subscores (social interaction, abnormalities in communication, restricted and repetitive behaviors). The analysis aimed to verify that discovered phenotypes align with established ASD diagnostic measures.

Statistical reporting: Figures and tables include example correlation matrices (e.g., Figure 2), t-values for group differences (Figure 4), BH procedure visualization (Figures 7–8), and a connectivity difference heatmap (Figure 9). A table (TABREF0) lists p-values for significant connections, and a table (Figure 6) reports Pearson correlations between connectivity and phenotypes with corresponding p-values. No details on random seeds, train/test splits, or effect sizes are provided.

title: A community based case-control study to determine the risk factors of dengue fever in Bangladesh
research_question:
Research question: Which socio-demographic, lifestyle, and household factors are associated with dengue virus infection among hospitalized patients in Chattogram, Bangladesh, during the 2019 epidemic?

Hypotheses: (1) Behavioral exposures (e.g., living/working with dengue patients, travel to high-prevalence areas, daytime sleep) increase dengue risk; (2) Household and housing characteristics (e.g., house type/structure/age, crowding) are associated with higher odds of infection; (3) Certain occupations confer differential risk. Support for these hypotheses would be indicated by statistically significant associations (p<0.05) in chi-square tests and/or logistic regression with ORs >1 (risk) or <1 (protective) and 95% CIs excluding 1. Null findings would refute or nuance these hypotheses. The study also explored whether environmental features (e.g., stagnant water within 250 m, indoor daylight/ventilation, nearby bus stands/garages, construction sites) were associated with dengue risk.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Community-based case-control study conducted in Chattogram district, Bangladesh, during July–November 2019, coinciding with an unprecedented dengue epidemic. Cases were hospitalized dengue patients confirmed by NS1 antigen tests admitted to CMCH (tertiary government hospital) and BITID (specialized hospital/research center) in August–September 2019. Controls were non-dengue patients admitted to other departments of the same hospitals, frequency-matched by age, gender, and geographic location.

Sample: N=300 (150 cases; 150 controls). Demographics were matched: age categories (≤15, 16–30, 31–45, 46–60, ≥61) and gender (male 70.0%; female 30.0%) were balanced. Cases were predominantly 16–30 years (63.3%) and urban residents (60.7%); 77.3% were permanent residents.

Questionnaire and data collection: A 24-variable structured questionnaire (demographics, travel history, daily activities, family status, housing and surroundings) was developed in English and translated to Bengali. The instrument was reviewed by two specialists (medicine and epidemiology) and pre-tested. Trained investigators from One Health Center for Research and Action conducted telephone interviews. Verbal informed consent was obtained; confidentiality assured. Participation was voluntary with no incentives. Response rate was 57.47% due to invalid/inactive numbers, unresponsive contacts, and relatives answering. Incomplete interviews were excluded.

Data processing and analysis: Data were entered into Excel, checked for completeness/consistency, and analyzed in SPSS v26. Chi-square tests assessed group differences and screened variables. Stepwise binary logistic regression identified significant predictors; p<0.05 defined significance. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs quantified associations. Model diagnostics included the Omnibus test, Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, Cox & Snell and Nagelkerke pseudo-R², and a classification table. Predicted vs observed plots were examined to assess calibration.

Ethics: Ethics approval was obtained from Chattogram Veterinary and Animal Sciences University. Participants (or guardians for children) were informed that data would be kept private and used for research only. Participants could withdraw at any time.

title: Beliefs About COVID-19 During Lockdown in France: Evidence From Two Representative Surveys
research_question:
The study asks: (1) How accurate are individuals’ beliefs about COVID-19 risks (IFR, own risk, others’ risk, expected prevalence) during lockdown, and how do these beliefs vary by demographics? (2) Do individuals exhibit comparative optimism (own risk < others’ risk), and does this change over time? (3) How do beliefs evolve between early and late lockdown, and what factors drive these changes?

Hypotheses: H1: Beliefs are well-calibrated relative to available evidence and mediated by socio-demographic characteristics (gender, age, education). H2: Comparative optimism is present (own risk < others’ risk), potentially due to limited information and familiarity bias. H3: Beliefs change during lockdown: Bayesian learning predicts rational updates with new information (own risk and prevalence adjust), whereas representativeness heuristics predict persistence of priors. Outcomes supporting H1 include alignment of IFR and prevalence with hospital data and demographic associations. H2 is supported if own risk < others’ risk. H3 is supported if own risk and prevalence shift significantly across surveys, with IFR potentially stable if updated slowly.
reference_methodology:
Design: Two cross-sectional online surveys of the French general population aged ≥18 years, conducted during the first national lockdown (March 17–May 11, 2020). Survey 1: March 31–April 2, 2020 (two weeks after lockdown). Survey 2: April 23–27, 2020 (two weeks before lockdown end). Samples: n=1,005 (Survey 1) and n=1,004 (Survey 2), drawn from an IFOP online panel (>750,000 households) stratified to match census distributions for sex, age, occupational status, education, town size, and region. Ethical approval: University Hospital Institute Méditerranée Infection (2020-018). Written informed consent obtained.

Measures: Four quantitative risk beliefs: Q1 IFR ("Out of 100 infected, how many die?"); Q2 own risk to catch/catch again (0–100 scale); Q3 others’ risk (0–100 scale); Q4 expected prevalence (0–100 scale). Survey 1 included Q1bis (seasonal influenza IFR) and qualitative items: Q5 relative risk (0–10), Q6 worry (0–10), Q7 contagiousness (0–10), Q8 seriousness (0–10), with influenza counterparts (Q7bis, Q8bis). Confidence in Q2 and Q3 was assessed (very high/high/moderate/low/very low). Health items: self-rated general health; chronic illness; personal COVID-19 diagnosis/illness; relatives’ illness; expected epidemic duration (0–52 weeks). Survey 1 also included sleep problems and cultural profiles; these were excluded from the current analysis.

External data: Hospital deaths and diagnosed cases by gender, age, and region from Santé Publique France (publicly available). Population denominators from INSEE (January 1, 2020). IFR computed as deaths/cases; prevalence as cases/population. Regions grouped into low (Nouvelle-Aquitaine, Bretagne, Normandie, Pays de la Loire, Occitanie), medium (Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur, Center-Val-de-Loire, Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, Hauts-de-France, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, Corse), and high incidence (Île-de-France, Grand-Est). Time fixed at the center of each survey interval.

Statistical analysis: GLMs with logit link and quasibinomial distribution to model determinants of Q1–Q4 (first survey only and pooled). Post-stratification weights applied (survey package); average marginal effects computed with margins (Delta method).
