Calibration assessed via paired t-tests: (a) IFR vs expected prevalence (one-sided, given IFR<prevalence); (b) COVID-19 vs seasonal influenza IFRs (two-sided); (c) qualitative contagiousness and seriousness (regressions without intercept). The “50-blip” was examined by fitting beta distributions to each item’s distribution, estimating excess 50s, and regressing demeaned answers on an indicator of 50 responses; significance at p<0.05. Software: R 3.7.0. Supplementary Tables 6–7 report unweighted GLM estimates.

title: PROPERTIES OF THE RIEMANN-LEBESGUE INTEGRABILITY IN THE NON-ADDITIVE CASE
field_subfield: Mathematics — Real Analysis (Vector-valued integration, non-additive measures)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can the Riemann-Lebesgue integral be generalized to vector functions with respect to arbitrary non-negative set functions while preserving classical properties (linearity, monotonicity, continuity of the integral set function)? (2) How does the generalized RL integral relate to Birkhoff simple and Gould integrals in non-additive settings? (3) Under what conditions on the set function m (e.g., σ-additivity, monotone σ-subadditivity, finite variation) do RL and Gould integrals coincide?

Hypotheses/predictions: (H1) For bounded f and finite m(T), f is |RL| integrable, and the integral satisfies standard bounds (e.g., ∫|f| dm ≤ ||f||_∞ m(T)). (H2) RL integrability implies Birkhoff simple integrability with coinciding integrals. (H3) Under σ-additivity or monotone σ-subadditivity with finite variation, RL and Gould integrals coincide; without these assumptions, equivalence may fail. (H4) The integral set function I_f inherits finiteness, absolute continuity, and order/exhaustive properties from m under boundedness and finiteness of m(T).

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if Proposition 3.3 and Theorem 3.9 are proved. H2 is supported if Theorem 4.2 shows RL ⇒ Birkhoff simple with equality. H3 is supported if Proposition 4.5 and Theorem 4.7 establish equivalence under the stated conditions, and Example 4.6 refutes equivalence without them. H4 is supported if Theorem 3.12 proves finite variation, ε-δ absolute continuity, and inheritance of order/exhaustive properties.
reference_methodology:
Setting: Let T be a nonempty, at least countable set; A a σ-algebra of subsets of T; N* = {1, 2, 3, …}. A partition P of T is a finite or countable family of pairwise disjoint nonempty sets whose union is T. Refinement P ≤ P′ means every set in P′ is contained in some set of P. The common refinement P ∧ P′ is {A_i ∩ B_j}. The class of all partitions is P; for A ∈ A, P_A denotes partitions of A.

Set functions: m: A → [0, ∞] with m(∅) = 0. Properties: monotone (m(A) ≤ m(B) if A ⊆ B); subadditive (m(A ∪ B) ≤ m(A) + m(B) for disjoint A, B); σ-subadditive (m(∪_{n∈N} A_n) ≤ Σ_{n∈N} m(A_n) for pairwise disjoint (A_n)); submeasure (monotone + subadditive); σ-additive; exhaustive (lim_{n→∞} m(A_n) = 0 for pairwise disjoint (A_n)); null-additive (m(A ∪ B) = m(A) if m(B) = 0); property (σ) (the ideal of m-zero sets is stable under countable unions). For finitely additive m, m̄(A) = inf{m(B); A ⊆ B, B ∈ A} is defined; m̄ is monotone and super-additive on P(T), and m̄ = m for finitely additive m; subadditivity (σ-subadditivity) implies finite (σ-)additivity.

Vector-valued functions and integrals: Let (X, ||·||) be a Banach space. The authors define absolute RL (|RL|) and unconditional RL (RL) integrals of f: T → X with respect to m. f is |RL| m-integrable on T if there exists b ∈ X such that for every ε > 0 there exists a countable partition P_ε of T so that for every finer countable partition P = {A_n} with tags t_n ∈ A_n, the series Σ_{n∈N} f(t_n)m(A_n) is absolutely convergent and ||Σ f(t_n)m(A_n) − b|| < ε. The RL integral requires unconditional convergence of the series in place of absolute convergence. The integral on a subset A ∈ A is defined analogously; Theorem 3.2 shows integrability on T implies integrability on every A, and fχ_A integrability on T is equivalent to integrability on A with ∫_A f dm = ∫_T fχ_A dm.

Key theorems and propositions: Proposition 3.3: If f is bounded and m(T) < ∞, then f is |RL| integrable and ||∫ f dm|| ≤ ||f||_∞ m(T). Theorem 3.5: Linearity: (a) αf is |RL| integrable with ∫ αf dm = α ∫ f dm; (b) f is |RL| integrable with respect to αm with ∫ f d(αm) = α ∫ f dm; (c) f ± g is |RL| integrable with ∫ (f ± g) dm = ∫ f dm ± ∫ g dm. Theorem 3.8: If f is |RL| integrable with respect to m1 and m2, then f is |RL| integrable with respect to m1 + m2 and ∫ f d(m1 + m2) = ∫ f dm1 + ∫ f dm2. Theorem 3.9: If m(T) < ∞ and sup_{t∈T} ||f(t) − g(t)|| < ∞, then ||∫ f dm − ∫ g dm|| ≤ sup ||f − g|| m(T). Theorem 3.10: If f, g: T → R are m-integrable and f ≤ g, then ∫ f dm ≤ ∫ g dm. Theorem 3.12: If f is |RL| integrable on T, then I_f is finitely additive. If f is bounded and m(T) < ∞, then I_f is ε-δ absolutely continuous and of finite variation; if m is order-continuous (exhaustive), then I_f is order-continuous (exhaustive).

Comparative integrals: Birkhoff simple integral (Bs): a ∈ X exists such that for every ε > 0 there exists P_ε with lim sup_{n→∞} ||Σ_{k=0}^n f(t_k)m(A_k) − a|| < ε for all finer P with tags. Theorem 4.2: RL integrability implies Birkhoff simple integrability with coinciding integrals. Gould integral (G): the net σ(P) = Σ_{i=1}^n f(t_i)m(A_i) over finite partitions ordered by refinement converges; equivalently, for every ε > 0 there exists a finite P_ε so that for all finer finite P with tags, ||σ(P) − a|| < ε. Proposition 4.5 and Theorem 4.7: For bounded f, if m is σ-additive (or monotone and σ-subadditive) with finite variation, then f is Gould m-integrable iff RL-integrable, and the integrals coincide. Example 4.6: For T = N, A = P(N), m(A) = 0 if |A| < ∞, m(A) = 1 if |A| = ∞, f(n) ≡ 1 is RL-integrable with integral 0 but not Gould-integrable.

title: Enhancers in T Cell development and malignant lesions
field_subfield: Immunology — T cell biology and oncology
research_question: The review addresses two overarching questions: (1) How do enhancers regulate gene expression during normal T cell development (ETP, DN, DP, SP), and which enhancers and TFs are critical for TCR assembly, lineage marker expression, and signaling pathways? (2) How do enhancer dysregulation and viral enhancer insertions contribute to T cell malignancies, and what therapeutic strategies can selectively disrupt oncogenic enhancer-promoter loops? The implied hypotheses are: (a) Disrupting specific enhancer-promoter loops or targeting Mediator subunits that bind eRNAs will selectively suppress oncogenic transcription in T cell malignancies; (b) BET/CDK inhibitors and chromatin-modifying agents can reduce enhancer-driven oncogene expression and improve outcomes in pre-clinical models; (c) Standardized enhancer classification (e.g., super-enhancers) will enable more precise therapeutic targeting. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include reduced proliferation/apoptosis in T-ALL models with BET/CDK inhibitors, identification of super-enhancers driving oncogenes, and mechanistic evidence that Mediator subunits (MED1, MED12) interface with eRNAs to activate promoters. Refutation would involve lack of efficacy, off-target toxicity, or failure to translate to in vivo models.
reference_methodology:
As a narrative review, the article synthesizes findings from diverse experimental modalities rather than reporting new experiments. Key methodologies cited include: (1) Chromatin immunoprecipitation-based profiling of histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) to annotate enhancers; (2) CRISPR/Cas9 functional screens to test enhancer activity and gene regulation in human cells; (3) Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) to quantify enhancer activity across contexts; (4) Single-cell RNA sequencing to resolve enhancer activity and lineage-specific programs; (5) Pre-clinical models for therapeutic testing: T-ALL cell lines, primary patient T cells, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) mice; (6) Viral enhancer studies using HTLV1 and MuLV to model enhancer hijacking and leukemogenesis.

The review compiles evidence across developmental stages: ETP enhancers (e.g., E BAB for Bim; GATA2 and NOTCH1 enhancers affecting ETP numbers and apoptosis), DN/DP enhancers (TCR α/β/γ/δ enhancers; HES1/5; ETS1; pTα enhancer regulated by E47 and PU.1), and SP enhancers (CD4 enhancers Eα/β/δ and E4p/E4m; CD8 enhancers E8I–VI; FOXP3 demethylation and lineage commitment). In malignancy, it integrates genomic analyses of super-enhancers (e.g., TIAM2 in adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma; GIMAP, TP73, BCL11b, MYC super-enhancers) and viral enhancer insertions (HTLV1, MuLV) that dysregulate ETS1, ELF1, SRF, and MYC.

Therapeutic strategies summarized include: gene editing to remove abnormal enhancers; BET inhibitors (JQ1, dBET6, OTX015, ARV-825, I-BET151) and CDK inhibitors (dinaciclib, alvocidib, PIK-75) that disrupt enhancer-promoter looping and RNA Pol II phosphorylation; and HDAC/HAT inhibitors that modulate acetylation-dependent enhancer function. Clinical trials (phase 1) are summarized from clinicaltrials.gov, with reported adverse events (AEs) including anemia, neutropenic fever, nausea, fatigue, and thrombocytopenia. No new datasets, statistical analyses, or preregistration are reported by the authors.

title: Early stages of agglomeration of adhesive particles in fully-developed turbulent pipe flows
field_subfield: Fluid Mechanics — Multiphase Flow and Turbulence
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does particle response time (St_e, St_L) affect agglomeration rates, agglomerate sizes, and deposition patterns in fully-developed turbulent pipe flows? (2) How does adhesiveness (Ad) modulate the fraction of particles in agglomerates and the spatial distribution of agglomerates? (3) Can a two-way coupled LES–DEM framework with JKR adhesion and rolling resistance robustly capture early-stage agglomeration and deposition across parameter ranges?

Hypotheses: (H1) Intermediate Stokes numbers maximize agglomeration due to optimal collision rates and shear-lift-driven centering of agglomerates. (H2) Increasing adhesiveness increases the fraction of particles in agglomerates and shifts deposition toward the wall. (H3) Reducing particle stiffness while scaling adhesion appropriately preserves collision outcomes, enabling stable, computationally feasible simulations. Outcomes supporting H1 include a peak in average agglomerate size at St_e ≈ 6.4 (St_L ≈ 46.4) and a center-peaked agglomerate number density at this St. Outcomes supporting H2 include monotonic increases in the fraction of particles in agglomerates with Ad and wall-peaked agglomerate number density at high Ad. Outcomes supporting H3 include near-identical agglomeration dynamics for λ = 500 vs λ = 5000 when Ad is scaled by λ^(2/5).
reference_methodology:
Flow and domain: Fully developed turbulent pipe flow at Re = U D/ν = 10,000. The domain is periodic in the streamwise direction with length L/D = 4 (L+ ≈ 2500), chosen to avoid coherent structures extending across the domain. The cross-section is discretized with three meshes (Table 1): Coarse (N_θ, N_r, N_x) = (160, 90, 160), Δθ+max = 12, Δx+max = 15; Medium = (200, 110, 200), Δθ+max = 10, Δx+max = 12.5; Fine = (240, 140, 240), Δθ+max = 8, Δx+max = 10. The DEM domain is also periodic to maintain constant φ.

Fluid solver: Finite-volume LES with PISO pressure–velocity coupling. Time advancement uses an implicit second-order scheme; spatial discretization is second-order accurate. Subgrid-scale viscosity ν_sgs is modeled with the WALE model (C_w = 0.325), which vanishes at walls without damping functions. The momentum exchange term R_pf = K_pf (u − v) is included, with K_pf computed from local fluid forces on particles in each cell (implicit Crank–Nicolson scheme). A momentum source term β δ_1,i balances the pressure gradient across the periodic domain.

Particles and DEM: Soft-sphere DEM tracks translational and angular motion of primary particles (mass m_i, radius r_i, I_i = (2/5) m_i r_i^2). Equations of motion: m_i d^2x_i/dt^2 = F_i,con + F_i,fluid; I_i dω_i/dt = M_i,con + M_i,roll + M_i,fluid. Time integration uses velocity Verlet. Gravity is neglected; Brownian motion is negligible for the particle sizes considered. Collision detection uses a potential partner list updated every 10 Δt_DEM to reduce O(n_p^2) checks.

Fluid forces on particles: Drag is modified by a clustering correlation (Benyahia et al.) based on Hill–Koch–Ladd to account for finite volume fraction and Reynolds number; in the dilute, low-Re limit it reduces to Stokes drag. Lift combines shear and rotational components via a lift coefficient formulation with coefficients from Loth & Dorgan (valid up to Re_p < 50). The collision Stokes number St* = (m_p + C_M m_f) v/(6π μ r_p) with C_M = 0.5 is used to assess viscous dissipation during collisions.

Adhesion and rolling resistance: JKR theory governs adhesive contact with normal spring F_spring,n = −(4E/3R) a_n^3, adhesive force F_JKR,n = 4 π γ E a_n^3, and damping F_damp,n = −(2/5) β S_n m v_n, where β = ln(e)/(ln 2(e) + π^2), S_n = 2E/(R δ_n), and e is the coefficient of restitution. Tangential forces include a spring F_spring,t = −S_t Δs_t with S_t = 8G √(R δ_n) and damping F_damp,t = −(2/5) β S_t m v_t. The total tangential force is truncated to |F_con,t| ≤ μ_s |F_N + 2F_C|, with F_C = 3π R γ the critical force to separate adhered particles. Rolling resistance torque M_r = k_r ξ for ξ < ξ_crit and M_r = k_r ξ_crit for ξ ≥ ξ_crit, with k_r = 4 F_C (a/a_0)^(3/2) and ξ_crit = a_0 (Δγ/γ)/12; Δγ/γ = 0.5 is used. The contact radius a is obtained from the JKR quartic relation solved analytically (Parteli et al.).

Parameterization and coupling: Particle response time τ_p = ρ_p d_p^2/(18 μ) is varied via Stokes numbers St_e = τ_p/τ_e and St_L = τ_p/τ_L (τ_L from velocity autocorrelation ρ(s) = u_x(t) u_x(t+s)/u_x(t)^2). Adhesiveness is parameterized by Ad = γ/(ρ_p U^2 d_p). To reduce stiffness while preserving collision outcomes, λ is reduced (λ_mod = λ/1000 in text; λ = 500×10^3 realistic; λ_mod = 500 used in main runs) and Ad is scaled as Ad_mod = Ad (λ_mod/λ)^(2/5). The fluid time step is set by a maximum convective Courant number of 0.5 (D/(U Δt_CFD) = 160). The DEM time step is Δt_DEM = Δt_CFD/500, sufficient to resolve collisions without altering outcomes (validated by binary collisions).

title: Caffeine administration prevents retinal neuroinflammation and loss of retinal ganglion cells in an animal model of glaucoma
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does caffeine administration reduce OHT-induced retinal neuroinflammation and microglial activation? (2) Does caffeine protect RGCs from OHT-induced loss? (3) Does caffeine lower IOP in OHT animals? (4) Does caffeine affect optic nerve structural integrity and retrograde axonal transport? (5) Does OHT alter adenosine receptor expression (A1R, A2AR) in the retina?

Hypotheses: (a) Caffeine will attenuate OHT-induced microglial activation and inflammatory cytokine expression via antagonism of A2AR (upregulated by OHT), thereby reducing neuroinflammation. (b) Caffeine will increase RGC survival despite ongoing IOP elevation. (c) Caffeine will partially reduce IOP in OHT animals but may not normalize it. (d) Caffeine will not restore impaired retrograde axonal transport, as this is tightly coupled to IOP magnitude/duration. (e) OHT will upregulate A2AR mRNA while leaving A1R unchanged. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include reduced MHC-II/TSPO mRNA and protein, decreased TNF/IL-1β, higher Brn3a+ RGC counts, partial IOP reduction, unchanged retrograde transport deficits, and increased A2AR mRNA.
reference_methodology:
Animals: Adult female albino Sprague Dawley rats (8–10 weeks; Charles River Laboratories) were housed under 12 h light/12 h dark with standard diet and water ad libitum. All procedures were approved by the University of Murcia Ethical and Animal Studies Committee and complied with ARVO and EU guidelines.

Caffeine administration: Rats were randomly assigned to receive caffeine (1 g/L) in drinking water or water. Caffeine was provided for two weeks before OHT induction and continued until study end. The dose was based on prior protective effects reported in the literature.

OHT induction and IOP: OHT was induced in the left eye under anesthesia (xylazine 10 mg/kg, ketamine 60 mg/kg) via a single session of diode laser burns (532 nm) to limbal/episcleral vessels. IOP was measured non-sedated using a rebound tonometer (Tonolab, Icare) in both eyes at baseline and days 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7. IOP was considered elevated when the mean increased by ≥30% from baseline. Topical Tobramycin ointment was applied post-surgery.

Retrograde tracing: One day after laser photocoagulation, 3% Fluorogold (FG) in 10% DMSO saline was applied to both superior colliculi. Retinas were analyzed 6 days later (day 7 post-OHT).

Immunodetection and imaging: After euthanasia (20% sodium pentobarbital) and transcardial perfusion (saline then 4% PFA), retinas were flat-mounted and permeabilized (0.5% Triton X-100). Brn3a immunostaining used goat anti-Brn3a (1:750) with Alexa Fluor 568 secondary. Retinal cryosections (18 μm) were prepared for Iba1/MHC-II immunohistochemistry. Confocal microscopy was used for imaging; nuclei were DAPI-stained.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM): Optic nerves (~1 mm from chiasm) were fixed (2.5% glutaraldehyde; 1% osmium tetroxide), dehydrated, embedded in epoxy resin, and sectioned (70 nm). Ultrathin sections were stained (uranyl acetate, lead citrate) and imaged (Tecnai G2 Spirit BioTWIN, 100 kV). Axonal damage was graded by masked observers (Grade 1: 0–25% myelin disarrangement; Grade 2: 25–75%; Grade 3: 75–100%). Inter-observer agreement was κ = 0.607 (p < 0.001).

qPCR: Total RNA from retinas was extracted (Trizol), reverse-transcribed (1 μg RNA), and analyzed by SYBR Green qPCR (StepOnePlus). Relative quantification used 2^-ΔΔCt. Housekeeping genes (Tbp, Hprt, Ywhaz, Rhodopsin) were evaluated; Ywhaz was most stable (NormFinder). Genes: A1R, A2AR, TNF, IL-1β, MHC-II, TSPO, CD11b, TREM2.

ELISA: Retinal lysates were prepared (20 mM imidazole-HCl, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 1 mM EGTA, 1 mM EDTA, 10 mM NaF, 1% Triton X-100; protease/phosphatase inhibitors), sonicated, and centrifuged. IL-1β and TNF concentrations were quantified (Peprotech) and normalized to total protein (BCA assay).

Image analysis: Whole-mount retinas were photographed (Axioscop 2 Plus; ProgRes c10; ProScan H128; Image-Pro Plus 5.1). Automated cell counting subroutines quantified FG+ and Brn3a+ cells. Isodensity maps displayed density distributions (cells/mm^2).

Statistics: Data are mean ± SEM. Normality was assessed (Shapiro–Wilk). Analyses used Kruskall–Wallis with Dunn’s multiple comparisons or Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc tests (GraphPad Prism 6.0).

title: SECOND LIFE: SECOND CHANCE -A netnographical study of the online virtual world Second Life as a place of conspicuous consumption and parallel identity creation
field_subfield: Marketing — Consumer Research; Sociology — Netnography and Virtual Worlds
research_question:
Central research question: As people construct parallel identities online, what kind of consumer society is being established inside Second Life? Sub-questions: Who inhabits SL? Why inhabit SL? Are SL avatars direct projections of users’ alter egos? Does the avatar or the person behind control interaction, or is it enhanced by environment and societal norms?

Hypotheses/predictions: (1) SL residents engage in conspicuous consumption of avatar appearance and virtual goods/services to signal status and gain social acceptance, reflecting symbolic consumption and Veblenian dynamics. (2) Avatar appearance strongly influences social interaction and inclusion; residents with more attractive, well-styled avatars receive more attention and invitations. (3) SL’s consumer society is autonomous from RL: consumption is for online use only, and social norms are shaped by in-world visibility and etiquette rather than RL credentials. (4) Social norms in SL mirror RL norms (e.g., politeness, greetings), but the publicness of SL amplifies the role of appearance and etiquette. Support for these hypotheses would be evidenced by interview and observation accounts of appearance-driven social dynamics, reported spending on appearance, and qualitative accounts of in-world social practices. Refutation would involve evidence that appearance is irrelevant to interaction, that consumption is primarily functional, or that SL norms diverge substantially from RL.
reference_methodology:
Design: Exploratory qualitative netnography combining passive observation, semi-structured interviews, and active participation in SL. The approach is justified as appropriate for complex, context-rich phenomena and for capturing social norms and identity work in a virtual community.

Data sources and collection: (1) Passive participant observation of an active SL resident (MRH, a 26-year-old graphic designer) on April 8, 2007 (login 20:29–22:30). The observer documented first-contact initiation, avatar appearance choices, and interactions across settings (e.g., Ungdomshus, a club, a battle simulator). (2) Fifteen semi-structured, in-world interviews conducted by the researcher’s avatar (“Janus Janus”) across multiple regions and languages (Danish, English, German). Interviews were conducted over approximately one month, with the researcher online nearly every second night. Interviews were recorded and transcribed; documentation is available upon request. (3) Active participation by the researcher’s avatar undergoing a professional stylist-led makeover (with SL magazine “FOR the love of MEN”) to test whether conspicuous appearance increases social acceptance. The makeover included purchasing a shape (Hugh, GB design), skin (semi-tanned with facial hair), and hairdo (blond half-long), costing 2,800 L$ (≈ US$11.20). The researcher revisited prior locations to compare interaction patterns before and after the makeover.

Setting and participants: SL is described as a 3D virtual world launched in 2003 by Linden Lab. Basic membership is free; premium membership costs US$9.95/month. Communication is via typed chat, IM, and pre-recorded animations. The study references secondary statistics (e.g., resident counts, spending) from SL’s official site and media reports. Interviewees included diverse avatars (e.g., a 32-year-old Hamburg resident with extensive appearance investments; a 47-year-old Scottish male; a 50-year-old German with a full-back tattoo; an 18-year-old shop owner/building bar). The researcher’s own avatar (“Janus Janus”) initially used a default appearance and later adopted a styled appearance.

Analytic approach: Thematic analysis of interviews and observation notes, triangulated with secondary data. Themes included social consumption/conspicuous consumption, interaction dynamics, choices and risks, and the concept of “Escapistemology.” The study cross-validates findings by comparing the researcher’s pre- and post-makeover experiences and by referencing prior literature on social norms in virtual environments.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. The text notes that all parties could log off at any time and that interviews were conducted on SL’s terms, but no formal consent procedures, anonymity safeguards, or institutional approvals are described.

title: Numerical Method for Modeling of Acoustic Waves Propagation
research_question:
The central questions are: (1) Can a third-order Euler-based CAA postprocessor accurately model acoustic wave propagation and near-field noise when provided with unsteady mean flow data from arbitrary CFD solvers? (2) What mesh resolution is required for stable and accurate propagation in uniform mean flow? (3) How well does the EAP reproduce near-field and far-field SPL spectra compared to CFD (SAS/uRANS) and experiments?

Hypotheses: (H1) A third-order accurate Euler solver is sufficient to capture acoustic propagation in tested regimes, with mesh resolution ≥5 points per wavelength ensuring accuracy. (H2) The EAP can reproduce near-field SPL spectra from CFD pressure data (SAS/uRANS) with high fidelity. (H3) Far-field SPL predictions depend on boundary placement and CFD accuracy; proximity to the outer boundary and coarse CFD grids may degrade agreement with experiments.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if numerical solutions match analytical pulse propagation and non-reflective boundary behavior. H2 is supported if EAP near-field spectra closely match SAS. H3 is supported if EAP with SAS data captures main far-field frequency and SPL but shows discrepancies near boundaries, and if uRANS data overestimate SPL and miss broadband content.
reference_methodology:
Governing equations: The method solves the full nonlinear Euler equations for acoustic fluctuations, decomposing variables into mean (Q0) and fluctuating parts. Conservative variables Q = [ρ, ρu, ρv, ρw, ρE]^T and fluxes E, F, G are defined in Cartesian coordinates, with primitive fluctuating variables (u, v, w, p) expressed in terms of conservative fluctuating variables and mean values. The equations are written as ∂Q/∂t + ∂E/∂x + ∂F/∂y + ∂G/∂z = 0.

Numerical scheme: A third-order accurate scheme in space and time is used. The authors state that third-order accuracy is sufficient for acoustic modeling, supported by comparisons with analytical solutions. The exact discretization (e.g., WENO, RK scheme, flux splitting) is not detailed here; prior works are cited for full descriptions.

Boundary conditions: Non-reflective boundary conditions are applied on all outer boundaries. For the speaker–cavity case, the speaker is modeled via a time-dependent boundary condition p(t)=A cos(2πft) with A=2 Pa and f=771.69 Hz. For the cylinder/airfoil case, pressure data on solid boundaries from CFD (SAS/uRANS) serve as boundary conditions for EAP.

Validation setup (pulse test): A 2D Gaussian acoustic pulse is propagated in a uniform mean flow with Mach number 0.5. The numerical solution is compared to an analytical solution to determine mesh resolution requirements. The authors report that at least five mesh points per wavelength are needed for correct propagation.

Speaker–cavity setup: The computational domain comprises seven blocks with approximately 0.3 million nodes. The cavity is located ~0.4 m behind the speaker; cavity depth 0.45 m, width 0.2 m. Mean flow velocity is 0 m/s. Non-reflective boundary conditions are applied on the upper boundary and at inlet/outlet. SPL is computed as SPL = 20 log(p_rms/p_ref), where p_rms = sqrt((1/n) Σ p_i^2) over n=10 instantaneous states per period.

Cylinder/airfoil setup: The test case follows Jacob et al. (2002) with Ma ~0.2 around a cylinder and airfoil. CFD simulations are performed with SAS and uRANS turbulence models. The EAP uses the unsteady pressure distributions on the solids from CFD as boundary conditions. For EAP, a uniform mesh of about 100,000 nodes is used, with non-reflective boundaries on all outer boundaries. A near-field monitor point (monitor point 1) is used to compare EAP with SAS, and a far-field monitor point at (x=0.04 m, y=1.85 m) is used to compare with experimental SPL spectra (reported ~110.7 dB ±0.5 dB at 90°).

Analysis: SPL spectra are compared qualitatively and quantitatively where possible. The number of instantaneous states used for RMS averaging is n=10. No additional statistical tests, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are reported. Details such as time step Δt, grid spacing, and exact boundary condition formulations are not provided in the text.

title: BIOACCUMULATION OF ELEMENTS AND OXIDATIVE STRESS MARKERS IN THE MUSCLE TISSUE OF SEA TROUT SMOLTS (SALMO TRUTTA L.) FROM S£UPIA BASIN
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do juvenile sea trout smolts from different Słupia tributaries exhibit spatially variable bioaccumulation of Mn, Cu, Zn, Fe, Ca, and Mg in muscle tissue? (2) Are oxidative stress markers (TBARS, OMB) and antioxidant defenses (SOD, GPx, catalase, glutathione reductase) elevated in tributaries with higher metal burdens, consistent with pollution-induced oxidative stress? (3) Can muscle tissue biomarkers differentiate tributaries with distinct contamination profiles?

Hypotheses (implicit): (H1) Tributaries with higher anthropogenic contamination (e.g., Skotawa, Kamienna) will show higher muscle tissue metal concentrations (Mn, Cu, Zn, Fe) and elevated oxidative stress markers (TBARS, OMB) relative to less impacted tributaries (Glaźna, Kwacza). (H2) Antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, GPx, catalase) will be upregulated in response to oxidative stress, particularly in tributaries with higher metal burdens. (H3) Differences in Ca and Mg will reflect local geochemistry and water hardness, potentially modulating metal toxicity and biomarker responses.

Support/refutation criteria: Significant between-river differences (p<0.05) in metal concentrations and biomarker levels, with higher metals and oxidative markers in tributaries with known contamination sources, would support H1–H3. Null differences would refute or nuance these hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Study area and sampling: Juvenile sea trout smolts were collected from four tributaries of the Słupia River: Glaźna, Skotawa, Kamienna, and Kwacza. Electrofishing was used for capture in collaboration with the Dolina Słupi Landscape Park and the Polish Angling Association (Słupsk). Sampling was conducted in the smolt stage, when fish undergo physiological changes preparing for seawater migration.

Tissue collection and preparation: From each fish, muscle tissue was sampled from the dorsal fin above the lateral line. Tissue was homogenized in cold 0.1 M Tris-HCl buffer (pH 7.2) at a 1:10 ratio (tissue:buffer). Protein content was quantified by the Bradford method (1976).

Elemental analysis: Muscle tissue was mineralized in a mixture of nitric acid (HNO3) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Trace and macroelements (Mn, Cu, Zn, Fe, Ca, Mg) were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectrometry (AAS) using an Analyst 300 spectrometer. Wavelengths: Mn 279.5 nm; Cu 324.8 nm; Zn 248.3 nm; Fe 285.2 nm; Ca 422.7 nm; Mg 213.9 nm. To eliminate phosphate interference for Ca and Mg, lanthanum chloride (LaCl3) was added to all samples to achieve 0.5% La3+ concentration. Units: Mn, Cu, Zn, Fe in mg/kg wet weight; Ca, Mg in mg/100 g wet weight.

Oxidative stress markers: Lipid peroxidation was assessed via TBARS (products reacting with 2-thiobarbituric acid), expressed as nmol/mg protein. Oxidative modification of proteins (OMB) was quantified as aldehydic and ketonic derivatives of amino acid residues, expressed as nmol/mg protein (Levine et al. 1990; Dubinina et al. 1995).

Antioxidant defenses: Superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity was measured using the quercetin oxidation method (Kostiuk et al. 1990; Koroliuk et al. 1988). Glutathione peroxidase (GPx) activity was determined using Ellman’s reagent (Moin 1986). Catalase activity was measured by standard methods (cited). Glutathione reductase activity was also assessed (method cited). Activities were expressed as U/mg protein.

Statistics: Group comparisons among tributaries were reported with arithmetic means and standard deviations (M±m) and p-values (p<0.05). The specific statistical tests, sample sizes, and confidence intervals were not reported. No water quality measurements, fish size/sex distributions, or seasonality controls were provided.

Ethics: Institutional approvals and permits are not reported. Collaboration with the Landscape Park and Angling Association is noted.

title: Evaluation économique des impacts du changement climatique pour la forêt et le secteur bois en France Revue de littérature
field_subfield: Economics — Environmental Economics (Forestry and Climate Change)
research_question:
The review is guided by the following questions: (1) What are the principal physical changes in French forests under climate change, and how do they translate into economic impacts for forest owners, markets, and non-market services? (2) How will productivity changes (e.g., CO2 fertilization, species range shifts) and disturbance regimes (droughts, fires, storms, insects) affect wood supply, prices, and regional competitiveness? (3) What adaptation strategies are feasible and economically efficient, and how do rigidities and reconstruction constraints amplify shock costs? (4) How should national-level analyses account for spatial distribution, transport costs, and biomass energy development to avoid misestimating impacts?

No explicit hypotheses are tested, but the synthesis evaluates whether: (a) increased global supply and lower prices will reduce Europe’s market share; (b) repeated shocks will induce irreversible sectoral adjustments (e.g., bankruptcies, underinvestment in certain uses); and (c) proactive adaptation can mitigate losses relative to reactive measures. Outcomes supporting these expectations include projections of higher global supply and lower prices, evidence that rigidities multiply shock costs (2–4×), and documented price collapses after major storms. Outcomes refuting them would include sustained European competitiveness despite climate change or negligible cost multipliers from rigidities.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative literature review synthesizing findings from IPCC AR4 (Alcamo et al., 2007; Fischlin et al., 2007; Nabuurs et al., 2007) and related studies on forest ecosystems and economic impacts. The review compiles physical projections (species distribution, productivity, disturbance regimes) and economic implications (market dynamics, non-market services, adaptation) for France and Europe, with attention to regional heterogeneity (notably the Mediterranean). It integrates results from ecosystem modeling (e.g., Schröter et al., 2005), species distribution modeling (Badeau et al., 2004), disturbance risk assessments (Pausas, 2004; Moreno, 2005; Moriondo et al., 2006), and economic analyses of timber markets (Sohngen and colleagues). The review also references studies on storm damage (Nilsson et al., 2004; Schumacher and Bugmann, 2006), frost damage timing (Redfern and Hendry, 2002), and non-market valuation (Montagné and Niedzwiedz, 2007; Thorsen and Kjaer, 2007). An annex provides a structured grid of questions and needs (problem severity, affected regions, current capacity, future severity, additional needs, cross-sectoral impacts, irreversibility thresholds, and limits to current economic reasoning).

No primary data collection, statistical tests, or formal meta-analysis are reported. The review does not specify inclusion/exclusion criteria, search strategy, or quality assessment procedures. It relies on cited studies’ quantitative projections and qualitative assessments (e.g., migration speeds, NPP trends, fire risk increases) to infer economic consequences. The analysis highlights the absence of national-level economic models that integrate spatial distribution, transport costs, and biomass energy development, and calls for scenario-based analyses to evaluate policy options under uncertainty.

title: Point-of-care SARS-CoV-2 sensing using lens-free imaging and a deep learning-assisted quantitative agglutination assay
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a portable LFHM–agglutination biosensor detect SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus with sensitivity comparable to RT-PCR while providing rapid POC readouts? (2) Does a deep learning–assisted classification pipeline improve robustness and speed over traditional thresholding in heterogeneous samples containing cell debris and non-specific aggregates? (3) What are the LOD and dynamic ranges achievable with this system, and how do control media (DMEM vs PBS) affect high-concentration behavior?

Hypotheses: (H1) The LFHM–agglutination assay will achieve an LOD within an order of magnitude of RT-PCR (≤10^4–10^5 copies/mL) using 40 µL of sample and 3-hour processing. (H2) A residual CNN trained on bead/cluster/debris patches will reduce variability and enable a reliable LOD determination compared to thresholding. (H3) DMEM will induce non-specific binding that reduces BR at high viral loads, making PBS a more appropriate negative control for high-sensitivity assays. (H4) The assay will exhibit a blind spot between 1.5×10^5 and 1.5×10^6 copies/mL due to BR LLOD < BR < BR LOD, but this can be mitigated by increasing bead concentration or adding a positive-control mixing step.

Support/refutation: H1 is supported by a conservative LOD of 4.74×10^3 copies/mL. H2 is supported by lower variability (SD 3.89% vs 10.66%) and a reliable LOD. H3 is supported by observed BR trends toward PBS controls at high concentrations. H4 is supported by the identified blind spot and proposed mitigation strategies.
reference_methodology:
Pseudovirus preparation: SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus was generated as an HIV-1-derived lentiviral particle expressing the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and luciferase. Production used HEK293T cells engineered to express ACE2 (receptor). Cells were lysed with Bright-Glo Luciferase Assay System (Promega E2610). Lysates were transferred to 96-well plates and measured on a Cytation 5 reader; luciferase luminescence scales linearly with pseudovirus copies, enabling calculation of copies/mL. Initial pseudovirus concentration was 3×10^6 copies/mL.

Agglutination assay: 2 µm polystyrene beads (Nanocs PS2u-SV-1) were diluted to 0.005% w/v in 1× PBS. Biotinylated ACE2 (Sino Biological 10108-H08H-B) was added to 5.0 µg/mL (≈50,000 molecules/bead). Beads and ACE2 were incubated 2 hours at 25°C on a shaker (1200 rpm). Functionalized beads were stored at 4°C.

Sample preparation and mixing: Pseudovirus was filtered (0.22 µm) to remove debris. DMEM dilutions were prepared in half-log steps from 3×10^6 to 3×10^2 copies/mL, plus a pure DMEM control. Functionalized beads were mixed 1:1 with each dilution for triplicates per dilution, yielding 30 samples (0.0025% bead concentration; pseudovirus 1.5×10^6 to 1.5×10^2 copies/mL). A single bead-only sample in PBS served as a negative control. Only 40 µL of viral sample was required per test. Samples were incubated 2 hours at 25°C (1200 rpm), then 25 µL were pipetted into the imaging chip.

Imaging chip and LFHM setup: The chip is a 65 mm² microfluidic chamber made from two laser-cut polycarbonate layers and a No.1 glass coverslip (125 µm center layer; 250 µm upper layer with inlet/outlet ports). Coverslips were cleaned with piranha (30% H2O2:H2SO4 1:3, 1 hour), rinsed with Milli-Q water, and assembled with UV-curable adhesive (Norland 7230B). The LFHM uses a 15-LED array positioned 15 cm above the sample; LEDs illuminate sequentially for 120 ms each with 15 ms delays, capturing 15 sub-pixel shifted images over 2.025 s. Spatial coherence is provided by 180 µm pinholes below each LED; temporal coherence by a 532 nm, 3 nm bandpass filter. A CMOS monochromatic sensor (ON Semiconductor AR1335, 1.1 µm pixels) records holograms. A custom 3D-printed PLA housing (<800 g; 15 × 15 cm footprint) blocks ambient light and allows hinged access for chip placement.

Image reconstruction and analysis: LR holograms are divided into 5×7 overlapping patches. PSR synthesizes HR holograms per patch, which are back-propagated to the sample plane with cardinal-neighbor regularization (weight 200) and twin-image suppression. HR patches are stitched to a full FOV image. Processing averages 20 minutes per image on HPC clusters. Two quantification methods are used: (1) thresholding to isolate monomers/clusters via connected components, with area/eccentricity boundary to separate monomers from clusters; BR = clusters/FOV beads; (2) a residual CNN classifying 60×60-pixel patches into 1–4-bead clusters and debris. BR LOD is defined as µControl + 3σControl; BR LLOD is defined as µControl − 3σControl.

CNN training and evaluation: 1,410 hand-labeled patches (5 classes: 1–4 beads, debris) were augmented by rotation and mirroring to 11,280 images. 75% were used for training and 25% for validation. Training used SGD with momentum and L2 regularization; loss minimized weighted log-likelihood. Training ran for 30 epochs (1,980 iterations; batch size 128) on a 2-core Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (2.29 GHz). Validation accuracy plateaued at 82.06%; training time was 175 s; inference time per FOV was 14.11 s (2.74× faster than thresholding, 38.65 s).

title: Biosynthesis of plant tetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloids through an imine reductase route †
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can IR45 be engineered to accept bulky 1-aryl 6,7-dimethoxy-DHIQs while maintaining high stereoselectivity and efficiency? (2) Can CNMT methylate bulky S-THIQs to THIQAs with high conversion? (3) Can these steps be assembled into minimal biosynthetic pathways in E. coli to achieve high-yield, stereoselective THIQA production, including overcoming permeability barriers for PIAs?

Hypotheses: (i) Engineering residues away from the steric bottleneck (e.g., F190, W191) will expand IR45’s substrate scope without severely compromising catalytic parameters. (ii) CNMT exhibits relaxed substrate specificity sufficient to methylate bulky THIQs. (iii) Combining IRED, CNMT, and GDH in E. coli will enable complete conversion from DHIQ precursors to THIQAs, with N-methylation driving the imine reduction equilibrium and improving overall conversion. (iv) A chimeric system (crude IRED-GDH enzymes + CNMT-expressing cells) will overcome membrane permeability limitations for PIAs, achieving high yields without SAM.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (i) is supported if engineered mutants convert bulky 1-aryl DHIQs with high ee and measurable kcat/Km. Hypothesis (ii) is supported if CNMT converts all S-THIQs to THIQAs with 100% conversion. Hypothesis (iii) is supported if E. coli systems achieve 100% conversion and high isolated yields. Hypothesis (iv) is supported if the chimeric system improves conversion of 2a and 3a to 100% with high isolated yields.
reference_methodology:
Substrates: Five DHIQ precursors (1a–5a) corresponding to cryptostyline I–III (PIAs) and laudanosine analogs (BIAs) were synthesized chemically in 90–95% yields (ESI). The THIQ products (1b–5b) and final THIQAs (1–5) were targets.

Enzymes and engineering: The IRED IR45 was used as the starting enzyme. Structural modeling was based on Q1EQE0 (PDB: 3ZHB; 64% identity). Site-directed mutagenesis targeted F190 and W191 to expand substrate tolerance. Single mutants W191X (X = 19 residues) were screened for activity on 2a and 3a; W191F showed marginal activity (2a: 3%; 3a: 2%). Double mutants F190X-W191F were evaluated; F190L-W191F achieved 75% conversion (2a) and 100% (3a) within 24 h with high ee. Kinetic parameters (kcat, Km, kcat/Km) were measured for selected substrates (e.g., 2a: kcat 0.003 s⁻¹, Km 0.307 mM, kcat/Km 0.011 s⁻¹ mM⁻¹; 3a: kcat 0.032 s⁻¹, Km 0.372 mM, kcat/Km 0.087 s⁻¹ mM⁻¹). For 1-benzyl substrates, wild-type IR45 converted 4a and 5a with 100% conversion and >99% ee; F190M-W191F improved kcat/Km to 0.989 and 0.306 s⁻¹ mM⁻¹ for 4a and 5a, respectively, and improved activity on 1a (2.23× and 3.79× over WT and F190L-W191F, respectively).

CNMT: Coclaurine N-methyltransferase (CNMT) from Coptis japonica was codon-optimized for E. coli. CNMT converted all S-THIQs (1b–5b) to THIQAs with 100% conversion. Docking into CNMT (PDB: 18) indicated binding with methylenedioxy/methoxy groups near F322 and W329; W329F reduced activity, confirming its critical role.

In vitro assays: Enzymatic reductions were performed with purified IR45 mutants and GDH (NADPH recycling from glucose). Conversions and ee were quantified (HPLC/chiral analysis). Kinetic parameters were determined for representative substrates (Table 2; Table S1/S2 in SI).

Whole-cell systems: E. coli strains co-expressing IR45 mutants (pET28a) and GDH (pACYCDuet) were used for imine reduction; CNMT was expressed in pACYCDuet. Temperature (25, 30, 37°C) and IPTG (20, 50, 100 mM) were screened; optimal conditions were 20 mM IPTG and 30°C. Under these conditions, 4a and 5a were efficiently reduced (100%), while 1a–3a showed poor-to-medium conversion (6.5–50%) due to membrane permeability. CNMT-expressing cells converted 1b–5b to THIQAs with 100% conversion.

Chimeric system: To overcome permeability, F190L-W191F + GDH were overexpressed in E. coli, lysed by sonication, and crude enzymes were added to CNMT-expressing cells at OD600 0.7 with IPTG, DHIQ substrates (50 mg L⁻¹), and NADP (1.1% w/v). This setup achieved 100% conversion for 2a and 3a with isolated yields of 93% (2) and 96% (3).

title: Core circadian clock genes Per1 and Per2 regulate the rhythm in photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis
field_subfield: Neuroscience — Circadian Biology and Retinal Physiology
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are Per1 and Per2 required for the circadian rhythm of POS phagocytosis under DD? (2) Which retinal cell type (RPE vs photoreceptors) exhibits transcriptional changes preceding and during the phagocytic peak? (3) Can a candidate RPE gene network be inferred from time-resolved transcriptomics and mutant comparisons that plausibly initiates the phagocytic peak?

Hypotheses: (H1) Per1 and/or Per2 are necessary components of the molecular clock that drive the daily POS phagocytosis peak; thus, Per1-/-Per2 Brdm1 mice will lack a rhythmic phagocytic peak under DD. (H2) The transcriptional program initiating the phagocytic peak is located in the RPE, not photoreceptors; WT RPE will show significant DEGs at the peak time point, whereas photoreceptors will not. (H3) A subset of RPE genes upregulated at the peak and downregulated after the peak in WT, filtered for photoreceptor contamination, will form a coherent network enriched in pathways implicated in phagocytosis initiation (e.g., neurotransmission, ion homeostasis, cell junctions).

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if phagocytosis is rhythmic in WT but absent in mutants under DD. H2 is supported if WT RPE exhibits time-dependent DEGs at the peak time point, while photoreceptors do not. H3 is supported if the candidate gene set shows pathway enrichment and a plausible protein interaction network.
reference_methodology:
Animals: Homozygous Per1-/-Per2 Brdm1 double-mutant mice (C57BL/6/J × 129 SvEvBrd F2) and WT littermates on mixed background were maintained under 12h light/12h dark (LD; 300 lux light phase) at 22 ± 1°C. Only male mice were used for RNA-seq; both sexes were used for qPCR and phagocytosis assays. Age-matched controls were used. All procedures complied with ARVO and EU Directive 2010/63/EU.

Genotyping: Tail DNA PCR with primers targeting deleted genomic regions (Per1: 5′-GTC TTGGTCTCATTCTAGGACACC; 5′-AACATGAGAG CTTCCAGTCCTCTC; Per2: 5′-AGTAGGTCGTC TTCTTTATGCCCC; 5′-CTCTGCTTTCAACTCCTGT GTCTG) and recombinant alleles (Per1-/-: 5′-ACAAACTCACAGAGCCCATCC; 5′-ACTTCCATTTGTCACGTCCTGCAC; Per2 Brdm1: 5′-TTTGTTCTGTGAGCTCCTGAACGC; 5′-ACTTCC ATTTGTCACGTCCTGCAC).

Phagocytosis quantification: Under DD, mice were sacrificed at eight circadian time (CT) points (CT0–CT23). Eyes were immersion-fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, cryoprotected, sectioned (10 μm), permeabilized, blocked, and stained with anti-rhodopsin (Rho-4D2) and Alexa 488 secondary. DAPI stained nuclei. Phagosomes were defined as Rho-4D2-positive inclusions >1 μm within the RPE subcellular space. A 150 μm × 150 μm grid was aligned to the POS/RPE interface and displaced dorsally/ventrally; 20 grids per section were counted. Twelve sections per eye (1 eye/animal) were analyzed; means per section represent data points. Representative images are blurry due to out-of-focus fluorescence; Rho-4D2 staining of OS was oversaturated to enhance phagosome visualization.

qPCR: Retinas were collected immediately after sacrifice, homogenized (RNAble), and mRNA extracted. DNAse I treatment (0.1 U/μl, 30 min, 37°C), phenol/chloroform/isoamyl alcohol extraction, and sodium acetate/isopropanol precipitation were used. RNA quality (RIN 7.8–9). Reverse transcription used random primers and High Capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit. qPCR employed TaqMan assays (Table 1) on 7300 Real-Time PCR System; program: 95°C 10 min; 40 cycles of 95°C 15 s and 60°C 1 min. Each reaction was run in duplicate. Amplification efficiencies were 1.8–2.0. No-template controls were included. Data were analyzed with qBase; normalization used Hprt and Tbp (cosinor P-values for rhythmicity: WT Hprt P=.676; Tbp P=.992; KO Hprt P=.219; Tbp P=.347). Relative expression was normalized to the average across six time points (rescaled to 1), and cosinor fitting assessed rhythmicity (P<.05).

LCM and RNA-seq: Eyes were enucleated under dim red light (<5 lux), embedded in OCT, cryosectioned (10 μm), cresyl violet stained, and microdissected (PALM LCM) to isolate RPE and photoreceptors. Each eye yielded 116–258 sections; WT used 183 ± 10.18 slices vs 201.3 ± 8.91 in mutants (P=.19). RNA was extracted (RNeasy Micro), quantified (NanoDrop), and quality assessed (Bioanalyzer). RIN: photoreceptors 7–9.8 (three samples 3.2, 4.1, 4.1); RPE 5–9.5. Libraries were prepared with KAPA mRNA HyperPrep: 20 ng RNA for photoreceptors (n=1/genotype/time point) and 30 ng for three additional batches (n=3/genotype/time point); RPE used 20 ng RNA. Low-yield samples were pooled to three biological replicates per genotype/time point. Libraries were 50 bp single-end sequenced (Illumina HiSeq 4000).

Bioinformatics: Quality control with FastQC, Picard Tools, and dupRadar. Adapter trimming with Trimmomatic (v0.32). Alignment to mouse genome (Ensembl GRCm38.p6) with HISAT2 (v2.1.0). Gene-level counts with HTSeq (v0.11; -stranded=reverse; Ensembl GTF release 93). Differential expression used limma/voom (precision weights) and edgeR; genes with >2 counts in ≥4 photoreceptor or ≥3 RPE samples were retained. Pairwise DE between adjacent time points and time-affected genes were tested with moderated t-tests/F-tests; FDR correction applied (photoreceptors adjusted P<.05; RPE adjusted P<.1). Annotation via biomaRt (photoreceptors release 94; RPE release 98). Pathway enrichment used g:Profiler with g:SCS FDR correction (adjusted P<.05). STRING analysis (confidence threshold 0.25) examined protein–protein interactions among candidate genes.

Statistics: Data are mean ± SEM. Normality assessed by Shapiro–Wilk; non-normal data analyzed by ANOVA on ranks. Cosinor fitting used y = y0 + c·cos[2π(t−ϕ)/24] with constraints ϕ<24, ϕ>0, c>0; rhythmicity required P<.05. One-way or two-way ANOVA with Holm–Sidak post hoc tests were used as indicated.

title: A NOTE OF CAUTION ON COVARIANCE-EQUIVALENT MODELS IN INFORMATION SYSTEMS Completed Research Paper
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How prevalent are covariance-equivalent model structures in IS studies that use CB-SEM to test main theoretical models? (2) How do such equivalences affect the conclusions drawn from those studies? (3) What modeling and design strategies can researchers adopt to mitigate or avoid equivalent models?

Hypotheses/predictions: The authors do not test formal hypotheses but advance the following expectations: (a) A nontrivial fraction of IS CB-SEM studies contain saturated blocks enabling covariance-equivalent models; (b) Equivalent models can reverse or reconfigure hypothesized causal directions while maintaining identical fit, thereby altering hypothesis support; (c) Saturated structural models are especially problematic because they are statistically equivalent to CFA models, rendering structural constraints untestable; (d) Longitudinal/experimental designs and theory-driven constraints (e.g., fixing exogenous covariances) reduce the number of plausible equivalent models and strengthen causal claims. Outcomes supporting these expectations include identifying saturated blocks, demonstrating identical fit with reversed paths, and showing swapped significance patterns across hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Survey of IS literature: The authors reviewed four highly ranked IS journals (MISQ, ISR, JMIS, JAIS) for studies published between 2004 and 2010 (inclusive) that used CB-SEM to test their main theoretical models. They excluded studies that used CB-SEM for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) but then moved to regression or PLS for hypothesis testing. From this corpus, they identified 61 studies. They then screened these for the presence of saturated blocks (variables sharing identical antecedents with all pairwise connections) and applied the Lee & Hershberger (1990) replacement rule to generate covariance-equivalent models. They found 22 studies (36.1%) exhibiting problematic equivalent models.

Detailed replication example: For Li et al. (2005), the authors used the published covariance matrix to replicate the CB-SEM analysis. They report the same degrees of freedom (df=176) and sample size (N=273) as the original study. Differences in parameter estimates relative to Li et al. are attributed to rounding in the reported covariance matrix, missing value handling, estimator choice, software, or unreported sample/estimation characteristics. The original model posits PU→PE (H3). Because PU and PE share identical antecedents, the replacement rule allows reversing the PU→PE path to PE→PU, yielding a covariance-equivalent model with identical χ² fit. The authors compared path coefficients and significance across the original and equivalent models (Table 1). They also note that free covariances among exogenous latent variables (attachment motivation, relationship commitment, perceived critical mass) create a larger saturated block, implying many equivalent models.

Further examples: The authors qualitatively assess additional studies where covariance matrices were not available. They identify saturated blocks or shared antecedents enabling equivalent models (e.g., Pavlou & Gefen, 2004; Malhotra et al., 2004; Jiang et al., 2006; Lopes & Galletta, 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Mishra et al., 2007; Tarafdar et al., 2007; Zahedi & Song, 2008; Kim, 2009; Beaudry & Pinsonneault, 2010). They also note seven additional studies where exogenous variables jointly determine a single consequent, and free exogenous covariances permit reversed regressions.

Analytic approach: The paper relies on model equivalence theory (replacement rule) and CB-SEM fit properties (χ² equivalence). It does not report software, estimators, or full replication code for all cases. No IRB/ethics approvals are applicable because the analysis uses published data and models.

title: Echinacea purpurea for the Long-term Prevention of Viral Respiratory Tract Infections during COVID-19 Pandemic: A Randomized, Open, Controlled, Exploratory Clinical Study Authors
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does EF administered as a preventive regimen reduce the incidence of viral RTIs, including SARS-CoV-2, compared with no EF? (2) Does EF reduce virus load during symptomatic RTI episodes compared with no EF? (3) Does EF mitigate symptom severity (e.g., fever days) during RTI episodes? (4) Is EF safe and well tolerated in healthy adults?

Hypotheses: (H1) EF will reduce the incidence of viral RTIs, with a specific effect against enveloped viruses and SARS-CoV-2. (H2) EF will significantly reduce virus load (lower Ct values; higher log10 ΔCt) during symptomatic RTI episodes compared with control. (H3) EF will reduce fever days and other symptom severity markers during RTI episodes. (H4) EF will have an acceptable safety profile with no serious adverse events attributable to EF.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 supported if adjusted RR/OR for incidence is <1 with p<0.05; H2 supported if log10 ΔCt reductions are significantly greater in EF vs control at prespecified time points; H3 supported if fever days and temperature metrics are significantly reduced; H4 supported if AEs are non-serious and not causally related to EF.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Randomized, parallel, open, no-treatment controlled, exploratory clinical study conducted at one center (Diagnostics and Consultation Center Convex EOOD, Sofia, Bulgaria) from November 30, 2020 to May 29, 2021. Ethical approval: Ethics Committee at Diagnostics and Consultation Center Convex Ltd (registration nr: 116/26.10.2020). Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05002179. Conducted per ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki (2013). Written informed consent obtained.

Participants: Healthy adults aged 18–75 years residing in Sofia and neighboring regions. Baseline characteristics (N=120): mean age 36 years; 100% Caucasian; smokers 36.7% (EF 41.7% vs control 31.7%; p=0.256). Co-morbidities overall 26.7% (EF) vs 10.0% (control; p=0.018), with hypertension more frequent in EF (6.7% vs 0%). Exclusion criteria: age <18 or >75; positive pregnancy test/no contraception; long-term antimicrobials/antivirals/immune-suppressors; surgical intervention within 3 months; diabetes mellitus; bronchopulmonary dysfunctions/diseases; immune/metabolic disorders; serious health conditions; known allergy to EF; participation in a clinical study within 30 days.

Randomization and groups: Random assignment to EF prevention (N=60) or control (N=60) using SAS/PLAN. Safety group (SAF) included all with at least one EF intake; ITT group included all with at least one evaluable effectiveness variable (SAF=ITT). Baseline SARS-CoV-2 positivity by RT-qPCR/serology: EF 20, control 17 (p>0.05).

Intervention: EF tablets (A. Vogel AG, GMP-compliant) contained 400 mg liquid extract (65% v/v ethanol; 95% aerial parts, 5% root; DER 1:11–12). Prevention regimen: 800 mg three times daily (2400 mg/day) during three cycles of 2, 2, and 1 months, with 1-week breaks between cycles. Acute RTI treatment: 800 mg five times daily (4000 mg/day) for up to 10 days. Control group received no EF; participants could continue prior treatments and use concomitant therapies during RTIs. Compliance assessed by weighing returned bottles (±20% tolerance).

Procedures and sampling: Monthly visits (V1–V7) for routine NP/OP swabs and venous blood (7.0 mL). Intensified sampling during symptomatic RTI episodes on days 1, 2, 5, and 10. SARS-CoV-2 positive participants in quarantine were visited every 5 days until RT-qPCR negative. Symptom diaries recorded severity (Likert 0–3) for 12 symptoms and axillary temperature per Jackson (1958). AEs recorded via diaries and visits, coded by MedDRA v17.1GE; concomitant medications recorded and coded by WHO ATC L3.

Laboratory methods: NP/OP swabs for general RTIs collected with sterile FLOQ swabs in eNAT medium; RT-qPCR using VIASURE Respiratory Panel IV (CerTest BIOTEC) targeting rhinoviruses, enteroviruses, adenoviruses, and enveloped viruses (influenza A/B, parainfluenza 1–4, RSV A/B, coronaviruses 229E/NL63/OC43/HKU1, metapneumovirus, bocavirus). NP/OP swabs for SARS-CoV-2 collected with Σ-Transwabs in Amies medium; RT-qPCR using TaqPath COVID-19 (ThermoFisher). Serology: Elecsys Anti SARS-CoV-2 (Roche) for IgG/IgM. Samples stored at −80°C; analyses performed at Bodimed (Sofia) per manufacturer protocols. Ct values pooled (S/N/ORF1ab) for load estimation. Ct values below detection set to 45 (respiratory panel) or 40 (SARS-CoV-2). Missing Ct due to hospitalization replaced by last observation carried forward to day 10.

Statistical analysis: Descriptive biometric approaches with pre-specified primary endpoint (incidence of viral RTIs). Power calculation (nQuery Advisor 7.0): two-group chi-square, α=0.05, 80% power to detect a 0.12 difference (absolute rates 0.10 EF vs 0.23 control) with N≥50/group; planned N=120 (60/60). Adjusted RR/OR for relative observation time; two-sided p<0.05 significant. SAS 9.4 used.

title: EMBO Mol Med (2021) 13: e13180
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do intraductal xenografts of ILC-derived cell lines and patient-derived cells model human ILC biology (growth, invasion, metastasis, histopathology, ER/PR signaling)? (2) What tumor cell-intrinsic molecular programs distinguish ILC from non-lobular ER+ HER2− breast cancers? (3) Is ECM remodeling a targetable feature of ILC, and does LOX/LOXL1 inhibition impair tumor growth and metastasis?

Hypotheses: (a) Intraductal grafting will yield robust ILC xenografts that recapitulate LCIS-like in situ growth, invasion, and ILC-typical metastatic patterns. (b) Purified ILC tumor cells will exhibit an ECM remodeling signature distinct from non-ILC ER+ HER2− tumors. (c) LOX/LOXL1 activity is required for ILC ECM remodeling and tumor progression; pharmacologic LOX inhibition and LOXL1 knockdown will reduce growth and metastasis and disrupt collagen organization. Supportive outcomes include: higher matrisome scores in ILC, LOXL1 upregulation in ILC tumor cells, BAPN-induced growth/metastasis reduction and collagen disruption, and LOXL1 knockdown impairing invasion and proliferation. Refutation would involve lack of ECM signature enrichment, no LOXL1 expression in ILC, or absence of therapeutic effects of LOX inhibition.
reference_methodology:
Human samples: Tissue collection was approved by the Commission Cantonale d’éthique de la recherche sur l’être humain (CER-VD 38/15; PB_2016-01185). Informed consent was obtained. After margin inking and pathologist assessment, tumor tissue was transported in DMEM/F12, mechanically and enzymatically dissociated, erythrocytes lysed, and single cells prepared with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA, DNase I, and filtration (70 μm). Cells were transduced with ffLuc2/eGFP lentivirus (CMV promoter) via spin infection (25°C, 400 g, 2.5 h).

Animals and grafting: NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) and NSG-EGFP mice (JAX 021937) were used. Female mice (8–12 weeks) were anesthetized (xylazine 10 mg/kg; ketamine 90 mg/kg) and intraductally injected into the 3rd thoracic and 4th inguinal ducts with 4–8 μl PBS containing 200,000–500,000 cells. Engraftment was monitored by bioluminescence imaging (Xenogen IVIS 200) after intraperitoneal luciferin (150 mg/kg, 10 min prior). For metastasis detection, mice received 300 μl luciferin 7 min before sacrifice; organs were imaged and luminescence normalized to ungrafted controls.

Histology and imaging: Mammary glands were fixed (4% paraformaldehyde), paraffin-embedded, sectioned (4 μm), and stained with H&E, carmine alum, picrosirius red, or DAPI. IHC/IF used standard antigen retrieval (10 mM sodium citrate, pH 6.0, 95°C, 25 min), blocking (1% BSA), primary antibodies (Appendix Table S1), and secondary antibodies. Confocal imaging used Zeiss LSM700; stereo-microscopy used Leica M205 FA. GFP/RFP area ratios and corrected total cell fluorescence (CTCF) were quantified in ImageJ. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) imaging used a Leica SP5 2-photon microscope (800 nm excitation; NDD1 400/15 nm; NDD2 460/50 nm; 20×/1.00 water objective).

Pharmacology and genetics: BAPN (Sigma-Aldrich A3134) was administered intraperitoneally (800 mg/kg daily) or in drinking water (3 mg/ml). For LOXL1 knockdown, GIPZ shRNA lentiviruses targeting human LOXL1 (V3LHS_361816 selected for 85% transcript reduction by qRT-PCR) or non-silencing control (RHS4346) were used. Cells were transduced, sorted by FACS for GFP, and grafted intraductally. Randomization was performed to equalize baseline radiance; investigators were not blinded to group allocation.

RNA-seq and computational analysis: For PDXs, GFP+ tumor cells were FACS-sorted; ~20,000 cells per sample were RNA-seq’d (NuGEN Ovation RNA-Seq V2; Illumina HiSeq 2500). For SUM44, libraries were prepared in two steps and sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 500 (85 nt single-end). Reads were aligned to mm9 (TopHat v2.0.11), counted (FeatureCounts), normalized (TMM; voom), and differentially expressed genes analyzed with edgeR GLMs (GLM likelihood-ratio test; P<0.05). GSEA and REACTOME/MSigDB pathway enrichment used ClusterProfiler and ReactomePA. TCGA analyses used matrisome signatures (44 collagens, 195 glycoproteins) and LOX family expression, adjusting for tumor purity (Aran et al.).

title: Cephalometric Changes Induced by Splitting of the Midpalatal Suture on a Lateral Cephalometric Roentgenogram
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What cephalometric angular changes (SNA, SNB, ANB) occur in children following rapid midpalatal suture splitting using a fixed split acrylic appliance? (2) Are these changes statistically significant and clinically meaningful? (3) Are the changes predictable across patients and occlusal classes?

Hypotheses (implicit from aims): (a) Rapid expansion advances the maxilla (increases SNA), (b) the mandibular plane drops (decreases SNB), and (c) the maxillomandibular relationship shifts (increases ANB). Support would be directional increases in SNA and ANB and decreases in SNB with statistically significant t-tests. Null outcomes would be nonsignificant changes. Alternative possibilities include no change or inconsistent directionality, which would suggest limited or variable treatment effects.
reference_methodology:
Design: Retrospective analysis of pre- and post-treatment lateral cephalometric roentgenograms from 31 North American Caucasian children who underwent rapid palatal expansion. No control group was included.

Participants: N=31; age 10–15 years; 19 girls, 12 boys; 12 late mixed dentition, 19 early permanent dentition; occlusal classes: 14 Class I, 9 Class II, 8 Class III. Selection criterion: completeness of records and confirmed midpalatal suture opening.

Imaging: Lateral head cephalograms taken in a standing position using a Cephalometrix Cephalostat. Efforts were made to standardize technique to enable superimposition and valid angular/linear measurements. Films were obtained before appliance placement and at the end of rapid expansion (typically 10–15 days).

Appliance and activation: Tissue-borne fixed split acrylic maxillary palatal expansion appliance (Haas-type) with a central jackscrew across the midline. Rocky Mountain conventional type A-611 expansion screw; approximately 0.8–0.9 mm per 60° turn; ~0.2 mm per patient turn. Anchorage: bands on maxillary first premolars and first molars; buccal and lingual bars contoured close to gingiva and soldered for strength; occasionally extended to canines/second molars. Activation protocol: 2–3 turns upon placement and 2–3 turns daily (older patients sometimes 2 turns/day), typically continued until ~4–6 mm activation (10–15 days). Appliances were used as retainers for 4–6 months.

Measurements: Angular measurements to the nearest 0.5° using the Loyola University Cephalometric Analysis: SNA (A-point position relative to SN), SNB (B-point position relative to SN), and ANB (difference SNA–SNB). Landmarks included S (sella), N (nasion), A (subspinale), B (supramentale). Tracings were performed on matte acetate.

Control accuracy: One cephalogram was traced five times on separate days; means and SDs were computed for SNA, SNB, and ANB (Table I). Reported means: SNA 76.2° (SD ±0.24°), SNB 73.5° (SD ±0.45°), ANB 2.7° (SD ±0.4°).

Statistical analysis: Student’s t-tests compared pre- and post-treatment means for SNA, SNB, and ANB. Directional change counts were tabulated (Table II). Means and SDs before and after are reported (Table III). Probability thresholds were interpreted as: SNA t=1.55 (0.15<P<0.10), SNB t=0.319 (0.35<P<0.20), ANB t=1.972 (0.05<P<0.01).

title: Kawasaki disease: serial transthoracic echocardiography and coronary artery Z-scores in the diagnostic work-up
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does serial TTE with coronary artery Z-score monitoring detect early coronary involvement and support KD diagnosis when initial clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic findings are inconclusive? (2) How do coronary artery Z-score distributions compare between complete and incomplete KD? (3) In incomplete KD, how frequently is echocardiography (including serial TTE) required for diagnosis, and does it enable timely treatment without significant delay?

Hypotheses: (a) Serial TTE will reveal significant increases in coronary artery Z-scores over short intervals, enabling KD diagnosis even when initial TTE is normal. (b) Z-score distributions will not differ markedly between complete and incomplete KD, but incomplete KD will more often require echocardiography for diagnosis. (c) Early diagnosis rates will be comparable between complete and incomplete KD when serial TTE is used. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include statistically significant Z-score increases between serial TTEs, a high proportion of incomplete KD cases diagnosed via echocardiography, and similar median days to diagnosis between groups.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Retrospective analysis of clinical records from the Children’s University Hospital Regensburg (KUNO-Clinic St. Hedwig). Study period: March 2002–May 2018. Ethical compliance: Declaration of Helsinki; IRB approval University of Regensburg (file 14-101-0206). Exclusions: missing clinical reports, initial treatment before hospitalization, history of vascular/cardiovascular disease, hematological disorders.

Participants: 124 KD patients aged 2 months–17 years. KD diagnosis per AHA guidelines: complete KD if ≥5 days fever, unresponsive to systemic antibiotics, and ≥4 major criteria; incomplete KD if ≥5 days fever, <4 major criteria, with compatible labs or echocardiographic abnormalities (dilation, ectasia, aneurysm). Demographics and medical history were recorded on admission. Laboratory tests included complete blood count, electrolytes, AST, ALT, γGT, and CRP. Body surface area (BSA) was calculated using Haycock’s formula. The first reported day of fever was defined as day 0.

Interventions and management: Standard KD therapy included IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10 h and acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) 40–100 mg/kg in four divided doses within 24 h until afebrile for 48–72 h, followed by low-dose ASA 3–5 mg/kg once daily for 6–8 weeks. IVIG unresponsiveness was defined as recrudescent or persistent fever ≥36 h after treatment completion; second IVIG or prednisolone 2 mg/kg was administered as needed.

Echocardiography protocol: Pediatric cardiological evaluation included 12-lead ECG and TTE. Serial TTE was performed when KD could not be diagnosed with clinical findings, laboratory tests, and initial TTE. Equipment: Toshiba Xario XG (since 2013 Aplio 500 CV); transducers 6.5, 5.0, or 3.0 MHz (PST65-BT, PST-50BT, PST-30BT). Positions: supine or left lateral decubitus. Views: parasternal short- and long-axis. Measurements: LMCA, RMCA, LAD, LCX diameters 5 mm distal to ostium; trailing edge to leading edge; if LMCA short stem (<5 mm), measured mid between ostia and branch. Distal segments were considered within normal range if proximal diameters were normal. Z-scores were computed per Dallaire et al. using BSA normalization. Categories: normal (<2 SD), dilation (2–<2.5 SD), small aneurysm (2.5–<5 SD), medium (5–<10 SD), large (≥10 SD or absolute ≥8 mm). Studies were digitally stored for offline analysis and follow-up.

Statistical analysis: Categorical variables summarized as counts and percentages; continuous variables as median (Q1, Q3). Group comparisons: chi-squared test for categorical variables; Mann–Whitney U for continuous variables. Paired Student’s t-tests for changes in Z-scores between serial TTEs. Z-score categories compared between complete and incomplete KD using chi-squared. Significance threshold p<0.05. Software: IBM SPSS Statistics 25.

title: Study of electronic prescribing rates and barriers identified among providers using electronic health records in New York City
field_subfield: Health Informatics — Electronic Health Records and Prescribing
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the trajectory of eRx adoption among NYC primary care providers using PCIP EHRs over 1.5 years (Jan 2009–Jul 2010)? (2) Which practice characteristics are associated with achieving the meaningful use eRx threshold (>40%)? (3) What barriers do providers perceive as limiting eRx use, and how do these align with pharmacy readiness and patient preferences?

Hypotheses (implicit): (a) eRx rates are increasing over time as EHR adoption matures and incentives accrue; (b) practices with greater support staff capacity and longer EHR experience will exhibit higher eRx rates; (c) perceived barriers (patient preference for paper prescriptions, limited pharmacy acceptance, and DME/mail-order exclusions) will be salient among providers. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include a positive linear trend in eRx rates, statistically significant associations between support staff ratios and eRx rates, and qualitative evidence of patient- and pharmacy-related barriers. Outcomes refuting them would include flat or declining eRx rates, no association with support staff ratios, or minimal perceived barriers.
reference_methodology:
Design: Observational analysis of aggregate, de-identified EHR utilization data from PCIP practices, complemented by provider surveys and a pharmacy map.

Setting and participants: 376 primary care practices (internal medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics/gynecology) in medically underserved NYC communities, serving ≥30% Medicaid/uninsured patients. Practices transmit de-identified data monthly to PCIP. A subset of 37 providers participated in phone/in-person surveys.

Data sources: (1) PCIP database of aggregate de-identified counts of EHR utilization, including eRx, transmitted monthly from Jan 2009 to Jul 2010; (2) PCIP EHR database of NYC pharmacies accepting eRx with addresses, used to produce a map; (3) Provider surveys (n=37) assessing attitudes toward eRx and perceived barriers.

Definitions and measures: eRx was defined as an electronically generated prescription using certified EHR technology transmitted directly to a pharmacy system. Fax-based transmission did not qualify as eRx. eRx rate was computed as the number of office visits with an eRx divided by the number of office visits with any prescription, calculated monthly per provider. Aggregate analyses summarized rates across practices and compared groups (e.g., EHR adoption duration).

Statistical analysis: Chi-square tests examined associations between achieving eRx >40% and practice characteristics: number of office visits with prescriptions, number of prescriptions written, and support staff to full-time equivalent provider ratio. Significance threshold was p<0.05. Analyses and graphics were performed in SPSS. No multivariable modeling, effect sizes, or confidence intervals were reported.

Procedures: Monthly aggregate counts were extracted from PCIP’s EHR network. A pharmacy map was generated to visualize eRx-enabled pharmacies and provider locations. Surveys captured provider perceptions of eRx benefits, workflow impacts, and barriers. The study also contextualized findings with literature on eRx benefits and incentives (e.g., CMS eRx incentive program).

Ethics: Data were de-identified and HIPAA-compliant; no patient-level identifiers were used. IRB approval and consent procedures were not reported.

title: Comprehensive and Professional Solutions for all Heritage Related Matters
research_question:
The Terms of Reference define the study’s objectives: (1) identify all archaeological/historical cultural heritage resources within the proposed development footprint; (2) assess their significance across archaeological, historical, scientific, social, religious, aesthetic, and tourism values; (3) describe potential impacts of the proposed development; (4) propose mitigation measures; and (5) review applicable legislation. The implicit research questions are: Are there cultural heritage resources within the direct footprint of Shafts 7 and 10? What is their significance? What are the likely impacts of the proposed underground mining and associated infrastructure? What mitigation is required?

The working hypothesis is that the proposed development will not impact significant cultural heritage resources within the direct footprint, but that some historical mining-related features may exist and require mitigation. Alternative possibilities include the presence of subterranean or previously undocumented prehistoric/early Iron Age remains, or unmarked burials, which would necessitate additional assessment and protection. Outcomes supporting the hypothesis include the absence of significant resources in the footprint and the identification of only non-significant, non-protected historical structures. Outcomes refuting it would include discovery of protected structures (>60 years), graves, or significant archaeological sites within the footprint.
reference_methodology:
Design: A Heritage Impact Assessment (HIA) following standard phases: pre-assessment/scoping, baseline assessment, Phase I impact assessment, exemption letter (if applicable), Phase II mitigation/rescue, and Phase III management plan. The study combined literature review, field survey, and documentation.

Literature review: Historical sources and maps were consulted to contextualize the area. Key references include Bergh (1999) for regional archaeological and historical context, and Lombard et al. (2012) for the Stone Age sequence. The Chief Surveyor General (CSG) database provided 1916 survey documents (Portion 1: Document No. 10547601; Portion 3: Document No. 10I7KPO1). A 1914/1952 Brakpan Mines map (updated annually) was provided by Mr. Herbie Trouw, indicating mining features and two "Native Cemeteries".

Field survey: Conducted per generally accepted HIA practices, focusing on areas around Shafts 7 and 10, with some broader area inspection due to illegal mining risks. The team was accompanied by a client representative and security personnel. GPS was used to record coordinates where possible; detailed photographs were taken. Oral histories were considered when applicable but were not systematically conducted in this case. The assessment documented sites, features, and objects according to minimum standards, including locality coordinates and descriptions.

Project description: The Gedex Project involves re-equipping two incline shafts (7# for personnel/materials; 10# for ore/waste) for underground mining. Mining will occur at ~60–150 mbs, with the current water level at 153 mbs and operations planned ~25 m above the water level. Surface infrastructure includes perimeter fencing, unpaved roads (sealed with chemical dust suppressant), steel headgears (12 m at 7#, 21 m at 10#), winders housed in shipping containers, a 500 T headgear bin at 10# (timber-lined), and covered employee drop-off areas. Hoisting will operate 24 h; hauling 12 h/day (06:00–18:00). Ore will be transported by 20 T trucks to Modder East for processing; tailings will be deposited at Modder East’s existing facility. Approximately 440 employees will be employed across three 8 h shifts; transport from Modder East to 7# will be by bus (single bus seating 60; ~30 min roundtrip). The suburb of Sherwood Gardens (~700 m from 10#) will provide municipal services.

Legislation and ethics: NHRA protections include permits for altering/demolishing structures >60 years and destruction permits for archaeological sites. Graves require permissions from descendants, health departments, provincial authorities, and police, with handling by registered undertakers or institutions under the Human Tissues Act. NEMA mandates surveys and evaluations for developments changing the environment, minimizing disturbance to cultural heritage landscapes. The report notes that many historical structures near the shafts are less than 60 years old and thus not protected under NHRA.

title: Limitations of Atomistic Molecular Dynamics to Reveal Ejection of Proteins from Charged Nanodroplets
