field_subfield: Chemistry — Physical Chemistry (Mass Spectrometry and Molecular Dynamics)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the likelihood of ejection of unstructured linear macromolecules (PEG, protonated peptides, proteins) from aqueous charged droplets in the size window accessible to atomistic MD? (2) Can atomistic MD observations of macromolecule charging and ejection be extrapolated to larger droplets? (3) What additional factors (e.g., droplet curvature, conical fluctuations, jets) govern macromolecule charging and ejection in larger droplets?

Hypotheses: (H1) Atomistic MD will show low ejection probability for proteins and peptides in small droplets, implying that observed ejection in experiments likely occurs via jets in larger droplets. (H2) Droplet curvature and conformational dynamics will modulate macromolecule charging, producing a critical droplet size above which charging is transient. (H3) Conical fluctuations near RL will assist extrusion by capturing segments or facilitating repulsion with co-ions. Support for H1 would be rare ejection in small droplets; for H2, transient vs permanent sodiation across droplet sizes; for H3, extrusion events coinciding with conical fluctuations and Na+ accumulation.
reference_methodology:
Software: NAMD 2.12 for PEG and peptides; GROMACS 2018.3 for myoglobin comparisons. Visualization: VMD 1.9.2.

PEG systems: PEG54 (54 monomers) in aqueous droplets with ~5×10^3 and ~10^4 H2O molecules and Na+ ions near the Rayleigh limit (RL). Na+ counts: 18 (5×10^3 H2O) and 25–29 (10^4 H2O). Temperatures: 300 K and 350 K. Water model: modified-TIP3P (mTIP3P). Surface tension values used for RL: 0.0523 N/m (300 K) and 0.0432 N/m (350 K). Equilibrium runs placed droplets in spherical cavities (radius 20.0 nm) to allow shape fluctuations; non-equilibrium runs evaporated droplets in vacuo. Time step: 1.0 fs; Langevin thermostat (damping 1 ps^-1). Long-range forces computed directly.

Protonated peptides: Sequences (Val6–Lys+)3–Val6, (Val10–Lys+)3–Val10, and Val10–Lys+–Val10 embedded in ~2100 H2O with 11 Na+ to achieve total charge +14 (first two) or +12 (last). Water model: mTIP3P. Equilibrium runs at 300 K and 350 K; non-equilibrium runs at 350 K. Equilibrium runs: ~100 H2O evaporated to establish vapor pressure in a 20.0 nm cavity. Non-equilibrium runs: quintuples at 350 K. Initial conformations: equilibrium conformations established within cavities; non-equilibrium runs started from equilibrium states.

Myoglobin: Two PDBs (1MBN, 1WLA) with similar sequences (134/153 identical). Charge states: 1MBN 17+ and 23+; 1WLA 22+[A,C]. 1MBN modeled with CHARMM36m; 1WLA with CHARMM36. Water: mTIP3P (1MBN) and TIP4P/2005 (1WLA). Solvent counts: ~2.0×10^4–2.25×10^4 H2O. Total system charge: +36 (1MBN 23+ with 13 Na+; 1MBN 17+ with 19 Na+). Initial conformations: 1MBN generated by stretching in gas phase, zeroing charges, and relaxing to a loose coil; 1WLA 22+[A,C] prepared by gas-phase relaxation (100 ns) and solvation. For 1MBN, additional runs restrained the protein near the droplet surface for 5 ns before evaporation. 1WLA simulations at 370 K used a cubic box (999 nm), 333 nm cutoffs, direct long-range electrostatics, and trajectory stitching (removing water >100 nm from the COM every 250 ps; velocities reassigned to Boltzmann distribution). Simulation length: 40 ns.

Analysis: Rayleigh fissility parameter X = Q^2/(64π^2γε0R^3) used to assess stability (X<1 stable; X>1 unstable). Radius of gyration (RG) distributions for PEG54 were computed (Figure 5). Ejection events were identified by loss of the macromolecule from the droplet; partial extrusion was tracked via RG and snapshots. Conical fluctuations were qualitatively assessed via shape deformations and Na+ accumulation near the chain.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable (computational study).

title: High Accuracy WiFi-Based Human Activity Classification System with Time-Frequency Diagram CNN Method for Different Places
field_subfield: Computer Science — Wireless Communications and Machine Learning
research_question:
Research question: Can converting WiFi CSI into time-frequency diagrams and classifying them with a CNN improve cross-environment robustness for human activity classification (including fall detection) compared to raw CSI-based DNNs and handcrafted feature classifiers?

Hypothesis: For the same human action performed in different static environments, the frequency components in CSI’s channel frequency response (CFR) remain similar, while amplitude varies with environment. Therefore, time-frequency diagrams derived from CSI will be more invariant to environmental changes than raw CSI amplitude/phase or handcrafted features, enabling higher accuracy when tested in different locations.

Predictions: (1) In same-place testing, the proposed CNN on time-frequency diagrams will match or exceed SVM and DNN baselines. (2) In cross-environment testing, the proposed method will maintain high accuracy (≥90%), whereas SVM and DNN baselines will drop substantially. (3) Holding objects during falls will not significantly alter the time-frequency patterns, indicating robustness to certain perturbations. Outcomes supporting the hypothesis include higher cross-environment accuracy for the proposed method and stability of time-frequency patterns across objects and locations.
reference_methodology:
Data collection: Experiments were conducted in a 6 m × 6 m conference room with a commercial AP as Tx and a laptop with an Intel 5300 NIC as Rx in LOS, 3 m apart (Figure 5). Four actions were recorded: bed, fall, sit down, and walk. Sampling rate was 1 kHz. Five volunteers performed each action multiple times: falls >10, sit >20, walk >30, bed >30. Safety measures included crash mats, pads, and removal of unnecessary furniture. The study used all necessary safety equipment and was supervised by laboratory directors.

Data sources: The online dataset [16] contained six actions (bed, fall, walk, run, sit down, stand up). The authors used four actions (bed, fall, walk, sit down) due to limited entries for run and stand up. For training/testing, the authors’ collected data were used for cross-environment evaluation; the online dataset was used for same-place evaluation.

Signal processing: CSI was collected using a Linux 802.11n CSI tool and denoised via Discrete Wavelet Denoising (DND) with Symlet-4 (sym4) to preserve abrupt changes and reduce noise. The rationale for Symlet-4 is its higher symmetry and reduced distortion in reconstruction. Alternative denoising methods (WMA, Butterworth filter) were discussed but not used in the final pipeline. Phase sanitization was mentioned for phase errors but not detailed in the final implementation.

Feature transformation: Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) was applied to denoised CSI to produce time-frequency diagrams. The authors argue that for the same action, frequency components in CFR remain similar across environments, while amplitude varies, making time-frequency diagrams more robust to environmental changes.

Classification: The time-frequency diagrams were treated as images and fed into a pretrained GoogLeNet (Inception) classifier implemented via NVIDIA DIGITS. The study used five-fold cross-validation for evaluation. For comparison, an SVM classifier used eight features: variance, normalized STD, MAD, IQR, signal entropy, offset of signal strength, mean of velocity of signal change, and max of velocity of signal change. A DNN baseline used denoised CSI as input without STFT; the authors note that the DNN’s lower accuracy may partly reflect insufficient data and lack of STFT-derived features.

Evaluation protocol: Same-place testing used the online dataset [16] with five-fold cross-validation. Cross-environment testing used the authors’ collected data from five volunteers, with the same actions and LOS setup. The study reports per-class and average accuracies for both same-place and different-place conditions. No additional statistical tests (e.g., confidence intervals) or hyperparameter details (e.g., STFT parameters, CNN fine-tuning specifics) are reported.

title: Maximal Isometric Handgrip Strength and Strength-Endurance in Recreational and Ambitious Sport Climbers: A Time-Series Analysis Across Arm-Hand Positions
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do maximal isometric handgrip strength and strength-endurance (SDI) differ between recreational and ambitious climbers? (2) How do these metrics vary by limb dominance (left vs right) and climbing-specific arm–hand positions (upper straight vs lifted)? (3) Is the strength decrement index (SDI) sensitive to differences in climbing level? (4) Are asymmetry levels (left–right differences) associated with climbing level and position?

Hypotheses: The authors hypothesized that the time course of grip strength decline would differ between ambitious and recreational climbers, with a steeper decline and lower maximal grip strength in recreational climbers. They further anticipated that maximal grip strength would be higher on the dominant (right) side and that climbing-specific positions might modulate performance. Outcomes supporting the hypothesis would include significant group differences in SDI and/or maximal strength across positions, with larger declines and lower absolute strength in recreational climbers. Outcomes refuting the hypothesis would include no group differences in SDI despite differences in maximal strength, and consistent side effects independent of group.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional, within-subjects repeated-measures study comparing recreational and ambitious climbers on maximal isometric handgrip strength and repetitive strength-endurance across two climbing-specific arm–hand positions and left/right sides.

Participants: Twenty-eight right-handed young adult indoor sport climbers (recreational n=17; ambitious n=11). Inclusion criteria: ≥1 year of indoor climbing; no acute/chronic cardio-circulatory, metabolic diseases, health complaints, or prior injury. Climbing level reported as best redpoint ascent (UIAA metric) within the current year; ambitious group required ≥8.0 UIAA. Anthropometrics included body mass, height, BMI, and ape index (arm span/body height). Demographics (Table 1): recreational (n=17) vs ambitious (n=11) vs total (n=28): sex (f/m) 3/14 vs 0/11 vs 3/25; age 25.1±7.4 vs 30.6±8.2 vs 27.2±8.0 years; body mass 70.2±9.2 vs 72.2±8.2 vs 71.4±8.8 kg; height 1.78±0.05 vs 1.81±0.09 vs 1.79±0.07 m; BMI 21.5±2.0 vs 21.8±1.9 vs 21.6±1.9 kg/m²; ape index 1.06±0.23 vs 1.01±0.03 vs 1.05±0.18; climbing level 6.8±0.5 vs 8.7±0.6 vs 7.6±1.0 (UIAA); training frequency 2.0±0.9 vs 2.5±1.1 vs 2.2±1.0 times/week. Only climbing level differed significantly (p<0.001).

Ethics: Informed consent obtained; study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013). Ethical approval: German Sport University (127/2020). Data were collected during standard handgrip screening.

Apparatus and familiarization: Hydraulic handgrip dynamometer (Saehan, Masan, Korea). Participants practiced trials and hand mobilizations to familiarize with the device. Heart rate monitored via Polar Accurex Plus chest strap. Perceived exertion (RPE) recorded using the 6–20 Borg scale.

Positions and order: Four positions from seated: (a) upper arm straight beside trunk, no abduction/rotation, elbow 90°; (b) lifted arm, 90° abduction and 90° external rotation; mirrored for left and right hands. Order of the four positions was inter-individually randomized.

Protocol: Two sets of the four positions were performed. Within each set, the four positions were tested sequentially with 5-minute breaks between positions; a 10-minute break separated the two sets. The best trial of each position was retained for analysis. Before endurance testing, maximal isometric handgrip strength was assessed in each of the four positions. Each endurance attempt consisted of 12 consecutive work–relief cycles at maximal effort. Work period: 4 s; relief: 1 s; acoustic cues signaled work and relief. Verbal encouragement (“go, go, go, go”) during work and “relax” during relief were provided. Force–time data were recorded at 100 Hz using a Sony HandyCam DCR-DVD 201E PAL.

Outcomes: Maximal isometric handgrip strength (kg) and relative force (kg/kg body mass). Strength-endurance quantified via SDI (%): SDI = ((mean_first_three_work_phases − mean_last_three_work_phases)/mean_first_three_work_phases) × 100. Heart rate (bpm) and RPE were recorded before and after each endurance set; RPE was collected after the final repetition.

Statistical analysis: Normality (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) and homogeneity (Levene) were tested. Demographics analyzed via MANOVA with follow-up univariate tests. Side comparisons (left vs right) for maximal grip strength, SDI, and RPE were analyzed with 2 (group: recreational vs ambitious) × 2 (side: left vs right) repeated-measures ANOVAs for upper and lower positions. Time-course of maximal grip strength was analyzed with a 2 (side) × 2 (position: upper vs lower) × 12 (time: 12 cycles) repeated-measures ANOVA. Tukey’s HSD post hoc tests were used for significant main or interaction effects. Heart rate analyses followed the same repeated-measures framework. Spearman correlations assessed asymmetry (left–right differences) in upper and lower positions separately for each group. Effect sizes: partial eta squared (ηp²) for ANOVAs (small ≥0.01; medium ≥0.059; large ≥0.138) and Cohen’s d for pairwise comparisons (trivial <0.2; small 0.2–0.49; moderate 0.5–0.79; large ≥0.8).

title: PathoFact: a unified metagenomic pipeline for simultaneous prediction of virulence factors, bacterial toxins and antimicrobial resistance genes with mobile genetic element localization
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a unified pipeline accurately and efficiently predict virulence factors, bacterial toxins, and ARGs from metagenomic assemblies while contextualizing these features by their localization on MGEs? (2) Does integrating multiple tools and databases improve detection compared to existing workflows (MOCAT2, HUMAnN3) on simulated datasets? (3) Do virulence factors, toxins, and ARG categories differ between disease and control metagenomes in public case-control datasets (CDI, psoriasis, Parkinson’s disease)?

Hypotheses: (H1) A combined HMM plus random forest classifier will outperform standalone HMM or MP3 for virulence prediction, achieving high sensitivity/specificity. (H2) A toxin HMM database combined with SignalP will achieve high specificity with reasonable sensitivity. (H3) Merging DeepARG and RGI will yield high accuracy for ARG prediction and improved detection compared to individual tools. (H4) On simulated data, PathoFact will detect more virulence/toxin features than MOCAT2/HUMAnN3 and perform comparably for ARGs. (H5) In disease vs control metagenomes, specific toxin domains and ARG categories will be differentially abundant, reflecting disease-associated pathogenic potential and resistance profiles.

Support/refutation: H1–H3 are supported by reported metrics (virulence sensitivity 0.886, specificity 0.957; toxins sensitivity 0.777, specificity 0.989; AMR combined sensitivity 0.963, specificity 0.994). H4 is supported by ANOVA showing higher virulence/toxin predictions for PathoFact (p<0.05). H5 is partially supported: several toxin domains and ARG categories were differentially abundant in disease vs control, but virulence factor abundance differences were not significant.
reference_methodology:
Design: The study develops and validates PathoFact, a modular metagenomic pipeline, and evaluates it on curated validation datasets, a simulated CAMI high-complexity dataset, and three public case-control metagenomes (CDI, psoriasis, Parkinson’s disease). The pipeline integrates three workflows (virulence factors, toxins, ARGs) and MGE localization.

Implementation: Written in Python (v3.6) with Snakemake (v5.5.4) and conda (v4.7). Inputs are contig FASTA files. ORFs are predicted with Prodigal (v2.6.3). MGEs are predicted from the assembly; a mapping file aggregates results. Outputs include module-specific and consolidated reports with confidence levels, resistance mechanisms, and MGE localization.

Virulence factor prediction: Training set comprised 8945 positive sequences (VFDB core) and 7995 negative sequences (DEG), clustered at 90% identity (CD-HIT) to reduce redundancy. HMMER3 (v3.2.1) annotated HMM profiles against PFAM-A, TIGR, KEGG, MetaCyc, and SwissProt; best hits were selected if HMM score exceeded log2(target genes). HMM profiles were concatenated into a virulence HMM database (hmmpress). A random forest classifier (scikit-learn v0.21.3) used five features: amino acid composition (AAC), dipeptide composition (DPC), composition (CTDC), transition (CTDT), and distribution (CTDD). The model had 1600 trees with maximum depth 340. SignalP (v5.0) predicted secretion to distinguish secreted vs non-secreted virulence factors.

Toxin prediction: Training set compiled from T3DB and DBETH-derived sequences, clustered at 90% identity (CD-HIT-2D) to remove redundancy. Toxin HMM profiles were identified from PFAM, TIGR, KEGG, MetaCyc, and SwissProt, and combined with existing toxin-domain HMMs. A toxin library listed HMM profiles, names, aliases, and source databases. HMMER3 (v3.2.1) hmmsearch was used; SignalP (v5.0) distinguished secreted vs non-secreted toxins.

ARG prediction: DeepARG (v1.0.1) and RGI (v5.1.0) were used. DeepARG integrates CARD, ARDB, and UNIPROT and reduces false negatives; RGI identifies mutation-driven resistance. For validation, NCBI resistance gene database (5265 sequences) was used as positive set; DEG provided negatives (equal size). DeepARG default settings with model LS and type prot; RGI default settings with input-type protein.

MGE prediction: PlasFlow (v1.1) for plasmids; VirSorter (v1.0.6) and DeepVirFinder (v1.0) for phages. Predictions were merged to classify localization as plasmid, phage, genome, unclassified, or ambiguous.

Validation datasets: Virulence validation set: 2639 positive (VFDB) and 2628 negative (DEG) sequences, non-overlapping with training. Toxin validation set: 202 positive (EMBL-EBI UniProt-annotated bacterial toxins, filtered to exclude hypothetical/probable; clustered at 90% identity) and 202 negative (housekeeping genes). AMR validation set: NCBI resistance gene database (5265) positive and DEG (5265) negative.

Case-control datasets: CDI (PRJNA297269), psoriasis (PRJNA281366), PD (ERP019674). Reads were processed and assembled with IMP (v2). FeatureCounts (v1.6.4) quantified reads per functional category; relative abundance of toxin genes used Rnum_Gi; differential abundance used DESeq2 (v1.24).

Simulated dataset: CAMI high-complexity toy test with 5 time series, 596 genomes, 478 circular elements. Reads were assembled with IMP (v2) and analyzed with PathoFact; MOCAT2 and HUMAnN3 were run on original reads with default settings.

Metrics: Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy defined as standard classification metrics. Similarity between training and validation sets was assessed with sourmash after removing 90% identity overlaps.

title: Oral amelanotic malignant melanoma: a case report
research_question: The implicit clinical questions are: (1) How can oral amelanotic melanoma be reliably diagnosed when pigmentation is absent? (2) What surgical and adjuvant strategies are appropriate for localized oral melanoma, and what short-term outcomes can be expected? The working hypotheses are: (a) Immunohistochemistry is necessary to confirm AMM in clinically amelanotic lesions, given the absence of melanin and potential histologic mimicry; (b) Wide local excision with adequate margins combined with adjuvant radiotherapy can achieve disease control in localized oral melanoma, potentially improving short-term outcomes. Supportive outcomes would include IHC positivity for melanocyte markers (e.g., melan A, S-100) with absence of epithelial or mesenchymal markers (e.g., AE1/AE3, CD34, P63), negative staging imaging for distant disease, and recurrence-free survival at follow-up. Refuting outcomes would include negative IHC for melanocyte markers, evidence of distant metastasis, or early local recurrence despite treatment.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-patient clinical case report with diagnostic imaging, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, surgical intervention, and short-term follow-up.

Patient: 42-year-old woman with a 3-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful gingival mass in the anterior maxilla. No significant medical history. Symptoms included pain, bleeding during meals, and loss of the left central incisor.

Clinical examination: Extraoral view showed an exophytic mass causing mild superior labial swelling and preventing lip closure. Intraoral examination revealed a pink, sessile, non-pigmented mass measuring 4 cm, firm with an uneven surface and residual blood spots. The lesion occupied the anterior maxillary sector and vestibule, extending to the anterior third of the hard palate and displacing teeth 11 and 22, which were highly mobile.

Imaging: Craniofacial computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a superior soft tissue process extending to the maxillary bone and hard palate with integrity of the maxillary sinus. Thoraco-abdominal CT showed no evidence of distant metastasis. CT coronal and axial views documented palatal bone destruction and a soft tissue mass arising in the anterior maxilla with bone erosion.

Biopsy and histopathology: Incisional biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated proliferation of spindle-shaped cells with round or oval nuclei, moderate nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and numerous mitotic figures. No melanin pigment was identified in the cells.

Immunohistochemistry: Tumor cells strongly expressed melan A and S-100. AE1/AE3, CD34, and P63 were negative. These findings supported a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

Surgical management: Under general anesthesia, tumor resection with 2 cm safety margins was performed. A partial maxillectomy from tooth 15 to 25 was conducted, with removal of part of the vestibule and hard palate. Therapeutic neck dissection was not performed due to absent clinical or radiologic evidence of lymph node metastasis.

Adjuvant therapy and follow-up: The patient underwent adjuvant radiotherapy and received dental care and prosthetic reconstruction. At 9 months post-surgery, clinical examination showed absence of local recurrence, lymphatic involvement, or distant metastasis.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported.

title: ''Now, I know my life is not over!': Introduction and Adaptation of the RESPECT HIV Intervention, OraQuick, and Trauma-Informed Care for Female Victims of Non-Partner Sexual Violence in Haiti
field_subfield: Public Health — HIV Prevention and Trauma-Informed Care
research_question:
The study posed six research questions: (1) Are contextual characteristics of NPSV in Cité Soleil consistent with prior reports, and do they heighten HIV susceptibility? (2) Are key concepts in the Haitian Kreyòl RESPECT EBI understandable and acceptable to NPSV victims and health providers? (3) Is the Haitian Kreyòl RESPECT feasible to implement in Cité Soleil? (4) Can NPSV victims demonstrate knowledge gain in administering and interpreting OraQuick oral fluid HIV testing? (5) Can NPSV victims establish the necessary social support that is part of RESPECT? (6) Is a TIC approach desired by victims and health providers?

Implicit hypotheses were that: (a) NPSV characteristics would align with prior findings and elevate HIV risk; (b) the Haitian Kreyòl RESPECT would be understandable, acceptable, and feasible; (c) participants would correctly interpret OraQuick results; (d) TIC would be desired to mitigate stigma and support agency. Supportive outcomes would include convergent qualitative evidence of acceptability/feasibility, correct interpretation of OraQuick procedures/results, and endorsement of TIC. Refutation would involve low acceptability, misunderstanding of OraQuick, or rejection of TIC.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative adaptation study (ADAPT-ITT Phase 3: Administration/Adaptation) using focus groups to assess acceptability, feasibility, and preliminary knowledge gain.

Setting and participants: Cité Soleil, Haiti, a densely populated shantytown with high poverty and gang violence. Purposive sampling recruited 32 stakeholders: 16 female NPSV victims (ages 18–41; mean 24; 20% married; 20% reported income as food vendors) and 16 health providers (ages 24–42; mean 27.8; 100% single; 43.75% employed; professions included social workers, nurses, physicians, psychologists). Two focus groups were held with victims and two with health providers (8 per group). Recruitment was constrained by safety and financial limitations; a small sample was justified for rich stakeholder insights and ADAPT-ITT requirements.

Procedures: Focus groups were conducted at the El Rancho Hotel in Pétion-Ville (20-minute drive from Cité Soleil) to maximize safety and privacy. Each session lasted ~120 minutes with two 15-minute breaks; food/drink provided; no monetary incentive. The primary author (PA), fluent in Haitian Kreyòl, moderated using motivational interviewing (MI) to enhance safety, respect, and reflective listening while addressing coercive risk profiles. The PA summarized prior NPSV findings, defined EBIs, introduced RESPECT’s core elements and timeframe, and demonstrated RESPECT via role play with a volunteer. Participants then viewed two OraQuick videos: (1) sample collection and result interpretation; (2) placing the sample in the solution bottle and interpreting a reactive result. The PA introduced TIC principles, linked them to NPSV experiences, and facilitated discussion on acceptability, feasibility, and desirability. Participants provided verbal feedback on RESPECT, OraQuick, and TIC.

Data collection and management: Informed consent was obtained; participants summarized purpose, voluntariness, benefits/risks, and alternatives. Audio recordings were made with permission; OREZON colleagues witnessed signed consent. A bilingual transcriptionist transcribed Haitian Kreyòl to English; the PA reconciled discrepancies with audio. Transcripts were imported into ATLAS.ti 6.2 for analysis.

Analysis: A structured codebook guided open and axial coding. The PA conducted open coding, then grouped codes into categories. ATLAS.ti’s hermeneutic framework supported code groundedness (frequency) and code density (linkages). Axial coding used network views to explore relationships among categories and retrieve supporting texts. Rigor steps included bilingual transcription, moderator notes, consensus on transcripts and codes, and mitigation of groupthink (encouraging divergent perspectives, offering post-session contact). No quantitative outcomes were collected; findings are qualitative with illustrative quotes and counts of participants (e.g., 100% correct interpretation of OraQuick results from videos).

title: Seismic waveforms and velocity model heterogeneity: Towards a full-waveform microseismic location algorithm
field_subfield: Geophysics — Seismic Monitoring and Wave Propagation
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do velocity model choice and source frequency affect microseismic event location accuracy when using a ray-based eikonal solver? (2) Can a wide-angle one-way acoustic wave equation with velocity model interpolation provide accurate travel-time and amplitude predictions suitable for full-waveform microseismic location, and what interpolation density (N) is required as a function of frequency and heterogeneity? (3) How do travel-time and amplitude errors from the one-way solver compare to an exact wide-angle solution, and where do discrepancies arise (e.g., near velocity transitions)?

Hypotheses: (H1) Ray-based eikonal solvers will underperform in strongly heterogeneous, borehole-relevant settings, yielding larger location errors when the velocity model used for location does not match the true model. (H2) A wide-angle one-way acoustic solver with modest interpolation (N≈3–4) can predict travel-times within typical picking errors (2–3 ms) across practical frequencies (e.g., 150 Hz), while amplitude accuracy requires higher N. (H3) Increasing the number of velocity interpolants (N) will monotonically improve agreement with the exact wide-angle solution for both amplitude and travel-time, with frequency-dependent sensitivity. Outcomes supporting H1 include larger mislocations for mismatched models and larger confidence ellipses for strongly heterogeneous models. Outcomes supporting H2/H3 include travel-time errors within 2–3 ms at N=3–4 and reduced amplitude errors as N increases, with frequency-dependent trends.
reference_methodology:
Synthetic data generation: Nine synthetic microseismic datasets were created by combining three depth-dependent 2D velocity models (3-layer surface seismic, 13-layer VSP, and 34-layer sonic log) with three geometrically equivalent events at dominant source frequencies of 40, 150, and 300 Hz. Finite-difference simulations used E3D (Larsen and Harris, 1993), a staggered-grid, fourth-order accurate in space and second-order accurate in time solver for isotropic 2D/3D viscoelastic media (Virieux, 1984; 1986). P- and S-wave travel times were manually picked from the synthetics.

Ray-based location evaluation: A fast marching eikonal solver (Madagascar implementation; Sethian, 1996; Sethian and Popovici, 1999) generated discrete travel-time tables from each subsurface point to receivers. Akima interpolation (Akima, 1978) produced continuous travel-time surfaces for the neighborhood algorithm (Sambridge, 1999a,b) to estimate the optimal event location and 90% confidence ellipses. The objective function minimized the root-mean-square misfit between observed and predicted travel times. Nine permutations were evaluated by pairing each synthetic model with each location model (3×3), enabling assessment of model mismatch effects.

One-way wave equation feasibility study: The wide-angle one-way acoustic wave equation (Thomson, 2005) was implemented for 3D acoustic media. The phase propagator P1 and transmission coefficient Q were computed for each extrapolation step along the preferred axis x1, with lateral coordinates xα (α=2,3). To reduce computational cost, a linear velocity wavefield interpolation (LVWI) scheme was used: the velocity model was discretized into N velocities Vi spanning the model’s Vmin to Vmax; for each step, N wavefields φi were computed via the wide-angle equation and then linearly interpolated to the continuous velocity at each lateral grid point. The number of interpolants N was varied from 2 to 7. The Horn River Basin 6-layer P-wave velocity model (Maxwell, 2009) was used, with a vertical array of 128 geophones spaced 6.3 m (aperture ~800 m) at a lateral distance of 250 m from the source. Six dominant source frequencies (50, 100, 125, 150, 250, 500 Hz) and three source depths (2399 m in Muskwa shale; 2490 m in Mid-Devonian carbonate; 2510 m in Evie shale) were tested.

Error metrics: For the one-way solver, travel-time error was computed as the cross-correlation time lag between primary arrivals of the LVWI solution and the exact wide-angle solution. Amplitude error was computed after time alignment as the percentage difference between the maximum amplitudes of the two time-corrected waveforms. For the eikonal-based locations, mislocations and 90% confidence ellipses were reported relative to the true source location. No explicit random seeds, grid sizes, or frequency-domain parameters were reported. No IRB/ethics approvals were applicable.

title: Association of genetic polymorphisms CYP2A6*2 rs1801272 and CYP2A6*9 rs28399433 with tobacco-induced lung Cancer: case-control study in an Egyptian population
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are CYP2A6*2 (rs1801272) and CYP2A6*9 (rs28399433) genotypes associated with lung cancer risk in an Egyptian population? (2) Do these genotypes modify the association between smoking and lung cancer risk? (3) Are there differences in genotype distributions by smoking status, pack-years, age, sex, or histology?

Hypotheses: Based on prior literature, the authors hypothesized that slow-metabolizer variants (CYP2A6*2 and/or *9) would be associated with lower lung cancer risk, potentially via reduced activation of tobacco-specific nitrosamines and/or altered smoking behavior (e.g., lower cigarette consumption). Alternative outcomes include no association with lung cancer risk or higher risk if slow metabolism leads to compensatory smoking patterns or altered exposure to other carcinogens. Outcomes supporting the hypothesis would include significantly lower odds of lung cancer among carriers of CYP2A6*2 and/or *9 compared to wild-type CYP2A6*1AA after adjustment for confounders. Outcomes refuting the hypothesis would include null associations or higher odds among carriers.
reference_methodology:
Design: Case-control study with 150 unrelated adult lung cancer cases and 150 unrelated controls. Cases were recruited from the National Cancer Institute (NCI), Cairo University; controls were randomly sampled. The study was approved by the National Research Center ethics committee, and all participants provided written informed consent.

Participants: Cases were patients with primary lung cancer; controls were unrelated adults without lung cancer. Demographics: mean age cases 56.7 ± 9.79 years vs controls 43.3 ± 11.1 years (p < 0.001). Gender distribution differed (cases 76% male, 24% female; controls 48.7% male, 51.3% female; χ² = 25.82, p < 0.0001). Smoking prevalence was higher in cases (62%) than controls (20%), p < 0.0001; adjusted OR for smoking vs non-smoking 2.78 (95% CI 2.0–3.86).

Data collection: Standardized questionnaires captured demographic information, smoking history (including pack-years), occupational history, and family history of malignancy. Smoking status and pack-years were used as covariates in analyses.

Biospecimen and DNA extraction: Peripheral blood was collected via venipuncture into EDTA tubes. Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA extraction kit following the manufacturer’s protocol.

Genotyping: Two SNPs were genotyped using TaqMan SNP Genotyping Assays on an ABI 7500 Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems). Assay IDs: CYP2A6*2 (1799 T > A; rs1801272; assay ID: C_27861808_60) and CYP2A6*9 (−48 T > G; rs28399433; assay ID: C_30634332_10). Specific VIC/FAM probe sequences were not reported in the provided text. Genotyping quality control included negative controls for all SNPs and duplicate testing of 10% of samples, with 100% concordance.

Statistical analysis: Analyses were conducted in SPSS v18. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Genotype distributions were compared between groups using chi-square (χ²) tests; likelihood ratio tests were used when expected counts were <5 in >20% of cells. Associations between genotype and lung cancer risk were estimated using odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from logistic regression models adjusted for age, smoking status, and pack-years. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. No additional sensitivity analyses, multiple-testing corrections, or interaction tests were reported.

title: Correlation between lamina directions and the mechanical characteristics of laminated bamboo composite for ship structure
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do laminate orientations (unidirectional 0° vs bidirectional 45°/−45° and 0°/90°) affect tensile, bending, and impact properties of laminated bamboo composites? (2) Does adding Waru fiber improve mechanical performance relative to bamboo-only laminates? (3) Do the resulting properties meet BKI thresholds for ship structural applications?

Hypotheses: (H1) On-axis (0°) laminate orientation will yield superior tensile, bending, and impact properties compared to off-axis orientations due to favorable load transfer and stiffness. (H2) Incorporating Waru fiber will increase tensile and bending strengths relative to bamboo-only laminates at the same compaction pressure. (H3) Only on-axis and certain bidirectional orientations (0°/90°) will meet BKI thresholds; 45°/−45° will likely fail due to reduced stiffness and strength. Support for H1 would be higher mean values and lower variability for 0° across tests; support for H2 would be positive percentage increases in tensile and bending strengths with Waru fiber; support for H3 would be compliance with BKI tensile (98 MPa), impact (147 MPa), and modulus thresholds for specific orientations.
reference_methodology:
Materials: Apus bamboo (Gigantochloa apus) culms (3 years old; 1–4.5 m height) were sourced from Bondowoso, East Java. Bamboo slats were prepared by cross-cutting, splitting, and planing to 400 mm × 20 mm blades. Slats were preserved in 2.5% sodium tetraborate and dried to <13% moisture (4–6 h oven drying). Waru (Hibiscus tiliaceus) bast fibers were collected from Tulungagung, East Java, soaked in water for 7 days, combed, and dried by wind convection for 5 days. Surface modification: 5% NaOH at 27°C for 2 h, followed by 0.5% methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane in distilled water (pH adjusted to ~3 with acetic acid), soaking for 4 h, rinsing to pH 7, drying at room temperature for 1 day, then 40°C for 1 h. Epoxy matrix: Bakelite EPR 174 (diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A; epoxy equivalent 189 ± 5 g/eq) with hardener V-140 (cycloaliphatic amine; amine hydrogen equivalent 86 g/eq; viscosity 0.5–1 poise at room temperature). Mix ratio: 2:1 (resin:hardener) by weight; degassed in vacuum for ~20 min.

Manufacturing: Hand lay-up of seven layers with Waru fibers interlayered. First layer: epoxy applied to bamboo surface. Second layer: Waru fibers applied. Slats and fibers were aligned to form boards (40 cm × 20 cm). Cold press at 1.5 MPa; clamp tightened; cure for 24 h. Laser cutting produced specimens per test standards. Mass fractions: bamboo:waru:epoxy = 50:30:20 wt.

Testing: Tensile (ASTM D3039) on WE-1000B UTM (1,000 kN). Specimen: 250 mm × 25 mm × 10 mm. Bottom side clamped; crosshead displacement recorded. Calculations: ultimate tensile strength σmax = Pmax/Ao; tensile stress σi = Pi/A; tensile strain εi = δi/Lg; MOE as slope of stress–strain curve. Bending (ASTM D7264) on WE-1000B at 2.0 mm/min crosshead speed. Specimen: 130 mm × 13 mm × 10 mm; simply supported with midspan load. Flexural stress σ = 3PL/(2bh); flexural strain ε = 6δh/L2; flexural modulus Eflex from stress–strain slope. Charpy impact (ASTM D256) on DB-300A. Specimen: 55 mm × 25 mm × 10 mm with 45° notch. Test conditions: impact energy 150 J (little hammer), speed 5.2 m/s, pendulum angle 150°. Impact resistance Is = (Es − ET)/t, where Es is dial reading breaking energy, ET is total correction energy (accounting for windage and friction), and t is specimen width or notch width.

Sample sizes and statistics: Tensile, bending, and impact tests each used n=4 specimens per orientation. Reported means and standard deviations (SD) are provided in tables. No environmental conditioning (e.g., seawater immersion) or statistical hypothesis testing beyond descriptive statistics was reported.

title: Light and nutrient effects on the growth and photosynthesis of two Bolivian rain forest tree seedlings
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do light availability and nutrient supply affect growth and photosynthesis of S. macrophylla and S. parahybum seedlings? (2) Do nutrient effects depend on light regime? (3) Are growth and photosynthetic performance correlated? (4) Do interspecific differences in growth reflect differences in photosynthetic traits or allocation strategies?

Hypotheses: (1) Seedling growth is responsive to light availability; (2) the growth response to light is affected by nutrient supply; (3) growth and photosynthetic performance are correlated; (4) these responses reflect inter-species differences in photosynthetic traits. Support for (1) would be monotonic growth responses to RLI. Support for (2) would be significant light-by-nutrient interactions on growth. Support for (3) would be significant correlations between growth metrics (e.g., D²H) and photosynthetic parameters (e.g., Amax). Support for (4) would be consistent interspecific differences in photosynthetic traits (e.g., a, Amax, LCP) explaining growth differences. The study further explores whether differences in carbon allocation (e.g., H/D) could explain growth disparities when photosynthetic capacity is similar.
reference_methodology:
Plant material: Seeds of Swietenia macrophylla and Schizolobium parahybum were collected from a plain rainforest in the Bolivian Amazon (1993). Seeds were sown in April 1997 in plastic trays with a volcanic-origin substrate. After two months, seedlings were transplanted in June 1997 to Wagner pots (19.5 cm long, 17.5 cm diameter) filled with Akahoya volcanic ash soil (moderate texture, average organic carbon 1.95%, total nitrogen 0.09%).

Experimental design: Five light regimes were imposed using black polypropylene shade nets over 1.6 m × 1.6 m × 1.6 m frames: 100% (1.00 RLI), 60% (0.60 RLI), 36% (0.36 RLI), 13% (0.13 RLI), and 5% (0.05 RLI). A 20-cm gap between the net bottom and ground allowed air movement; pots were placed ≥40 cm from frame edges to avoid edge effects. Three nutrient treatments were applied: control, 5 g NPK fertilizer (N1), and 10 g NPK fertilizer (N2). Each treatment combination was replicated five times. Sets of 15 seedlings were randomly assigned within each shade frame and an open site. Initial seedling heights and diameters were 17 cm and 2 mm (S. macrophylla) and 14 cm and 3 mm (S. parahybum). Seedlings were watered to maintain field capacity.

Environmental conditions: Mean temperature 24.1°C, maximum 27.5°C, minimum 20.8°C; mean relative humidity 77%; mean monthly rainfall 350 mm (Miyazaki Meteorological Agency, 1997). Growth measurements were taken at the start (June 1997) and end (October 1997).

Growth measurements: Height (H) and stem diameter (D) at the root collar were measured at both time points. Growth increments were calculated as height increment (HI) and diameter increment (DI). Biomass growth was approximated by D²H (square of diameter multiplied by height). Stem slenderness ratio (H/D) was computed from final measurements.

Photosynthesis measurements: Leaf-level CO2 assimilation was measured with an infrared CO2 analyzer (HORIBA ASSA-1110) in an assimilation chamber. PPFD levels included 1140, 700, 400, 225, and lower values (partially garbled in the text). A water filter between the chamber and light projector blocked thermal radiation. Chamber air humidity was maintained at 60–70% via a water bath. Leaf net photosynthetic rate (Pn) and dark respiration (Rdark) were calculated following Von Caemmerer and Farquhar (1981). Apparent quantum yield (a) was determined as the slope of the linear regression of Pn on PPFD below 80 μmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Maximum net photosynthesis (Amax) was estimated from maximum gross photosynthesis (Pgmax) using Yoda (1982). The third or fourth leaf from the shoot apex was used for measurements; only leaves fully expanded after treatment initiation and without senescence were included.

Statistical analysis: ANOVA assessed effects of light, nutrient, and their interactions on growth and photosynthetic parameters. LSD tests indicated significant differences (P<0.05). Multiple regression examined relationships between growth and photosynthetic traits. Significance thresholds were P<0.05, 0.01, 0.001. Survival at 5% RLI was noted qualitatively for S. parahybum.

title: Extensive Screening of Green Solvents for Safe and Sustainable UiO-66 Synthesis
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which green solvents, selected under REACH-compliant criteria, can replace DMF to synthesize high-quality UiO-66 (pure phase, high crystallinity, microporosity, and BET) under a standardized protocol? (2) How do solvent physical properties (dielectric constant, boiling point, viscosity) and toxicological profiles relate to UiO-66 crystallinity, morphology, and porosity? (3) Can alternative zirconium sources and modulators maintain UiO-66 quality without DMF? (4) Do selected green solvents exhibit process safety advantages (higher flash points, reduced VOC dispersion) and recyclability?

Hypotheses: (a) Several green solvents with high polarity and appropriate boiling points can substitute DMF to yield UiO-66 with crystallinity and porosity comparable to DMF-synthesized material. (b) A composite green assessment integrating solvent properties and MOF quality will identify preferred solvents. (c) Alternative Zr salts (e.g., ZrOCl2·8H2O) and modulators (e.g., HCOOH) can produce UiO-66 without compromising quality. Support would be evidenced by XRPD patterns with characteristic UiO-66 peaks, low FWHM (111), BET values in the 700–1600 m²/g range, and yields comparable to DMF. Refutation would involve amorphous products, co-phases, low BET, or poor crystallinity across solvents.
reference_methodology:
Solvents: Approximately 40 solvents spanning alcohols, esters, carbonates, ketones, aromatics, ethers, and dipolar aprotic classes were selected under REACH-compliant criteria (low cost, low toxicity, biodegradability). Examples include GVL, PC, 1-(2-HE)-2-P, TAME, 1,3-propanediol, DMC, DMA, DEC, methyl laurate, and others (Table 2). Boiling points, viscosities, and toxicological profiles were considered for green assessment.

Synthesis optimization in DMF: A literature-based DMF synthesis (ZrCl4, H2-BDC, water) was optimized by increasing reagent concentration (from 0.05 M to 0.125 M) and adding 30 equivalents AcOH modulator. The optimized protocol used 4 mL solvent, H2-BDC (83 mg, 0.5 mmol), water (27 μL, 3 eq), AcOH (860 μL, 30 eq), ZrCl4 (116 mg, 0.5 mmol) in a screw-capped 4 mL vial, sonication to dissolution, then 120°C for 16 h in a Teflon reactor. Post-reaction, solids were centrifuged, washed with MeOH (two times, one-hour soaking), water (one time, one-hour soaking), and acetone (one time, one-hour soaking; one time overnight), then dried at 80°C for 2 h. Figure 1 schematizes the reaction.

Green solvent screening: The same optimized conditions were applied to each green solvent (4 mL, 3 eq H2O, 30 eq AcOH, 120°C, 16 h). Selected solvents with high boiling points (>80°C) were prioritized to minimize evaporation and pressure risks. Solvent stability was assessed by 1H NMR comparing neat and reacted solvents (Supporting Information: S8, S13, S18, S27, S32). TGA was used to determine molecular formulas and solvent retention (weight loss above 200°C to 600°C plateau indicating ZrO2; PC retained solvent as indicated by TGA and 1H NMR).

Characterization: XRPD was used to confirm UiO-66 phase and crystallinity (FWHM of (111) peak). BET surface area and micropore volume were measured by N2 adsorption/desorption. Yield was determined gravimetrically. FE-SEM images (S33) assessed morphology. Defectivity was inferred from XRPD (broad low-angle peaks) and high BET.

Alternative Zr sources and modulators: In GVL, the authors varied Zr salt (ZrCl4 vs ZrOCl2·8H2O) and modulator (AcOH vs HCOOH) (Table 6). XRPD patterns (Figure 4) showed similar crystallinity even without modulator.

Green assessment: A color-coded scheme (green/yellow/red) was applied to solvent greenness, boiling point, viscosity, crystal size, and BET. A composite default ranking emphasized crystal size (Table 3b), with a discussion-adjusted ranking balancing solvent greenness and MOF quality (Table 2). Extremely low boiling point solvents (≤50°C) were excluded for safety/processing reasons. DMF was included as a reference and ranked not recommended due to toxicity.

title: Highly luminescent hetero-ligand MOF nanocrystals with engineered massive Stokes shift for photonic applications
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can co-assembling DPA (donor) and DPT (acceptor) into isostructural Zr-MOF nanocrystals produce a large Stokes shift with high fluorescence QY and fast kinetics? (2) Does diffusion-mediated Förster ET from DPA to DPT occur efficiently within the MOF framework, enabling ultrafast activation of low-energy emission? (3) Do hetero-ligand MOF nanocrystals in a polymer matrix yield scintillation composites with higher light output and improved outcoupling than homo-ligand composites?

Hypotheses: (i) The short ligand center-to-center distance (11.7 Å) and complementary spectra of DPA and DPT will enable efficient diffusion-mediated ET with high φET, producing a large Stokes shift (ΔE ≈ 750 meV) and high QY (~70%). (ii) The green emission lifetime will mirror that of DPT monomers (≈11 ns), indicating minimal aggregation and preserved single-molecule behavior. (iii) In PDMS composites, the hetero-ligand design will suppress reabsorption, increase scintillation yield (e.g., ~5000 ph/MeV), and improve geometrical detection efficiency (β) relative to Zr-DPA composites. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include dilution-invariant green/blue emission ratios, single-exponential lifetimes matching DPT monomers, theoretical φET ≈ 0.9 at low DPT loading, and measured scintillation metrics exceeding homo-ligand benchmarks.
reference_methodology:
Synthesis: Zr-DPT:DPA-x% MOFs were prepared by solvothermal assembly of ZrCl4, DPT (5,12-bis(4-carboxyphenyl)tetracene), and DPA (9,10-bis(4-carboxyphenyl)anthracene) in DMF with acetic acid at 120°C for 22 h. Powders were filtered, washed, and activated at 130°C under high vacuum. DPT ligand synthesis is provided in the Supplementary Information. Homo-ligand MOFs (Zr-DPA, Zr-DPT) were synthesized analogously. Composition matched feeding ratios (0.1–8% DPT/DPA), confirmed by 1H NMR of digested samples.

Structural and physicochemical characterization: PXRD with Rietveld refinement established cubic Fm-3m fcu topology, consistent with Zr-DPA and Zr-DPT. Twelve ligands coordinate each Zr6(μ3-O)4(μ3-OH)4(CO2)12 node, forming interconnected octahedral and tetrahedral cavities. SEM showed homogeneous octahedral nanocrystals; Zr-DPT:DPA-8% had average size 185 ± 20 nm. N2 adsorption at 77 K showed high surface areas up to 3000 m2/g with stepwise isotherms and pore sizes of 10.8 Å and 14.5 Å. Hyperpolarized 129Xe NMR confirmed pore patency and homogeneity; Zr-DPT:DPA-8% exhibited δ = 96.5 ppm, the weighted average of Zr-DPA (δ = 94.6 ppm) and Zr-DPT (δ = 117.0 ppm), with no residual homo-ligand signals. FT-IR, 13C MAS NMR, and TGA verified connectivity, purity, and thermal stability.

Photophysics: Absorption and PL spectra were recorded in THF (0.1 mg/mL) using a Cary Lambda 900. Excitation spectra were measured at 550 nm. Dilution series (Zr-DPT:DPA-1%) were analyzed under 355 nm excitation to assess ET dependence on acceptor concentration. Time-resolved PL (TCSPC) was performed with PicoHarp300 (32 ps/bin) and MCS6A (800 ps/bin). Temperature-dependent PL was measured on 0.1 cm-thick films in a closed-cycle He cryostat.

Scintillation and radioluminescence: Steady-state RL was measured at room temperature using a Jobin-Yvon Symphony II CCD with Triax 180 monochromator (100 lines/mm). X-ray excitation used a Philips 2274 tube (W target, 20 kV) through a Be window; dose rate 0.2 Gy/s (calibrated via 90Sr-90Y and quartz OSL). For PL under X-ray, the same detection system was coupled to a 405 nm pulsed diode laser via fiber. Pulsed X-ray excitation employed a Hamamatsu N5084 tube driven by a 405 nm picosecond diode laser (1 MHz), with energies up to 25 keV. Scintillation light was collected in reflection by an HPM 100-07 hybrid PMT (Becker & Hickl), processed by an ORTEC 9237 discriminator, and recorded with a chronologic xTDC4 TDC. A 450 nm band-pass filter (40 nm FWHM) suppressed air excitation. Scintillation pulses were fitted by convolving the system IRF (FWHM 180 ps) with an intrinsic scintillation rate.

Light propagation modeling: Monte Carlo ray-tracing simulated photon transport in a 10 × 10 × 5 mm scintillator with measured absorption/emission spectra and emission efficiencies (ΦPL = 67% for Zr-DPT:DPA-8%; ΦPL = 27% for Zr-DPA). Scattering was modeled as an artificial absorption background from 0 to 20 cm−1. Geometrical detection efficiency β was computed as the fraction of scintillation photons reaching the detector.

title: An Iterative Multiuser Detector for DS-CDMA Systems in Multipath Fading Channels
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can an iterative multiuser detector for Turbo-coded DS-CDMA that conditions MAP estimation on both the received signal and an estimated MAI outperform conventional iterative IC that subtracts MAI before decoding? (2) Does incorporating channel side information (CSI) into the MAP-based detector improve performance in multipath fading channels? (3) Can the detector’s complexity be kept linear in the number of users while achieving these gains?

Hypotheses: (H1) The proposed MAP-based detector with MAI as side information will achieve lower bit error rates (BER) than conventional iterative IC under comparable settings (e.g., 3 iterations, 10 users, unit energy). (H2) Incorporating CSI into the likelihood computation will yield additional BER gains in multipath fading, with larger gains as multipath severity increases (e.g., more paths, more RAKE fingers). (H3) The detector’s computational complexity will scale linearly with the number of users, making it practical for larger systems.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if BER curves show consistent gains over conventional IC at the same SNR. H2 is supported if CSI-enabled variants achieve dB gains at specified BERs (e.g., >1.5 dB at 1e-3; >2 dB at 1e-2). H3 is supported if the algorithm’s operations per user are additive and independent across users.
reference_methodology:
System model: A Turbo-coded, asynchronous BPSK DS-CDMA uplink is considered. The received signal comprises contributions from the desired user, MAI, side interference (SI), and AWGN. The channel is modeled as a time-delay impulse response with an exponential Multipath Intensity Profile (MIP), where the second moment of fading gains decays exponentially with path delay. Fading gains are Rayleigh distributed. A RAKE receiver with M fingers is used for diversity combining; the output is a weighted sum of matched-filter outputs across taps.

Detector design: The receiver is derived from MAP estimation of the desired user’s transmitted code bit, conditioned on the received signal and an estimate of MAI. The algorithm estimates code bits (not information bits) to avoid re-encoding before interference cancellation. The joint probability density function (PDF) of the received sequence and the estimated MAI is assumed jointly Gaussian with correlation r, and variances σ_Y² (received signal) and σ_I² (MAI estimate). For a Turbo code with coding rate 1/3, the LLR for the desired code bit is expressed as a function of the received sequence, the MAI estimate, and the correlation r, incorporating extrinsic information from the previous iteration. For the case with channel side information (CSI), the joint PDF is extended to include the fading gain parameter h, with its expectation E[h] over paths used in the likelihood computation.

Iterative procedure: The detector and Turbo decoder exchange soft information. At each iteration, the detector computes LLRs conditioned on the current received signal and the current MAI estimate, using the Gaussian joint model. The Turbo decoder updates the information bit LLRs and provides extrinsic code-bit LLRs to the detector. The MAI estimate is then updated using the refined code-bit LLRs. The process repeats for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 3 in simulations).

Simulation settings: The constituent encoder is a recursive systematic convolutional (RSC) code with octal representation (7,5). Frame length is 200. The number of active users is 10. A unit energy constraint is applied. The conventional baseline is an iterative receiver that subtracts the estimated MAI from the received signal prior to decoding (as in prior work). Performance is evaluated via BER vs SNR curves. Reported gains are at specific BER targets: 1.0E-3 and 1.0E-2. Figures 2–4 compare the proposed “Turbo IC” against the conventional “Conv Iter. IC” in AWGN and multipath fading. Multipath scenarios include: (i) single fading path with PG 15; and (ii) three fading paths with three RAKE fingers. The number of iterations is three for all comparisons. Exact SNR grids, random seeds, and CSI estimation procedures are not reported in the provided text.

title: A Dual Model for Restoring Images Corrupted by Mixture of Additive and Multiplicative Noise
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a unified variational model automatically detect and adapt to mixed additive and multiplicative noise per pixel, improving restoration quality over single-type denoisers? (2) Can a dual MAP formulation yield an adaptive fidelity term whose weights serve as noise detectors with interpretable statistical and convex optimization perspectives? (3) Does integrating strong priors (e.g., CNNs) with the adaptive fidelity improve PSNR/SSIM across a range of mixture ratios and noise parameters? (4) Can an operator-splitting algorithm ensure practical solvability and convergence guarantees for the inner denoising subproblem?

Hypotheses: (H1) An adaptive fidelity derived from a dual MAP estimator will produce per-pixel weights that accurately classify noise type and level, improving restoration over fixed-fidelity mixed models. (H2) The soft-max interpretation of the weights will provide a principled convex-dual basis for the detector. (H3) Combining the adaptive fidelity with strong priors (e.g., IRCNN) will yield consistent PSNR/SSIM gains over ROF, AA, BM3D, and single-type denoisers, especially at intermediate mixture ratios (α ≈ 0.4–0.6). (H4) The splitting algorithm will converge for the inner u-subproblem and produce restorations with better detail preservation and fewer artifacts. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include quantitative PSNR/SSIM improvements, visual comparisons, and convergence analysis.
reference_methodology:
Noise model and assumptions: The observed image f is modeled as a mixture of additive Gaussian noise and multiplicative Gamma noise with unknown mixture ratio α = P(A), where A denotes additive noise. The additive noise N is Gaussian with mean 0 and variance σ²; the multiplicative noise V is Gamma with mean 1 and shape parameter L. The latent clean image U follows a Gibbs prior with potential φ and normalization T. The forward model is f = U + N with probability α and f = U·V with probability 1−α. The parameters α, σ², and L are unknown.

Fidelity derivation: Using Bayes’ rule and log-likelihoods, the MAP estimator is converted to a minimization problem over (u, Θ, w), where Θ = (α, σ², L) and w are per-pixel weights. Expanding the ln-sum term via an EM-equivalent identity yields a dual formulation. The adaptive fidelity term is expressed as a weighted combination of additive and multiplicative log-likelihoods with weights w that adapt to local noise characteristics. The continuous functional J is derived, and the soft-max interpretation is provided: for ε>0, the soft-max operator is convex, and its Fenchel-Legendre transform yields the dual variables (weights) that classify noise.

Regularization: The regularization φ(u) can be TV, BM3D, or a deep CNN prior (e.g., IRCNN). For model-based regularizers (TV, BM3D), existence of a minimizer is established; for data-driven CNN priors, numerical experiments are used to assess performance.

Algorithm: The model is solved via operator splitting. The discrete BV space is used with rectangular integration and central differences for TV derivatives. The u-subproblem is solved with an augmented Lagrange method (ALM) and ADMM inner iterations: u is updated by a Gaussian denoiser (ROF, BM3D, or IRCNN) with a penalty term; a dual variable d is updated by solving a cubic equation; a Lagrange multiplier p is updated. Closed-form updates are derived for α and σ² from first-order conditions. The Gamma shape parameter L is estimated via digamma-based approximation (within ~1.5% confidence). The algorithm alternates between denoising and a dual process that updates w and Θ.

Evaluation: Metrics are PSNR and SSIM. Test images: 10 grayscale images; two color images (Lena 512×512×3, House 256×256×3); real ultrasound and CT images. Noise settings: α ∈ {0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1}; σ² ∈ {0.005, 0.01}; L ∈ {10, 20, 30}. For IRCNN, the trained denoiser from [27] is used in a plugin-and-play manner. Comparators include ROF, AA, BM3D, and IRCNN. Visual comparisons and quantitative averages across 10 images are reported. Convergence analysis shows the inner u-subproblem converges to its minimizer under standard conditions.

title: Spray Combustion Dynamics under Thermoacoustic Oscillations
field_subfield: Mechanical Engineering — Combustion Science and Thermoacoustics
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do global equivalence ratio (GER) and injector atomization (SMD) determine the stability boundaries and flame regimes in a kerosene-fueled LDI combustor? (2) What acoustic and thermal signatures accompany transitions between stable and unstable regimes? (3) Can high-amplitude acoustic pressure induce secondary droplet breakup, thereby altering combustion mode and stability characteristics?

Hypotheses: (H1) Increasing GER will sequentially drive the combustor through a stable regime, a first unstable regime with diffusion-dominated burning, and a second unstable regime with premixed-like characteristics due to enhanced acoustic coupling and altered flame structure. (H2) Finer atomization (lower FN, smaller SMD) will delay the onset of the second unstable regime (higher GER), whereas coarser atomization (higher FN, larger SMD) will shrink the first unstable region. (H3) High acoustic pressure amplitudes will cause droplet deformation and secondary breakup, particularly for larger droplets, leading to increased vaporization and a transition to a pre-vaporized premixed-like regime.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if spectral coupling emerges at resonance with increasing GER and limit cycles appear with characteristic frequency shifts and harmonic content. H2 is supported if stability maps show delayed second-regime onset for lower FN injectors and reduced first-regime extent for higher FN injectors. H3 is supported if TAB simulations predict higher deformation and breakup likelihood for larger droplets under high acoustic forcing, consistent with observed regime transitions.
reference_methodology:
Experimental setup: Tests were conducted at Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University on a cylindrical 75 kW LDI, swirl-stabilized combustor fueled with kerosene. Air inlet temperature was 293 K. The combustor section was a sudden expansion (dump) combustor 1270 mm long with 127 mm internal diameter; the flow-conditioning section was 864 mm long with 76 mm internal diameter. Optical access was provided via three rectangular fused-silica windows. A 45° axial swirler yielded a geometric swirl number of 0.81. Fuel was injected via a full-cone pressure-swirl simplex injector. Pressure measurements used dynamic pressure transducers mounted along the combustor and flow-conditioning sections. Heat release rate was measured using a photomultiplier tube with optics and signal conditioning to capture OH* chemiluminescence. Temperature measurements were taken in the combustor and in air/fuel feed lines. Data acquisition used an 8-channel simultaneous sample-and-hold card with anti-aliasing filtering.

Operating conditions and mapping: The combustor operating range was mapped under atmospheric pressure, constrained by injector/fuel pump capacities, air supply, and thermal loading. A Delavan WDB-1.00 solid-cone burner atomizer (FN = 3.42) served as the baseline. Stability was mapped over GER by varying air and/or fuel flow rates. Two additional injectors were used: WDB-0.75 (FN = 2.56; orifice 0.234 mm; mass flow 2.380 kg/h at 0.862 MPa) and WDB-1.50 (FN = 5.13; orifice 0.330 mm; mass flow 4.761 kg/h at 0.862 MPa). Spray characterization under non-reacting conditions used Phase Doppler Anemometry (PDA) to obtain droplet size distributions.

Measurements and analysis: Stability was assessed via power spectral densities (PSDs) of acoustic pressure and acoustically driven heat release rate. Acoustic velocity was estimated from closely spaced wall-mounted pressure transducers in the flame zone. Temperature profiles were measured in the flame zone and upstream burner section. Mean heat release rate was derived from OH* chemiluminescence averaged over the window area. Limit-cycle frequency and amplitude were identified from PSD peaks. The combustor quarter-wave resonance frequency was 123 Hz. The study reports SPL values, frequency shifts, temperature changes, and relative pressure oscillation amplitudes.

Analytical model: A modified Taylor Analogy Breakup (TAB) model was used to simulate droplet deformation under combined aerodynamic and acoustic forcing. The 1D TAB equation included surface tension (restoring), viscous damping, aerodynamic drag, and acoustic pressure forces. Drag was shape-dependent (deforming sphere), following prior work. Simulations used a droplet velocity of 5 m/s and fuel properties, acoustic pressure, and advective flow values corresponding to GER = 0.6. Breakup was declared when non-dimensional deformation exceeded a criterion (z_ss > 0.5).

title: PSC-powered intelligent-curtain electrochromic devices with alkynyl-substituted viologens
field_subfield: Materials Science — Electrochromic devices and photovoltaics
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can alkynyl-substituted viologens (mono- vs di-substituted) in all-in-one gel ECDs overcome radical cation aggregation to deliver high stability and fast, light-sensitive switching? (2) Can PSCs power ECDs to achieve automatic, real-time light adjustment and energy storage sufficient to power external devices? (3) Do DPV and MPV enable distinct color palettes (deep blue vs magenta-blue) that correlate with light intensity and stored energy?

Hypotheses: (H1) DPV with two alkynyl groups will reduce radical cation aggregation, increasing coloration efficiency, cycling stability, and response speed relative to MPV. (H2) Inverted-structure PSCs will provide adequate VOC and JSC to drive ECDs and charge ECSs, enabling multi-color, light-intensity-responsive operation. (H3) PSC-powered ECDs will maintain stable switching under varying light/no light conditions and store sufficient energy to power a red LED. Outcomes supporting H1 include higher η, longer ΔT retention, and faster response times for DPV; outcomes supporting H2/H3 include PCE ≥18%, stable ΔT under dynamic illumination, and successful LED powering.
reference_methodology:
Synthesis: MPV (1-(pent-4-yn-1-yl)-[4,4′-bipyridin]-1-ium chloride) was synthesized by reacting 4,4′-bipyridine (0.3 g, 1.9 mmol) with 5-chloro-1-pentylene (0.176 g, 1.7 mmol) in 2 mL DMF at 90°C for 16 h, followed by concentration, silica gel purification, and drying to yield 0.1 g (20%). DPV (1,1′-di(pent-4-yn-1-yl)-[4,4′-bipyridine]-1,1′-diium dichloride) was synthesized by reacting 4,4′-bipyridine (0.3 g, 1.9 mmol) with 5-chloro-1-pentylene (0.49 g, 4.8 mmol) in 2 mL DMF at 110°C for 48 h, filtration, washing (DMF 3×2 mL), and vacuum drying to yield 450 mg (66%). Characterization included 1H/13C NMR (Bruker 400 MHz) and HRMS (m/z calcd/found: MPV C15H15N2 [M]+ 223.1230/223.1231; DPV C20H22N2 [M]2+ 145.0886/145.0889).

ECD fabrication: Gels were prepared by dissolving 0.1 mmol viologen, 150 mg propylene carbonate (PC), 23 mg ferrocene, 160 mg LiTFSI, and 300 mg PVB in 1.5 mL dried CH3OH under N2 for 3 h, then degassing. Gels were injected into liquid crystal cells with 70 μm electrode spacing (parafilm) and an effective area of 2 cm² (radius 0.8 cm). Electrochemical tests: cyclic voltammetry at 100 mV/s; chronoabsorptometry with switching between colored (1.6 V, 10 s) and bleached (−0.3 V, 10 s) states; current–time switching between 1.6 V (colored, 20 s) and 0 V (bleached, 20 s); galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) at 3–10 mA/cm². Coloration efficiency η=ΔOD/ΔQ was computed from linear ΔOD–ΔQ slopes. Areal capacitance C=IΔt/SΔV was computed from GCD curves.

PSC fabrication: ITO glass was cleaned (DI water, acetone, IPA) and UV-ozone treated (20 min). PTAA (2 mg/mL in chlorobenzene) was spin-coated at 5000 rpm for 25 s and annealed at 100°C for 10 min. A two-step spin-coating deposited PbI2 (60 μL of 600 mg/mL in DMF:DMSO 95:5) at 1500 rpm, followed by FAI:MABr:MACl (60:6:6 mg in 1 mL IPA) at 1300 rpm for 30 s, with annealing at 150°C for 15 min in ambient air (20–30% RH). C60 (40 nm)/BCP (8 nm)/Ag (100 nm) were thermally evaporated under <10−4 Pa base pressure.

PSC testing: J–V curves were measured under AM1.5G (100 mW/cm²) using a 300 W Xe lamp solar simulator (Enlitech SS-F7-3A) and Keithley 2400, with an NREL-calibrated Si cell for intensity control. A mask (0.0576 cm² aperture) was used. Scans: forward (−0.2 to 1.2 V) and reverse (1.2 to −0.2 V) at 0.01 V steps, integrating 10 ms after 10 ms delay.

PSC-powered ECD testing: UV–vis spectra and colorimetry (CHN Spec CS-820) with a waveform generator (Rigol DG4102) were used to monitor transmittance and L*/a*/b* under varying light intensities. Natural sunlight tests assessed multi-color transitions. Stability tests under strong/no light in air were conducted for 2000 s. LED powering tests used two connected ECDs in deep-colored states.

title: Derivation of an extended Bjerrum equation for the activity coefficient of ions based on an analysis of Coulombic forces
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a model based on nearest-neighbor Coulombic interactions with a concentration-dependent cutoff reproduce the dilute-limit cube-root law for ln γ± and extend it to higher concentrations and nonzero ion sizes? (2) Does this framework generalize to asymmetric salts (2:1, 3:1) and to higher valencies (2:2, 3:3) without resorting to DH’s square-root law? (3) How well does the model predict osmotic coefficients and diffusion trends compared to experimental data and simulations?

Hypotheses: (H1) In the dilute limit, ln γ± scales as −b c∞^(1/3) with b = α z^2 λB NA^(1/3), where α ≈ 1 for symmetric salts; for 1:1 salts at 298 K, b ≈ 0.0605 (mM)^−1/3. (H2) Including ion size via a size factor q yields an extended Bjerrum equation that fits 1:1 salts across 1–1000 mM and asymmetric salts up to moderate concentrations. (H3) For higher valencies, the cube-root law is insufficient; numerical evaluation of the full integral (Eq. (5)) is required. (H4) The model’s osmotic coefficients and diffusion relations align with experimental datasets and RPM simulations. Support for H1–H4 is evaluated by comparing model predictions to NaCl/KCl activity coefficients, HCl datasets, RPM ion pair energies, asymmetric salts (K2SO4, LaCl3), 2:2 (MgSO4) and 3:3 (LaFe(CN)6) salts, and osmotic/diffusion data.
reference_methodology:
Model derivation: For symmetric z:z salts, the ion pair energy IPE is computed from Coulomb’s law with potential ψ(x) = −z^2 λB/x (kT units), where λB = e^2/(4πεr ε0 kT). The probability distribution f(x) of finding the pair at separation x is defined over x_min = 2⟨a⟩ (sum of ion radii) to x_max, with f(x) ∝ exp(−ψ(x)) x^2. The maximum separation x_max is set by the concentration via n∞ = c∞NA = x_max^−3 (α = 1 empirically for symmetric salts). IPE is obtained by integrating ψ(x) f(x) over x. Multiplying IPE by n∞ gives the free energy density; differentiating with respect to n∞ and dividing by 2 yields the electrostatic contribution to ln γ±. In the dilute limit (x_max ≫ a), series expansion of the integrals yields ln γ± = −(3/2) z^2 λB / x_max, which, with x_max ∝ n∞^−1/3, becomes ln γ± = −b c∞^(1/3), with b = α z^2 λB NA^(1/3). For 1:1 salts at 298 K (εr = 78.3), λB = 0.716 nm and b ≈ 0.0605 (mM)^−1/3.

Asymmetric salts: For 2:1 salts, the triplet energy ITE is computed by integrating over two anions around a central divalent cation with attractive (cation–anion) and repulsive (anion–anion) interactions, using spherical coordinates (xα, xβ, ϑ, φ) with x_min = ac + a− and x_max determined by total ion concentration (3/2 n∞ = x_max^−3). For 3:1 salts, the quadruplet energy IQE integrates over three anions around a central trivalent cation, with x_max set by 2 n∞ (4/2 n∞ = x_max^−3). The mean activity coefficient is obtained by differentiating n∞·ITE or n∞·IQE with respect to n∞ and dividing by 3 or 4, respectively.

Extended Bjerrum equation: To include ion size effects, the model adds a size factor q = (⟨a⟩/λB)^2 − 1/48 to the dilute-limit law, yielding ln γ± = −b c∞^(1/3) − (1/3) b q c∞^(1/3) + … (Eq. (27)). For 1:1 salts, b = 0.0605 (mM)^−1/3; for 2:2 salts, b scales as 4× the 1:1 value, with an additional factor on the size term (q ≈ 0.23) to match data. For 3:3 salts, full numerical evaluation is required.

Osmotic coefficient: Using Gibbs–Duhem (∂Π/∂c∞ = 2 c∞ ∂μi/∂c∞ for z:z), the model derives φ = 1 − (1/4) b c∞^(1/3) for 1:1 salts (Eq. (10)), with φ ≈ 1 − 0.151 c∞^(1/3) (M), consistent with historical cryoscopic estimates (0.146–0.225; mean ~0.17).

Data and comparisons: Experimental datasets include NaCl/KCl activity coefficients (Hamer & Wu, 1972; 1–100 mM), HCl datasets (Carmody, 1932; Hills & Ives, 1951), and asymmetric salts (K2SO4, LaCl3; Malatesta et al.). RPM simulations (Lamperski, 2007) provide ion pair energies for 1:1 salts (a = 0.212 nm; εr = 78.65). Diffusion fits use Frank & Thompson (1959) D_eff vs c∞^(1/3) data. Calibration notes: ln γ± datasets are vertically shifted by a constant when plotted against c∞^(1/3) to extrapolate to the origin; this shift depends on assumed limiting law (cube-root vs square-root).

title: Main points of the PhD thesis Changes in gene expression and metabolic processes during stress adaptation in plants
field_subfield: Plant Biology — Stress Physiology and Molecular Genetics
research_question:
The thesis articulates six research questions: (I) How does light intensity influence gene expression in wheat during cold hardening, and which genes change significantly in response to cold and illumination? (II) What protective compounds underlie satisfactory frost tolerance in wheat? (III) Do ascorbate- and salicylic acid-deficient Arabidopsis genotypes differ in cold tolerance? (IV) How do Arabidopsis genotypes’ frost defense strategies change with temperature, and which physiological factors contribute to improved tolerance? (V) What anti-stress pathways are responsible for satisfactory frost tolerance in Arabidopsis? (VI) Which genes govern shade avoidance under low temperature in Arabidopsis introgression lines?

Implicit hypotheses include: (a) Light intensity modulates cold-induced gene expression in wheat, with genotype-specific responses; (b) In Arabidopsis, polyamines (e.g., putrescine) are more critical for frost tolerance than ascorbate or SA; (c) SA and NO pathways interact with cold signaling to influence survival and physiological markers; (d) A SAS QTL exists under low temperature and low R/FR, implicating ER/ERL genes. Support would be indicated by differential expression patterns with illumination and genotype, freezing survival differences among mutants/transgenics, physiological shifts (e.g., increased putrescine, altered PSII parameters), and QTL mapping to ER/ERL loci. Refutation would involve no illumination-dependent expression changes, uniform survival across genotypes, or QTL mapping outside ER/ERL regions.
reference_methodology:
Plant materials and growth conditions: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) winter variety Mv Emese and spring variety Nadro were grown in soil at 20°C with normal light (NL) PPFD 250 µmol m-2 s-1 in a phytotron (Agricultural Institute, Martonvásár). Cold hardening was conducted for 12 days at 5°C under either NL (250 µmol m-2 s-1) or low light (LL) (20 µmol m-2 s-1). For Arabidopsis thaliana, wild-type Columbia (Col-0) and mutants vtc2-1 (ascorbate-deficient), eds5 (low SA), sid2 (SA synthesis-deficient), and noa1 (NO-deficient mitochondrial cGTPase) were used, along with transgenics GLOase (complements vtc2-1) and NahG (degrades SA). Seeds were germinated in soil at 23°C for 3 weeks under short-day illumination (PPFD 50 µmol m-2 s-1), then grown at 21°C under long-day illumination (PPFD 150 µmol m-2 s-1). Cold hardening occurred from week 8 at 4°C for 4 days (PPFD 90 µmol m-2 s-1). Freezing tests were performed at -9°C and -11°C in the dark for 24 h; survival was counted 21 days post-treatment.

QTL mapping: NIL2-8 plants with Ler genetic background and a Cvi introgression were used. Seeds were germinated at 4°C in the dark on Lehle medium, then grown at 21°C under long-day illumination (PPFD 130 µmol m-2 s-1). From week 3, low R/FR illumination (PPFD 100 µmol m-2 s-1) at 16°C was applied to induce shade avoidance. Photomorphogenetic changes were evaluated visually. Genotyping targeted chromosome 2: 12.65 Mb and 11.61 Mb regions with allele-specific In/Del markers, and 11.16 Mb with an SMP marker.

RNA isolation and microarray: Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol (Invitrogen). RNA amplification and labeling followed Agilent 4×44K Wheat Chip manufacturer protocols. Primary analysis used LIMMA (ImFit and eBayes), with p-values adjusted by Benjamini–Hochberg. The Agilent annotation was incomplete; genes were reannotated to GO categories.

Physiological and biochemical assays: PSII quantum efficiency parameters Fv/Fm and ΔF/Fm' were measured with a PAM-2000 (Walz). Plants were dark-adapted 30 min prior to Fv/Fm measurement. Relative chlorophyll content was measured on the third fully developed leaf using a CL-01 chlorophyll meter (Hansatech). Electrolyte leakage was quantified from frozen leaf samples shaken in distilled water, measured by conductance (ASA610, Agro Science). Proline was quantified via ninhydrin reaction (Bates et al., 1973). Polyphenols were measured using the gallic acid equivalence method (Salluca et al., 2008). Ascorbate (AA) was extracted in metaphosphoric acid; total AA was determined by dithiothreitol reduction and isocratic HPLC (Waters 2690); oxidized AA was computed as total minus reduced. Antioxidant enzymes were isolated (Janda et al., 1999) and measured spectrophotometrically: GR activity via DTNB reduction at 412 nm (Smith et al., 1988); APX via AA consumption at 290 nm; CAT via H2O2 decrease at 240 nm; GPX via guaiacol oxidation (Ádám et al., 1995); MDHAR via dehydro-ascorbate to AA conversion at 265 nm (Krivosheeva et al., 1996). SA was extracted with methanol; ortho-anisinic acid was the internal standard and para-hydroxybenzoic acid the extraction carrier; HPLC was performed on a Waters instrument (Meuwly and Métraux, 1993). Polyamines were extracted with perchloric acid and derivatized with dansyl chloride (Smith and Davies, 1985) for HPLC (Waters). ACC and MACC were prepared per Tari and Nagy (1994) with modifications; ACC was measured by GC after conversion to ethylene (Lizada and Yang, 1979); MACC was calculated as ACC before minus after hydrolysis.

Statistics and replication: Most results are means of 5×3 measurements. Student’s two-sample t-test assessed significance; principal component analysis (PCA) was used for similarity analysis. Exact sample sizes per treatment, randomization, and blinding were not reported.

title: The Great Game Will Never End: Why the Global Financial Crisis Is Bound to Be Repeated
