field_subfield: Finance — Financial Regulation and Systemic Risk
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Do the principal explanations of the GFC—product complexity, behavioral biases, systemic risk, and regulatory arbitrage/capture—share a common underlying cause? (2) Are existing regulatory and market-based measures sufficient to prevent future crises? (3) What policy changes could credibly align incentives and reduce gaming?

Hypotheses: (H1) Gaming by bankers and regulators is the common underlying cause of the GFC and its recurrence, enabling leverage, maturity mismatch, and complexity to privatize profits and socialize losses. (H2) Post-crisis reforms (Basel III, stress tests, macroprudential buffers) are insufficient to prevent future crises because they are gameable, pro-cyclical, or misaligned with incentives. (H3) Personal liability for bankers and simpler, judgment-based regulatory frameworks (e.g., Bufferati) would materially reduce gaming and systemic risk. Outcomes supporting H1 include documented cases of complexity-driven risk transfer, arbitrage of capital rules, and regulatory capture. Outcomes supporting H2 include evidence of continued leverage and low market value capital ratios despite reforms, and stress-test weakening. Outcomes supporting H3 would be credible commitments to personal liability and adoption of simpler, releasable buffers; the paper argues feasibility is low but effectiveness is high.
reference_methodology:
Design: Narrative synthesis and policy analysis of the GFC’s causes and policy responses. The paper integrates regulatory documents, official reports (e.g., Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission; Basel Committee; FSB; European Parliament), academic literature (e.g., Dowd; Nijskens & Wagner; Besar et al.), and case studies (AIG, LIBOR manipulation, Archegos, Evergrande). It also reports quantitative indicators from secondary sources (e.g., UK banks’ market capitalization and price-to-book ratios; ECB analysis of fund suspensions; Basel III buffer parameters).

Data: Secondary data and published statistics (e.g., CDO issuance volumes; bank losses; leverage ratios; fund suspension durations; household share of fund assets). No primary data collection, experiments, or formal statistical tests are reported. The paper references tables summarizing UK banks’ market capitalization (2006 vs 2020) and price-to-book ratios (2020) and cites ECB findings on fund suspensions.

Procedure: The authors (i) outline the GFC’s origins (securitization, leverage, maturity mismatch, bonus systems, implicit government put); (ii) review four principal explanations (product complexity, behavioral biases, systemic risk, regulatory arbitrage/capture); (iii) argue for a common cause (gaming); (iv) assess the effectiveness of post-crisis measures (Basel III, stress tests, macroprudential tools) during the COVID-19 shock; (v) propose policy responses (product liability insurance, stress-tested design, centralized derivatives exchanges, accounting reforms, retail restrictions, stronger buffers, Bufferati, personal liability, market-based regulation). Ethical approvals are not applicable. Funding: none. Conflicts of interest: none declared.

title: A woman with abdominal pain, jaundice and elevated CA 19.9
research_question:
Research question: In a patient with obstructive jaundice and extremely elevated CA 19-9, does the clinical workup confirm cholangiocarcinoma or reveal a benign biliary obstruction? Secondary questions: What is the diagnostic performance of CA 19-9, CT, PET/CT, and EUS in this context, and how should discordant findings be reconciled?

Hypothesis: Given US findings of distal biliary obstruction and a CA 19-9 level of 9606 IU/mL, the authors initially hypothesized malignancy (cholangiocarcinoma). Alternative hypothesis: The obstruction is benign (choledocholithiasis and gallstones), and the elevated CA 19-9 reflects cholestasis-driven secretion/absorption rather than tumor burden. Outcomes supporting malignancy would include imaging or endoscopic evidence of a mass, vascular invasion, or malignant stricture; outcomes supporting benign obstruction would include stones/calculi, absence of mass, and resolution of obstruction with normalization of labs and CA 19-9. The observed outcomes (EUS showing stones and sludge without mass; ERCP removal of stones; normalization of bilirubin/transaminases; CA 19-9 reduction to 600 U/mL; benign pathology) support the benign obstruction hypothesis.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-patient clinical case report with sequential diagnostic evaluation and therapeutic intervention.

Participant: 54-year-old woman with 3 months of weight loss (14 kg), asthenia, hyperchromic urine (7 days), and jaundice (3 days). Past medical history unremarkable. Initial outpatient treatment with ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily and esomeprazole was ineffective.

Laboratory assessment: SGOT 403 IU/L (RR 10–35), SGPT 650 IU/L (RR 10–40 in females), total bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL (RR 0.2–1.2), conjugated bilirubin 6.90 mg/dL (RR <0.3), CRP 4.33 mg/dL (RR <0.5). Complete blood count and electrolytes were normal.

Imaging and endoscopic procedures: Initial US showed a distended gallbladder with diffuse wall thickening, dilated intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, and a hyperechogenic material in the intrapancreatic bile duct, suggesting distal cholangiocarcinoma. CA 19-9 was measured at 9606 IU/mL (RR 0–27). Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a normal liver, diffuse calcified gallbladder wall consistent with "milk of calcium" gallbladder, a calcified stone at the gallbladder infundibulum, and two hyperdense stones in the CBD causing significant biliary dilatation. PET/CT did not show focal FDG-avid lesions. EUS revealed CBD dilation (maximum diameter 9.3 mm), biliary sludge at the confluence of the cystic and common hepatic ducts, an 8.9 mm calculus in the CBD behind the ampulla of Vater, a full gallbladder with stones and slightly thickened walls (maximum 5 mm), and no vascularization, indicating benign obstruction. ERCP was performed to remove gallstones; the patient improved clinically, with bilirubin and transaminases normalizing. CA 19-9 decreased to 600 U/mL within 5 days. An elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed 1 month later; pathology showed no malignancy. Three months postoperatively, the patient was in good health with CA 19-9 at 12.5 U/mL.

Analytical framework: The diagnostic workflow integrated literature-based performance metrics (Table 1) to interpret discordant findings. US sensitivity/specificity 73.5%/61.5%; CT accuracy 79%; PET/CT sensitivity 82% (95% CI 78–85), specificity 75% (95% CI 65–84), AUC 0.89; EUS sensitivity 89.5%, specificity 100%, accuracy 90.9% (and sensitivity 90.5%, specificity 100%, accuracy 94.1% in another study). Likelihood ratios were derived from reported sensitivities/specificities.

Ethics: Informed consent was obtained. Procedures complied with institutional/national ethical standards and the 1964 Helsinki declaration and amendments. No animal studies were performed.

title: Mechanized Production of Cotton in Texas
field_subfield: Agricultural Engineering — Cotton Production and Mechanization
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Which mechanized equipment and operating parameters optimize efficiency, yield, and quality across Texas’ diverse environments? (2) How do varietal characteristics and cultural practices (e.g., thinning, defoliation, residue disposal) interact with mechanical systems to affect performance? (3) What fertilizer placement and timing strategies avoid germination inhibition while maximizing yield? (4) How do mechanical thinning, flame, and cultivator attachments compare in weed control and stand establishment? (5) What defoliant application rates and conditions minimize green boll contamination and maximize opening for mechanical or hand harvest?

Hypotheses: (a) Proper residue disposal and seedbed preparation improve planting uniformity and reduce interference with cultivation and harvesting. (b) Fertilizer placed 2.5 inches to the side and 2–3 inches below the seed avoids salt injury and improves germination. (c) Mechanical thinning at 9–15 inch spacing yields higher than hand-thinning or late thinning. (d) Strippers achieve high efficiencies when plants are mature or defoliated; picker performance depends on varietal traits (e.g., boll openness, fluffiness, storm resistance). (e) Defoliation with calcium cyanamide at 20–35 lb/acre under heavy dew/high humidity accelerates opening and improves harvestability. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include higher efficiencies, better stands, improved grades, and reduced foreign matter; refutation would entail lower efficiencies, poor stands, or degraded grades under these conditions.
reference_methodology:
The bulletin aggregates findings from multiple station experiments and field trials conducted at College Station (East Central Texas) and Lubbock (High Plains), with additional references to Temple, Nacogdoches, Brazos River Valley, and other Texas locations. Key methodological elements reported include:

- Residue disposal: Rolling stalk cutters (two- or three-row units; custom four- or five-row units) operated at 4–5 mph; tractor-mounted shredders with two rotating cylinders cutting stalks in standing position, producing 2–4 inch sections; tandem disk harrows used for green cover crops and stalk cutting. Coverage rates: four-row cutters at 4–5 mph covered 50–70 acres/day.

- Seedbed preparation: Listing vs. bedding depending on rainfall; plowing depths (e.g., 6 inches at College Station) compared to disking; harrowing and spike-tooth harrows to break clods; Cropmaker for cutting and reforming beds; chisel tools in the High Plains. Row spacing typically 40 inches.

- Planting: Seed quantity 8–32 lb/acre depending on soil; seed viability testing; seed treatments to reduce rot; delinted vs. fuzzy seed effects on depth and emergence; planting depth by soil type (sandy loam: 1/4–2 inches; clay: 1.5–3 inches); furrow openers (knife/runner vs. shovel) and coverers (press wheels, fish-tail scrapers); press wheel types (open-center vs. solid); fertilizer placement at planting (2.5 inches side, 2–3 inches below seed) to avoid salt injury; planting timing after frost risk; drainage management to prevent standing water.

- Fertilizer application: Planter attachments for side/below seed placement; cultivator attachments for side-dressing; furrow-sole application not popular; liquid/gas fertilizers limited due to water logistics.

- Thinning and spacing: Trials across 3–36 inch spacing in 3-foot rows; 9–15 inch spacing optimal; thinning at 4–6 leaves vs. later; mechanical thinners vs. hand; flame thinning with half-cylinder cups and three burners; cross plowing; hill-drop rotary valve adjustments (notch depth ~3/4 inch, width ~1 inch, rounded bottom).

- Cultivation: Winged sweeps (4–32 inch sizes), rotary hoe attachments (3–4 wheels), broadcast rotary hoes (6–8 mph), flame cultivation (butane/propane), lister cultivators (four-row, power-lift), spoke wheel cultivators; timing to control weeds early.

- Insect control: Dusts (2,4-D sensitivity noted) and sprays; ground dusters (tractor-mounted, 4–8 rows) and airplanes (350+ acres/hour dusting; 3–5 cents/pound contract rates); repeat applications if washed within 24 hours; chlorinated camphene, BHC, DDT for fleahopper not requiring repeats.

- Defoliation: Calcium cyanamide dust at 20–35 lb/acre; soluble monosodium cyanamide sprays; application under heavy dew/high humidity with 2–3 hours dew retention; green boll separation at harvester/gin.

- Harvesting: Strippers (roller surfaces, angles 25–30°, peripheral speed 25–50% faster than forward speed; travel speed effects; field losses <1% for storm-resistant bolls from small plants); extractors (18-inch saw, 48-inch length) and cleaners; pickers (spindle barbs, moisture, RPM, spacing, synchronized movement; varietal dependence; drying and cleaning impacts).

Statistical analyses are referenced (e.g., effects of length/fineness due to immaturity), but detailed protocols, sample sizes, and test statistics are not provided in the text.

title: Whole genome phylogenies reflect the distributions of recombination rates for many bacterial species
field_subfield: Biology — Microbial Genomics and Population Genetics
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Can clonal phylogenies be reconstructed from whole-genome alignments in bacteria where recombination is frequent? (2) Do phylogenies reconstructed from many loci reflect clonal ancestry or population structure? (3) What is the quantitative extent of recombination and how does it vary across lineages? (4) Can n-SNP frequency distributions and strain-specific entropy profiles reveal structured recombination patterns?

Hypotheses: (H1) In many bacterial species, recombination is so frequent that clonal segments are rare and phylogenies at loci are highly incongruent with any single clonal tree. (H2) Phylogenies reconstructed from many loci reflect population structure (heterogeneous recombination rates among lineages) rather than clonal ancestry. (H3) n-SNP frequency distributions will be long-tailed and heterogeneous across strains, indicating a continuum of recombination rates. (H4) Pairwise SNP-density analyses will show that most divergence derives from recombination even for close pairs, and that phylogeny changes are frequent along the genome. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include: high fractions of clashing SNPs relative to supporting SNPs; low clonal fractions at modest divergences; frequent phylogeny changes; and power-law-like n-SNP distributions with heterogeneous entropy profiles.
reference_methodology:
Data: 91 wild E. coli strains (SC1 collection) sequenced with Illumina HiSeq 2000 (100 bp paired-end; 125–487× coverage; 4 strains >1000×). K12 MG1655 used as reference. Core-genome alignment (Realphy; Bowtie2) required presence in all strains, ≥10× coverage per strain, and ≥95% agreement per position. Core alignment length: 2,756,541 bp; polymorphic fraction: 10.8% (6.7% excluding a 9-strain outgroup). Sequencing error rate bounded at <1.1×10^-7 (posterior 99%).

Pairwise analysis: For each pair, slide 1 kb windows (100 bp step) over the core alignment; compute SNP density per window. Fit mixture model: Poisson (clonal) + negative binomial (recombined) to estimate clonal fraction fc and recombination segment length distribution. For very close pairs (divergence <0.002), use a two-state HMM (clonal vs recombined) to parse recombined segments. Define mostly clonal (fc>0.9), fully recombined (fc<0.1), and transition pairs. Fit linear models to relate divergence to fc and to map the fraction of SNPs in recombined regions to fc.

SNP-based phylogeny checks: For each SNP column, classify as supporting or clashing with a branch split of the core tree. Compute per-branch support fractions S/(S+C). Also compute pairwise SNP compatibility vs genomic distance. To quantify phylogeny changes, iterate along the alignment and count minimal number of phylogeny changes C required to maintain compatibility of SNP sets.

Homoplasy estimation: Fit a simple substitution model to observed frequencies of columns with 1–4 nucleotides (including transition/transversion bias r=3) to estimate expected mutations per column μ* and homoplasy fraction fh. Validate on simulated data (fh=2.56% true; estimated 2.43%). Remove 5% or 10% of most inconsistent SNP columns to generate homoplasy-corrected alignments.

Simulations: Wright-Fisher model with neutral mutation μ and homologous recombination ρ per base per generation; population size N=3600; sample size S=50; genome length Lg=2,560,000 bp; recombination segment length Lr=12 kb; μ set so polymorphic fraction ≈0.9 (Nμ=0.012). Vary ρ/μ from 0 to 10; draw a single clonal phylogeny (Kingman coalescent) and reuse it across simulations. Track per-branch clonal inheritance fractions, per-position overwriting counts, and recombination segment lengths.

n-SNP and entropy profiles: For each SNP, map to a binary string (minority allele 1, majority 0) to define SNP types. Count frequencies of n-SNP types (pair, triplet, etc.). Fit power-law P(f)∝f^-α. For each strain s, compute entropy Hs(n) over n-SNP types in which s participates. Compare profiles across strains using Fisher exact test.

title: Vascular Tissue Engineering for Small-Caliber Vascular Grafts: A Review
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which scaffold fabrication techniques and biomaterials have been most effective for small-caliber vascular grafts, and what mechanical and biological properties do they achieve? (2) What in vivo outcomes (patency, remodeling, endothelialization, intimal hyperplasia) have been reported across animal models and early human trials? (3) What design principles (e.g., porosity, alignment, biofunctionalization) are associated with improved performance? (4) What limitations and failure mechanisms persist, and what are the implications for clinical translation?

No explicit hypotheses are tested in this narrative review. The synthesis evaluates whether specific techniques/materials and biofunctionalizations correlate with improved endothelialization, reduced thrombosis/intimal hyperplasia, and durable patency, and whether cell-free versus cell-seeded approaches offer practical advantages for off-the-shelf small-caliber grafts.
reference_methodology:
The review was conducted via a PubMed search using the terms “tissue engineering and vascular grafts,” with analysis of abstracts of original papers published in the last 5 years. The authors report surveying the distribution of techniques (electrospinning, decellularization, lyophilization, 3D printing/bioprinting) and polymers used in VTE over this period (Figures 2 and 7). They also summarize in vivo studies in animal models and early human trials, extracting quantitative outcomes (e.g., mechanical properties, patency, remodeling) from cited primary studies.

Specifics of the search strategy (databases beyond PubMed, date ranges, inclusion/exclusion criteria, language restrictions, PRISMA flow, risk-of-bias assessment, and data extraction protocols) are not reported. The review does not provide systematic review registration or protocol details. Figures 1–7 illustrate trends in publication counts, technique distributions, and representative scaffold architectures and materials. The review collates methodological details from primary studies (e.g., electrospinning parameters, decellularization protocols, lyophilization steps, bioprinting bioinks) and in vivo outcomes (patency, histology, mechanical tests) as reported by the original authors. Ethical approvals and animal/human study details are not summarized in the review text beyond those explicitly reported in the cited trials.

title: Influence of low and moderate grade leg ischaemia on the skin microcirculation parameters in peripheral arterial occlusive disease patients Wpływ niewielkiego i zaawansowanego niedokrwienia na przepływ w mikrokrążeniu skórnym u pacjentów z miażdżycowym niedokrwieniem kończyn dolnych
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do skin microcirculation parameters (SBF, vasomotion bands, TcpO2) and systemic endothelial function (FMD, NMD) differ across PAOD severity strata (advanced vs mild) and healthy controls? (2) Do atherosclerosis risk factors (diabetes, smoking, hypertension) significantly modify microcirculatory parameters within PAOD and control groups? (3) Are provocative tests (thermal and ischemic stimulation) necessary to detect functional microcirculatory reserve deficits that may be masked by resting measures?

Hypotheses: (a) Advanced PAOD (Rutherford 3–4) will show greater impairment in microcirculatory reserve (reduced SBF and VFBs during thermal/ischemic stimulation, lower TcpO2) than mild PAOD (Rutherford 0–1) and controls. (b) Mild PAOD will already exhibit systemic endothelial dysfunction (reduced FMD) and local hypoxia (lower TcpO2) relative to controls. (c) Diabetes and smoking will significantly worsen endothelial function and tissue oxygenation, respectively, while hypertension may have limited independent effects on microcirculation in this cohort. (d) Resting SBF may not differentiate groups due to collateralization in advanced disease, whereas provocative tests will reveal deficits. The reported results support these hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional comparative study with three groups: Group 1 (advanced PAOD, Rutherford 3–4; n=137), Group 2 (mild PAOD, Rutherford 0–1; n=79), and Group 3 (healthy controls; n=27). Inclusion criteria for PAOD: hemodynamically significant femoral–popliteal lesions or occlusions; ABPI <0.9. Imaging modalities included duplex Doppler, angioCT, and angioMRI to localize and quantify lesions. Exclusion criteria: hemodynamically significant lesions in iliac, common femoral, popliteal, tibial, or sagittal arteries; limb ulcers/necrosis; pregnancy; chronic venous insufficiency; renal failure requiring dialysis; neoplastic, allergic, rheumatic, or inflammatory diseases; diffuse dermatologic lesions; uncontrolled or untreated arterial hypertension and vasomotor disorders; prior ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, spinal cord injury; prior pharmacologic sympathectomy; limb edema; and intake of steroids, immunosuppressants, vasomotor, or phlebotropic medications.

Pharmacotherapy: All participants received antiplatelet therapy (acetylsalicylic acid 100–150 mg/day or clopidogrel 75 mg/day) and statins (simvastatin or atorvastatin 20–40 mg/day). Patients with arterial hypertension were treated without beta-blockers or calcium antagonists. Patients with hypertension, diabetes, or hyperlipidemia had their conditions managed per standard care, with confirmation via repeated blood pressure, lipid profile, glucose, and HbA1c measurements.

Testing conditions: All tests were performed in the morning in an air-conditioned room at 21°C, with participants supine after 15 minutes of rest. Participants abstained from caffeinated/tea and alcoholic beverages for ≥2 hours and avoided exercise beyond painless distance for 6 hours prior. The last dose of antihypertensive medications was taken ≥12 hours before testing.

Measurements: ABPI was measured. Microcirculation was assessed using a laser Doppler probe (PF 457; Perimed, Stockholm, Sweden) at the dorsal foot (midpoint between the second and third metatarsals). Fast-Fourier transform analysis (Perisoft PSW v2.50; Perimed) decomposed the laser Doppler signal into vasomotion frequency bands: endothelial (0.01–0.02 Hz; VFB_E), neurogenic (0.02–0.06 Hz; VFB_N), myogenic (0.06–0.15 Hz; VFB_M), respiratory (0.15–0.40 Hz; VFB_R), and heartbeat (0.40–1.60 Hz; VFB_H). Results were reported in Power Density Units (PU/Hz). Tests were performed at rest, during thermal stimulation (44°C), and after post-ischemic hyperemia. TcpO2 was measured using a Clark electrode (tc electrode REF 945-605, E 5250-TcpO2; Radiometer Medicals Aps, Denmark) with the PF 5040 TcpO2/pCO2 module of the Periflux System 5000. Endothelial function was assessed by brachial artery FMD and nitroglycerin-mediated dilation (NMD) per International Brachial Artery Reactivity Task Force guidelines.

Statistics: Analyses used STATISTICA v9 (StatSoft). Between-group comparisons used Mann–Whitney tests; within-group comparisons used Wilcoxon tests. Spearman correlations were used where applicable. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

Ethics: Approval was obtained from the local bioethics committee of the Medical University of Poznan.

title: Distinct epigenetic reprogramming events rewire transcription during life cycle transitions in Arabidopsis
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How is chromatin accessibility reprogrammed across the sporophyte-to-gametophyte transition in Arabidopsis pollen, and what are the cell-type-specific ACRs? (2) How do repressive epigenetic marks—H3K9me2/DNA methylation in the vegetative cell and H3K27me3 in sperm—shape accessible chromatin and transcription? (3) Do accessible chromatin changes in sperm forecast the sporophytic transition in the next generation?

Hypotheses: (a) The vegetative cell undergoes loss of constitutive heterochromatin and DME-mediated DNA demethylation at cis-regulatory regions, increasing accessibility and enabling binding of methylation-sensitive TFs to drive VC differentiation. (b) Sperm chromatin accessibility is reprogrammed by loss of H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 priming, exposing cis-regulatory elements at genes required for early sporophytic development. (c) The extent of chromatin accessibility reprogramming between closely related haploid cell types (SN vs VN) is greater than between closely related sporophytic cell types, reflecting deterministic epigenetic reprogramming accompanying life-form transitions.

Predictions: VN-specific ACRs will be enriched for pericentromeric features, H3K9me2, TE insertions, and pollen siRNAs; DME-targeted ACRs will overlap VN-specific ACRs and contain methylation-sensitive TF motifs with reduced methylation in WT VN and increased methylation in dme-2/+ VN; SN-specific ACRs will overlap somatic H3K27me3 domains and show H3K4me3 priming; genes near H3K27me3-repressed ACRs will be downregulated when H3K27me3 removal is compromised. Outcomes supporting these predictions would validate the hypothesized roles of DME and H3K27me3 in reprogramming accessible chromatin and transcription.
reference_methodology:
Plant materials and growth: Arabidopsis thaliana lines included ProHTR10:HTR10-Clover (sperm marker) and dme-2/+ (DME hypomorph). Plants were grown under long-day conditions (16 h light/8 h dark) at 22°C.

Constructs and transformation: ProVCK:NTF (vegetative cell marker) and ProDUO1:MDB-NTF (germ cell marker) were generated via MultiSite Gateway. NTF (nuclear envelope-targeted GFP) was fused to a stop codon and driven by the VCK promoter; MDB (CYCB1;1 destruction box) fused to NTF was driven by the DUO1 promoter. Constructs were transformed into a homozygous ProUBQ14:BirA marker line (Col-0 background). Primer sequences for cloning are provided.

Cell isolation: Dry pollen was harvested and nuclei isolated by FANS using Galbraith buffer (with 1% Triton X-100), β-mercaptoethanol, and protease inhibitors. A 488 nm laser and 530/30 nm filter were used for GFP/Clover detection. Microspores were isolated by FACS from unopened buds using PEB buffer, gating on SSC and GFP autofluorescence. Germ cell nuclei were isolated from ProDUO1:MDB-NTF spores by FANS, exploiting G2/M accumulation of MDB-NTF and APC/C-mediated turnover post-mitosis.

RNA-seq: VN nuclei were sorted directly into Trizol; RNA-seq libraries were prepared with Smart-seq2. Libraries were sequenced on Illumina HiSeq 2500 (50 bp paired-end for VN; single-end for pollen). Adapter trimming used TrimGalore v0.4.1. Reads were aligned to TAIR10 with STAR v2.5.2a. TPMs were computed with Kallisto v0.43.1. Published sperm RNA-seq datasets were reanalyzed. PCA used mean TPMs across replicates. DESeq2 v1.22.2 identified DEGs in dme-2/+ vs WT pollen (FDR-adjusted p<0.1; genes with ≥10 counts in at least one sample). GeneOverlap assessed overlap enrichment.

ATAC-seq: For GN, SN, VN, ~50,000 nuclei were incubated with Nextera Tn5 (37°C, 1 h). For microspores, ~50,000,000 spores were lysed and transposed. Libraries were sequenced on Illumina HiSeq 2500 (50 bp paired-end). Adapter trimming used cutadapt v1.9. Reads were mapped with Bowtie2 v2.1.0 (end-to-end, -X 2000). Duplicates were marked with Picard v1.141. Only mapQ>10 reads were retained. BigWig coverage was generated with deepTools v2.2.4 (normalizeTo1x119146348, binSize=10, smoothLength=100). Replicate cross-correlation used deepTools v2.5.0.1. Peaks were called with MACS2 v2.1.0 (BAMPE, q=1e-5). Annotation used ChIPseeker v1.6.7 (TxDb.Athaliana.BioMart.plantsmart28; region range to TSS=900 bp). Enrichment of peak features used HOMER v4.9 annotatePeaks.pl.

Differential accessibility: A master peak set was defined by combining SN and VN peaks and merging peaks within 50 bp; sporophyte-specific peaks were microspore peaks not overlapping this set. For each replicate, reads mapping to the master set were counted with featureCounts (Subread v2.0.1) to compute FRiP. DESeq2 v1.22.2 performed pairwise differential analysis. VN-specific and SN-specific peaks were defined by FDR-adjusted p<0.05 and |log2FC|>1; common peaks had |log2FC|≤1.

Epigenomic and sRNA analyses: H3K9me2, H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K27me1, H3K9me1, and H1 ChIP-seq data were reanalyzed. sRNA-seq reads (18–30 nt) were trimmed with cutadapt v1.9.1 and aligned with STAR v2.7 (zero mismatches, ≤100 multiple end-to-end alignments). Multimappers were reassigned with readmapIO.py. siRNA levels were normalized to RPM over peaks ±10 bp. DNA methylation was reanalyzed from bisulfite-seq (Bismark v0.22.2; Methylpy v1.2.9) to identify DMRs and DMCs (FDR≤0.05; DMCs collapsed within 250 bp; DMRs required ≥5 DMCs). DME-targeted ACRs were defined as VN ACRs overlapping hyper-DMCs in dme-2/+ VN vs WT.

Motif and TF analyses: DAP-seq motifs for 50 VN-expressed TFs were used (MEME suite v5.0.4; AME). Motif enrichment was tested against all ACRs. Binding fold-changes for DAP-seq vs ampDAP-seq were from prior work. Predicted TF binding sites within DME-targeted ACRs were identified with FIMO (p<1e-5; background from all ACRs). HINT-ATAC was used for DNA footprinting to infer TF activity. Gene lists for pollen-tube growth (SIVPT) and embryogenesis were from prior studies.

title: A conformational switch high-throughput screening assay and allosteric inhibition of the flavivirus NS2B-NS3 protease
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can an SLC-based conformational switch assay reliably detect NS2B conformational changes induced by active-site inhibitors and allosteric modulation? (2) Does a pocket unique to the inactive NS2B-NS3 structure enable identification of allosteric inhibitors that prevent the NS2B conformational switch? (3) Do identified inhibitors reduce protease activity and viral replication in vitro and in relevant cell types? (4) What is the inhibition mechanism (competitive vs non-competitive) and binding site of the lead compound?

Hypotheses: (i) Active-site inhibitor binding will induce NS2B closure, increasing SLC signal; allosteric inhibitors will suppress this NPGB-induced SLC enhancement. (ii) Virtual screening of the inactive NS2B-NS3 pocket will yield compounds that bind allosterically and inhibit protease activity. (iii) Effective allosteric inhibitors will reduce viral titers and RNA/protein expression in infected cells. (iv) Mechanistically, inhibition will be non-competitive (reduced Vmax, unchanged Km) and allosteric, with binding to the inactive-state pocket and stabilization of the complex (ΔTm >0.5°C). Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include dose-dependent suppression of NPGB-induced SLC by allosteric inhibitors, submicromolar IC50/EC50 values, non-competitive kinetics, and mutagenesis/PTSA evidence of pocket involvement.
reference_methodology:
Constructs and expression: DENV2 NS2B-NS3 protease (NS2B aa 48–95; NS3 aa 1–185) was cloned into pET28a with a G4SG4 linker (covalently linked). A thrombin cleavage site was engineered to generate unlinked NS2B/NS3. ZIKV NS2B-NS3 (PRVABC59) with a 3C cleavage site was codon-optimized and synthesized. The SLC conformational switch construct (N2CN3N) fused CLuc (aa 398–550) between NS2B C-terminus and NS3 N-terminus (GGSGG linker) and NLuc (aa 1–398) between NS3 aa 119–120. Mutants (e.g., A125C, A125W; K74A, I123A, N152A, V154A) were generated by site-directed mutagenesis. All constructs were verified by sequencing.

Protein expression and purification: Proteins were expressed in E. coli Rosetta 2(DE3) and purified via Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, followed by gel filtration (Superdex 200 16/60). For unlinked complexes, thrombin and/or 3C protease digestion was performed on-column or post-purification.

SLC conformational switch assay: In 96-well format, N2CN3N (150 nM) or full-length firefly luciferase (FLuc) (150 nM) was incubated with DMSO, DTNB, or candidate compounds (various concentrations) in test buffer (1× PBS, 0.05% CHAPS, 0.5% DMSO) for 30 min. NPGB (30 μM) was added to induce active-site binding. D-luciferin (5 μg/ml) in substrate buffer (1× PBS, 2 mM MgCl2, 4 mM EGTA, 4 mM ATP, 5 mM DTT) was added for 30 min. Luminescence was recorded (5 s integration) on a Veritas luminometer. Controls included FLuc alone to assess specificity.

Virtual screening: NCI Diversity Set II (1,364 compounds) was converted to PDB (Open Babel). AutoDock Vina docked compounds into a pocket unique to the inactive NS2B-NS3 structure (PDB 2FOM) with a 30 Å box centered at the pocket and exhaustiveness 8. Top 29 compounds were selected.

Protease inhibition assays: DENV2 or ZIKV NS2B-NS3 (150 nM) was preincubated with compounds (100 μM or serial dilutions; DMSO control) for 30 min at 4°C. Substrates: Abz-RRRRSAG-nTyr (50 mM stock; 100 μM working) or TAMRA-RRRRSAG-QXL570 (50 mM stock; 10 μM working). Reactions were monitored at 37°C for 1 h (Abz: Ex/Em 360/420 nm; TAMRA: 520/575 nm). Rates in the linear range were normalized to DMSO control. Kinetics used Abz substrate at 400–25 μM (2-fold dilutions) with NSC135618 (3 μM) preincubation; initial rates (0–10 min) were analyzed by Lineweaver–Burk.

Cell assays: A549 cells were infected with DENV2 (MOI 0.1) or ZIKV (MOI 0.1 for A549; MOI 2 for HPECs/hNPCs) in the presence of compounds. Viral titers were quantified by plaque reduction assays (Vero monolayers; 3–8 tenfold dilutions; 0.6% agar overlay; neutral red overlay on day 2). EC50 values were derived by sigmoidal fits. Cytotoxicity was measured by MTT (260594) or WST-8 (135618) assays; CC50 was determined by sigmoidal fits. Immunofluorescence (IFA) used anti-E antibody 4G2 and DyLight 488 secondary; Hoechst nuclear stain. qRT-PCR used TaqMan assays (ZIKV: CCGCTGCCCAACACAAG and CCACTAAYGTTCTTTTGCAGACAT with Cy5 probe; DENV2: CAGGTTATGGCACTGTCACGAT and CCATCTGCAGCAACACCATCTC with FAM probe) on Applied Biosystems 7500; 2−ΔΔCT quantification.

PTSA: DENV2 NS2B-NS3 (WT or mutants; 2.5 μM) was mixed with compounds (4.8 μM) in 1× PBS, 1.6% DMSO; SYPRO Orange fluorescence was monitored from 25–80°C on an Applied Biosystems 7500 Fast. ΔTm = Tm-comp − Tm-DMSO; ΔTm >0.5°C indicates binding.

Western blot and MS: ZIKV-infected A549 cells were lysed; SDS-PAGE (12%) and probed with anti-ZIKV NS3 (GTX133309) and anti-GAPDH (CB1001). High-MW bands were excised, trypsin-digested, and analyzed by LC–MS/MS (CapLC–QSTAR XL) with Mascot 2.5 (peptide mass tolerance 0.3 Da; MS/MS 0.3 Da; up to 2 missed cleavages; variable mods: Met oxidation, Cys carbamidomethylation). Significant identifications were at 95% confidence.

Statistics: Data are means ± SD of triplicates unless noted. Dose–response curves were fitted with sigmoidal models (Origin 6.0). One-way ANOVA assessed significance (p<0.05 to p<0.01).

title: Characterization of the Domestic Cat Population of Uruguay: Breeds, Coat Colors, Hair Length, Lifestyle, Sex and Spay/Neuter Status According to Guardian Report
field_subfield: Veterinary Science — Companion Animal Demography and Welfare
research_question:
Research question: What are the demographic characteristics of owned domestic cats in Uruguay with respect to sex, age, spay/neuter status, lifestyle (indoor vs. outdoor), breeds, coat colors, and hair length, and how are these traits associated with one another?

Hypotheses/predictions: The study did not state explicit hypotheses. Implicitly, the authors sought to estimate national-level distributions and test for associations among variables (e.g., sex, age, spay/neuter status, breed, coat length, lifestyle). Outcomes supporting associations would include statistically significant chi-square tests (p<0.05) for differences in proportions across categories. Outcomes refuting associations would include non-significant tests (p≥0.05). The study also aimed to document the prevalence of purebred vs. non-purebred cats and the distribution of coat colors and hair lengths, with the expectation that non-purebreds would predominate (as in most regions) and short-haired cats would be common among non-purebreds.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional, online survey using Google Forms. The survey was administered in Spanish, with scientific terminology accompanied by colloquial clarifications for public comprehension. Guardians were required to be ≥18 years, Uruguayan residents, and guardians of at least one cat. The survey period was March–July 2020.

Sample size and recruitment: Based on an estimated 68% of guardians owning at least one cat and Uruguay’s population (3,252,091), with a 95% confidence level and 5% margin of error, the minimum required sample size was 385. A total of 2572 completed surveys were received; 2561 met inclusion criteria after review. The achieved margin of error was 0.27%.

Survey instrument: Five blocks: (1) Guardian demographics; (2) cat basic information (age, sex, spay/neuter status); (3) physical characteristics (breed, coat length, coat color); (4) home, lifestyle, environment, and coexistence; (5) optional suggestions and photo upload. Question types included numeric fields, multiple choice, multiple answer, binary (Yes/No), and open-ended with “Don’t know/Does not answer” and “Others” options. Hair color options included representative photos. Indoor/outdoor classification was binary: indoor-only (no exterior access at any time) vs. outdoor (any exterior access; no gradation of supervision).

Data handling and quality control: Each survey was individually reviewed for completeness and eligibility. “Other” responses were classified, and guardians were contacted to clarify doubtful data. Repeated or incomplete surveys were excluded.

Statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics summarized proportions for sex, age, breed, coat colors, hair length, lifestyle, and spay/neuter status. Associations among variables were tested using chi-square tests at a 95% significance level. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.1.2). Reported tests included overall distributions and subgroup associations (e.g., sex by age strata, spay/neuter by age, lifestyle by breed/sex/neuter). Figures summarized distributions (Figure 1: age, sex, spay/neuter; Figure 2: age by lifestyle; Figure 3: multilevel Sankey linking lifestyle with breed, sex, and spay/neuter; Figure 4: coat color patterns; Figure 5: coat length examples).

Ethics: The study adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki. Privacy and data confidentiality were maintained. Data security complied with Law No. 18331 (Uruguay). Guardians’ full names and emails were collected for follow-up and photo use authorization. A specific ethical agreement was not required in Uruguay for this type of survey. Informed consent was obtained via a form legend detailing scientific use and anonymization. No IRB approval was indicated as necessary by local regulations for this survey type.

title: Predicting psychological symptoms when Facebook's digital wellbeing features are used: A cross-sectional survey
field_subfield: Psychology — Social Media and Digital Wellbeing
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the extent of awareness and adoption of Facebook’s six digital wellbeing features among US-based Facebook users? (2) Are these features associated with better mental health outcomes (lower DASS-21 depression, anxiety, stress scores) after accounting for time spent on Facebook and sociodemographics?

Hypotheses: (a) Users would show high awareness but variable adoption of wellbeing features. (b) Greater use of features designed to reduce attentional capture and social comparison (e.g., Unfollow, Notification Settings) would be associated with lower DASS-21 scores. (c) Time-monitoring features (Your Time on Facebook, Set Daily Reminders) might reduce symptoms by curbing excessive use. (d) Baseline time spent on Facebook would positively predict DASS-21 scores. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include significant negative associations between feature use and DASS-21 subscales, increased explained variance when adding features to models, and robustness across models controlling for demographics and time spent. Outcomes refuting them would include null associations or inconsistent patterns across models.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional survey. Recruitment: Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) panel, June 2021. Eligibility: age ≥21, English proficiency, US-based, positive MTurk track record (HIT approval rate >95%, >500 HITs approved). Sample: 608 participants; 10 failed attention checks (1.6%), yielding n=598. Ethics: Written informed consent per Declaration of Helsinki; USD $0.50 compensation. Approvals: Yale-NUS College Ethics Review Committee (2021-CERC-001). Preregistration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04967846).

Measures: Survey hosted on Qualtrics (link: https://osf.io/9z4dy/). Reading level: 7th grade. Pilot-tested. Baseline Facebook use: self-reported hours per week on Facebook; frequency of nine activities (reading news feed, posting status updates, posting photos, posting original content, browsing friends’ timelines, viewing friends’ photos, commenting on friends’ posts, sharing friends’ content, using Messenger) on 7-point scales (never to >once/day). Awareness and adoption of six features: participants viewed screenshots and indicated whether they had heard of each feature (Yes/No). If Yes, whether they had used it (Yes/No). For repeated-use features (Unfollow, Snooze, Off-Facebook Activity, Your Time on Facebook), frequency was rated on a 5-point scale (never to daily). Demographics: age, gender, race, religion, marital status, education, employment, family income, household size, living setting. Mental health: DASS-21 (21 items; 7 items per subscale: depression, anxiety, stress). Cronbach’s alphas: depression 0.87; anxiety 0.89; stress 0.89. Items rated 0–3; subscale scores summed and multiplied by two.

Statistical analysis: Data cleaning included two attention checks (CAPTCHA-like verification). Descriptive statistics: counts/percentages and medians/IQRs. Primary analyses: linear regression models predicting each DASS-21 subscale. Model 1: time spent on Facebook (log-transformed) as predictor. Model 2: Model 1 + six binary indicators of feature use (Unfollow, Snooze, Off-Facebook Activity, Your Time on Facebook, Set Daily Reminders, Notification Settings). Model 3: Model 2 + demographics (age, gender, race, religion, marital status, education, employment, family income, household size, living setting). Type I error controlled at α=0.05; power set at 0.80 to detect small effects (f²=0.05). Software: SPSS 27 and R 4.0.3. Sensitivity analyses: Models 2 and 3 repeated without time spent on Facebook; key findings unchanged (Appendix 1, Tables S1–S3).

title: Hypoxia and Ezrin Expression in Primary Melanoma Have High Prognostic Relevance
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are hypoxia indicators (CD34 capillary density, HIF-1α) and EMT markers (Ezrin, L1CAM) in primary melanoma associated with sentinel lymph node metastasis and tumor-specific survival? (2) Do these markers correlate with each other and with established clinicopathologic factors (e.g., Breslow thickness)?

Hypotheses: (a) Lower capillary density (hypoxia) and higher HIF-1α activity will be associated with worse survival and increased SLN metastasis. (b) EMT markers Ezrin and L1CAM will be elevated in more aggressive tumors and correlate with hypoxia markers. (c) Ezrin and L1CAM will independently predict survival beyond traditional factors. Supportive outcomes would include significant inverse correlations between capillary density and EMT markers, positive associations between HIF-1α and EMT markers, and significant hazard ratios for survival in Cox models. Refuting outcomes would include null associations between hypoxia/EMT markers and outcomes or lack of correlation with clinicopathologic features.
reference_methodology:
Design and cohort: Retrospective observational cohort of 49 patients with primary cutaneous malignant melanoma treated at the University Hospital of Zurich between 1999 and 2002. All patients had tissue available for additional staining. Two patients with missing follow-up were excluded from survival analyses; a sensitivity analysis comparing mean Breslow thickness (2.83 mm) between groups showed no significant difference (t=0.043, p=0.9659). Follow-up ended on 29 May 2022; median follow-up for survivors was 96 months (mean 110; range 12–263). Twelve patients died of melanoma-related causes.

Participants: Age 18–75 years (median 54; mean 53.53). Tumor type: 26 nodular melanomas. SLN status: 15/49 (30.6%) positive. Breslow thickness: mean 2.83 mm (median 2.20). Melanoma-related deaths: 12/49 (25.5%).

Tissue and IHC: TMA from a prior SLN study. IHC performed for Ezrin, CD34, and L1CAM; Ki67 and HIF-1α IHC data were available from a previous study. Ezrin and HIF-1α were scored using the German Immunohistochemical Scoring (GIS) system: percentage of positive cells (0: negative; 1: ≤10%; 2: 11–50%; 3: 51–90%; 4: >90%) multiplied by staining intensity (0: negative; 1: weak; 2: moderate; 3: strong). L1CAM was consistently strong positive; only percentage of positive cells was recorded. CD34-positive capillaries were counted per TMA core (0.28 mm²). A capillary count <20 per core was categorized as low; >20 as high. Ki67 was assessed in hot spots by counting positive cells per 100 tumor cells.

Pathology: Two experienced pathologists (U.M., D.M.-P.) evaluated IHC. Weak background staining was considered negative.

Ethics: Conducted under the ethics committee of Canton Zurich (BASEC-Nr. PB 2017−27). Informed consent obtained from all subjects.

Statistical analysis: Normality assessed via Q–Q plots. Correlations between numerical predictors with >2 categories used Kendall’s tau B. Comparisons between dichotomous and ordinal variables used Mann–Whitney U; between dichotomous variables used chi-square. Survival curves constructed via Kaplan–Meier and compared with Mantel–Haenszel log-rank tests. Numerical and ordinal predictors were dichotomized into low/high using clinically meaningful cut-points. Univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations with survival time (diagnosis to last follow-up or death). Due to limited events, multivariable models included only two predictors, chosen a priori based on theoretical significance. Patients with missing independent variables were excluded from individual analyses. Model diagnostics checked proportional hazards (survival and log–log plots, time interaction terms), multicollinearity, and independence of cases; no violations were detected.

title: Effects of Neuropeptides and Mechanical Loading on Bone Cell Resorption in Vitro
research_question:
Research question: Do neuropeptides CGRP and VIP suppress bone resorptive activity through the RANKL/OPG pathway in a manner similar to mechanical loading via OFF-induced shear stress, and do combined neuropeptide and mechanical stimuli produce additive effects?

Hypotheses: (1) Both CGRP and VIP will decrease RANKL and increase OPG mRNA and protein, thereby reducing the RANKL/OPG ratio and suppressing osteoclast formation/activity. (2) OFF-induced shear stress will produce similar decreases in RANKL and increases in OPG, consistent with prior findings. (3) Combining neuropeptides with mechanical loading will further enhance suppression of RANKL/OPG signaling beyond either modality alone, indicating additive or synergistic effects.

Alternative outcomes: If neuropeptides and loading converge on overlapping pathways, combined treatment may not yield additive changes. If only one modality is effective, the other would show no significant modulation. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses include significant reductions in RANKL and increases in OPG across all treatments, with combined groups showing greater suppression than single treatments. Outcomes refuting the hypotheses would include no change in RANKL/OPG or additive effects only in one modality.
reference_methodology:
Cell systems: MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblastic cells and RAW 264.7 murine monocytic macrophages were co-cultured to assess osteoclastogenesis. For osteoclast formation, cells were co-cultured at a 25,000:10,000 ratio in α-MEM (GIBCO) with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. M-CSF (25 ng/mL; Peprotech) and 1α,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (10 nM; Sigma-Aldrich) were added on Days 1, 3, 5, and 7 to induce RANKL and osteoclast formation. Neuropeptides VIP (10 μM; Sigma-Aldrich) or CGRP (10 nM; Sigma-Aldrich) were added on Days 1, 3, 5, and 7. Cells were maintained at 37 °C, 5% CO2. TRAP staining (Sigma-Aldrich) was performed on Day 9. TRAP-positive multinucleated cells with ≥3 nuclei were counted by three blinded independent observers using a 20× objective.

Mechanical loading: MC3T3-E1 cells were cultured in α-MEM with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. 1α,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (10 nM) was added on Days 1 and 3. VIP (1 μM) or CGRP (10 nM) were added on Days 1 and 3. On Day 5, cells were subcultured on glass slides (~7 × 10^5 cells/cm^2) for either osteoclast formation or OFF experiments. On Day 6, slides were placed in custom-built parallel plate flow chambers under sterile conditions. Dynamic OFF was generated using a glass syringe connected to rigid tubing and the flow chamber, driven by an actuator delivering a precise flow rate at 1 Hz with a peak shear stress of ±1 Pa for 1 h. Control cells were placed in flow chambers without flow. Six groups were tested: Control, Load, CGRP, CGRP+Load, VIP, VIP+Load.

Gene expression: After 1 h OFF, cells were lysed and total RNA extracted using Tri-Reagent (Sigma-Aldrich). Real-time RT-PCR (Applied Biosystems) with TaqMan Gene Expression Assays quantified RANKL and OPG mRNA. Expression was normalized to the housekeeping gene 18S (TaqMan). Each RNA sample was analyzed in triplicate.

Protein quantification: After 1 h OFF, slides were incubated in 10 mL fresh serum-free media for 1 h at 37 °C, 5% CO2. Supernatants were collected to measure secreted RANKL and OPG by ELISA (Quantikine Mouse RANKL and OPG Immunoassays; R&D Systems). Cell lysates were prepared with lysis buffer (1% Triton X-100, 0.5% Nonidet P-40, 10 mM Tris pH 7.4, 0.2 mM PMSF, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 30 mM Na4P2O7) and total protein quantified by Quick Start Bradford Protein Assay (Bio-Rad).

Statistics: ANOVA followed by Fisher’s least significant difference (LSD) post hoc test was used. Significance threshold was p<0.05. Blinding was applied for TRAP counting. Sample sizes for qPCR/ELISA and randomization procedures were not reported.

title: Research on intrusion and large arch bulge in lining structure for highway's mudstone tunnel
field_subfield: Civil Engineering — Geotechnical Engineering (Tunneling and Rock Mechanics)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the primary mechanisms driving large deformation and lining intrusion in the YK209+500–YK210+030 mudstone tunnel section? (2) How do water-induced softening and rheological behavior of mudstone influence time-dependent deformation and stress redistribution in the surrounding rock and lining? (3) What roles do tunnel depth, in-situ stress, and swelling forces play in controlling deformation magnitude and convergence time? (4) Can a 3D viscoelastic–plastic model calibrated via inverse analysis reproduce observed deformation and stress patterns, and what parameter values best capture the field behavior?

Hypotheses: (H1) Water seepage into mudstone reduces strength and stiffness, accelerates macroscopic fissure growth, and induces plastic flow that drives large invert arch bulges and lining intrusions. (H2) The surrounding rock exhibits pronounced rheology (attenuating and stable creep), with deformation rates decaying over time, and lining deformations remain small after initial lining. (H3) Tunnel depth and stress levels are primary controls on unloading deformation and convergence time, whereas swelling forces are secondary. (H4) A composite Burgers–Mohr–Coulomb model, calibrated to field data, can reproduce observed displacement time histories and stress distributions. Support for H1–H4 would be evidenced by: (i) measured displacement magnitudes and patterns consistent with water-softening; (ii) time-dependent displacement decay; (iii) simulated stress concentrations at arch feet and low lining stresses; and (iv) close agreement between model and field data. Refutation would involve alternative mechanisms (e.g., swelling dominance) or poor model-data fit.
reference_methodology:
Site and geology: The highway tunnel traverses eroded and accumulated loess with elevation 1248–1536 m. Rock attitude is 44°–28°∠30°. Joints include J1: 7°∠30° and J2: 13°∠86°. The problematic section is YK209+500–YK210+030. Groundwater was encountered in boreholes at YK209+650 and YK209+845; distribution is uneven.

Field monitoring: Thirty-six monitoring sections were installed along YK209+500–YK209+850 at 10 m intervals. Monitoring began after initial lining completion and continued through pre-application of secondary lining, with per-section durations of 18–41 days. Displacement sensors were placed on the arch top, arch shoulders, arch waist, and invert arch. Measuring points #1–#9 were evenly distributed on the invert arch; buried points #10–#20 were aligned along a vertical line through #3, spaced 2 m apart (except #19–#20 at 5 m), with #3–#20 spanning 25 m.

Ground stress testing: Hydrofracturing was used to measure in-situ stresses. Expandable rubber packers isolated a borehole segment at a set depth; liquid was pumped to fracture the rock, and in-situ stresses were inferred from characteristic pressure values. Reported stresses: max horizontal 1.0–2.2 MPa, min horizontal 0.7–1.8 MPa, vertical 5.1–5.9 MPa. The stress field is dominated by dead-weight stress.

Laboratory tests: Mudstone cores from the problematic section were tested for physical and mechanical properties. Physical properties (Table 1): particle density 2.16–2.23 g/cm3; water content 8.37–9.63%; water filling rate 8.52–9.77%; porosity 17.49–19.04%. Mechanical properties (Table 2): uniaxial compressive strength decreased markedly upon saturation (e.g., 6.75 MPa to 1.02 MPa; 6.22 MPa to 3.67 MPa across depth intervals); deformation modulus decreased (e.g., 1.13 GPa to 1.04 GPa; 1.35 GPa to 1.24 GPa); Poisson’s ratio ~0.30–0.31. Additional parameters (Table 3) for natural and saturated mudstone included: deformation modulus 800 MPa (natural) vs 300 MPa (saturated); Poisson’s ratio 0.32 vs 0.35; unit weight 22 vs 23 kN/m3; cohesion 200 vs 60 kPa; friction angle 30° vs 25°; tensile strength 50 vs 15 kPa.

Numerical simulation: A 3D finite difference model (FLAC3D) was built to simulate deformation and stress under natural and water-softened conditions. Domain boundaries: 68 m from the tunnel centerline on both sides, top 60 m, bottom 50 m, and 20 m along the tunnel axis. Mesh: 151,800 elements; 161,637 nodes. Excavation diameter: 12.38 m; inner diameter behind lining: 10.86 m; burial depth ~237 m. Lining design: SVb: I20a steel I-beam at 100 cm spacing; 26 cm C25 shotcrete; Φ6 double-layer mesh; 3.5 m R25 hollow grouting anchors at 75×100 cm spacing; 50 cm C30 reinforced concrete lining; main cavern design limit 10.25×5 m.

Constitutive modeling and calibration: A composite model combined a Burgers viscoelastic model (Maxwell and Kelvin elements in series) with Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, where viscoelastic and plastic strain rates act in series. The model captures attenuating and stable creep stages and elastic–plastic volumetric changes. Parameters for natural and saturated mudstone were taken from Tables 1–3. Inverse analysis of field displacement time series was used to calibrate rheological parameters (Table 4). Reported natural-state parameters: EM=2.4 GPa, Ek=0.25 GPa, ηk=0.18 GPa·d, ηm=1,000 GPa·d. The plasticity criterion used a composite Mohr–Coulomb shear damage and tensile damage with yield functions f_s and f_t (equations provided). The model’s validity was assessed by consistency with field data; details of the inverse procedure (objective function, solver, uncertainty) were not reported.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human or animal subjects. Funding: No financial support reported. Conflict of interest: One author employed by CCCC Second Highway Consultants Co., Ltd.; others declare no conflicts.

title: Path Diversified Retransmission for TCP over Wireless Mesh Networks
field_subfield: Computer Science — Networking (Wireless Mesh Networks, Transport Protocols)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can multipath routing be made viable for TCP in WMNs without degrading throughput or fairness? (2) Does separating original and retransmitted packets and routing them along distinct QoS-optimized paths mitigate RTT underestimation and reordering-induced spurious retransmissions? (3) How does the proposed cross-layer design compare to single-path routing and naive multipath in terms of throughput, stability, and fairness?

Hypotheses: (H1) PDR, by routing original packets over max-bandwidth paths and retransmitted packets over min-delay paths, will avoid RTT underestimation (since Karn’s algorithm excludes retransmissions) and reduce reordering, thereby improving TCP throughput relative to naive multipath. (H2) PDR will maintain TCP fairness comparable to single-path routing because retransmissions are distributed across flows, preventing disproportionate degradation of any single flow. (H3) PDR will reduce throughput fluctuations compared to naive multipath by minimizing spurious retransmissions and timeouts.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if PDR shows higher throughput than naive multipath and single-path baselines across scenarios, with reduced loss-recovery time. H2 is supported if Jain’s fairness index under PDR is similar to single-path and higher than naive multipath. H3 is supported if time-series throughput variability is lower under PDR than naive multipath.
reference_methodology:
Simulation platform: ns-2. Scenarios: (a) 40-node random WMN in a 1000m × 1000m square field; (b) 100-node grid (10 × 10) with 200m spacing. Radio parameters: propagation range 250m; carrier sensing distance 550m. MAC: IEEE 802.11 RTS/CTS/Data/ACK; channel data rate 11Mbps. Transport: TCP-Veno. Routing baselines: AODV (single-path) and AOMDV (naive multipath with even split). Proposed: PDR with QAOMDV.

Traffic scenarios: (1) 1 TCP flow; (2) 1 TCP flow and 7 UDP flows; (3) 8 TCP flows. For each scenario, 30 independent runs with different random seeds were executed and results averaged to mitigate randomness. Additional large-scale evaluation: 100-node grid with 10 TCP flows between randomly chosen source–destination pairs; 30 runs.

Throughput metric: average number of packets received per time unit. Fairness metric: Jain’s fairness index. Additional observation: time-series throughput variability to assess stability.

Parameter estimation (QAOMDV): Available bandwidth estimated by passively monitoring channel idle/busy periods; available bandwidth = channel capacity × (idle time / total time). Delay between nodes measured as the time interval between sending and receiving the same packet. Initialization: nodes broadcast probe packets; after route establishment, real data packets are used for estimation. Periodic updates via exponential weighted moving average (EWMA).

Routing QoS metrics: QAOMDV extends AOMDV to maintain both max-bandwidth and min-delay routes. Minimum bandwidth calculation: if hopcount n ≤ 4, available bandwidth is inversely proportional to hopcount; if n > 4, available bandwidth is set to 1/4 of raw channel bandwidth (empirically chosen parameter). RREQ header carries min-bandwidth and delay; intermediate nodes update these fields. RREP header carries bandwidth and delay to establish forwarding paths. Route updates follow AOMDV rules, inserting disjoint paths with better QoS.

Classifier and scheduler: A classifier between transport and IP layers marks packets as original or retransmitted by comparing incoming TCP sequence numbers against the most recent sequence number. Original packets are routed over the max-bandwidth path; retransmitted packets are routed over the min-delay path. The scheduler maintains two queues (original, retransmitted) with higher priority for retransmissions.

Analysis: The authors extend a TCP Veno throughput model to multipath, deriving expressions for expected loss-recovery time and throughput under PDR. They show that if the retransmission path has lower delay, PDR reduces loss-recovery time and improves throughput.

title: ANCA-associated pauci-immune glomerulonephritis in a patient with bacterial endocarditis: a challenging clinical dilemma
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological features of ANCA-associated pauci-immune GN occurring during IE? (2) How should such cases be diagnosed and managed, particularly when coexisting infections and chronic viral hepatitis complicate immunosuppression? (3) What is the prevalence and prognosis of ANCA-mediated GN in IE based on available case reports?

Hypotheses/predictions: (a) Infection can induce PR3-ANCA formation and pauci-immune GN, necessitating immunosuppression beyond antimicrobials; (b) Renal biopsy is critical to differentiate immune complex GN from ANCA-associated vasculitis, as treatment strategies diverge; (c) Reported cases will show subacute/chronic infection courses and left-sided IE predominance, with variable renal recovery depending on timely immunosuppression. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include biopsy evidence of pauci-immune GN with PR3-ANCA positivity, clinical improvement with immunosuppression in literature cases, and challenges in initiating immunosuppression in the presence of active infection and chronic hepatitis B/C.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-patient clinical case report with systematic literature review.

Case identification and setting: A 59-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and C coinfection presented with AKI and Enterococcus faecalis IE. He had a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, chronic left bundle branch block, and a prophylactic biventricular ICD. He denied recreational drug use and recent sexual activity.

Clinical course and diagnostics: Initial presentation included progressive low back pain, weight loss, and AKI (creatinine 418 µmol/L). CT spine revealed chronic discitis/osteomyelitis of the lower thoracic spine. Blood cultures grew Enterococcus faecalis. Transthoracic echocardiography identified a 1.5 × 1 cm mass on the anterior tricuspid valve leaflet and a 1 × 0.5 cm echodense mobile mass on the ICD wire (right atrial side). The ICD was extracted; the LV lead was tunneled to the right side. Creatinine rose to 720 µmol/L with microscopic hematuria and proteinuria. Laboratory testing showed low complement (C3 0.5 g/L; C4 0.07 g/L) and strongly positive PR3-ANCA (>8.0 AI), with negative p-ANCA. Renal biopsy demonstrated focal segmental proliferative and necrotizing GN affecting >50% of glomeruli with cellular and fibrocellular crescents and segmental sclerosis. Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy showed paucity of immune complexes, supporting pauci-immune GN consistent with ANCA vasculitis.

Interventions: After blood cultures sterilized (~1.5 weeks prior), the patient received IV methylprednisolone 250 mg daily for 3 days, followed by oral prednisone taper starting at 60 mg daily. Due to chronic inactive hepatitis B/C coinfection and dialysis status, standard induction therapies (e.g., cyclophosphamide, rituximab) were not administered. The patient developed pneumonia and candidemia, became anuric, and required intermittent hemodialysis. Cardiovascular surgery deemed surgery too high risk. He died 3 months after admission.

Literature review methods: PubMed, Web of Science, Proceedings First, and Papers First were searched using terms: “anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody,” “glomerulonephritis,” and “endocarditis.” Inclusion criteria: biopsy-proven pauci-immune GN with ANCA positivity in culture-positive IE; abstracts from International Society of Nephrology proceedings were also reviewed. Five cases met criteria. Data extracted included organism, valve involvement, infection duration, ANCA profile, extrarenal manifestations, treatments, and renal outcomes.

title: Investigation of Quantitative Polarographic Measurements of Oxygen Tension in Tissue
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can polarographic measurements provide quantitative estimates of tissue oxygen tension in vivo when electrode stability and steady-state conditions are controlled? (2) Does the polarographic diffusion current (i_d) correlate with tissue pO2 calculated from Krogh-type models using measured blood flow, oxygen extraction, and hemoglobin oxygenation? (3) What diffusion coefficient for oxygen in saline can be reliably obtained using a diffusion chamber and polarography, and how does it compare to literature values?

Hypotheses: (H1) Under controlled steady-state conditions, polarographic i_d will scale with tissue pO2 in a manner consistent with Krogh-type diffusion models, enabling quantitative inference of tissue oxygenation. (H2) The measured diffusion coefficient for oxygen in saline will be within the range of literature estimates, validating the polarographic diffusion setup. (H3) Variability in polarographic tissue measurements will be primarily attributable to electrode stability (adsorption, catalytic effects) and tissue factors (flow, metabolism, geometry), rather than the polarographic method per se.

Predictions: If H1 holds, polarographic i_d and calculated pO2 will show close agreement (within ~10%) across repeated measurements under steady conditions. If H2 holds, the measured D will match literature values (≈10^-5 cm²/s range). If H3 holds, excluding unstable electrodes and non-steady tissue states will reduce variability to within ~5–10%.
reference_methodology:
Diffusion coefficient measurement in saline: A custom diffusion chamber (two compartments separated by cellophane membrane) was constructed. Each compartment had a platinum analysis electrode (20-gauge platinum-iridium wire) positioned at known distances (e.g., ~1 cm diffusion path). The diffusion path diameter was ~0.43 inches (0.43 cm). One compartment was equilibrated with oxygenated saline (e.g., 0.91 M NaCl), and the other with deoxygenated saline. The chamber was mounted on a plastic float in an oil bath to minimize vibration. Polarographic measurements were recorded at a constant applied potential (e.g., −0.59 V vs SCE) using a modified interrupted polarographic circuit that alternated applied potential and periodically shorted the analysis electrode to the reference to stabilize solid electrodes. Calibration curves (i_d vs concentration) were obtained from polarograms at known oxygen concentrations. The diffusion coefficient D was estimated by fitting error-function solutions of the diffusion equation to the time course of oxygen concentration changes at the second electrode, using tabulated error-function values and correcting for temperature (≈1.3–1.65% per °C increase at physiological temperatures). Reported conditions: 23°C, 0.91 M NaCl.

In vivo tissue measurements: White rabbits (1.4–3.8 kg) were anesthetized with pentobarbital (30–50 mg/kg IV, with supplemental doses). Heparin (1 U/kg IV) prevented clotting. Tracheal cannulation ensured airway patency and allowed inspired gas control (N2/O2 mixtures). For ear experiments, the cervical sympathetic nerve was cut to denervate vessels; for muscle, the nerve to the muscle was cut to prevent neural stimulation. Polarographic electrodes (platinum-iridium wire, 10–65 gauge) were implanted in the ear or muscle. Electrodes were stabilized with a cotton ball and covered with multiple coats of collodion to minimize movement and adsorption. A T-bar support held electrodes perpendicular to muscle fibers and limited motion. Temperature was controlled using a water bath (ear) or water pack (muscle), monitored by platinum resistance thermometers or thermistor probes.

Blood flow and oxygen extraction: Blood flow was measured gravimetrically using calibrated pipettes and microcatheters (e.g., Intramedic polyethylene catheters, ID 0.011 in, OD 0.024 in). Approximately 0.1 mL blood was collected at the tip of the pipette, and the time to fill additional 0.1 mL increments was recorded until flow stabilized. Arterial blood samples were drawn immediately after flow measurements. Oxygen content was determined by van Slyke–Neil or Copeland–Nathanson methods (0.03 mL blood samples), with oxygen absorbed into sodium thiosulfate containing anthraquinone and measured as partial pressure. Hemoglobin concentration was measured spectrophotometrically (Klett spectrophotometer, 540 nm) using standard hemoglobin reagents and calibration curves.

Data analysis and criteria: For each condition, a calibration curve (i_d vs concentration) was recorded before and after tissue measurements to assess electrode stability. Data were excluded if calibration changed substantially, if temperature drifted, or if blood flow varied by >10% from control. Mean tissue pO2 was calculated from Krogh’s model using measured capillary oxygen tension (Po), oxygen extraction (Q), and geometric factors (capillary radius r, tissue radius R, and D). The study reports comparisons between polarographic i_d-derived pO2 and calculated pO2 for multiple experiments in ear and muscle.

title: Transportin 3 (TNPO3) as a carrier of SRSF1 during myogenesis in C2C12 cells
field_subfield: Cell Biology — Nuclear Transport and Myogenesis
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does TNPO3 expression and localization change across myogenic differentiation stages in C2C12 myoblasts? (2) Does TNPO3 colocalize with its cargo SRSF1 during differentiation, and how does this colocalization shift between nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments? (3) Do these localization dynamics align with canonical markers of myogenesis (MRFs, MyHC-1, Desmin) and myomiRNA expression profiles?

Hypotheses: (a) TNPO3 expression and nuclear localization increase in differentiating myotubes, reflecting a role in nuclear import of splicing factors during myogenesis. (b) TNPO3 colocalizes with SRSF1, with a shift from cytoplasmic to nuclear colocalization as differentiation progresses. (c) TNPO3–SRSF1 dynamics are temporally coordinated with myogenic marker expression and myomiRNA regulation. Supportive outcomes would include increased TNPO3 nuclear signal in myotubes versus myoblasts, increased nuclear colocalization of TNPO3 and SRSF1 at later stages, and concordant upregulation of myogenic markers and myomiRNAs. Refutation would involve stable or decreased TNPO3 nuclear localization, minimal colocalization with SRSF1, or discordant marker profiles.
reference_methodology:
Cell culture and differentiation: Murine C2C12 myoblasts (ATCC CRL-1772; RRID:CVCL_0188) were cultured at 37°C, 5% CO2 in complete medium. At 80% confluence, differentiation was induced by switching to differentiation medium. Stages: T0 (undifferentiated), T1 (24 h), T3–T5 (3–5 days), T10 (10 days). Media: Growth medium—DMEM + 1% L-glutamine + 1% penicillin/streptomycin + 10% heat-inactivated FBS. Differentiation medium—DMEM + 1% L-glutamine + 1% penicillin/streptomycin + 1% heat-inactivated equine serum (HS).

RNA extraction and qRT-PCR: Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol and purified by chloroform/isopropanol. Quantity/quality were assessed by NanoDrop ND-2000. One microgram RNA was reverse-transcribed (RevertAid First Strand cDNA Synthesis). qPCR used Maxima SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix 2X on a Bio-Rad IQ5. Reaction efficiency (E) was calculated per prior method. qPCR was performed in triplicate; CT values were normalized to GAPDH. Primers (Table 2) targeted Tnpo3, MyoD, Myf5, Desmin, Pax7, MyoG, Myf6, and GAPDH.

MicroRNAs and exosomes: For miRNA analysis, cells at each stage were enzymatically harvested and 2.5×10^6 cells stored at −80°C. Exosomes were isolated from supernatants by centrifugation (300 g, 10 min, 4°C), 0.2 μm filtration, and ultracentrifugation (120,000 g, 70 min, 4°C). miR-1, miR-206, miR-133a/b were isolated and analyzed per prior protocol.

Protein extraction and subcellular fractionation: Total lysates used RIPA buffer with protease inhibitors and Na3Va4; lysates were incubated 30 min on ice and centrifuged (12,800 g, 20 min). For nuclear/cytoplasmic fractions, 1–5×10^6 cells were pelleted and lysed in hypotonic buffer; nuclei were pelleted (1,850 g, 5 min), then incubated (1,850 g, 15 min) to separate cytoplasmic (supernatant) and nuclear (pellet) fractions. Cytoplasmic fraction was clarified (40,000 g, 30 min) in S100 buffer. Nuclear fraction was rinsed with low/high salt buffers (20 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 25% glycerol, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM EDTA; and 1.2 M KCl), incubated on ice (30 min), and centrifuged (13,225 g, 30 min, 4°C). Protein concentration was measured by DC Protein Assay (Bio-Rad) using BSA standards. Buffers (Table 3) included RIPA (25 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 50 mM NaCl, 0.5% Na-deoxycholate, 1% NP-40, 0.1% SDS), hypotonic lysis buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl, EDTA-free protease inhibitors), S100 buffer (0.3 M HEPES pH 7.9, 30 mM MgCl2, 1.4 mM KCl, EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and low/high salt buffers.

Western blotting: 40 μg lysate per lane were resolved on 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose. Membranes were blocked (TBS-Tween 0.1% + 5% milk, 1 h, RT), incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (Table 4), washed (TBS-Tween 0.05%), and probed with HRP-conjugated secondaries (1 h, RT). Detection used Clarity Western ECL. Densitometry used ImageJ; signals were normalized to actin. Statistics used t-tests. Primary antibodies included TNPO3 (ab71388), SRSF1 (Thermo 96), Myosin (F59), Myogenin (5FD), MyoD (G-1), Actin (I-19). Secondary antibodies included HRP-conjugated anti-mouse/rabbit/goat and DyLight-conjugated secondaries for IF.

Immunofluorescence: Cells (1×10^4 cells/cm²) were seeded on LabTek slides. Primary antibodies were incubated overnight at 4°C; secondary antibodies for 1 h at 37°C; nuclei counterstained with Hoechst. Slides were imaged on a Nikon A1 confocal microscope with 60×/1.4 NA objective and 405/488/561 nm lasers. Acquisition parameters (laser power, gain, offset) were fixed. Z-stacks were acquired at 210 nm/pixel, 12-bit, 4096 gray levels, pinhole 1 Airy unit, z-step 500 nm. Image analysis and 3D rendering used NIS-Elements. TNPO3 fluorescence intensity was quantified by measuring mean intensity in 50 ROIs (64-pixel diameter) in nucleus and cytoplasm.

IEM: Cells were fixed (1% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer pH 7.4, 30 min RT; then 45 min), scraped, pelleted (1,200 g, 20 min), dehydrated in ethanol, and embedded in London Resin White at 60°C. Thin sections were immunolabeled for TNPO3 (goat anti-rabbit conjugated with 10 nm colloidal gold; 1:20), stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate, and imaged on a Zeiss EM 109. Controls lacked primary antibody; no gold particles were detected in controls.

SIM: 3D N-SIM used a Plan-Apochromat 100×/1.49 Oil TIRF objective with 405/488/561 nm lasers. For each axial plane, 1024×1024 px images at 4096 gray levels were acquired in 3 rotations and 5 phases. Final images were reconstructed at 125 nm z-step. Colocalization was quantified using Mander’s Overlap coefficient (percentage ± SD). Pixels with intensity >50% of 4096 were included. 3D cluster analysis quantified colocalized volumes.

title: Behavioral Responses to Fevers and Other Medical Events in Children With and Without ASD
research_question:
The study asked: (1) Do participants exhibit behavioral changes during a fever, and if so, do these differ for children with ASD? (2) Do behavioral changes during fever differ from changes during non-febrile illnesses? (3) What phenotypic characteristics characterize children who show positive behavioral changes during fever?

Implicit hypotheses included: (a) Children with ASD would show distinct behavioral responses to fever compared to TD peers (e.g., differential worsening or improvement); (b) Behavioral changes during fever would differ from changes during non-febrile illnesses, potentially implicating fever-specific mechanisms; (c) A subset of children with ASD might show improvement during fever, identifiable via consistent positive changes across multiple fevers. Support for (a) would be indicated by significant diagnosis-by-condition interactions in multilevel models; support for (b) would be indicated by significant differences between fever and non-febrile illness conditions; support for (c) would be indicated by case-level consistency of positive changes across ≥2 fevers and characterization of associated phenotypes. Null findings for (a) and (b) would suggest no overall group differences or that fever-related changes are not unique to fever.
reference_methodology:
Design: Prospective observational study with three-month behavioral tracking via a custom smartphone app. Weekly baseline behavioral surveys were collected at times without events, and event-specific surveys were triggered by reported medical events (fever, non-febrile illness, other) and non-medical “out of the ordinary” events. Temperature was recorded each time an event or survey was submitted to mask hypotheses and reduce biased reporting.

Participants: N = 244 children (141 ASD; 103 TD), 70% male. Ages 2–7 years. Recruitment occurred through research databases, word-of-mouth, and flyers in local autism clinics, pediatric offices, daycares, and schools in Los Angeles, San Francisco, and New York areas. Inclusion criteria: age 2–7 years; fever in the prior 12 months; independent walking. For ASD recruitment, parents provided documentation of a clinical ASD diagnosis. Exclusion criteria: severe sensory impairment; for TD recruitment, any diagnosis or receipt of services for a developmental or psychiatric disorder.

Measures: Behavioral survey (11 items) rated child mood/behavior on a 5-point Likert scale (lower = less than usual; higher = more than usual). Items 9–10 (irritability, anxiety) were reverse-coded so a score of 5 indicated lessening symptoms. Items were recoded to -2 to 2 for interpretability (negative = worsening; 0 = same as usual). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with oblique rotation yielded three factors: Factor 1 (Social Behaviors: happy/cheerful, talk to others, physically active, social/interested, communicating ideas, play); Factor 2 (Emotional/Behavioral Problems: anxious, managing behaviors, irritable); Factor 3 (Somatic Symptoms: eat, sleep). Factor scores were computed as average item ratings within each factor.

Covariates: PPVT-4 (receptive vocabulary; standard scores); Mullen Scales of Early Learning nonverbal subtests (Visual Reception, Fine Motor) if PPVT basal not obtained (age equivalents used to compute ratio IQ/developmental quotient); Vineland-3 Adaptive Behavior Composite (ABC) standard score; SRS-2 total T-score; PSI-4 SF total stress score; ABC-C Irritability and Hyperactivity subscales; CBCL/1.5–5 and CBCL/6–18 Internalizing and Externalizing subscales.
