Event categorization: Baseline (weekly no-event reports); Fever (≥100.0°F); Week After Fever (7 days following the last fever report); Non-fever Medical (any medical event without fever); Other (non-medical events).

Statistical analysis: Multilevel models (SAS PROC MIXED) with behavioral factor scores as outcomes. Model 1: unconditional ICC to quantify within-person variance. Model 2: fixed effects of condition (baseline, fever, week after) with random intercepts and slopes to capture within-person associations and between-person variability. Model 3: added diagnosis (TD reference) and diagnosis-by-condition interactions to test group differences. Separate models compared fever vs non-febrile medical events. Model fit indices (AIC, BIC; smaller is better), variances explained, and fixed/random effects were reported. Significance thresholds: p < .05, p < .01 as indicated in tables.

title: СИСТЕМНИЙ ПІДХІД У ЗАБЕЗПЕЧЕННІ ІНФОРМАЦІЙНОЇ БЕЗПЕКИ
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How can information security in corporate information and telecommunication systems be conceptualized as an emergent property of a network of relations among components and users? (2) Can a formal hypergraph model across SDLC phases capture the organizing relations (processes) that define ISCS properties? (3) What systemic thinking characteristics should guide ISCS design, implementation, operation, and disposal to ensure alignment with CITS goals and user needs? (4) How should governance be structured to balance hierarchical control with peer-to-peer interactions?

Hypotheses/claims: (a) A hypergraph representation of CITS-ISCS relations will better capture systemic properties than component-centric models. (b) Prioritizing processes and explicitly modeling inter-component relations will improve ISCS effectiveness and alignment with CITS objectives. (c) Incorporating systemic thinking principles (e.g., moving from parts to whole, shifting focus across levels, explaining in terms of the external environment) will mitigate common ISS shortcomings. (d) A hybrid governance (hierarchical + peer-to-peer) is necessary to manage dynamic, interdependent components. The paper does not test these hypotheses empirically; they are argued conceptually and supported by alignment with ISO/IEC 27001 and systemic theory.
reference_methodology:
Design: The study is a theoretical/methodological contribution. It synthesizes systemic thinking and constructs a formal model of ISCS within CITS using hypergraphs and SDLC phases.

Conceptual framework: The author adopts systemic thinking principles: (1) emergent properties arise from relations among parts; (2) properties of the whole are not reducible to parts; (3) focus shifts across system levels; (4) phenomena are explained in terms of the external environment; (5) knowledge is a network of interdependent concepts; (6) all scientific concepts are approximate and context-dependent. The SDLC is used as a temporal scaffold: Initiation, Development/Acquisition, Implementation/Assessment, Operation/Maintenance, Disposal.

Formal model: The CITS-ISCS network is modeled as a hypergraph H_k^0 = (X_k^0, U_k^0) in phase k, where X_k^0 is the set of vertices (structured products/components) and U_k^0 is the set of edges (processes) with each edge a subset of two or more vertices. Higher-level hypergraphs H_k^1 are derived by: (i) mapping lower-level vertices to edges via f_k: X_k^0 → U_k^1; (ii) defining edges as pairwise intersections of lower-level edges via g_k: U_k^0 × U_k^0 → U_k^1. The model emphasizes that processes (edges) are primary; components (vertices) are secondary patterns within the network. The model is instantiated across SDLC phases, with figures depicting the hierarchy of objects (HS, ITS, CITS, ISCS) and the network of relations (Figure 4) and a fragment of the hypergraph (Figure 5).

Application guidance: In each SDLC phase, ISCS goals should be defined without pre-specifying elements; attention to any element must include its organizing relations and role in system properties. ISCS should be designed as a hybrid governance system combining hierarchical control with peer-to-peer interactions. The approach is aligned with ISO/IEC 27001’s process-oriented ISMS lifecycle (creation, implementation, operation, continual control, analysis, support, improvement).

Standards and references: The paper cites ISO/IEC 27001:2005 and NIST SP 800-64 Rev2 for SDLC security considerations, and Ukrainian DSTU/ND TZI documents for technical protection and evaluation of security services. No datasets, experiments, or statistical analyses are reported. No IRB/ethics approvals are applicable.

title: A wash-free ER marker to monitor micropolarity during ER stress and visualize ER-Golgi transport
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can an alkylated NBD fluorophore be engineered to selectively target the ER and report micropolarity quantitatively in live cells? (2) Does ER micropolarity change measurably under ER stress-induced G1/S arrest and G2/M arrest, and is the change cell line–specific? (3) Can the probe visualize ER-to-Golgi transport in live cells and be used for wash-free imaging across diverse biological samples?

Hypotheses: (i) Increasing hydrophobicity (longer alkyl chains) will enhance ER targeting via membrane partitioning while balancing cellular permeability; among congeners, the longest-chain NBD-Oct will show the best ER specificity, fastest diffusion (FRAP), and photostability. (ii) ER stress and cell cycle arrest will increase ER micropolarity (red-shifted spectra) relative to homeostasis due to altered protein composition and lipid environment. (iii) The probe will partition into Golgi over time, enabling visualization of ER-to-Golgi transport; pharmacological inhibition (Brefeldin A) will reduce ER–Golgi colocalization. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include high PCC with ER markers, linear solvatochromism, increased emission maxima under stress/arrest, time-dependent Golgi colocalization, and reduced colocalization upon BFA treatment.
reference_methodology:
Synthesis: Three alkylated NBD dyes (NBD-Bu, NBD-Hex, NBD-Oct) were synthesized by substituting 4-chloro-7-nitrobenzofurazan (NBD-Cl) with butylamine, hexylamine, or octylamine in methanol at 298 K for 10 minutes with triethylamine, followed by silica gel chromatography (30–40% ethyl acetate/hexane). Yields were 70–88%. Structures were confirmed by 1H/13C NMR and mass spectrometry (Figures S1–S9). Spectroscopic purity was verified by overlapping absorption and excitation spectra (Figure S10).

Spectroscopy: UV–Vis and fluorescence spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu 1800 UV–Vis spectrophotometer and a Horiba Jobin Yvon Fluorolog 3 (450 W Xe lamp), 1 cm quartz cuvettes, 1 nm slit widths. Absolute quantum yields were measured with a QuantaPhi integrating sphere. Solvatochromism was assessed across solvents with varying polarity; emission maxima vs ET(30) were linear (R2 = 0.92) (Figure 1C).

Cytotoxicity and uptake: MTT assays in BHK-21, A549, MDA-MB-231, and HeLa cells (24 h) yielded IC50 ~20 µM (Figure S11). For imaging, 2 µM probe was used to maintain ~80–90% viability. Optimal uptake time was 10 minutes (Figure S15). cLogP values (DataWarrior) were 1.65 (NBD-Bu), 2.55 (NBD-Hex), and 3.47 (NBD-Oct); ER Tracker Red had cLogP 6.79.

Cell culture and microscopy: Cells were cultured in phenol red–free DMEM with 10% FBS and 1% antibiotic cocktail at 37 °C, 5% CO2. For imaging, cells were grown to ~80% confluence in 35 mm glass-bottom dishes (170 ± 5 µm). Confocal imaging used an Olympus FV3000 LSM with sequential scanning to avoid cross-talk. Excitation/emission settings: 488 nm (alkylated NBD probes) 500–540 nm; 561 nm (ER/Lyso/Mito Tracker Red) 570–620 nm; 594 nm (LipidSpot 610) 600–640 nm. Laser powers: 0.2% (488), 0.5% (561), 1% (594). Confocal aperture: 1.0 Airy Unit; dwell time: 8 µs/pixel; identical laser power/gain/offset across experiments.

FRAP: Live BHK-21 cells were imaged with 488 nm excitation (0.2% power), bleached at 5% power for 2 s, and recovery monitored at 1, 5, and 10 s (Figure 3). Diffusion coefficients were estimated using the Soumpasis equation Drn = 0.224 rn^2/τ1/2, with rn the bleached spot radius and τ1/2 the half-recovery time. Photostability was assessed by time-lapse imaging (Figure S16) and compared to ER Trackers (Figures S17–S18).

ER isolation and staining: Subcellular fractionation of live BHK-21 cells followed a standard protocol: lysis on ice, centrifugation at 3000 rpm to pellet nuclei, removal of mitochondria/lysosomes/endosomes at 12,000 rpm, and ultracentrifugation at 70,000 rpm for 1 h to obtain ER. ER pellets were resuspended in membrane buffer (100 mM KAc, 50 mM HEPES, 5 mM MgCl2, 250 mM sucrose) and co-stained with NBD-Oct and ER Tracker Red for 10 min before imaging (Figure 4A–B). Fixed cells were stained after 4% paraformaldehyde fixation (Figure 4C).

Micropolarity quantification: Lambda scanning (488 nm excitation, 500–675 nm emission) was performed in live cells to compare ER emission spectra with bulk water spectra (Figure 5). Experiments were repeated across BHK-21, A549, MDA-MB-231, and HepG2 under homeostasis and after 24 h treatments: tunicamycin (100 ng·mL^-1) for G1/S arrest and 5-fluorouracil (100 ng·mL^-1) for G2/M arrest.

ER–Golgi transport visualization: Cells were co-stained with NBD-Oct and ER Tracker Red or BODIPY TR ceramide and imaged immediately and after 24 h (Figure 7). Brefeldin A (5 µM, 24 h) was used to inhibit ER-to-Golgi transport and assess colocalization changes (Figure S24).

Tissue and model organism imaging: 3D tumoroids (BHK-21) were stained with NBD-Oct for 10 min and imaged (Figure 6A). C. elegans (N2) were grown in NGM containing 2 µM NBD-Oct at 20 °C for 60 h, paralyzed with 5 mM levamisole, and imaged (Figure 6B). Mouse liver tissue sections (4 µm) were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and stained with NBD-Oct for 15 min; z-stacks and extended focus images were acquired (Figure 6C–K).

title: Genetic links in angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL), clonal hematopoiesis and concomitant hematologic malignancies provide insights into the cell of origin, etiology and biomarker discovery for AITL
field_subfield: Hematology/Oncology — Molecular Hematology and Hematologic Malignancies
research_question:
Primary questions: (1) Do AITL/PTCL-NOS and concomitant myeloid/B-cell malignancies share common mutated HSC clones detectable in BM/PB? (2) Are CH-associated mutations early events in AITL/PTCL-NOS pathogenesis, while additional non-CH mutations arise later? (3) Do TET2 mutation burden and allelic burden in CH predict risk of CHN? (4) Are smoking-associated mutational signatures enriched in late AITL/PTCL-NOS mutations, and is lung cancer prevalence elevated in AITL/PTCL-NOS?

Hypotheses: (a) AITL/PTCL-NOS originate from mutated HSC clones associated with CH, evidenced by shared truncal mutations in BM/PB and tumors and higher VAFs in BM/PB than in tumor-involved compartments. (b) Late, non-CH mutations are enriched for missense and C>A substitutions, consistent with smoking-related mutagenesis. (c) CH harboring ≥2 pathogenic TET2 variants with high VAF is an independent risk factor for CHN. (d) AITL/PTCL-NOS patients exhibit higher lung cancer prevalence than age-matched controls and CLL, reflecting smoking-associated mutational processes.

Support/refutation criteria: Shared truncal mutations with high VAF in BM/PB and tumor; enrichment of C>A in late mutations; significant survival differences by TET2 burden; and higher lung cancer prevalence in AITL/PTCL-NOS vs controls.
reference_methodology:
Cohort and samples: 25 AITL and 2 PTCL-NOS patients (n=27 total) diagnosed/confirmed June 2010–December 2019 at NYP/Weill Cornell Medical Center per WHO criteria. Four cases were PTCL with TFH phenotype and included as AITL per WHO 2016. Matched BM (n=23) or PB (n=4) samples were available. One BM sample had concomitant MPN (Patient #20). Ethics: IRB approval; written consent obtained.

DNA extraction and library prep: Genomic DNA from LN and BM/PB (QIAamp DNA Mini Kit). Library quantification by Tape Station and Qubit. T-cell targeted panel: 538 genes covering recurrently mutated T-cell neoplasms and translocations (~3.2 Mb). Libraries prepared with KAPA HyperPlus; hybrid selection with Twist Library Prep. Sequencing on Illumina HiSeq4000 (150-bp paired-end). Myeloid panel: 45 genes (Raindance Thunderstorm system; 726 amplicons) with microdroplet-based PCR enrichment; Illumina MiSeq (260-bp paired-end). Clinical lab CLIA-certified and CAP-accredited.

Bioinformatics: NEXTGENe (Softgenetics) for SNV/INDEL calling with manufacturer-recommended settings. Variant calling thresholds: VAF ≥5%, population frequency ≤0.01%, strand bias ≤1:5. Tumor burden (TB) estimation for BM/PB with lymphoma involvement used histology, immunophenotyping, and TCR gamma rearrangement. CH-associated mutations were defined as variants in BM/PB with VAFs exceeding TB estimates or detected in uninvolved BM/PB; tumor-associated variants were those with VAFs consistent with TB. Validation: CH-associated mutations confirmed in purified neutrophils in PB for one patient (Patient #24).

Mutational signature analysis: Transition (Ti)/transversion (Tv) rates and base substitution patterns (C>T, C>G, C>A) were compared between CH-associated and late, non-CH mutations. Case-level C>A enrichment was assessed by t-test.

Survival analysis: Combined with an external AITL cohort (n=22) to yield n=49. Patients stratified by TET2 status: wild-type vs pathogenic TET2 mutant; and further by high TET2 burden (≥2 pathogenic TET2 variants with VAF ≥15%) vs no/low burden. Kaplan-Meier curves (log-rank test, p<0.05) and Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs. Performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV) were computed for the high TET2 burden biomarker.

Lung cancer prevalence comparison: AITL/PTCL-NOS cohort (n=28; including one PTCL-NOS without matched BM/PB) compared to CLL (n=1329) and age-matched general US population (n=153,798,075; age 40–80+). CLL data from published cohort; general population data from CDC (https://gis.cdc.gov/Cancer/USCS/DataViz.html).

title: Pulsed Laser Activation Method for Hydrogen Storage Alloys
research_question:
Research question: Can a nanosecond pulsed laser treatment (PLA) rapidly restore hydrogen storage activation in air-aged Ti11V30Nb28Cr31 without altering bulk crystalline phases, and what surface modifications underlie this restoration?

Hypotheses: (1) PLA-induced near-surface remelting and rapid solidification will modify the surface microstructure and oxide layer, restoring hydrogen permeability. (2) PLA will not significantly change bulk phase composition (BCC and minor C15 Laves), preserving the alloy’s intrinsic hydriding behavior. (3) Increased oxide fraction and microcracking on the surface after PLA will facilitate hydrogen transport, enabling kinetics comparable to pristine samples.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if aged+PLA samples exhibit restored hydrogen absorption kinetics and surface features (remelting, cracks) consistent with activation. Hypothesis (2) is supported if XRD shows no significant phase changes after ageing or PLA. Hypothesis (3) is supported if XPS indicates increased oxide species after ageing and complete oxidation after PLA, and SEM reveals microcracks post-PLA. Failure to restore kinetics or evidence of bulk phase changes would refute the hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Alloy synthesis: Ti11V30Nb28Cr31 was produced by arc melting under argon using high-purity elements (>99.5%). Ti-getter pieces were melted prior to each fusion to minimize oxygen contamination. The ingot was remelted 10 times, flipping between remelts to improve homogeneity. Post-melting, samples were stored and handled in an MBRAUM glovebox under argon with O2 and H2O <0.5 ppm.

Sample preparation: Small fragments were prepared under three conditions: (1) Pristine: crushed inside the glovebox to avoid air exposure; (2) Aged: removed from the glovebox, crushed, and exposed to air for 30 days at 21–23 °C and 50–70% RH; (3) Aged+PLA: a portion of the aged sample subjected to PLA.

PLA procedure: Aged samples (0.5 g) were spread over a 12×16 mm stage. A Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm, 10 ns pulses, 10 Hz, 0.8 W average power) with a f=15 cm focusing lens scanned the fragments at 400 mm/min. The entire area was scanned four times, yielding ~3 min processing time. The setup used computer-controlled x–y translation stages (Figure 1).

Hydrogen absorption kinetics: Sieverts-type measurements (PCT-Pro SETARAM) were performed at 25 °C and 25 bar H2 on fragmented samples for pristine, aged, and aged+PLA conditions. The aged+PLA sample was transferred to the Sieverts apparatus after PLA; handling occurred on air for ~2 h during transport.

Structural characterization: XRD (Bruker D8 Advance ECO, Cu-Kα) was conducted on pristine, aged, and aged+PLA samples before and after hydrogenation to assess phase changes. SEM (XL30 Philips FEG) collected secondary electron images of pristine and aged+PLA samples before and after hydrogenation to evaluate surface morphology and crack formation.

Surface chemistry: XPS (Scienta Omicron ESCA+) used an Al Kα source with a low-energy electron flood gun for charge compensation. High-resolution spectra were acquired with a pass energy of 30 eV and 0.05 eV increments. Binding energies were referenced to adventitious carbon (C–C/C–H at 284.8 eV). Data analysis used CasaXPS. XPS focused on Nb 3d, Ti 2p, Cr 2p, and V 2p regions to quantify oxidation states.

Reproducibility: All experiments (aging and XPS) were reported at least twice with good reproducibility. No details on statistical analysis, error bars, or replicate counts for kinetics were provided.

title: Which Measures of Beliefs About Others' Prosociality Predict Prosocial Behavior in Economic Games?
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do beliefs about others’ prosociality—operationalized as perceiver effects (global positivity of first-impression judgments) and generalized trust—predict prosocial behavior in economic games? (2) Does honesty–humility predict prosocial behavior across games? (3) Are associations between beliefs and behavior specific to situations affording dependence under uncertainty? (4) Do trait-specific perceiver effects for prosocial traits (honesty–humility, agreeableness) beyond global positivity predict behavior? (5) Do perceiver effects and generalized trust capture distinct constructs?

Hypotheses: (a) Perceiver effects and generalized trust will predict prosocial behavior in games affording dependence under uncertainty (PGG, TG-Trustor). (b) Honesty–humility will predict prosocial behavior across all games (PGG, TG-Trustor, TG-Trustee, MG). (c) The relation between beliefs and behavior will hold after controlling for honesty–humility. (d) Trait-specific perceiver effects for honesty–humility and agreeableness will uniquely predict behavior beyond global positivity. (e) Perceiver effects and generalized trust will show modest overlap but distinct nomological networks.

Support/refutation: The main hypotheses were largely refuted for perceiver effects and partially supported for generalized trust (unique prediction in PGG only). Honesty–humility robustly predicted behavior across games.
reference_methodology:
Design: Preregistered main study (https://aspredicted.org/HPM_VCX) with a follow-up analysis preregistered separately (https://aspredicted.org/SP3_3W6). The main study used a large, heterogeneous German sample recruited via a professional panel provider. Participants received monetary compensation and bonus payments contingent on their and matched partners’ behavior in games.

Participants: Main study N = 962 (436 female, 524 male, 2 diverse; M[SD]age = 43.67[12.25]). Follow-up analysis N = 1,020 (466 female, 552 male, 2 diverse; M[SD]age = 43.35[12.35]). The follow-up sample largely overlapped with the main study (78%).

Procedure: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three behavioral games (PGG, TG-Trustor, TG-Trustee) and all completed the MG. Timing: self-reported personality and demographics at wave 1; perceiver effects at PPP follow-up wave 2020-05c (24 weeks after wave 1); behavioral games at wave 6 (19 weeks after wave 1). In the follow-up, generalized trust was measured at wave 5 (16 weeks after wave 1).

Behavioral games: PGG (n = 316): groups of 4; endowment 4.00€; contributions in 0.50€ increments; contributions doubled and split equally; dependence under uncertainty. TG-Trustor (n = 321): dyads; endowment 3.00€; transfers in 0.50€ increments; trustee receives tripled amount; dependence under uncertainty. TG-Trustee (n = 325): dyads; trustee chooses return proportion; strategy method (trustors’ transfers known ex post); no dependence under uncertainty. MG (n = 962): choose a number 1–8; report whether it matches a randomly drawn number; “yes” yields 2€; chance of winning 12.5%; analyzed with RRreg to account for chance.

Measures: Perceiver effects via O-TAPE: participants rated 10 standardized Facebook profile screenshots on six HEXACO bipolar adjective scales (emotionality reverse-keyed for stability). Perceiver effect scores were averaged across targets per dimension; global positivity was the average across dimensions (z-scores used in analyses). Descriptive statistics (Table 1): dimension means ranged 4.70–5.56 (αs .60–.75); positivity M = 5.30, SD = 0.57, α = .90. Honesty–humility via HEXACO-60 (German version): M = 3.62, SD = 0.63, α = 0.76. Generalized trust via GTS (German version): M = 3.48, SD = 0.66, α = .90.

Analyses: For each game, four regression models were estimated: Model 1 (perceiver effects only), Model 2 (perceiver effects + age + gender), Model 3 (honesty–humility only), Model 4 (perceiver effects + honesty–humility + age + gender). MG analyses used RRreg to adjust for chance responses. For the follow-up, the same models were estimated with generalized trust replacing perceiver effects. Zero-order correlations and full regression outputs are available on OSF. Some models excluded the two participants identifying as diverse (e.g., PGG n = 316; TG-Trustor n = 320; TG-Trustee n = 324; MG n = 960).

title: The landscape of reported VUS in multi-gene panel and genomic testing: Time for a change
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the rates of inconclusive results due to VUS in diagnostic MGPs versus ES/GS? (2) How do panel size, trio-based analysis, and exome versus genome sequencing influence VUS rates? (3) How do VUS sub-tier distributions differ by test type? (4) Do VUS rates vary by disease area?

Hypotheses: (a) ES/GS will have lower VUS rates than MGPs due to clinical correlation and family data that guide selective reporting despite analyzing more genes. (b) VUS rates in MGPs will increase with panel size as gene–phenotype specificity diminishes. (c) Trio-based testing will reduce VUS rates compared with less-than-trio analyses. (d) Exome versus genome sequencing will not materially affect VUS rates. (e) In disease areas with strong gene–phenotype correlations, ES/GS will show lower VUS rates than MGPs; in areas with weaker correlations, differences may be smaller.

Support/refutation: The data support (a)–(d). Hypothesis (e) is partially supported: ES/GS had lower VUS rates than MGPs in cardiovascular, neurologic/muscular, metabolic, and neurodevelopmental/intellectual disability/autism, but not in hematologic/rheumatologic/immunologic or dysmorphic/skeletal.
reference_methodology:
Design: Observational, multi-laboratory aggregate analysis of deidentified diagnostic sequencing test results from 19 North American clinical laboratories (2020–2021). The study focused on symptomatic (diagnostic) testing only.

Data sources and scope: Tests included MGPs and ES/GS. Single-gene tests were collected but excluded from analysis due to inconsistent diagnostic use and ordering tracking. Custom add-on genes, untracked panel sizes, and cases where providers opted out of VUS reporting (notably in large neurodevelopmental/neurological panels) were excluded. If a patient had multiple tests, only the largest panel was counted to avoid double-counting overlapping genes.

Categorization: MGPs were grouped by total genes analyzed into bins: 2–10, 11–25, 26–50, 51–100, 101–200, >200 genes. ES/GS were categorized by exome versus genome and by family inclusion: trio (both parents and patient) versus less-than-trio (patient only, single parent, multiple siblings, or other combinations). Some laboratories further categorized tests by disease area across 12 indications (cardiovascular, hereditary cancer/cancer syndrome, neurodevelopmental/intellectual disability/autism, neurological/muscular/neuromuscular, retinal disease, hearing loss, renal/gastrointestinal, endocrine, metabolic, dysmorphic/skeletal, hematologic/rheumatologic/immunologic, dermatologic, or other). For disease-area comparisons, the average number of genes per test was computed using midpoints (e.g., 6 for 2–10 genes; 201 for >200 genes).

Outcome definition: The primary outcome was the rate of inconclusive test results due to at least one VUS. Inconclusive cases without a VUS (e.g., single heterozygous pathogenic variant in a recessive disease) were excluded. To control for differences in positive yield, VUS rates were also compared among combined positive and inconclusive results for 17/19 laboratories (97.9% of MGPs and 95.3% of ES/GS) where positive-result VUS rates were provided.

Laboratory reporting practices: MGPs typically reported all VUS for symptomatic individuals. ES/GS labs used clinical correlation, segregation analysis, and strength of pathogenicity evidence to determine which VUS, if any, to report. Two laboratories reported VUS sub-tiers (VUS-High, VUS-Mid, VUS-Low), enabling analysis of evidence-level distributions.

Statistical analysis: Chi-square tests with Yates correction were used. Statistical significance was defined as p<0.001; p-values down to 0.0001 were reported. Diagnostic yields (positive-result rates) were computed but not compared across test types due to differing tested populations (e.g., MGPs included more low-yield cancer testing).

title: Continuous microfluidic synthesis of zirconium-based UiO-67 using a coiled flow invertor reactor
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a CFIR microreactor continuously synthesize UiO-67 with reduced reaction time while maintaining crystallinity? (2) Does CFIR-enhanced mixing and RTD narrowing yield smaller, more uniform particle sizes than batch synthesis? (3) What are the practical throughput and space-time yield of the continuous process?

Hypotheses: (H1) CFIR operation at 140 °C with a 30 min residence time will produce crystalline UiO-67 in a fraction of the batch time (24 h at 120 °C). (H2) The CFIR’s Dean vortices and narrow RTD will reduce particle size and narrow the size distribution relative to batch. (H3) The continuous process will achieve a non-trivial space-time yield comparable to prior continuous MOF syntheses.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if PXRD confirms UiO-67 phase and if reaction time is reduced. H2 is supported if SEM shows smaller, more uniform particles and if Scherrer estimates indicate smaller crystals. H3 is supported if STY is reported and comparable to literature benchmarks.
reference_methodology:
Reactor and setup: A CFIR was constructed by coiling PTFE tubing (0.79 mm ID, 1/16" OD) around a 3D-printed support (Formlabs high-temp resin) designed in AutoCAD. The support comprised four helical segments with 90° inversions to induce Dean vortices. The total coil length was ~3.146 m. The CFIR was submerged in a silicon oil bath on a magnetic stirrer hotplate for uniform heating. Inlets/outlets used IDEX flangeless fittings and luer adapters (catalog numbers XP-283 and P-628). Tubing was coiled tightly through inlet/outlet holes and secured. Product was collected in a 100 ml glass flask.

Temperature and residence time control: The oil bath was set to 140 °C (chosen over 120 °C based on batch testing indicating faster reaction at higher temperature). Residence time was controlled by volumetric flow rate using t = V/Q with V = (π d² L)/4. For d = 0.79 × 10⁻³ m, L = 3.146 m, and Q = 0.052 ml/min, t ≈ 30 min. At this flow, 10 ml of solution required ~3 h to pass through the system.

Reactants and procedure: ZrCl4 (0.26 mmol), benzoic acid (1.28 mmol), and DMF (10 ml) were combined in a dry beaker; initial DMF addition minimized HCl evolution from ZrCl4. The mixture was sonicated for 1 min. BPDC (0.26 mmol) and water (0.25 ml) were added, followed by 3 min sonication. Water increases pH, accelerating linker deprotonation and growth. A 10 ml syringe containing a 5 mm magnet was loaded with the mixture. Before connection, 2 ml fresh DMF (exceeding the 1.72 ml internal tubing volume) was flushed to clear residual material. The syringe was connected to the CFIR and placed in a Chemyx Fusion 101 syringe pump. A small magnetic stirrer plate (~1500 RPM) above the syringe maintained reactant solubility. The pump was started at 0.052 ml/min. The reaction ran for 2.5 h until the stirrer bar stopped. The syringe was replaced with 5 ml fresh DMF and 2 ml flushed at the same flow; then 2 ml was flushed at 1 ml/min to remove settled material. No severe blockages were observed.

Post-processing and characterization: Product was washed with fresh DMF (2 × 15 ml), methanol-soaked (15 ml) for 72 h (changed every 24 h), centrifuged (6000 rpm, 20 min), and dried overnight at 110 °C. PXRD used a Bruker D8 diffractometer (Cu Kα, 2θ = 5–45°, 45 min scan, 0.033° step). SEM used a Carl Zeiss EVO MA15 with 25 nm Ir sputter coating. A simulated UiO-67 pattern (VESTA) was used for comparison.

Timing and yield: Synthesis run 2.5 h; washing 72 h; drying 12 h. Yield ≈70 mg. Production rate 0.81 mg h⁻¹. STY 524 kg m⁻³ day⁻¹ (based on DMF volume).

title: Simulación numérica de una célula solar a través del método de elementos finitos
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a finite element method formulated in weighted Sobolev spaces accurately solve the axisymmetric, effective-mass Schrödinger eigenvalue problem with discontinuous coefficients arising from wetting layer–barrier contrasts? (2) Does the discrete scheme exhibit theoretically predicted convergence rates for eigenvalues and eigenfunctions? (3) What physical conclusions about QD eigenstates (ground vs excited) and parameter sensitivities emerge from the simulations?

Hypotheses: (H1) The variational formulation with a(ξ,v) and b(ξ,v) is well-posed (bounded, symmetric, elliptic), ensuring existence and uniqueness of solutions and a discrete spectrum. (H2) The discrete operator T_h converges in norm to T, and eigenvalue errors decrease proportionally to h² under mesh refinement. (H3) In the modeled axisymmetric QD/wetting layer geometry, the ground state (no z-nodes) is physically representative, while excited states with nodes are not. (H4) Ground state energy is sensitive to QD height, radius, effective mass, and wetting layer thickness.

Support/refutation: H1–H2 are supported by theorems and numerical convergence tables (rates approaching 2). H3–H4 are supported by the thesis’s physical analysis and conclusions, though direct experimental validation is not provided in this text.
reference_methodology:
Model: Time-independent Schrödinger equation under the effective mass approximation for electrons in a semiconductor heterostructure. The full 3D equation is reduced to 2D axisymmetric form by assuming θ-independence and separation of variables Φ(r,θ,z)=ξ(r,z)φ(θ), with φ(θ)=exp(inθ) satisfying ∂²φ/∂θ² + n²φ=0. The resulting 2D equation includes effective mass m_eff(x), effective potential V_eff(x), and angular term n²/r². Dirichlet boundary conditions ξ=0 are imposed on ∂Ω to reflect confinement and to study wetting layer–QD coupling.

Mathematical formulation: The axisymmetric equation is cast in weighted Sobolev spaces H^1_r(Ω) and L^2_{1/r}(Ω) to handle the 1/r weighting from cylindrical coordinates. The variational problem seeks (E,ξ)∈R×H with ξ≠0 such that a(ξ,v)=E b(ξ,v) for all v∈H, where a(ξ,v)=∫Ω [γα∇ξ·∇v + (β/r² + V_eff) ξ v] r dr dz and b(ξ,v)=∫Ω ξ v r dr dz. Here γ=h²/2, α=1/m_eff, β=γ α n². Bilinear forms are shown bounded, symmetric, and elliptic under assumptions on coefficients, ensuring a well-posed eigenvalue problem. The solution operator T is self-adjoint and compact, yielding a discrete sequence of positive eigenvalues converging to zero.

Discretization: A regular family of triangular meshes {T_h} with size h is used. The finite element space V_h consists of piecewise linear functions on T_h, with V_{h,0}={v_h∈V_h: v_h=0 on ∂Ω}. The discrete problem seeks (E_h,ξ_h)∈R×V_h with ξ_h≠0 such that a_h(ξ_h,v_h)=E_h b_h(ξ_h,v_h) for all v_h∈V_h. The discrete bilinear forms a_h and b_h are assembled via weighted integrals over elements. The discrete operator T_h is defined analogously to T and shown to converge in norm to T as h→0.

Implementation: The linear system Aξ=b is solved internally by FEniCS, using Lagrange P1 basis functions and Dirichlet boundary conditions. Mesh refinement studies are conducted on Ω=(0,1)×(0,1) for the axisymmetric Laplacian to quantify convergence. Units are discussed (e.g., h=1.054571817×10^-34 J·s; 1 eV=1.602×10^-19 J; 1 nm=1×10^-9 m), though specific material parameters for the QD/wetting layer simulations are not reported in the provided text.

Error analysis: Cea’s lemma and interpolation bounds yield ∥u−u_h∥_V ≤ C inf_{v_h∈V_h} ∥u−v_h∥_V and ∥u−u_h∥_V ≤ C h ∥u∥_{H^2_r(Ω)}. For eigenvalues, the error decreases proportionally to h² under sufficient regularity. Theorems establish boundedness, symmetry, and ellipticity of a(·,·) and b(·,·), and norm convergence of T_h to T.

title: AVALIAÇÃO DOS ÍNDICES ZOOTÉCNICOS DE POEDEIRAS EM SISTEMA DE PRODUÇÃO CAGE-FREE Evaluation of the zootechnical indexes of laying hens in a cage-free production system
research_question:
Research question: In a commercial cage-free laying hen system with specified enrichment and management, what are the zootechnical indices (start of laying, peak production, daily egg output, feed conversion, and mortality) over a 62-week production period, and are they comparable to conventional expectations?

Hypotheses (implicit): (1) Cage-free housing with adequate enrichment and bedding will achieve early onset of laying and competitive peak production relative to conventional systems. (2) Feed conversion in the cage-free system will be near conventional benchmarks (approximately 2 kg feed per dozen eggs). (3) Mortality will remain low if management mitigates known risks (e.g., crowding, vent prolapse). Support for these hypotheses would be demonstrated by early onset (≤20 weeks), peak production in the mid-20s, feed conversion near 2 kg/dozen, and mortality ≤5%. Refutation would involve delayed onset, substantially lower peak production, feed conversion far above 2 kg/dozen, or high mortality.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-site case study of a commercial cage-free laying hen barn. Location: Jacutinga, north of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Period: April 2019 to February 2020.

Facility: A 120 m² brick barn, divided into two compartments, with a total capacity of 6.66 birds/m². The barn was covered with tarps and had a curtain system for manual temperature control. Perches were wooden, installed on one side; nests were wooden, with five birds per nest, and lined with 10 cm pine maravalha. The opposite side housed nest boxes. The floor was covered with pine maravalha at 250 cm² per bird. Feeders were tubular; drinkers were pendulous, alternated and positioned along the center, occupying the full length of the barn. A natural wind barrier of trees protected the external area.

Animals and sample: 400 Isa Brown laying hens, 12 weeks of age at placement. No randomization or replication across flocks is reported.

Management and environment: Lighting program used artificial light from 20:00 to 22:00 and 03:00 to 07:00, with 5 hours of darkness and natural light otherwise, to encourage nesting and reduce early-morning floor laying. Eggs were collected manually twice daily at 07:30 and 15:00. Temperature was manually controlled by opening/closing curtains. Water was artesian, chlorinated, and annually evaluated for physicochemical and microbiological parameters.

Diet and feeding: Isocaloric and isoproteic diets formulated per phase following Brazilian tables (Rostagno et al., 2017): initial (12–15 weeks), pre-lay (to 17 weeks), and lay (17–62 weeks). Feeding occurred twice daily (morning and afternoon). Feed intake was adjusted as production progressed (e.g., 87 g/bird/day at week 17; 120–125 g/bird/day by week 21; 135 g/bird/day at week 24; 128 g/bird/day post-peak).

Variables and data collection: Daily data were collected from week 17 to week 62 on (i) start of laying (weeks), (ii) peak production (weeks), (iii) egg production (units), (iv) feed intake (g/bird/day), and (v) mortality (%). Mortality causes were recorded (e.g., trampling, vent prolapse). No statistical analyses, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests are reported. No egg quality metrics (e.g., shell quality, contamination) were measured. Ethical approvals are not reported.

title: Feature Point Tracking-Based Localization of Colon Capsule Endoscope
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a visual-based feature-point tracking model, combined with a local cylindrical approximation of the colon and distributional priors, reconstruct the large intestine trajectory from CCE videos with clinically useful accuracy? (2) How do priors on colon radius and sampling frequency affect reconstruction fidelity and section-wise localization accuracy? (3) Does incorporating cleanliness-aware post-processing reduce error propagation from poor-quality frames? (4) Do intra-capsule camera-head reconstructions agree, indicating robustness?

Hypotheses: (H1) A geometric visual odometry approach with appropriate priors can reconstruct CCE paths with low average path differences and high section-wise accuracy. (H2) Priors on colon radius will have a larger impact on reconstruction quality than priors on sampling frequency. (H3) Cleanliness-aware post-processing will mitigate overestimation of speed and orientation in poor-quality frames. (H4) Intra-capsule camera-head reconstructions will agree for robust prior choices, but may diverge for uniform-only priors.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if average path differences are small (on the order of the colon radius) and section-wise accuracy is high. H2 is supported if T–T outperforms combinations with uniform priors. H3 is supported if post-processing reduces speed overestimation and stabilizes estimates. H4 is supported if cumulative speed distributions from both camera heads overlap within confidence intervals for robust priors.
reference_methodology:
System and data: The PillCam COLON2 capsule (two camera heads; 172° FOV each; total 344° coverage) records frames at variable frequencies (4–35 Hz). Videos were extracted using RAPID software, converting to a common format and compressing to fixed frames per second, which lost exact sampling timestamps. The study used 42 patients (84 videos) from a prior dataset (Kobaek-Larsen et al., 2018), with each frame converted to grayscale.

Geometric model: The colon is locally approximated as a cylinder of radius R. For a point P at distance D from the camera center, its polar angle θ satisfies θ = arctan(R/D). Between frames, the capsule moves distance d, yielding θ_{t+1} = arctan(R/(D−d)). Solving for d gives d = R [tan(θ_{t+1})/(tan(θ_{t+1}) − tan(θ_t))]. Feature points (edges, corners, blobs, ridges) are detected and matched across frames using SURF, with RANSAC filtering to remove outliers. Feature points are mapped to Cartesian coordinates (x = Lφ/(2π), y = r), enabling linear displacement estimation.

Orientation and motion estimation: Speed v_{t+1} is estimated by maximizing the ensemble distribution P(f_{t+1} d_{t+1}), where f_{t+1} is the sampling frequency. Roll γ_{t+1} is estimated by maximizing P(Δx_{t+1}). Tilt magnitude Ω_{t+1} and direction ω_{t+1} are derived from pairwise angular changes between matched points, with Ω computed as the normalized difference of angular changes for opposite points and ω from the distribution of φ. Pitch and yaw are α_{t+1} = Ω cos(ω) and β_{t+1} = Ω sin(ω). Orientation is updated via rotation matrices R_x, R_y, R_z, and integrated into an observer frame using a state vector [x, y, z, s] with a transition matrix T that incorporates v_{t+1} and f_{t+1}.

Cleanliness post-processing: An SVM classifier (trained on expert input) labels pixels as clean/dirty; frames with over-/underexposure are excluded. Cleanliness levels L ∈ {0,1,2,3} (0 unacceptable; 1 poor; 2 fair; 3 good). If L=0 or matched features <20, the update uses the previous tracking matrix T_t with additive Gaussian noise on v, f, α, β, γ (zero mean; variance σ_h^2 computed from prior means). This prevents overestimation in poor-quality frames.

Priors and parameters: Colon diameter 2R has mean μ_{2R}=4.6 cm, SD σ_{2R}=0.7 cm, bounds [2.5, 9] cm (from Gilroy et al. and Ohgo et al.). Sampling frequency f_{t+1} is drawn either from a uniform U(a,b) or a truncated Gaussian with μ_f, σ_f, and bounds [a,b]. For tilt estimation, ξ=0.25 is used. For demonstration, a 400-frame sequence at 2 Hz with R=5 cm is shown.

Evaluation design: Reconstructions are initialized from the anus (Section I) with an ad hoc direction. For each video, 25,000 path reconstructions are generated under prior combinations: T–T (truncated Gaussian for radius and frequency), T–U (truncated radius, uniform frequency), U–T (uniform radius, truncated frequency), U–U (uniform radius and frequency). Path differences Δ_S are computed within six anatomical boxes (I–VI) and aggregated across videos. Expert panel annotations label Sections III and V; Section I is used as origin, enabling labeling of II, IV, VI. Intra-capsule validation compares cumulative speed distributions between the two camera heads.

title: Leveraging AutoML to provide NAFLD screening diagnosis: Proposed machine learning models
field_subfield: Computer Science — Machine Learning; Medicine — Hepatology
research_question:
Research question: Can AutoML models trained on easy-to-measure anthropometric variables achieve high discrimination for NAFLD screening, comparable to or exceeding ultrasound-based approaches, while maintaining low computational cost?

Hypotheses: (1) Anthropometric-only AutoML models will demonstrate good discrimination (AUC >0.75) for NAFLD screening on the Huang et al. cohort. (2) Among candidate algorithms, ensemble methods (e.g., RGF) will achieve the highest AUC due to their capacity to handle nonlinearity and interactions in anthropometric data. (3) The models will be computationally efficient, enabling practical deployment in resource-limited settings.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if AUCs exceed 0.75; (2) is supported if ensemble methods outperform individual models; (3) is supported if training times are short relative to clinical constraints. The study does not explicitly state alternative hypotheses or predefined thresholds beyond the AUC interpretation schema.
reference_methodology:
Data source: Huang et al. (2015) cohort (PLoS One) comprising 4,053 participants (2,436 men; 1,617 women) aged 20–88 years. Exclusions: patients with comorbidities and those lacking hepatic ultrasonography data. Anthropometric and biochemical variables were measured using standardized methods with negligible measurement error. BMI ≥24 kg/m² was defined as overweight (per Zhou, 2002), differing from South Asian standards (≥25 kg/m²). NAFLD diagnosis on ultrasonography followed Graif’s criteria.

Outcome definition: NAFLD status (binary) derived from ultrasonography per Graif’s criteria. The study emphasizes discrimination (AUC-ROC) as the primary outcome due to class imbalance.

AutoML framework: MLjar (zero-code AutoML) was used for data loading, preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, hyperparameter selection, and result interpretation. Preprocessing included one-hot encoding for categorical features. System specifications: 8 CPUs, 15 GB RAM. Validation: 15-fold cross-validation with shuffling of samples and stratification of classes in folds. Tuning mode: Perfect mode (25–35 models). Time limit: 5 minutes per model. The study reports training times and AUCs for individual models and ensemble averages where available.

Models and evaluation: Eight algorithms were trained: XGBoost, LightGBM (LGBM), Random Forest (RF), Regularized Greedy Forest (RGF), Extra Trees (ET), k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Logistic Regression (LR), and Neural Network (NN). AUC-ROC was computed and interpreted per Lau et al. schema (AUC >0.9 excellent; >0.75 good; >0.5 random). Ensemble averaging was computed for RGF, RF, ET, LR, and KNN; LGBM and NN ensemble averages were not reported. No additional metrics (e.g., calibration, sensitivity/specificity, confidence intervals, or statistical tests) were reported. No external validation or test set evaluation was performed.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. Funding: none. Conflicts of interest: none declared.

title: How Efficacious Must a COVID-19 Coronavirus Vaccine be to Prevent or Stop an Epidemic by Itself
research_question:
Research question: What vaccine efficacy thresholds are required for a COVID-19 vaccine to prevent or largely extinguish an epidemic without additional non-pharmaceutical interventions, and how do coverage and vaccination timing modulate these thresholds?

Hypotheses: (1) Vaccines that prevent infection will substantially reduce attack rates and peak incidence compared with vaccines that only reduce viral shedding. (2) There exists a non-linear relationship between vaccine efficacy, coverage, and timing; higher efficacy lowers required coverage and allows later vaccination, while lower efficacy necessitates higher coverage or earlier deployment. (3) To prevent or largely extinguish an epidemic without other measures, a vaccine must prevent infection with at least 70% efficacy when vaccination occurs within 90 days and coverage is ≥60%. (4) Vaccines with 40–70% efficacy can still reduce burden under certain conditions (e.g., ≥75% coverage), but such coverage may be unachievable in practice.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypotheses are supported if simulations show large reductions in attack rates and peaks with ≥70% efficacy and sufficient coverage/timing, and limited impact with lower efficacies or shedding-only vaccines. Refutation would occur if lower efficacies suffice to prevent epidemics without high coverage or if shedding-only vaccines achieve comparable outcomes.
reference_methodology:
Model structure: A discrete-time, one-day-step simulation of the U.S. population (N=357,157,434) over 2.5 years. Individuals transition among five mutually exclusive states: susceptible (S), exposed (E), infectious asymptomatic (Ia), infectious symptomatic (Is), and recovered/immune (R). On day 1, a seed set of individuals starts in Ia or Is; the remainder are S. Transmission is modeled by β*S*(Is + 0.5*Ia), where β = R0/(infectious period duration × population). Exposed individuals transition to infectious at rate 1/latent period duration. Infectious period durations are drawn from a distribution (4–15 days), including the day before symptom onset. Individuals moving to I draw a duration and transition to R at rate 1/infectious period duration. Symptomatic probability governs Is vs Ia.

Vaccination: Vaccination creates a V state. Two modes: (a) prevent infection: vaccinated individuals in E transition to R with probability equal to vaccine efficacy; failures transition to Ia or Is. (b) reduce viral shedding: vaccinated individuals in E transition to Ia with reduced probability of Is (efficacy). Protection is immediate (on day of vaccination) and does not affect already infected/exposed individuals.

Clinical progression and costs: Symptomatic cases traverse a probability tree: mild illness, ambulatory care or telemedicine, progression to severe disease and hospitalization, ICU admission, ARDS, ventilator use, sepsis, and mortality. Age-specific clinical probabilities, durations, utilities, and costs are drawn from scientific literature and national data (Appendix Table 1). Costs include direct medical costs (third-party payer) and societal costs (direct plus indirect productivity losses). Productivity losses are proxied by hourly wages (all occupations), with absenteeism during symptomatic illness and lifetime earnings foregone due to premature mortality. Costs are discounted at 3%.

Scenarios and analysis: Baseline unmitigated epidemics are simulated for R0=2.5 and R0=3.5. Vaccination scenarios vary vaccine efficacy (20–100%), population coverage (50–100%; includes vaccinated plus otherwise immune), vaccination timing (0–180 days from epidemic start), and R0 (2.5–3.5). Experiments include vaccines that prevent infection and vaccines that reduce viral shedding. Each scenario comprises 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations varying parameters within their ranges (Appendix Table 1). Results are reported as medians with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs). Seeding of initial infections is parameterized to match U.S. case data as of March 24, 2020. Age-specific COVID-19 data reflect the U.S. context as of March 16, 2020. Outputs include epidemic curves, attack rates, peak daily cases, clinical outcomes, resource use (bed days, ventilator days), and costs.

title: Master's Degree Programme in International Business Management
field_subfield: Business — Supply Chain Management and Corporate Social Responsibility
research_question: The study posed two research questions: (1) What HSEQ and corporate responsibility issues should be evaluated in Algol Chemicals’ supplier selection process? (2) How should these aspects be integrated into the process? The work did not test formal hypotheses; instead, it sought actionable, context-specific guidance grounded in company policies, customer inquiries, and stakeholder interviews. Evidence that would support the integration plan includes: identification of non-negotiable legal and ethical criteria (e.g., forced/child labor, corruption, money laundering), prioritization of documentation needs (SDS, labels, COAs, traceability), and stakeholder agreement on the feasibility of checklists, supplier self-assessment, and centralized reporting. Evidence that would refute or complicate the plan includes supplier resistance to documentation, lack of feasible compliance mechanisms, or cultural barriers that render the approach impractical. The study’s action-research design aimed to produce implementable recommendations rather than generalizable causal claims.
reference_methodology:
Design: Inductive, qualitative, action-research approach (Easterby-Smith et al., 2008; Freebody, 2003). The researcher actively participated in the change process, engaging stakeholders (Quality & Environment Manager, Business Development Director, HSEQ Manager, Sourcing Manager) through discourse.

Setting and participants: Algol Chemicals Ltd., a Finnish subsidiary of the Algol Group (family-owned, multi-branch), sells industrial chemicals B2B with a global supplier network. The study focused on supplier selection and valuation practices at Algol Chemicals.

Data sources and phases: Phase 1 (document analysis) examined Algol Group’s corporate responsibility and HSEQ policies: Code of Business Conduct (CoBC), Health, Safety & Environment (HSE) Policy, and Quality Policy. Phase 2 (customer inquiries) analyzed HSEQ department records of customer questionnaires and general inquiries (Jan 2012–Oct 15, 2013). Phase 3 (interviews) conducted semi-structured interviews with six segment leaders (three in Espoo; three via Google Hangouts) and the Quality & Environment Manager (in person).

Document analysis: Manual conceptual content analysis (Colorado State University, 2013) of CoBC/HSE/Quality Policy to identify HSEQ/CSR issues relevant to suppliers. For customer inquiries, the study extracted themes (e.g., SDS, labels, certifications) and computed descriptive statistics (counts, percentages) for industry distribution and questionnaire counts. Some records were missing from the shared drive (11 in 2012; 21 in 2013), limiting completeness.

Interviews: Semi-structured interviews (Saunders et al., 2009) explored current supplier selection practices, legal/ethical criteria, documentation needs, and integration ideas. Interviews were conducted 7–11 October 2013. Notes were taken during interviews and analyzed post hoc. The interview guide covered topics such as legal supplier criteria, preliminary supplier information needs, and process improvements.

Analysis: Thematic coding of documents and interview notes; descriptive statistics for inquiry counts and industry distributions. No inter-rater reliability, coding scheme, or software tools were reported. The study did not report formal statistical tests or effect sizes.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. The CoBC’s anti-corruption and anti-money laundering clauses are explicitly referenced as non-negotiable.

title: Running out of farmland? Investment discourses, unstable land values and the sluggishness of asset making
field_subfield: Geography — Political Economy of Land and Finance
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Under what conditions does farmland become a financial asset, and how is this process assembled? (2) Are global claims of rising farmland values and scarcity valid across regions, or are they selective and context-dependent? (3) In the post-Soviet region, did investor discourse and institutional changes create the prerequisites for asset making, and what mechanisms led to subsequent stagnation and de-assetization? (4) How do standardization practices (e.g., yield gap, soil fertility) interact with material constraints (climate, water) to shape asset formation?

Hypotheses: (H1) Asset making in farmland requires a conjunction of scarcity, profit potential, liquidity, standardization, and legitimacy; absent or weak conditions will impede or reverse asset formation. (H2) Global claims of universal farmland value appreciation are overstated due to selective data and regional heterogeneity. (H3) In Russia/Ukraine, supply exceeds demand in most regions, leading to stagnation or declines in land prices after initial increases. (H4) Overreliance on soil fertility and standardized yield-gap indicators, without accounting for climate/water variability, will fail to close yield gaps and undermine profitability. The study tests these hypotheses through discourse analysis of investor reports/indices and empirical fieldwork in the post-Soviet region.
reference_methodology:
Design: Mixed-methods combining discourse analysis of global investor reports/indices and a multi-sited empirical case study of farmland investment in Russia and Ukraine. The typology of asset making (scarcity, profit potential, liquidity, standardization, legitimacy) is developed from valuation studies, resource making, and sociology of finance, then applied to both global and regional contexts.

Data sources: (1) Global investor reports and indices: Savills (2012) Global Farmland Index; Knight Frank and Citi Private Bank (2011) Wealth Report; World Bank and other development agency publications (e.g., Deininger et al. 2011). (2) Media and company reports (e.g., Economist 2012; RT 2008; Kuzmenko 2012). (3) Fieldwork in Russia and Ukraine (2011–2014): web searches in English and Russian (general and investor-oriented media, company websites), interviews with foreign-owned agroholdings (4 Scandinavian, 2 German, 2 Dutch), expat farm managers/consultants, and participation in investor conferences/meetings in Ukraine, Russia, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands. Interviewees included CEOs, farm staff, and investors; identities are not disclosed. (4) Secondary literature on yield gaps, soil fertility, and institutional reforms (e.g., Li 2014; McMichael 2012; Visser et al. 2012; Kuns et al. 2014).

Procedures: (a) Discourse analysis of investor narratives and visualizations (e.g., Savills’ graph of people per hectare; Knight Frank’s table of country-specific price changes) to identify claims of scarcity and value appreciation and assess selection and data reliability. (b) Case study analysis of post-Soviet institutional changes (land code reforms enabling free land sales; state-subsidized/guaranteed credit; commodity exchanges; foreign ownership loopholes) and investor practices (aggregation, REITs, stock listings) to evaluate liquidity and standardization. (c) Interviews with investors and managers to document expectations (e.g., 50% yield gains; 50–70% capital gains), operational realities (equipment, personnel investments), and organizational structures (finance-led boards). (d) Synthesis of biophysical constraints (temperature, rainfall variability, water availability) and their interaction with standardized indicators (average rainfall) to explain yield gap failures.

Analysis: Qualitative thematic analysis of discourse and interviews; triangulation with media and reports. No statistical tests or formal econometric models are reported. Ethical approvals/consent procedures are not described. The study acknowledges limitations in data reliability for Global South contexts and selection bias in indices.

title: Agenda setting in primary care visits for chronic pain: a qualitative taxonomy and quantitative association with topics discussed and patient experience
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do primary care physicians open chronic pain visits, and can a standardized taxonomy of opening styles be developed? (2) Is agenda setting associated with fewer surprise topics and improved visit organization? (3) Is agenda setting associated with better patient experience and lower physician-perceived visit difficulty?

Hypotheses: (a) Agenda setting (eliciting or reframing) will be associated with fewer surprise topics and fewer returns to prior topics, reflecting better upfront organization. (b) Agenda setting will be associated with improved patient experience and lower physician-perceived difficulty. (c) Non-agenda opening styles (open-ended question, patient launch, physician launch) will be associated with more surprise topics and poorer organization. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include lower mean counts of surprise topics and returns among agenda-setting visits, higher patient experience scores, and lower physician difficulty scores. Null or opposite findings would refute or nuance these hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative observational study with inductive taxonomy development (conversation analysis) followed by quantitative association analyses.

Setting and participants: Video-recorded primary care visits at the University of California Davis Medical Center. Physicians were second- or third-year internal medicine or family medicine residents. Patients were established adults planning to discuss pain management with an enrolled physician during a routine appointment. Exclusion criteria: non-English language during visits, active cancer treatment or palliative care, or receiving an opioid prescription from a non-primary care physician. Demographics were collected at enrollment.

Measures: Post-visit physician difficulty was assessed using the 10-item Difficult Physician-Patient Relationship Questionnaire (DPPRQ), scored 10–60 (higher = more difficult). Patient experience was measured via four instruments: short-form Wake Forest trust scale, a 3-item agreement with treatment plan measure, CAHPS Adult Visit Survey communication assessment, and a patient-facing DPPRQ. Exploratory factor analysis indicated a single latent construct; these were combined into a standardized score (mean=0, SD=1), with higher values indicating better experience.

Qualitative coding: Two coders (a primary care physician and a medical sociologist trained in conversation analysis) watched videos in tandem. For visit openings, they reviewed 20 videos, then expanded to 45 to reach saturation, developing a taxonomy of opening styles. Agenda setting was defined as strategies to explicitly elicit or confirm an upfront list of topics before discussing the first topic; open-ended questions alone did not qualify. Agenda reframing was defined as reframing patient talk into an explicit agenda before engaging the first topic. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. The final 5-level opening taxonomy was applied to all 83 visits.

Topic-level coding: A tandem inductive review of 15 visits established coding rules for topic types and occurrence. The final scheme coded total topics, major topics (comprehensive discussions), surprise topics (patient-initiated topics not on the agenda; if no agenda setting, all patient-initiated topics were surprise), return topics (mentions >1), and visit length. Topics initiated by patient companions were counted as patient-initiated. Coding was applied to 41 visits: all 9 with agenda setting and 32 additional visits via maximum variation sampling to represent resident type, opening styles, and a wide range of patient experience and physician difficulty scores.

Statistical analysis: For openings (n=83), linear regressions modeled patient experience and physician difficulty as outcomes with agenda setting (present/absent) and opening style (5-level categorical; open-ended question as reference). For topic-level variables (n=41), linear regressions assessed differences in total topics, major topics, surprise topics, return topics, and visit length by agenda setting (present/absent) and by opening style (5-level categorical). Models controlled for patient age, sex, and race (white vs non-white) and used generalized estimating equations to account for clustering of patients within physicians. Analyses were conducted in SAS 9.4. Ethics: UC Davis IRB approval; written consent obtained.

title: Gold(I)-catalyzed 6-endo hydroxycyclization of 7-substituted-1,6-enynes
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can cationic gold(I) complexes catalyze a 6-endo-dig hydroxycyclization of o-(alkynyl)-3-(methylbut-2-enyl)benzenes (1,6-enynes with a condensed aryl ring at C3–C4) under mild conditions? (2) How do catalyst identity, solvent polarity, and nucleophile (water vs methanol) influence selectivity between 6-endo and 5-exo pathways? (3) What is the diastereoselectivity of the 6-endo pathway for E/Z enynes? (4) Does a gold carbenoid intermediate mediate the cyclization, as supported by labeling experiments?

Hypotheses: (i) Cationic gold(I) complexes will enable a 6-endo-dig cyclization to a gold carbenoid intermediate, followed by nucleophilic attack and deprotonation to give dihydronaphthalenes. (ii) The presence of water or methanol will favor 6-endo hydroxycyclization over 5-exo pathways. (iii) Catalysts with stronger σ-donating ligands and appropriate counterions will enhance 6-endo selectivity. (iv) Solvent polarity will modulate the balance between 6-endo and 5-exo products, with more polar solvents promoting 5-exo hydroxycyclization. (v) E-enynes will exhibit higher diastereoselectivity for 6-endo products than Z-enynes. (vi) D2O labeling will incorporate deuterium at the cyclization site, supporting the proposed mechanism.

Outcomes that would support the hypotheses include high 6-endo selectivity with water/methanol, improved selectivity with specific catalysts, solvent-dependent shifts in product distribution, single-isomer formation for E-enynes, and D2O incorporation at the expected position.
reference_methodology:
Substrate preparation: o-(alkynyl)-3-(methylbut-2-enyl)benzenes (1a–k) were synthesized via two routes. Route A: o-(bromo)-3-(methylbut-2-enyl)benzene was prepared from 2-methyl-1-propenylmagnesium bromide and 2-bromobenzyl bromide using CuI and 2,2′-bipyridyl, then coupled with terminal alkynes using Cs2CO3 and PdCl2(MeCN)2/XPhos. Route B: o-(alkynyl)bromobenzenes were prepared by Sonogashira coupling of o-bromoiodobenzene with terminal acetylenes, followed by bromine–lithium exchange and reaction with 3,3-dimethylallyl bromide in TMEDA. Additional substrates 1m and 1n were prepared from 2′-(phenylethynyl)acetophenone via lithium reagents and Wittig reactions (details in Supporting Information File 1).

Catalysis and conditions: Model substrate 1a was reacted with (Ph3P)AuNTf2 (Gagosz catalyst) in CH2Cl2, then in CH2Cl2/MeOH (10:1) and CH2Cl2/H2O (20 equiv). Catalysts screened included (Ph3P)AuNTf2, XPhosAuNTf2, IPrAuCl/AgSbF6, and (JohnPhos)(NCMe)AuSbF6. Solvents tested were CH2Cl2, CH2Cl2/Me2CO (1:1), CH2Cl2/dioxane (1:1), and CH2Cl2/dioxane (1:1) with various ligands/counterions. Reactions were run at 0.1 mmol (1a) or 0.3 mmol (substrate scope) with H2O (2.2 mmol, 0.04 mL) in 0.4 mL (1a) or 1.2 mL (scope) solvent until complete consumption (overnight), monitored by GC–MS and/or TLC. Isolated yields were determined by column chromatography. For substrate scope, reactions were typically performed in CH2Cl2 unless otherwise noted.

Selectivity and product analysis: Selectivity ratios (6-endo/5-exo) were determined by 1H NMR of crude mixtures. Products were isolated and characterized by NMR; X-ray crystallography confirmed 7a (CCDC-945504). Diastereoselectivity was assessed for E-enyne 1m (single isomer 7m) and Z-enyne 1n (2.5:1 mixture of 7n and 3n). Methoxycyclizations used (JohnPhos)(NCMe)AuSbF6 in CH2Cl2/MeOH (30:1), with yields and ratios reported.

Mechanistic probe: A D2O labeling experiment on 1b under the same catalytic conditions produced [D]-7b in 75% yield with >90% deuterium incorporation at C4, consistent with deuterodemetallation from a vinylgold species formed after nucleophilic attack on a gold carbenoid intermediate.

Controls and scope: Terminal enyne 1l (R=H) served as a control for 5-exo behavior. Substrates with electron-rich aryls, alkenyls, halogenated aryls, alkyl alkynes, trimethylsilyl, phenylthio, and terminal alkynes were evaluated to map substrate effects on selectivity and yield. Reaction times for some substrates (e.g., 1k) were extended (48 h).

title: Linguistic fairness in the U.S.: The case of multilingual public health information about COVID-19
field_subfield: Public Health — Health Literacy and Linguistic Equity
research_question:
The study addresses four central questions: (1) What is the extent of multilingual coverage of state-specific COVID-19 guidance across U.S. states? (2) Which factors predict the presence of non-English COVID-19 guidance at the state level (e.g., total language user counts versus limited English proficiency)? (3) How readable are Spanish-language COVID-19 materials from CDC, FDA, and state health departments relative to recommended standards for the general public? (4) How do these materials compare in difficulty to other Spanish corpora spanning genres and complexities?

Implicit hypotheses include: (a) Coverage is limited and uneven, with larger language communities more likely to be served; (b) Limited English proficiency, rather than total user counts, better predicts guideline presence; (c) Spanish-language materials often exceed recommended readability levels; and (d) Public health Spanish materials are more complex than simpler Spanish corpora (e.g., subtitles, fairy tales, TED transcripts). Support for these hypotheses would be indicated by Bayesian model selection favoring LEP predictors, readability scores above the 8th-grade threshold for most materials, and latent rank comparisons placing public health corpora among more complex genres.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional observational study of official non-English COVID-19 information from CDC, FDA, and all 50 U.S. state health departments. Two complementary analyses were conducted: (1) a state-level language coverage model; and (2) a readability analysis of Spanish-language materials.

Language coverage model: Between March 1 and March 15, 2021, the authors reviewed the websites of all 50 state health departments and the District of Columbia for non-English COVID-19 information. For each state, they recorded: number of languages represented; presence of automated translation options; reference to CDC’s multilingual resources (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/pubs/other-languages?Sort=Lang%3A%3Aasc); and availability of ASL videos. Content and accessibility were not assessed; a state received credit for a language if any content (original or linked) existed in that language. State-level language user counts were obtained from the 2009–2013 American Community Survey (U.S. Census Bureau). Language labels in the Census data vary in granularity (e.g., family-level aggregations or regional terms); the authors cross-referenced the widest available label to avoid undercounting coverage (overestimating coverage).

Modeling: A Bayesian logistic model predicted the presence of COVID-19 guidelines for a language in a state: g(−1(Rij)) ∝ αi + βj + f(nij), where Rij is a binary variable for presence/absence, αi and βj are state and language fixed effects, and f(·) is a smooth function of the number of users nij. The model was implemented in brms (v2.15.0) using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS). Posterior predictive checks indicated the model captured observed data distributions. Model selection compared two predictors: total users versus limited English proficiency (LEP). On the subset with LEP data, the model with LEP outperformed the total-users model by ELPD difference −15.3 (SE 5.3).

Readability analysis: Spanish-language materials were scraped from CDC (153 pages under “Su salud” and “Vacunas”), FDA (26 pages, e.g., FAQs, vaccine information sheets), and 12 states (21 pages) with Spanish FAQs and among the top 20 by fraction of Spanish speakers. Scraping dates: CDC/FDA March 24, 2021; states April 24, 2021. Text preprocessing (headers/footers, captions, extraneous content) used Readability Studio Professional (v2020). Five Spanish-specific readability formulas were applied: FRASE Graph (categorical difficulty), Gilliam-Peña-Mountain Graph (grade level), Läsbarhetsindex (Lix), Rate Index (Rix), and SOL (grade level). Extreme scores were capped (Lix/Rix ≥13→13; SOL ≥19→19; Gilliam-Peña-Mountain “too difficult”→17). Readability Studio Professional computed scores. A Plackett-Luce latent rank was inferred for 13 benchmark Spanish corpora (fairy tales, subtitles, TED transcripts, Wikipedia, news, medical, bureaucratic) across the five measures to contextualize public health corpora.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported.

title: Intravenous peramivir vs oral oseltamivir in high‐risk emergency department patients with influenza: Results from a pilot randomized controlled study
research_question:
Research question: In CDC-defined high-risk ED patients with laboratory-confirmed influenza, is single-dose intravenous peramivir non-inferior to a 5-day oral oseltamivir regimen for key clinical outcomes (symptom severity, disease severity, clinical status, and functional status) and comparable in safety and complications? Secondary questions include feasibility of ED-based enrollment and follow-up, adherence differences between regimens, and semi-quantitative changes in influenza viral load over time.

Hypotheses: (1) Peramivir will be non-inferior to oseltamivir on FLU-PRO, PGIS, Ordinal Scale, and Karnofsky Performance Scale trajectories up to day 14, with non-inferiority defined by P<0.05 in t-tests. (2) Safety profiles (adverse events, serious adverse events, complications) will be similar between groups. (3) Viral load (Ct) will decrease or remain stable over time, with no clear superiority of one regimen over the other. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses include comparable endpoint trajectories and safety profiles; outcomes refuting them would include inferior peramivir trajectories or higher complication rates. The study was not powered to detect absolute efficacy differences but aimed to establish feasibility and non-inferiority.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Open-label randomized controlled pilot trial at two academic EDs: Johns Hopkins Hospital (Baltimore, MD) and Maricopa Medical Center (Phoenix, AZ). Recruitment occurred 24/7 from 11/2015–04/2016 (JHH only) and 11/2016–04/2017 (both sites).

Participants: Adults (≥18 years) with ED-confirmed influenza by rapid molecular assay (Cepheid GeneXpert Flu/RSV), meeting 2011 CDC antiviral treatment criteria, symptom onset <96 hours, able to consent, and willing to comply with follow-up (daily diaries and phone calls). Exclusions: language barriers (English at JHH; English/Spanish at MMC), inability/unwillingness to consent, prior enrollment in the same season, inability to take oral medication, neuraminidase inhibitor use within 7 days, known allergy to neuraminidase inhibitors, pregnancy/breastfeeding, end-stage renal disease, end-stage liver disease, G6PD deficiency, or immunodeficiency.

Randomization and allocation: Internet-based randomization (www.random.org) without block randomization, aiming for 1:1 allocation; not stratified by site. Random numbers were independent per patient and site. The sample size (50–150) was set for feasibility.

Interventions: Dosing based on creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault). Oseltamivir: 30 mg once daily, 30 mg twice daily, or 75 mg twice daily for 5 days. Peramivir: 100 mg, 200 mg, or 600 mg as a single IV dose. The first dose was administered in the ED. For oseltamivir, patients were instructed to take remaining doses at home or inpatient. For peramivir, discharged patients received no further study drug; admitted patients could continue IV peramivir at the same dose for up to 4 days; if not improved after 5 days, continuation for another 5-day course was possible with infectious disease and pharmacist consultation. Peramivir was discontinued at discharge.

Outcomes: Primary feasibility and descriptive outcomes. Clinical endpoints included FLU-PRO (32-item symptom score, 1–5 scale), PGIS (0–3 severity), Ordinal Scale (1–6 clinical status), and Karnofsky Performance Scale (0–100). Follow-up was via daily diaries and phone calls through day 28. A biorepository collected nasopharyngeal swabs at day 1 (clinical testing) and day 3 (research) using flocked swabs and universal viral transport media. Day 1 clinical testing used Xpert Flu; aliquots were stored at JHH for future assays. Day 3 specimens were transported and stored at JHH.

Viral load analysis: Cepheid GeneXpert Xpress Flu/RSV Ct values were used as a semi-quantitative surrogate for viral load; Ct=40 was considered undetectable. Analysis was performed on paired samples available for both time points.

Statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics; chi-square tests for baseline characteristics, adherence, complications, and relevant side effects. Non-inferiority t-tests for daily outcomes (P<0.05 indicated non-inferiority). Sensitivity analyses used 15 multiple imputations per outcome/time point. Analyses were intent-to-treat. Ethics: IRB approvals at both sites; trial registration NCT02609399.

title: Arsenic(V) Immobilization in Fly Ash and Lead-Zinc Mine Tailing based Geopolymer: Performance and Mechanism Insight
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do NaOH concentration, FA content, As(V) content, GY content, and curing time affect UCS and As(V) immobilization in FA/MT geopolymers? (2) What are the dominant mechanisms of As(V) immobilization in these geopolymers? (3) Can FA/MT geopolymers meet hazardous waste leaching standards while achieving construction-relevant strengths?

Hypotheses: (H1) Increasing NaOH concentration accelerates aluminosilicate dissolution and geopolymer gel formation, increasing UCS and As immobilization efficiency. (H2) There exists an optimal FA content that balances Na/Al ratio for gel formation; beyond this, UCS decreases. (H3) Prolonged curing reduces porosity and enhances crystallization (e.g., calcium silicate, CSH), decreasing As leachability. (H4) As(V) is immobilized via initial physical encapsulation in geopolymer gels, followed by incorporation into crystalline phases with longer curing. (H5) FA/MT geopolymers can achieve ≥95% As immobilization and meet GB 5085.3-2007 leaching limits while attaining ≥25 MPa UCS.

Outcomes supporting/refuting: H1–H3 are supported by UCS trends with NaOH, FA, and curing time; H4 is supported by XRD/FTIR/SEM evidence of gel-to-crystal transitions and reduced As leachability with curing; H5 is supported by TCLP results (≤2.6 mg/L; ≥95.4% immobilization) and UCS values (≥25 MPa).
reference_methodology:
Materials: Class F fly ash (FA) and FGD gypsum (GY; kidney-shaped CaSO4·2H2O, 10–55 μm) were sourced from Jiangsu Nanre Power Generation Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China). Lead–zinc mine tailings (MT) were from Nanjing Yinmao Pb–Zn Mining Industry Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China). Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 96%) and sodium silicate (SS; Si:Na2O molar ratio 2:2–2.31) were from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) and Ganjiashan Yourui Refractories Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China), respectively. Sodium arsenate dibasic heptahydrate (Na2HAsO4·7H2O, 98%) was from Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai, China). Deionized water was used throughout.

Specimen preparation: FA and MT were dry-blended at FA contents of 28, 44, 54, or 61 wt.% (by total solid mass). NaOH (5, 8, or 10 M) and 25 g SS were added with deionized water to achieve a liquid-to-solid (L/S) ratio of 0.3–0.4, mixing gently to a homogeneous paste. For As(V) immobilization, sodium arsenate was added to achieve 0.01, 0.03, or 0.05 wt.% As(V). GY was added at 2.5 or 5 wt.% (by total solid mass). Paste was cast into 20 × 20 × 20 mm3 steel molds at room temperature for 24 h, demolded, and cured at 65 °C for 24 h, then at room temperature for 7, 14, or 28 days. All specimens were prepared in triplicate.

Mechanical testing: UCS was measured on a WDW-100 universal testing machine (Jinan Fangyuan Test Instrument Co., Ltd., China) at 5 MPa/s per ASTM C109M-2008. Each sample was tested in triplicate; averages were used.

Leaching tests: TCLP (US EPA Method 1311) was performed in triplicate. Leachates were filtered (0.45 μm), acidified with ultrapure nitric acid, and analyzed for As(V) by ICP-OES (PerkinElmer Optima 8000). Immobilization efficiency (%) was computed as (C0 − Cf)/C0 × 100, where C0 is the initial As(V) concentration in the TCLP suspension (assuming 100% leachability) and Cf is the measured leachate concentration (mg/L). The Chinese hazardous waste leaching standard GB 5085.3-2007 (≤5.0 mg/L) was used for compliance assessment.

Microstructural characterization: Crushed UCS specimens were milled to fine powders. XRD (Shimadzu XRD-6100) used Cu-Kα radiation (40 kV, 30 mA), step size 0.02°, scan rate 5°/min. SEM (Hitachi SU1510) operated at 1.5 kV. FTIR (Thermo Nicolet Is5) used KBr pellets. Calculated initial mixture ratios (Si/Al, Na/Al) are reported in Table 1; final gel ratios may differ.

Design and controls: The study varied NaOH concentration, FA content, As(V) content, GY content, and curing time to isolate effects on UCS and leaching. GY content was primarily 2.5 wt.% (5 wt.% was also tested and found to reduce UCS). Curing at 65 °C for 24 h was used to accelerate early strength development. Triplicate testing was applied to UCS and TCLP. No explicit randomization or blinding is described; no statistical tests beyond triplicates are reported.
