title: New Regenerative Cycle for Vapor Compression Refrigeration
field_subfield: Mechanical Engineering — Refrigeration and Heat Transfer
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a two-phase ejector used as a second-stage compressor increase the COP of a vapor compression refrigeration cycle relative to a conventional single-stage cycle? (2) Under what operating conditions (inter-stage pressure, motive pressure, entrainment ratio U, ejector compression ratio Π) does the system satisfy the thermodynamic condition U > W for COP improvement? (3) How do ejector geometry (mixing chamber diameter, nozzle diameter) and motive pressure affect entrainment, compression, and net COP? (4) How do refrigerant properties (R-507/R-404A vs R-22 vs propane) influence feasibility and magnitude of COP gains?

Hypotheses: (H1) The system achieves higher COP when the ejector’s entrainment ratio U exceeds the dimensionless work potential W derived from liquid pump compression and refrigerant properties. (H2) Higher entrainment ratios and lower ejector compression ratios (Π) will increase COP, but net gains will be constrained by the additional power required to pump the motive liquid and by external losses. (H3) Smaller nozzle diameters (smaller ejector module b) will increase U but require higher motive pressures; smaller mixing chambers may improve performance but will still face limits. (H4) Refrigerants with lower W for a given Π (e.g., propane) will be easier to improve than R-507/R-404A, though ODP may restrict practical use.

Support/refutation: H1 and H2 are supported by thermodynamic analysis and experiments showing COP increases with U and lower Π but plateaus due to pump power. H3 is supported by nozzle and geometry tests. H4 is supported by calculations indicating lower W for propane but limited by ODP and experimental constraints.
reference_methodology:
Thermodynamic analysis: The cycle is analyzed on p–h and T–s diagrams with isentropic compression in the mechanical compressor and isentropic liquid pumping. Key variables include inter-stage pressure pm (and temperature tm), motive pressure pp (and temperature tp), and entrainment ratio U. The dimensionless work potential W is defined as the ratio of specific work of isochoric liquid compression (pp→pk) to isentropic vapor compression (2→2′). The system’s operating point is determined by the intersection of two characteristic lines: (i) system demand U(Π) derived from energy and momentum balances (isobaric mixing, isentropic expansion/compression) and (ii) ejector performance U(Π) from momentum and energy transfer models. The COP is computed as COP = Q̇o/(Ṗc + Ṗp), with internal and external power terms and heat balances (Eqs. 1.10–1.22; 4.1–4.17; 4.20–4.22). The condition for COP improvement is U > W (Eq. 1.19), with isentropic case U > Ws (Eq. 1.20).

Experimental apparatus: A dedicated R-507 test rig (Fig. 2.4) includes a BOCK F1 open compressor (with motor and oil separator), a Hydra-Cell G03B liquid pump, two-phase ejectors (Ejector I: mixing chamber 6.0 mm, diffuser outlet 18.00 mm; Ejector II: mixing chamber 4.0 mm, diffuser outlet 11.95 mm), interchangeable sharp-edge motive nozzles (Dn = 2.00, 1.01, 1.20 mm), and plate heat exchangers for evaporator (SWEP B25TH x 20/1P-SC-S 2x22U) and condenser (SWEP B25TH x 80/1P-SC-S 2x22U). A frequency converter (ABB ACS50) controls compressor speed. Instrumentation: Coriolis mass flow meters (E&H Promass 40E/83F DN15), electronic throttling valves (CAREL E2V/E3V), pressure transducers (WIKA S-10, 0.25 class), T-type and K-type thermocouples (CZAKI TP-201), and a NI SCXI DAQ system. Sensors were calibrated per ISO 9000 procedures; thermocouples were calibrated to ±0.2 K. The system was purged with a two-stage vacuum pump and charged with R-507; refrigerant charge was verified via sight glasses.

Experimental procedures: Two modes were used. Mode I (ejector-only characterization): valve (a) closed, (b) open; the evaporator acts as a high-pressure vapor generator with controlled vapor pressure, superheat, liquid temperature, and mass flow. Mode II (system-level): valve (a) open, (b) closed; the ejector is integrated into the refrigeration cycle. Tests varied motive liquid pressure and mass flow (via pump capacity), inter-stage pressure pvi, and nozzle diameter. For Ejector I, tests were conducted with Dn = 2.00 mm (b = 0.111) and then Dn = 1.01 mm (b = 0.028). For Ejector II, tests used Dn = 1.01 mm (b = 0.064) and Dn = 1.20 mm (b = 0.090). For each condition, steady-state data were averaged over 100 readings. COP was computed via internal parameters (Eq. 4.15), external parameters (Eq. 4.16), and heat balances (Eqs. 4.12–4.15). A reference cycle (ejector body as a dummy discharge line) established baseline COP vs evaporation temperature (Fig. 4.1). A COP ratio Ψ compared system with ejector vs reference under matched condensation/evaporation pressures (Eq. 4.20).

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable. Randomization, blinding, and preregistration are not reported.

title: 'I take my tablets with the whiskey': A qualitative study of alcohol and medication use in mid to later life
field_subfield: Public Health — Geriatrics and Substance Use
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do older adults in mid-to-later life describe their experiences of concurrent alcohol and medication use? (2) How do they use alcohol for medicinal purposes (e.g., pain, sleep, mental health)? (3) How do they perceive and interact with health professionals regarding alcohol use and medication? (4) What gender- and context-specific patterns emerge?

The study did not state explicit hypotheses. Implicit expectations, grounded in prior literature, were that co-use is common, that alcohol is used as self-medication for pain and mental health, and that clinician engagement with alcohol use is limited. Outcomes that would support these expectations include reports of concurrent use despite contraindications, narratives of alcohol substituting for medication, and accounts of clinicians not inquiring about alcohol. Outcomes that would nuance or refute expectations include widespread clinician screening, minimal co-use, or absence of self-medication narratives. The analysis sought to identify themes that capture these patterns and their nuances.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative study situated in the interpretivist paradigm, employing semi-structured interviews and focus groups to capture individual experiences and socially negotiated norms. Data were analyzed using grounded theory to derive themes from the data.

Participants and sampling: Purposive sampling targeted adults aged 50+ with experience of drinking alcohol, recruited from three Age UK branches and two alcohol services in North East England. Twenty-four interviews were conducted (12 men, 12 women; ages 51–90) between 19/11/09 and 15/03/10. Three focus groups were facilitated between 15/03/10 and 19/10/10 (n=27; 6 men, 21 women; ages 50–95). Recruitment initially yielded a high proportion of recovering dependent drinkers; strategic snowballing added non-service users. Recruitment sources: nine via Age UK, 13 via alcohol services, two via snowballing. Focus groups were recruited from Age UK membership; participants were not required to disclose personal details beyond age and date of birth.

Procedures: One experienced post-doctoral researcher (GW) conducted all interviews and focus groups, lasting 40–150 minutes, at participants’ homes or organizational offices. Topic guides (supplementary files) covered drinking in later life, service use/support, and how support could be improved, with specific prompts about prescription medications, alcohol effects, and clinician discussions. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, anonymized, and imported into NVivo v10. Focus groups were facilitated to encourage general views rather than personal disclosures.

Analysis: Grounded theory analysis involved iterative reading of transcripts, coding, and theme development. Early analysis informed later data collection. Authors discussed divergent cases to refine themes and consider demographic influences (e.g., gender). Focus group data were used to triangulate interview themes, assessing social norms and negotiated meanings.

Ethics: Ethical approval was granted by Newcastle University Research Ethics Committee (application no. 000224/2009). Written informed consent was obtained; participants consented to data publication. Data are not publicly available due to sensitivity; requests can be directed to the ethics committee.

Sample characteristics: Table 1 details participant drinking status and household composition (e.g., dependent drinker; recovering dependent drinker with abstinence durations; occasional minimal drinker; household members including spouses, adult children, and other residents).

title: Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug Use Among Persons With Chronic Kidney Disease in the United States
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the prevalence of current NSAID use among US adults by CKD status (no CKD, mild CKD, moderate-to-severe CKD)? (2) How does NSAID use differ by CKD awareness? (3) What is the pattern of NSAID use (OTC vs prescription), duration (long-term vs short-term), and co-prescription with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and loop diuretics among CKD patients? (4) Are findings robust to alternative CKD staging equations and additional covariate adjustments?

Hypotheses: (a) NSAID use is present among CKD patients despite recommendations; (b) awareness of CKD is not associated with reduced NSAID use; (c) OTC NSAIDs predominate; (d) co-prescription with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and loop diuretics is common among CKD patients using NSAIDs. Supportive outcomes would include higher or similar prevalence of current NSAID use in CKD versus non-CKD, no significant difference in current use between CKD-aware and CKD-unaware individuals, a majority of NSAID use being OTC, and non-trivial co-prescription rates with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and loop diuretics. Refutation would involve low prevalence in CKD, lower use among CKD-aware individuals, predominance of prescription NSAIDs, or minimal co-prescription with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and loop diuretics.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Cross-sectional analysis of NHANES 1999–2004, a nationally representative survey of noninstitutionalized US civilians using standardized in-home interviews, physical examinations, and specimen collection at mobile centers. The survey employed a complex, multistage probability sampling with oversampling of certain subpopulations. Response rates for completing both interview and examination were 76% (1999–2000), 80% (2001–2002), and 76% (2003–2004), totaling 14,213 participants.

Participants: 12,065 adults aged ≥20 years who responded to the analgesic questionnaire and had available serum creatinine and urine albumin/creatinine measurements were included. Exclusions: pregnancy and eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2. All participants provided written informed consent; the protocol was approved by the National Center for Health Statistics Research Ethics Review Board.

Measurements: Interviews captured demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity), socioeconomic status (education, income), health care access, diagnosed diseases/conditions, and current/past use of analgesics via computer-assisted personal interviewing. Participants brought bottles of all prescription medications taken in the past month for recording. Physical examinations included height, weight, and blood pressure. Laboratory measurements: serum creatinine by modified kinetic Jaffe method with analyzer-specific corrections; urine albumin by solid-phase fluorescence immunoassay; urine creatinine by modified Jaffe kinetic method.

NSAID definitions: Current NSAID use was defined as self-reported daily or nearly daily use of ibuprofen, naproxen, sulindac, piroxicam, indomethacin, tolmetin, or diclofenac (with brand names and combinations identified) for the last 30 days. Long-term use was defined as ≥1 year of use. Current NSAID prescriptions were identified from the prescription medication database. Aspirin and acetaminophen were excluded from NSAID definitions due to lower nephrotoxicity and recommended use in CKD (pain relief for acetaminophen; cardiovascular prevention for aspirin).

Covariates: Comorbidities included self-reported cardiovascular disease (coronary artery disease, angina, myocardial infarction, stroke, congestive heart failure), hypertension (self-report, antihypertensive use, or measured BP ≥140/≥90 mm Hg), and obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). CKD awareness was defined as a yes response to having been told by a health professional that they have weak or failing kidneys.

Statistical analysis: Unweighted characteristics were compared by CKD status. Weighted prevalence estimates (unadjusted and adjusted) of current NSAID use were calculated by CKD category using survey design weights, strata, and primary sampling units. Variance of proportions was estimated via Taylor series linearization. Sensitivity analyses included: (1) defining reduced kidney function using the CKD-EPI equation; (2) additional adjustment for demographics and clinical conditions; and (3) stratification by arthritis status. All analyses used Stata 10.0 SVY commands. Statistical significance was set at P<.05.

title: Plasma-chemically brominated single-walled carbon nanotubes as novel catalysts for oil hydrocarbons aerobic oxidation
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do plasma-chemically brominated SWCNTs catalyze aerobic oxidation of hydrocarbons, and how does their activity compare to untreated SWCNTs and brominated MWCNTs? (2) Is catalytic activity proportional to the bromine content on the CNT surface? (3) Do (Br)n-SWCNTs outperform industrial Mn naphthenate catalysts in oil oxidation at lower loadings? (4) What is the plausible mechanism of catalytic action?

Hypotheses: (H1) Bromination increases catalytic activity by promoting ROS formation due to altered electron density on CNT surfaces; (H2) Higher Br content yields higher catalytic activity; (H3) (Br)n-SWCNTs will accelerate cumene oxidation at 60°C under 20 kPa O2; (H4) (Br)n-CNTs will surpass Mn naphthenate in oil oxidation at reduced catalyst loading. Supportive outcomes would include increased oxygen consumption rates in the model system with Br content–dependent acceleration, and higher acid numbers/yields of SPA in the oil oxidation at lower (Br)n-CNT loadings versus Mn naphthenate. Refutation would involve no acceleration, inverse dependence on Br content, or inferior performance to Mn catalysts.
reference_methodology:
Materials: SWCNTs (Elicarb, Thomas Swan & Co. Ltd., UK) were brominated via plasma-chemical technique using bromine vapor at 100 W (continuous wave) and 9 Pa. XPS quantified surface composition: Sample 1 (1 h exposure): C 94.8%, O 3.3%, Br 2.0% (O/C = 0.035; Br/C = 0.021); Sample 2 (2 h exposure): C 87.3%, O 6.3%, Br 6.4% (O/C = 0.072; Br/C = 0.073); Sample 3 (untreated): C 96.9%, O 3.1% (O/C = 0.032). Model hydrocarbon: cumene (98% purity, Sigma-Aldrich). Initiator: 2,2-azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN), purified by recrystallization from benzene and ethanol. Petroleum feedstock: naphthenic-paraffinic concentrate from Azerbaijan (Baku) crude oil diesel cut (Oil Refinery "Azernefteyag") after de-aromatization and de-paraffination. Table 1 reports physico-chemical properties of the crude diesel cut and naphthenic concentrate.

Model cumene oxidation: Conducted in batch at 60°C (±0.02°C) under oxygen pressure PO2 = 20 kPa (air), with reaction mixture volume 10 ml. Initiation rate Wi = 6.8 × 10^-8 M s^-1 was achieved by adding 10 mg AIBN. (Br)n-SWCNT loadings: 0 g/l (reference), 2.0 g/l (Br-81-120509), 4.0 g/l (Br-82-120514, untreated), and 4.0 g/l (Br-80-120504). Oxygen consumption was measured volumetrically using a simple laboratory device (Fig. 1). Oxidation rates (WO2) were determined from slopes of oxygen uptake curves (steady-state) or by differentiation during induction periods. Experiments were performed at least in triplicate; kinetic parameter accuracy was 3–7%.

Oil oxidation: A glass laboratory flow reactor (Fig. 2) was used at 135–140°C with an air stream of 100–120 L/h for several hours. Feedstock: 128 g (150 ml) of the 220–350°C naphthenic fraction. Catalyst loadings: (Br)n-SWCNT 1.6 g/kg (1.3 g/L) and (Br)n-MWCNT; industrial Mn naphthenate 15 g/kg. Conversion criteria: acid number (AN) of the oxidate and yields of SPA and oxy-synthetic petroleum acids (OSPA). Acidic components (SPA + OSPA) were isolated by alkali treatment (NaOH or KOH), acidified with mineral acids, and separated by light benzene or petroleum ether. IR spectroscopy (Specord M-80, Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany) characterized SPA.

Comparative data: Brominated MWCNT (Br content 17.8%) was tested in the model oxidation (Fig. 4) under identical conditions to (Br)n-SWCNTs. No explicit details on reactor geometry, mixing, or oxygen mass transfer coefficients were provided. No statistical tests beyond triplicate runs were reported.

title: Auditory localization reflects higher-level cognitive processing in disorders of consciousness: a multimodal clinical, neuroimaging and neurophysiological study
research_question:
Primary research question: Does auditory localization reflect higher-level cognitive processing and qualify as an MCS sign rather than a UWS reflex? Secondary questions: (1) Does the probability of auditory localization increase with consciousness level? (2) Do UWS patients with auditory localization (LOCA) have better outcomes than those without (NO-LOCA)? (3) Do LOCA patients show greater brain metabolism and connectivity in auditory/awareness-related networks than NO-LOCA? (4) Are LOCA patients more similar to MCS− than NO-LOCA on brain metrics?

Hypotheses: (a) Auditory localization prevalence increases with consciousness level (UWS < MCS− < MCS+ < EMCS). (b) LOCA patients recover better than NO-LOCA (higher survival and functional improvement). (c) LOCA vs NO-LOCA show greater metabolism and connectivity in cortical networks linked to auditory processing and awareness. (d) LOCA patients’ brain activity is more similar to MCS− than NO-LOCA. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include graded prevalence, survival advantages, metabolic/functional connectivity differences favoring LOCA, and convergence of LOCA with MCS− on brain metrics.
reference_methodology:
Design: Multimodal observational study combining clinical assessment, FDG-PET, resting-state fMRI, and hdEEG in DOC patients. Primary cohort: 186 severely brain-injured patients (66 females; mean age 39±16 years; median time since injury 9 months [1–29 years]) with prolonged DOC (>28 days post-injury). Etiologies: traumatic brain injury (TBI) 100 (53.8%) and non-TBI (NTBI) 86 (46.2%). CRS-R-based diagnoses: UWS 64 (34.4%), MCS− 28 (15%), MCS+ 71 (38.2%), EMCS 23 (12.4%). Experienced clinicians conducted ≥5 CRS-R assessments per patient to ensure reliable diagnosis. Auditory localization was defined as presence in ≥1 of the minimum 5 assessments; repeatability was the proportion of assessments with localization.

Outcomes: Follow-up to 2 years using the extended Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended (GOSE; 1=death to 8=good recovery). Survival was GOSE≠1; improvement thresholds: GOSE>2 (UWS), >3 (MCS), >4 (EMCS).

Statistical analyses: Group comparisons used one-way ANOVA/Chi-square for demographics; Fisher’s exact and Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney for etiology/time since injury; independent-sample t-tests and Fisher’s exact for age/gender. Presence of auditory localization and repeatability were compared via Chi-square and Kruskal–Wallis H. Multinomial logistic regression predicted consciousness level (UWS, MCS−, MCS+, EMCS) from age, etiology, time since injury, and auditory localization. Survival and improvement differences were tested with Fisher’s exact.

FDG-PET: Resting-state [18F]FDG-PET (Gemini Big Bore TF, Philips) compared UWS LOCA (n=8) and NO-LOCA (n=30) to 34 age-matched HCS (mean age 43±15 years; 15 women). SPM12 GLM identified decreased metabolism; covariates: standardized age (mean-centered, SD-scaled) and log10-transformed time since injury. Significance: voxel-wise p<0.05 FDR-corrected (whole-brain).

fMRI: 3T Siemens Trio Tim; structural T1 and resting-state T2* fMRI (300 volumes). Preprocessing in SPM12. Seed-based connectivity (CONN 16b) for auditory network (7 ROIs), default-mode network (DMN; 9 ROIs), and fronto-parietal network (FPN; 11 ROIs). Second-level one-sided tests contrasted patient groups (UWS LOCA, UWS NO-LOCA, MCS−) vs HCS, and UWS LOCA vs NO-LOCA, and UWS vs MCS−. Covariates: standardized age and log time since injury. Significance: cluster-wise p<0.05 FDR-corrected (non-parametric permutation cluster-mass) with voxel-wise p<0.001 uncorrected.

hdEEG: 256-channel recordings (~20 min; 500 Hz; Electric Geodesics). Preprocessing per prior work. Power spectra decomposed into delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4.1–8 Hz), alpha (8.1–12 Hz), beta (12.1–30 Hz) using multi-taper method. Mean power and connectivity (debiased weighted PLI) computed for whole brain and regional networks; graph theory measures included participation coefficient. Non-parametric multivariate permutation tests (5000 permutations; MATLAB 2018a) tested group differences in connectivity and graph metrics; covariates: standardized age and log time since injury. Region-wise analyses used FDR correction across 12 regions (p<0.05).

Ethics: Institutional ethics approval; written informed consent from legal representatives and healthy participants.

title: Personal Preference Analysis for Emotional Behavior Response of Autonomous Robot in Interactive Emotion Communication
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a camera-based, Laban-inspired fuzzy inference system (FEIS) reliably recognize human emotions from motion and map them to robot emotional behaviors in real time? (2) How do human participants subjectively evaluate robot emotional responses across different human–robot emotion combinations? (3) Are there consistent patterns or individual differences in preferences for robot emotional behaviors, and can these be quantified using weighted composite scores and inter-subject correlations?

Hypotheses (implicit): (H1) FEIS will produce human emotion classifications (JOY-F, ANG-F, SAD-F, REL-F) that align with human-elicited emotions (JOY-H, ANG-H, SAD-H, REL-H) and trigger corresponding robot behaviors (JOY-R, ANG-R, SAD-R, REL-R). (H2) Human participants will prefer robot responses that are congruent with their own emotions (e.g., JOY-R for JOY-H) and may prefer encouraging responses (e.g., JOY-R for SAD-H). (H3) Individual preferences will vary, with some combinations eliciting strong positive or negative impressions.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if FEIS outputs and robot behaviors track human-elicited emotions over time. H2 is supported if weighted composite scores (σ) are higher for congruent or encouraging combinations. H3 is supported if inter-subject Spearman correlations (ρ) show both positive and negative associations across combinations.
reference_methodology:
Design: Within-subject, interactive experiment with two participants (Subject A and Subject B) performing 16 human–robot emotion combinations over 40-second trials. The study focuses on four basic emotions: JOY, ANG, SAD, REL.

Participants: Two university students (age not reported). Both were asked to imagine specific situations to elicit target emotions (Table 3). No further demographics or inclusion criteria were reported.

Apparatus: A pet-type robot (AIBO ERS-7, Sony) with 20 degrees of freedom. The robot’s program was controlled via a personal computer using a dedicated memory stick. A CCD camera captured human motion at 3–5 frames/s. FEIS ran on a computer, sending outputs to the robot via wireless LAN. An observer monitored FEIS outputs in real time.

Human motion capture and features: Subjects wore five colored markers (head, both hands, both feet) in distinct colors (red, yellow, green, blue, pink). The system extracted Laban-based features: Time Effort (TE: speed of the center of gravity), Flow Effort (FE: hand acceleration), Table-Plane Shape (TPS: body area), and Door-Plane Shape (DPS: height of the center of gravity). Weight, shape effort, and wheel plane were excluded due to measurement difficulty.

FEIS pipeline: (1) Measure human motion via CCD camera. (2) Extract Laban features (TE, FE, TPS, DPS). (3) Fuzzy inference to compute pleasure/unpleasure (Rx) and arousal/sleep (Ry). (4) Map Rx/Ry to Russell’s circumplex to determine basic emotion and strength Ei. (5) Express robot emotion based on inferred emotion value.

Membership functions and fuzzy rules: Membership functions for La (area), Lp (position), Lv (velocity), Lh (hand acceleration), and Rx/Ry are defined with singleton values (Table 2). Fuzzy rules (Table 1) map combinations of La, Lp, Lv, Lh to Rx/Ry classes (e.g., NUS, NEU, PPL, PAS, PAM, PAL, NSS, NSL, NSM). The emotion value Ei is computed as Ei = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2) / |sin(π − 2θ)|, where θ = arctan(Ry/Rx), with quadrants mapping to JOY (0 ≤ θ < π/2), ANG (π/2 ≤ θ < π), SAD (π ≤ θ < 3π/2), REL (3π/2 ≤ θ < 2π).

Robot behaviors: Four canonical expressions were used: JOY-R (raise both hands), ANG-R (drop both hands to the ground), SAD-R (hang head), REL-R (stretch legs). Each robot expression lasted 3–6 seconds and was repeated 3–5 times within a 40-second trial.

Procedure: For each trial, subjects (a) selected an emotion-easy situation (Step 1), (b) expressed the target emotion freely (Step 2), (c) FEIS recognized human emotion (Step 3), (d) the computer sent FEIS output to the robot (Step 4), (e) the robot expressed emotion for all human–robot combinations (Step 5), (f) the subject observed the robot while expressing emotion (Step 6), (g) steps 2–4 were repeated within 40 seconds (Step 7), and (h) post-experiment questionnaires were completed (Step 8). The 16 patterns covered all combinations of JOY-H/ANG-H/SAD-H/REL-H with JOY-R/ANG-R/SAD-R/REL-R.

Outcome measures: Six adjectival pairs were rated on 7-point scales (−3 to 3): animal-like–mechanical (S1), interesting–boring (S2), complex–simple (S3), familiar–unfamiliar (S4), natural–unnatural (S5), likable–dislikable (S6). A weighted composite score σ was computed as σ = Σi αi Si, where αi were subject-provided weights reflecting perceived importance of each pair. Weights obtained: Subject A (α1, α2, α3, α4, α5, α6) = (0.15, 0.05, 0.15, 0.15, 0.0, 0.5); Subject B = (0.15, 0.1, 0.025, 0.1, 0.125, 0.5). Spearman rank correlations (ρ) were computed between Subject A and Subject B for each combination.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported.

title: Influence of Supplemental Protein on the Life Expectancy and Reproduction of the Chinese Citrus Fruit Fly, Bactrocera minax (Enderlein) (Tetradacus minax) (Diptera: Tephritidae)
research_question:
Research question: Does supplementing adult B. minax diets with protein (yeast extract or peptone) improve survival, mating behavior, ovarian development, egg load, and oviposition compared to water or sucrose alone?

Hypotheses: (1) Protein-supplemented diets (F2, F3) will increase adult survival metrics (LT50, LT90) and delay mortality peaks relative to non-protein diets (F0, F1). (2) Protein supplementation will increase mating frequency and duration, with earlier mating onset and higher cumulative mating ratios. (3) Protein supplementation will accelerate ovarian development and increase egg load and oviposition. (4) Yeast extract will outperform peptone in enhancing survival and reproduction due to additional vitamins and micronutrients. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include statistically significant improvements in survival time-to-event metrics, higher mating frequencies and longer mating windows, earlier ovarian maturation, and higher egg counts on protein diets, with yeast showing superior performance where applicable. Null outcomes would include no differences between diets or worse performance on protein diets.
reference_methodology:
Source population and rearing: Mature larvae of B. minax were collected from orange orchards in Songzi, Hubei, China (20 Oct–10 Nov 2015). Larvae were reared in plastic containers (21 cm diameter) with sterilized sand (15% water content; sand sterilized at 60°C for 24 h) at room temperature (4.8–22.6°C; 75% RH ± 5%). Adults emerged from late April to 27 May 2016.

Diet preparation: Solid diets were prepared by mass: sucrose 4 g (Tianjin Beilian Fine Chemicals Development Co. Ltd.), sucrose + yeast extract (3 g + 1 g; 3:1), and sucrose + peptone (3 g + 1 g; 3:1) (Guangdong Huankai Microbial Sci & Tech. Co. Ltd.). Diets were mixed evenly and placed on Petri dishes (diameter 9 cm). Four diets were tested: F0 (water), F1 (sucrose), F2 (sucrose + yeast extract), F3 (sucrose + peptone).

Experimental design: Adults were separated into cohorts. Survival study: 60 newly emerged flies (30 males, 30 females) per replicate were placed in wire mesh cages (30 × 30 × 30 cm) with a white cloth bottom. Five replicates per diet were used. Flies received 4 g of solid food per day, replaced every 24 h. Water (7 ml) was provided twice daily (morning/evening) on a cotton bud (diameter 0.5 cm), replaced weekly. Mortality was recorded daily.

Mating and oviposition study: Virgin adults (0–24 h post-emergence) were assigned to diets (F0–F3) with 30 males and 30 females per replicate; five replicates per diet. Fresh orange fruit was provided for oviposition (adapted to oviposition through thick skin) and replaced every 3 days. Mating frequency was observed and recorded every 30 minutes from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

Ovarian development study: 800 females were maintained in four cages (200 females/cage) with the four diets. Twenty females were dissected every 5 days for 20 days to assess ovarian development and egg load under a stereomicroscope. Ovarian stages were classified as: stage 1 (original, small, nondeveloped, with subsidiary silks; diameter slightly greater than oviduct), stage 2 (growing, swelling; subsidiary silks diminish; primary ovary formation and yolk precipitation), stage 3 (growing larger; hardening yolk; eggs visible in oviducts; mature eggs present before/after oviposition onset). Stage ratios were computed as (number with stage)/(total dissected) × 100.

Statistical analysis: Life expectancy was calculated as (∑ survival days per insect)/total tested adults. Mortality ratio (MR%) = daily mortality/total lifetime mortality × 100; cumulative mortality ratio (CMR%) = Σ MR1…MRn. Cumulative mortality was transformed to probability units and analyzed by logistic regression y = a/(1 + Exp(b − kx)) to estimate LT50 and LT90. Age-specific cumulative mortality was arcsine-transformed and analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test (P = 0.05). Mating metrics: lifetime mating frequency per sex = Σ (daily mating times/daily surviving individuals). Cumulative mating ratio (CMR) computed analogously to mortality. Cumulative mating was transformed to probability units and analyzed by logistic regression to estimate mating onset (16%), peak (50%), and end (84%). Age-specific mating data were arcsine-transformed and analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test (P = 0.05). Oviposition per female = Σ (weekly fecundity/weekly average surviving females). Ovarian egg load was counted as mature oocytes per ovary. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test (P = 0.05). Analyses were performed in SPSS 17.0.

title: Proverbiogenesis: The Phases of Proverbial Birth
research_question:
Central questions: (1) What are the necessary and optional phases that constitute proverbial birth (proverbiogenesis)? (2) How do definitional criteria (closed units, generic meaning, currency, human activities, authorial anonymity) interact with these phases? (3) What mechanisms drive exposure and dissemination, and how do propagating agents shape the process? (4) When and how does reference loss occur, and is it necessary for full proverb status? (5) How common are polygenetic origins, and how do modifications (syntactic/lexical/semantic) arise?

Hypotheses: (a) Proverbiogenesis comprises at least five phases—induction, coinage, exposure, dissemination, and reference loss—rather than a single creation followed by acceptance. (b) Dissemination proceeds via mixed diffusion from multiple simultaneous sources, not a single localized origin. (c) Reference loss is a critical, often prolonged phase that completes proverbial birth by achieving authorial anonymity. (d) Polygenesis is possible but statistically unlikely; many formulas attributed to famous authors are later borrowings or propagating agents. (e) Facilitators (e.g., brevity, figurativeness) and modifications (often media-driven) can occur at multiple points and influence success. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include corpus-based evidence of multi-source diffusion, temporal sequences from archives/corpora showing prolonged acceptance, and cases where authorial attribution persists despite widespread use.
reference_methodology:
Design: The paper is a theoretical framework supported by illustrative case studies and corpus-linguistic evidence. It does not report formal experiments, statistical tests, or preregistration.

Data sources: Modern corpora and archives are emphasized to mitigate temporal gaps. Specifically, the Global Web-based English (GloWbE) corpus is used to analyze usage patterns and authorial attribution (e.g., Life is like a box of chocolates). Newspaper archives (e.g., New York Times) and the Dictionary of Modern Proverbs are cited for historical references and dating. The author also references secondary sources (e.g., Mieder 2004, 2015; Taylor 1931, 1934; Firth 1926) for conceptual grounding.

Procedure: The author synthesizes prior literature to define proverbs via multi-criteria and then applies this definition to trace phases in exemplar formulas. For each case, the paper identifies: (1) induction (stimulus from real-life experience), (2) coinage (formulation), (3) exposure (primary propagating agents such as advertisements, films, books, or speeches), (4) dissemination (micro-propagating agents and secondary exposures), and (5) reference loss (anonymity). The author also examines modifications (syntactic/lexical/semantic) and their sources (e.g., slogans, media). For duration estimation, the paper collates first recorded instances, earliest written references, and later common usage to infer time spans.

Analysis: The analysis is qualitative and descriptive, using corpus counts and historical records to substantiate claims. For Life is like a box of chocolates, the paper reports GloWbE counts (42 entries; 27 with film references) to argue limited reference loss. For Garbage in, garbage out, the paper cites first written references (1957–1959), computing manuals (1964–1966), NYT usage (1965), press commonality (1972), and a 1983 press label as a “folk saying.” For What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas, the paper notes slogan origin (2002), ads (2003), and proverbial usage by 2008. The dissemination model is illustrated via a simplified mixed diffusion representation (Table 1) showing primary exposure to hearers (square nodes) and subsequent dissemination (round nodes).

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human subjects or sensitive data are involved.

title: Conditional Generation Net for Medication Recommendation
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can explicitly modeling historical medication recommendations via a copy-or-predict mechanism improve the accuracy and safety of medication recommendations compared to instance-based and longitudinal baselines? (2) Does a hierarchical selection mechanism (visit-level and medication-level) effectively leverage longitudinal history and improve performance as the number of visits increases? (3) Are diagnosis and procedure information, graph-based medication relations (EHR co-occurrence and DDI), and beam search integral to performance? (4) How does medication label ordering affect training and final performance?

Hypotheses: (H1) COGNet will outperform instance-based baselines (LR, ECC, LEAP) and longitudinal baselines (RETAIN, DMNC, GAMENet, MICRON, SafeDrug) on Jaccard, F1, and PRAUC. (H2) The copy module and hierarchical selection will be integral; removing either will degrade performance. (H3) Performance will improve with more historical visits due to better historical information capture, outperforming RNN-like methods (e.g., MICRON) that suffer from error accumulation. (H4) Appropriate label ordering (e.g., Rare first) will mitigate imbalance and improve performance; chronological orderings will be suboptimal. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include higher Jaccard/F1/PRAUC than baselines, ablation degradation when removing key components, monotonic gains with more visits, and superior performance under Rare-first ordering.
reference_methodology:
Dataset: MIMIC-III (PhysioNet) with 46,520 patients and 58,976 admissions (2001–2012). The authors use the data processing script from [28] and retain patients with at least two visits. Medications are restricted to the top 300 by occurrence to improve training speed. Top-40 severity DDI types are extracted from TWOSIDES (reported by ATC Third Level codes). NDC drug codes are transformed to ATC level codes to compute DDI scores. Data are split into train/validation/test with ratios 2/3, 1/3, 1/3. Medication frequencies are counted on the training set and sorted in ascending order for all patients.

Model inputs: For each visit, diagnosis codes D, procedure codes P, and medication codes M are embedded via E_D, E_P, E_M (dimension d). Diagnosis and procedure sets are encoded with Transformer-based encoders (multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward, residual connections, LayerNorm) to obtain D′ and P′. Medication representations are learned via two-layer GCNs on EHR co-occurrence and DDI graphs, then fused to obtain relation-aware medication features. The decoder generates medications sequentially, maintaining relation-aware representations of partially generated medications and aligning with D′ and P′ to guide coverage of diseases.

Training: The model is trained to minimize cross-entropy over the medication sequence. Teacher forcing is used: at step t, the decoder uses the ground-truth (t−1)-th medication as input; the first step uses a special ⟨START⟩ token. Implementation details: PyTorch 1.9.0, Python 3.9.6, Intel Xeon 8255C with 315 GB RAM and 8 NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. Hyperparameters: embedding dimension d=64; beam search width=4; maximum generation length=45; Adam optimizer with learning rate 1×10^−4; batch size=16; 50 epochs; random seed=1203. Evaluation uses bootstrapping: 10 rounds of random sampling 80% of the test set; mean and standard deviation are reported.

Metrics: Jaccard Similarity (intersection over union of predicted and ground-truth medications), Average F1 (harmonic mean of precision and recall), Precision–Recall AUC (PRAUC), and DDI rate (fraction of DDI pairs among recommended medications). For PRAUC, each medication’s probability is taken at its generation step; for others, the average across steps is used. DDI rate is computed using the DDI adjacency matrix A and indicator 1{·}.

Baselines: LR (logistic regression), ECC (Ensemble Classifier Chain with multihot encoding and SVMs), LEAP (LSTM-based generation on diagnoses), RETAIN (attention/gate-based longitudinal encoder), DMNC (memory-augmented encoder), GAMENet (memory+graph), MICRON (recurrent residual learning on medication changes), SafeDrug (drug molecular graph + DDI graph).

title: Approaches to determining the stages of the language teaching methods development in Western Ukraine (1867-1939)
field_subfield: Education — Language Education (Foreign Language Teaching Methods)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What criteria can validly periodize FLTM development in Western Ukraine (1867–1939) given its historical and social context? (2) How did FLTM evolve across distinct stages, and what methods, curricula types, and didactic principles characterized each stage? (3) Which provisions of translation-based and direct methods persisted across stages, and how did they adapt to regional conditions?

Hypotheses: (H1) A periodization grounded in historical/social/political factors, foreign FLTM influence, and changes in methodological science will capture the evolution of FLTM in Western Ukraine. (H2) FLTM in Western Ukraine progressed through identifiable stages with distinct methodological emphases (e.g., grammar translation in Stage I; direct method in Stage II; mixed method in Stage III). (H3) Core provisions of translation-based and direct methods (e.g., reliance on native language translation, spoken language primacy, phonetic rules) persisted across stages, while additional provisions (e.g., reading–writing integration, individualization, dramatisation) emerged regionally. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include consistent alignment of stage boundaries with political transitions, documented curricular and textbook evidence of method shifts, and explicit identification of persistent and emergent provisions.
reference_methodology:
Design: Historical-methodological analysis combining critical source analysis, narrative periodization, and hermeneutic interpretation. The study integrates multiple historical-methodological approaches to structure and interpret the evolution of FLTM in Western Ukraine.

Data sources: The author analyzed 131 curricula, 61 textbooks, and numerous educational periodicals from Galicia, Bukovyna, Transcarpathia, and Western Volyn. Periodicals included Galician titles such as “Uchytel,” “Nasha Shkola,” “Uchytelske slovo,” “Uchytelskyj holos,” “Kalendar ‘Oswita’,” “Shkilnyj calendar na zwychajnyj shkilnyj rik,” “Shljach vychovanja i navchanja,” “Ukrajinska shkola,” “Muzeum”; Bukovynian titles such as “Kamenjari,” “Shkolnaja chasopys,” “Bukowiner Schule,” “Bukowiner pädagogische Blätter,” “Bukowiner Schul-Zeitung”; Transcarpathian titles such as “Podkarpatsksja Rus,” “Uchytel,” “Nasha Shkola”; and Western Volyn titles such as “Rilnyk,” “Do prazi.” These sources documented pedagogical debates, curricular prescriptions, and textbook content.

Analytic procedures: (1) Critical analysis of Ukrainian and foreign psychological, linguistic, and methodological literature, educational documents, curricula, and FL textbooks; (2) Monitoring and summarizing teachers’ positive experiences by extracting didactic principles, techniques, and methodological solutions that improved teaching efficiency; (3) Narrative method to arrange historical events chronologically; (4) Hermeneutic method to preserve authentic meanings and period-specific terminology while summarizing results with contemporary FLTM terms; (5) Historical-structural method to organize accumulated historical-methodological information and correlate it with historical periods; (6) Historical-genetic method to trace the origin of FLTM in Western Ukraine and derive subsequent stages; (7) Historical-comparative method to compare FLTM development in Western Ukraine with European, Russian Empire, and USSR contexts and identify specific features.

Curriculum and textbook analysis: Curricula were evaluated against criteria including compliance with social order, approval by state educational authorities, clarity of objectives/content/periodization, availability of methodological guidelines, alignment with school type requirements, availability of language/speech material per year, recommendations for formative/summative assessment, and availability of authorized textbooks. Textbook analysis followed Borysko’s hierarchical scheme (1999) for structural and content evaluation.

Scope and periodization: The study spans 1867–1939, acknowledging political transitions (Austro-Hungarian rule; interwar national affiliations; Soviet administration after 1939). Stage boundaries were set at 1867–1890 (Stage I), 1890–1918 (Stage II), and 1918–1939 (Stage III), with Stage III’s upper limit discussed as 1938 given the 1939 Soviet–German treaty. The analysis emphasizes English, German, and French, with Latin and Greek also present in curricula.

title: Brave New Surfactant World Revisited by Thermoalkalophilic Lipases: SDS as a Potential Substrate Analog
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does SDS mimic non-ionic substrate analogs and stabilize the active conformation of thermoalkalophilic lipases at ambient temperature? (2) Does SDS induce partial denaturation of surface structures at elevated temperatures, and how does this affect catalytic function? (3) How do SDS concentration, temperature, and oligomeric state (monomer vs dimer) modulate SDS–lipase interactions and activity?

Hypotheses: (H1) At 298 K, SDS binds to the sn-1 acyl-chain pocket of the open conformation and induces an open-like state in the closed conformation, preserving the catalytic triad and increasing activity. (H2) At 373 K, SDS partially unfolds surface structures (e.g., the β-flap) while leaving the core intact, reducing activity unless oligomerization protects surface regions. (H3) Activation by SDS is concentration- and temperature-dependent, with optimal SDS concentrations shifting with temperature and CMC, and oligomerization (dimers) reducing SDS accessibility at the interface. Support for H1 would be observed as SDS occupancy in the sn-1 pocket, intact triad, and increased activity at low SDS; support for H2 would be increased RMSF in surface regions and loss of secondary structure without core unfolding; support for H3 would be reduced SDS contacts and surface flexibility in dimers and experimental activity maxima near or above CMC at higher temperatures.
reference_methodology:
Protein structures: Two members of the thermoalkalophilic lipase family (family I) were used: open conformation (PDB 2W22) and closed conformation (PDB 1KU0). Sequences are ~95% identical. For 1KU0 (a dimer in crystal), chain A was used for simulations. Structures were stripped of crystal waters and ligands; zinc and calcium ions were retained. Protonation was set to pH 7.0. Systems were solvated in cubic boxes with at least 10 Å padding.

Solvent systems: Three solvents were modeled: water; SDS-water with 20 SDS molecules; SDS-water with 180 SDS molecules. SDS-containing systems were generated with PACKMOL. Resulting systems were neutralized with Na+ and Cl−. Equilibration: 40,000-step energy minimization; 0.25 ns NVT (solvent only, protein fixed); then 40,000-step minimization and 0.25 ns NVT (all atoms); final 5 ns NPT at 298 K, 1 atm (Langevin thermostat, piston pressure). System densities and SDS concentrations were verified; control water systems matched experimental density (~0.99 g/L). SDS concentrations after equilibration were ~1.4% w/v (~50 mM) for 20-SDS systems and ~12.8% w/v (~440 mM) for 180-SDS systems.

Production simulations: NPT at 1 atm, 298 K or 373 K, 2 µs per system (12 total). Software: NAMD 2.13 with CHARMM36 force field (correction map). Water modeled with TIP3P. PME with 1.2 Å grid spacing; 12 Å non-bonded cutoff; 2 fs timestep; periodic boundary conditions.

Analysis: Visual inspection in VMD; all-to-all RMSD (MDAnalysis); essential dynamics via PCA (Bio3D); fraction of native contacts (Q1); SDS–protein contacts (<5 Å); hydrogen bonds (SDS–lipase, SDS–SDS, SDS–water); radial distribution functions (COM–COM SDS–lipase); tunnel analysis with Caver 3.0 (bottleneck radius 1.5 Å). Dimer simulations were also performed with 20 SDS at 298 K and 373 K for 500 ns to assess oligomerization effects.

Enzyme assays: Recombinant Bacillus thermocatenulatus lipase 2 (BTL2) was expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) using pMCSG7, purified by Ni-affinity chromatography, buffer-exchanged to 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, concentrated to 2 mg/mL, and stored at 4°C. Activity was measured colorimetrically using pNPP (p-nitrophenyl palmitate) at 410 nm. Initial rates were obtained from triplicate samples measured every minute for 2 minutes. Stability assays: 1 mg/mL enzyme incubated at 25, 70, or 100°C with SDS at 0–13% w/v for 10 min; residual activity was normalized to water at 25°C. SDS CMC values were approximated from literature: 25°C ~0.236% w/v (0.0082 mol/L), 70°C ~0.302% w/v (0.0105 mol/L), 100°C ~0.418% w/v (0.0145 mol/L).

title: Laparoscopic radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy: preliminary experience with 10 cases
research_question:
Research question: Is laparoscopic radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy (LRAMPS) technically feasible and safe in well-selected patients with left-sided pancreatic cancer, and does it achieve adequate oncologic margins and lymphadenectomy?

Hypotheses: (1) LRAMPS can be completed laparoscopically without conversion or transfusion in selected patients. (2) Perioperative outcomes (operative time, EBL, complications, hospital stay) will be acceptable. (3) Oncologic adequacy will be high, with R0 resection and adequate lymph node retrieval. (4) Early recurrence rates will be comparable to expectations for distal pancreatectomy in this population.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (1) is supported if all cases are completed laparoscopically without conversion. Hypothesis (2) is supported if operative times and EBL are within reasonable ranges and complication rates are acceptable. Hypothesis (3) is supported if R0 resection is achieved and lymph node counts are adequate. Hypothesis (4) is supported if early recurrence is low; however, given short follow-up, it remains preliminary.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-center, consecutive case series of 10 patients undergoing LRAMPS for pancreatic cancer from December 2018 to February 2020. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of Zhejiang Provincial People’s Hospital and The First People’s Hospital of Jiashan. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients.

Participants: Ten patients (6 male, 4 female), median age 64 years (range 55–80), mean BMI 24.1 ± 2.9 kg/m². Two patients had prior laparotomy (one cholecystectomy, one appendectomy). Tumor locations: 6/10 (60%) in the pancreatic body and 4/10 (40%) in the tail. All tumors were away from the celiac axis. Imaging included CT and MRI for all; EUS with FNA in 2 cases; PET in 6 cases. One case had a 125 × 108 mm cystic neoplasm in the body with clear margins, multilocular cavity, enhanced internal septa, and thick wall; nine had solid masses in body/tail without retroperitoneal invasion.

Interventions: All patients underwent posterior RAMPS without robotic or hand-assisted assistance. No conversions occurred. The operative technique involved supine positioning with head slightly elevated. Trocar placement: one 10-mm port below the umbilicus for laparoscopy; four additional ports (one 12-mm, three 5-mm) in left upper flank, left flank, right upper flank, and right flank arranged in a V-shape. Entry into the lesser sac via division of the gastrocolic ligament with harmonic scalpel. Mobilization began at the inferior border to visualize the superior mesenteric vein (SMV), splenomesenteric confluence, and portal vein (PV), then proceeded at the superior border. Lymphadenectomy along the common hepatic artery (CHA) and gastroduodenal artery (GDA) was performed. A tunnel was created behind the pancreas neck, which was transected with an endoscopic linear stapler (Endocutter 60 staple; white/blue cartridges). Lymphadenectomy around the celiac trunk followed. The splenic artery and vein were divided. Lymph nodes anterior to the aorta between the celiac artery and SMA, and anterior/left of the SMA, were dissected. The distal pancreas was dissected medial-to-lateral. The posterior RAMPS approach was used. The distal pancreas and spleen were resected en bloc with lymphadenectomy. The specimen was bagged and retrieved via an enlarged umbilical incision. One drain was placed near the proximal pancreatic remnant. Drains were removed on postoperative day 3 if drain amylase was <3× upper normal serum value; otherwise, drains were maintained until amylase normalized.

Outcomes and follow-up: Data collected included demographics, operative time, EBL, conversion, transfusion, postoperative hospital stay, morbidity (including PF graded per ISGPF), mortality (30-day), pathology (tumor size, lymph node count, margin status), and follow-up. PF was graded per ISGPF; grade A biochemical leaks were not counted as complications. Follow-up was outpatient, with final follow-up in February 2020. Recurrence or distant metastasis was diagnosed by pathology (resection, biopsy, cytology) and/or radiology. All patients received chemotherapy postoperatively.

Statistical analysis: Not reported. No randomization or control group.

title: Dissecting the mechanisms of a 5-year decline in antibiotic prescribing
field_subfield: Public Health — Infectious Disease/Health Services Research
research_question:
Research question: What are the relative contributions of reduced observed disease (fewer outpatient visits for infectious conditions) and improved antibiotic stewardship (lower per-visit prescribing probability) to the decline in outpatient antibiotic prescribing in Massachusetts between 2011 and 2015?

Hypotheses: (1) Both mechanisms contributed to the decline; (2) Reduced observed disease would be a major driver, particularly for respiratory conditions, potentially linked to PCV13 and other prevention efforts; (3) Improved stewardship would also contribute meaningfully across conditions. Supportive outcomes would include significant declines in monthly visit rates for antibiotic-meriting conditions and significant declines in monthly per-visit prescribing rates, with projections indicating substantial avoided prescriptions attributable to each mechanism. Refuting outcomes would include no significant changes in visit rates or per-visit prescribing rates, or projections showing minimal avoided prescriptions from either mechanism.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: Massachusetts All-Payer Claims Database (APCD), 5th edition, covering insurance claims for 94% of Massachusetts residents under age 65 (2011–2015). The analysis was limited to September 2015 to avoid ICD-10 coding changes that could shift observed prevalence. Outpatient physician encounters were identified via APCD medical claims associated with outpatient CPT codes (e.g., 99201–99215, 99241–99245, 99354–99355, 99381–99397, 99441–99444, 99429, 99499). Each visit included a unique patient identifier, age, service date, and up to seven ICD-9 diagnoses. Pharmacy claims for antibiotics were extracted using previously described methods; each claim included a unique patient identifier, age, and fill date. Individuals aged ≥65 were excluded because most use traditional fee-for-service Medicare (not included in APCD).

Condition mapping and linkage: Each outpatient diagnosis was mapped to one of 20 antibiotic-meriting conditions previously defined. For each visit, the diagnosis with the highest antibiotic appropriateness ranking was designated the primary diagnosis. Antibiotic prescriptions were linked to visits using patient identifier and timing: a prescription could be linked to at most one visit; if multiple visits occurred within one week of a fill, the nearest visit was linked. Prescriptions were not linked if the associated visit was not an outpatient physician visit (e.g., dentistry, hospital follow-up), if the prescription was written without a formal outpatient visit (phantom prescribing), if the fill occurred more than one week after the visit, or if different insurance products were used for the visit and fill (different patient IDs).

Outcomes and covariates: Primary outcomes were (a) the projected number of antibiotic prescriptions that would have been given over the study period in the absence of long-term trends in observed disease; (b) monthly antibiotic prescribing rates per 1,000 individuals overall and by age; and (c) the actual number of antibiotic prescriptions given. Outcomes were measured for each of the 20 conditions. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for beneficiary age, sex, and county.

Statistical analysis: For each condition, monthly outpatient visit rates per 1,000 individuals and monthly antibiotic prescriptions per 1,000 individuals were computed (denominator: number of individuals enrolled in an insurance product for the entire month). The monthly per-visit prescribing rate was calculated as prescriptions per 1,000 divided by visits per 1,000. LOESS regression highlighted seasonal variation. To estimate avoided prescriptions due to reduced observed disease, the slope of the monthly visit rate per 1,000 was estimated via linear regression. A counterfactual visit rate with zero slope (same intercept) was projected; multiplying this by the actual per-visit prescribing rate yielded projected prescriptions per 1,000. The difference between actual and projected prescriptions per 1,000 quantified avoided prescriptions due to reduced disease. A similar procedure projected avoided prescriptions due to improved stewardship by setting the per-visit prescribing rate slope to zero and multiplying by actual visit rates.

National observed disease trends: Using NAMCS (2002–2015), annual visit rates per 1,000 for antibiotic-meriting (tiers 1 and 2) and non-antibiotic-meriting (tier 3) conditions were analyzed. Linear regression estimated slopes; piecewise-linear regression with a single breakpoint (January 1 or July 1 of each year) identified changes in trend. Seasonal analysis for under-5 prescribing used a sinusoidal model with linearly changing upper and lower envelopes to compare winter vs summer declines.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. Code availability: https://github.com/skissler/disease-stewardship-ms.

title: Impacts of Early Interventions on the Age-Specific Incidence of COVID-19 in New York, Los Angeles, Daegu and Nairobi
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do age-specific contact patterns and demographic structures shape COVID-19 transmission and outcomes across cities with different age profiles? (2) What are the age-specific effects of key NPIs (school closure, WFH, mobility reduction, quarantine) on infections, hospitalizations, and deaths? (3) How does the timing of interventions (e.g., one week earlier) affect epidemic trajectories and outcomes? (4) Can coordinated, age-targeted NPIs achieve high suppression without strict lockdowns?

Hypotheses: (a) Younger populations, with higher contact rates, will drive higher transmission but lower fatality rates, leading to more infections but fewer deaths in younger cities. (b) Quarantine of exposed/symptomatic individuals will be more uniformly effective across age groups than social distancing measures, which will have stronger age-specific effects. (c) Early implementation of NPIs will substantially reduce infections and deaths compared to delayed implementation. (d) Combining moderate social distancing with high quarantine rates will suppress the epidemic more effectively than single strategies or strict distancing alone.

Support/refutation: The simulations support (a) and (b), showing higher infections in Nairobi and age-specific benefits of school closure (younger) and mobility reduction (older). They support (c) with quantified reductions in deaths and infections from one-week earlier interventions. They support (d), with combinations achieving 80–99% suppression depending on scenario.
reference_methodology:
Model: An age-specific SEIR-HQD model with seven states: Susceptible (S), Exposed (E), Infectious (I), Recovered (R), Hospitalized (H), Quarantined (Q), and Dead (D). The model incorporates age structure, birth and death rates, and city-specific contact matrices. The population is stratified into nine age groups (0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, 80+). The system is modeled over 365 days.

Transmission: Transmission rates are derived from country-level contact matrices adjusted by local age structure. The contact matrix is scaled by the proportion of each age group in the city population, and the dominant eigenvalue method is used to estimate age-specific transmission probabilities. The basic reproduction number R0 is set to 2.92 (95% CI 2.28–3.67). The average incubation period is 6.4 days; infection duration is 7–11 days (assumed to grow with age). Initial infected counts are 200 or 500 per million (per literature). Hospitalization and fatality rates vary by age and are taken from published sources (e.g., Verity et al., Ferguson et al.). Quarantine rate is varied between 0% and 80% in scenarios.

Interventions and scenarios: Seven scenarios test age-specific NPIs (Table 2): A) school closure 100%; B) WFH 50%; C) WFH 80%; D) reduction in other mobility 50%; E) reduction in other mobility 80%; F) quarantine 10%; G) combined (school closure 100%, WFH 50%, mobility reduction 50%, quarantine 10%). A second set of scenarios shifts the timing of interventions one week earlier than observed policy timelines to assess the impact of early action.

City-specific data and policies: Demographic age structures and contact matrices are adapted to each city (Daegu, Los Angeles, New York, Nairobi). Policy timelines are reconstructed from public records (Appendix 1 lists dates and measures). The model assumes closed systems (no in/out migration) and does not include population movement or air pollution effects.

Outcomes: Simulated outcomes include infections, hospitalizations, deaths, and avoided cases relative to no-intervention baselines. Age-specific avoided infections are reported for each scenario. The model also evaluates the risk of second waves if interventions are relaxed after 8 months.

Ethics and funding: The funder had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or writing. Authors report no competing interests. Data are publicly available; code is open-source.

title: Non-linear ultrasonic defectoscopy of concrete structures for nuclear industry
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does non-linear wave modulation spectroscopy (NWMS) compare to conventional ultrasonic and resonance NDT in detecting and quantifying damage in concrete subjected to thermal loading? (2) Does NWMS provide earlier or more sensitive detection of microcracking than linear NDT? (3) How do mechanical properties (flexural, tensile splitting, compressive strength) and modulus of elasticity change with increasing thermal conditioning, and how do these changes relate to NWMS-derived non-linearity?

Hypotheses: (H1) NWMS will show a pronounced increase in the non-linear parameter β at lower temperatures (e.g., 400 °C) due to initial microcrack formation, outperforming linear NDT in early damage detection. (H2) Conventional NDT (ultrasonic pulse, resonance) will exhibit substantial decreases in modulus of elasticity with temperature, reflecting macroscopic stiffness loss, but with less sensitivity to early microcracking. (H3) Mechanical properties will degrade markedly with increasing temperature, with flexural and tensile splitting strengths showing larger relative reductions than compressive strength. Support for H1 would be a large, early increase in β relative to reference; refutation would be minimal β change. Support for H2 would be large, linear decreases in modulus with temperature; refutation would be weak or non-linear trends. Support for H3 would be larger percentage drops in flexural/tensile strengths than compressive strength at 600 °C.
reference_methodology:
Materials: Ordinary concrete with water-to-cement ratio 0.5, silica sand, and Portland cement CEM II 32.5. Four series were prepared: reference and three heated series at 400 °C, 500 °C, and 600 °C.

Specimens: For each series, six cylinders (diameter 100 mm, height 200 mm), eight cubes (edge length 100 mm), and nine prisms (40×40×160 mm) were cast. After casting, specimens were covered with plastic for two days to prevent excessive drying, demolded, and left to air-cure for 28 days.

Thermal conditioning: After 28 days, all specimens were weighed, dimensioned, and tested non-destructively. Three series were then heated: 400 °C reached in 10 minutes; 500 °C and 600 °C reached in 2 hours. Dwell time at the final temperature was 2 hours for all heated series, followed by natural cooling. Post-heating, dimensions and mass were remeasured, and non-destructive and destructive tests were repeated.

Non-destructive testing (NDT): (1) Ultrasonic pulse method per ČSN 73 1371 (Non-destructive testing of concrete — Method of ultrasonic pulse testing of concrete, 2012) to estimate modulus of elasticity (Ebu). (2) Resonance method per ČSN EN 73 1372 (Non-destructive testing of concrete — Testing of concrete by resonance method on prisms, 2012) to estimate longitudinal (EbrL) and transverse (Ebrf) modulus of elasticity. Measurements were performed on prisms (40×40×160 mm) and cylinders (diameter 100 mm, height 200 mm). Averages and standard deviations were reported.

Destructive testing: (1) Compressive strength on cubes, cylinders, and prisms per ČSN EN 1015-11 (Testing methods for mortar for masonry — Part 11: Determination of compressive and flexural strength of hardened mortars, 2000) and ČSN EN 12390-3 (Testing of hardened concrete — Part 3: Compressive strength, 2002). (2) Tensile splitting strength on cubes per ČSN 73 1318 (Determination of tensile strength of concrete, 1986). (3) Flexural strength on prisms per ČSN EN 1015-11 (2000). Results were reported as averages with standard deviations.

Non-linear wave modulation spectroscopy (NWMS): Two sequential ultrasonic signals were transmitted: a low-frequency signal (f1 ≈ 5–20 kHz) and a high-frequency signal (f2 ≈ 70–120 kHz), or two signals with similar frequencies. In the present study, f1 = 153 kHz and f2 = 180 kHz were used, producing an intermodulation at f12 = f1 + f2 = 333 kHz. The first signal modulates crack openness (closing during compression, opening during tension). The second signal’s amplitude is altered by the crack state. The recorded signal was analyzed via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). For undamaged material, only input frequencies appear; damage manifests as sidebands and higher harmonics. The non-linear parameter β was computed as β = A12/(A1·A2), where A12, A1, and A2 are amplitudes of the intermodulation and input peaks, respectively. Six values per specimen were measured for each group; averages and standard deviations were reported.

Outcomes: Bulk density changes, mechanical properties (flexural, tensile splitting, compressive strength), modulus of elasticity (Ebu, EbrL, Ebrf), and NWMS β were compared across reference and heated conditions. No IRB/ethics approvals were applicable.

title: Teukrosit'in yara iyileştirme potansiyelinin değerlendirilmesi
research_question:
Research question: Does teucroside enhance in vitro wound healing as measured by fibroblast migration/proliferation in a scratch assay?

Hypothesis: Teucroside will increase wound closure compared with untreated control, reflecting enhanced fibroblast migration and/or proliferation. Supportive outcome: A statistically significant increase in percent wound healing at 24–48 h relative to untreated control at the selected non-cytotoxic concentration. Refuting outcome: No increase or a decrease in wound closure relative to untreated control, or no difference after accounting for vehicle effects.

Alternative explanations considered: If teucroside reduces viability (cytotoxicity) at the tested concentration, wound closure would be impaired; if it is non-cytotoxic but does not alter migration/proliferation, wound closure would be similar to control. The study’s results align with the latter alternative, indicating no wound-healing effect under the tested conditions.
reference_methodology:
Cell line and culture: L929 mouse fibroblasts were obtained from Ege University Animal Cell Culture and Tissue Engineering Laboratory. Cells were cultured in DMEM-high glucose supplemented with 10% FBS at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 95% air and 5% CO2. Media were changed every 2 days.

Compound preparation: Teucroside was extracted, isolated, and identified per prior work by Dr. Elmastaş and his team. Stock solutions were prepared at 200 µg/ml in DMSO (<0.1% final in culture medium) and filter-sterilized before use.

MTT viability assay: L929 cells were seeded at 4×10^4 cells/ml in 96-well plates and incubated for 24 h. Ten concentrations of teucroside were tested, spanning 200 µg/ml down to 0.4 µg/ml. Cells were exposed to teucroside for 48 h. After incubation, 100 µl of MTT solvent (5 mg/ml) was added to each well and incubated at 37°C for 3 h. Formazan was dissolved in 100 µl DMSO, and absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a multimode microplate reader. The concentration with the highest viability relative to negative control was selected for the scratch assay.

Scratch assay: L929 cells were seeded at 5×10^4 cells/ml in 6-well plates and grown to 90% confluence. A straight-line wound was created with a sterile p200 pipette tip; debris was removed, and the wound edge was smoothed by washing with culture medium. Cells were incubated with teucroside at 50 µg/ml (selected via MTT). Images were captured at 0, 24, and 48 h using phase-contrast inverted microscopy. Quantification of wound closure was performed with Olympus image analysis software. Percent wound healing was calculated and plotted.

Controls and comparisons: The untreated control was used for comparison. The text does not specify a vehicle-only control (DMSO) for the scratch assay. No details are provided on replicate numbers, randomization, blinding, or statistical analyses. No additional parameters (e.g., scratch width, number of scratches, or software settings) are reported.

title: การศึกษาเรื่อง แนวทางการจัดการชุมชนหมู่บ้านจัดสรรโครงการ "บ้านฉางเพลส" เพื่อนำไปสู่ชุมชนเข้มแข็ง อำเภอบ้านฉาง จังหวัดระยอง
field_subfield: Social Sciences — Community Development and Urban Planning
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How has the Ban Chang Phleas housing project evolved in terms of community development? (2) What management practices of the housing committee have contributed to building a strong, resilient community? (3) How do leadership, communication, and participation mechanisms operate within these practices?

The study does not state explicit hypotheses. Implicit expectations include that participatory governance, two-way communication, and community-led problem-solving will improve security, environmental conditions, and shared-service compliance, thereby advancing community empowerment. Outcomes that would support these expectations include documented reductions in crime, improved environmental quality, increased participation in meetings and activities, and sustained compliance with shared-service fees. Outcomes that would refute them would include persistent insecurity, unresolved environmental issues, low participation, and continued non-compliance despite interventions.
reference_methodology:
Design: Qualitative case study using interviews and participant observation to document community development and management practices in the Ban Chang Phleas housing project.

Setting and population: The project spans ~40 rai with 171 houses and approximately 500 residents in Ban Chang, Rayong Province. The community is described as a housing project with mixed residential types (commercial buildings, single-family homes, etc.).

Participants and sampling: Eight key informants were interviewed, selected based on relevance to the project’s development and management: (a) project owner and staff (e.g., Mr. Somkri Angsirikultharn, project owner; Ms. Nattika, project staff); (b) housing committee members (e.g., Mr. Songtham, committee chair; Mr. Sopon, committee member; Ms. Siriporn, secretary); and (c) long-term residents with deep local knowledge (e.g., Mr. Phirap, elder resident; Ms. Nattanong, active resident). Selection criteria emphasized involvement in community management, leadership roles, and knowledge of historical and current conditions.

Data collection: (1) Semi-structured interviews (in-depth, individual and group) to elicit narratives on community history, management practices, challenges, and outcomes; (2) Participant observation at monthly community meetings and activities (e.g., opening of buildings, social events, committee sessions), with field notes and photographs; (3) Contextual documentation (e.g., meeting minutes, project plans, environmental complaints). Data collection occurred over four months (January–April 2013).

Analysis: Qualitative content analysis was used to synthesize themes and processes. The analysis integrated theoretical frameworks on communication, leadership, and community empowerment to interpret observed practices and outcomes. No statistical tests or quantitative metrics were reported.

Ethics: No ethics approval, consent procedures, or data protection details are reported in the provided text.

Timeline: The study references the project’s development from 2007–2012, with the qualitative data collection in 2013.

title: Characterization and elimination of linkage-drag associated with Fusarium wilt race 3 resistance genes
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the magnitude and genetic basis (pleiotropy vs linkage drag) of the association between I-3 and reduced fruit size and increased bacterial spot sensitivity in modern tomato germplasm? (2) Can reducing the I-3 introgression size from >5 Mb to a minimal interval eliminate these negative associations while preserving Fol3 resistance? (3) Does I-7 confer Fol3 resistance without negative associations to bacterial spot or fruit size in Florida-adapted backgrounds?

Hypotheses: (H1) Large I-3 introgressions reduce fruit size and increase bacterial spot sensitivity via linkage drag rather than pleiotropy of I-3. (H2) A minimal I-3 introgression (~140 kb) will retain Fol3 resistance but eliminate negative associations with bacterial spot and fruit size. (H3) I-7 will confer Fol3 resistance without negative horticultural associations. Supportive outcomes would include: additive I-3 effects on fruit size and bacterial spot; significant improvements in bacterial spot and fruit size when replacing large I-3 introgressions with minimal I-3; and no differences in bacterial spot or fruit size when minimal I-3 is introgressed into susceptible backgrounds. Refutation would involve persistence of negative associations with minimal I-3 or evidence of I-7-associated horticultural drawbacks.
reference_methodology:
Field trials were conducted at the Gulf Coast Research and Education Center (Balm, FL). Seed was sown in peat-lite soilless media (128-cell trays; 39 cm^3 cells) and transplants grown in a greenhouse before field planting. Field beds (20 cm high, 81 cm wide) were fumigated with chloropicrin + 1,3-dichloropropene (Pic-Clor 60 EC; 300 lbs per treated acre) and covered with black plastic mulch. Beds were spaced 152 cm apart; plants were staked and tied; drip irrigation was used. A recommended fertilizer and pesticide program was followed.

Effect of large I-3 introgressions on fruit size: Two UF/IFAS parental lines segregating for I-3 were used: Fla. 7907B (I-3 on ~5.1 Mb introgression) and Fla. 8814 (I-3 on ~4.2 Mb introgression). Plants were genotyped with I-3-linked markers and grouped by genotype (i-3/i-3, i-3/I-3, I-3/I-3). Spring 2015: sown Jan 22, 2015; transplanted Feb 27, 2015; RCBD with 3 replications of 8 plant plots. Spring 2016: sown Feb 1, 2016; transplanted Mar 21, 2016; RCBD with 4 replications of 12 plant plots. Mature fruit were harvested three times and graded by USDA standards (S, M, L, XL). Fruit counts and weights per category were recorded; average fruit size was calculated. Data were checked for normality and homoscedasticity; ANOVA (PROC GLIMMIX, SAS 9.4) with mixed models treating blocks nested within season and both block and season as random effects. Least squares means with Tukey adjustment (P = 0.05) were used for comparisons.

Reducing the I-3 introgression: RILs R12 (proximal I-3 introgression including I-3 at 63.52 Mb) and R18 (distal I-3 introgression including I-3 at 63.32–63.51 Mb) were intercrossed; F1 self-pollinated. Flanking markers 7g728 (63.32 Mb) and 7g6362 were used to screen F2 for recombination products yielding a minimal I-3 introgression. A plant with the minimal introgression was self-pollinated to obtain Fla. 8978. Whole-genome sequencing (Illumina) of five lines (including Fla. 7946 minimal I-3 NIL) was used to define introgression boundaries by SNP frequency (cultivated vs wild tomato). SNP frequency peaked between 63.44–63.57 Mb in the minimal I-3 NIL, defining ~140 kb.

Fol3 seedling assays: Fol3 isolate GEV1400 was grown on PDA at 28 °C ~1 week, then suspended in water to ~10^5, 10^6, or 10^7 spores/mL. Seeds were sown in Black Beauty spent coal; seedlings (~2 weeks) were root-dipped and transplanted to peat-lite trays. Susceptibility was scored by external symptoms (stunting, yellowing, wilting, stem enlargement/collapse) and/or vascular browning in roots/stems. Symptomless plants were considered resistant. Assays were repeated twice and pooled. Chi-square tests compared proportions of healthy plants.

Bacterial spot and fruit size trials of minimal I-3 and I-7: Minimal I-3 (Fla. 8978) was backcrossed into UF/IFAS lines: Fla. 7907B(i-3/i-3), Fla. 7946 (I-3 on ~4.2 Mb), Fla. 8059, and Fla. 8814(i-3/i-3). I-7 was backcrossed into Fla. 8059 using 'Tristar' as donor. Field trials (spring 2017–2019) used segregating backcross F2 populations genotyped by markers (7g728 for introgression size; I-7 marker) and sorted by genotype. Horsfall–Barratt disease severity ratings were converted to percent disease for analysis. Fruit size was measured as above. Data were analyzed by ANOVA (PROC GLIMMIX) with blocks nested within seasons, block and season as random effects, and Tukey-adjusted LSMeans (P = 0.05).

title: Highly Memorable Images are more Readily Perceived
research_question:
Research question: Does intrinsic image memorability predict perceptual detectability under brief presentation, and if so, is the effect consistent with statistical regularity (prototypicality) or distinctiveness?

Hypotheses: If memorability is driven by distinctiveness (statistical irregularity), high memorability images would require longer exposure durations to reach 70.7% accuracy in an intact/scrambled task. If memorability is driven by prototypicality/statistical regularity, high memorability images would require shorter durations. A null outcome (no difference) would suggest that memorability is not linked to detectability or that distinctiveness and regularity effects cancel out. The authors further predicted that the effect would generalize across datasets and persist even when the memorability manipulation is weaker. Outcomes supporting the prototypicality account include shorter detection durations for high memorability images; outcomes supporting the distinctiveness account include longer durations; a null result would refute the link between memorability and detectability.
reference_methodology:
Design: Two within-subjects psychophysical experiments using an intact/scrambled detection task to estimate durations required to reach 70.7% accuracy for high versus low memorability natural scenes. Categories, color contrast, and image size were controlled between conditions. Memorability differences were verified using ResMem. Nonparametric tests were used due to violations of normality.
