Participants: Experiment 1 recruited 25 participants (11 women, 9 men; Mage=20.34) from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign participant pool; 20 were analyzed (5 excluded for Weibull fit failure). Experiment 2 recruited 65 participants (34 women, 12 men; Mage=20.20); 45 were analyzed (1 excluded for low accuracy, 6 for high duration, 13 for Weibull fit failure). All provided informed consent under IRB approval; self-reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision. No preregistration.

Stimuli: Experiment 1 used 300 natural scenes (150 high, 150 low memorability) from LaMem, resized to 512×512; aspect ratio changes were similar across conditions (high: M=0.317, SD=0.163; low: M=0.427, SD=0.173). For each intact image, a phase-scrambled version was created by randomizing phase while preserving amplitude. A synthetic texture mask (Portilla & Simoncelli) was randomly assigned to each intact and scrambled image. Categories were balanced across conditions (animal, architecture, nature, object, people). Memorability was verified with ResMem (high .89, range .64–.98, SD=.06; low .53, range .41–.75, SD=.09). Experiment 2 used 160 scenes (80 high, 80 low) from FIGRIM (categories: castle, golf course, house, skyscraper), with identical preprocessing and masking. Memorability verification: high .64 (range .44–.88, SD=.10) vs low .58 (range .41–.77, SD=.09).

Apparatus and procedure: Stimuli were presented on an 85 Hz CRT monitor (1280×960) using PsychoPy 2021.2.3 (Python 3.6.6). Participants viewed from a chinrest at 59 cm. Each trial: fixation cross, target (intact or scrambled), then mask. Responses indicated intact vs scrambled via keyboard keys (counterbalanced). Practice: 60 trials with fixed durations (intact 118 ms; mask 494 ms) and feedback (incorrect: red text and 100 Hz tone; correct: black text). Main experiment: 1-up 2-down staircases (Experiment 1: 300 trials per staircase; Experiment 2: 160 trials per staircase), initial duration 118 ms, step size 12 ms, maximum 247 ms; the first six trials were excluded from analysis. No feedback in the main experiment. Order of high vs low memorability staircases was counterbalanced.

Exclusion criteria: Participants were excluded if staircases reached 200 ms in the last 50 trials (indicating divergence from prior research), if overall staircase accuracy <60% (chance=50%), or if Weibull fits failed to converge. Sample size was determined via pilot studies and G*Power (paired t-test). Experiment 1 pilot (N=13) yielded d=.86; Experiment 2 pilot (N=36) yielded d=.46.

Analysis: Psychometric functions were fit with a two-parameter Weibull to estimate durations at 70.7% accuracy. Average sum of squared errors for fits: Experiment 1 M=0.20 (range 0.01–0.44, SD=0.12); Experiment 2 M=0.24 (range 0.01–1.12, SD=0.17). Group-level comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Experiment 1 two-sided; Experiment 2 one-sided).

title: Fair and Robust Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Optimal Policies in Multilevel Studies
field_subfield: Computer Science — Machine Learning (Fairness); Statistics — Causal Inference
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a CATE estimation framework be formulated to incorporate multilevel fairness constraints (individual, cluster, and intersectional) while maintaining statistical efficiency and interpretability? (2) How do fairness constraints at different levels (individual vs cluster vs intersectional) affect the fairness–utility trade-off in optimal policies? (3) Does enforcing multilevel fairness reduce disparities in CATE estimates and recommendations compared to individual-only constraints in real multilevel data?

Hypotheses: (H1) A linear projection of the CATE under multilevel fairness constraints can be estimated via a convex, doubly robust program that is computationally tractable. (H2) Enforcing fairness will reduce mean unfairness across fairness functions but incur a small utility loss; correctly specified multilevel constraints (including intersectional) will yield better trade-off efficiency than individual-only constraints. (H3) In multilevel observational data, policies that are fair at the individual level may still be unfair at the cluster level; adding cluster-level constraints will eliminate such disparities.

Support/refutation: The simulations and HSLS:09 application support H1–H3: the estimator is doubly robust; fairness enforcement reduces unfairness with ~1% utility loss; and multilevel constraints eliminate disparities that persist under individual-only constraints.
reference_methodology:
Setup: J clusters (e.g., schools), n_j individuals per cluster, total n = Σ_j n_j. Treatment T_ij ∈ {0,1} (e.g., advanced math course), outcome Y_ij (e.g., 9th-grade weighted math GPA), pre-treatment covariates W_ij = (S_ij, X_ij) with q-dimensional sensitive S_ij and (p−q)-dimensional insensitive X_ij. Potential outcomes Y_ij(1), Y_ij(0) under SUTVA. CATE τ(w) = E{Y_ij(1) − Y_ij(0) | W_ij = w}. The estimand is the best linear approximation β′ = argmin_β E[τ(W_ij) − W′_ij β]^2.

Fairness constraints: K constraints E[uf_k(O_ij) W′_ij β] ≤ δ_k, where uf_k(O) encodes fairness criteria (e.g., statistical parity, conditional statistical parity, separation/equalized odds, within-cluster versions). Examples: individual-level statistical parity uf_k(O) = 1 − S^(1)_1ij E{1 − S^(1)_1ij} − S^(1)_1ij E{S^(1)_1ij}; conditional statistical parity uf_k(O) = (1 − S^(1)_1ij)1(L_ij = l) / E[(1 − S^(1)_1ij)1(L_ij = l)] − S^(1)_1ij 1(L_ij = l) / E[S^(1)_1ij 1(L_ij = l)]; within-cluster versions condition on cluster identifier C_j; cluster-level analogs replace S^(1)_1ij with S^(2)_1j; intersectional parity across S^(1)_1ij and S^(2)_1j uses group indicators S* = (S^(1)_1ij, S^(2)_1j).

Estimation: Nuisance models via GLMMs: logit(π_1(W_ij)) = γ_0 + γ′_W W_ij + V_j, V_j ∼ N(0, σ^2_V); outcome model Y_ij = β_0 + β_T T_ij + β′_W W_ij + β′_{T×W} T_ij W_ij + U_j + R_ij, U_j ∼ N(0, σ^2_U), R_ij ∼ N(0, σ^2_R). Augmented inverse probability weighted estimators φ_t(O; η) = 1(T = t)[Y − μ_t(W)] / π_t(W) + μ_t(W). The estimator solves β* = argmin_β (1/2) β′ P_n(W W′)β − P_n{φ_1 − φ_0} W′ β subject to P_n uf_k(O) W′ β ≤ δ_k, where P_n is the cluster-averaged sample operator. The program is convex and solvable with off-the-shelf solvers (e.g., ADMM, conic/SDP via MOSEK). Proposition 1 establishes √n-consistency if one of π_t or μ_t is correctly specified and cluster sizes are uniformly bounded.

Simulation designs: Design 1 (no intersectionality) and Design 2 (intersectionality) each use 300 clusters × 25 individuals per cluster. Data-generating processes (Appendix S1) induce unfairness in individual- and cluster-level sensitive variables; Design 2 adds intersectional unfairness. Evaluation metrics: CATE MSE (Equation 15), relative utility (Equation 16), mean unfairness across K fairness functions (Equation 17), and fairness–utility trade-off metrics FURG and FUTR (Equations 18–19). Simulations are repeated 500 times.

Empirical application: HSLS:09 restricted-use data (9,910 students from 800 schools). Treatment: 9th-grade advanced math course (geometry or higher). Outcome: 9th-grade weighted math GPA. Covariates: 11 student-level (e.g., 8th-grade math proficiency, math club participation, math utility, math identity) and 12 school-level (e.g., student-to-math-teacher ratio, math course requirements, school type). Sensitive variables: student-level race (white vs black) and school-level proportion of black students (high vs low; threshold 20%, median in data). Fairness functions: statistical disparity for school-level sensitive variable; conditional statistical disparity for student-level race conditioned on pre-high-school math above average. Covariates imputed via predictive mean matching. Two δ values: 20 (unfair) and 0.0001 (fair). For comparison, an individual-only constraint scenario is also evaluated.

title: CoFe2O4 supported g-C3N4 nanocomposite for sensitive electrochemical detection of dopamine
field_subfield: Materials Science — Electrochemistry; Analytical Chemistry — Electrochemical Sensors
research_question:
Research question: Can a CoFe2O4@g-C3N4 nanocomposite, synthesized via a dual-template method, serve as an antifouling, selective, and sensitive electrochemical platform for dopamine detection in biological samples?

Hypotheses: (1) The CoFe2O4@g-C3N4 heterostructure will increase electrochemically active surface area (EASA) and reduce charge-transfer resistance (Rct), improving electron transfer and catalytic activity for DA oxidation. (2) The composite will exhibit wide linear dynamic ranges, low detection limits, and high selectivity against common interferents (e.g., UA, AA). (3) The sensor will demonstrate operational stability, repeatability, and reproducibility suitable for real-sample analysis.

Predicted outcomes: CV and i-t measurements will show higher peak currents and lower Rct for the composite-modified GCE versus bare, g-C3N4, and CoFe2O4 alone; calibration curves will display high linearity (R² ≥ 0.99); LODs will be in the sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar range; selectivity will be maintained in the presence of interferents; and real-sample recoveries will be accurate with low RSD.
reference_methodology:
Materials synthesis: g-C3N4 was prepared by thermal polymerization of 5 g melamine in a boat crucible in a tubular furnace at 550°C for 3 h under N2, yielding a yellowish powder (g-C3N4). CoFe2O4 nanoparticles were synthesized hydrothermally: stoichiometric Co2+ and Fe3+ salts (Co2+:Fe3+ = 1:2) were dissolved in deionized water with stirring; pH was adjusted to 12 by NaOH addition to form a homogeneous solution. The mixture (180 mL total volume) was sealed and heated at 180°C for 12 h. The precipitate was collected by centrifugation with DI water and ethanol, dried overnight at 100°C, and calcined at 400°C for 4 h to obtain CoFe2O4. The composite CoFe2O4@g-C3N4 was formed by mixing 20 mg g-C3N4 and 60 mg CoFe2O4 in 20 mL DI water, sonicating for 2 h, centrifuging, and drying to obtain the powder.

Electrode fabrication: A glassy carbon electrode (GCE; surface area 0.072 cm²) was polished with a polishing cloth, washed, and dried. CoFe2O4@g-C3N4 was dispersed at 2 mg/mL in DI water by ultrasonication for 1 h. A 6 µL aliquot was drop-cast onto the GCE to form CoFe2O4@g-C3N4/GCE. For comparison, bare GCE, g-C3N4/GCE, and CoFe2O4/GCE were also prepared.

Electrochemical setup and procedures: A three-electrode system was used with a CHI 1211c workstation. The working electrode was GCE (0.072 cm²), the counter electrode was Pt wire, and the reference electrode was Ag/AgCl (3 M KCl). CV measurements were performed in 0.05 M phosphate buffer (PB) over 0–0.4 V at 0.05 V/s. Amperometry (i-t) was conducted at a fixed potential (reported as 0.16 V in the electrode fabrication section and 0.18 V in the amperometric detection section) with a rotation speed of 1200 rpm. pH dependence was evaluated by varying PB pH from 3.0 to 11.0 with 100 mM DA.

Characterization: XRD assessed crystalline phase and purity; SEM/TEM/HRTEM examined morphology; XPS identified elemental composition and chemical states. EIS used a Randles equivalent circuit to quantify Rct and infer electron-transfer kinetics. EASA was calculated from CV peak currents using the Randles–Ševčík equation (Ip = 2.69×10^5 × n^(3/2) × ACD^(1/2) v^(1/2)). Kinetic behavior was assessed by varying scan rates (0.02–0.20 V/s) and plotting Ip vs v^(1/2).

Selectivity and stability: Selectivity was tested against 13 interferents (including UA and AA) under the optimized conditions. Stability was evaluated by monitoring steady-state current over 3000 s at +0.18 V and 1200 rpm. Repeatability (single electrode, five runs) and reproducibility (four electrodes, three runs) were assessed at 50 mV/s and 100 mM DA in 0.05 M PB (pH 7.0).

Real-sample analysis: Urine and blood serum samples were collected from Chang-Gung Memorial Hospital (Taiwan). Experiments complied with IRB No. 201801660B and institutional ethics approvals; informed consent was obtained. Urine was centrifuged and diluted with DI water without pre-treatment. Known DA was spiked into urine and serum; 10 µL of phosphate-mediated solution was added. Standard addition was used to quantify DA and calculate recoveries.

title: Survival for Patients with Metastatic Disease e How Good are Radiation Oncologists at Predicting Survival?
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How accurate are radiation oncologists’ predictions of whether a patient will survive beyond 1 year following their first palliative RT visit? (2) Do factors such as academic vs community practice setting, years in practice, and disease site predict the accuracy of these predictions? (3) How do observed time-to-death distributions differ between patients expected to live beyond 1 year versus those expected to die within 1 year?

Hypotheses: The authors implicitly test whether physicians’ 1-year survival predictions are accurate and whether specific clinician or disease factors are associated with prediction accuracy. Outcomes supporting accuracy would show prediction concordance with observed survival (e.g., high proportion of patients expected to live >1 year actually surviving >1 year). Outcomes refuting accuracy would show systematic misclassification (e.g., overestimation of survival). Predictors of accuracy would be identified if univariate or multivariate models demonstrate significant associations (e.g., practice setting, years in practice, disease site).
reference_methodology:
Design: Retrospective cohort study of patients receiving palliative-intent RT for metastatic, recurrent, or primary non-recurrent disease across a network.

Setting and participants: 1,586 patients treated by 35 physicians at 18 sites between February 2016 and December 2016. Patients evaluated after December 31, 2016 were excluded to ensure ≥1 year of follow-up. For each patient’s first visit with a given physician, the physician’s pathway entry indicating whether they would be surprised if the patient died within the next year was reviewed.

Outcomes: Primary outcome was accuracy of physicians’ 1-year survival predictions, operationalized as whether the patient died within 1 year following the first appointment date. Secondary outcomes included time-to-death among those who died within 1 year, stratified by physicians’ expectations.

Statistical analysis: Chi-square analysis assessed the association between physicians’ predictions and observed 1-year survival. Univariate and multivariate binary logistic regression identified predictors of prediction accuracy, including academic vs community practice setting, physician years in practice, and disease site. Reported p-values: p<0.001 for the primary association; p=0.236 for academic vs community setting; p=0.047 for years in practice (<15 vs ≥15); p<0.001 for disease site. Multivariate analysis retained disease site as significant (p<0.001). Time-to-death medians and ranges were reported by expectation category.

Data handling: The study used the first visit per physician-patient pair to avoid duplicate assessments. No additional patient-level covariates (e.g., performance status, comorbidities, prior therapies) were reported. No details on missing data handling, model diagnostics, or adjustments for confounding beyond the listed predictors were provided.

Ethics: Not reported.

title: Drinking and Driving: A Pilot Study of Subjective Norms, Attitudes and Behaviors of German and American Students
research_question:
Research questions: (RQ1) Does TRA provide an accurate foundation to predict drinking-and-driving intentions among German and American students? (RQ2) Do attitudes influence drinking-and-driving intentions? (RQ3) Do subjective norms influence drinking-and-driving intentions? (RQ4) Are there differences in drinking-and-driving attitudes, norms, and behaviors between German and American students?

Hypotheses: (H1) Attitudes and subjective norms will be associated with intentions to drink-and-drive, consistent with TRA. (H2) Attitudes (e.g., perceived harmfulness) will be negatively associated with intentions; affective attitudes (e.g., excitement) may be positively associated. (H3) Subjective norms (e.g., perceived approval/disapproval of family/friends) will be negatively associated with intentions. (H4) U.S. students will report higher risky drinking and drinking-and-driving than German students, reflecting cultural differences in norms and infrastructure (e.g., public transport, legal ages). Outcomes supporting H1–H3 would show significant associations between attitudes/norms and intentions; H4 would be supported by higher prevalence and frequency of drinking-and-driving in the U.S. Conversely, null associations or no cross-cultural differences would refute or nuance these hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Design: Mixed-methods pilot study combining qualitative focus groups and an online survey. The focus groups informed survey item development; the survey quantified attitudes, subjective norms, beliefs, and behaviors.

Participants: College-age students enrolled at a U.S. university (Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis, IUPUI) and a German university (University of Regensburg). Recruitment was via professors; participation was voluntary. IRB approval was obtained. Focus groups were conducted in English. The pilot survey was distributed via university email lists; extra credit was at professors’ discretion.

Procedure: Phase 1 (focus groups): In July 2013, the author contacted professors at the University of Regensburg to recruit students for focus groups. Three focus groups (each ~7–15 students) were conducted in Regensburg on February 4 and 7, 2014. In the U.S., a large focus group (~30 students) was conducted at IUPUI on January 29, 2014. A semi-structured guide elicited definitions of drinking-and-driving, contributing factors, and injunctive norms. Sessions were digitally recorded. Phase 2 (pilot survey): After focus group analysis, professors emailed the survey to students. The survey was administered via Qualtrics for approximately one month (shortened due to scheduling constraints).

Measures: Focus groups used open-ended prompts (e.g., definitions of drinking-and-driving, reasons for/against drinking-and-driving, peer/family reactions). Thematic content analysis identified attitudes, subjective norms, and beliefs. The pilot survey included: (a) Likert-type scales (1–7) for cognitive and affective attitudes (e.g., “drinking-and-driving is bad/good,” “exciting/unfavorable”), injunctive norms (e.g., perceived approval/disapproval of parents, friends, partner), and beliefs about contributing factors (e.g., public transport availability, college pressure, legal drinking age, education, rural residence, cost of license); (b) multiple-choice items for behaviors and demographics (age, gender, residence, GPA, race/ethnicity [optional], fraternity/sorority membership). Behavioral items included frequency of drinking/drinking-and-driving in the past 30 days, heavy episodic drinking (≥5 drinks in a row) in the past week, likelihood to drink-and-drive at the next party (1=Extremely Unlikely to 5=Extremely Likely), and likelihood to arrange transportation to avoid drinking-and-driving.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics summarized demographics and behaviors. Independent t-tests compared U.S. and German groups on attitudes, subjective norms, beliefs, and behaviors. Levene’s tests assessed equality of variances; when unequal, Welch’s t-tests were used. Reported statistics include F, p, t, df, and two-tailed p-values. The author notes that the pilot was intended to refine instruments and inform future research rather than to draw population-level conclusions.

title: Side-by-Side Comparison of Clean and Biomass-Derived, Impurity-Containing Syngas as Substrate for Acetogenic Fermentation with Clostridium ljungdahlii
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do biomass-derived syngas (with impurities) versus matched clean syngas affect growth, product distribution (acetate vs ethanol), yields, productivities, and carbon fixation in C. ljungdahlii fed-batch fermentations? (2) How do gas composition (CO/CO2/H2) and flow rates modulate these outcomes? (3) Do impurities primarily reduce carbon fixation and alter product ratios, or do gas composition effects dominate?

Hypotheses: (H1) Biomass-derived syngas will reduce carbon fixation and productivity relative to clean syngas due to impurities. (H2) Clean syngas will favor acetate formation and higher acetate-to-ethanol ratios, especially at lower H2 and higher CO2 flows. (H3) At lower gas flow rates, biomass-derived syngas may increase ethanol productivity due to impurity-driven metabolic shifts. Outcomes supporting H1 include lower EC,total and productivity in biomass-derived syngas; H2 is supported by higher acetate-to-ethanol ratios in clean syngas; H3 is supported if biomass-derived syngas at lower flow yields higher ethanol productivity than clean. The study also tests whether simultaneous H2 and CO consumption occurs across syngas types and how growth cessation correlates with H2 uptake decline.
reference_methodology:
Organism and medium: Clostridium ljungdahlii DSM 13528 was cultivated in Tanner’s medium (MES buffer; pH adjusted to 5.9 before autoclaving). Pre-cultures were prepared from a single glycerol stock stored at −80°C. A 100 mL serum flask with 50 mL medium and 10 g/L fructose was inoculated and grown 48 h at 37°C. Two subsequent passages were performed with 10% inoculum. For the last passage, three 250 mL serum flasks (150 mL medium each) were inoculated; each fermenter received a 10% inoculum (150 mL).

Experimental design: Ten fed-batch fermentations were conducted in triplicates (n = 3) over ~93 h. Set-ups 1–6 compared biomass-derived syngas with matched clean syngas: (1) Bioliq straw syngas with impurities; (2) clean syngas matching Bioliq composition; (3) Bioliq syngas at lower flow; (4) clean syngas matching Bioliq at lower flow; (5) clean syngas mimicking TNO beech wood syngas; (6) clean syngas mimicking TNO lignin syngas. Set-ups 7–8 used clean syngases based on LNEG (limestone-cleaning at 850°C) and ENEA (updraft gasifier with O2/steam) compositions. Set-ups 9–10 were custom clean mixtures with lower H2 and varied CO2.

Gas compositions and flows: Table 1 reports average off-gas compositions and flows. Standard conditions (from prior work) were 32.5% CO, 16% CO2, 32.5% H2 (rest N2), 18 mL/min, Cin = 0.4 mmol/min, H2,in = 0.26 mmol/min. For set-ups 3–4, flows were adjusted to maintain H2,in = 0.26 mmol/min (Cin reduced). Impurities in Bioliq syngas (pre-CO2 cleaning) included HCN 0.91 ppm, NH3 150 ppm, H2S 54.1 ppb, COS 12.3 ppb; CH4 and HCl were 0 ppm. For LNEG/ENEA-based syngases, CH4 was included in custom mixtures to replace N2 for off-gas flow calculation.

Analytical methods: Off-gas was analyzed by GC-2010 Plus AT (Shimadzu) with ShinCarbon ST 80/100 column (2 m × 0.53 mm ID) and Rtx-1 capillary column (30 m × 0.25 mm ID, 1 µm). Four samples per day (2–3 h intervals) were collected; OD, acetate, ethanol, and residual fructose (first 24 h) were measured. pH was monitored online. Gas usage and fixation were computed from off-gas flows; CO fixation was calculated by accounting for CO2 production when CO2 usage was negative. Product yields (YP/S to fed, used, fixed), productivities, and EC,total were computed per grams of substrate and biomass.

Comparative metrics: For each pair of biomass-derived vs clean syngas, end-point productivity and productivity up to the end of maximum CO fixation were compared. Gas consumption profiles (CO, CO2, H2) and maximum overall usage intervals were quantified (Table 4).

title: Implications of uremic cardiomyopathy for the practicing clinician: an educational review
research_question:
The review addresses the following questions: (1) What are the current definitions, epidemiology, and pathophysiological mechanisms of uremic cardiomyopathy in CKD? (2) Which diagnostic modalities and biomarkers best detect UC, quantify myocardial fibrosis, and predict outcomes? (3) What are the evidence-based management strategies for UC, including pharmacotherapy, dialysis modalities, and renal transplantation? (4) What are the gaps in knowledge and the priorities for future research to translate mechanistic insights into clinical practice?

No explicit hypotheses are tested, as this is a narrative review. The implicit expectations are that: (a) multimodal imaging (especially cMRI with T1/T2 mapping and strain analysis) will improve detection and risk stratification of UC; (b) heart failure–directed therapies (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) will confer cardioprotective benefits in CKD; (c) renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, transplantation) will influence cardiac remodeling and outcomes, with transplantation offering the greatest benefit; and (d) emerging targets (e.g., FGF-23/Klotho axis, salvianolic acid B, iron/vitamin D) may provide disease-modifying effects. The review evaluates whether the literature supports these expectations and identifies where evidence is insufficient.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative educational review. The text does not report a systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, databases queried, time windows, or risk-of-bias assessments. Instead, it synthesizes findings from prior studies and clinical observations cited in the references. The review structure follows thematic sections: clinical background, pathogenesis, screening and diagnosis, new diagnostic methods, disease management, and future directions.

Epidemiologic context is drawn from national projections and cohort analyses: estimates that 2 million people in the USA will require dialysis by 2030, and that LVH is present in approximately 70% of ESRD patients. Cardiovascular mortality accounts for roughly half of deaths in ESRD, with graded associations between reduced GFR and cardiovascular events/death in large cohorts.

Diagnostic modalities are described with their clinical utility and limitations. ECG is highlighted for accessibility and for detecting Q waves, ST changes, prolonged QRS, and tachycardia; advanced ECG parameters (QT interval, spatial QRS-T angle, signal-averaged ECG, heart rate variability, T-wave alternans) associate with mortality in dialysis patients, though causality is unclear. TTE is widely used for LV mass estimation and prognostication, but a large meta-analysis found no clear association between LV mass changes and cardiovascular mortality in CKD, limiting its use as a surrogate endpoint. Cardiac CT can delineate myocardial fibrosis, a strong predictor of cardiovascular death. cMRI provides reproducible quantification of coronary flow, perfusion, scarring, and interstitial fibrosis and is considered the standard where available. PET can assess perfusion, viability, inflammation, and coronary flow reserve.

Advanced imaging techniques include T1/T2 mapping on cMRI to quantify DIF; feature-tracking cMRI to derive longitudinal strain; and STE to quantify LV global longitudinal strain in patients with preserved LVEF. Native T1/T2 mapping can avoid gadolinium exposure. GLS by 2D echocardiography is reported to be more sensitive than LVEF for detecting myocardial dysfunction in ESRD.

Therapeutic management is summarized from clinical trials and observational studies: ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce renal and vascular damage in CKD; carvedilol improves LV end-diastolic pressure, LV end-systolic volume, and LV function in dialysis patients; spironolactone reduces LV mass and aortic stiffness in early CKD. Statins show mixed results in UC populations. Hemodialysis can reverse some UC sequelae; peritoneal dialysis may be preferable for some patients but can have worse long-term CV outcomes if not adequately monitored; renal transplantation improves survival and cardiac function (LVEF, LVH reduction). Experimental therapies include salvianolic acid B (preclinical efficacy), vitamin D (positive LV fiber shortening), and intravenous iron (reduced adverse CV events and mortality in low-ferritin dialysis patients). ESAs improve quality of life and reduce transfusions but may increase stroke risk without survival benefit.

Ethical approvals are not applicable for this review. Competing interests are disclosed. Data availability is stated as not applicable.

title: Does Excessive Dynamic Airway Collapse Have Any Impact on Dynamic Pulmonary Function Tests?
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the quantitative relationship between tracheal cross-sectional area reduction, AP-distance, and flow resistance under physiologic airflows and varying obstruction lengths? (2) In COPD patients, does EDAC observed during cough and forced expiration correlate with PFTs (PEF, FEV1)?

Hypotheses: (a) Flow resistance increases sharply when cross-sectional area reduction exceeds ~70–80% for a 3 cm obstruction, particularly at low flows, and increases with longer obstruction length. (b) EDAC during peak expiratory maneuvers in COPD does not significantly correlate with PFTs, implying minimal impact on PEF/FEV1. (c) AP-distance can be mapped to area reduction with high accuracy, enabling practical clinical estimation.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (a) would be supported by model data showing steep resistance increases beyond ~70–80% area reduction and by a ~3.5-fold resistance increase when obstruction length quadruples. Hypothesis (b) would be supported by null correlations between EDAC severity and PEF/FEV1 in the patient cohort. Hypothesis (c) would be supported by a strong AP-distance vs area reduction relationship (high R²) and by consistent clinical mapping.
reference_methodology:
Model study: A garden hose (Hozelock Ltd., Birmingham, UK) with wall thickness 3.5 mm and inner diameter 18 mm (cross-sectional area ~2.54 cm²) was used to simulate the adult trachea (Weibel’s mean ~2.54 cm²; length ~12 cm). The hose was inserted into a 12 cm brass pipe (inner diameter 24 mm) with approximately half the circumference removed. A 10 mm external pipe was placed over the exposed hose segment and compressed via four screws in 8 steps to simulate posterior wall protrusion. Step 1: no pressure; step 8: AP-distance 1 mm (80% luminal reduction). Flow was measured downstream using an ASV Flowmeter (DFM-350-100-1000; ASV Stubbe GmbH & Co. KG, Vlotho, Germany) from a pressurized air tank ~2 m upstream. Intraluminal pressure was measured upstream and downstream of the obstruction using 2 mm external cannulas and a Maximal Respiratory Mouth Pressure Monitor (Pollard Electronic Design, Stockport, Cheshire, UK; range 0–769 cm H2O). Airflow was set stepwise from 1 L/s (60 L/min) to 9 L/s (540 L/min). Driving pressure across the obstruction was computed from upstream and downstream pressures. Two series were performed: (1) 3 cm obstruction length (lower trachea); (2) 12 cm obstruction length (full tracheal length). Gas temperature was recorded upstream (~21°C) and downstream (10–16°C); for calculations, the obstruction temperature was assumed 17°C. Cross-sectional area and AP-distance were quantified from digital photos of the cut hose end (white paint contrast) using Canvas v6 (Deneba Systems Inc., Miami, FL). Reynolds numbers were calculated to assess flow regime; turbulent flow was expected for most conditions.

Patient study: Prospective cohort of 104 COPD patients (64 male) admitted to Glittreklinikken AS for a 4-week rehabilitation program (June 2004–March 2006). Inclusion: current or ex-smokers; no current signs/symptoms/history of malignancy; no tumor on chest x-ray at inclusion; no current COPD exacerbation. Bronchoscopy was performed via the mouth in a semirecumbent position after premedication (diazepam 5 mg PO; hydrocodone 5 mg PO; atropine sulfate 0.3 mg SC; alfentanil 0.5 mL IV; lidocaine 2 mL PO and 1 mL via bronchoscope). After subsegmental inspection and sampling, the scope was positioned ~5 cm proximal to the carina. Patients performed cough and forced expiration; the shortest AP-distance (mm) was estimated during both maneuvers. PFTs were performed per ERS/ATS guidelines with EFSR reference equations using Jaeger Master Screen/Master Lab (Erich Jaeger GmbH, Hoechberg, Germany). AP-distance was converted to cross-sectional area reduction using the model-derived polynomial (Table 2). Statistical analysis: normality, linearity, and homogeneity checks; Spearman correlations; linear regression; two-sided p<0.05 considered significant. Analyses used MS Excel 2003 and IBM SPSS Statistics v19. Ethics: approved by the regional committee for medical research ethics (Oslo, Norway); written informed consent obtained.

title: ECS Journal of Solid State Science and Technology
field_subfield: Materials Science — Semiconductor Technology (Cleaning and Surface Science)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can non-chemical electrolysis of UPW produce amphoteric electrolyzed water (EW) with stable near-neutral pH and controlled ORP suitable for EUV cleaning? (2) Does EW achieve high particle removal efficiency (PRE) on EUV-relevant substrates and masks, comparable to or exceeding conventional methods (H2W+SC1, SC1 alone), while minimizing surface modification and chemical residue adsorption? (3) Are the cleaning mechanisms in EW consistent with the colloidal DLR model, or do nanoscale, non-equilibrium water cluster dynamics dominate?

Hypotheses: (H1) Electrolysis splitting UPW into H+ and OH− streams and remixing them will yield amphoteric EW with pH ~6.5–6.7 and ORP ~−540 to −560 mV, stable over days and temperatures up to ~90°C. (H2) EW will achieve high PRE across inorganic, organic, and metallic particles on EUV masks and substrates, surpassing H2W+SC1 and comparable to or better than SC1 alone, without observable pattern damage or film loss. (H3) Because hydronium and hydroxide ions are physically and electronically separated in EW and water clusters hinder recombination, cleaning mechanisms will differ from DLR, potentially involving dynamic surface tension changes in water clusters.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if measured pH/ORP and stability are as stated. H2 is supported if PRE exceeds H2W+SC1 and shows minimal residue/haze risk. H3 is supported if removal efficiency is similar across particle types and mechanistic arguments align with non-equilibrium cluster dynamics rather than DLR.
reference_methodology:
Electrolysis system: UPW was split into an H-cell and an OH-cell at a 4:1 flow ratio (4 L/min to H-cell; 1 L/min to OH-cell). Platinum-coated electrodes (40 × 130 mm, 15 mm inter-electrode separation) were used in each cell. The system was conditioned by applying up to ~15 V for several hours; when voltage decreased to ~8 V, the platinum surfaces were considered clean and ready for electrolysis. Operation used 8 V with ~20–30 W power. Ions produced at electrodes were selectively collected via commercial membranes. The H-cell produced H+-rich water at the cathode (pH 6.6–6.8; ORP ~−550 mV; hydrogen evolution), and the OH-cell produced OH−-rich water at the anode (pH 6.0–6.5; ORP ~800 mV; oxygen evolution). The streams were remixed to form amphoteric EW for cleaning.

Operating variables: water flow rates, flow ratio (4:1), voltage (8 V), current (up to 3 A in experiments), and mixing ratio (fixed at 0.25 for subsequent tests). ORP and pH were monitored during electrolysis and storage. The amphoteric EW exhibited pH 6.5–6.7 and ORP −540 to −560 mV at room temperature.

Cleaning trials: Substrates included MoSi2 films, quartz, and partially processed EUV masks (4× nm). Megasonic cleaning was performed at 3 MHz with 4–8 W for 5–15 minutes. Comparative treatments included cold EW (room temperature), hot EW (40°C), hydrogen cavitation water (H2W), and SC1 (RCA). For residue analysis, sulfuric peroxide mix cleaning was followed by rinses in UPW or EW. AFM was used to assess surface modification after cleaning and exposure to cleanroom air. TOF-SIMS quantified desorbed F− and Cl− ions from MoSi2 and quartz after sulfuric peroxide cleaning and rinsing.

Storage and temperature stability: EW was stored in glass and plastic containers. ORP remained ~−550 mV for several days and was stable up to ~90°C. The amphoteric behavior was maintained up to OH-cell/H-cell flow ratios of 1.0; at higher ratios, amphoteric behavior deteriorated.

Data and analysis: PRE was reported for masks with intentional contamination (reference particles). Quantitative PRE values are provided in Table I. Megasonic assistance effects are summarized in Table II with ranges across test energies. No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are reported. No IRB/ethics approvals are applicable.

title: A novel noncontrast CT marker, multihematoma fuzzy sign, predicts acute traumatic intraparenchymal hematoma expansion: a prospective observational study
research_question:
Research question: Does the presence of a multihematoma fuzzy sign on admission NCCT predict acute tICH expansion in patients with primary hemorrhagic contusion, and does it generalize across clinical subgroups and external settings?

Hypotheses: (1) The multihematoma fuzzy sign is independently associated with acute tICH expansion after adjustment for confounders and propensity score matching. (2) The marker demonstrates superior discrimination (AUC) compared with common predictors (multiple hematomas, time to baseline CT, baseline volume). (3) The association holds across subgroups (sex, age, GCS, baseline volume, time to CT, coagulopathy) and is stronger in moderate/severe GCS patients. (4) The marker retains predictive value when restricted to patients with ≥3 hematomas, indicating it captures heterogeneity beyond simple multiplicity.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypotheses are supported if adjusted/matched ORs are significantly elevated with the fuzzy sign, ROC AUCs exceed those of comparators, subgroup interactions are non-significant (except GCS), and sensitivity analyses in ≥3-hematoma patients remain significant.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Prospective observational study with development and external validation cohorts. Development cohort: First Affiliated Hospital and Second Affiliated Hospital of Shantou University Medical College (May 2013–June 2018). External validation cohort: Affiliated Jieyang Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (March 2014–June 2018). All patients treated per institutional protocols.

Participants: Adults (>18 years) with primary hemorrhagic contusion confirmed on baseline CT. Inclusion required baseline and follow-up CT. Exclusions: baseline CT >6 h post-injury; follow-up CT >48 h; prior hematoma evacuation before follow-up; brain tumor; prior brain trauma. In the development cohort, 5.57% of patients with baseline tICH volume <2 mL were excluded due to measurement difficulty.

Clinical data: Demographics and clinical variables (Table 1). Coagulopathy defined as aPTT ≥36 s, INR >1.2, or platelet count <120×10^9/L at admission.

Imaging acquisition and reader workflow: Axial NCCT with standardized local protocols; baseline CT slice thickness 5 mm. Two blinded readers (D.Z., S.C.) assessed multihematoma fuzzy sign on baseline CT; discrepancies adjudicated by a senior neuroradiologist (J.Y.) blinded to prior readings.

Imaging marker definition: Multihematoma fuzzy sign requires (1) ≥3 adjacent hyperdense hematomas within a contusion region; (2) a relative hypodense fuzzy signal between them; and (3) a ≥20 HU difference between hyperdense hematomas and the hypodense area. Multiple hyperdense hematomas separated by normal gray/white matter do not qualify. The fuzzy area is interpreted as fresh liquid blood.

Volumetry and expansion criteria: Hematoma volumes measured semiautomatically (General Electric software) using fixed HU thresholds (window 110/50 HU). Regions of interest were manually selected and automatically segmented; adjacent voxels were summed to compute volume. When multiple ICHs were present in the contusion region, total volume was calculated. Acute tICH expansion defined as ≥30% relative growth or ≥5 mL absolute growth from baseline.

Statistical analysis: Continuous variables summarized as mean (SD) or median (IQR); categorical as counts (%). Associations between fuzzy sign and tICH expansion analyzed via multivariable logistic regression. Propensity score (PS) estimated using a nonparsimonious multivariable logistic regression with fuzzy sign as dependent variable and all baseline covariates (Table 1) as covariates. PS matching: 1:1 without replacement (greedy algorithm), caliper 5% of PS. Balance assessed by standardized differences (<10% indicates acceptable balance). In matched cohorts, paired McNemar’s test (binary) and paired t-tests (continuous) were used. Cox proportional hazards models stratified on matched pairs estimated adjusted risks. Sensitivity analyses restricted to patients with ≥3 hematomas. Subgroup analyses and interaction tests (predefined: sex, age <65 vs ≥65, GCS 13–15 vs 3–12, baseline volume <10 vs ≥10 mL, time to CT 0–3 vs 3–6 h, normal coagulation vs coagulopathy) assessed heterogeneity. ROC curves compared predictive performance of fuzzy sign vs multiple hematomas, time to CT, and baseline volume. Two-tailed P<0.05 considered significant. Analyses performed in SPSS v22. Reporting followed STROBE guidelines.

title: Review of the marine tourism industry in the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage area.
field_subfield: Environmental Science — Marine Conservation and Tourism Management
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Is the proposed shift from individual permits to spatial management via Zoning Plans, statutory Plans of Management, and generic licenses robust, practicable, and capable of meeting management and industry needs? (2) How should latent capacity (unused permits and underutilized capacity) be managed to avoid unintended ecological and amenity pressures? (3) What tenure and allocation policies best balance security, investment, and environmental protection? (4) What consultative mechanisms ensure transparent, inclusive decision-making?

Hypotheses/predictions: (a) Spatial management and generic licenses will improve control of cumulative impacts and industry flexibility compared to permit-based systems; (b) First-come-first-served allocation will better align with environmental suitability and market demand than auctions; (c) Extending license tenure to 15 years, with clear procedures for amendment/revocation, will enhance investment security without compromising environmental protection; (d) A dual-license structure will increase fungibility and innovation; (e) Formalizing a competency-based TAG will improve transparency and industry-government collaboration. Outcomes supporting these include documented reductions in anchor damage, improved access management, and stable industry operations under the new regime; refutation would involve persistent cumulative impacts, market distortions, or administrative infeasibility.
reference_methodology:
Design: Policy review and strategic assessment conducted by a Steering Committee with assistance from the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority (GBRMPA) and the Office of National Tourism (ONT). The review synthesized existing data, stakeholder input, and prior studies to evaluate the proposed management regime and recommend policy changes.

Data sources: Environmental Management Charge (EMC) returns (visitor-days), CRC Reef Research Centre studies, GBRMPA reports (e.g., Protection for Profit), industry economic estimates (Coopers & Lybrand), and international visitor surveys (IVS) and Domestic Tourism Monitor (DTM). The report also draws on prior reviews (e.g., Carey 1993; Kelleher & Dinesen 1993, 1994; Dinesen 1995; Honchin 1996) and technical workshop outputs (State of the GBR World Heritage Area Report).

Scope: Marine tourism operations (air and water-borne) within the GBRMP boundaries; infrastructure located within the Marine Park. Excluded: management of tourism components of adjacent coastal developments (e.g., resorts, marinas), and the Environmental Management Charge/Visitors’ Charge policy changes.

Procedures: The Steering Committee convened meetings (e.g., 18 Feb 1997; 5 and 29 May 1997), engaged a Working Group (ONT, Queensland Department of Tourism, Small Business and Industry, GBRMPA), and consulted with a Tourism Advisory Group (TAG) established in January 1997. The review analyzed industry structure (number of operations, vessel counts, market concentration), visitation patterns (seasonality, regional distribution), latent capacity (permitted vs actual use), ecological and social impacts (anchor damage, sensitive cays, amenity), and proposed management tools (Plans of Management, licenses, codes, non-regulatory instruments).

Analysis: Narrative synthesis of quantitative indicators (e.g., visitor-days, market shares, permit caps) and qualitative assessments of impact mechanisms and management effectiveness. The report evaluates the feasibility and equity of allocation policies (first-come-first-served vs auctions), tenure length (6 vs 15 years), and the separation of generic licensing provisions from Plans of Management. It also assesses the role of non-regulatory instruments (codes, associations, accreditation) in complementing regulation.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human subjects research reported. The report emphasizes environmental, cultural, and heritage obligations under the GBRMP Act and World Heritage Properties Conservation Act 1983.

title: On the use of Locally Dense Basis Sets in the Calculation of EPR Hyperfine Couplings: A study on Model Systems for Bio-inorganic Fe and Co complexes
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can locally dense basis sets—core-property basis sets on coupled atoms (metals and first-sphere N) and smaller basis sets on non-coupled atoms—accurately reproduce EPR hyperfine coupling constants (AFC, ASD, APSO) for Fe and Co model systems compared to a reference calculation with large basis sets on all atoms? (2) What minimal basis set choices on non-coupled atoms and first-sphere N atoms are sufficient to achieve ≤1% accuracy for each contribution? (3) How do basis set choices affect the relative importance of AFC, ASD, and APSO across Fe (d5) and Co (d7) complexes? (4) Do these conclusions generalize to larger gas-phase models relevant to P450cam and coenzyme B12, and do computed couplings align with experimental values?

Hypotheses: (H1) Locally dense basis sets will yield hyperfine couplings within ≤1% of reference values for most contributions, enabling substantial computational savings. (H2) AFC will be the dominant contribution for Fe, while ASD will dominate for Co; APSO will be smaller for Fe but significant for Co. (H3) For Fe, single-polarization Pople-style basis sets on non-coupled atoms suffice; for Co, double-polarization (e.g., 6-31G(2d)) may be required for ASD. (H4) Using 6-31G-Juc on first-sphere N atoms will be a viable, smaller alternative to aug-cc-pVTZ-J without significant loss of accuracy. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include small deviations from reference values across basis set choices and consistent trends in contribution magnitudes.
reference_methodology:
Model systems: Two small complexes were optimized for the basis set study: [Fe(III)(OOH)(SH)(en)2]+ (Ia; Fe, d5) and [Co(II)(NH3)(CN)(en)2]+ (IIa; Co, d7). Two larger gas-phase models were also studied: Ib (larger P450cam compound 0 model) and IIb (larger coenzyme B12 model). All systems were doublet spin states.

Geometry optimization: Ia and IIa were optimized at B3LYP/aug-cc-pVDZ using Gaussian09. Ib and IIb were optimized at B3LYP/6-311G(d). All optimizations used Gaussian09 (Revision B.01).

Electronic structure and properties: Hyperfine coupling tensors were computed with ORCA. Contributions were decomposed into isotropic Fermi contact (AFC), anisotropic spin-dipolar (ASD), and second-order paramagnetic spin–orbit (APSO). ASD and APSO for first-sphere N super-hyperfine couplings were negligible and reported in Supporting Material. AFC and ASD expressions followed standard theory; APSO was evaluated per Neese (2003) using an effective two-electron operator based on effective potential and mean-field approaches. Scalar relativistic effects and finite nuclear volume effects were not included, as they modify rather than add new contributions and were not expected to be sensitive to basis set choice on non-coupled atoms.

Basis sets: Metals (Fe, Co) used aug-cc-pVTZ-Juc (uncontracted) core-property basis sets. Equatorial N atoms (N1–N4) used aug-cc-pVTZ-J (contracted) or 6-31G-Juc (uncontracted) core-property basis sets. Non-coupled atoms used a broad set of CC and Pople-style basis sets (Table 1), including 6-31G, 6-31+G, 6-31++G, 6-31G(d), 6-31G(2d), 6-31G(2df), 6-31G(d,p), 6-31G(2d,2p), 6-31G(2df,2pd), 6-311G, 6-311+G, 6-311++G, 6-311G(d), 6-311G(2d), 6-311G(2df), 6-311G(3df), 6-311G(d,p), 6-311G(2d,2p), 6-311G(2df,2pd), cc-pVDZ, cc-pVTZ, aug-cc-pVDZ, aug-cc-pVTZ. Total contracted basis function counts for Ia are provided in Table 1. Reference calculations used aug-cc-pVTZ-Juc on metals and aug-cc-pVTZ-J on all other atoms.

Functional sensitivity: Main text reports B3LYP; Supporting Material includes PBE and PBE0, with analogous basis set dependence and conclusions.

Evaluation criteria: Accuracy was assessed relative to the reference calculation. Deviations were reported in MHz and as percentages. For Fe, acceptable accuracy was defined as ≤0.1 MHz (≤0.7%) for AFC and ASD; for APSO, ≤0.5 MHz. For Co, acceptable accuracy was ≤1% (≈0.5 MHz) for AFC and ASD; APSO deviations were assessed similarly.

title: Grasses (Poaceae) of the District of Coronel Rosales (Province of Buenos Aires, Argentina)
research_question: The study’s objectives were to: (1) update knowledge of Poaceae in Coronel Rosales; and (2) identify ecological characteristics and ethnobotanical uses of the species present. The work does not state explicit hypotheses. Implicit expectations include that the district hosts a diverse and ecologically significant Poaceae assemblage, with notable representation of native and endemic species, and that species exhibit habitat fidelity to dunes and salinas. Outcomes supporting these expectations would include a high number of species relative to the district’s flora, a substantial proportion of native/endemic taxa, and documented habitat-specific distributions. The study also anticipates practical uses (forage, dune fixation, ornamentals, etc.) that align with local environmental conditions and human needs. Evidence that would refute or nuance these expectations would include low species richness, dominance of introduced taxa, or absence of habitat-specific distributions and uses. The authors’ results largely support the anticipated patterns, though they note the need for eco-physiological studies to explain habitat fidelity.
reference_methodology:
Study area: Coronel Rosales, Province of Buenos Aires, Argentina, located in the south-western part of the province, bordered by Bahía Blanca to the west/north-west, Coronel Pringles to the north, Coronel Dorrego to the south-east (natural boundary: Río Sauce Grande), and the Argentine Sea to the south. The landscape is predominantly flat with a stepped relief decreasing toward Bahía Blanca. Two geomorphological units are recognized: a general planation surface and a coastal/litoral environment. The climate is temperate with an annual mean temperature of ~15°C and well-defined thermal seasons; annual precipitation averages 540 mm, concentrated in late spring and early summer; winds are moderate, predominantly from the NNO. Soils include Argiustoles (northern sector), Ustipsammentes and Haplustoles (coastal/litoral), and Ustifluventes ácuicos in depressions and pediments. The vegetation includes psammophilous herbaceous steppe, halophilous shrub steppe, and halophilous shrublands.

Sampling design and fieldwork: Fieldwork occurred in 2006, 2007, and 2008 across localities: Punta Alta, Pehuen-Có, Villa del Mar, Villa Arias, Paso Mayor, Bajo Hondo, and Calderón, covering dunes and salinas. Over 40 collection trips were conducted to capture flowering and fruiting periods. Inventories were performed in natural, rural, and urban areas. Sampling was described as random, though no spatial sampling frame, plot sizes, or effort quantification are reported.

Specimen processing and identification: Collected material was herbarized following Carter et al. (2007). Taxonomic determinations used Flora de la Provincia de Buenos Aires (Cabrera, 1970) with updates from Flora Argentina online (http://www.floraargentina.edu.ar; consulted July 2015). Determined specimens are deposited in the UNS herbarium (BBB). For species descriptions and use information, the authors referenced BBB and literature (e.g., Grun, 1998; Pensiero, 1999; Scarpa, 2000; Steibel, 1997).

Data synthesis: Species were organized by scientific name and summarized by ecological traits (life form: perennial/annual; seasonality: warm/cool; photosynthetic pathway: C3/C4) and ethnobotanical uses (forage, medicinal, dune fixation, ornamentals, lawn, food, industrial uses). The study also noted habitat fidelity patterns (taxa restricted to salinas or dunes). No statistical analyses, effect sizes, or uncertainty estimates are reported. Ethical approvals/permits are not mentioned.

title: Benefit of chemotherapy as part of treatment for HPV DNA-positive but p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What explains the observed improvement in CSS for OSCC between 1999–2001 and 2003–2005 in South East Scotland? (2) Is the survival improvement dependent on HPV and p16 status, and do these biomarkers define distinct prognostic subgroups? (3) Does chemotherapy use account for the cohort effect?

Hypotheses: (a) The survival improvement is driven by increased use of concurrent chemoradiotherapy in Cohort-2 rather than by demographic shifts alone; (b) HPV+/p16− tumors form a distinct subgroup with intermediate prognosis that benefits from chemotherapy; (c) p16 status is not a perfect surrogate for HPV status, with notable discordance. Supportive outcomes would include: significant cohort effects in PH models that attenuate when chemotherapy is included; a marked survival gain in HPV+/p16− patients in Cohort-2; and evidence of discordance between HPV and p16 statuses. Refutation would involve no cohort effect after adjusting for treatment, no survival difference in HPV+/p16−, or near-perfect concordance between HPV and p16.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Retrospective, population-based cohort study of all patients with OSCC referred to the Edinburgh Cancer Centre (regional referral center for ~1.4 million) between 1999–2001 (Cohort-1) and 2003–2005 (Cohort-2). The 2002 transition year marked a change in management policy. The Scottish Cancer Registry confirmed population coverage.

Participants: 254 patients total (118 Cohort-1; 136 Cohort-2). Minimum follow-up: 83 months (Cohort-1) and 48 months (Cohort-2). Patients with metastatic neck nodes only (no primary) were excluded. Patients without FFPE blocks were excluded from HPV/p16 subgroup analyses but included in overall survival analyses.

Treatments: Prior to 2002, treatment favored surgery±postoperative radiotherapy or radiotherapy alone; neck dissection was performed for N2/N3 disease pre-radiotherapy in Cohort-1. After 2002, concurrent chemoradiotherapy became the treatment of choice; neck dissection was performed after concurrent chemo-irradiation if a complete response at the primary site was achieved. Radiotherapy schedules: 4-week schedule in Cohort-1 and 6.5-week schedule in Cohort-2; doses converted to EQD2 using α/β=10. Intensity-modulated radiotherapy was not used. Chemotherapy regimens: cisplatin or carboplatin±5-fluorouracil; methotrexate used in a small number in Cohort-1 (UKHAN trial). Follow-up was by specialist teams.

Biomarker assays: One FFPE block per case was selected. For HPV, a 10-μm section underwent proteinase K digestion (15 h), DNA purification (Qiagen DNA mini kit), and genotyping with INNO-LiPA HPV Genotyping Extra (SPF10 primers; detects HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 40, 43, 44, 45, 51, 52, 53, 54, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 69/71, 70, 73, 74, 82). HLA-DPB1 served as a specimen integrity control; samples negative for both human gene and HPV types were considered invalid. For p16, a 3-μm section was stained using the CINtec Histology kit (clone E6H4) on a BOND-maX automated stainer with standardized protocol (epitope retrieval, peroxidase quenching, primary antibody, polymer detection, DAB, hematoxylin counterstain). Staining was scored as negative, focal positive, or positive based on diffuse cytoplasmic and nuclear staining in tumor cells; negative controls (normal cervix) and positive controls (cervical high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia) were included.

Outcomes and statistics: Cause-specific survival (CSS) and relapse were analyzed. Kaplan–Meier methods estimated CSS and relapse; Mantel–Cox tests compared curves. Univariate analyses assessed cohort, age, sex, deprivation, smoking, drinking, subsite, grade, stage, T/N stage, radical surgery, radical radiotherapy, EQD, radical chemotherapy, p16, and HPV status among radically treated patients. Cox PH models evaluated independent prognostic factors; variables with >20% missing data or non-significant in preliminary PH were excluded. Significance thresholds: exploratory 0.05; quoted results 0.01; 95% CIs reported. Ethics approval: Lothian Research Ethics Committee 2.

title: Quantitative Analyses of Plant Remains from the NAN Ranch Ruin, Grant County, New Mexico
research_question:
Research question: Did the pithouse-to-pueblo transition at the NAN Ranch Ruin coincide with increased agricultural dependence, as reflected in macrobotanical remains?

Hypotheses: (1) If agricultural dependence increased in the Classic period, then ubiquity of cultigens (maize, cotton) and agricultural weeds (Chenopodium, Amaranthus, Portulaca) should be higher in Classic samples than Late Pithouse samples; ubiquity of non-weedy edible wild taxa should be lower. (2) Maize and weed percentages (relative to total fruits/seeds) should be higher in Classic samples. (3) Taxonomic diversity and richness should decline in Classic samples due to intensified maize agriculture and field disturbance. (4) Sample size effects should be minimized by standardized five-liter sub-samples; context-matched comparisons should yield clearer diachronic signals than combined-context analyses.

Predicted outcomes: Significant increases in ubiquity and percentages for maize and weeds; significant decreases in diversity and richness in Classic samples; and robust patterns when comparing similar contexts. Null outcomes would include no significant differences between periods or patterns attributable to context composition rather than agricultural dependence.
reference_methodology:
Site and chronology: NAN Ranch Ruin (Grant County, New Mexico) contains Late Pithouse (Three Circle phase) pithouses overlain by Classic Mimbres surface rooms. Dating employed dendrochronology, radiocarbon, archaeomagnetism, relative stratigraphy, and ceramic microstyle seriation.

Sampling: 47 flotation samples were analyzed: 17 Late Pithouse (fire-pit: 2; midden: 8; room-fill: 7; floor: 0) and 30 Classic Mimbres (fire-pit: 17; midden: 8; room-fill: 4; floor: 1). Samples were from well-provenienced contexts (Table 2). Fire-pit samples included intramural features (e.g., rooms 12, 22, 25, 28, 29, 39, 62, 63, 94) and extramural adobe-surface fire-pits (SF20, SF22, SF27; SF46). Midden samples included West Plaza (Unit 5) and Southeast Midden (Units 15, 39). Room-fill samples were from stratified units in pithouse 14 (Late Pithouse) and room complex 11/22 (Classic), with one floor sample from room 18.

Flotation and sub-sampling: Water flotation used a ~208 L drum with a screen-bottomed insert, inlet, and spout; light fractions were captured in a cloth-lined basket (mesh <0.425 mm). Heavy fractions were captured on ¼ inch mesh but were excluded from quantitative analyses due to incomplete availability and low plant content. To control sample size, each flotation sample was converted to a representative 5 L sub-sample using a conversion factor (flotation sample volume / excavated sediment volume). Sub-samples were randomly selected via a grid method (overlapping trays) to ensure equal probability of particle size representation. Sub-samples were sorted by size fractions and identified under 6–25× magnification. Only maize fragments ≥2 mm were retained for analysis; degraded, unknown, and cheno-am (Chenopodium/Amaranthus-like) specimens were excluded from numerical analyses but counted toward totals.

Identification and categories: Remains were identified to genus (commonly), with maize and cotton to species. Weeds were defined by high seed production, rapid growth, and disturbance affinity (Chenopodium, Amaranthus, Portulaca). Non-cultigen taxa included Yucca, Vitaceae, Poaceae, Opuntia, Prosopis, Trianthema, Asteraceae, Atriplex, Mentzelia, Juniperus, Helianthus, Echinocactus, Coryphantha, Descurainia, and others. Uncarbonized remains were treated as modern contaminants.

Quantification and statistics: Ubiquity was computed as the percentage of samples containing a taxon, grouped by context (fire-pit, midden, room-fill) and combined contexts, and by independent samples (one sample per unit/feature). Spearman’s rank correlation (rs) tested correlations between Late Pithouse and Classic ubiquity rankings. Maize and weed percentages were computed as taxon counts divided by total fruits/seeds per sample; Mann-Whitney U tests compared Late Pithouse vs Classic. Diversity (Shannon-Wiener H′) and richness (number of taxa) were computed at generic and familial levels; Mann-Whitney U tests compared periods. Sample size effects were assessed via Spearman’s rs correlations between sample size (fruits/seeds per sample) and percentages/diversity/richness, and via Mann-Whitney U tests comparing sample sizes between periods and contexts.

title: IMAGES OF PUBLIC PLACES: EXTENDING THE COPYRIGHT EXEMPTION FOR PICTORIAL REPRESENTATIONS OF ARCHITECTURAL WORKS TO OTHER COPYRIGHTED WORKS
research_question: Research question: Should the statutory exemption for pictorial representations of architectural works visible from public places (17 U.S.C. §120(a)) be extended, in modified form, to all copyrightable works that are ordinarily visible from public places, limited to photographic images? The article advances the hypothesis that such an extension is justified by (1) substantial public benefits in communication, autonomy, and democratic discourse; (2) minimal costs to creators’ incentives for works whose value is not tied to photographic reproductions; and (3) the superiority of a bright-line rule over balancing tests for consumer clarity and consistency. Alternative positions considered include reliance on licensing markets and fair use. The paper argues that market failure and the ad hoc nature of fair use make these alternatives inadequate for consumers, and that a bright-line rule better aligns with public expectations and reduces chilling effects.
reference_methodology:
The article employs doctrinal legal analysis. It examines statutory provisions (17 U.S.C. §§106, 107, 120(a)), case law (e.g., Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Davis v. The Gap, Inc., Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc., Leicester v. Warner Bros.), and secondary sources (e.g., Ginsburg on architectural copyright, Landes & Posner on IP economics, Lessig on digital culture). It analyzes the scope and limitations of de minimis (as applied to substantial similarity, as a separate defense, and within fair use) and the uncertainty of fair use, including the role of the four statutory factors and the Sony presumptions for noncommercial and commercial uses. The paper also engages with market failure theory (transaction costs, externalities) to argue that licensing is impractical for consumers and that statutory clarity is preferable.

The author constructs five illustrative examples to map potential uses and their legal implications (e.g., selling prints, posting online, distributing posters, contest entries). It synthesizes industry data (e.g., growth in digital camera sales from under one million units in 1996 to 12.5 million by 2003; total camera sales rising from ~16 million to ~25 million between 1996 and 2003; one-time camera sales from 72 million to 211 million) to contextualize technological change and increased photographic activity. No empirical study, human subjects, or statistical tests are conducted. The analysis is normative and policy-oriented, grounded in statutory interpretation, case law, and economic reasoning. Ethical approvals are not applicable as no human subjects research is reported.

title: A New Constructive Algorithm for Architectural and Functional Adaptation of Artificial Neural Networks
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a constructive algorithm that jointly adapts architecture (number of layers and neurons per layer) and functional specialization (via distinct training sets per neuron) improve generalization and compactness compared to existing constructive and nonconstructive methods? (2) Does an AdaBoost-like training set strategy for individual hidden neurons reduce redundancy and accelerate learning? (3) Does a layer-addition criterion that incorporates functional dissimilarity between consecutive neurons prevent unnecessary layer growth and improve performance? (4) What is the computational complexity of the proposed approach relative to standard BP training?

Hypotheses: (H1) NCA will produce ANNs with fewer hidden neurons and layers and better generalization (lower TER/STE) than baselines. (H2) Training each hidden neuron on a distinct, AdaBoost-weighted dataset will increase functional dissimilarity among neurons, reducing redundancy and improving generalization. (H3) A layer-addition criterion based on both training error reduction and functional dissimilarity will avoid unnecessary layer growth and improve performance relative to criteria based on training error alone. (H4) NCA’s computational complexity will be O(W × Pt × τ), comparable to BP training for a fixed architecture. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include lower TER/STE and smaller architectures than baselines, empirical evidence of increased functional dissimilarity under NCA, and complexity analysis showing O(W × Pt × τ).
reference_methodology:
Datasets: Ten UCI benchmark problems (8 classification, 2 approximation) with varying difficulty and size (e.g., cancer, glass, thyroid, heart, card, gene, iris, flare, letter, and two approximation tasks). For all except letter, the first P1 examples were training, next P2 validation, and last P3 test (Table I). For letter, 1000/500/4000 examples were used for train/validation/test.

Networks: Feedforward ANNs with sigmoid hidden neurons. Each hidden layer receives inputs from all preceding layers; the output layer receives inputs from all hidden layers. One bias neuron with fixed input +1 is used for hidden and output layers. For classification, logistic sigmoid activation is used for hidden and output layers; for approximation, the output uses identity activation.

Initialization and training: Initial connection weights are randomly initialized between −0.5 and +0.5. BP learning is used with learning rate 0.10 and momentum 0.8. The number of training epochs per neuron (τ) is set to 20 for all problems except letter (τ=50). Control parameters: ε1=2e−3 (error reduction threshold) and ε2=0.20 (functional dissimilarity threshold). The error metric E is a mean squared error percentage (normalized by output coefficient range omax−omin and number of outputs m), following Prechelt’s recommendation to reduce dependence on dataset size and output count.

Algorithmic procedure (NCA): Start with a minimal 3-layer ANN (input, one hidden neuron, output). Label the hidden layer C and neuron I. For each newly added neuron: (1) create a new training set via AdaBoost-like weighting (increase weights of misclassified examples; decrease weights of correctly classified examples) from the current training set; (2) initial partial training: train the neuron for τ epochs using BP; (3) check if training error reduces by ε1; if not, assume local optimum and proceed; (4) final partial training: add Gaussian noise with mean 0 and variance 1 to input/output weights, then train for τ epochs; (5) freeze weights if no further improvement; (6) decide to add a neuron to the current C-labeled layer if training error reduction criterion (E(i)−E(i+τ) ≤ ε1) is met but functional dissimilarity criterion (average |yk(p)−y(k+1)(p)| ≤ ε2) is not; otherwise, add a new hidden layer with one neuron (C-labeled) above existing layers. Termination uses a combined criterion: stop when generalization loss GL(τ) > training progress Pk(τ), where GL(τ) = (Eva(τ)/Eopt(τ) − 1) and Pk(τ) measures average training error over the last k epochs relative to its minimum.

Variants: NCAST (no functional adaptation; all neurons trained on the same dataset) and NCAWL (no layer addition; only one hidden layer). Parameter sensitivity studies vary τ (10–50 for glass/heart; 30–80 for letter), ε1 (1e−4 to 3e−3), and ε2 (0.05 to 0.30). Statistical comparisons use t-tests at 95% confidence level for TER/STE, number of hidden neurons, and epochs where applicable.

title: First Report of Alternaria Leaf Spot on Gerbera (Gerbera Jamesonii L.) in North of Iran
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What is the causal agent of leaf spot disease observed on Gerbera jamesonii in northern Iran? (2) Do isolated fungi reproduce the disease symptoms on healthy Gerbera plants? (3) What are the morphological characteristics of the pathogen consistent with known Alternaria species?

Hypotheses: (H1) The causal agent is Alternaria alternata, identifiable by standard morphological traits (colony color, conidiophore/conidial morphology). (H2) Inoculation of healthy Gerbera plants with conidia of the isolated fungus will produce typical leaf spot symptoms within two weeks under greenhouse conditions. (H3) Re-isolation from inoculated leaves will yield morphologically identical colonies, supporting Koch’s postulates.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if colony and conidial features match A. alternata descriptions. H2 is supported if inoculated plants develop brown, coalescing lesions within the specified timeframe. H3 is supported if re-isolated colonies match the original isolate’s morphology.
reference_methodology:
Sampling: Gerbera leaves with leaf spot symptoms were collected from five greenhouses in the north of Iran. Leaves were transported to the laboratory for fungal isolation.

Isolation and culture: Symptomatic leaves were cut into small pieces, surface-sterilized with 1% NaOCl for 1 minute, rinsed in sterile distilled water, and dried on sterile filter paper. Tissue pieces were placed on potato dextrose agar (PDA) and incubated at 25±1°C for 10 days to promote fungal growth and sporulation. Fungal growth was isolated to pure culture using single spores and hyphal tips, and maintained on PDA plates.

Morphological characterization: Colony and conidial/conidiophore characteristics were examined. Colonies were described as effuse, olivaceous black with dark olive margins; surface initially greyish white, later darkening to greenish black or olive brown. Conidiophores were branched, straight, pale brown to olive brown, 25–60 μm long and 3–3.5 μm thick. Conidia were pale brown to light brown, produced in long branched chains, obclavate to obpyriform or ellipsoid with a short conical beak or beakless, 20–63 μm long and 9–18 μm wide, with 2–3 transverse septa and several longitudinal septa.

Pathogenicity test: A conidial suspension was prepared from 10-day-old PDA cultures and adjusted to 2×10^5/ml using a hemacytometer. Healthy Gerbera plants were grown in pots with sterile soil mixture. Plants were spray-inoculated with 100 ml of the spore suspension per pot. Immediately after inoculation, plants were placed in a humid chamber at 100% relative humidity and 25°C for 24 hours. After 24 hours, plants were uncovered and maintained at constant humidity by spraying tap water. Plants were kept in a greenhouse at 25–30°C for 2 weeks to allow symptom development. Disease incidence was recorded as 22.6% (7 spotty leaves in 31 healthy leaves). The pathogen was re-isolated from inoculated leaves on PDA and compared morphologically to the original isolate.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human or animal subjects. Statistical analysis: Not reported.

title: Denoising Diffusion Models of Matrix-Factorization User Embeddings for Collaborative Filtering
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can denoising diffusion models applied to MF user embeddings improve recommendation quality compared to standard MF baselines? (2) How does the choice of MF backbone (IALS, MF-BPR, PureSVD) for generating user factors affect diffusion performance? (3) Does conditioning diffusion on prompt user factors from an alternative MF model improve ranking or beyond-accuracy metrics? (4) What is the trade-off between ranking accuracy and beyond-accuracy metrics when diffusion is applied to user factors?

Hypotheses: (H1) Diffusion on MF user embeddings will improve beyond-accuracy metrics (coverage, novelty, diversity) relative to non-diffusion MF, potentially at the cost of ranking accuracy. (H2) MF-BPR user factors, which are less concentrated than PureSVD, will be more amenable to diffusion, yielding a favorable accuracy–exploration trade-off. (H3) Prompt conditioning will modestly improve ranking accuracy and/or coverage metrics by guiding denoising toward relevant directions. (H4) Increasing diffusion steps will increase exploration (coverage) but decrease NDCG.

Support/refutation: The results support H1 and H2 (MF-BPR diffusion improves coverage and diversity with slight NDCG loss; PureSVD diffusion degrades accuracy). H3 is nuanced: prompt conditioning has minimal impact on ranking accuracy overall, with dataset-specific gains. H4 is supported: NDCG decreases with more diffusion steps, while coverage metrics increase.
reference_methodology:
Datasets: CiteULike-a (5,551 users; 16,980 items; 204,987 interactions), Movielens10M (69,878 users; 10,681 movies; 10,000,000 explicit ratings), Pinterest (55,187 users; 9,916 items; implicit interactions). Dataset statistics (user/item counts, sparsity, profile lengths) are summarized in Table 4.1.

MF backbones for user factors: IALS (implicit ALS), MF-BPR (Bayesian personalized ranking), PureSVD (truncated SVD). Hyperparameters for these MF models were optimized via Bayesian search (Scikit-Optimize) over 35 cases per algorithm (first 5 random). Search ranges: neighborhood sizes k ∈ [5, 800], shrink term h ∈ [0, 1000], α and β ∈ [0, 2]. Implementation follows Ferrari Dacrema et al. [7].

Data partitioning: Two-stage splits. First, URM is split using an interactions holdout: 80% training, 10% validation, 10% test. Second, user factors obtained from MF models on the URM train split are split using a users holdout: 80% train, 10% validation, 10% test. The same split applies to prompt user factors (from alternative MF models). For final evaluation, the URM train and validation are used together to train MF models and generate user factors for diffusion.

Diffusion model training: Diffusion models are trained on the user-factor train split to minimize reconstruction loss on the validation split. A cosine noise schedule is used, with β_t = 1 − α_t / α_{t−1} and α_t derived from a cosine function (s = 0.008) and clipped at 0.999 to avoid singularities. Time-step conditioning is implemented via sinusoidal positional encodings (Transformer-style) injected as inputs to the denoising network. Early stopping is applied with a 30-epoch threshold and a maximum of 700 epochs. Hyperparameters optimized include denoising architecture parameters (encoding size, next-layer multiplier, max hidden layers, activation, batch normalization, dropout, dropout rate), diffusion training parameters (betas_offset, noise_time_steps, learning_rate, batch_size). Optimization uses Optuna (TPE) for 12 hours on NVIDIA P100 GPUs.

Evaluation: Offline holdout evaluation on the URM test split. Metrics include NDCG, Precision, Recall, Coverage, Coverage Hit, and beyond-accuracy metrics (novelty, diversity). For beyond-accuracy, the study reports Coverage Item, Coverage Item Hit, average popularity, novelty, and inter-list diversity (MIL). Cutoff k = 10 is used for reported tables. Figures 5.13–5.15 plot NDCG vs diffusion steps; Figures 5.16–5.18 plot Coverage Item; Figures 5.19–5.21 plot Coverage Item Hit. KDE plots (Figures 5.1–5.9) visualize user-factor distributions pre/post diffusion; cosine similarities (Figures 5.10–5.12) quantify distributional change. Baselines include unpersonalized (TopPop, Random, GlobalEffects), linear (SLIM), k-NN (UserKNN, ItemKNN), graph (P3α, RP3β), neural (EASE-R, MultVAE), and MF (PureSVD, IALS, MF-BPR). Baseline hyperparameters are reported in Appendix A.

title: Influence of Vacuum Sublimation Deposited Metal Layer Thickness on Metrological Parameters of the Amperometric Gas Sensor with Nafion Membrane
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does relative humidity (0%, 33%, 54%, 76%, 86%) affect the sensitivity, response time, and calibration linearity of an SO2 amperometric sensor with a Nafion membrane and a vacuum-sublimated gold working electrode? (2) How do RH conditions modulate the electrochemical transport regime (activation vs. diffusion control) and the associated charge transfer and diffusion resistances? (3) What are the long-term stability implications of operating at different RH levels?

Hypothesis (as proposed by the authors): Moderate RH enhances analyte transport via thin water films on hydrophobic membrane regions, increasing sensitivity and shortening response time relative to dry conditions. High RH increases diffusion resistance and charge transfer limitations, reducing sensitivity and slowing response. Long-term moistening, even at moderate RH, can degrade performance due to metal delamination. Outcomes supporting the hypothesis include higher sensitivity and faster response at moderate RH, lower Warburg coefficients and diffusion-to-activation resistance ratios at moderate RH, and increased Warburg coefficients and slower response at high RH. Outcomes refuting the hypothesis would include monotonic decreases in sensitivity with RH or no change in EIS-derived transport parameters.
reference_methodology:
Sensor design: A three-electrode amperometric sensor was constructed with a cylindrical gas-flow body, a measurement cell containing the internal electrolyte, and a container with hygrostatic solutions to set RH. The cell included a baffle and was filled with 5 mol m⁻³ H2SO4. The Nafion 350 membrane (Aldrich) separated the gas stream from the internal electrolyte. The working electrode was a gold layer vacuum-sublimated directly onto the Nafion surface from the gas side. The counter electrode was a gold plate; the reference electrode was Hg/Hg2SO4.
