The casing was PEEK. The Nafion thickness was 250 µm; the gold layer thickness was ~100 nm. The geometric working electrode area was 0.4 cm²; the counter electrode area was >10× larger.

Humidity control: RH was set using saturated salt solutions in a desiccator: MgCl2 (33%), Mg(NO3)2 (54%), NaCl (76%), and KCl (86%). RH was calculated from water vapor pressure relative to saturation (RH = P/Ps = exp(−m_s/M1·1000·φ), where m_s is saturation molality, M1 is water molecular mass, and φ is the osmotic coefficient). Sensors were conditioned for several days to saturate the membrane with the internal electrolyte and stabilize the working electrode area.

Electrode preparation: Nafion membranes were dried prior to deposition to remove water traces, then placed in a mold to ensure reproducible geometry. Vacuum sublimation was performed at 10⁻⁴ mm Hg using tungsten electrodes at 4 V (UZ Tesla 800). Post-deposition, membranes swelled upon electrolyte absorption; preparation errors could cause metal delamination.

Gas and flow: Synthetic air and a certified air/SO2 mixture (1000 ppm v/v) were supplied via Messer GmbH cylinders. Mass flow meters (Tylan General) provided 0–100 cm³/min flow. Voltamograms were recorded in synthetic air and in 200 ppm SO2 mixtures at 5 mV/s scan rate. Calibration curves (I vs. c) were obtained at selected constant potentials (e.g., 700 mV) using precisely defined SO2 concentrations. Preliminary polarization curves were recorded to select analytically useful potentials.

Electrochemical instrumentation: A Solartron SI 1287 potentiostat and PC with software were used for potentiostatic measurements. For EIS, a Solartron SI 1260 frequency response analyzer was added, with 10 mV perturbation amplitude and frequency range 10 mHz–1 MHz. Analysis used Zplot and ZView. Impedance spectra were recorded at potentials corresponding to activation control (e.g., 300 mV) and diffusion control (e.g., 700 mV), with 200 ppm SO2 and 50 cm³/min flow.

Response time measurement: Step changes in SO2 concentration (0→200 ppm) were applied at 50 cm³/min flow. The time constant was defined as the time to reach 63.2% of the maximum signal (I_t/I_max = 1 − exp(−t/τ)). Geometry, dead volume, and system inertia influenced τ; achieving ideal step changes was challenging under flowing conditions.

Stability assessment: Long-term stability was evaluated over two months for sensors at RH 0% and RH 54%.

title: Savouring the Present to Better Recall the Past
field_subfield: Psychology — Emotion Regulation and Autobiographical Memory
research_question:
Primary research questions: (1) Does real-time manipulation of savouring during positive events increase the salience and positivity of the associated memories one week later? (2) Does increased memory salience mediate the effect of savouring on recalled positivity? Secondary question: Do specific savouring strategies differentially affect memory phenomenology dimensions (accessibility, coherence, sensory details, visual perspective, vividness)?

Hypotheses: (1) Savouring (vs control) will increase (a) memory salience and (b) recalled positivity. (2) Increased memory salience will mediate the effect of savouring on recalled positivity (mediation model). Secondary analyses were exploratory without pre-specified hypotheses regarding differential strategy effects on memory dimensions. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses would include significant main effects of savouring on salience and positivity, significant indirect effects of salience on positivity, and, for secondary analyses, significant strategy-specific effects on memory dimensions.
reference_methodology:
Design: Two-week study with two phases. Phase 1 (EMA): daily prompts to report ongoing positive events; Phase 2 (recall): surprise recall one week after each event.

Participants: n=97 (79 female, 18 male), mean age 25.75 (min 18, max 61, SD 9.21). Sample size determined via power analysis (simr in R) assuming linear mixed-effects models; with β=0.40, power ≥95% at n=97 for models with five predictors (α=0.05). Recruitment via online ads and fliers; participants were told the study was a two-week free training to improve resilience and positive emotional regulation; the recall phase was not disclosed initially to avoid bias.

EMA phase: Two semi-randomized prompts per day (10:00–16:00 and 16:00–22:00) via Qualtrics. If a positive event was reported (specific, significant, with clear time and place and pleasant emotions), participants were randomly assigned to control or one of four savouring strategies (within-subjects factor). Control: written description and positivity rating (1–7). Experimental: same plus instructions to upregulate positive emotions. Strategies (based on Quoidbach et al., 2015): (1) Situation modification: modify the situation to enhance positive impact (e.g., small changes to amplify enjoyment). (2) Attentional deployment: focus attention on positive details and sensory feelings. (3) Cognitive change: reappraise the event as special and meaningful, reflecting on fortune and positive outcomes. (4) Response modulation: express positive emotions outwardly (e.g., smile, laugh, joke, jump for joy). Situation selection was excluded because events were already ongoing.

Recall phase: One week after each event, an email-based survey prompted a surprise recall of the event, including the same positivity rating (1–7) and the short-form MEQ (31 items; five subscales used: accessibility, coherence, sensory details, visual perspective, vividness). Manual comparison of momentary and retrospective descriptions confirmed accurate recall; no exclusions.

Measures: MEQ subscales showed good internal consistency (between-individual α: accessibility 0.89; coherence 0.78; sensory details 0.80; visual perspective 0.88; vividness 0.79; within-individual α: accessibility 0.79; coherence 0.71; sensory details 0.62; visual perspective 0.86; vividness 0.78) and strong inter-item correlations (mean r=0.674). PCA suggested a single component accounting for 69% of variance; component scores formed memory salience (α=0.88).

Procedure: Participants accessed an online survey via QR code, provided demographics and email, and received daily prompts. No time limit was enforced; links expired before subsequent prompts. In Phase 2, an email with the recall task was sent 7 days after each event, with a reminder the next day.

Ethics: Approved by BLINDED ethics committee (CD/57/2019); informed consent obtained. Participants could withdraw at any time.

Analysis: Conducted in R. Linear mixed-effects models (maximum likelihood) with random intercepts and all possible random slopes per participant; predictors included t0 positivity; interactions with sex (dichotomous) and age (grand-mean-centered). Multiple comparisons corrected with Tukey’s method. Mediation analyses used the mediation R package with 1000 bootstraps. Exploratory models tested strategy-specific effects on each memory dimension.

title: Use of Social Media Tools for Library Services during the Critical Condition of Covid-19 in University Libraries of Odisha
field_subfield: Library and Information Science — Social Media and Library Services
research_question: The study’s objectives, rather than formal hypotheses, guide the inquiry: (1) identify the most prominent social media tools used by library professionals; (2) assess awareness and depth of knowledge about platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, WhatsApp, LinkedIn, and YouTube; (3) analyze the purposes for which social media tools are used in library services; (4) determine how library services are applied through social media tools; and (5) identify LIS professionals who actively use social media to promote library services and products. The study does not state explicit directional hypotheses. Outcomes that would support the objectives include high adoption rates of specific platforms, frequent usage patterns, clear rationales for use (e.g., resource sharing, professional networking), and evidence of active promotion. The study’s descriptive design focuses on quantifying these aspects rather than testing causal claims.
reference_methodology:
Design: Quantitative survey using stratified random sampling. The sampling frame comprised library professionals and related stakeholders (students, research scholars, library staff) across six universities in Odisha, India: Sambalpur University, Utkal University, G.M. University, Berhampur University, Fakirmohan University, and North Orissa University. The study period corresponds to the COVID-19 lockdown period, though exact dates are not specified.

Sample: N=100 completed questionnaires. Distribution by university: Sambalpur University (n=20), Utkal University (n=15), G.M. University (n=10), Berhampur University (n=20), Fakirmohan University (n=20), North Orissa University (n=15). Respondent categories: students (n=71), research scholars (n=10), library staff (n=19). Demographics: gender—male 57% (n=57), female 43% (n=43); age—20–30 years 48% (n=48), 31–40 years 34% (n=34), 41–50 years 12% (n=12), 51+ years 6% (n=6).

Instrument: A questionnaire covering social media platform usage, frequency of use, reasons for use, and components employed. The instrument’s item wording, scale anchors, validation procedures, and reliability metrics are not reported. The survey included multiple-choice items, as indicated by the note that percentages exceed 100% in several tables due to multiple selections.

Procedure: Questionnaires were distributed to students, research scholars, and library professionals at the six universities. The exact mode of distribution (online vs. paper), recruitment procedures, response rate, and data collection timeline are not reported. No details are provided on consent procedures, anonymity, or data protection.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics (counts and percentages) were computed for platform usage, preference frequency, usage frequency, reasons for use, and components used. No inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are reported. No subgroup analyses (e.g., by role or age) are presented.

Ethics: No information is provided on ethical approval, informed consent, or data privacy safeguards.

title: Investigating the dynamics of Leishmania antigen in the urine of patients with visceral leishmaniasis: a pilot study
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do Leishmania antigen concentrations in urine vary across the day (08:00, 12:00, 16:00) in VL patients, and if so, which time point yields the highest median concentration? (2) Are urinary antigen concentrations higher in patients with relapse/treatment failure compared with primary VL cases?

Hypotheses: (H1) Early-morning urine (08:00) contains higher Leishmania antigen concentrations than midday (12:00) and afternoon (16:00) samples, consistent with CLSI guidance that early-morning urine maximizes urinary component concentrations. (H2) Patients with relapse/treatment failure have higher urinary antigen levels than those with primary VL, reflecting higher parasite loads in relapse disease.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 would be supported if the median antigen concentration at 08:00 is significantly higher than at 12:00 and 16:00. H2 would be supported if median antigen levels differ significantly between type-1 (primary) and type-2 (relapse/treatment failure) groups. Non-significant differences would refute or fail to support the respective hypotheses.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Pilot observational study conducted at the Emerging Infections and Parasitology Laboratory, International Centre for Diarrheal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b), between 15 March and 30 April 2016.

Participants: Convenience sample of 16 hospitalized VL patients at Surya Kanta Kala-azar Research Centre (SKKRC), the only specialized VL treatment hospital in Bangladesh. Grouping: type-1 (primary VL) and type-2 (relapse VL or treatment failure). Inclusion criteria: VL diagnosis per national guidelines (endemic area, fever >2 weeks, splenomegaly, positive rK39 rapid diagnostic test; Kalazar Detect, InBios Intl., USA). Clinical and demographic characteristics were summarized (Table 1; details not provided in the text).

Specimen collection: Midstream urine (50 ml) collected at 08:00, 12:00, and 16:00 hours into tubes containing 0.1% NaN3. Samples were stored at −20°C immediately after collection and transported under cold chain to icddr,b. For analysis, 2 ml aliquots were used.

Assay: Leishmania Antigen ELISA (VL ELISA; Kalon Biological Ltd., UK) targeting non-proteic Leishmania antigens with polyclonal antibodies. Samples were diluted 1:20 in kit-provided assay diluent. A total of 100 µl of diluted urine was tested in triplicate per well on 96-well plates, alongside duplicate calibrator standards. After room temperature incubation, optical density (OD) was read at 450 and 620 nm (Biotek microplate reader). OD620 was subtracted from OD450 for calculations. A four-parameter logistic standard curve was constructed per plate using the kit calibrators. Antigen concentrations were expressed in Urinary Antigen Units (UAU/ml), acknowledging that the antigenic components remain largely uncharacterized.

Statistical analysis: Within-subject differences across time points were assessed using the Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test. Spearman’s rank correlation tested associations between antigen concentrations at different time points and age. Mann–Whitney U tests compared antigen concentrations between sexes and between type-1 and type-2 patients. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 7.03 and SPSS 20.0.

Ethics: Approved by the icddr,b Ethical Review Committee (protocol PR-14093). Written informed consent was obtained from participants or legal guardians (children).

title: Geographical Research Bulletin
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How does the timing of mild drought (flowering vs pod-setting stage) affect peanut yield components, plant N accumulation, and N distribution among organs? (2) How do N fertilizer levels (0, 90, 180 kg/ha) modulate N uptake, transport efficiency to kernels, and N use efficiency under well-watered and drought conditions? (3) Are there stage- and dose-specific patterns in N recovery, residual, and loss that can inform precision N management under drought?

Hypotheses: (H1) Drought reduces peanut yield and plant N accumulation, with flowering-stage drought exerting a larger negative impact than pod-setting-stage drought due to critical reproductive development during flowering. (H2) Under drought, plants reallocate N to kernels, increasing kernel N accumulation and N transport efficiency to kernels. (H3) Medium N (90 kg/ha) under drought optimizes N use efficiency (higher recovery, lower loss) compared to low and high N, whereas high N under drought does not improve recovery and may increase environmental losses. Support for H1 would be evidenced by greater yield and N accumulation reductions under flowering-stage drought. Support for H2 would be increased kernel N fractions and higher N transport efficiency to kernels under drought. Support for H3 would be higher recovery and lower loss at 90 kg/ha under drought relative to 0 and 180 kg/ha.
reference_methodology:
Site and period: Agricultural experimental station in Sichuan Province, China, characterized by flat terrain, sandy loam soil (pH 6.5), and an alternating drought–wet climate with ~700 mm annual precipitation concentrated in summer. The experiment spanned two consecutive years (Dec 2022–Dec 2024), covering the full peanut growth cycle (sowing, flowering/pegging, pod-setting, maturity, harvest).

Experimental design: A factorial arrangement with three water regimes and three N fertilizer levels. Water regimes: (1) Well-watered: field capacity maintained at 75–80% (control, fully irrigated); (2) Mild drought during flowering (pegging) stage: field capacity maintained at 55–60%; (3) Mild drought during pod-setting stage: field capacity maintained at 55–60%. N fertilizer levels: (1) Low N: 0 kg N/ha; (2) Medium N: 90 kg N/ha; (3) High N: 180 kg N/ha.

Measurements: Yield indices included total peanut yield (kg/ha) and organ-specific components (kernel, pod shell, root weights). N accumulation indices included plant N content in leaves, stems, roots, kernels, and other organs to compute total plant N accumulation. The 15N tracer technique quantified N fertilizer uptake, transport, and distribution across organs, enabling calculation of N derived from fertilizer and organ-specific N fractions. N use efficiency indices included: (1) N fertilizer recovery rate (proportion of applied N absorbed by crops); (2) N fertilizer residual rate (proportion of applied N remaining in soil after crop uptake); (3) N fertilizer loss rate (proportion of applied N lost via volatilization, runoff, or leaching).

Statistical analysis: One-way ANOVA assessed differences among treatment groups for yield, N accumulation, and N use efficiency indices. When ANOVA indicated significant differences, multiple comparisons (e.g., Tukey’s HSD) identified specific pairwise differences. Regression analysis modeled relationships between N application rates and yield/N absorption efficiency, and predicted optimal N rates under different water conditions. Data were visualized using bar charts, line graphs, and scatter plots to compare treatments and reveal dynamic trends.

Unreported details: The text does not specify replication numbers, randomization/blocking, cultivar, soil background N status, 15N labeling protocol (source, application timing, enrichment), sampling schedule, analytical instruments (e.g., isotope ratio mass spectrometry), or statistical parameters (alpha, effect sizes, confidence intervals). Ethical approvals are not applicable for agronomic field trials and are not reported.

title: МЕТОД ФОРМИРОВАНИЯ ЦИКЛОВЫХ ПОДКЛЮЧЕЙ НА БАЗЕ ЛИНЕЙНЫХ РЕГИСТРОВ СДВИГА В РАСШИРЕННЫХ ПОЛЯХ GF (2N)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a key schedule based on an LFSR over GF(2^n) with a carefully designed nonlinear filter function meet stringent cryptographic requirements (long period, statistical randomness, high avalanche/completeness, and high complexity of solving key-output systems)? (2) Does such a design achieve practical performance comparable to or better than block-cipher-based PRSGs used in key schedules? (3) Can the approach be implemented with low platform dependence and minimal key-dependent operations?

Hypotheses: (H1) An LFSR over GF(2^32) with a two-layer S-box filter and fixed bit/byte permutations will pass NIST STS tests and exhibit strong avalanche and completeness metrics, indicating robust statistical properties. (H2) The proposed key schedule will expand keys at least as fast as a block-cipher-based PRSG, and likely faster, due to the lightweight nature of LFSR updates and fixed permutations. (H3) The design will avoid key-dependent nonlinearities in the filter, enabling reuse across block ciphers without constant-tuning overhead.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if all NIST STS tests pass with Pj > 0.001 and no failures, and if avalanche/completeness metrics are close to 1. H2 is supported if measured keys/s exceeds the block-cipher PRSG baseline under identical cryptographic operations. H3 is supported if the filter uses only fixed cryptographic operations and no key-dependent constants.
reference_methodology:
Design: The key schedule is a nonlinear filter generator over GF(2^32). The LFSR has 17 states (s[1]…s[17]), each 32 bits, with characteristic polynomial P(X) = X^17 + X^15 + X^4 + α over GF(2^32), where α = 0x000001000 (equivalently, a specific polynomial in x and y). The recurrence is s[t+17] = s[t+16] ⊕ s[t+15] ⊕ s[t+4] ⊕ α. The LFSR period is T = 2^544 − 1, realized by decomposing the field LFSR into 32 parallel binary LFSRs of length 544.

Filter function: The nonlinear filter F takes 160 bits formed by concatenating four 32-bit states (s[t+16], s[t+13], s[t+6], s[t+1]) and one additional state (s[t+16]) at each time t. To match the 128-bit cryptographic operations, the 160-bit vector is compressed to 128 bits via pairwise XORs of adjacent states: σ′(t) = s[t+16] ⊕ s[t+13] ⊕ s[t+13] ⊕ s[t+6] ⊕ s[t+6] ⊕ s[t+1] ⊕ s[t+1]. The 128-bit input X is processed by: (1) byte permutation Pbyte(n=2) across 64-bit words; (2) two layers of 8×8 S-box substitutions (S1 and S2); (3) a uniform bit permutation Pbit within each 64-bit word; and (4) a second byte permutation Pbyte(n=2). The output ν(t) = F(σ′(t)) is used to generate round keys.

Key schedule mapping: The Tornado block cipher’s specification defines the key schedule as a block transformation: input is 7 half-blocks of the user key (7 × 64 = 448 bits); output is 4 × 5 + 4 half-blocks of the expanded ("raw") working key ((4 × 5 + 4) × 64 = 1536 bits). The paper evaluates the statistical and correlation properties of this mapping.

Statistical testing: The NIST STS suite (16 tests; 189 total tests including multiple templates) was applied to sequences generated by the proposed key schedule. Acceptance criteria were Pj > 0.001 and rj ≥ 0.96015 per test. The same methodology was used to evaluate a block-cipher-based PRSG in prior work.

Correlation analysis: Three metrics were computed for the key schedule: (1) N, the number of bits changed in the expanded key when any single bit of the user key is flipped; (2) avalanche coefficient da; (3) strict avalanche coefficient ds; and (4) completeness dc. Expectations M and variances D were reported for N, da, ds, and dc. The analysis treated the key schedule as a block transformation with 448-bit input and 1536-bit output.

Performance evaluation: Key expansion throughput was measured on a Celeron-600 PC under Windows 2000. The number of 128-bit user keys expanded per second to a 1536-bit expanded key was recorded for the proposed LFSR-based schedule and for a block-cipher-based PRSG used in Tornado. Identical cryptographic operations were used in the filter to isolate the effect of the generator design.

title: Breast Ultrasound Microvascular Imaging and Radiogenomics
research_question:
The review addresses three interrelated questions: (1) Do microvascular US techniques (SMI without contrast; CEUS with contrast) improve diagnostic performance for differentiating malignant from benign breast lesions compared with conventional Doppler and B-mode US? (2) Do microvascular US features correlate with histologic microvessel density (MVD) and other markers of tumor aggressiveness (e.g., ER/HER2 status, Ki-67)? (3) Can US vascular phenotypes predict gene expression patterns associated with angiogenesis, proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and drug resistance, thereby informing prognosis and therapy?

Implicit hypotheses are: (a) SMI and CEUS will detect more microvessels and irregular vascular patterns than conventional Doppler, improving sensitivity/specificity and AUC for malignancy detection; (b) SMI/CEUS metrics (e.g., VI, CEUS time-intensity parameters) will correlate with MVD and adverse histologic features; (c) specific US vascular phenotypes will associate with distinct gene expression signatures linked to angiogenesis and drug resistance. Supportive outcomes include higher pooled sensitivity/specificity and AUC in meta-analyses, significant correlations with MVD and molecular markers, and statistically significant differential gene expression (e.g., >4-fold) associated with US-defined vascular patterns. Refutation would involve no improvement over conventional methods, null correlations with MVD/molecular markers, or absence of gene expression differences.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review synthesizing clinical studies and meta-analyses on microvascular US techniques for breast cancer. The text does not report a systematic review protocol, search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessment. It summarizes findings from multiple observational studies and meta-analyses.

SMI studies: Comparative evaluations of SMI versus conventional color/power Doppler assessed lesion vascularity characterization and diagnostic performance. Examples include: Park et al. (n=191 masses) comparing SMI, color, and power Doppler; Ma et al. (n=123 lesions) grading vascularity (0–3); Zhan et al. (n=82 lesions categorized 3/4 and avascular on color Doppler) evaluating penetrating vessels. A meta-analysis pooled 15 SMI studies to estimate sensitivity, specificity, and AUC for malignancy detection. Objective SMI metrics included the vascular index (VI), defined as the ratio of Doppler signal pixels to total lesion pixels, measured via built-in or offline analysis packages.

CEUS studies: Qualitative assessment of enhancement patterns (degree relative to normal tissue, enhancement order, margin, internal homogeneity, penetrating vessels, perfusion defects) and quantitative time-intensity curve analysis (peak intensity, time-to-peak, mean transit time, wash-in velocity, area under the curve) were performed using region-of-interest placement in the strongest enhancement. A meta-analysis pooled 9 studies comparing CEUS and B-mode US, and 5 studies comparing B-mode US plus CEUS versus B-mode US alone. CEUS acquisition used low mechanical index (<0.3) and contrast-specific modes to prolong microbubble stability and isolate nonlinear contrast signals.

Histopathologic correlations: SMI semiquantitative grades and VI correlated with MVD using Spearman’s rank correlation (r=0.63–0.82). CEUS quantitative features correlated with MVD (r=0.43–0.57). Associations with molecular markers included perfusion defects with ER negativity and HER2 positivity, penetrating vessels with poor histologic grade, and stiff wash-in slope with Ki-67 positivity.

Radiogenomic study: A study of 31 breast cancers profiled RNA sequencing and 13 US phenotypes (B-mode, SMI, CEUS). Differential expression analyses identified 340 genes with >4-fold up- or downregulation associated with US-defined vascular features. Examples include: penetrating vessels associated with CST1 (6.3-fold) and AGR2 (4.3-fold) upregulation; elevated SMI VI associated with MIR1307 (11.6-fold) upregulation, HIST2H2BE (4.1-fold) upregulation, and MIR597 (6.2-fold) downregulation; SMI complex morphology associated with CRIPAK downregulation (5.4-fold) and FZD8 upregulation (4.1-fold). Statistical significance thresholds included p<0.05 and log2FC >2.0 or <−2.0 for volcano plot visualization.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported in the provided text.

title: Observed strong pervasive positive selection in the N-terminal domain, receptor-binding domain and furin-cleavage sites of SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein sampled from Zimbabwean COVID-19 patients
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What evolutionary patterns (selection pressures) are evident in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike gene among sequences sampled from Zimbabwean COVID-19 patients? (2) Is there evidence of recombination in the Zimbabwean SARS-CoV-2 dataset? (3) How do lineage distributions and temporal sampling relate to observed evolutionary patterns?

Hypotheses: (H1) Pervasive positive selection (β > α) is present in the Spike protein, particularly in functionally critical regions (NTD, RBD, furin-cleavage site). (H2) Recombination signals are detectable in the dataset if present. (H3) Temporal clustering of sequences reflects variant waves and increased divergence over time.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if FUBAR identifies sites with posterior probability >0.9 for β > α and elevated Bayes factors (>15). H2 is supported if any RDP method detects recombination; absence of detection across multiple methods would refute H2. H3 is supported if the phylogenetic tree shows clustering by collection year and divergence from the reference sequence over time.
reference_methodology:
Data: High-coverage SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences from GISAID were downloaded along with patient metadata and the GISAID S gene reference sequence. The approximate S gene region (nucleotides 21,500–25,500) was extracted using Biopython, Pandas, and NumPy, allowing ~100 nucleotides on each end to accommodate variable genome lengths.

Sequence processing and alignment: Sequences were aligned using Clustal Omega within Jalview 2.11.1.3. Redundant sequences and those with a high number of unidentified nucleotides were removed. Using the GISAID S reference as a guide, flanking regions were sliced to retain the S gene. Codon alignment was performed in MEGA X (Clustal Omega prerequisite for FUBAR).

Recombination analysis: Following Martin et al. (2011), the RDP 4.100 suite was used with default settings to test for recombination using RDP, GENECONV, Chimaera, MaxChi, and BootScan. A Monte Carlo-based method, SISCAN, was additionally applied. The authors report no evidence of recombination by any method.

Selection analysis: The codon-aligned S dataset was uploaded to Datamonkey for FUBAR analysis. The fitted phylogenetic tree (Newick format) was exported and visualized in iTOL. A CSV table of site-specific selection parameters (synonymous α vs non-synonymous β rates) was exported. Posterior probability thresholds of 0.9 were used to identify sites under strong positive selection (β > α) and strong negative selection (α > β). A bar plot of Bayes factors was used to visualize sites with strong positive selection.

Lineage distribution and visualization: Patient metadata were processed in Pandas to summarize lineage distribution and sample collection dates. WHO Greek-letter groupings were used to categorize variants. Visualization was performed with Matplotlib and Seaborn. A consensus sequence of Zimbabwean sequences was generated and compared to the GISAID S reference to assess identity.

Ethics/IRB: Not reported. The study uses publicly available genomic data; no individual-level consent or approvals are described.

title: Symmetry of Attractors and the Karhunen-Lo eve Decomposition
field_subfield: Mathematics — Dynamical Systems and Applied Mathematics
research_question:
Central questions: (1) Can symmetry of attractors be detected generically using ergodic sums of equivariant observables under the assumption of an SBR measure? (2) How do symmetry properties of the underlying attractor manifest in the KL decomposition for PDEs, and when does the reduced system inherit the correct symmetry? (3) Can one construct a KL-based observable that recovers the correct symmetry type (e.g., distinguishing SO(2) from O(2)) in cases where the standard kernel fails?

Hypotheses: (H1) For SBR attractors, ergodic-sum-based detectives (polynomial observables spanning all nontrivial irreducible representations) generically recover the attractor’s symmetry group. (H2) The KL correlation kernel K(U) and operator K_U are at least (A)-equivariant, where (A) is the attractor’s symmetry group, but may possess additional symmetry in specific cases (e.g., scalar PDEs with SO(2) symmetry). (H3) Extending the KL observable to (U, U_t) enables distinguishing symmetries that the standard kernel cannot (e.g., SO(2) vs O(2)). (H4) The reduced Galerkin system from KL eigenfunctions is (A)-equivariant and independent of the choice of attractor within its symmetry orbit.

Support/refutation: Theorems 3.3 and 4.3 support H1; Propositions 6.1 and 6.3 support H2; Example 6.4 and the extended kernel construction support H3; Propositions 8.1 and 8.3 support H4.
reference_methodology:
Detectives and SBR measures: Let a finite group Γ act orthogonally on R^n. For an open set A with piecewise-smooth boundary and satisfying the dichotomy A=ΓA or A∩ΓA=∅, define the symmetry group (A)={γ∈Γ: ΓA=A}. An equivariant observable φ:R^n→W (W a finite-dimensional Γ-representation) yields an observation K(A)=∫_A φ dμ (Lebesgue measure). The isotropy subgroup of K(A) contains (A); observables for which equality holds generically are detectives. The authors recall a Lebesgue-integration detective theorem (Theorem 2.4) and introduce ergodic sums for attractors A (future basin U): K_E(A)=lim_{N→∞} (1/N)∑_{j=0}^{N−1} φ(f^j(x)), which, under an SBR measure μ on A, equals ∫_A φ dμ for Lebesgue a.e. x∈U. An SBR measure satisfies: support(A)=A, ergodicity on U, and for Lebesgue a.e. x∈U, the ergodic average equals the integral over A for all continuous observables.

Ergodic-sum detectives: For polynomial observables φ spanning all nontrivial irreducible representations W(Γ) (with trivial component W0), Theorem 3.3 proves φ is an SBR-detective: for each SBR attractor (f;A;μ;U), almost all near-identity Γ-equivariant diffeomorphisms γ satisfy (γ(A))=(A). Proposition 3.4 shows that if A is invariant under a subgroup Λ⊆Γ, then μ is Λ-invariant and the ergodic sum is Λ-invariant almost everywhere.

PDE context: Consider PDEs ∂_t U=G(U) on a domain Ω with boundary conditions, with symmetry group Γ=Γ_r×Γ_d (range and domain symmetries). Define an SBR attractor A⊆X_0 (X_0⊂L^2(Ω) with boundary conditions) with an SBR measure μ: (i) neighborhood N of A with S(t)U→A; (ii) S(t)A⊆A; (iii) μ invariant and ergodic on A, and for U_0 in a dense, symmetric open subset N_0⊂N, lim_{T→∞} (1/T)∫_0^T φ(S(t)U_0)dt=∫_A φ dμ for continuous φ. The time-average of a continuous φ is (U_0)=lim_{T→∞} (1/T)∫_0^T φ(S(t)U_0)dt.

KL decomposition: For a trajectory U(t), define the temporal ensemble average h·i and the correlation kernel K(U)(x,y)=⟨L(U)(x,y)⟩, where L(U)(x,y)=U(x)U(y)^T (m×m matrices with entries in L^2(Ω×Ω)). Under μ, K(U)=⟨L(U)⟩=∫_A L dμ. The KL operator K_U is the integral operator with kernel K(U), which is non-negative and compact under standard assumptions, yielding eigenfunctions {φ_k} and coefficients a_k(t) with ha_k a_ki=λ_k δ_{jk}. The KL decomposition U(x,t)=∑_{k=1}^∞ a_k(t)φ_k(x) holds almost everywhere with respect to μ.

Symmetry analysis: Proposition 6.1 shows K(U) is equivariant with respect to Γ_r∩(A): for γ=(γ_r,γ_d)∈(A), γ_r K(U) γ_r^T=K(γ_d U). Proposition 6.3 shows K_U is (A)-equivariant: K_U=γ K_U γ^T for all γ∈(A). Example 6.4 (scalar PDE on the line with periodic BCs, Γ=SO(2) or O(2)) shows K(U) can be written as a periodic function of x−y, implying O(2)-equivariance even if the attractor is SO(2)-symmetric. Example 6.5 (complex Ginzburg–Landau with S1 range symmetry) shows the standard kernel K_c(x,y)=⟨U(x)U(y)⟩ is S1-invariant and cannot distinguish range symmetries.

Extended observable: For discretized PDEs (cells z_j with m≥2 equations and p≥3 cells), Theorem 7.1 shows φ(z)=z z^T is a detective. For scalar PDEs (m=1), the authors propose extending the observable to (U,U_t) and redefining L_e(V)(x,y)=((V(x),V_t(x)) (V(y),V_t(y))^T, enabling distinction between SO(2) and O(2) via the cross-correlation component F_2(x−y)=⟨U(x)U_t(y)⟩.

Reduced system: Truncate KL eigenfunctions to M modes with λ_{M+1}<λ_M. Decompose the M-dimensional space X=span{φ_1,…,φ_M} into (A)-irreducible subspaces X=⊕_{j=1}^N X_j. The reduced ODE system is equivariant (Proposition 8.1) and independent of the choice of attractor within its orbit (Proposition 8.3). Numerically, approximate K_U by N_U and symmetrize it (N_U=Z N_U) to enforce (A)-equivariance before solving the eigenproblem.

title: Saddle Point Criteria in Semi-Infinite Minimax Fractional Programming under Φ, ρ -Invexity
field_subfield: Mathematics — Optimization (Semi-Infinite Programming; Fractional Programming; Generalized Convexity)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Under what generalized convexity conditions can an optimal solution of a semi-infinite minimax fractional program with inequality and equality constraints be characterized as a saddle point of a vector-valued Lagrangian? (2) Can Φ, ρ-invexity provide parametric saddle point criteria that extend beyond prior generalized convexity frameworks?

Hypotheses: (H1) If a saddle point of the vector-valued Lagrangian exists for (SMFP), then the associated primal point is optimal. (H2) If a feasible point x is optimal and satisfies the necessary optimality conditions with multipliers (λ, µ, v, w_0, t, s), and if the objective and constraint components satisfy one of seven Φ, ρ-invexity hypothesis sets (A–G) with a sign-consistent sum of ρ-parameters, then x, λ, µ, v, w_0, t, s is a saddle point. Outcomes supporting H1/H2 are proven via Theorems 3.7 and 3.8; failure of equivalence under other generalized convexity notions is demonstrated by the example, indicating that Φ, ρ-invexity is necessary to cover the considered nonconvex cases.
reference_methodology:
Problem formulation: Let X ⊂ R^n be a nonempty convex open set. The semi-infinite minimax fractional program (SMFP) is:

min_{x∈X} max_{i∈I} f_i(x)/i(x), subject to G_j(x, t) ≤ 0 for all t ∈ T_j (j = 1,…,q), and H_k(x, s) = 0 for all s ∈ S_k (k = 1,…,r), where I = {1,…,p}. For each i, f_i: X → R with f_i(x) ≤ 0 and i(x) > 0 for all x ∈ X. The parameter sets T_j and S_k are compact subsets of a complete metric space. The functions t ↦ G_j(x, t) and s ↦ H_k(x, s) are continuous in t and s, respectively, for x satisfying constraints. The feasible set is D = {x ∈ X : G_j(x, t) ≤ 0 ∀ t ∈ T_j, H_k(x, s) = 0 ∀ s ∈ S_k}.

Minimax representation: Lemma 3.4 shows ϕ(x) = max_{i∈I} f_i(x)/i(x) = max_{λ∈Λ} Σ_{i=1}^p λ_i f_i(x)/Σ_{i=1}^p λ_i i(x), where Λ = {λ ∈ R^p : λ_i ≥ 0, Σ_i λ_i = 1}.

Necessary optimality conditions: Theorem 3.5 (Zalmai and Zhang) states that if x ∈ D is optimal with value v = max_i f_i(x)/i(x), the generalized Abadie constraint qualification holds at x, and the cone spanned by gradients of active constraints is closed, then there exist λ ∈ Λ, integers w_0 and w with 0 ≤ w_0 ≤ w ≤ n+1, indices j_m and k_m, points t_m ∈ T_j_m(x) and s_m ∈ S_k_m, and multipliers µ_m > 0 (m = 1,…,w_0) such that:

Σ_{i=1}^p λ_i ∇f_i(x) − v Σ_{i=1}^p λ_i ∇i(x) + Σ_{m=1}^{w_0} µ_m ∇G_j_m(x, t_m) + Σ_{m=w_0+1}^w µ_m ∇H_k_m(x, s_m) = 0 (Equation (2)), and λ_i f_i(x) − v i(x) = 0 for all i (Equation (3)).

Lagrangian and saddle point: The vector-valued Lagrangian L has components L_i(z, λ, µ, v, w, w_0, t, s) = λ_i f_i(z) − v i(z) + (1/p)[Σ_{m=1}^{w_0} µ_m G_j_m(z, t_m) + Σ_{m=w_0+1}^w µ_m H_k_m(z, s_m)] (Equation (4)). A saddle point (x, λ, µ, v, w, w_0, t, s) satisfies: (i) L_i(x, λ, µ, v, w, w_0, t, s) ≤ L_i(x, λ, µ, v, w, w_0, t, s) for all µ ∈ R^w; (ii) L(x, λ, µ, v, w, w_0, t, s) ≤ L(x, λ, µ, v, w, w_0, t, s) for all x ∈ D (Definition 3.6).

Φ, ρ-invexity: For differentiable f: X → R^k, f is Φ, ρ-invex at u if there exists Φ: X × X × R^{n+1} → R with Φ(x, u, •) convex on R^{n+1}, Φ(x, u, (0, a)) ≥ 0 for all x and a ∈ R_+, and scalars ρ = (ρ_1,…,ρ_k) such that f_i(x) − f_i(u) ≥ Φ(x, u, ∇f_i(u), ρ_i) for all x ∈ X (Definition 2.1). Special cases include convexity, invexity, ρ-convexity, F-convexity, F, ρ-convexity, b, F, ρ-convexity, and others (Remark 2.3).

Proof strategy: Theorem 3.7 proves that a saddle point implies optimality by combining the saddle inequalities with feasibility and complementary slackness. Theorem 3.8 proves the converse under seven alternative Φ, ρ-invexity hypothesis sets (A–G), each specifying invexity for objective and constraint components and a nonnegativity condition on the sum of ρ-parameters (e.g., Σ_i λ_i ρ_i + Σ_m ρ_Gjm + Σ_m ρ_Hkm − Σ_m ρ_Hkm ≤ 0 in A). The proofs use convexity of Φ(x, x, •), the necessary optimality conditions, and convex combinations of gradients to derive contradictions unless the saddle inequalities hold.

Example (P1): In R^2 with f_i(x) = (x_1^2 + x_2^2 + i)/(2i + arctan(x_1 x_2)), G_1(x, t) = −t/(1 + t) − x_1 x_2 ≤ 0 for t ∈ [0, 1], and x = (0, 0) feasible, the author defines Φ(x, x, (ς, ρ)) = (1/2)(ς_1 + ς_2)(x_1^2 − x_1^2 + x_2^2 − x_2^2) + 2(2ρ − 1)(x_1 − x_1)(x_2 − x_2) with ρ_fi = 1, ρ_i = −1, ρ_G1 = −1. Under these, all functions are Φ, ρ-invex at x, and Theorem 3.8 yields a saddle point; Theorem 3.7 then implies optimality. The example also shows that equivalence under other generalized convexity notions may fail because stationary points are not global minimizers.

title: Multi-Omics Analysis in β-Thalassemia Using an HBB Gene-Knockout Human Erythroid Progenitor Cell Model
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does HBB deletion in human erythroid progenitors upregulate HBG1/2 via H3K4me3-mediated genetic compensation response (GCR)? (2) What molecular pathways and regulatory changes accompany HBB loss, and do they implicate oxidative stress and stress erythropoiesis? (3) Are these mechanisms reflected in patient hematopoietic stem cell single-cell transcriptomes?

Hypotheses: (H1) HBB deletion increases HBG1/2 expression without H3K4me3-mediated GCR; (H2) HBB loss induces oxidative stress and HIF1-mediated stress erythropoiesis, leading to slowed cell cycle progression and increased apoptosis; (H3) These stress responses elevate HBG1/2 expression; (H4) Patient HSC scRNA-seq shows partial erythroid differentiation consistent with stress erythropoiesis. Predictions: If H3K4me3-mediated GCR drives HBG1/2 upregulation, H3K4me3 enrichment at HBG1/2 promoters should increase and exogenous HBB nonsense transcripts should induce HBG1/2 upregulation. If oxidative stress and HIF1 activation are central, ROS and HIF1α should increase, and GSEA should show HIF1 pathway activation; phosphoproteomics should indicate reduced CDK activity consistent with cell cycle slowdown. If stress erythropoiesis is operative, erythroid differentiation markers and γ-globin should increase, and patient HSC scRNA-seq should show a higher erythroid cell proportion.
reference_methodology:
Cell model: HUDEP2 human umbilical cord blood-derived erythroid progenitor cells were engineered for homozygous HBB knockout (HBB-KO) using CRISPR/Cas9. Potential off-target sites for guide RNAs were identified via CCTop; the top six sites were PCR-amplified and Sanger-sequenced, revealing no off-target cleavage. A series of HBB nonsense mutant plasmids producing truncated proteins were constructed (KOD-Plus-Mutagenesis Kit) and transfected into HEK-293T (Lipofectamine 3000) and K562 cells (P3 primer cell 96-well Nucleofector kit). After 12 h transfection, media were replaced with complete medium; cells were collected at 48 h.

Molecular assays: RT-qPCR used TRIzol extraction, RNeasy Mini Kit, HiScript III RT SuperMix, and SYBR Green. Ct values were normalized to GAPDH; fold changes were calculated as 2^-ΔΔCt. CUT&Tag employed anti-H3K4me3 antibody (Abcam) with the NovoNGS CUT&Tag 3.0 High-Sensitivity Kit (Illumina) on HUDEP2 WT (n=3) and HBB-KO (n=3). ATAC-seq followed manufacturer protocols; libraries were prepared with NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit and sequenced on Illumina NextSeq500 (paired-end 150 bp). Quality control used FastQC; analyses followed ENCODE guidelines for unreplicated ChIP-seq. Genomic tracks were visualized in UCSC Genome Browser.

Omics profiling: ATAC-seq used three biological replicates per condition (WT, HBB-KO). RNA-seq and proteomics used three biological replicates per condition. Proteomics employed 6-plex TMT labeling (FASP trypsin digestion), HPLC separation, and LC-MS/MS on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 coupled to an EASY-nLC 1000. Two-column system: 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile (B). Gradient: 2–5% B for 2 min; 5–28% B for 98 min; 28–35% B for 5 min; 35–90% B for 2 min; 90% B for 13 min at 200 nL/min. Data-dependent acquisition selected top 15 ions per MS scan for HCD fragmentation. Raw data were processed with Proteome Discoverer 1.4 (Mascot 2.3) against Homo sapiens (UP000005640). Differential expression thresholds: fold change ≥ 2 or ≤ 0.5 with FDR ≤ 0.05. PCA used factoextra in R; heatmaps used pheatmap; GO and GSEA used clusterProfiler; kinase activity analysis used KSEA; subcellular localization used WoLF PSORT.

Functional assays: ROS content was measured (DCFH probe), viability by trypan blue, apoptosis by flow cytometry and capillary electrophoresis, cell cycle progression by flow cytometry and CCK8 assays, and HIF1α expression by RT-qPCR. Erythroid differentiation was induced in WT and HBB-KO cells; samples were collected before (WT_B, HBB-KO_B) and after (WT_A, HBB-KO_A) differentiation. Surface markers CD71 and CD235a were assessed by flow cytometry; γ-globin and erythroid markers (KLF1/3, FOG1, AHSP, NFE2, EPOR, GFI1B) were quantified by RT-qPCR.

Patient data reanalysis: Single-cell RNA-seq data from CD34+ HSCs (GEO GSE133181) were analyzed to compare erythroid cell proportions across normal, β-thalassemia, and sickle anemia cohorts.

title: Erythromelanosis follicularis faciei et colli: clinico-epidemiological profiles and dermoscopic findings in a series of 8 patients
research_question:
Research questions: (1) What are the clinico-epidemiological profiles of EFFC in a consecutive series of patients? (2) What dermoscopic features are consistently observed in EFFC, and how do they align with histopathological findings? (3) Can dermoscopy aid in differentiating EFFC from clinically similar pigmentary erythematous disorders? (4) What is the prevalence of associated keratosis pilaris and family history in this cohort?

Hypotheses: (a) EFFC presents with a characteristic triad of erythema, pigmentation, and follicular papules predominantly on the face and neck, with early onset and a benign course; (b) polarized dermoscopy reveals a consistent pattern of follicular keratotic plugs, reddish-brown background, gray-blue peppering, telangiectasias, and twisted/coiled hair within follicles, corresponding to histopathological features of hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, and pigmentary incontinence; (c) dermoscopy can reduce the need for invasive biopsy by providing diagnostic confidence and aiding differentiation from mimics; (d) rosettes, while present in EFFC, are not specific to the condition and reflect optical effects of polarized light on follicular structures.

Outcomes supporting the hypotheses include concordance between dermoscopic findings and histopathology, consistent clinical triad across cases, and the presence of non-specific rosettes. Outcomes refuting would include discordant dermoscopy–histopathology findings, absence of the clinical triad, or rosettes showing high specificity for EFFC.
reference_methodology:
Design: Consecutive case series of patients presenting with clinically suggestive EFFC.

Participants: Eight consecutive patients (ages 11–24 years; mean 16.1) with no reported sex predominance. Disease onset occurred between ages 7 and 13 years; mean duration ranged from 2 to 10 years. All patients reported mild to moderate photosensitivity and xerosis or a granular feel. Keratosis pilaris (KP) was present in all patients; 3/8 had a positive family history for KP.

Inclusion criteria: Presence of hyperpigmentation, erythema, and follicular papules involving mainly the face extending to the sides of the neck.

Exclusion criteria: Not explicitly stated.

Procedures: After informed consent, patients underwent history and clinical examination. Dermoscopy was performed using a handheld DermLite DL4 dermoscope (3Gen, USA) at ×10 magnification. Polarized light was used; rosettes were documented when present. Histopathological confirmation was obtained in cases where the clinical diagnosis was doubtful. No standardized treatment protocol was applied; management recommendations included sun protection, regular moisturization, and low-dose oral retinoids in one patient.

Clinical assessments: Sites of involvement were recorded, with cheeks most commonly affected, followed by preauricular areas, temporal regions (6/8), and submandibular/neck areas (5/8). Telangiectasias were noted in 4/8. Follicular papules on the forehead and ear helices were observed in 2 patients.

Dermoscopy assessments: Features recorded included reddish-brown background, numerous follicular keratotic plugs, whitish scales (perifollicular distribution), gray-blue dots and granules (peppering), telangiectasias, white rosettes under polarized light, and twisted/coiled hair within follicular prominences with overlying inflamed papules.

Histopathology: In three cases, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at ×4 magnification showed hyperkeratosis, dilated infundibula with follicular plugging, increased basal membrane pigmentation, and mild perivascular and periadnexal chronic inflammatory infiltrate.

Analysis: Descriptive statistics (counts and proportions) were reported. No inferential statistics, inter-rater reliability, or diagnostic accuracy metrics were provided. No IRB/ethics committee details were reported beyond informed consent.

Ethics: Informed consent was obtained. Funding: none. Competing interests: none.

title: Characteristic Analysis and Risk Control of Syngas Explosion during Underground Coal Gasification
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a simplified thermodynamic framework reliably estimate key explosion characteristics (maximum temperature, pressure, pressure rise rate, KG, stoichiometric concentration, LEL/UEL, oxygen safety limit) for UCG syngas across realistic initial temperatures and compositions? (2) How do initial temperature and syngas calorific value influence these parameters, and what are the implications for risk in different UCG areas? (3) Can the framework inform targeted prevention and control measures for UCG operations?

Hypotheses: (H1) Increasing initial temperature will increase maximum explosion temperature and UEL but decrease maximum pressure, LEL, and oxygen content safety limit; (H2) Explosion thermal effect, pressure rise rate, and KG will show limited dependence on initial temperature but will scale with syngas calorific value; (H3) The framework’s predictions will align with prior experimental trends for gas explosions and provide actionable thresholds for UCG risk management. Support for H1 would be demonstrated by monotonic shifts in temperature, LEL/UEL, and oxygen safety limit with temperature; support for H2 would be shown by small temperature-induced changes in pressure rise rate and KG but clear proportionality to calorific value; support for H3 would be evidenced by consistency with literature and by practical, implementable safety measures derived from the computed parameters.
reference_methodology:
Study design: The authors develop a simplified thermodynamic calculation framework for UCG syngas explosion characteristics and apply it to syngas produced by multiple gasification processes in the Huating UCG industrial test. The framework integrates reaction stoichiometry, enthalpy calculations, adiabatic temperature rise, ideal gas pressure estimation, isothermal flame speed-based pressure rise rate, and empirical formulas for explosion limits and oxygen safety limits.

Syngas composition and operating conditions: The Huating UCG test (closed mine, Ankou Town, Huating County, Gansu, China) produced syngas via air (A), air-steam (AS), oxygen-enriched (O), oxygen-enriched steam (OS), and two-stage (TS) processes. Average syngas compositions and calorific values (Table 3) include, for example, air gas (A1: H2 14.92%, CH4 1.61%, CO 11.45%, CO2 13.72%, O2 0.06%, N2 58.24%, calorific value 3.65 MJ/Nm3; A2: 15.41/2.13/12.36/11.35/0.00/58.76, 4.00 MJ/Nm3), oxygen-enriched gases (e.g., 36% O: H2 18.07%, CH4 1.59%, CO 22.19%, CO2 21.48%, O2 0.00%, N2 36.67%, 5.35 MJ/Nm3), air-steam (AS1: 13.27/1.64/15.91/10.90/0.00/58.28, 4.04 MJ/Nm3; AS2: 19.82/2.86/10.76/16.85/0.10/49.61, 4.54 MJ/Nm3), oxygen-enriched steam (e.g., 83% OS: 26.75/3.44/22.70/34.34/0.00/12.77, 7.02 MJ/Nm3), and two-stage water gas (TS-W: 41.95/9.32/20.33/0.63/31.89/0.06/7.75, 10.88 MJ/Nm3). Initial temperature range for explosion analysis is 381–1473 K (production well measurements 381–676 K, average 448 K; gasification process maxima 1073–1473 K).

Reaction stoichiometry: UCG syngas is approximated as C_aH_bO_cN_d, with reaction in air (f=3.77) or oxygen (f=0). The method assumes sufficient oxygen (positive oxygen equilibrium) to maximize heat release and determine products (CO2, H2O, N2). Stoichiometric coefficients (a,b,c,d,e,f) are computed from measured syngas composition and oxidant ratio (Table 5). For zero oxygen equilibrium, the amount of substance decreases by ~10% after complete reaction of 1 mol syngas and air.

Thermodynamics: Enthalpy of reaction ΔrHm(T) is computed via Kirchhoff’s equation using standard formation enthalpies and temperature-dependent heat capacities (298–3000 K; Table 1; Figure 2). Constant-volume heat effect QV1 is obtained from ΔrHm(T) and the ideal gas law. Maximum temperature Tf is derived under constant-volume adiabatic conditions by equating heat released to heat absorbed by products, using fitted Cp(T) and ΔfH(T) relations (Figure 2). Maximum pressure pm follows from the ideal gas law using initial and final moles and temperatures (Equation 8).

Pressure rise rate and KG: For a cavity (spherical, V≈523.60 m3, diameter 10 m; Table 4), the pressure rise rate dP/dt is modeled isothermally with flame speed v(T) (Figure 3) and turbulence factor α=1: dP/dt = (v Ap0)/(V p0) (Equation 9). For tube-like spaces (roadways, wells), dP/dt = (v p0)/(L p0) (Equation 10). KG is the product of peak dP/dt and V^(1/3) (Equation 12), noting applicability for L/D ≤ 2:1 and V ≥ 1 m3.

Explosion limits and oxygen safety limit: Stoichiometric concentration Cst is computed from reaction coefficients (Equation 13). LEL and UEL for multicomponent mixtures use Le Chatelier’s formula (Equations 14–17), with inert corrections (CO2, N2). Temperature-dependent LEL/UEL for H2 and CO are fitted from literature (Equations 20–23), and CH4/C2H4 limits are taken from literature (Table 2). Oxygen safety limit CLO(T) is estimated from stoichiometric oxygen demand at the LEL (Equation 24).

title: Design and Implementation of a General Web-based Course Teaching Management System
field_subfield: Computer Science — Web Systems; Educational Technology
research_question: The paper does not state explicit research questions or hypotheses. Its stated objective is to design and implement a general, comprehensive web-based course teaching management system that can be used by different teachers across different colleges to manage courses and teaching activities. The implicit expectations are that the system will: (1) provide flexible administration from colleges to curriculum subjects; (2) support teacher–student interaction via message boards; (3) enable online assignment submission and evaluation and attendance checking; and (4) offer rich learning resources. Outcomes that would support these expectations include successful deployment across multiple courses, functional modules for the listed features, and permission-based access control. No alternative hypotheses or quantitative benchmarks are proposed.
reference_methodology:
System architecture: A two-tier web application with a PHP front-end and MySQL back-end. The front-stage provides user-facing functionality (login, query/search, resource downloads, assignment submission/viewing, score and attendance queries, message board). The back-stage provides administrative and teacher-facing management (college/major/course/student/teacher management; attendance, assignments, notices; password changes).

Database design: Eighteen MySQL tables are defined to store website information (Figure 3). Key tables include: achievement_table (attendance and assignment management), admin_table (administrator credentials), assignments_table (teacher-set assignment information), assignment_table (student-completed assignment information), class_table (class information), download_table (uploaded/downloaded materials), attends_table (daily attendance), attend_table (student attendance for a course), faculty_table (college/department information), grade_table (grade information), major_table (major information), note_table (latest news, electronic courseware, simulated tests, assignments), messagebox_table (message board messages), referencebook_table (reference book details), student_table (student details), subject_table (subject details), teacher_subject_table (teacher–subject correspondence), and teacher_table (teacher details). The paper provides sample table structures (Figure 4) but does not report schema normalization level, indexes, or constraints.

Programming and data handling: PHP is used as the core programming language with MySQL for data storage. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are used for web page design. PHP superglobals are leveraged: $_GET for URL parameters (e.g., announcement IDs), $_POST for form submissions (e.g., login credentials, assignment data), $_FILES for file uploads (requiring enctype="multipart/form-data"), and $_SESSION for session variables (created via session_start(), destroyed via session_destroy()).

Login module: Pages include login.php, check.php, logout.php, and welcome.php. login.php sends account, password, and permission via POST to check.php, which queries teacher_table or student_table based on permission. On successful authentication, check.php creates $_SESSION variables, stores user information, and redirects to welcome.php. welcome.php retrieves login information from $_SESSION and displays it. Logout is handled by logout.php calling session_unset() and session_destroy(), returning to login.php.

Notice board module: Pages include index.php, note_list.php, shownote.php, note.php, and error.php. note_list.php (embedded in index.php) queries note_table with an SQL ORDER BY clause to sort results in descending order and displays the six most recent announcements. Clicking an announcement passes its ID via GET to shownote.php, which displays details by querying note_table with the provided ID. note.php checks $_SESSION['name'] and $_SESSION['admin'] (1=admin, 2=teacher, 3=student) to enforce permissions; students can only view notices. The parameter "action" in note.php can be list, create, or save to control listing, creating, or saving notices.

Assignment management module: Pages include admin.php, header.php, assignments_list.php, and assignment_list.php. header.php (embedded in admin.php) provides an "assignment management" link to assignments_list.php. assignments_list.php uses action parameters list, create, edit, save, del to control listing, creating, editing, saving, and deleting assignments. Initially, action defaults to list, which queries assignments_table by the user’s name (from $_SESSION['name']) to display all the user’s assignments. For create, assignments_list.php allows setting assignments; for edit, it retrieves the assignment by ID and permits modification; for delete, it executes a DELETE command on assignments_table. The save action uses POST data to either INSERT (create) or UPDATE (edit) assignments_table. assignment_list.php is activated when a user clicks an assignment name, receiving action=list and assignmentid=$fid (from assignments_table). It queries assignment_table using $_SESSION['name'] and assignmentid to display student-side assignment management and results.

Deployment and evaluation: The system is reported to be running for management of multiple courses across different teachers, offering an effective teaching and learning environment. No user counts, performance metrics, security audits, or comparative evaluations are reported.

title: Giant Star-shaped Nitrogen-doped Nanographenes
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a C3-symmetric precursor strategy enable the synthesis of highly soluble, giant star-shaped nitrogen-doped nanographenes with diameters exceeding 3.0 nm while maintaining monodispersity? (2) How do size-dependent structural features (diameter, ring count) influence optoelectronic properties (absorption/emission energies, molar absorptivity) and electrochemical levels (ELUMO, EHOMO, Egap)? (3) What are the intrinsic charge transport characteristics (carrier mobility proxies) of these SNGs in the solid state, and do they exhibit n-type behavior?

Hypotheses: (i) A C3-symmetric precursor with appropriately spaced diones and solubilizing tert-butyl/TIBS groups will facilitate iterative cyclocondensation to yield giant SNGs with high solubility. (ii) Increasing the π-system diameter will bathochromically shift absorption bands and increase molar absorptivity, while lowering ELUMO and Egap, consistent with n-type semiconductors. (iii) TRMC will reveal localized states but overall n-type charge transport (dominant electron transport) with φΣµmax on the order of 10^-4 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1.

Support/refutation criteria: Success is indicated by (a) isolation of SNG-G1 and SNG-G2 with diameters 4.1 and 6.5 nm and monodisperse HRMS; (b) bathochromic shifts and increased ε with size; (c) ELUMO becoming more negative and Egap decreasing with size; (d) TRMC showing φΣµmax ≈ 10^-4 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1 and τ1/2 in the microsecond range without oxidation in CV.
reference_methodology:
Synthesis: The team first attempted cyclocondensation of precursor A (dibenzodiazatetracene core with terminal protected ketones at the pyrene end and diamino groups at the quinoxaline end) with HKT (cyclohexane-1,2,3,4,5,6-hexaone) under standard conditions. The reaction yielded an inseparable mixture that, upon MnO2 oxidation (Bunz conditions), evolved to a major compound identified as a linear C2 ribbon-like adduct C with 13 fused aromatic rings. This outcome was attributed to early formation of dihydro intermediates that were aromatized by MnO2 and to steric/nucleophilicity factors favoring C2 over C3 condensation.

To overcome this, a C3-symmetric precursor (SNG-G0) was designed by condensing pyrene diketone D (obtained in 4 steps from pyrene and 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexaaminobenzene) with HAB-derived HAB (3 steps from 1,3,5-trichlorobenzene). The cyclocondensation proceeded cleanly to SNG-G0 in 45% yield. Deprotection of terminal o-diones with TFA/H2O afforded SNG-G0-Q (70%). Cyclocondensation of A with SNG-G0-Q yielded SNG-G1 (32% yield). Subsequent deprotection (water/TFA) and cyclocondensation with A afforded SNG-G2 (38% yield). The iterative strategy leveraged tert-butyl and tri-iso-butylsilyl (TIBS) groups to enhance solubility and avoid steric hindrance during triple cyclocondensation.

Characterization: All SNGs were highly soluble in toluene and chlorinated solvents at room temperature. Structural assignments were supported by 1H/13C NMR (sharp signals; integrations matched expected aromatic and diketal patterns) and MALDI-TOF HRMS (M+Ag+ m/z: 1553.5692, 4211.1790, 6868.7884 Da for SNG-G0, SNG-G1, SNG-G2). Isotopic distributions were recorded for SNG-G0 and SNG-G1; SNG-G2 was at the detection limit. Single crystals suitable for XRD were not obtained.

Computational modeling: GFN-xTB (Geometry, Frequency, Non-covalent, eXtended Tight-Binding) was used to model conformations and stable disk-like structures for SNG-G0, SNG-G1, and SNG-G2, yielding diameters of 1.7, 4.1, and 6.5 nm, respectively. Due to computational cost, TIBS groups on acetylenes were replaced by H atoms in TD-DFT calculations (B3LYP/6-31g(d)) for SNG-G0-H, SNG-G1-H, SNG-G2-H to compare with experimental spectra and frontier orbital energies. Differences between GFN-xTB and TD-DFT were reported as small and mostly negligible.

Optoelectronic measurements: UV-vis absorption spectra were recorded in CHCl3, revealing α, ρ, β bands and their vibronic features. Photoluminescence spectra were measured in CHCl3 with excitation wavelengths λex = 340 nm (SNG-G0), 524 nm (SNG-G1), and 540 nm (SNG-G2). Quantum yields were estimated using 9,10-diphenylanthracene in hexane (SNG-G0) and oxazine in MeOH (SNG-G1/SNG-G2) as references.

Electrochemistry: Cyclic voltammetry was performed in CH2Cl2 with 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 and ferrocene/ferrocenium (Fc/Fc+) as internal standard. Reduction waves were analyzed; oxidation processes were not observed within the solvent-electrolyte window.

Charge transport: Time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC) was conducted on solid powders (λ = 355 nm; I0 = 9.1×10^15 photons/cm^2). Pseudo-photoconductivity φΣµmax (Σµ × φ) and half-lives τ1/2 were extracted.

title: The optical properties of low redshift radio galaxies
research_question:
The central questions are: (1) Do radio galaxies’ host galaxies differ from normal ellipticals in structural and photometric properties (luminosity, size, Kormendy relation, ellipticity, isophote shape, interaction signatures, colors)? (2) Are there systematic differences between FRI and FRII hosts beyond the classical radio power segregation? (3) What is the prevalence and optical significance of nuclear point sources in radio galaxies, and how do they relate to radio core power? (4) Do outer light excesses indicate interaction-induced features or intrinsic components (disks/halos)?

Hypotheses: (H1) Radio hosts are structurally similar to normal ellipticals, with modest interaction signatures. (H2) FRI hosts are brighter and larger than FRII hosts, consistent with classical segregation. (H3) Nuclear point sources are common and correlate with radio core power but not with host luminosity. (H4) Outer light excesses are primarily due to disks/halos rather than interactions. Support for H1–H4 would be indicated by Kormendy relations matching normal ellipticals, similar ellipticity and c4 distributions, low δ and ΔPA, and a nuclear luminosity–core power correlation. Refutation would involve significant deviations in structural relations, strong interaction signatures, or lack of nuclear–radio correlations.
reference_methodology:
Sample: 79 low-redshift (z ≤ 0.12) radio galaxies selected from two complete radio surveys: the 2.7-GHz 2-Jy all-sky survey (WP) and the EK survey. Radio morphologies were classified per Fanaroff–Riley (FRI/FRII) using published radio images; unresolved sources were marked as U. Radio data include 408 MHz fluxes (PKS catalog), 2.7 GHz fluxes (WP/EK), and 4.8 GHz core fluxes (Morganti et al. 1993; upper limits when unavailable). The average radio power at 2700 MHz is 1.1 × 10^25 W Hz−1.

Imaging and photometry: R-band imaging for all 79; B-band for 29. Observations were obtained at ESO (La Silla) and NOT (La Palma). Surface photometry and quantitative morphology were performed with the AIAP package, chosen for interactive analysis in crowded fields. For each frame, the point spread function (PSF) was determined by combining radial profiles of stars of different magnitudes, enabling accurate PSF modeling in the core and wings. Errors on profiles followed Fasano & Bonoli (1990) prescriptions.

Profile decomposition: Radial brightness profiles were fit with a de Vaucouleurs bulge (I ∝ r1/4) plus optional components: (i) a nuclear point source modeled by the PSF; (ii) an exponential component (I ∝ r) to represent outer disks/halos. Fitting strategies ranged from visual inspection of residuals to χ2 minimization. For each galaxy, the authors report m_ps (nuclear), m_r1/4 (bulge), m_exp (disk/halo), Re (bulge), Rd (disk), χ2, and component notes (Table 2). Component statistics are summarized in Table 3.

Derived quantities: Integrated magnitudes within μR = 24.5 and total magnitudes from profile extrapolation were computed. Effective radius Re (semimajor axis enclosing half the total light) and effective surface brightness μe were derived. Absolute magnitudes M_HOST(24.5) and M_HOST(tot) were corrected for Galactic extinction, K-corrections (Paper I–II), and nuclear-component contributions (Table 5). Colors (B−R) and color gradients Δ(B−R)/Δlog r were computed for the 29 B-band objects, corrected for extinction, K-corrections, and nuclear components.

Structural and interaction metrics: Ellipticity ε and position angle PA were measured; c4 (Fourier coefficient) quantified isophote shape (boxy c4 < 0; disky c4 > 0). Isophote decentering δ = ΔR/R at Re quantified non-concentricity (Xc, Yo centers; Xo, Yc outer isophote centers). Isophotal twisting ΔPA was defined as the maximum absolute PA variation over observed isophotes, excluding radii < 5″ and PA errors > 8° to mitigate seeing effects.

Statistics and comparisons: Kolmogorov–Smirnov (K–S) tests compared distributions between radio galaxies and normal ellipticals. The Kormendy relation μe–Re was fit for the full sample and FRI/FRII subsamples, and compared to normal ellipticals (Hamabe & Kormendy 1987). Color distributions and gradients were compared to Peletier et al. (1990). Radio power relations (core vs total) were examined (Giovannini et al. 1988). Cosmology: H0 = 50 km s−1 Mpc−1, q0 = 0.

title: The adipose tissue endocannabinoid system in periparturient dairy cows: implications for metabolism, inflammation, and appetite
field_subfield: Animal Science — Ruminant Metabolism and Endocrinology
research_question:
The review addresses the following questions: (1) How does the ECS in bovine adipose tissue regulate adipogenesis, lipogenesis, and lipolysis during the periparturient period? (2) What are the biosynthetic and degradative pathways for key eCBs (AEA, 2-AG) in ruminant AT, and how do their expression/activity relate to metabolic status (weight loss, insulin sensitivity)? (3) How does ECS activation modulate mitochondrial function and inflammatory responses in AT, and what are the implications for periparturient metabolic health? (4) What is the role of ECS in appetite regulation and nutrient uptake in dairy cows, and how might ECS-targeted interventions influence feed intake and energy balance?

No explicit hypotheses are tested in this narrative review. Implicit propositions include: (a) ECS activation in AT during periparturient stress promotes lipogenesis/adipogenesis and suppresses lipolysis, thereby attenuating negative energy balance; (b) higher eCB levels and altered enzyme expression (e.g., MAGL) accompany intense lipolysis and insulin resistance; (c) ECS signaling intersects with inflammatory pathways in AT and reproductive tissues, with context-dependent anti- or pro-inflammatory effects; and (d) CB1-mediated modulation of appetite and intestinal barrier function could improve intake and reduce systemic inflammation. Support or refutation of these propositions is evaluated by collating quantitative and qualitative evidence from cited studies.
reference_methodology:
This is a narrative review synthesizing published literature on the ECS in bovine adipose tissue during the periparturient period. The text integrates mechanistic pathways (biosynthesis, degradation, receptor signaling) with quantitative findings from dairy cow studies. Key data points include: plasma 2-AG concentrations during the dry period and one month postpartum; AT AEA and 2-AG levels in cows with high vs low postpartum weight loss; MAGL and FAAH protein abundance in AT stratified by weight loss and insulin sensitivity; expression of ECS biosynthetic enzymes (NAPEPLD, DAGL) and receptors (CNR1, CNR2) in relation to lipolysis and inflammation; and lipoxygenase expression (ALOX5, ALOX15) dynamics across the periparturient period.

Specific study designs and sample sizes are not detailed in the provided text. Where available, the review reports numerical values and fold-changes (e.g., 2–4-fold changes in eCB-degrading enzymes in endometritis; 2.5–4-fold increases in eCB synthesis components). The review also references mechanistic studies in monogastric models (e.g., 3T3-F442A preadipocytes, human preadipocytes) to contextualize pathways, but these are not primary data for the ruminant-specific claims. No systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessments are reported in the provided text. Ethical approvals and animal welfare details are not applicable to this review format.

title: A Match Made in Cyberspace: Applicant Perspectives on a Virtual Residency Application Process
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How satisfied were residency applicants with the 2020–2021 virtual Match, and what benefits and concerns did they report? (2) Which program-provided resources (e.g., websites, virtual programming, social media) were most helpful for evaluating program fit? (3) What policy changes do applicants support for future cycles (application limits, interview limits, preference signaling), and should virtual interviews continue when in-person options are available?

The study did not state explicit hypotheses. Implicit expectations, based on prior literature, included: virtual interviews would be perceived as cost-saving and feasible; applicants might express concerns about evaluating fit and equity; and there would be mixed views on policy interventions. Outcomes that would support these expectations include high satisfaction and perceived financial access, significant concerns about interview hoarding and resource disparities, and majority support for interview limits and preference signaling.
reference_methodology:
Design: Cross-sectional post-Match survey of residency applicants who participated in the 2020–2021 NRMP cycle.

Instrument: A 30-question survey combining 5-point Likert-type items and free-response questions was developed with input from a national medical student committee focused on medical education, 2020–2021 residency applicants, and survey methodology experts. The instrument referenced NRMP and specialty-specific surveys. Five M.D. and/or Ph.D. methodology experts pre-tested the instrument for appropriateness. A pilot study with 20 fourth-year medical students assessed clarity before wide distribution.

Sampling and distribution: The survey was emailed to members of a national medical student organization; 11,243 students viewed the correspondence. The authors estimated 25% eligibility (students apply in their final year), yielding 2,811 eligible recipients. Grassroots social media efforts were also used, but overlap with the email list could not be determined. Total responses: 158; estimated response rate ≈5%.

Participants: Respondents represented 24 states and 31 specialties (including 8 combined programs). Demographics (Table 1): MD 71.5% (113/158), MD/PhD 4.4% (7/158), MD/MPH 4.4% (7/158), DO 17.0% (27/158), DO/MPH 0.6% (1/158), Other 1.9% (3/158). Gender: Female 58.9% (93/158), Male 38.6% (61/158), Non-binary 1.2% (2/158), Prefer not to answer 1.2% (2/158). Ethnicity: Non-Hispanic White 60.1% (95/158), Asian 15.8% (25/158), Hispanic/Latino 13.3% (21/158), Non-Hispanic Black/African American 3.8% (6/158), Multiracial 3.8% (6/158), Other 0.6% (1/158), Prefer not to answer 2.5% (4/158). Match result: Matched 95.6% (151/158), Unmatched 3.8% (6/158), Prefer not to answer 0.6% (1/158).

Analysis: Response percentages, 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and statistical significance were computed using a customized Python computing package. For Likert items, categories were collapsed: Agree/Strongly Agree → Agree; Disagree/Strongly Disagree → Disagree; Helpful/Extremely Helpful → Helpful; Unhelpful/Extremely Unhelpful → Unhelpful. Statistical significance was determined by testing for non-overlap among 95% CIs for Agree/Neutral/Disagree (for agreement items) and Helpful/Neutral/Unhelpful (for helpfulness items). Free-response items were thematically analyzed by three independent reviewers; discrepancies were resolved by discussion. IRB: The Vanderbilt Human Research Protections Program granted Institutional Review Board exemption.

title: COVID-19 Vaccine Booster Dose Willingness Among Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease on Infliximab and Vedolizumab: A Cross-Sectional Study
research_question: Research questions: (1) What is the prevalence of willingness to receive or receipt of a third (booster) dose of BNT162b2 among IBD patients on infliximab or vedolizumab? (2) Does booster willingness/receipt differ by initial COVID-19 vaccine type (BNT162b2 vs ChAdOx1 nCoV-19), gender, age, biologic therapy (infliximab vs vedolizumab), and nationality? The study does not state explicit a priori hypotheses. The analyses test for differences across these categories using chi-square tests at α=0.05. Outcomes supporting differences would include statistically significant chi-square results indicating higher or lower willingness/receipt in specific subgroups; null findings would indicate no significant differences.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Cross-sectional observational study at Mubarak Al-Kabeer University Hospital, Kuwait. Recruitment occurred in the gastroenterology infusion room from January 1 to March 31, 2022.

Participants: Adults (≥18 years) with confirmed IBD diagnosis (ICD-10: CD K50/K50.1/K50.8/K50.9; UC K51/K51.0/K51.2/K51.3/K51.5/K51.8/K51.9). Inclusion required two prior COVID-19 vaccine doses and current treatment with infliximab or vedolizumab for at least six weeks. Exclusions: confirmed or suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection after the second dose; corticosteroid use within two weeks of study start; severe adverse effects from prior COVID-19 vaccination.

Data collection and verification: Third-dose counseling was provided by healthcare providers during clinic/infusion visits before recruitment. Vaccination status was verified at two separate infusion-room visits eight weeks apart. Electronic medical records (EMRs) were used to extract demographics, disease characteristics, and vaccination details.

Outcomes: Primary outcome was the percentage of patients willing to receive or who had received a third (booster) dose of BNT162b2 among IBD patients on infliximab or vedolizumab. Secondary outcomes assessed differences in booster willingness/receipt by initial vaccine type (BNT162b2 vs ChAdOx1 nCoV-19), gender, age, biologic therapy, and nationality.

Statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics summarized frequencies and proportions. Chi-square tests evaluated differences in booster willingness/receipt across categories. Statistical significance was set at α=0.05. Analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2017). Reporting followed STROBE guidelines.

Sample flow and characteristics: Of 575 interviewed patients, 76 were excluded for post-second-dose infection, yielding 499 IBD patients. Median age was 34.5 years; 54.9% were female. Disease distribution was 40% CD and 60% UC. Median BMI was 25.1 kg/m²; 22.0% were smokers. Comorbidities included asthma (11.2%), diabetes (8.0%), and hypertension (6.6%). Median duration of infliximab and vedolizumab therapy was 12 and 11 months, respectively. Among infliximab users (n=400; 80.2%), 275 (68.7%) were on concomitant immunosuppressants.

title: 西准噶尔紫苏花岗岩成因岩石学研究
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Are the charnockites in the Miaoergou Batholith igneous in origin? (2) What are their crystallization temperatures and pressures, and what source(s) generated them? (3) Do charnockites and coeval alkaline granites share a common magma source? (4) What tectonic processes (e.g., underplating) governed their formation in the post-collisional ECAOB?

Hypotheses: (H1) Charnockites are igneous charnockites formed by partial melting of juvenile lower crust, not metamorphic residues. Support would include igneous textures, pyroxene thermometry/geobarometry consistent with crustal depths, and trace element signatures typical of igneous charnockites. (H2) Charnockitic magmas incorporated melt from a depleted mantle source prior to crystallization, indicated by lower εNd in restitic enclaves relative to host charnockites. (H3) Charnockites and alkaline granites share a common source, evidenced by overlapping εNd values and similar REE patterns, with alkaline granites representing more evolved, shallower-level differentiation. (H4) Post-collisional mantle upwelling and underplating triggered lower crustal melting to produce charnockites, followed by extension and emplacement of alkaline granites at upper crustal depths.
