Outcomes refuting these hypotheses would include metamorphic textures/mineral assemblages, P–T conditions inconsistent with crustal depths, isotopic disequilibrium between host and enclaves, or isotopic/geochemical divergence between charnockites and alkaline granites.
reference_methodology:
Sampling and field context: Charnockites occur as giant enclaves or pendants within the Miaoergou Batholith (Western Junggar), intruding early Carboniferous basalts and tuffaceous volcanics and later intruded by 240–270 Ma Miaoergou alkaline granites. The charnockites are interpreted to be late Paleozoic in age.

Mineral chemistry: Electron microprobe analyses (Cameca SX51) were conducted at the Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Accelerating voltage 15 kV; beam current 20 nA; counting times 10–20 s; PAP correction applied. Representative pyroxene compositions (Table 1) include orthopyroxene with En = 29.1–49.1% and clinopyroxene with Wo = 40.7–43.8%. Amphibole Mg/(Mg+Fe2+) = 0.38–0.51 (hornblende), biotite TiO2 = 3.76–5.27%, Mg/(Mg+Fe2+) = 0.27–0.56. Plagioclase An ≈ 26.4%; alkali feldspar Or ≈ 71%. Olivine Fe/(Mg+Fe2+) = 0.91–0.93 (fayalite-rich).

Whole-rock geochemistry: Major elements by XRF at the Chinese Academy of Nonferrous Metals Research Institute; FeO verified by wet chemistry. Due to abundant zircon, Zr was measured by XRF. Analytical precision: 5% for major elements; 5–10% for Zr. Trace elements by VG-PQ-3 ICP-MS (University of Hong Kong). Sm–Nd isotopes were measured at the Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. 143Nd/144Nd ratios were normalized to 146Nd/144Nd = 0.7219. εNd(T) was calculated using zircon U–Pb age of 320 Ma.

P–T estimation: Temperature constraints from pyroxene thermometry: Wood & Banno binary thermometer (orthopyroxene–garnet) yielded T = 709–826 °C; Lindsley ternary geothermometer (Di–En–Hd–Fs) for clinopyroxene coexisting with orthopyroxene gave 700–800 °C. Pressure constraints from olivine–pyroxene geobarometry (Muller, calibrated for 700–800 °C): P = −41.224 + 23.709 XopxFe + 18.263 XolFe + 0.0143 T (°C), yielding P = 3.78–4.88 kPa (15–20 km). A FeO–MgO–CaO–SiO2 barometer (Davidson & Lindsley) using the opx–olivine–quartz assemblage at 800 °C gave P = 378–575 kPa. Reported P–T ranges are 700–820 °C and 378–525 kPa (15–20 km).

Isotopic and trace element modeling: Chondrite-normalized REE patterns (Figure 5a) show mild LREE enrichment (La/Sm)N = 1.65–1.99 and Eu negative anomalies (Eu/Eu* = 0.59–0.89). Primitive mantle-normalized patterns (Figure 4) show LREE enrichment and negative Nb–Ti–P anomalies with positive K–Zr–Sr–Ba anomalies. Sm–Nd isotopes (Table 4) give 143Nd/144Nd = 0.51275–0.51282 and εNd(T) = +4.8 to +5.9; T(DM) = 690–790 Ma. Enclaves (Figure 5b) have εNd(T) = +2.6 to +3.5 and similar REE patterns to host charnockites.

Comparative analysis: Alkaline granites from the same region have εNd(T) = +5.0 to +5.8, similar REE patterns, but stronger Eu–Sr–Ba negative anomalies and are interpreted to have crystallized at 7–8 km depth.

title: The Role of Investments in Energy in Enhancing Environmental Sustainability in Developing Countries
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do energy investments (private participation and public-private partnerships) affect CO2 emissions in developing countries? (2) Do GDP per capita and its square (EKC) exhibit the expected inverted-U relationship with emissions? (3) How does FDI influence emissions, and does its effect vary by income level? (4) What is the role of health expenditures in environmental sustainability? (5) What are the short-run adjustment dynamics toward long-run equilibrium?

Hypotheses: H1: Energy investments (EIP, EIPP) increase CO2 emissions in developing countries due to fossil fuel dominance and growth-driven energy demand. H2: GDPPC exhibits a positive long-run effect on CO2, while GDPPC² exhibits a negative effect (EKC). H3: FDI increases CO2 in developing countries (Pollution Haven Hypothesis), but the effect may be negative in higher-income countries with stricter environmental policies. H4: Higher health expenditures reduce CO2 via productivity gains and policy shifts toward greener technologies. H5: Short-run deviations from equilibrium are corrected over time (negative ECT). Support for H1–H4 is evaluated via long-run CS-ARDL coefficients; H5 via ECT significance. Alternative outcomes include null or negative effects of EIP/EIPP in higher-income groups if investments are directed toward renewables and efficiency improvements.
reference_methodology:
Design: Panel econometric analysis using second-generation CS-ARDL to estimate long-run and short-run relationships between CO2 emissions and determinants across income groups.

Sample and data: 88 developing countries (1990–2022). Of 134 developing countries, 46 were excluded due to missing energy investment data. Data sources: World Development Indicators (WDI). Variables: Dependent variable CO2 (metric tons per capita). Regressors: GDPPC (% annual), GDPPC² (EKC), EIP (investment in energy with private participation, % of GDP), EIPP (investment in energy with public-private partnerships, % of GDP), FDI (net inflows, % of GDP), HE (out-of-pocket health expenditure, % of current health expenditure). Summary statistics (Table 4) show non-normal distributions (Jarque–Bera p=0.000) and large skewness/kurtosis for EIP and EIPP.

Pre-estimation diagnostics: Second-generation panel unit root tests indicate mixed integration orders. For developing countries, GDPPC, HE, FDI, and CO2 are I(1); EIP and EIPP are I(0). For low-income countries, GDPPC, HE, and CO2 are I(1); EIP, EIPP, and FDI are I(0). Lower-middle and upper-middle groups exhibit similar mixed orders. Pesaran’s CD test indicates cross-sectional dependence. Slope homogeneity tests (Delta and HAC-adjusted Delta) show homogeneous slopes (e.g., Delta test p=0.000; HAC-adjusted Delta p=0.000 across groups).

Estimation: CS-ARDL with lagged cross-sectional averages to address cross-sectional dependence and weak exogeneity. The model yields mean-group long-run coefficients and short-run dynamics via an error correction term (ECT). The specification includes GDPPC and GDPPC² to test EKC, EIP and EIPP to capture energy investment channels, FDI to test Pollution Haven Hypothesis, and HE to proxy social sustainability. No explicit lag lengths, weighting schemes, or robustness checks beyond CS-ARDL are reported in the provided text. No IRB/ethics approvals are applicable.

Statistical reporting: Long-run and short-run coefficients with significance stars (1%, 5%, 10%) are presented in Table 9. ECT coefficients and standard errors are reported. No confidence intervals or effect sizes (e.g., elasticity magnitudes) are provided. No details on software, random seeds, or data cleaning procedures are included in the provided text.

title: Hydrological Analysis of Agricultural Reservoir Watersheds Based on Water Utilization System Using the Catchment Hydrology Cycle Analysis Tool Model
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does subdividing the Hantan River Dam upstream watershed into smaller units (including reservoir-informed sub-basins) improve hydrological simulation efficiency compared to a single-basin or coarser subdivision? (2) How do agricultural reservoir operations and wastewater discharge influence model performance and water balance estimates? (3) Can the CAT model reproduce observed reservoir water level dynamics under normal and drought conditions, and what discrepancies arise? (4) What are the implications of observed hydrologic anomalies (e.g., 2014 drought) for water management in a transboundary basin?

Hypotheses: (H1) Finer watershed subdivision that reflects reservoir presence will increase model efficiency (higher NSE) by better capturing spatial heterogeneity and management controls. (H2) Including wastewater discharge as an input will improve overall performance, particularly post-drought, by closing a portion of the water balance. (H3) Reservoir water level simulations will align with observations under normal conditions but will deviate during droughts due to external supply and data gaps. (H4) The 2014 drought will manifest as reduced inflows and altered runoff rates, with evidence of out-of-basin inflows and snowmelt contributions.

Support/refutation: H1 is supported by higher NSE in 27 sub-basins vs. single basin. H2 is partially supported: overall performance improved post-2014 with wastewater inclusion, but scenario-wise differences remained. H3 is supported: 2014 drought shows mismatches (e.g., Hagal Reservoir) and missing pumping data. H4 is supported by 2014 inflow reduction (221.90 vs. 778.31 million m³ average) and monthly outflow/inflow patterns.
reference_methodology:
Study area: The Hantan River Dam upstream watershed (Han River basin) spans 1,285.73 km² with a maximum elevation of 1,172.52 m. The Hantan River joins Namdaecheon Stream, merges with the Imjin River, and flows into the Han River. The basin is transboundary, with 2/3 of the Imjin basin upstream in North Korea, complicating data availability and management. There are 7 water level observation stations and 11 precipitation stations. Land cover (2010) is based on the Ministry of Environment’s 2010 land cover map using Landsat 7; the upper reaches (mostly North Korea) are 68% forest and 24% agricultural land. Impermeable area is 26.33 km² (2% of the basin). Average elevation is EL 423.49 m; average slope is 20.94%.

Data: Spatial datasets include topography (Korea National Geography Institute, 1:5,000), soil (Korea Rural Development Administration, 1:25,000; soil properties including texture, porosity, wilting point, field capacity, saturated hydraulic conductivity), land cover (1:25,000), precipitation (Korea Meteorological Administration, daily, 2010–2017), streamflow (Han River Flood Control Office, daily, 2010–2017), reservoir operation data (Korea Rural Community Corporation, 2010–2017; storage volumes, bottom surfaces, saturated permeability coefficients, spillway/outlet dimensions, on-site confirmation elevations), groundwater usage (National Groundwater Information Center, 2010–2017), and wastewater discharge (Korea Ministry of Environment, 2012–2017). Groundwater usage data comprise 34,811 records from 3,133 tube wells (2007–2016), with 4,498 (13%) reported; 30,313 (87%) lacked location or were closed. Of reported locations, 86% are household and 12% agricultural. Annual groundwater usage in the standard watershed is 13.33 million m³. Wastewater discharge averaged 4.67 million m³ annually.

Model setup: The CAT model divides the watershed into permeable and impermeable areas, simulating infiltration, evaporation, and groundwater flow at each spatial unit. Soil and aquifer are represented as single layers; groundwater intake is considered. Evapotranspiration uses the Penman–Monteith method. Infiltration options include Rainfall Excess, Green–Ampt, and Horton. Channel routing uses Muskingum, Muskingum–Cunge, or kinematic wave methods. The watershed was delineated into three scenarios: (1) one basin, (2) five sub-basins per standard criteria, and (3) 27 sub-basins incorporating 11 agricultural reservoirs. Reservoir stage–storage curves (2010–2017) were derived from 11 reservoirs; overflow heights were field-verified, with field data overriding specifications for the Jail reservoir. External water supply and leakage in the water supply network were included.

Calibration and evaluation: Parameters were calibrated using groundwater usage, wastewater discharge, sewage usage, and wastewater processing volume. Model efficiency was evaluated using Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) computed from groundwater and wastewater discharge data. Simulations were performed for 2010–2017, with scenario-wise comparisons and year-specific analyses (including 2014 drought).

title: Probabilistic reconstruction of measles transmission clusters from routinely collected surveillance data
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a Bayesian MCMC model using age, location, genotype, and onset date reconstruct measles transmission clusters and infer importation status from routine surveillance data with accuracy comparable to contact-tracing-derived clusters? (2) How does incorporating spatial connectivity (exponential gravity model) affect precision and sensitivity of inferred clusters? (3) How do different importation status assumptions (ideal, epidemiological, inferred) and thresholds for removing unlikely links (λ) influence cluster size distributions and importation identification? (4) Can the inferred cluster size distributions and derived metrics (importation-to-subsequent cases ratio, reproduction numbers) identify pockets of susceptibility and transmission intensity across states?

Hypotheses: (i) Including spatial connectivity will improve cluster reconstruction by reducing spurious long-distance links and aligning inferred clusters with reference clusters. (ii) When importation status is known (ideal or epidemiological), inferred clusters will closely match reference clusters. (iii) Inferring importation status without prior information will be challenging, with sensitivity to λ; combining prior importation information with inference will yield the best agreement with reference clusters. (iv) The model will identify high-transmission pockets (e.g., states with large outbreaks) and characterize heterogeneity in transmission potential (e.g., many cases with no onward transmission; a small fraction with high onward transmission).
reference_methodology:
Design: Bayesian MCMC inference of probabilistic transmission trees and importation status using routinely collected variables: age (5-year groups), location (county centroid), genotype (N-450-based), and rash onset date. The model estimates infection dates, infector assignments, and importation status, and infers cluster size distributions.

Likelihood components: For each case i with infector j and infection time ti, the individual log-likelihood L_i(ti, j, θ) is the sum of (i) the incubation period likelihood f(ti − T_i), where T_i is onset date; and (ii) the connection likelihood L_ij(ti, tj, θ). The connection likelihood combines: (a) temporal probability w_k(ti − tj) for k generations between i and j, with w_k obtained by convolving the generation time distribution k times; (b) a geometric distribution for the number of missing generations k given the conditional report ratio ρ; (c) age-specific contact probabilities a(α_i, α_j, k) from POLYMOD; (d) genotype compatibility G(g_i, g_tree), where each tree has at most one reported genotype; and (e) spatial connectivity s(r_i, r_j | a, b) using an exponential gravity model with parameters a (population scaling) and b (distance decay), computed from county population centroids and inter-county distances.

Priors and parameters: ρ (conditional report ratio) is assigned a beta prior informed by the proportion of clusters whose first case was not classified as imported. Spatial parameters a and b are assigned uniform priors on [0, 5]. Incubation period and generation time distributions are taken from prior studies. Age contact probabilities are from POLYMOD (UK), with cross-country comparability argued to be reasonable.

Pre-clustering: To reduce search space, potential infectors are restricted to same-genotype cases within γ = 100 km and within δ = 30 days of onset (above the 97.5% upper quantile of the generation time with a missing generation). Cases with no potential infector are considered importations. Cases are grouped by shared potential infectors.

MCMC and proposals: A Metropolis–Hastings algorithm samples parameters (ρ, a, b) and transmission trees. Eight proposals are used: five adapted from outbreaker2 (change generations, ρ, infection time, infector, swap infector–infectee), two to update a and b (recomputing spatial probabilities), and one to change the ancestor of a tree while preserving the number of trees. The maximum number of missing generations is capped at 2 when estimating a or b. A short preliminary run (30,000–70,000 iterations) identifies unlikely links using a threshold λ (absolute or relative quantile of individual log-likelihoods). The minimum number of importations is added to the initial tree for the long run. The long run (100,000 iterations) is thinned and burn-in removed; unlikely links are deleted per iteration, and clusters are identified.

Evaluation: Performance is assessed by comparing inferred clusters to contact-tracing-derived reference clusters via sensitivity (proportion of reference cluster members inferred with i) and precision (proportion of inferred cluster members that are in the reference cluster) per case, and by comparing cluster size distributions. State-level importation-to-subsequent cases ratios and inferred reproduction numbers are computed from the posterior samples. Convergence is assessed via posterior traces (Supplement Figure S3).

title: phbuilder: a tool for efficiently setting up constant pH molecular dynamics simulations in GROMACS
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can phbuilder automate the preparation of constant pH MD simulations in GROMACS from initial protein structures and from existing systems, ensuring correct structure/topology modifications, parameter files, ion/buffer neutralization, and stable simulations? (2) Can phbuilder streamline parameterization of new titratable groups by providing a two-step workflow (fast TI + Boltzmann reweighting) that yields accurate V_MM fits, evidenced by flat λ-coordinate distributions at pH=pKa with zero barrier? (3) Does the tool’s solvation cleaning script reliably remove waters erroneously placed inside the protein without disrupting the system?

Hypotheses: (H1) Automated setup via phbuilder will produce stable constant pH MD simulations with evolving protonation states across diverse systems (soluble proteins and a membrane protein). (H2) The two-step parameterization will correct initial TI biases, producing flat λ distributions after reweighting, indicating improved V_MM accuracy. (H3) The solvation cleaning algorithms will effectively remove internal waters while preserving the solvated structure. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include 10 ns stable runs with evolving λ-trajectories, flat λ distributions post-reweighting for arginine, and qualitative success of the cleaning script. Refutation would involve unstable runs, non-flat λ distributions after reweighting, or failure to remove internal waters.
reference_methodology:
Tool inputs and dependencies: phbuilder requires a structure file (.pdb or .gro) and a target pH. It currently supports a modified CHARMM36m force field with dihedral modifications for improved sampling of titratable side chains. The GROMACS constant pH implementation is used. phbuilder reads a global configuration file (lambdagrouptypes.dat) that defines titratable group types (atom names, charges per protonation state, pKa values, and polynomial coefficients for V_MM). Users can optionally specify ion concentration and buffer particle count.

Core components: (1) gentopol: selects residues to be titratable, modifies the structure to add dummy hydrogens, regenerates the topology (via gmx pdb2gmx), assigns initial λ-values based on the target pH, and saves the mapping between λ-coordinates and residues. If needed, systems can be solvated using gmx editconf and gmx solvate. (2) neutralize: ensures net-neutral charge by adding ions (0.1 M Na+/Cl− by default unless specified) and buffer particles to compensate for charge fluctuations during constant pH. Buffer count defaults to the number of titratable sites (N_sites), with guidance to keep buffer λ near 0.5; increasing buffers up to ~2N_sites can reduce charge fluctuations but may alter solvent properties. (3) genparams: generates .mdp files with constant pH parameters, group type descriptions (from lambdagrouptypes.dat), and atom-to-group mappings.

Solvation cleaning: A Python script (clean_after_solvate.py) removes waters inside the protein using two algorithms. Algorithm 1 counts the number of water atoms within a sphere of radius R (default 10 Å) around each water molecule; waters inside the protein have fewer neighbors than Ncutoff=120 (default), and are removed. Algorithm 2 identifies the N_neighbors nearest residues (default 20) and removes waters if the fraction of water neighbors is below a threshold (default 3). Default parameters may require tuning per system.

Parameterization workflow: For new titratable groups, phbuilder automates (i) fast TI to obtain an approximate V_MM polynomial fit and (ii) reweighting using Boltzmann inversion on long sampling runs at pH=pKa with zero barrier. The reweighting corrects initial TI biases by adjusting V_MM so that the λ distribution becomes flat. Scripts provided: create_parameterization.py (prepares directories and .mdp for parameterization runs), fit_parameterization.py (computes optimal V_MM coefficients and updates lambdagrouptypes.dat and .mdp), and create_titration.py (prepares titration runs).

Simulation systems and setup: Three systems were prepared: (1) cardiotoxin V (PDB 1CVO) with 4 titratable groups; (2) barnase–barstar (PDB 1BRS) with 30 titratable groups; (3) GLIC (PDB 6ZGD) embedded in a POPC bilayer (prepared via CHARMM-GUI). For cardiotoxin V and barnase–barstar, proteins were placed in cubic boxes with 2.0 nm buffer, solvated with ~17,000 and ~31,000 CHARMM TIP3P waters, respectively, and neutralized with 0.1 M Na+/Cl−. For GLIC, the system contained ~62,000 TIP3P waters, 489 POPC lipids, and 0.15 M Na+/Cl−. Arginine was modeled as an Ala–Arg–Ala tripeptide with capped termini in a ~5×5×5 nm^3 box, ~5,000 TIP3P waters, and 0.15 M Na+/Cl−.

Simulation parameters: CHARMM36 all-atom force field with dihedral modifications; PME electrostatics (1.2 nm real-space cutoff; 0.14 nm grid); Lennard-Jones with switching from 1.0–1.2 nm; v-rescale thermostat at 300 K (0.5 ps^-1); c-rescale barostat at 1 bar (5.0 ps; semi-isotropic for GLIC); leapfrog integrator; 2 fs timestep; LINCS for bonds to H; SETTLE for water. For constant pH, Asp, Glu, and His were titratable with reference pKa values: Asp 3.65, Glu 4.25, His HSD 6.53, His HSE 6.92. λ-particles: mass 5 a.u.; thermostat 2.0 ps^-1; biasing barrier 7.5 kJ/mol. Equilibration: 10 ps NVT (fixed λ), 10 ps NPT (fixed λ). Production: 10 ns constant pH at pH=4 (cardiotoxin V; GLIC) and pH=7 (barnase–barstar). For arginine parameterization: 1 ns fixed-λ runs; then 10 replicas of 100 ns at pH=pKa with zero barrier; reweight V_MM; then another 10 replicas of 100 ns at pH=pKa with zero barrier using updated V_MM.

title: Fidesz, liberal democracy and the fundamental law in Hungary
field_subfield: Political Science — Comparative Politics and Constitutional Law
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Do specific provisions of the 2012 Fundamental Law violate liberal democratic principles as defined by embedded democracy? (2) Are such violations linked to Fidesz’s populist ideology, particularly in weakening checks and balances and curtailing minority rights?

Hypotheses: (H1) Populist governments will primarily target institutions that serve as counterweights to majority decisions (separation of powers, especially judicial review), thereby weakening horizontal accountability. (H2) Populist governments will curtail civil rights protections for minorities, consistent with a homogeneous “people” narrative. (H3) Some reforms will not violate liberal democratic principles if they align with standard practices in other democracies or do not reduce individual rights/access to courts.

Expected outcomes: Support for H1 would be indicated by constitutional changes that reduce judicial independence or remove judicial review in core policy areas (e.g., budget). Support for H2 would be indicated by provisions that politicize minority rights (e.g., religious recognition). H3 would be supported if reforms mirror international norms (e.g., two-thirds judicial selection) or preserve individual rights (e.g., limiting ex-post review to personal cases).
reference_methodology:
Design: Comparative legal analysis of seven institutional changes in Hungary’s constitutional order, operationalizing Merkel et al.’s embedded democracy criteria into dichotomous indicators. The approach follows a two-step process: (1) screen each change against indicators to detect potential backsliding; (2) qualitatively assess severity using Merkel et al.’s thresholds and comparative analysis to determine whether the change breaches liberal democratic principles.

Data: The 1949 Basic Law and the 2012 Fundamental Law; transitional provisions (not originally constitutional but later given constitutional rank); secondary legal literature and comparative references (e.g., Germany, Poland, Italy, Austria, Switzerland). Quantitative context: Hungary’s public debt at 84.5% of GDP; OECD data indicating debt has not fallen below 50% since 1995.

Operationalization: The authors adapt Merkel et al.’s five partial regimes into indicators (e.g., universal suffrage; free and fair elections; judicial independence; separation of powers; effective power to govern). Indicators are framed as dichotomous questions (yes/no), where an affirmative answer signals a backslide. Thresholds from embedded democracy theory guide classification of defective democracies (exclusive, illiberal, delegative, domain). Comparative analysis is used to contextualize reforms (e.g., Germany’s proportional electoral commission for constitutional court nominations; Verfassungsbeschwerde vs. actio popularis).

Cases analyzed: (1) Appointment of HCC President (Article 24): Parliament selects with two-thirds majority for 12 years. (2) Selection method for HCC judges: Subcommittees reflect parliamentary strength; two-thirds majority required. (3) HCC competencies in budgetary matters (Article 37 IV): Full review only if debt <50% of GDP; otherwise limited to specific rights. (4) Civil rights—abolishment of actio popularis: Ex-post review limited to personal cases. (5) Effective power to govern—Budget Council (Article 44): Three-member council (President of Republic appoints one; President of National Bank of Hungary; President of State Audit Office) must consent to budget; failure to approve by March 31 allows dissolution. (6) Transitional—National Office for the Judiciary (NOJ): President elected by Parliament for 9 years; powers include case reassignment and judge appointments/removals (later amended). (7) Transitional—Recognition of religious communities (Article 21): Parliamentary recognition with higher thresholds (1,000 petitioners; 20 years presence or 100 years international operation).

Analysis: For each case, the authors assess whether the change reduces judicial independence, removes judicial review in core areas, politicizes minority rights, or creates non-elected veto power over reserved domains. They then evaluate whether the change breaches liberal democratic principles using Merkel et al.’s criteria and thresholds. No statistical tests are reported; the study is qualitative and legal-comparative.

title: Giant-magnetoimpedance-based sensitive element as a model for biosensors
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Does a thin ferrofluid layer on a Co-based amorphous ribbon measurably alter the MI response compared to an uncovered ribbon, and how does this dependence vary with applied bias field, excitation current amplitude, and frequency? (2) Can the MI-based prototype detect fringe fields from magnetic nanoparticles embedded in ferrofluid, supporting a two-step biosensing workflow? (3) What field range and operating conditions maximize sensitivity and stability?

Hypotheses: (H1) Ferrofluid coverage increases the MI ratio at zero field (ΔZ/Z(H=0)) across frequencies, with the largest enhancement at an intermediate frequency (e.g., ~3.5 MHz). (H2) The MI response of the covered sensor will differ in shape and magnitude from the uncovered sensor, particularly near zero field, due to ferrofluid-induced changes in surface magnetic field and permeability. (H3) There exists a critical bias field (~6–7 Oe) above which ferrofluid particle agglomeration and increased damping reduce the MI response of the covered sensor relative to the uncovered sensor. (H4) The MI-based prototype can serve as a biosensor for detecting fringe fields from nanoparticles, leveraging high sensitivity and robustness in aggressive media.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if ΔZ/Z(H=0) is higher for the covered sensor across frequencies. H2 is supported if the covered sensor exhibits distinct MI curve shapes (e.g., single vs double peaks) and higher induced voltages at low fields. H3 is supported if the covered sensor’s response crosses below the uncovered sensor’s response above ~6–7 Oe. H4 is supported if the setup demonstrates detectable field changes attributable to nanoparticle fringe fields and if the sensor’s properties align with biosensing requirements.
reference_methodology:
Materials: Vitrovac 6025 amorphous ribbons (Co67Fe4Mo1.5Si16.5B11) produced by single-roller quenching. Ribbon dimensions: 1×0.02×100 mm. Post-processing: annealed at 340 °C for 1 h under Ar to enhance magnetic softness and reduce oxidation. Saturation magnetostriction: 2.8×10^-7.

Sensor geometry and setup: The ribbon is mounted horizontally as the sensitive element. A Cu-lead imprinted circuit is used for a four-point impedance measurement. The induced voltage is measured over a 60 mm active length. The active surface area of the prototype without isolation is ~100 mm², with a ferrofluid volume of ~2.5 mm³. Ferrofluid (Ferrotec Corporation, USA) is applied uniformly in a shadow zone (central area) such that the ribbon is narrower than the ferrofluid application area, avoiding direct contact between the ferrofluid and the Cu pickup lead.

Excitation and measurement: A sinusoidal drive current flows along the ribbon’s longitudinal axis. Frequency range: 0.3–10 MHz. Drive current amplitudes: I_rms = 1.5 mA and 11 mA. Lower currents yield weaker field sensitivity; higher currents reduce reproducibility, likely due to nonlinear circuit effects. The induced voltage U(V) is recorded using a Tektronix 2232 oscilloscope. A bias magnetic field is applied via a pair of Helmholtz coils parallel to the ribbon axis. Longitudinal hysteresis loops were measured inductively at 48 Hz.

Definitions and metrics: The giant MI ratio is defined as ΔZ/Z(H) = 100×[Z(H)−Z(H_max)]/Z(H_max), with H_max = ±150 Oe. Field dependence is assessed for both increasing (up) and decreasing (down) fields to probe hysteresis. Frequency dependence is evaluated at multiple points, with 3.5 MHz selected for detailed analysis due to the largest difference between covered and uncovered responses.

Controls and comparisons: Measurements are performed on the same ribbon both with and without ferrofluid coverage. The response is compared across two excitation currents (1.5 mA and 11 mA) and across a range of bias fields. The MI curve shape (double vs single peak) and induced voltage magnitude are compared qualitatively and quantitatively where possible.

Unreported details: Exact environmental conditions (temperature, humidity), calibration procedures, number of replicates, randomization, and statistical tests are not reported. No explicit mention of sample preparation variability or long-term stability tests.

title: Steady-State Statistical Sputtering Model for Extracting Depth Profiles from Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Dynamic SIMS
field_subfield: Chemistry — Surface Science and Analytical Chemistry
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a revised SSM that uses steady-state MD parameters (sputtering and displacement distributions) accurately reproduce depth profiles and their evolution with erosion? (2) How do the sputtering information depth (width of the sputtering distribution) and interlayer mixing (displacement coefficients) influence the shape, width, and peak position of depth profiles? (3) How sensitive are predictions to layer thickness and to the inclusion of mixing? (4) Can the model explain and predict experimental observations, such as depth resolution in Ni:Cr multilayers and the improvement in depth profiles with sample rotation?

Hypotheses: (H1) Parameters extracted from the steady-state region will yield depth profiles that match MD trends in layer filling versus monolayer equivalents removed. (H2) Increasing mixing (larger D_{j,j′}) will shift the ARF peak deeper and lengthen the trailing edge decay, with minimal impact on width. (H3) Broadening the sputtering distribution (information depth) will primarily increase ARF width and affect all ARF parameters, not only the leading edge growth length. (H4) Depth profiles are largely insensitive to layer thickness up to ~rms roughness. (H5) Sample rotation reduces rms roughness and narrows sputtering distributions, producing narrower ARFs with peaks closer to the true delta-layer position.

Support/refutation criteria: Agreement between SS-SSM and MD layer filling trends supports H1. Observed shifts in ARF peak and trailing edge with mixing support H2. Increased ARF width with broader sputtering distributions supports H3. Minimal changes in profiles across layer thicknesses up to ~rms roughness supports H4. Reduced rms roughness and narrower ARFs under random azimuthal incidence support H5.
reference_methodology:
System and indices: The target is Ag(111) bombarded by 20 keV C60 at normal incidence. The system is discretized into space-fixed layers with index i (1 ≤ i ≤ N) and reference-level layers with index j = i − i_av, where i_av is the average surface level (e.g., i_av = 3 in Figure 1). The filling factor θ_i is defined as θ_i = n_i / N_atoms, with n_i the current number of atoms in layer i and N_atoms the number of atoms in a fully filled layer (0 ≤ θ_i ≤ 1).

Differential equations: The SS-SSM solves dθ_i/dx = −C_j θ_i − ∑_{i′ ≠ i} D_{j,j′} θ_i (1 − θ_{i′}) + ∑_{i′ ≠ i} D_{j′,j} θ_{i′} (1 − θ_i), where x is the number of monolayer equivalents removed. Sputtering losses are proportional to C_j θ_i; displacement terms represent gains/losses between layers via D_{j,j′} θ_i (1 − θ_{i′}) and D_{j′,j} θ_{i′} (1 − θ_i). The average surface level i_av is updated when (Y/N_atoms) ∑_i C_j θ_i equals 1 over consecutive integration steps, indicating removal of one monolayer equivalent; Y is the total sputtering yield.

Parameter extraction from MD: The steady-state region is identified from a “divide and conquer” MD simulation (20 keV C60 on Ag(111) normal incidence) where rms roughness stabilizes and the average surface level recedes at a constant rate (Figure 2). For each impact in the steady-state region, atoms are binned into layers of thickness 0.94 nm (four Ag(111) atomic layers). The average surface level is computed as the mean of the highest atom positions in columns; rms roughness is the root-mean-square deviation of the highest atom positions relative to the average surface level. Parameters are averaged over 1000 impacts. The average filling factor ⟨θ_j⟩ is computed per layer (Figure 3). For each impact, the sputtering yield per layer γ_{j,k} is evaluated; the average sputtering yield per layer Γ_j = (1/K) ∑_k γ_{j,k} (K = number of impacts) is obtained (Figure 4–5). The total sputtering yield Y = ∑_j Γ_j (eq 4). Sputtering coefficients are defined as C_j = 0 if ⟨θ_j⟩ = 0; otherwise C_j = Γ_j / (Y ⟨θ_j⟩) (eq 5), with normalization ∑_j C_j ⟨θ_j⟩ = 1 (eq 6). Displacement coefficients D_{j,j′} are defined as 0 if ⟨θ_j⟩ = 0 or ⟨θ_{j′}⟩ = 1; otherwise D_{j,j′} = Δ_{j,j′} / (Y ⟨θ_j⟩ (1 − ⟨θ_{j′}⟩)) (eq 7), where Δ_{j,j′} is the average number of atoms displaced from layer j to j′.

Depth profile computation: The differential equations are integrated to obtain θ_i(x). To reconstruct depth profiles of original layers, the system is decomposed into N subsystems, each tracking the evolution of particles originating from one initial layer. Each subsystem starts with a single occupied layer at its initial filling factor and is integrated independently. The fate of particles from each initial layer is tracked, and the total depth distribution is obtained by summing across subsystems. Depth profiles are computed as the negative derivative of the fraction of particles from an initial layer that remain in the system. The Dowsett ARF is fitted to SS-SSM outputs: ARF(x) = N[(1 − erf(ξ1)) exp((x − x0)/λ_g + σ^2/(2λ_g^2)) + (1 + erf(ξ2)) exp(−(x − x0)/λ_d + σ^2/(2λ_d^2))], with ξ1 and ξ2 defined in terms of x, x0, σ, λ_g, and λ_d (eq 8–9). The integral of the ARF is constrained to unity.

Sensitivity analyses: (1) Layer thickness is varied from 0.47 nm (two Ag(111) layers) to 4.72 nm (Figure 8). (2) Mixing is varied by selectively retaining interlayer displacement terms (Figure 9) and by scaling D_{j,j′} relative to C_j (Figure 10). (3) The sputtering distribution width is varied by scaling Γ_j while maintaining normalization (Figure 11). (4) For 70° incidence, parameters are computed for a single azimuthal angle and for random azimuthal angles (computational equivalent of sample rotation) (Figure 12–13).

title: A Large Sporadic Intra-abdominal Desmoid-Type Fibromatosis in a Young Male: A Case Report
research_question:
Research question: In a symptomatic, large sporadic intra-abdominal desmoid-type fibromatosis arising from the ileocolic mesentery, can complete surgical resection with negative margins be achieved safely and effectively, and what are the short-term outcomes and recurrence status?

Hypothesis: For a symptomatic, progressive, and operable intra-abdominal DTF with mass effect on bowel and organs, surgical resection with en bloc removal of involved bowel segments and primary anastomosis will yield negative margins and short-term recurrence-free status, supported by multidisciplinary imaging and histopathologic confirmation.

Predicted outcomes supporting the hypothesis include: (1) successful en bloc resection with negative margins on resected bowel segments; (2) absence of residual or recurrent disease on early postoperative imaging; and (3) favorable short-term recovery. Outcomes refuting the hypothesis would include positive margins, early recurrence, or significant postoperative complications. The case report evaluates these outcomes over a 3-month follow-up period.
reference_methodology:
Design: Single-patient case report with retrospective diagnostic assessment, surgical intervention, and short-term follow-up.

Patient: 24-year-old male with a 4-week history of increasing abdominal pain and progressive weight gain; otherwise healthy; no prior surgery or medical interventions; family history notable for a sister with thyroid cancer at age 18; social history included prior service in the Marines; reported bicycle trauma to the abdomen 1 month prior to presentation.

Clinical examination: Distended abdomen, firm, non-tender, no guarding or rebound; abdomen non-tympanic.

Imaging: Abdominal/pelvic CT identified a large intra-abdominal mass up to 30 cm. MRI delineated a 31 × 25 × 12 cm homogeneous intraperitoneal/mesenteric mass with internal vascularity exerting mass effect on adjacent bowel loops and intra-abdominal organs (Figure 1). Preoperative CT angiography mapped the vascular pedicle arising from a distal branch of the SMA near the ileocolic region, sparing other mesenteric vessels (Figure 2).

Biopsy and pathology: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy. Immunohistochemistry: negative for AE1/3, D2-40, EMA, MUC4, BCL2; weakly positive for CD68 and cytoplasmic beta-catenin; rarely positive nuclear calretinin; microfocal positivity for muscle-specific actin; scattered cells with cytoplasmic smooth muscle actin positivity. These findings, together with clinical presentation, were consistent with DTF. No evidence of FAP or Gardner syndrome was identified.

Genetic testing: No mutation of the APC gene. Beta-catenin staining was weakly cytoplasmic with no nuclear positivity.

Surgical procedure: Open laparotomy. The tumor was well-defined and encapsulated but densely adherent to the right lateral abdominal wall, liver, and right retroperitoneum. Posteriorly, it was intimately associated with the terminal ileum, cecum, and ascending colon with loss of tissue planes. The vascular pedicle was identified and confirmed to originate from the ileocolic artery. The team performed an en bloc resection of the tumor with terminal ileum, cecum, and ascending colon, followed by primary ileocolic anastomosis.

Perioperative course: The patient tolerated surgery well, ambulated by POD 1, passed flatus by POD 3, resumed full diet by POD 4, and was discharged home.

Follow-up: Postoperative visit at 9 days showed good recovery and return to baseline activity. Surveillance MRI at 3 months showed no residual or recurrent lesion (Figure 3). The patient continued surveillance with clinical evaluation and repeat MRI every 3–6 months at an outside institution.

Ethics: Written informed consent was obtained for publication of potentially identifiable images/data. Institutional review board approval is not reported.

title: Non-Intrusive Electric Load Monitoring in Commercial Buildings
field_subfield: Building Science — HVAC and Electrical Monitoring
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can centralized NILM at a building’s HVAC service entrance detect on/off transitions of major HVAC equipment (chillers, pumps, fans) with sufficient accuracy to support control confirmation and fault detection? (2) Which filtering strategies best separate impulses from edges to quantify power changes while preserving transient features (e.g., shutdown dips)? (3) Can NILM reveal controller tuning faults (e.g., high gains) and suboptimal chiller staging via power oscillations and discontinuities? (4) Can stator current harmonic analysis from a central point detect motor fault indicators (e.g., rotor eccentricity sidebands) in a commercial setting?

Hypotheses: (H1) With low steady-state variability (~5 kW SD), NILM can detect devices >5 kW at the 5% significance level using modest sample sizes (e.g., 10 samples). (H2) A median filter with an appropriately chosen window will remove impulses while preserving edges, yielding stable estimates of on/off power changes. (H3) Large power oscillations will correlate with high controller gains and exhibit FFT spikes at controller sample frequencies; suboptimal chiller staging will produce measurable power discontinuities. (H4) Stator current sampled slightly above 2×60 Hz will reveal sidebands indicative of rotor eccentricity, though larger motors may mask smaller-motor signatures.

Support/refutation: H1–H3 are supported by the reported SDs, filter comparisons, and observed oscillations/staging discontinuities. H4 is supported in laboratory tests but remains to be validated in the field.
reference_methodology:
Study design: Field installation of a watt transducer on the 480V 3-phase electrical service feeding HVAC equipment in two campus buildings. The system included two identical 500-ton centrifugal chillers, associated chilled water pumps (50 hp) and condenser water pumps (40 hp), and two large supply fans (125 hp and 100 hp) with adjustable-speed drives (ASDs). Maximum total system power was ~1000 kW. One-second average samples of real power were stored on a portable computer.

Filters and parameters: Three filters were evaluated. (1) Hart’s three-point sliding window averaging with a user-defined tolerance defining steady power; (2) an integral filter that integrates data after a change exceeding a user-defined tolerance to distinguish impulses (no change in before/after integrals) from steps; (3) a median filter with a user-defined window width (11-point window used). The median filter sorts values in its window and preserves the median, removing impulses while preserving edges. The integral filter requires an acceptable agreement parameter for before/after comparisons. The median filter required only a single parameter (window width), chosen based on the minimum temporal feature of interest (≈5 s maximum window width permitted by data characteristics).

Statistical testing: To quantify detection thresholds, the authors computed minimum detectable mean differences at the 5% significance level for normal differences between two means, given a 5 kW standard deviation during steady periods. Sample sizes of 5–30 were considered (Table 1). For example, with n=10, the minimum detectable difference was 5.3 kW.

Experimental procedures: (a) Pump tests: A 50 hp condenser-water pump was cycled on/off while the other condenser pump ran continuously. Power changes were measured and filtered using the three filters. (b) Fan tests: A 125 hp supply fan was cycled on/off twice, followed by one on/off cycle for a 100 hp fan. ASDs provided soft-start behavior; no power spikes were observed at start-up. (c) Fault detection: Time-series power data were examined for oscillations and discontinuities; FFT analysis identified controller sample-time frequencies. (d) Chiller staging: Power discontinuities were compared to optimal switch points from prior literature (Braun et al.) to assess suboptimality.

Motor fault detection: Laboratory tests analyzed stator current harmonic spectra for three motors (two fractional-horsepower single-phase and one larger three-phase). A belt under tension was applied to one single-phase motor to induce torque and potential eccentricity. Current was sampled slightly above 2×60 Hz (e.g., 666 Hz in related work) and low-pass filtered (sixth-order Butterworth) to prevent aliasing. Sidebands relative to the fundamental were examined. Field spectra were not yet analyzed in this study.

Ethics/IRB: Not applicable; no human subjects or sensitive data were involved.

title: Институты развития: рамки анализа
field_subfield: Economics — Development Economics and Institutional Economics
research_question:
Central questions include: (1) What is the role of institutional structures in shaping development outcomes in post-Soviet higher education and broader economies? (2) How do transaction costs and institutional dynamics constrain or enable development, and what policy implications follow? (3) Is market transition sufficient to ensure economic progress, or are institutional quality and social capital prerequisites? (4) How should higher education reforms (commercialization, Bologna Process) be designed to balance competing stakeholder interests and maintain quality?

Implied hypotheses: (H1) Institutions are the primary determinant of development, with property rights, contract enforcement, and social capital reducing transaction costs and enabling innovation and efficient production. (H2) Market transition alone does not guarantee growth; without robust institutions and social capital, marketization can exacerbate transaction costs and rent-seeking. (H3) In higher education, commercialization and Bologna Process integration require careful balancing of state, firms, students, parents, and universities to sustain stability and quality. (H4) Development strategies should prioritize long-term, feedback-oriented institutional design over short-term marketization. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include evidence that institutional quality correlates with lower transaction costs and higher innovation/productivity, and that marketization without institutional safeguards fails to deliver sustained growth.
reference_methodology:
The paper is a theoretical and methodological essay synthesizing literature from classical political economy, development economics, and institutional economics. It draws on Schumpeter’s theory of economic development, Marx’s analysis of capital and speculation, Smith’s moral sentiments and utility norms, and Keynes’s institutionalization of speculative norms. The author also references the Bologna Process and commercialization trends in post-Soviet higher education to illustrate institutional dynamics and stakeholder multiplicity.

No empirical data, samples, or statistical analyses are reported. There are no explicit procedures, datasets, or evaluation metrics. The analysis is conceptual, emphasizing institutional structures as the "carrying structure" of socio-economic systems and transaction costs as a central metric for development. The paper discusses transition economies’ institutional voids following the destruction of old formal institutions and the erosion of social capital, and argues that building new institutions requires time and resources with delayed returns and risks of rent-seeking capture. The author calls for long-term, feedback-oriented management in higher education and for development strategies that account for temporal lags in institutional payoff.

Ethical approvals, preregistration, and data/code availability are not applicable or not reported. The work does not specify operational indicators for institutional quality or transaction costs, nor does it present case studies or comparative analyses. The methodological contribution is the articulation of an analytical framework linking institutions, transaction costs, and development, rather than a reproducible empirical protocol.

title: Model training periods impact estimation of COVID-19 incidence from wastewater viral loads
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can a Bayesian deconvolution model and a log-linear regression reliably estimate COVID-19 incident cases and Re from wastewater viral loads? (2) How does the adequacy of the training period (as defined by relative rates of change in testing and cases) affect the accuracy and robustness of these estimates? (3) Do wastewater-derived Re estimates align with Re from clinical cases, and can they reveal transmission dynamics not captured by testing data?

Hypotheses: (H1) Training periods with adequate testing (testing rate increases faster than cases) will yield case estimates that align with observed trends and Re values consistent with transmission dynamics. (H2) Training periods with inadequate testing will bias case estimates downward and degrade Re estimation. (H3) Wastewater-derived Re may diverge from clinical-case Re during periods of testing inadequacy, potentially indicating ongoing transmission not reflected in reported cases.

Support/refutation criteria: H1 is supported if models trained on adequate periods produce higher, trend-consistent case estimates and Re values that track observed dynamics. H2 is supported if models trained on inadequate periods systematically underestimate cases and show poor alignment with observed trends. H3 is supported if wastewater-derived Re exceeds 1 when clinical-case Re is below 1, indicating undetected transmission.
reference_methodology:
Study sites and period: Wastewater influent samples were collected from three Northern California communities (Davis, Woodland, UC Davis) from December 1, 2021 to March 31, 2022. Community screening program data (daily cases and total tests) were obtained from Healthy Davis Together (HDT) and Healthy Yolo Together (HYT).

Wastewater sampling: Davis and Woodland used Teledyne ISCO 5800 refrigerated autosamplers; UC Davis used a Hach Sigma 900 autosampler. Davis collected 400 mL every 15 pulses (1 pulse = 10,000 gallons) with ~24 pulses/day (average influent 3.6 MGD). Woodland collected 100 mL every 15 minutes over 24 hours. UC Davis collected ~200 mL every 20 minutes over 24 hours. Sample collection dates corresponded to autosampler program completion. Samples were stored at 4°C, transported weekly on ice, and heat-inactivated at 60°C for 30 minutes before processing in a BSL2-certified lab. Davis and UC Davis provided 12 mL samples in 15 mL polypropylene tubes; Woodland provided 1 L in washed, sterilized Nalgene bottles.

Laboratory assay and QC: ddPCR (Bio-Rad) quantified SARS-CoV-2 N1 and N2 targets with PMMoV as a process control. Positive controls used synthesized gene fragments (GenBank MN975262 for N1/N2; M81413 for PMMoV). Bovine coronavirus (BCoV) was spiked for standard addition. LOD/LOB were determined per manufacturer guidance using 15 negative wastewater extracts (four replicates each). LOB was set at the 95th percentile rank of droplet counts; LOD = LOB + 2×SD. Reported LOB (copies/mL wastewater): N1 13.605 (SD 5.547), N2 18.544 (SD 6.712); LOD: N1 24.700, N2 31.967. Samples with merged droplets below thresholds (N1: 3; N2: 4) were excluded; if both targets were below threshold, concentration was reported as 0. Runs with extraction control blanks >15 positive droplets in either N1 or N2 were reprocessed.

Data processing: The wastewater signal was N/PMMoV (average SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentration divided by PMMoV). Wastewater data were smoothed with a 10-day moving average; cases were smoothed with a 7-day moving average to harmonize with wastewater signals. Weekly rates of change in tests (rT) and cases (rc) were computed to classify training periods as adequate (rT > rc) or not adequate.

Models: Two approaches were used. (1) Bayesian deconvolution: Daily wastewater concentrations Ci were modeled as a convolution of incident infections Ii with an exponential shedding distribution parameterized by b, with normalization B and system constant M (assumed in B). The deconvolution was approximated via Richardson–Lucy. The observational model assumed Ii ~ Negative Binomial with mean μi and overdispersion parameters ω=2 and α=0.05 (σ²i = ωμi + αμi²). Priors: b ~ Gamma(shape 2, scale 1); B ~ Gamma(shape 2, scale 2/1e-4). Posterior inference used t-walk MCMC. Shedding duration m was selected by DIC over m ∈ {6,…,10}. (2) Linear regression: log(Ii) = β log(Ci) + εi, εi ~ N(0, σ²). Re was estimated from observed cases and from reconstructed cases using Cori et al.’s framework.

Training period selection: For Davis, two periods were contrasted: TA (adequate) Jan 9–Feb 2, 2022 and TNA (not adequate) Dec 12, 2021–Jan 8, 2022. Similar adequacy classifications were applied to Woodland and UC Davis (supplement).

title: Exploring Hidden Local Ordering in Microemulsions with a Weak Directive Second Order Parameter
research_question:
Research questions: (a) What local structure exists within the correlation volume near a hydrophilic surface in bicontinuous microemulsions? (b) How can this structure be made visible via scattering and depth-resolved measurements? (c) Do additional order parameters (directive) describe the inner structure and its persistence beyond the bulk correlation length? (d) Does the presence of a directive order parameter manifest in rheological signatures at low shear rates?

Hypotheses: (1) Near-surface ordering depends on surfactant efficiency: less efficient surfactants (e.g., C8E3) will exhibit gyroid-like ordering, while more efficient surfactants (e.g., C12E5) will show lamellar ordering and capillary condensation. (2) The ordered interphase extends deeper than the bulk correlation length ξ, indicating a weak directive order parameter that aligns local correlation volumes into strings/arrays. (3) Rheology at very low shear rates will reveal high viscosities consistent with a directional network of correlation volumes. Supportive outcomes include GISANS patterns consistent with gyroid or lamellar near-surface structures persisting beyond ξ, and rheological data showing elevated viscosity at low shear rates. Refutation would involve isotropic scattering persisting to depths comparable to ξ and rheology matching simple Newtonian behavior without directional network signatures.
reference_methodology:
Materials: N-decane (Sigma Aldrich); non-ionic surfactants C8E3, C10E4, C12E5 (Bachem); deuterated n-decane and heavy water (Armar). Critical micelle concentrations (CMCs): 7.5, 0.68, and 0.064 mmol/L for C8E3, C10E4, and C12E5, respectively. Deionized water (18.2 MΩcm). Formulations: C10E4 at 17% vol surfactant; C8E3 and C12E5 at 27.0/0.0/36.5/32.3/4.2 and 8.0/3.6/42.4/46.0/0.0 (surfactant/H2O/D2O/n-decane/d-decane). Samples are thermodynamically stable and form after short shaking. Phase inversion temperatures ~20 °C (C8E3) and ~36 °C (C12E5) were selected for scattering experiments. Bulk isotropy was confirmed by crossed polarizers; at these symmetric compositions, no spherical micelles coexist.

GISANS: Instrument KWS1 at MLZ (FRM-2). Wavelength λ = 10.5 Å for C8E3 and C12E5. Silicon slab substrate: 15 × 5 × 2 cm³. Sample cell thickness: 0.5 mm. Temperatures set to phase inversion. Apparent detector distances: 4 m and 8 m with symmetric slit collimation 40 × 4 mm²; real distances 3.7 m and 7.7 m due to stage offset. Scattering length density of the overall microemulsion: 2.46 × 10⁻⁶ Å⁻². Critical angle αc = 0.21°; scattering depth Λ0 = 450 Å at αi = 0. Scattering depth Λ below αc defined as Λ = Λ0 × (1 − αi²/αc²)⁻¹/²; near/above αc, the 1/e depth z1/e is defined via characteristic functions involving absorption, incoherent, and coherent small-angle cross sections. Bulk scattering modeled by the Teubner–Strey formula I(Q) = 1/(k0² + (Q² − k0²)² + Q⁴) with k0 = 2π/d; parameters d and ξ taken from literature. Intensities corrected for detector efficiency to a common scale. Near-surface analysis used Laplace transforms of depth profiles with parameters for near-surface structure depth d and transition region depth ζ; linearized forms were fit to intensity trends vs Λ.

Rheology: Viscosity of the C10E4 microemulsion measured as a function of shear rate (solid symbols) and compared to a PEP5-PEO15 diblock copolymer sample (open symbols). The Carreau model was discussed as a reference for network-like behavior but was not observed here. Specific rheometer model, geometry, temperature control, and data acquisition parameters are not reported in the provided text.

title: Magnitude, global variation, and temporal development of the COVID-19 infection fatality burden
field_subfield: Epidemiology — Infectious Disease Epidemiology and Demography
research_question:
The study asks: (1) What is the magnitude and global variation of the COVID-19 cIFR over the first year of the pandemic? (2) How did cIFR develop over time within and across countries? (3) What factors drive cross-country differences in cIFR? (4) How sensitive are cIFR estimates to input data and modeling choices, including baseline IFRs, deaths sources, and infection age structures? (5) How would cIFR respond to plausible changes in age-specific IFRs (e.g., due to variants, treatment improvements, vaccination)?

Hypotheses/predictions include: (a) cIFR will vary strongly across countries but remain relatively stable within countries over time once age structures stabilize; (b) cIFR will be higher in older populations and in countries with older infected populations; (c) cIFR will be lower for women due to lower age-specific IFRs; (d) cIFR levels will be sensitive to baseline IFRs and data sources, but broad patterns will be robust; (e) increases in age-specific IFRs (e.g., +60%) will raise cIFR, with larger effects in countries with older infected populations. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include strong correlations between cIFR and median ages, stable within-country trajectories, sex differences consistent with lower female IFRs, and scenario analyses showing proportional increases in cIFR with scaled IFRs.
reference_methodology:
Data sources: (1) COVerAGE database provides daily reported COVID-19 deaths and confirmed cases by 5-year age groups (0–4, …, 95+) and sex for 111 countries since 3 January 2020; the study used data from 14 April 2021. (2) STMF provides weekly all-cause mortality by age for 38 countries; the study used input files as of 15 March 2021 and national vital statistics for Mexico and Peru. (3) UNWPP provides 2019 demographic indicators (remaining life expectancy by age, population size by age, median age) for all COVerAGE countries. (4) Spanish seroprevalence (ENE-COVID) provides sex-specific seroprevalence by 5-year age groups (0–4, …, 90+) with 95% CIs from four rounds (March–November 2020; n=51,409). (5) Baseline IFRs by 10-year age groups (both sexes combined) from Verity et al. (China), Salje et al. (France), and Levin et al. (universal regression).

Estimation framework: The cIFR is defined as total deaths divided by total infections. For a country of interest (COI) at time t, cIFR_t^COI = D_t^COI / I_t^COI, where D_t^COI is cumulative deaths by age and I_t^COI is the cumulative infected population by age. The infected population by age is estimated as I_x,t^COI = D_x,t^COI / IFR_x^COI, where IFR_x^COI is the scaled age-specific IFR for COI.

Scaling IFRs: Baseline IFRs (Verity, Salje, Levin) are interpolated onto a fine age grid using cubic splines. The demographic scaling model assigns the same IFR to individuals with the same remaining life expectancy (e_x) across the reference country (RC) and COI: IFR_{e_x}^{RC} = IFR_{e_x}^{COI}. Scaled IFRs are then aggregated to 5-year age groups. Sex-specific scaling uses 2019 abridged life tables by sex. For Spain, sex-specific baseline IFRs by age are derived from ENE-COVID seroprevalence and COVerAGE/STMF deaths, with 95% CIs from survey uncertainty.

Infection age structure: I_x,t^COI is estimated from D_x,t^COI and scaled IFR_x^COI. Estimation occurs only when cumulative deaths ≥200 to avoid small-number issues. The study also explores using excess deaths (STMF-based) and approximating I_x,t^COI with the age structure of confirmed cases (COVerAGE) as sensitivity checks.

Uncertainty: 95% prediction intervals for cIFR are computed by propagating the 95% credible intervals of baseline IFRs (Bayesian analyses) through the scaling and estimation formulas. Scenario analyses multiply scaled IFRs by factors 0.4–1.6 to simulate changes (e.g., improved treatment, vaccination, deadlier variants).

Sex-specific cIFR: Using sex-specific inputs (Spanish baseline IFRs by age and sex, and COVerAGE deaths by sex), cIFR is estimated separately for women and men.

Quality considerations: COVerAGE provides harmonized age bands and metadata/quality indicators; STMF data quality may be affected by date-of-death definitions and delayed registration; ENE-COVID seroprevalence is considered high quality given timing relative to antibody waning.

title: Acoustic Mode Frequencies of the Sun during the Minimum Phase between Solar Cycles 23 and 24
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do high-degree p-mode frequency shifts vary spatially and temporally across the solar disk during the extended minimum between cycles 23 and 24? (2) What is the relationship between these frequency shifts and local magnetic activity, and how does it compare to correlations with global activity indices? (3) Do latitudinal analyses reveal a consensus epoch for the solar minimum, and how does it compare with activity indices? (4) Are there quasi-biennial signals or multiple minima in the smoothed indices, and how do they relate to helioseismic minima?

Hypotheses/predictions: (a) Frequency shifts will correlate with local magnetic activity, but the strength of this correlation will weaken at low magnetic activity levels. (b) Disk-averaged frequency shifts will show moderate correlation with global activity indices (e.g., MMAI, R_I, F10.7), with correlation magnitudes bounded by prior high-degree global-mode results. (c) Latitudinal analyses may reveal multiple minima and a lead of helioseismic minima relative to activity indices, reflecting different sensitivities of mode frequencies to subsurface dynamics. (d) Quasi-biennial variability may be present in smoothed indices, potentially influencing inferred minimum epochs. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include weak or anti-correlated shifts at low MAI, moderate correlations with global indices (≤~72%), latitudinally varying minima epochs, and evidence of quasi-biennial structure in smoothed activity metrics.
reference_methodology:
Data: GONG ring-diagram data for high-degree p-modes (180 ≤ ℓ ≤ 1000) over Carrington rotations 2056–2099 (26 April 2007–7 August 2010). The dataset comprises 189 dense-packed, overlapping tiles, each 16°×16° in heliographic latitude and longitude, tracked for 1664 minutes (one ring-day) using a model solar velocity. Tile centers are spaced 7.5° in latitude and longitude, extending to ~52.5° from the disk center, covering most of the solar disk. Successive ring-days are overlapped by 27–30 minutes. The effective duty cycle ranges from 32% to 100% (mean ~90%); only data with duty cycle >70% were used, yielding 991 of 1056 ring-days and ~180,000 tiles.

Local magnetic activity index (MAI): GONG magnetograms sampled every 32 minutes are remapped and tracked identically to Dopplergrams, apodized with the same circular function, and averaged over pixels with field strength >2.5× the pixel noise to compute the MAI per tile. The MMAI is the mean MAI over the 189 tiles.

Frequency estimation and corrections: The ring-diagram technique computes three-dimensional power spectra via FFTs in space and time, fitted with Lorentzian profiles to obtain mode parameters. To mitigate foreshortening and duty-cycle biases, frequencies are corrected using a two-dimensional position-dependent model (function of distance from disk center ρ without cross-terms) combined with a linear duty-cycle term f(t). Coefficients a_i are determined by fitting over a two-year quiet period (1 September 2007–31 August 2009) for each (n, ℓ) mode. The linear terms are an order of magnitude smaller than quadratic terms (Figure 3). The corrected frequencies are used for analysis.

Spatial frequency shifts: For each ring-day, the frequency difference δν_{n,ℓ} is computed relative to a reference frequency, which is the error-weighted average of that mode across the 189 tiles. The spatial frequency shift δν_s for each tile is the error-weighted average of δν_{n,ℓ} over all modes present in the tile. Pearson’s linear correlation coefficient r_p between δν_s and MAI is computed for each ring-day.

Temporal frequency shifts: The mean disk-averaged frequency shift δν is computed as the error-weighted average of δν_{n,ℓ} over all modes and tiles, referenced to the ring-day of 11 May 2008. A 23-point running mean (≈1 Carrington rotation) is applied to reduce daily fluctuations. Additional smoothing with 91 and 365 points is used to test sensitivity. The minimum epoch is defined as the time of the lowest smoothed value.

Latitudinal analysis: Frequency shifts δν_lat are computed for latitudes on the central meridian by referencing δν_{n,ℓ} to the average frequency at that latitude across all ring-days. Running means (23-point) are applied, and Pearson’s r_p and Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients are computed between δν_lat and the MAI of tiles at the same latitude. Minimum epochs are identified as the lowest smoothed value per latitude band.

title: Lexicographic unranking algorithms for the Twelvefold Way *
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can one design a correct and efficient lexicographic unranking algorithm for set partitions of an n-set into k blocks (case 9) that operates directly on partitions in sequential form? (2) Can the same framework be adapted to ordered set partitions (case 7) and Bell’s set partitions (case 3)? (3) What is the bit-complexity of the resulting algorithms, and how do different implementations of the prefix-counting functions compare in practice?

Hypotheses: (H1) A normalization-based, prefix-counting approach using S and R will yield a correct lexicographic unranking algorithm for set partitions. (H2) The algorithm’s bit-complexity can be bounded in terms of n, k, and the bit-complexity of multiplication M(n), reflecting the size of Stirling numbers. (H3) On-the-fly computation with symmetry-exploiting variants (S_v2, S_v4) and a hybrid S_v5 will be competitive with precomputation (S_v6), with performance depending on k and n. (H4) The framework extends to ordered and Bell’s cases by replacing Stirling numbers with ordered Stirling numbers and Bell numbers, respectively.

Support/refutation: The paper proves correctness (Theorem 11) and provides a bit-complexity bound (Theorem 12). Experiments support H3, showing S_v5 nearly matches S_v6 and sometimes outperforms it for small k. Extensions are described for cases 7 and 3, with complexity deferred to a longer version.
reference_methodology:
Objects and order: The paper defines set partitions P_n^k of an n-set in sequential form, where each block B_i contains the smallest remaining element and is sorted. A total lexicographic order on partitions is induced by comparing blocks in order using a subset order on blocks. The authors also define prefixes of partitions (subsets of the first block) to enable prefix-counting.

Combinatorial core: The authors introduce S_n^k(ℓ, d), the number of partitions in P_n^k with a specified prefix of length ℓ ending at d, and derive a closed-form sum (Proposition 6) and a three-variable reduction S_n^k(d) (Proposition 7). They provide a recurrence for S_n^k(d) (Corollary 8) and a binomial transform representation (Proposition 9). They further define R_n^k(ℓ, d0, d1) to count partitions between two prefixes (Proposition 10), enabling binary search over candidate next elements.

Algorithm: The unranking algorithm Unranking(n, k, r) constructs blocks left-to-right. At each step, next_block(n, k, r) computes the first block by binary search over possible next elements d, using S and R to accumulate counts of smaller partitions. The algorithm maintains an accumulated rank (acc) and updates r by subtracting acc. The blocks are stored as index lists (normalization), and a final Extract step maps indices to values by removing elements from a list L = [1..n]. The ranking function (Appendix B) computes the rank by iterating over block prefixes and summing counts via S and R.

Complexity analysis: The authors analyze bit-complexity due to very large integers (order n ln n bits). They bound the number of S calls by O((n−k) ln n) and the cost of each S call by log(n choose k)/n · M(n), where M(n) is the bit-complexity of multiplying two n-bit numbers. Theorem 12 gives an overall bit-complexity bound O((n−k)^3 M(n) n ln n log k + k(n−k)^2 M(n) n ln n log n e^k). They note Go’s big integers use Karatsuba (Θ(n log 3)) for numbers > 2^40, which applies in most cases.

Implementations: Six S implementations are compared: S_v1 (naïve Proposition 7), S_v2 (symmetry-exploiting Proposition 7), S_v3 (naïve Proposition 9), S_v4 (symmetry-exploiting Proposition 9), S_v5 (hybrid choosing the more efficient of S_v2/S_v4 based on term counts), and S_v6 (precompute all Stirling numbers). Precomputation’s bit-complexity is bounded (Proposition 13), but memory is quadratic in n. Parallel computation of Stirling numbers is used to keep memory O(n) while maintaining time comparable to precomputation.

Experiments: Implemented in Go; hardware: Intel Xeon X5677, 32 GB DDR4, Debian GNU/Linux 12. For n=1000 and k from 2 to 992 (step 15), 500 uniform samples per k were unranked, and average times were recorded for S_v1–S_v6. A second experiment (Figure 2) explores larger partitions; the S_v5/S_v6 time ratio tends to 1 as n increases, with S_v6 becoming more favorable when k is near n.

title: Biological study on the impact of commonly used commercial fats and oil and threats of atherosclerosis
research_question:
Research question: How do commonly used commercial fats and oils (margarine, butter, vanaspati ghee, olive oil), when co-administered with a high-cholesterol diet, affect serum lipid profiles (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides), body weight, feed intake, and hematological parameters in hypercholesterolemic rats?

Hypotheses: (1) Saturated and trans fat–rich fats (butter, margarine, vanaspati ghee) will worsen atherogenic lipid profiles (increase total cholesterol and LDL; decrease HDL; increase triglycerides) relative to high-cholesterol diet alone. (2) Olive oil, rich in monounsaturated fatty acids and antioxidants, will attenuate adverse lipid changes and may improve HDL relative to other fats. (3) These dietary fats will influence body weight and hematological parameters, with saturated/trans fats potentially increasing weight gain and reducing hematological indices. Outcomes supporting the hypotheses would include statistically significant increases in total cholesterol and LDL and decreases in HDL in butter/margarine/vanaspati ghee groups versus G1, and the opposite pattern in olive oil. Refutation would be indicated by no significant differences or beneficial effects of saturated/trans fats.
reference_methodology:
Design: In vivo animal experiment with six groups (n=5 rats/group) over a defined induction and intervention period. Animals were housed at the National Institute of Food Science and Technology, University of Agriculture, Faisalabad, Pakistan.

Animals: Sprague Dawley rats (sex not reported). Acclimation: 1 week on regular diet and water ad libitum. Hypercholesterolemia induction: high-cholesterol diet (2% cholesterol) for 2 weeks, following a procedure cited as [7]. Diet composition: Normal diet contained 75% carbohydrates, 15% protein, 10% fat; high-cholesterol diet contained 75% carbohydrates, 15% protein, 8% fat, and 2% cholesterol of total kcal. After induction, baseline measurements were recorded.

Interventions: Six groups: G0 normal diet; G1 high-cholesterol diet; G2 high-cholesterol diet + margarine; G3 high-cholesterol diet + butter; G4 high-cholesterol diet + vanaspati ghee; G5 high-cholesterol diet + olive oil. Each fat/oil was administered at 10 g/100 g feed. The abstract states a 6-week intervention; the methods state a 2-week induction and 6-week study period. Diet consumption was monitored weekly; body weight was measured every 15 days.

Outcomes: Serum lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides) measured using standard protocols: cholesterol [9]; HDL/LDL [10]; triglycerides [11]. Hematological parameters (RBC, WBC, platelets) measured per Kamatani [12].

Statistical analysis: One-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests; significance threshold p<0.05. Software: Statistix 8.1 (Al-Okbi [13]).

Ethics: Ethical approval was granted by ORIC, University of Agriculture, Faisalabad, Pakistan. Conflict of interest: none declared.

Unreported details: Sex, age, randomization/blinding procedures, housing conditions (temperature, lighting), feed formulation beyond macronutrient/cholesterol percentages, exact assay kits/instruments, sample size justification, and any corrections for multiple comparisons beyond Tukey are not reported.

title: 8 O + 48 Ti elastic and inelastic scattering at 275 MeV
field_subfield: Physics — Nuclear Physics (Heavy-ion scattering and reaction theory)
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Can the initial-state interaction (ISI) for 18O + 48Ti at 275 MeV be determined by comparing elastic and inelastic scattering data to OM, DWBA, CC, and CCEP calculations using the SPP OP? (2) What is the strength and composition of couplings to low-lying collective excitations required to reproduce the measured angular distributions? (3) Does a TELP-based CCEP provide an effective ISI that captures coupling effects sufficiently for future DCE analyses? (4) How do these conclusions generalize to 54 MeV near the Coulomb barrier?

Hypotheses: (a) Channel couplings to low-lying collective states (2+1, 3-1) of 18O and 48Ti are necessary to describe elastic and inelastic scattering at 275 MeV, particularly at large momentum transfer where nonelastic channels compete with elastic scattering. (b) Including simultaneous 2+1 excitations of projectile and target will significantly improve agreement with data. (c) A TELP derived from CC will provide a reasonable elastic description but will underperform CC at high q. (d) Near-barrier (54 MeV) couplings will be less critical, with DWBA and CC giving similar results for inelastic transitions.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypotheses are supported if CC with the proposed coupling scheme reproduces data across the measured range, OM/DWBA fail without couplings, and CCEP performs adequately but not as well as CC. Discrepancies in specific channels (e.g., 48Ti(2+1) inelastic) would nuance the conclusions.
reference_methodology:
Experiment: Conducted at INFN-LNS (Catania) using the K800 superconducting cyclotron to accelerate fully stripped 18O8+ ions to 275 MeV. The beam was delivered to the object point of the MAGNEX large acceptance magnetic spectrometer. Beam spot size and angular divergence were reduced to 3 mm and 3 mr using a 2 mm diameter collimator and a 4 mm diameter antiscatterer placed 125 mm and 20 mm upstream of the target, respectively. The target was a 510 ± 25 μg/cm² TiO2 layer evaporated on a 216 ± 11 μg/cm² Al backing. Auxiliary measurements with WO3 + 27Al and 27Al targets under identical conditions were used to estimate background contributions from oxygen and aluminum; these were kinematically separated from the 48Ti signal in the analyzed energy/angle region. A copper Faraday cup (0.8 cm entrance, 3 cm depth) 15 cm downstream collected total charge; an electron suppressor at −200 V and a low-noise integrator yielded <10% charge collection accuracy.

Spectrometer and data acquisition: 18O ejectiles were analyzed in momentum by MAGNEX and measured by the focal plane detector (FPD). Data were acquired in three angular settings with the MAGNEX optical axis at θopt = 9°, 15°, and 21°, covering 4°–27° lab (6°–37° c.m.). In θopt = 15° and 21°, MAGNEX operated at maximum angular acceptance (50 msr). At θopt = 9°, full horizontal acceptance with reduced vertical acceptance was used to maintain event rates within FPD tolerance.

Data reduction: Following established procedures, the FPD positions were calibrated; particle identification selected 18O8+ ions; trajectories were reconstructed to the tenth order to extract the momentum vector at the target position. The missing mass method computed excitation energy Ex using the initial kinetic energy and laboratory scattering angle. The overall detection efficiency was evaluated to convert event yields to absolute differential cross sections. Angular slices (0.3°–4°) were used to fit Ex spectra. Each observed peak was modeled as a Gaussian; widths were fixed to the FWHM of the 48Ti(2+1) inelastic peak. For inelastic transitions populating bound excited states of 18O, Doppler broadening from in-flight γ decay was included. The achieved energy resolution was δEx ≈ 0.5 MeV (FWHM). Systematic uncertainties from total charge and target thickness were <10% and common to all points.

Theoretical modeling: Calculations were performed with FRESCO. The SPP OP was used for both real and imaginary parts: Uopt(r) = (NV + iNW) VSPP(r), with NV = 1 and NW = 0.78 for OM/DWBA and NW = 0.60 for CC. The SPP real part is a double-folding integral of the nucleon–nucleon interaction with ground-state densities; the imaginary part includes a Pauli nonlocality factor. Matter densities were two-parameter Fermi distributions (radius R, diffuseness a), spherical, with parameters from systematics; for 18O, a diffuseness of 0.61 fm (10% larger than SPP systematics) was adopted to account for two valence neutrons. Coupling schemes (CC-1 to CC-5) included low-lying collective states (2+1, 3-1) of 18O and 48Ti and their simultaneous excitations. Coupling potentials (λ = 2, 3) comprised Coulomb and nuclear components derived from multipole expansion of the OP and deformation lengths δλ related to M(Eλ). Experimental B(Eλ) and M(Eλ) were taken from literature; theoretical M(Eλ) were computed with KSHELL using interactions consistent with prior NUMEN work.
