CCEP used a trivially equivalent local polarization (TELP) potential derived from CC-5 to embed coupling effects in an effective OP. The 54 MeV data from Essel et al. were reanalyzed with the same framework to test energy dependence.

title: Leveraging Natural Language Processing and Geospatial Time Series Model to Analyze COVID-19 Vaccination Sentiment Dynamics from Tweets
field_subfield: Computer Science — Natural Language Processing; Public Health — Social Media Analytics
research_question: The study posed three questions: (1) What are the temporal trends of public sentiment toward COVID-19 vaccination on Twitter? (2) What are the geospatial patterns of sentiment across U.S. states over time? (3) What are the popular topics and key barriers to vaccination expressed in tweets? The authors did not state formal statistical hypotheses. Implicit expectations were that sentiment would vary over time and across states, and that topic analysis would reveal vaccine-related themes (e.g., specific brands, public health agencies, safety concerns). The analyses aimed to quantify these patterns and identify barriers that could inform targeted interventions. Outcomes supporting these expectations would include significant temporal fluctuations in sentiment, state-level heterogeneity, and coherent thematic clusters aligned with known vaccine hesitancy drivers (mistrust, safety concerns, misinformation).
reference_methodology:
Data source and collection: Tweets were collected via the Twitter API from January 2021 to February 2022. The public dataset contained daily COVID-19-related tweets; the team used the API to retrieve raw text and user profiles. Inclusion criteria: U.S.-based users (language and location filters), vaccine-related keywords (e.g., “vaccine,” “vaccination”), and removal of non-US tweets. Massively parallel processing accelerated data retrieval and filtering. User activity metrics (e.g., daily tweet counts) were computed locally to identify potential ghost writers.

Preprocessing: Irrelevant content (e.g., links) was removed. To mitigate topic drift, 100 tweets per month (n=1,400) were randomly sampled for annotation. Two annotators independently labeled 700 tweets each into positive, negative, irrelevant, and unsure; after discussion, labels were reconciled to three categories (positive, negative, irrelevant). Only tweets with clear sentiment (positive or negative) were retained for downstream analyses.

Data augmentation: To address limited labeled data and colloquial/typographical variability, back-translation was applied using Google Translate API. Tweets were translated iteratively into five intermediate languages (Chinese, German, French, Russian, Japanese) and then back to English, repeated across five rounds. Back-translation enriched vocabulary and syntax and improved model performance by >5% F1 on a 500-sample manual verification subset.

Modeling: Two BERT-based binary classifiers were trained using transfer learning. The pre-trained sentence BERT model (Hugging Face) provided contextualized embeddings; the [CLS] token captured global text features, and [SEP] separated sentences. The model architecture appended a fully connected layer with one hidden layer and a softmax output for classification. Training used back-translation-augmented data, with hyperparameters: epochs = 3 × number of intermediate languages, batch size = 4, learning rate = 1e-5, weight decay = 1e-5, max sequence length = 512. To mitigate class imbalance, the annotated data were split into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test. Two tasks were trained: (1) irrelevant content detection; (2) sentiment analysis (positive vs negative). Models were applied to the full dataset to filter irrelevant tweets and predict sentiment.

Topic modeling: Hashtags were analyzed using latent semantic analysis (LSA) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to identify and aggregate topics. State-level and temporal topic rates were computed (numerator: topic frequency in a state/time; denominator: total tweets in that state/time).

Geospatial and temporal analysis: Sentiment rates were computed by state and aggregated over time using weekly rolling averages (to account for weekend vaccination reporting gaps). Geospatial maps visualized state-level sentiment distributions and temporal trajectories. Qualitative synthesis of 2,500 tweets mapped barriers to vaccination onto Levesque’s access framework (Approachability, Acceptability, Availability/Accommodation, Affordability, Appropriateness).

title: A Comparison of Clinical and Ultrasound Estimation of Fetal Weight
research_question:
Primary research question: How accurate are clinical versus ultrasound fetal weight estimates in laboring women, and are they comparable? Secondary question: How does the accuracy of clinical estimation differ between 2nd-year resident physicians and 6th-year medical students?

Hypotheses (implicit from aims): (1) Clinical estimation by 2nd-year residents will be comparable in accuracy to ultrasound. (2) Clinical estimation by 2nd-year residents will be more accurate than by 6th-year students. (3) Accuracy will vary by neonatal weight category, with ultrasound potentially superior for <2,500 g and both methods tending to underestimate for >4,000 g. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses would include non-significant differences between resident clinical estimates and ultrasound, significant superiority of residents over students, and stratified accuracy patterns consistent with prior literature. Outcomes refuting them would include inferior resident accuracy to ultrasound, no difference between residents and students, or lack of stratified patterns.
reference_methodology:
Design: Analytical cross-sectional study.

Setting and period: Siriraj Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand; February 1 to March 1, 1999.

Participants: 266 singleton pregnant women admitted to the labor room. Exclusions: intrauterine fetal death, fetal abnormalities, uterine abnormalities, undiagnosed twins, inability to perform fetal biometry, and non-delivery within 24 hours. Final analyzed sample: 237 women (29 excluded for non-delivery within 24 hours).

Clinical estimation: Conducted by 2nd-year resident physicians and 6th-year medical students. Clinical assessment included fundal height, fetal head and body size, and amniotic fluid volume. The text notes that uterine size in transverse and vertical planes may also be used clinically, but specific protocols are not detailed.

Ultrasound estimation: Performed by a well-trained ultrasonographer within 24 hours before delivery. Measurements included biparietal diameter (BPD) and abdominal circumference (AC). Fetal weight was estimated using the Shepard formula. The Hadlock formula is referenced in the background but not used here.

Blinding: All estimations were blinded to each other.

Outcomes: Primary outcome was accuracy of fetal weight estimation, defined as whether the estimate was within a clinically acceptable range (exact thresholds not specified). Secondary outcomes included error direction (underestimation vs overestimation) and stratified accuracy by neonatal weight categories (<2,500 g, 2,500–4,000 g, >4,000 g).

Statistical analysis: Continuous variables summarized as mean ± standard deviation and range; categorical variables as counts and percentages. Comparisons between two groups used McNemar’s test; among three groups used Cochran’s Q test. Significance threshold p<0.05. No details on handling of missing data, inter-rater reliability, or calibration of ultrasound equipment are provided.

Ethics: No information on IRB approval, consent procedures, or data privacy is reported.

title: Identification of long non-coding RNA signatures in triple-negative breast cancer
research_question:
Research questions: (1) Which lncRNAs are differentially expressed in TNBC compared with normal breast tissue across independent microarray datasets? (2) Do these lncRNAs co-express with specific mRNAs that are enriched in cancer-relevant biological processes and pathways? (3) Are lncRNA–mRNA pairs or hub genes associated with relapse-free survival in TNBC?

Hypotheses: (a) TNBC exhibits a distinct lncRNA expression signature relative to normal tissue, detectable across multiple datasets. (b) Dysregulated lncRNAs co-express with mRNAs involved in core cancer processes (e.g., cell cycle, DNA/protein binding, PI3K-Akt, MAPK, ErbB, p53). (c) Expression levels of specific lncRNAs and their co-expressed mRNAs (hub genes) correlate with TNBC prognosis, with some conferring better and others worse relapse-free survival.

Support/refutation criteria: Hypothesis (a) is supported if multiple lncRNAs are differentially expressed across datasets with consistent directionality. Hypothesis (b) is supported if co-expressed mRNAs are enriched in cancer-related pathways. Hypothesis (c) is supported if Kaplan-Meier analyses show significant HRs (P < 0.05) for hub genes.
reference_methodology:
Datasets: Two TNBC lncRNA microarray datasets (GSE60689 and GSE64790) were downloaded from GEO (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). GSE64790 also included mRNA expression data.

Preprocessing and annotation: Raw data were reprocessed using GEO2R. LncRNA annotation was obtained from array additional files or LNCipedia v5.0 (http://www.lncipedia.org). If an lncRNA had an official HGNC symbol, that symbol was used; otherwise, accession or gene ID was used.

Differential expression: Differentially expressed lncRNAs were identified with |log2 fold change| ≥ 2.0 and P ≤ 0.05. Overlapping lncRNAs between datasets were determined using a Venn diagram tool (http://bioinformatics.psb.ugent.be/webtools/Venn/). Heatmaps were generated with Morpheus (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus/).

Validation: The TCGA BRCA RNA-seq dataset was accessed via TANRIC (http://ibl.mdanderson.org/tanric/_design/basic/index.html). LncRNA expression was quantified as log2 RPKM. Differential expression between TNBC and normal groups was tested using t or t' tests. The top 10 lncRNAs from each microarray and the 8 overlapping lncRNAs were validated.

Co-expression analysis: Using GSE64790 mRNA data, differentially expressed mRNAs were identified with the same criteria (|log2FC| ≥ 2.0; P ≤ 0.05). Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between lncRNAs and mRNAs using the expression matrix. Significant correlations were defined as P < 0.01. The co-expression network was constructed in Cytoscape v3.5.1. Hub genes were ranked by degree; the top 50 were selected for visualization and analysis.

Functional enrichment: Breast cancer–associated genes were compiled from literature via PALM-IST (http://www.hpppi.iicb.res.in/ctm/index.html). Overlap between this set and the co-expressed DEG set was used for enrichment. Metascape (http://metascape.org) performed GO (BP, CC, MF) and KEGG pathway enrichment. Significance thresholds: P < 0.01 and ≥3 genes per term. Terms were clustered by similarity (Kappa > 0.3), and the most significant term per cluster was retained.

Prognostic analysis: Kaplan-Meier Plotter (http://kmplo.t.com/analysis/) assessed associations between gene expression and TNBC relapse-free survival. Patients were split by median expression into high/low groups. The log-rank test evaluated group differences; HRs quantified associations. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.

Ethics: Not applicable for secondary analysis of public datasets.

title: Maternal Circulating Melatonin and 6-Hydroxymelatonin Sulfate Increase During Normal Singleton Pregnancy and Decrease After Delivery: Evidence for Placental Contribution
research_question:
Research questions: (1) How do maternal serum melatonin and 6-OHMS change across normal singleton pregnancy compared to non-pregnant women of childbearing age? (2) Do these levels change after delivery, and what is the contribution of the placenta? (3) Is placental 6-OHMS content associated with gestational age?

Hypotheses: (a) Maternal serum melatonin and 6-OHMS are elevated during pregnancy relative to non-pregnant controls; (b) melatonin increases across gestation; (c) post-delivery, maternal melatonin and 6-OHMS decrease, consistent with placental removal; (d) placental tissue contains 6-OHMS that increases with gestational age, supporting placental contribution. Outcomes supporting these hypotheses include significantly higher maternal melatonin/6-OHMS in all trimesters vs controls, a monotonic increase across trimesters, significant post-delivery declines, and a positive correlation between placental 6-OHMS and gestational age. Outcomes refuting would include no differences vs controls, no trimester trend, no post-delivery decrease, or no placental 6-OHMS correlation with gestation.
reference_methodology:
Design and setting: Two linked prospective studies (MEL-P and MEL-P2) at Aberdeen Maternity Hospital, NHS Grampian, Aberdeen, UK. Both were prospectively registered (NCT03014245; NCT03609086) and approved by research ethics committees (MEL-P: East Midlands, Nottingham 1, ref 16/EM/0412; MEL-P2: London-Bromley, ref 18/LO/0616). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Participants: MEL-P recruited healthy pregnant women with singleton pregnancies after first-trimester ultrasound (11–12 weeks), excluding those <16 or >45 years, multiple gestations, or pre-existing diabetes/hypertension, chronic kidney disease, or autoimmune disorders. Exclusions included ultrasound abnormalities. Non-pregnant controls were healthy women up to age 45, excluding chronic conditions and medication use (except oral contraceptives). MEL-P2 recruited pregnant women (16–45 years) with singleton pregnancies scheduled for elective CS, excluding those on chronic medication. Clinical outcomes (gestational age at parturition, preterm labor, gestational diabetes, pregnancy-induced hypertension/pre-eclampsia) were recorded.

Sampling schedule: MEL-P: morning venous blood (08:00–12:00) at 11–12, 19–21, and 27–29 weeks; follow-up to delivery. Non-pregnant controls: single morning sample (08:00–12:00). MEL-P2: morning serum 3–6 days pre-CS and 24 h post-delivery; placental tissue obtained within 15 min of delivery.

Sample processing: Blood collected into 5 ml clot activator-serum separator tubes, clotted, centrifuged within 2 h at 1,300 g for 10 min at room temperature; serum stored at −80°C. Placental tissue (1 cm^3) sampled from two diametrically opposed cotyledon sites halfway between center and border through full depth, washed twice in PBS, snap-frozen (FlashFREEZE; immersion in Novec 7000 to −80°C within 30 s), pulverized under liquid nitrogen, homogenized (200 mg tissue in 2 ml PBS), filtered (100 mm strainer), freeze–thawed twice, and centrifuged at 5,000 g for 5 min at 4°C.

Assays: Competitive ELISAs for melatonin (Wuhan Fine Biotech) and 6-OHMS (Abbexa Ltd.) per manufacturer instructions after dilution. Between-plate precision: 8.9% (melatonin) and 10.8% (6-OHMS) (n=6). Protein content measured by Bradford assay (Coomassie Brilliant Blue; BSA calibration). All assays performed in duplicate.

Statistical analysis: Data were non-normally distributed and presented as median [range]. Analyse-It for Microsoft Excel was used. Friedman test assessed trimester trends; Wilcoxon/Mann–Whitney tests compared groups; Spearman’s correlation assessed placental 6-OHMS vs gestational age. Significance threshold p<0.05.
